CCFT Study Guide

Certified CrossFit Trainer exam · reading companion for Javier Jaime

How to use this guide

This guide does not replace reading the articles — it makes your reading focused. For each PDF: read the chapter first, then open the PDF and read it deeply, hunting for the “focus while reading” points and working the concepts until you could apply them in coaching. Each chapter links to its PDF and maps to the exam’s Content Outline tasks.

The exam tests application, not memorization. 160 questions (140 scored), 3 hours 55 minutes, at Pearson VUE — some items use tables, photos, or video clips. Questions come from the Content Outline; the articles support it.

Prioritize your reading two ways at once: by confidence (Chase Ingraham method — know-nothing first, then know-but-fuzzy, then videos) and by exam weight (below). Training and Educating alone are 43% of the exam.

D1 · Screening & Ongoing Assessment

8% of exam · 11 questions
D1 · Screening & Ongoing Assessment 8% of exam Confidence tier: ___

2011-evidence-based-risk-assessment-and-recommendations-for-physical-activity-clearance-consensus-document-20111this.pdf

Open the PDF on Google Drive →

Why this is on the reading list

This consensus document is the evidence base behind pre-participation screening — the exact judgment Domain 1 tests. It establishes the 'risk paradox' (being inactive is far riskier than the transient risk of an acute bout of exercise), validates the PAR-Q/PARmed-X family of screening tools, and proposes a low/intermediate/high risk-stratification continuum that maps a 'yes' on a screening questionnaire to one of three actions: clear with minimal supervision, train under a qualified professional's guidance, or refer for medical clearance. For a CrossFit trainer it backs 1.1.1 (screen for medical issues via a health questionnaire), 1.1.2 (recognize conditions outside scope that require referral), and 5.2.3/7.2.2 (manage risk and obtain medical release), grounding the coach's daily decision of 'do I let this person train, scale them, or send them to a doctor first?'

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 1.1.1 Screen athlete for medical issues (e.g., health questionnaire)
  • 1.1.2 Recognize conditions/injuries outside CCFT Scope of Practice that require referral (risk factors)
  • 1.1.4 Assess psychological tolerance for training
  • 5.2.3 Manage risk for the athlete
  • 5.2.6 Recognize warning signs for possible injury or overexertion
  • 7.2.2 Obtain written, signed medical release when required
  • 7.4.1 Work within CCFT Scope of Practice

What to focus on while reading

  • The 'risk paradox' framing: habitual PA reduces long-term morbidity/mortality, yet an acute bout transiently raises the risk of nonfatal cardiovascular events and sudden cardiac death — and the net effect still favors being active. This is the single idea the whole document turns on.
  • What the PAR-Q is: a short self-completed questionnaire everyone fills out before a fitness assessment or before becoming much more active. A 'yes' to any question historically triggered automatic physician referral.
  • What the PARmed-X is: the second form a physician uses to address concerns the PAR-Q flagged — i.e., the medical-clearance side of the process.
  • The central reform: a 'yes' should NOT automatically mean physician referral. A qualified exercise professional can probe further and stratify the client instead — reducing unnecessary barriers to activity.
  • The three-tier risk continuum and the action each tier maps to: LOW = exercise at moderate intensity with minimal supervision; INTERMEDIATE = exercise under the guidance/advice of a qualified exercise professional (no automatic physician referral); HIGH = obtain medical clearance first, then exercise in a medically supervised setting that includes a qualified exercise professional. (Recommendation 59 — memorize the mapping, not the number.)
  • Why the old PAR-Q was 'unduly conservative': it screened OUT people (e.g., Bull et al. excluded 70% of 882 primary-care patients) who would have benefited from activity. Over-screening is itself a harm because it blocks beneficial movement.
  • The numeric anchors for how SAFE testing/training actually is — these quantify the risk paradox: cardiovascular event during maximal exercise testing <0.8 per 10,000 tests (~1 per 10,000 h); in healthy asymptomatic people, fatal 0.3–0.8 and nonfatal ~1.4 per 10,000 tests; fatality during participation well below 0.01 per 10,000 participant-hours.
  • The benefit side: routine PA cuts fatal/nonfatal cardiovascular events by 25%–50%. Active/fit individuals have a lower risk during exercise than inactive people have AT REST.
  • The intensity threshold that matters: transient cardiovascular risk is greatest with vigorous activity exceeding 6 METs. Note this is ABSOLUTE intensity — read the later discussion on how a deconditioned person's 'brisk walk' (3–6 METs) can be vigorous in RELATIVE terms.
  • The age-restriction reversal: there was insufficient evidence for the old 15–69 age limit; the PAR-Q should be used WITHOUT age restriction. Both very young and elderly benefit, and event risk is low at all ages.
  • The non-negotiable qualifier on the reform: only a genuinely QUALIFIED exercise professional may clear a 'yes' client. The document refuses to extend this to fitness personnel without the defined core competencies (see Recommendation 54's 15-item list). This is the scope-of-practice boundary.
  • Condition-specific red lines a coach should recognize even if they don't memorize them: osteoporosis → avoid trunk flexion and powerful trunk twisting (vertebral fracture risk); Down syndrome → screen for atlanto-axial instability before head/neck-stressing activities; type 1 diabetes → high hypoglycemia risk with exercise; cancer with extensive metastases or marked anemia → absolute contraindication.
  • Pregnancy conclusion: women with uncomplicated pregnancies (whether previously active or inactive) are LOW risk for both maternal and fetal adverse events with moderate-intensity activity — a reversal of the old 'rest while pregnant' advice.
  • Psychological-disorder conclusion: dementia, anxiety, psychosis, and intellectual disability are LOW risk for adverse PA events; the notable exception is Down syndrome / atlanto-axial instability. Note the consent-from-guardian recommendation.
  • The recurring structure of every condition section: state the benefit, state that adverse-event risk is low (single-digit percentages), then list the specific precautions/relative contraindications. Read for that pattern, not for every disease's numbers.

Concepts to understand

  • Screening is risk triage, not gatekeeping. The purpose is to route each person to the right level of support (self-clear, coach-guided, or doctor-first), and to remove barriers wherever the evidence says risk is low — not to find reasons to exclude.
  • The risk paradox in plain coaching terms: the safest thing you can do for almost any client is help them move; the riskiest thing is to leave them sedentary. A trainer who over-refers out of caution may be doing net harm.
  • Absolute vs. relative contraindication. Absolute = do not do this activity at all (rare — e.g., cancer with extensive metastases, excessive hyperglycemia with ketonuria). Relative = proceed with modification, lower intensity, supervision, or medical input. Most flagged conditions are relative, which is exactly why scaling — not exclusion — is usually the right move.
  • The three-tier stratification as a decision the coach actually makes: a questionnaire 'yes' is the start of a conversation, not an automatic stop. You probe, place the person in low/intermediate/high, and act accordingly.
  • Scope of practice as the hard boundary. A CrossFit trainer is NOT the 'qualified exercise professional' (university-trained clinical exercise physiologist with advanced certification) this paper empowers to clear clinical cases. When a condition is genuinely clinical, the trainer's correct move is referral + medical release, then coach within the cleared parameters.
  • Absolute vs. relative intensity, and why it changes risk judgment. The >6 MET 'vigorous' risk threshold is absolute. A deconditioned client whose peak capacity is ~5–6 METs may be working at vigorous RELATIVE intensity during a mere brisk walk — so 'easy' programming can still be demanding for them, and conversely their absolute workload rarely crosses the danger line.
  • Supervision is itself a risk-mitigation tool. The low adverse-event rates in the literature come largely from supervised, well-prescribed programs. A coach's attentive presence, sound scaling, and an emergency plan are part of why exercise is safe — not incidental to it.
  • Functional capacity (peak aerobic power, in METs) is a stronger predictor of mortality than traditional risk factors, and the ~5 MET / >17.5 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ mark recurs as a low-vs-higher-risk dividing line for several cardiovascular conditions. The takeaway for a coach: capacity matters, and building it is protective.
  • Psychological tolerance belongs in screening too (task 1.1.4). Activity broadly improves mood, anxiety, and self-efficacy, and most psychological conditions are low physical risk — but consent considerations (guardian/designate) and individualized approach still apply.
  • Screening tools are living documents. The PAR-Q+/ePARmed-X+ are designed to be revised as evidence changes (planned 5-year updates). The principle for a coach: use the current validated tool, don't treat any single form as permanent gospel.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenarios where a new or returning athlete discloses something on intake — chest discomfort with exertion, a recent stroke, uncontrolled asthma, pregnancy, type 1 diabetes, osteoporosis, a Down syndrome athlete wanting to do gymnastics — and you must choose the BEST next action: clear and coach, scale/modify and proceed, supervise closely, or stop and require medical clearance before training (tasks 1.1.1, 1.1.2, 7.2.2). The exam rewards the answer that neither over-refers low-risk people (blocking beneficial activity) nor under-refers genuine red flags (acting outside scope). Other items test the underlying judgment: recognizing relative vs. absolute contraindications, knowing that a 'brisk walk' can be relatively vigorous for a deconditioned client (5.2.3, 5.2.6), and staying inside CCFT scope by deferring clinical clearance decisions to a physician (7.4.1).

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

PAR-Q (Physical Activity Readiness Questionnaire)
A short self-administered screening questionnaire completed before a fitness assessment or before becoming much more active. A 'yes' to any item flags a possible medical concern; under the old model that meant automatic physician referral.
PARmed-X
The companion medical-evaluation form a physician uses to address concerns the PAR-Q raised — the medical-clearance side of the screening process. (A pregnancy-specific version, PARmed-X for PREGNANCY, exists.)
PAR-Q+ / ePARmed-X+
The revised, evidence-based versions produced by this consensus process. They add condition-specific probing questions and an online decision-tree (ePARmed-X+) so many people who answer 'yes' can be risk-stratified and cleared without a physician visit.
Pre-participation screening
The process of checking a person for medical/psychological issues before they start or intensify exercise, in order to route them to the appropriate level of support and identify the few who need medical input first.
Risk paradox
The finding that habitual physical activity lowers long-term illness and death, even though a single acute bout transiently raises the risk of cardiovascular events — with the net balance strongly favoring being active.
Risk continuum / risk stratification
Sorting clients into low, intermediate, or high risk. Low = moderate-intensity exercise with minimal supervision; intermediate = exercise under a qualified exercise professional's guidance; high = medical clearance first, then medically supervised exercise.
Qualified exercise professional
In this document, a university-trained exercise physiologist with advanced certification and defined core competencies who can safely serve clinical populations. It is a higher bar than a general fitness/CrossFit certification — important for knowing the limits of a CCFT trainer's scope.
Absolute contraindication
A condition under which a given activity should not be performed at all (e.g., cancer with extensive skeletal/visceral metastases; excessive hyperglycemia with ketonuria).
Relative contraindication
A condition that does not forbid activity but requires modification — lower intensity, avoided movements, supervision, or medical input. Most flagged conditions are relative, which is why scaling rather than exclusion is usually correct.
MET (metabolic equivalent)
A unit of exercise intensity (1 MET = resting energy expenditure). Transient cardiovascular risk is greatest above ~6 METs (vigorous). A peak capacity around 5 METs (~17.5 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹) recurs as a low-vs-higher-risk threshold for cardiovascular conditions.
Symptom-limited (maximal) exercise stress test
A graded exercise test taken to the point of symptoms or maximal effort, used to measure functional capacity and screen for cardiovascular disease. Very low event risk; capacity measured this way predicts mortality better than traditional risk factors.
Peak/maximal aerobic power
The highest rate of oxygen use a person can sustain (their aerobic ceiling), expressed in METs or mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹. A powerful, independent predictor of health and mortality.
Atlanto-axial instability
Excess mobility between the first two cervical vertebrae, present in a meaningful fraction of people with Down syndrome. Creates risk during activities that stress the head/neck (contact sports, diving, gymnastics, butterfly stroke) — a specific screening item for that population.
Autonomic dysreflexia
A potentially life-threatening blood-pressure surge that can occur in people with higher-level spinal cord injury during exertion; a reason such athletes need medical screening and supervised training.
Population-attributable risk
How much of a disease burden in a population is tied to a given factor. The document targets high-attributable-risk conditions (e.g., diabetes, cardiovascular disease) when deciding what to screen for.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • Symptoms of cardiovascular disease — chest pain/discomfort, unusual shortness of breath, palpitations, or angina with exertion: refer for medical clearance before intense training. Outside a CCFT trainer's scope to clear.
  • Stroke or spinal cord injury within the previous 6 months: requires medical clearance before becoming more active, then training under direct supervision.
  • Type 2 diabetes in middle-aged/older clients, or any diabetic with signs of cardiac/peripheral vascular or microvascular disease: higher cardiovascular risk; medical screening before activity more vigorous than brisk walking.
  • Type 1 diabetes: high risk of exercise-associated HYPOGLYCEMIA — ensure glucose management is in place; refrain from vigorous exercise with excessive hyperglycemia (fasting glucose >15 mmol/L) and/or ketonuria.
  • Uncontrolled asthma, or respiratory disease with significant arterial hypoxaemia (SaO₂ ≤85%) at rest or on exertion, pulmonary hypertension, or supplemental-oxygen use: medical clearance first, then supervised exercise.
  • Osteoporosis: avoid loaded trunk flexion and powerful trunk twisting (vertebral compression fracture risk). Advanced (stage III/IV) arthritis or severe joint damage: avoid heavy/high-intensity load-bearing.
  • Down syndrome athlete: screen for atlanto-axial instability before head/neck-stressing activities (gymnastics, diving, contact sports, butterfly stroke, high jump).
  • Cancer with extensive skeletal or visceral metastases, or marked anaemia: absolute contraindication. Patients currently undergoing cancer treatment, or with pulmonary/bronchogenic carcinoma, multiple myeloma, or head/neck cancers: higher risk — refer for evaluation and supervised programming.
  • Very high resting blood pressure (around or above 200 mmHg systolic / 110 mmHg diastolic), or hypertension with other cardiovascular risk factors/comorbidities: caution and further evaluation before intense exercise.
  • Chronic heart failure that is not medically stable, or NYHA class III–IV, or peak aerobic power <5 METs: high risk — physician clearance and medically supervised exercise.
  • Acute flare-up of arthritis, acute or serious low-back pathology (history of back surgery, spondylolysis/spondylolisthesis, neurological symptoms, spinal fracture): modify/avoid pain-provoking loading; refer when serious pathology is suspected.
  • Scope-of-practice boundary: a CCFT trainer is not the clinical 'qualified exercise professional' this document empowers to clear clinical cases. When a disclosure is genuinely clinical, obtain a signed medical release (task 7.2.2) and coach only within the cleared parameters.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. A 58-year-old new member completes your intake form and writes 'yes' to a question about chest tightness when she climbs stairs quickly. She feels fine right now and is eager to start the on-ramp class. What is the BEST next action?

  1. A. Start her in today's class but tell her to stop if she feels chest tightness
  2. B. Clear her yourself — the consensus document says coaches can clear a 'yes' so referral is unnecessary
  3. C. Refer her for medical clearance before intense training and obtain a signed medical release before she begins
  4. D. Tell her exercise is too risky for her and that she should not join until the symptom resolves on its own
  5. E. Have her sign the standard liability waiver and proceed at full intensity
Show answer

Answer: C — Exertional chest tightness is a cardiovascular red flag outside a CrossFit trainer's scope to clear. The document's reform lets a QUALIFIED clinical exercise professional clear some 'yes' responses, but a CCFT trainer is not that person (B is wrong, and it misreads who 'qualified' means). A and E proceed unsafely past a cardiac symptom. D over-refers in the wrong direction — it abandons the athlete rather than routing her to a physician — and the paper's whole thesis is that activity is beneficial once risk is appropriately managed. The correct path is referral, medical release, then coach within cleared parameters (tasks 1.1.2, 7.2.2, 7.4.1).

Scenario 2. A healthy, asymptomatic 34-year-old answers 'no' to every screening question and wants to begin CrossFit. He asks whether starting is dangerous given news stories about sudden cardiac death during exercise. Which response best reflects the evidence in this document?

  1. A. The risk of a serious cardiac event during exercise is real but very low for healthy people, and remaining inactive carries a markedly higher overall risk — so starting, coached and scaled, is the safer choice
  2. B. He should get a maximal stress test and physician sign-off before any CrossFit, regardless of symptoms
  3. C. Sudden cardiac death is common enough in exercisers that he should stick to walking only
  4. D. Because he is under 35 there is zero risk, so no screening or scaling is needed
  5. E. He should avoid anything above 6 METs permanently to eliminate all cardiac risk
Show answer

Answer: A — This is the risk paradox applied. For asymptomatic healthy people the event rate is very low (fatalities well below 0.01 per 10,000 participant-hours), and the net risk strongly favors becoming active. B over-screens a clean low-risk client — exactly the over-conservatism the document criticizes. C and E overstate the danger and would deny large benefits. D is false: low risk is not zero risk, and sound coaching/scaling still applies. A captures both the low absolute risk and the larger risk of inactivity (tasks 1.1.1, 5.2.3).

Scenario 3. An athlete with diagnosed osteoporosis has medical clearance to train. You are programming a class with heavy deadlifts, weighted sit-ups, and Russian twists. What is the MOST appropriate modification based on this document's precautions?

  1. A. No changes — she has clearance, so any movement is fine
  2. B. Avoid loaded/repeated trunk flexion and powerful trunk-twisting movements; substitute neutral-spine strength and progressive loading to tolerance
  3. C. Remove all resistance training and limit her to walking
  4. D. Keep the twists and sit-ups but drop the deadlift, since deadlifts are the only fracture risk
  5. E. Have her max out the deadlift to build bone density as fast as possible
Show answer

Answer: B — For osteoporosis the document specifically advises avoiding trunk flexion and powerful trunk twisting because of vertebral compression-fracture risk — so weighted sit-ups (loaded flexion) and Russian twists (powerful rotation) are the problems. Strength training is beneficial and should continue with neutral-spine loading progressed to tolerance, which makes B correct and C (over-restriction) wrong. A ignores a documented relative contraindication. D targets the wrong movement — the deadlift can be performed with a neutral spine, while it's the flexion/rotation drills that are contraindicated. E (maximal loading) is reckless for fragile bone. This tests recognizing relative contraindications and scaling rather than excluding (tasks 1.1.2, 5.2.3).

Scenario 4. A coach argues that to be safe, every member who checks any box on the health questionnaire should be sent to a physician before training. According to this consensus document, what is the main problem with that blanket policy?

  1. A. Physicians are not qualified to assess exercise risk, so referral is pointless
  2. B. It is unnecessarily conservative and creates barriers to activity for many low/intermediate-risk people who would benefit from exercising, and most adverse-event risks are very low
  3. C. It violates the law in every jurisdiction
  4. D. Liability waivers already eliminate any need for screening
  5. E. It is too expensive for the gym, which is the only real downside
Show answer

Answer: B — A core finding is that the original auto-referral process was 'unduly conservative,' screening OUT people who would have benefited (e.g., a trial excluded 70% of primary-care patients). Over-referral is itself a harm because it blocks beneficial activity, and most condition-specific adverse-event rates are low single digits. B states this. A is false — the document still relies on physicians for genuine clearance and even notes some have limited exercise-counseling skill, but that is not the argument against blanket referral. C and D are legally/clinically wrong (waivers don't replace screening). E names a side issue, not the main point: the central harm is the barrier to health-promoting activity (tasks 1.1.1, 5.2.3).

Scenario 5. A previously inactive woman who is 20 weeks pregnant, with an uncomplicated pregnancy and her physician's general okay to exercise, joins your gym and asks what she can do. Which approach best fits this document's conclusions?

  1. A. Advise her to rest until after delivery because exercise endangers the fetus
  2. B. Treat her as high risk and require a separate cardiac stress test before any activity
  3. C. Encourage regular moderate-intensity activity (e.g., scaled aerobic and strength work, walking, cycling, swimming, aquatic/pelvic exercises) — uncomplicated pregnancy is classified low risk for adverse maternal and fetal events
  4. D. Put her straight into unscaled high-intensity benchmark workouts since pregnancy needs no modification at all
  5. E. Refuse to train her at all because pregnancy is outside any coaching scope
Show answer

Answer: C — The systematic review found women with uncomplicated pregnancies — previously active OR inactive — are low risk for adverse maternal and fetal events with moderate-intensity activity, reversing the old 'rest while pregnant' advice (A is the outdated, incorrect view). B over-screens a low-risk client. The correct stance is to encourage and appropriately SCALE activity, which is C; D errs the opposite way by removing all modification and intensity judgment. E is wrong because coaching a cleared, low-risk pregnant member within sensible scaling is within scope. This tests applying the pregnancy risk classification and scaling for a special population (tasks 1.1.1, 5.2.3).

Scenario 6. An athlete with well-controlled type 1 diabetes (no cardiovascular symptoms, diagnosed 4 years ago, under 30) wants to do a high-intensity metcon. Beyond general fitness coaching, what is the single most important risk this document flags for you to manage?

  1. A. Vertebral fracture from spinal loading
  2. B. Exercise-associated hypoglycemia
  3. C. Atlanto-axial instability
  4. D. Autonomic dysreflexia
  5. E. Vitreous haemorrhage from retinopathy
Show answer

Answer: B — For type 1 diabetes the document states the risk of clinically significant adverse events is low EXCEPT for hypoglycemia, which is high and requires vigilance during and after exercise — so B is the key management priority (glucose monitoring, fueling, awareness of symptoms). A relates to osteoporosis, C to Down syndrome, D to higher-level spinal cord injury, and E to advanced diabetic retinopathy — none is the headline risk for an otherwise uncomplicated young type 1 diabetic. This tests matching the right precaution to the right condition (tasks 1.1.2, 5.2.6).

Scenario 7. During intake a member mentions she has an anxiety disorder and asks whether that disqualifies her from CrossFit. Based on this document, what is the best coaching response?

  1. A. Anxiety disorders make exercise dangerous; she needs cardiac clearance first
  2. B. She should be classified high risk and trained only under medical supervision
  3. C. Most psychological conditions (anxiety, depression, psychosis, intellectual disability) are low physical risk for adverse exercise events, and activity tends to improve mood and self-efficacy — so welcome her, build rapport, and individualize the approach
  4. D. She cannot participate because psychological tolerance is outside a coach's concern
  5. E. She must provide a psychiatric stress test before joining
Show answer

Answer: C — The review found a remarkably low risk of adverse PA-related events across psychological conditions (the notable exception being Down syndrome / atlanto-axial instability), and activity broadly improves psychological well-being. So A, B, and E over-restrict a low-risk person. D is wrong because psychological tolerance IS part of screening (task 1.1.4) and a coach should adapt rapport and approach accordingly. C reflects both the low physical risk and the trainer's role in assessing psychological tolerance and individualizing (tasks 1.1.4, 5.1.3).

Scenario 8. A coach claims that because peak aerobic power below ~5 METs marks higher cardiovascular risk, a deconditioned 60-year-old should never do anything 'vigorous.' How does this document refine that thinking on absolute vs. relative intensity?

  1. A. The >6 MET vigorous-risk threshold is absolute; for a very deconditioned person even brisk walking (3–6 METs) can be relatively vigorous, yet their absolute workload rarely crosses the danger zone — so appropriately scaled effort that feels hard for them is generally low absolute risk
  2. B. Relative intensity is irrelevant; only absolute METs matter for everyone
  3. C. Deconditioned people should train at maximal absolute intensity to improve fastest
  4. D. Vigorous activity is universally unsafe and should never be programmed for older adults
  5. E. METs cannot be applied to older or deconditioned individuals at all
Show answer

Answer: A — The document explicitly notes that for someone with a peak capacity of ~5–6 METs, a brisk walk can be vigorous in RELATIVE terms while still being a low absolute workload — and the >6 MET risk threshold is an absolute-intensity figure. So scaled training that feels demanding for a deconditioned client is usually low absolute risk, and the greatest health gains occur at the low end of the fitness continuum. B ignores the relative-intensity point the paper makes; C and D are unsafe or overly restrictive; E is false. A captures the nuance the exam wants you to apply when judging intensity for special populations (tasks 5.2.3, 5.2.6).

71_08_Measure_of_Man.pdf

PDF link not yet available

Why this is on the reading list

Lon Kilgore's 'The Measure of Man' teaches the foundational screening skill of reading an athlete's anthropometry (body-segment proportions) at a glance and recognizing that there is no one-size-fits-all template of body angles every athlete must hit. This directly backs Domain 1's assessment tasks because before a coach can judge whether a movement is 'sound,' they must first assess that athlete's capacity to assume the position given their build. The article reframes apparent 'faults' (bar low on the thigh, more horizontal back, wider stance) as correct adaptations for atypical limb/torso lengths, which is core to assessing functional-movement capacity and managing injury risk during screening.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 1.1.2 Recognize conditions/injuries outside CCFT Scope of Practice that require referral (here: recognizing when a structural difference is an anthropometric variation to accommodate vs. when something is outside scope)
  • 1.2.1 Assess capacity/capability to perform functional movements (judging whether an athlete's body can geometrically assume a given position)
  • 4.1.2 Identify sound mechanics (sound mechanics are athlete-specific; the same correct position looks different across body types)
  • 4.1.3 Identify faults in movement (distinguishing a true fault from a structurally-driven appearance)
  • 4.1.6 Identify root cause of faults (segment length as a root cause of how a position looks)
  • 4.2.6 Apply basic principles of anatomy and biomechanics (rudimentary anatomy and geometry of segment lengths)
  • 2.2.4 Design programming for injured athletes / modify movements when a standard technique is geometrically impossible (e.g., prescribing sumo deadlift)
  • 5.2.3 Manage risk for the athlete (avoiding forcing athletes into positions their body cannot assume increases efficiency and lowers injury risk)

What to focus on while reading

  • Katie's question — 'How do you know someone's arms are longer or shorter than normal?' — note that this practical assessment question is the entire premise; it is a screening/eye-development problem, not a textbook anatomy problem.
  • The definition of 'anthropometric and geometric influences' on movement: how body part sizes/proportions change how a movement looks AND performs.
  • Why the coach needs a REFERENCE TEMPLATE and a way to mentally/visually compare an athlete to 'average' — highlight that you cannot judge 'longer/shorter than average' without a baseline.
  • The Vitruvian Man / da Vinci proportion observations (arm span = height; chin-to-crown = 1/8 height; shoulder width = 1/4; elbow-to-fingertip = 1/5; elbow-to-armpit = 1/8). Understand these as a baseline concept, NOT numbers to memorize.
  • The 7.5-head and 8-head artist models for estimating total height and segment placement from head lengths.
  • The single most useful practical landmark given: in the 8-head model the ELBOW sits at about the level of the BELLY BUTTON (navel). Memorize the RELATIONSHIP, not as trivia but as a quick visual check.
  • How to interpret deviations: elbow well BELOW navel = longer-than-average arm/upper arm (if torso is average); elbow well ABOVE navel = shorter arm/upper arm OR longer torso.
  • The key principle stated bluntly: 'there isn't a one-size-fits-all template for body angles that every body must conform to.'
  • Specific accommodations the coach should pull out as a checklist — grip width in the snatch (short arms = narrower grip, long arms = wider grip), forearm length affecting rack/clean receiving grip width, big belly = wider stance with toes out, long thighs = higher hips + more horizontal back, short thighs = lower hips + steeper back, long arms = bar lower on the thigh in the power clean jump position.
  • The 'central triangle' of the deadlift start (Figure 4) — as one side (e.g., arm length) changes, ALL component angles change, so each correct start position looks different.
  • Figure 5's worked example: very long thighs make a standard deadlift setup (bar over mid-foot, under the shoulder blade) geometrically impossible, so the coach prescribes a SUMO deadlift as the safe, workable modification.
  • The Magilla Gorilla coaching warning: do NOT cue a long-armed athlete to hit the bar higher on the thigh — it forces them to pull with bent arms and breaks the lift.
  • The boundary statement: this level of analysis does NOT require naming a single muscle or bone — the skill is identifying SEGMENTS and assessing their length relative to average.
  • The explicit caveat that this is about STRUCTURE/geometry, NOT flexibility ('this is not in reference to flexibility issues') — do not confuse a mobility limitation with an anthropometric one.
  • The coach's problem-solving process for extreme deviations: think it through, draw it out, experiment, talk to other trainers — treat it as a complex geometry problem.
  • Who Lon Kilgore is (kinesiology professor, weightlifter, coauthor with Rippetoe of Starting Strength) — establishes why this sits on the reading list as foundational coaching-eye material.

Concepts to understand

  • Anthropometry as a screening input: an athlete's segment proportions (arm, forearm, thigh, shin, torso lengths, trunk girth) determine what a correct position looks like and what they are physically capable of, so reading anthropometry is part of assessing readiness and movement capacity.
  • Sound mechanics are athlete-relative: the SAME technically-correct position legitimately looks different on different bodies, so a coach cannot judge correctness against a single rigid picture of joint angles.
  • The 'average template' as a mental reference tool: developing a coaching eye starts with knowing typical segmental relationships (e.g., elbow ≈ navel) so you can quickly flag who deviates and where the deviation is localized (upper arm vs. forearm, thigh vs. shin).
  • Localizing a deviation: it is not enough to see that a limb is 'off' — you must determine WHERE (which segment) and whether the torso is the variable, because the accommodation differs depending on the source.
  • Geometry of the lift changes with the body: changing one segment length changes every joint angle in a position (the 'central triangle' idea), which is why prescriptive, one-template coaching fails.
  • Accommodating, not forcing: the coach's job is to place the athlete in the correct, efficient, safe position THEIR body can assume — never to force a body into a space it cannot geometrically occupy (distinct from a flexibility fix).
  • Differentiating a structural appearance from a true fault: a bar low on the thigh or a more horizontal back can be CORRECT for that athlete's build; cueing it as a fault makes the movement worse and can raise injury risk (root-cause analysis).
  • Movement modification as a last resort for extreme cases: when no standard setup works (e.g., very long thighs), the coach legitimately changes the exercise variant (conventional → sumo deadlift) to keep it safe and trainable, accepting it is not optimal for comprehensive development.
  • Practical, low-anatomy competency: meaningful movement screening at this level requires identifying segments and judging length vs. average plus knowing the key points of an effective position — detailed muscle/bone knowledge is not the prerequisite.
  • Risk management through accommodation: ignoring anthropometry can decrease efficiency and increase injury risk; recognizing it lets you maximize fitness gain safely, tying movement assessment to athlete risk management.
  • Equipment and skills are body-dependent too: oarlock adjustability, fight-style choices by reach ('tale of the tape'), and barbell grip widths all illustrate that effective coaching adjusts settings/positions to the athlete's measurements.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenario questions where an athlete's position 'looks wrong' (bar low on the thigh, hips high with a horizontal back, fingertips reaching the upper thigh) and you must decide whether to correct it or recognize it as a correct accommodation for their build — testing 4.1.2/4.1.3/4.1.6 (sound mechanics vs. fault vs. root cause) and 1.2.1 (capacity to perform the movement). Other items will present an athlete whose proportions make a standard setup impossible and ask for the best response, where the keyed answer is to modify the variant (e.g., sumo deadlift) rather than force the position — touching 2.2.4 and 5.2.3 (risk management). Watch for distractors that have you cue against the athlete's geometry (telling a long-armed lifter to hit the bar higher), assume a single 'correct' joint angle for everyone, or misread an anthropometric difference as a mobility problem.

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Anthropometry
The measurement of the human body's dimensions and proportions — limb lengths, torso length, girths — and how they vary between people.
Anatomical phenotype
An individual's particular set of body dimensions and segment lengths; the observable build that makes one person's proportions differ from 'average.'
Body segment
A distinct part of the body used as a unit for analysis (e.g., upper arm, forearm, thigh, shin, torso) whose length affects movement geometry.
Segmental length / segment-length variation
How long a given body segment is relative to the average; the core thing a coach learns to eyeball to explain why a position looks different on an athlete.
Vitruvian Man
Da Vinci's drawing of a man in a circle and square mapping average human proportions; used here as the historical origin of an 'average body' reference, not a rule to memorize.
Head-length model (7.5- or 8-head)
An artists' system that uses the height of the head as a ruler to estimate total body height and the placement of landmarks; a convenient beginner reference for average proportions.
Anatomical landmark
A reference point on the body (e.g., the navel/belly button, hip joint, armpit) used to judge whether a segment is longer or shorter than average — e.g., elbow ≈ navel level in the 8-head model.
Central triangle (of the deadlift start)
The triangular geometry formed at the deadlift/clean start position; changing any one side (such as arm length) changes all the angles, so correct start positions look different across builds.
Jump position (power clean)
The position from which the athlete extends/jumps in the power clean; with long arms the bar will sit lower on the thigh here, and that is correct for that build.
Sumo deadlift
A wide-stance deadlift variant with the hands inside the legs; used here as a modification that lets a long-thighed athlete align mid-foot, bar, and shoulder blade when conventional setup is impossible.
Coaching eye
The trained ability to assess body proportions and positions at a glance; it develops with experience and eventually needs less reliance on artificial reference models.
Geometric/anthropometric influence
The effect of body proportions on how a movement looks and performs, distinct from skill, strength, or flexibility.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • Do not force an athlete into a position their body cannot geometrically assume — this can decrease efficiency and increase injury risk; modify the position or variant instead.
  • Do not confuse an anthropometric/structural difference with a flexibility (mobility) limitation — the article explicitly excludes flexibility; accommodating a long thigh is different from fixing a tight hip.
  • Do not cue against the athlete's structure (e.g., telling a long-armed lifter to bring the bar higher on the thigh) — it induces compensatory faults like pulling with bent arms.
  • When a standard technique cannot be made safe for an athlete's build, change the exercise/variant (e.g., conventional → sumo deadlift) so the movement stays safe and trainable rather than loading a bad position.
  • Stay within scope: this is structural accommodation, not diagnosis — if an apparent structural anomaly suggests pain, deformity, or pathology beyond normal proportion variation, that is outside CCFT scope and warrants referral.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. A new athlete sets up for a conventional deadlift. With the bar correctly over the mid-foot and under the shoulder blade, his bar starts only about two inches above the knee and his back is noticeably more horizontal than the other athletes'. His arms are clearly long for his height. What is the best coaching response?

  1. A. Cue him to raise the bar higher on his thighs so his start matches the rest of the class.
  2. B. Tell him to drop his hips lower to make his back more vertical.
  3. C. Reinforce this as his correct start position, because his long arms make the bar sit lower and the back more horizontal.
  4. D. Stop him from deadlifting until his back angle improves.
  5. E. Add load so he learns to hold a 'flat-back' position under tension.
Show answer

Answer: C — Long arms legitimately place the bar lower on the thigh and create a more horizontal back; with the bar over mid-foot and under the shoulder blade, this IS the correct, structurally-driven start. C accommodates his anatomy. A forces the bar higher and causes him to pull with bent arms (the explicit warning). B and the other distractors fight his geometry and raise risk; D and E are unwarranted and unsafe.

Scenario 2. During a snatch session you have athletes with very different arm lengths. Athlete A has notably short arms; Athlete B has notably long arms. How should grip width be coached?

  1. A. Both should use the same standardized grip width for consistency.
  2. B. Athlete A (short arms) narrower grip; Athlete B (long arms) wider grip.
  3. C. Athlete A (short arms) wider grip; Athlete B (long arms) narrower grip.
  4. D. Grip width should be set only by hand size, not arm length.
  5. E. Both should grip at the collars regardless of build.
Show answer

Answer: B — The goal in the snatch is a grip as wide as feasible to reduce bar travel, and grip width tracks arm length: short arms call for a narrower grip and long arms a wider grip (B). A imposes a one-size template the article rejects; C inverts the relationship; D and E ignore arm length, the relevant variable.

Scenario 3. A tall female athlete has very long thighs. When you set up a conventional deadlift, lowering her hips pushes her shins forward, drives the bar out over her toes, and leaves her shoulders behind the bar — you cannot get mid-foot, bar, and shoulder blade to align with standard technique. What is the most appropriate action?

  1. A. Keep the conventional setup and accept the bar drifting over her toes.
  2. B. Tell her she lacks the mobility to deadlift and remove the lift entirely.
  3. C. Switch her to a sumo deadlift so mid-foot, bar, and shoulder blade can align.
  4. D. Have her round the back slightly to reach the bar.
  5. E. Elevate the bar on blocks so she never has to reach the floor.
Show answer

Answer: C — This is the Figure 5 case: very long thighs make the conventional geometric solution impossible, so the keyed solution is the sumo deadlift, which realigns mid-foot, bar, and shoulder blade — safe and trainable even if not optimal for comprehensive development. A loads a poor position; B misattributes a structural issue to flexibility; D introduces an unsafe fault; E is an unnecessary workaround that avoids rather than solves the geometry.

Scenario 4. You want to quickly judge whether an athlete's upper arm is longer or shorter than average without measuring anything. Using the 8-head reference model, which check is most useful?

  1. A. Compare arm span to height — they should be exactly equal.
  2. B. See whether the elbow sits at about the level of the navel; well below suggests a longer arm/upper arm, well above suggests a shorter segment or longer torso.
  3. C. Measure forearm length against shin length.
  4. D. Check whether the fingertips reach the knees when standing.
  5. E. Confirm the head fits 7.5 times into the body height.
Show answer

Answer: B — The article's practical landmark is that in the 8-head model the elbow sits roughly at navel level; an elbow well below indicates a longer arm/upper arm (if torso is average) and well above indicates a shorter segment or a longer torso (B). A is a true da Vinci proportion but doesn't localize the upper arm; C, D, and E don't isolate upper-arm length relative to average.

Scenario 5. An athlete's back looks more horizontal than you expect at the bottom of a clean pull. Before correcting it as a fault, what is the most important thing to assess first?

  1. A. Whether his shoes have an elevated heel.
  2. B. Whether his thigh length is long, which raises the hip start and makes the back more horizontal as a correct adaptation.
  3. C. Whether he ate before training.
  4. D. Whether the barbell is the standard 20 kg.
  5. E. Whether he is mentally focused on the lift.
Show answer

Answer: B — Segment length is a root cause of how a position looks: long thighs necessitate a higher hip start and therefore a more horizontal back, which is correct for that build. You must assess the structural source (B) before labeling it a fault — otherwise you risk cueing against his geometry. The other options are irrelevant to the appearance of the back angle here.

Scenario 6. A coach insists every athlete must hit the exact same torso angle and the exact same bar height on the thigh at the deadlift start, and drills the class until everyone looks identical. What is the core problem with this approach according to the article?

  1. A. Nothing — uniform positions are the safest way to coach a group.
  2. B. There is no one-size-fits-all template of body angles; segment-length differences make the same correct position look different, so a uniform standard forces some athletes into faulty, riskier positions.
  3. C. The problem is only that it takes too much class time.
  4. D. Identical positions are fine as long as the athletes are flexible enough.
  5. E. Uniformity is correct for beginners and only matters for advanced lifters.
Show answer

Answer: B — The article's central thesis is that there isn't a one-size-fits-all template of body angles every body must conform to; because changing a segment length changes all the joint angles, forcing uniformity pushes athletes with different builds into incorrect, less efficient, higher-risk positions (B). A and D ignore anthropometry; C trivializes the issue as time; E invents a beginner/advanced distinction the article does not make.

Scenario 7. An athlete with a large belly is setting up to pull a barbell from the floor and is struggling to find a comfortable start. What adjustment best fits his anthropometry?

  1. A. Narrow the stance and point the toes straight ahead to keep the bar close.
  2. B. Widen the stance somewhat and point the toes out a bit more to allow proper mechanics and give the belly room.
  3. C. Tell him to lose weight before he is allowed to deadlift.
  4. D. Have him pull with a rounded back to clear the abdomen.
  5. E. Raise the bar onto high blocks so he never bends past his belly.
Show answer

Answer: B — A larger-than-average trunk girth changes the geometry of the stance; the article's accommodation is a slightly wider stance with toes pointed out a bit more, allowing proper lifting mechanics and room for the belly (B). A constrains the geometry further; C is dismissive and outside the coaching task; D introduces an unsafe fault; E needlessly avoids the movement rather than adjusting the stance.

D1 · Screening & Ongoing Assessment 8% of exam Confidence tier: ___

PDF link not yet available

Why this is on the reading list

This article gives the coach a structured, repeatable way to answer the most fundamental assessment question in CrossFit: when an athlete's squat looks wrong, is it because they CAN'T move (mobility restriction) or WON'T/DON'T move correctly (motor-control dysfunction)? That distinction directly supports Domain 1's 'assess capacity/capability to perform functional movements' (1.2.1) by providing three concrete pass/fail screens (ankle dorsiflexion, knee flexion, hip flexion) plus hip-rotation and lumbar-extension checks. It also feeds the Training domain heavily, because correctly diagnosing root cause (4.1.6) dictates whether you cue, scale, or refer. For an 8% Screening domain that the exam expects you to APPLY at class scale, this is the canonical squat-assessment reference.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 1.2.1 Assess capacity/capability to perform functional movements
  • 1.1.2 Recognize conditions/injuries outside CCFT Scope of Practice that require referral (risk factors)
  • 4.1.1 Identify points of performance
  • 4.1.3 Identify faults in movement
  • 4.1.6 Identify root cause of faults
  • 4.2.1 Communicate cues to correct unsound mechanics
  • 4.2.2 Use multiple cueing strategies (visual, tactile, verbal)
  • 4.2.3 Utilize effective cues (short, specific, actionable)
  • 4.2.6 Apply basic principles of anatomy and biomechanics
  • 3.1.3 Use progressions to teach complex moves
  • 3.1.10 Teach the relationship between technique and intensity (threshold training)

What to focus on while reading

  • The article's central decision rule: ANALYZE MOBILITY FIRST. If adequate mobility exists in all necessary joints but movement quality is still below standard, the cause is motor control, not range of motion. This is the spine of the whole piece — highlight it.
  • The three foundational squat screens and their exact pass criteria: (1) ANKLE dorsiflexion — big toe one hand-width (~4 in) from wall, barefoot, bottom of a lunge, knee touches wall WITHOUT the heel lifting; (2) KNEE flexion — supine, bend knee until calf contacts posterior thigh; (3) HIP flexion — supine, pull thigh to chest, front of thigh contacts the stomach.
  • What passing all three screens means: the athlete has sufficient LOWER-BODY range of motion to squat to depth with all points of performance — so any remaining faults are almost always motor-control, addressable with squat therapy and cueing.
  • The squat points of performance taught in L1: shoulder-width stance, weight on heels, braced core, chest up, neutral spine; initiate by sending HIPS down and back (not knees forward); descend until hip crease is below the kneecap with knees tracking over the feet; finish fully upright with hips and knees extended.
  • The standard list of common squat faults the screens and cues map to: loss of neutral spine, weight shifting onto the toes, heels losing contact with the ground, feet rotating outward, lack of depth, and improper lateral knee tracking (knees caving / valgus).
  • The HIP-ROTATION screen: athlete sits on a box, upright torso; partner rotates the leg (foot inward = external rotation, foot outward = internal rotation), keeping the thigh pointed forward and stopping before the pelvis shifts. Normal ~40 degrees each direction. Note the faults limited hip rotation produces: feet turning out, loss of neutral spine, knees pushing out wider than the feet.
  • The LUMBAR-EXTENSION screen: athlete prone, props onto forearms; look for UNIFORM lumbar extension with hips flat on the ground. Dysfunction = hips rise off the ground, OR excessive hinge at one segment (often the thoracolumbar junction).
  • The note that thoracic-spine extension and shoulder mobility/stability matter increasingly in the overhead squat — and are covered in companion articles ('Analyzing the Handstand Position,' 'The Optimal Shoulder'). The squat is a family of movements with escalating demands.
  • The anatomy caveat: hip anatomy varies greatly between individuals; the ~40-degree target may be impossible for some, but even small mobility gains can meaningfully improve function. Do not force a number onto a body that isn't built for it.
  • MOTOR-CONTROL corrections by fault. Knees caving in (most common motor-control fault): usually weak/under-active glutes failing to control lateral knee motion (may be partly ankle); cues 'push the knees out,' 'spread the ground with your feet,' an external target (coach's hand at the knee), or a LIGHT resistance band around the knees used to drive glute activation, NOT to load/strengthen.
  • Loss of neutral spine into lumbar flexion: cue 'lift the chest' or raise the arms during the descent.
  • The set-up trap that mimics a mobility problem: an athlete starting with the lumbar OVER-extended tilts the pelvis anteriorly, which reduces the hip-socket ROM available for flexion; the spine is then forced into flexion to reach depth — the classic 'butt wink.' Fix the START position first; cue 'keep your ribcage down' to engage abs/glutes into neutral. Note the lesson: a poor set-up can fake a mobility restriction.
  • Balance/weight-distribution faults (toes-loaded, knees forward, shallow, lost spine) framed with the building-foundation analogy: if the base (foot weight distribution) is wrong, errors stack above. Cue hips down-and-back with weight on the heels, or add a COUNTERBALANCE (goblet KB or a light plate held in front) so a quads-dominant athlete can sit the hips back without falling; wean the weight as positioning is learned.
  • SQUAT THERAPY (the L1 corrective): athlete faces a wall in a proper set-up, squats slowly to a ~10-inch box / med ball, coach cues throughout. The wall blocks excessive forward travel of knees/trunk; the box gives a tactile depth target. It is the go-to starting drill for an athlete showing MULTIPLE faults.
  • The payoff principle: motor-control problems often resolve QUICKLY with the right cue, whereas mobility changes are slow and highly individual. With consistent correct practice, the corrected pattern becomes the athlete's default and transfers to other movements.
  • The 'relentless trainer' theme: even when some ROM is genuinely limited, a coach can almost always win small short-term improvements through creative cueing — don't accept 'I can't' at face value.
  • The cue taxonomy in action — note where the author uses VERBAL ('push knees out'), VISUAL/external-target (coach's hand, the wall, the box), and TACTILE (the band, holding the plate) cues. The article is a worked example of multi-modal cueing.
  • Functional/longevity framing: the squat is required to stand from a seat and stay independent with age, and is the prime developer of powerful hip extension / athleticism — i.e., why this assessment matters for every member, not just competitors.

Concepts to understand

  • Mobility vs. motor control as the two distinct causes of a faulty squat, and the diagnostic ORDER: test mobility first; if mobility is adequate, attribute the fault to motor control. Be able to apply this fork to a described athlete and pick the correct intervention (mobility work vs. cueing/squat therapy).
  • Mobility = the available range of motion at a joint. Motor control = the ability to coordinate muscle activation to USE that available range efficiently. An athlete can have the range and still move poorly — and that is a coaching/cueing problem, not a stretching problem.
  • How to administer and interpret each of the three foundational screens (ankle DF, knee flexion, hip flexion) and what a PASS on all three licenses you to conclude (sufficient lower-body ROM; remaining faults are motor control).
  • Ankle dorsiflexion as the highest-yield single restriction: it is among the most common ROM limits, can produce essentially every squat fault, and is research-linked to lower-extremity injury and faulty landing mechanics — so it is the first joint to clear.
  • How a single visible fault can have MULTIPLE possible root causes (e.g., knees caving = ankle restriction AND/OR weak glutes), and why the coach must test to find the actual driver rather than reflexively cueing — this is task 4.1.6 (identify root cause) in practice.
  • The set-up determines the rep: anterior pelvic tilt from a lumbar over-extension start steals hip flexion ROM and forces a 'butt wink'; therefore some apparent mobility problems are actually START-POSITION problems fixed before descent.
  • Counterbalance loading as a teaching tool (goblet KB / front-held plate): adding light load forward lets a quad-dominant athlete sit the hips back in balance; the load is a TRAINING WHEEL to be removed, not a strength stimulus.
  • Light resistance band at the knees as a TACTILE/activation cue: the resistance is intentionally light because its purpose is glute activation and proprioceptive feedback, not loading — combine it (band in warm-up) with live verbal cueing during the workout.
  • Squat therapy as the universal multi-fault starting drill, and WHY its two constraints work: the wall caps forward knee/trunk travel; the low box gives a tactile depth target; slow tempo + coach cueing rebuild the pattern.
  • The cueing hierarchy in modalities — verbal, visual, and tactile — and choosing the modality the individual athlete responds to (e.g., switch from a verbal 'knees out' to an external target if the words don't land). This directly serves tasks 4.2.1–4.2.3.
  • Mobility is the floor, not the ceiling: clearing the screens grants the CAPACITY to reach positions; it does not by itself produce a good squat. Capacity (1.2.1) and execution (Domain 4) are separate problems.
  • Individual variation in hip anatomy: standardized ROM targets are guides, not mandates; coach to the athlete's structure and value incremental gains over hitting an arbitrary degree count.
  • Escalating demand across squat variants: air squat → back/front squat → overhead squat add progressively greater thoracic-extension and shoulder mobility/stability requirements; the assessment must scale with the variation being coached.
  • Why motor-control wins are fast and durable: correct reps practiced consistently re-pattern the default movement and transfer to other lifts, whereas mobility change is slow and variable — this shapes where the coach spends effort first for the quickest safe improvement.
  • The functional/longevity rationale for prioritizing squat quality: independence in daily life (sit-to-stand) and athletic hip-extension power both ride on a sound squat, which is why screening every athlete's squat is foundational, not optional.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenarios that describe an athlete with a specific squat fault and ask for the BEST next coaching action — the right answer almost always requires you to first decide mobility-vs-motor-control (1.2.1, 4.1.6) and then pick the matching tool (a screen, a cue, a counterbalance, a band, squat therapy, or scaling). Items may hand you screen results (e.g., 'passes all three lower-body screens but knees still cave') and ask what that implies — the application is recognizing it's motor control and choosing a cue, not prescribing stretching. Others test cue selection by modality (4.2.1–4.2.3) and triage of the most egregious fault first (4.2.7), or hide a 'butt wink' caused by a set-up error to see if you fix the start position rather than chase phantom hip mobility. A small number can touch scope: persistent pain or a red-flag presentation moves from coaching into referral territory (1.1.2).

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Mobility
The available range of motion at a joint or set of joints — what the body CAN physically do. Tested first; improved slowly via stretching, myofascial release, joint mobilizations, or manual therapy.
Motor control
The ability to coordinate muscle activation to control movement THROUGH the available range — using the range you have. When mobility is adequate but the squat is faulty, motor control is the cause; it responds quickly to cueing and practice.
Ankle dorsiflexion
The motion of drawing the top of the foot toward the shin (knee traveling forward over the toes). One of the most common ROM limits; restriction can cause every squat fault. Screened with the knee-to-wall test, big toe ~4 in (one hand-width) from the wall, heel staying down.
Knee-to-wall test
Ankle-dorsiflexion screen: barefoot in the bottom of a lunge with the big toe one hand-width from a wall, the athlete touches the kneecap to the wall without the heel rising. Failure indicates limited ankle dorsiflexion.
Knee-flexion screen
Supine test for squat-depth capacity: the athlete bends the knee until the calf muscles contact the back of the thigh, confirming enough knee flexion to reach depth.
Hip-flexion screen
Supine test: the athlete pulls the thigh toward the chest; if the front of the thigh contacts the stomach, adequate hip flexion for squatting is present.
Hip-rotation screen
Seated on a box, upright torso; a partner rotates the leg (foot in = external rotation, foot out = internal rotation) keeping the thigh forward and stopping before the pelvis shifts. Normal ~40 degrees each way; limits cause feet turning out, lost neutral spine, and knees splaying past the feet.
Lumbar-extension screen
Prone press-up onto the forearms looking for uniform lumbar extension with hips flat. Dysfunction shows as hips lifting off the floor or excessive hinging at one segment (often the thoracolumbar junction).
Points of performance
The defining mechanical standards of a movement. For the squat: shoulder-width stance, weight on heels, braced/neutral spine, chest up, hips initiate down and back, hip crease below the knee, knees tracking over feet, full upright finish.
Butt wink
Posterior pelvic tilt with lumbar flexion at the bottom of the squat. Often driven by a set-up error (starting over-extended → anterior tilt → less available hip flexion), making a position fault masquerade as a mobility restriction.
Squat therapy
The L1 corrective drill for athletes with multiple faults: facing a wall in proper set-up, squat slowly to a ~10-in box/med ball with the coach cueing throughout. Wall limits forward knee/trunk travel; box gives a tactile depth target.
Counterbalance (goblet/plate)
Holding a light KB or plate in front of the chest so a quad-dominant athlete can send the hips back and stay balanced while learning the pattern; the load is a temporary teaching aid, reduced and removed as positioning improves.
Resistance band cue (knees)
A light band around the knees used as a tactile/activation cue to drive gluteal activation and discourage knees caving in — deliberately light because the goal is feedback and activation, not strength loading.
Tactile / visual / verbal cues
The three cueing modalities. Verbal ('push the knees out'), visual/external-target (coach's hand, the wall, the box), and tactile (the band, the held plate). Coaches select the modality the individual athlete responds to.
Knee valgus (knees caving in)
Inward tracking of the knees during the squat — the most common motor-control fault, usually from under-active glutes failing to control lateral knee motion (sometimes compounded by ankle restriction).
Neutral spine
The braced, natural-curve position of the spine maintained throughout the squat; losing it (into flexion or excessive extension) is a primary fault the screens and cues target.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • Pain (not just stiffness or tightness) during a screen or the squat, or a fault that does not respond to any cueing or mobility work, points beyond coaching — refer to a qualified medical professional rather than continuing to load (1.1.2). Note the author is a doctor of physical therapy; the COACH's job is screening and cueing, not diagnosing or treating injury.
  • Manual therapy, joint mobilizations, and hands-on mobility treatment are explicitly described as performed by TRAINED PROFESSIONALS — these fall outside the CCFT scope of practice. The coach stays in screening, cueing, scaling, and athlete-directed mobility drills.
  • A persistent 'I can't reach depth / it hurts' that is NOT explained by the three screens or a set-up error warrants caution: do not force range under load; scale the movement and consider referral if symptoms persist.
  • Do not chase an arbitrary ROM number (e.g., 40-degree hip rotation) on an athlete whose anatomy may not allow it — forcing range risks injury; coach to the individual's available structure.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. An athlete's knees collapse inward at the bottom of every air squat. You run the three foundational screens and he PASSES all three (knee-to-wall with heel down, calf-to-thigh knee flexion, thigh-to-stomach hip flexion). What is the best next step?

  1. A. Prescribe two weeks of daily ankle and hip stretching before he squats again
  2. B. Refer him to a physical therapist for the knee valgus
  3. C. Treat it as a motor-control fault: cue 'push the knees out' / 'spread the ground,' add a light band around the knees in warm-up, and cue during the workout
  4. D. Add load to the squat so the heavier weight forces the knees into a better position
  5. E. Tell him to stop squatting until his mobility improves
Show answer

Answer: C — Passing all three lower-body screens means mobility is adequate, so by the article's decision rule the remaining fault is motor control — addressed with cueing and a light activation band, not stretching (A), referral (B), more load (D), or stopping (E). The band is for glute activation, not strength.

Scenario 2. During the bottom of her back squat, an athlete shows a clear 'butt wink' (lumbar rounds under). She insists her hips are 'too tight.' On screening, her hip-flexion and ankle screens pass, but you notice she sets up with her lower back arched hard and ribs flared. What is the most likely root cause and best correction?

  1. A. True hip-flexion mobility deficit; assign hip-opener stretches
  2. B. Set-up error — starting over-extended tilts the pelvis anteriorly and steals hip-flexion ROM; coach a neutral start ('keep your ribcage down') before she descends
  3. C. Weak quads; add front squats for quad strength
  4. D. Ankle restriction; elevate her heels on plates permanently
  5. E. Nothing to correct — a butt wink at depth is unavoidable for everyone
Show answer

Answer: B — The screens passed, and an over-extended set-up produces anterior pelvic tilt that reduces available hip flexion and forces lumbar flexion at depth — a position fault disguised as a mobility problem. Fixing the start ('ribcage down') is the article's prescribed correction, not stretching (A), strength work (C), a permanent heel lift (D), or accepting it (E).

Scenario 3. You want to test whether an athlete has enough ankle dorsiflexion to squat well. How does the article say to perform and pass the screen?

  1. A. Standing, raise up onto the toes as high as possible
  2. B. Seated, pull the toes toward the shin with a band and measure the angle
  3. C. Barefoot in the bottom of a lunge with the big toe one hand-width (~4 in) from a wall, touch the kneecap to the wall WITHOUT the heel lifting
  4. D. Squat to depth with a barbell and see if the heels stay down under load
  5. E. Lie prone and press up onto the forearms, watching the heels
Show answer

Answer: C — The article's ankle screen is the knee-to-wall test: big toe ~one hand-width from the wall, knee touches the wall with the heel staying on the ground. A is plantarflexion; D adds a confound (load/balance); E is the lumbar-extension screen; B is not the described test.

Scenario 4. A new member demonstrates SEVERAL squat faults at once — shallow depth, weight on the toes, chest dropping, and knees drifting forward. Which single intervention does the article identify as the best STARTING point for an athlete with multiple faults?

  1. A. Load a heavy back squat to 'groove' the pattern
  2. B. Squat therapy: face a wall in a proper set-up and squat slowly to a ~10-inch box/med ball while you cue throughout
  3. C. Send her home with a list of mobility videos and reassess in a month
  4. D. Have her do max-effort box jumps to build power first
  5. E. Switch her straight to the overhead squat to force an upright torso
Show answer

Answer: B — Squat therapy is described as the L1 corrective that addresses all the most common mechanical errors and the great starting point for an athlete with multiple faults: the wall caps forward knee/trunk travel, the box gives a tactile depth target, and slow tempo plus coach cueing rebuild the pattern. Loading (A, E), deferring (C), or unrelated power work (D) do not address the faults.

Scenario 5. An athlete is quad-dominant: as he descends, his knees shoot forward and his weight rolls onto his toes, and he can't sit back without losing balance. Screens are clear. Which coaching tool does the article recommend to teach him to send the hips back in balance?

  1. A. A weightlifting belt to brace the trunk
  2. B. A heavy barbell on his back to anchor him down
  3. C. A counterbalance — holding a light kettlebell (goblet) or a plate out front — so he can sit the hips back without falling, then wean the weight as positioning improves
  4. D. Permanently elevating his heels so the knees can travel forward freely
  5. E. Telling him to simply 'go faster' out of the bottom
Show answer

Answer: C — A front-held counterbalance lets a quad-dominant athlete send the hips back and load them without losing balance; it is a temporary teaching aid to be reduced and removed. A belt (A) doesn't address balance/positioning, heavy load (B) worsens it, a permanent heel lift (D) accommodates rather than corrects the toes-forward pattern, and speed (E) ignores the fault.

Scenario 6. You cue an athlete 'push your knees out' and she immediately says 'I can't — my hips are too tight,' yet her hip and ankle screens pass. According to the article's coaching philosophy, what is the appropriate response?

  1. A. Accept the limitation and stop cueing — she knows her body best
  2. B. End the session and refer her out for tight hips
  3. C. Stay relentless and switch cue modality: use an external target like your hand at her knee or a light band, since screens show the range exists and the issue is motor control
  4. D. Immediately load a heavy squat to stretch the hips under tension
  5. E. Assign 30 minutes of static hip stretching before she may squat again
Show answer

Answer: C — The article stresses that athletes often blame ROM when the real issue is motor control, and that relentless coaches can almost always make short-term gains with creative cues — including switching from a verbal cue to an external target or tactile band. Passing screens confirms the range is present, so accepting defeat (A), referring (B), heavy loading (D), or stretching range she already has (E) are wrong.

Scenario 7. Why does the article direct coaches to analyze MOBILITY before concluding a fault is a motor-control problem?

  1. A. Because mobility problems are always more dangerous than motor-control problems
  2. B. Because if adequate mobility is present in all necessary joints but movement quality is still poor, the cause must be motor control — and that conclusion is only valid after mobility has been cleared
  3. C. Because motor control cannot be improved by a coach and must be referred out
  4. D. Because mobility work is faster to fix than motor control
  5. E. Because athletes prefer stretching to cueing
Show answer

Answer: B — The decision rule is sequential: test mobility first; only once you've confirmed the range exists can you correctly attribute a persistent fault to motor control. C is false (cueing IS the coach's job), and D is backwards — the article says motor control resolves faster than mobility. A and E are not the stated rationale.

Scenario 8. Which finding during the prone lumbar-extension screen indicates DYSFUNCTION rather than healthy uniform extension?

  1. A. The athlete props onto the forearms with hips flat and shows even extension across the lumbar spine
  2. B. The hips rise off the ground, or extension hinges excessively at one segment (often the thoracolumbar junction), instead of distributing uniformly
  3. C. The athlete can press all the way to straight arms
  4. D. The heels stay flat against the floor
  5. E. The athlete feels a mild stretch in the front of the hips
Show answer

Answer: B — The article defines dysfunction as hips lifting off the ground or excessive extension concentrated at a single segment (commonly the lumbar/thoracic junction), versus the healthy pattern of uniform lumbar extension with hips flat (A). Arm-straightening (C), heel position (D), and a mild hip stretch (E) are not the stated criteria.
