CFJ_2015_11_Aging_Kilgore2.pdf

PDF link not yet available

Why this is on the reading list

This article gives the coach an evidence-anchored mental model for how physical capacity declines with age and how training abates (never eliminates) that loss. It directly backs Domain 1's tasks on identifying fitness goals, setting age-appropriate expectations, quantifying and tracking performance, and judging readiness to progress, and it backs Domain 2's age-group scaling. Most importantly, it reframes the goal of training for the largest segment of paying clients (over-30s) away from elite numbers and toward function, health, and quality of life — the lens a CCFT must apply when setting and assessing goals for masters athletes.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 1.2.3 Identify athlete's fitness goals
  • 1.2.5 Identify when athlete is ready to progress to another goal/skill
  • 1.2.6 Quantify and track performance
  • 1.2.2 Evaluate athlete's work capacity
  • 1.2.1 Assess capacity/capability to perform functional movements
  • 1.2.4 Monitor athlete for signs of over- or under-training
  • 2.2.1 Scale by age group
  • 2.2.5 Scale by skill level
  • 2.3.1 Evaluate program success relative to athlete goals and needs
  • 2.3.4 Evaluate athlete progress relative to CrossFit's definition of fitness and their personal goal
  • 5.1.1 Provide athletes with goal setting
  • 6.1.4 Review basic health markers (relationship of fitness to mortality and disease risk)

What to focus on while reading

  • The decade-by-decade decline rates: roughly 10% loss of overall fitness capacity per decade until the 70s (13% in the 70s, 15% in the 80s); ~57% total overall performance loss by the 80s.
  • Table 1 — the differential decay rates by category. Note which capacities decay FASTEST and which are best PRESERVED, not the exact percentages.
  • Heavy power (the Olympic lifts) decays fastest — a 25% drop by age 40, twice the average and up to five times the rate of other categories. Ask yourself WHY (the article points to advanced mobility demands as a candidate).
  • Power speed (high/long jump) and light power (shot, discus, hammer) are the BEST-preserved capacities.
  • The ordering of categories on the strength-to-endurance spectrum: maximal strength, heavy power, light power, power speed, speed, endurance — and the example events in each.
  • The point that loss is COMPOUNDED if you don't train, but hard, intelligent training ABATES (not eliminates) the loss.
  • Octogenarians can improve strength by up to 200%; resistance training produces positive fitness/quality-of-life effects at any age (the Latham et al. systematic review is the cited evidence).
  • The training-progression population distribution: inactive 25%, physically active 40%, novice 20%, intermediate 10%, advanced 4%, elite 1% — and that these are the AUTHOR'S approximations, not hard data.
  • The mortality finding: lowest risk-of-death is in the upper THIRD for strength and the upper QUARTER for endurance; that band starts at the top of the novice standard and runs through elite.
  • The diminishing-returns nuance: mortality risk does NOT change much between intermediate and elite, but FUNCTION (and therefore quality of life) keeps rising with fitness.
  • The 'health vs. function' distinction: absence of disease (ACSM's definition of health) is not the same as functional capacity; health without function 'is just as problematic as ill health.'
  • Figure 3's logic — slope of decay is STEEPER for elite/advanced and SHALLOWER for untrained, but untrained people have little fitness to lose, so even small losses are catastrophic for them.
  • The cross-age comparison: an elite 70-year-old functions about like an intermediate 30-year-old; an intermediate 70-year-old like a physically active 30-year-old.
  • The timelines to move up levels: untrained-to-novice in a few months; untrained-to-intermediate ~2 years; advanced ~4-5 years; elite ~a decade of systematic training.
  • The honest limits the author flags: standards rest on a very limited data set; mobility/agility/balance/coordination affect quality of life but their lifespan-mortality relationship is NOT well established.

Concepts to understand

  • Age-adjusted expectations: a strength/performance standard built for a 30-year-old cannot be fairly applied to a 40-, 53-, 67- or 88-year-old. The coach must adjust expectations and goals downward by age when assessing and goal-setting.
  • Training abates decline, it doesn't stop it: aging guarantees some loss of capacity, but consistent hard training meaningfully slows the slope — so 'I'm getting older' is never a reason to stop, and progress is still expected from a new masters trainee.
  • Differential decay: not all fitness components age at the same rate. Olympic lifting/heavy power falls off fastest and earliest; throwing and jumping (light power, power speed) hold up best. A coach uses this to set realistic per-domain expectations and to choose where to push vs. preserve.
  • Function over numbers as the primary goal for masters athletes: for the over-30 majority of clients, the objective is health, vitality, independence and quality of life — not PRs or podiums. Goal-setting and program evaluation should be framed this way.
  • The fitness-mortality dose-response: moving from sedentary to merely 'physically active' yields the biggest single drop in all-cause mortality risk, but does NOT confer much fitness. Maximum risk abatement requires reaching roughly the upper third (strength) / upper quarter (endurance) of capacity — i.e., the top of novice through elite.
  • Diminishing mortality returns but rising function: past the intermediate level, additional fitness barely lowers death risk further, yet it keeps improving real-world function and quality of life — which is why a coach still pushes capable athletes higher.
  • Health is not the same as function: an athlete can be disease-free yet functionally impaired; the CrossFit coaching aim is functional capacity inside and outside the gym, not merely the absence of pathology.
  • It's never too late to start, and earlier is better: gains are available in every decade, but waiting reduces the ceiling you can reach relative to genetic potential. This shapes how a coach motivates and sets goals for an older beginner.
  • Relative, not absolute, framing of 'elite': only ~1% are elite, but you don't have to be elite — or set records — to capture the health and longevity benefits of training. Coaches should set attainable, individualized targets.
  • Cross-age perspective for motivation: a highly trained older athlete out-functions a less-trained younger one (elite-70 ≈ intermediate-30). Useful to reframe a discouraged masters athlete's self-assessment.
  • Progression timelines as readiness/goal-setting anchors: months to reach novice, ~2 years to intermediate, ~4-5 to advanced, ~a decade to elite. These set honest timeframes for when an athlete is ready to progress to a new goal.
  • Epistemic humility about standards: published referential data are sparse, much rests on experience/observation/estimation, and mobility-mortality links are largely unknown — so standards are guides for goal-setting, not rigid pass/fail gates.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenario questions where a masters or older-beginner athlete states a goal or compares themselves to a younger benchmark, and you must pick the response that sets age-appropriate expectations and reframes toward function/health (tasks 1.2.3, 1.2.5, 5.1.1, 2.2.1). Other items will give a coaching situation and ask how to track or interpret performance over time, or how to motivate a discouraged aging athlete using the training-abates-decline and function-over-numbers logic (tasks 1.2.6, 2.3.1, 2.3.4). Watch for distractors that promise elite outcomes regardless of age, treat a 30-year-old standard as universal, or define success purely as the absence of disease.

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Performance/fitness standard
A realistic expectation of what someone with given characteristics (sex, age, training experience) can do in a particular exercise — a reference point to help an athlete evaluate performance and set goals, not an absolute rule.
Fitness capacity (performance capacity)
The body's overall ability to produce work and movement across fitness components; it inevitably declines with age but is buffered by training.
Decay / performance decline
The age-related loss of fitness capacity; in this article ~10% per decade overall until the 70s, accelerating thereafter, with the rate differing by fitness component.
Heavy power
The Olympic lifts (snatch, clean and jerk) — high-velocity, high-load movements; the fitness category that decays fastest with age (25% by 40).
Light power
Throwing events (shot put, discus, hammer); among the best-preserved capacities across the lifespan.
Power speed
Jumping events (high jump, long jump); along with light power, the best-retained physical capacity with age.
Maximal strength
Peak force production (squat, bench press, deadlift); retains relatively well early but declines steadily with age.
Masters athlete
An older competitor (over-40 divisions and up); the population whose age-adjusted standards and function-focused goals this article addresses.
Training progression levels
A ladder of fitness — untrained/inactive, physically active, novice, intermediate, advanced, elite — used to classify athletes and frame realistic goals and timelines.
Physically active (vs. trained)
Accumulating ~30 minutes/day of above-baseline movement (e.g., stairs, walking) 3-5 days/week; lowers mortality risk substantially but yields little true fitness gain.
All-cause mortality / risk abatement
Risk of death from any cause; training lowers it most as one moves out of the weakest/least-enduring group, with maximal benefit in the upper third (strength) and upper quarter (endurance).
Health vs. function
Health framed as absence of disease (the ACSM-style definition) versus functional capacity (strength, endurance, mobility for real-world life); the article argues function is essential, not optional.
Quality of life
Real-world vitality, independence and pain-free capability that rises with fitness even after mortality benefits plateau — a primary aim of coaching older athletes.
Progressive resistance training
Systematically increasing resistance over time; the evidence base (Latham et al. review) shows it improves fitness and quality of life in older adults, including ~200% strength gains in octogenarians.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • Promising or implying elite/record-level outcomes for an aging athlete is unrealistic and a coaching error — set age-appropriate expectations instead.
  • Treating 'disease-free' as the finish line: an athlete can be healthy yet functionally impaired; the coach's job extends to restoring/preserving function and quality of life.
  • This article is performance/expectation-setting, not medical screening — it does not replace Domain 1 medical clearance, rhabdo risk assessment, or referral for conditions outside CCFT scope. Age alone is not a contraindication, but underlying medical issues still require the standard readiness screen.
  • Avoid catastrophizing or discouraging older beginners; the data support meaningful gains at every age, and small losses are most dangerous in the LEAST trained — making the case to start, not to quit.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. A 58-year-old new member says, 'My buddy who's 32 deadlifts 405. I want to hit that number this year to prove I'm not over the hill.' What is the best coaching response?

  1. A. Agree and program aggressively toward 405 within the year so he stays motivated.
  2. B. Tell him strength can't improve after 50, so he should focus only on cardio.
  3. C. Acknowledge that a 30-year-old's standard can't be fairly applied at 58, reset the goal to age-appropriate, consistent strength gains, and reframe success around improving function and quality of life.
  4. D. Tell him the number is irrelevant and refuse to track his deadlift.
  5. E. Refer him to a physician because wanting to lift heavy at his age is a medical red flag.
Show answer

Answer: C — C applies age-adjusted expectations (1.2.3, 2.2.1) and reframes toward function/QoL while still pursuing real gains. A sets an unrealistic, potentially unsafe target. B is false — older adults, even octogenarians, make large strength gains. D abandons performance tracking (1.2.6), which CrossFit and the client value. E mislabels a normal goal as a medical issue.

Scenario 2. Two 45-year-old athletes return to training after years off. One wants to chase a heavy snatch PR; the other wants general fitness. Based on the article's data on how capacities age, what should you tell the snatch-focused athlete to set expectations?

  1. A. Olympic-lifting capacity is among the best-preserved with age, so a lifetime PR is very likely.
  2. B. Heavy-power (Olympic-lift) capacity decays fastest and earliest with age, so while he can still improve and compete, a lifetime snatch PR may not be realistic — set goals against an age-appropriate standard.
  3. C. All fitness components decline at exactly the same rate, so the snatch is no different from any other lift.
  4. D. He should drop the snatch entirely because it is unsafe for anyone over 40.
  5. E. Throwing and jumping decay fastest, so he should expect his snatch to hold up better than his vertical jump.
Show answer

Answer: B — B matches the article: heavy power (the Olympic lifts) drops ~25% by 40, twice the average, so age-adjusted expectation-setting is warranted (1.2.3, 1.2.5, 2.2.1). A and E invert the data — power speed and light power are best preserved, heavy power is worst. C contradicts the differential-decay finding. D over-restricts; the lift can still be trained safely with appropriate scaling.

Scenario 3. A sedentary 67-year-old asks whether starting CrossFit is even worth it 'this late.' Which response best reflects the article's evidence?

  1. A. It's probably too late to gain meaningful fitness, so focus on staying comfortable.
  2. B. Gains are available in every decade; moving from untrained toward intermediate over a couple of years sharply lowers mortality risk and improves function — and the biggest single risk drop comes just from becoming active, so starting now is highly worthwhile.
  3. C. She should aim for elite fitness within a year to maximize the health benefit.
  4. D. Health is just the absence of disease, so as long as she has no diagnosis she gains nothing from training.
  5. E. Older untrained people lose fitness slowly, so there's no urgency and she can wait a few more years.
Show answer

Answer: B — B captures the dose-response and 'never too late' messages (1.2.3, 5.1.1): the largest mortality drop comes from leaving the sedentary group, and reaching upper-novice/intermediate maximizes risk abatement and function. A and D are defeatist and contradict the function-over-disease argument. C is unrealistic (elite ~ a decade, ~1% of people). E is misleading — although untrained people lose less in absolute terms, small losses are catastrophic for them and waiting lowers the attainable ceiling.

Scenario 4. You coach an intermediate 50-year-old who already moves well and has low disease risk. He asks why he should keep pushing his fitness when his health markers are fine. What is the most accurate, article-aligned answer?

  1. A. There's no further benefit past intermediate, so he should just maintain.
  2. B. Pushing higher will keep dramatically lowering his risk of death.
  3. C. Beyond intermediate, additional fitness adds little further reduction in mortality risk, but it continues to raise real-world function and quality of life — that's the reason to keep progressing.
  4. D. Higher fitness only matters for competition, not for everyday life.
  5. E. He should stop training hard because elite-level decay with age is steeper and therefore counterproductive.
Show answer

Answer: C — C reflects the diminishing-mortality-returns-but-rising-function point (2.3.1, 2.3.4, 5.1.1): mortality risk changes little from intermediate to elite, yet function and quality of life keep improving. A ignores the function gains. B overstates the mortality benefit past intermediate. D contradicts the article's emphasis on out-of-gym function. E misuses Figure 3 — steeper elite decay still leaves elite older athletes more functional than less-trained peers.

Scenario 5. A discouraged 70-year-old says she'll 'never be as fit as the young athletes,' and wants to quit. Which statement best uses the article to keep her engaged while staying honest?

  1. A. Tell her she's right and suggest a gentler hobby.
  2. B. Promise she'll match the 25-year-olds if she trains hard enough.
  3. C. Explain that a highly trained older athlete out-functions a less-trained younger one — an intermediate 70-year-old functions about like a physically active 30-year-old — so continued training preserves function, independence and quality of life even though youthful PRs aren't the target.
  4. D. Tell her age doesn't affect fitness at all, so any gap is just lack of effort.
  5. E. Advise her that since mobility's link to longevity is unproven, balance and range-of-motion work are a waste of time.
Show answer

Answer: C — C uses the cross-age comparison and function-over-numbers framing honestly (5.1.1, 1.2.3, 2.3.4): training keeps an older athlete more functional than less-trained younger people. A gives up on the athlete. B is a false, unsafe promise. D denies real age-related decline, undermining credibility. E misreads the article — the author notes mobility's mortality link is uncertain but still values mobility for quality of life, and balance/ROM remain important for an aging athlete.

Scenario 6. When setting realistic timelines and progression goals for a brand-new untrained 40-year-old, which expectation is most consistent with the article?

  1. A. He can reach elite fitness within about a year with hard training.
  2. B. Moving from untrained to novice can take a few months and to intermediate about two years; advanced is ~4-5 years and elite typically about a decade, so set near-term goals around novice-to-intermediate progress.
  3. C. Progression timelines are identical for everyone regardless of starting point, so plan one fixed schedule.
  4. D. He should expect no measurable progress in the first two years.
  5. E. Because he's 40, he should be held to the standard 30-year-old benchmark to stay competitive.
Show answer

Answer: B — B matches the article's stated timelines and supports honest readiness/goal-setting (1.2.5, 1.2.3, 2.3.1). A compresses a decade-long path into a year. C ignores that timelines depend on training level and individual factors. D contradicts the rapid early gains (untrained-to-novice in months). E reapplies a younger standard to an older athlete, the exact error the article warns against.

CFJ_Amundson_Goals.pdf

Open the PDF on Google Drive →

Why this is on the reading list

This article is the CCFT reading list's primary source on goal setting and the psychological/mental side of coaching, which Domain 1 tests under 'Identify athlete's fitness goals' and 'Assess psychological tolerance for training,' and which Domain 5 tests under 'Provide athletes with goal setting.' Amundson operationalizes how a coach helps an athlete define a goal (specific, positive tense, realistic-yet-challenging time frame), break it into milestones, and shape self-talk through positive reinforcement before, during, and after a workout. The exam will not ask you to recite his definition; it will hand you a coaching situation and ask which goal-setting or self-talk move best serves the athlete.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 1.2.3 Identify athlete's fitness goals
  • 1.1.4 Assess psychological tolerance for training
  • 1.2.5 Identify when athlete is ready to progress to another goal/skill
  • 1.2.6 Quantify and track performance
  • 5.1.1 Provide athletes with goal setting
  • 5.1.3 Establish rapport and adapt approach based on athlete response
  • 5.1.2 Create a culture/community of excellence and camaraderie
  • 4.2.1 Communicate cues to correct unsound mechanics
  • 4.2.3 Utilize effective cues (short, specific, actionable)
  • 4.2.8 Balance relentlessness with acknowledgement of improvement

What to focus on while reading

  • The article's working definition of a goal: 'a specifically desired end state, expressed in the positive tense, which provides motivation and direction on the path to achievement' — note all three load-bearing parts (end state, positive tense, motivation/direction).
  • The three 'points of performance' for a goal: (1) concise and specific, (2) expressed in the positive tense, (3) time frame that is challenging yet realistic and achievable. Be able to recognize each one in a scenario and spot which is missing.
  • Why 'specific' matters operationally: it enables precise planning/preparation/training AND lets the coach evaluate with precision when the goal has been met (links goal setting to measurement/tracking).
  • The example contrast for specificity: 'I want to complete 50 gymnastic kipping pull-ups in a single set' (good) vs. a vague aspiration.
  • The positive-tense example pair: 'I want to safely perform a backwards roll to support on the rings' vs. 'I don't want to fall off the rings while upside down.'
  • Amundson's claim about the subconscious: it does not process the negative tense, so stating what you DON'T want creates 'a blueprint for exactly what you intend to avoid.' Understand this as the rationale, not as a neuroscience fact to defend.
  • The time-frame balance: too far out = no urgency, no 'internal fire'; too short = discouragement and despair. The coach weighs motivation/challenge against high likelihood of success.
  • The self-assessment step that sets the time frame: ask the athlete their CURRENT baseline (e.g., 'how many consecutive pull-ups can you do right now?'). If they don't know, 'we need to find out immediately!' — baseline testing precedes time-framing.
  • The 5-vs-45 pull-up illustration: the same end goal (50) demands very different time frames and plans depending on the starting point.
  • The emphasis on the word ACHIEVE — the coach's job is helping athletes arrive at the end state, which builds a transferable pattern of success and creates lifelong clients and a referral base.
  • The milestone/mini-goal strategy: the 5-pull-up athlete chasing 50 hits 10, 15, 20 along the way; each increment is a 'mini-triumph' that reaffirms ability and builds confidence and motivation.
  • The three windows when an athlete is mentally/emotionally impressionable: (1) ~30 min before the workout up to '3-2-1...Go!', (2) DURING the workout (stated as perhaps most receptive), (3) after, depending on alertness and fatigue.
  • The 100-mile-run anecdote: the pace-runner's 'the next 50 miles will be the hardest yet' devastated him; his wife's 'you're gonna fly through these next few miles' instantly reversed his state. The lesson is the coach's unpredictable power over self-talk.
  • The parallel between movement cues and reinforcement: a coach should time and articulate positive reinforcement with the same skill used for cues like 'Drive through the heels!'
  • The positive-tense recue examples: 'Maintain your lumbar curve' instead of 'You're rounding your back'; 'Drive two inches deeper into the squat' instead of 'You missed the bottom.' Connect goal-setting language to actual movement coaching.
  • John Hackleman / Chuck Liddell example of 'scripting' an athlete's self-talk: 'You look strong, I'm proud of you,' never 'You're not tired' (which plants 'I'm tired').
  • The 'Five Coaching Tips' sidebar: (1) record goals + target date on a whiteboard section and in a personal journal, (2) encourage PUBLIC goal setting for trust and accountability, (3) ask athletes what they're working toward and teach them to formulate a goal, (4) publicly acknowledge achieved goals (whiteboard/website/newsletter), (5) listen to athletes' self-descriptive words and politely correct negative self-talk.
  • The framing that teaching goal setting and self-talk is 'just as important as instilling virtuosity in the foundational movements' — i.e., a core coaching responsibility, not a soft extra.

Concepts to understand

  • A well-formed goal has three required properties and a scenario can be diagnosed by which property is absent: vague vs. specific, negative vs. positive tense, no/poor time frame vs. challenging-yet-achievable time frame.
  • Specificity serves two functions a coach must both deliver: it sharpens planning AND it makes the goal measurable so completion can be objectively confirmed (ties goal setting to quantifying/tracking performance).
  • Positive-tense framing applies in two places: (a) when writing/stating the goal itself, and (b) in real-time movement cueing and reinforcement — the coach reframes a fault as the desired end state ('maintain lumbar curve,' 'drive two inches deeper') rather than naming the error.
  • Setting the time frame is an individualized, baseline-driven decision: the coach must learn the athlete's current capacity first; if unknown, test it before committing to a timeline (links to assessing capacity and quantifying performance).
  • Goal time frames are a risk/motivation balance: pick a horizon that creates urgency and challenge while preserving a high likelihood of success — too far kills urgency, too short breeds discouragement.
  • Breaking a large goal into progressive milestones is the mechanism that sustains motivation and confidence; each milestone is also a natural checkpoint for recognizing readiness to progress (1.2.5).
  • The coach materially shapes the athlete's self-talk; reinforcement is never neutral — even well-intentioned comments can be internalized negatively, so word choice and timing are a coaching skill on par with cueing.
  • There are specific high-leverage windows (pre-WOD, during, post-WOD) when athletes are most impressionable; a coach should deliberately deliver positive reinforcement in those windows, with 'during' called out as especially receptive.
  • Public goal setting and public recognition build accountability, trust, and community — connecting individual goal setting to gym culture and camaraderie (5.1.2).
  • Written and visible goals (whiteboard, journal) create a stronger athlete-goal connection than goals kept only in the head; documentation is part of the goal-setting practice and supports tracking.
  • Listening to how athletes describe themselves is a diagnostic for inner self-talk and psychological state; politely redirecting negative self-talk is part of assessing and supporting psychological tolerance for training (1.1.4).
  • Helping an athlete repeatedly set and ACHIEVE goals builds a transferable success pattern and drives retention/referrals — goal setting is both an athlete-development tool and a business/community asset.
  • Mental adaptation ('the greatest adaptation takes place between the ears') is treated as a trainable modality deserving the same diligence as physical training — relevant to assessing psychological readiness and tolerance, not just motivation.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenario items where an athlete states a vague, negative, or un-timed goal and you must choose the coach's best next move — most often: get a specific, positive-tense statement and establish the current baseline before setting a realistic time frame (1.2.3, 1.2.6). Other items will test self-talk and reinforcement judgment: choosing a positive-tense recue over naming a fault (4.2.1, 4.2.3), redirecting an athlete's negative self-talk (1.1.4, 5.1.3), or using milestones and public recognition to sustain motivation and build community (5.1.1, 5.1.2, 4.2.8). A common trap will be answers that sound supportive but are vague, negatively framed, or skip the baseline-assessment step.

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Goal (Amundson's definition)
A specifically desired end state, expressed in the positive tense, that provides motivation and direction on the path to achievement. Used here as a coaching tool, not a dictionary entry.
Points of performance (of a goal)
The three criteria a sound goal must meet: it is concise and specific, it is stated in the positive tense, and it has a time frame that is challenging yet realistic and achievable.
Positive tense
Phrasing a goal or cue in terms of the desired outcome to move toward ('maintain your lumbar curve') rather than the error or outcome to avoid ('don't round your back').
Self-talk
The internal dialogue an athlete runs about themselves and their performance; the article argues a coach's words directly shape it at conscious and subconscious levels.
Positive reinforcement
Deliberate, specific, encouraging communication from the coach—timed to impressionable moments before, during, and after a workout—intended to steer the athlete's self-talk toward productive content.
Milestone / mini-goal (incremental goal)
A smaller, nearer-term target on the path to a larger goal (e.g., 10, 15, 20 pull-ups en route to 50); each achievement reaffirms ability and sustains motivation.
Time frame
The deadline attached to a goal, set by balancing challenge and urgency against a high likelihood of success, and individualized to the athlete's current baseline.
Baseline / current capacity
The athlete's present performance level (e.g., consecutive pull-ups achievable now), which must be known—or tested immediately—before a realistic time frame can be set.
Public goal setting
Communicating goals to the coach and fellow athletes to create trust and accountability, reinforced by public recognition when goals are met.
Scripting self-talk
John Hackleman's practice of feeding an athlete specific positive statements ('You look strong; your punching is powerful') so their internal dialogue stays productive, deliberately avoiding negatively framed lines like 'You're not tired.'
Indomitable spirit
The resilient, optimistic mindset Amundson says coach and athlete forge together through goal setting and positive self-talk—'what the mind can believe the body can achieve.'
Firebreather
Informal CrossFit term for a top-performing, high-output athlete; Amundson is referred to as the 'original CrossFit firebreather.'

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • This article is motivational/psychological coaching, not medical screening. The mental 'toughness' framing must never override genuine signs of overexertion, injury, or distress—pushing an athlete who is at real risk is a safety failure regardless of positive self-talk.
  • Psychological tolerance assessment (1.1.4) has limits: persistent negative self-talk, signs of disordered thinking, or psychological distress beyond ordinary training nerves fall outside CCFT scope of practice and warrant referral, not amateur counseling.
  • Do not let 'mind over body' encouragement become a reason to ignore mechanical faults or fatigue warning signs; positive reinforcement supplements—never replaces—sound mechanics, scaling, and risk management.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. A new member tells you, 'My goal is to not be so bad at gymnastics.' What is the best coaching response under sound goal-setting practice?

  1. A. Accept it as stated and program more gymnastics volume right away.
  2. B. Help her restate it as a specific, positive-tense goal (e.g., 'perform 5 strict pull-ups'), then check her current baseline to set a realistic time frame.
  3. C. Tell her to stop being negative and just work harder in class.
  4. D. Set an ambitious public goal of a muscle-up in 30 days to create urgency.
  5. E. Wait several months until she is fitter before discussing any goal.
Show answer

Answer: B — The stated goal is vague and negatively framed. Best practice is to make it specific and positive, then establish the athlete's current capacity before assigning a challenging-yet-achievable time frame. A leaves it unmeasurable; C dismisses rather than redirects; D ignores baseline and likelihood of success; E needlessly delays the motivating practice of goal setting.

Scenario 2. Mid-WOD, an athlete's lumbar spine is rounding under a moderate deadlift load. Consistent with the article's approach to language, which cue is best?

  1. A. 'Don't round your back!'
  2. B. 'You're going to hurt yourself if you keep doing that.'
  3. C. 'Maintain your lumbar curve.'
  4. D. 'Stop—you missed the position.'
  5. E. 'Why do you always round your back?'
Show answer

Answer: C — Amundson advocates cueing the desired end state in the positive tense; 'maintain your lumbar curve' tells the athlete what to do. A and D name the fault negatively, B is fear-based and unspecific, and E is negative and unproductive. (Note: if the fault were severe enough to be unsafe, you would also reduce load or stop—positive language does not override risk management.)

Scenario 3. An athlete sets a goal of 50 consecutive pull-ups in three months but, when asked, says he isn't sure how many he can do right now. What should you do first?

  1. A. Lock in the three-month time frame since it sounds motivating.
  2. B. Tell him 50 is unrealistic and pick a different goal for him.
  3. C. Test his current consecutive pull-up capacity immediately, then set the time frame based on that baseline.
  4. D. Halve the goal to 25 to be safe.
  5. E. Assign daily max-effort pull-up sets until he can do 50.
Show answer

Answer: C — The article states that if the athlete doesn't know his baseline, 'we need to find out immediately,' because the right time frame for a 5-pull-up athlete differs greatly from a 45-pull-up athlete. A sets a time frame without data; B and D override the athlete's goal without justification; E is unscaled and risks overtraining/injury.

Scenario 4. Which approach best sustains a beginner's motivation while she works toward a distant goal of 50 pull-ups?

  1. A. Keep all focus on the final 50-rep target so she never loses sight of it.
  2. B. Break the path into milestones (10, then 15, then 20) and celebrate each as a mini-triumph.
  3. C. Avoid mentioning progress so she doesn't get complacent.
  4. D. Compare her weekly to the gym's strongest athletes to push her.
  5. E. Only acknowledge the goal once she reaches the full 50.
Show answer

Answer: B — Amundson's milestone strategy turns small increments into confidence-building wins that reaffirm the athlete's ability and maintain motivation. A is demotivating over a long horizon; C and E remove the reinforcement that drives persistence; D risks discouragement through unfavorable comparison.

Scenario 5. Per the article, when is an athlete generally MOST receptive to a coach's words, making reinforcement especially impactful?

  1. A. Only in a one-on-one meeting after class.
  2. B. During the workout itself.
  3. C. Only before the workout, prior to '3-2-1...Go!'
  4. D. Only by written feedback emailed later.
  5. E. Athletes are equally receptive at all times, so timing is irrelevant.
Show answer

Answer: B — Amundson identifies three impressionable windows—before, during, and after—and notes the athlete is 'perhaps... most receptive' DURING the workout. C and A capture only one window each; D is not discussed as a key window; E contradicts the article's point that timing of reinforcement matters greatly.

Scenario 6. An athlete keeps muttering 'I'm terrible at this, I'll never get it' during skill work. Which response best fits the article's guidance and stays within scope?

  1. A. Ignore it—self-talk is the athlete's private business.
  2. B. Politely redirect the negative self-talk toward positive, specific language and reinforce what she is doing well.
  3. C. Tell her she's right and should drop the skill.
  4. D. Refer her to a sports psychologist immediately as a first step.
  5. E. Match her energy by joking that the movement is impossible anyway.
Show answer

Answer: B — The article's fifth coaching tip is to listen for negative self-descriptions—which reflect inner self-talk—and politely correct them toward positive dialogue while reinforcing progress. A neglects a coachable moment; C reinforces the negative belief; D over-escalates for ordinary frustration (referral is for distress beyond normal training nerves); E undermines her further.

Scenario 7. You want to strengthen accountability and community around members' goals. Which practice best reflects the article's 'Five Coaching Tips'?

  1. A. Keep each member's goals confidential between you and them only.
  2. B. Encourage public goal setting and publicly acknowledge achievements on the whiteboard, website, or newsletter.
  3. C. Post only the goals members fail to hit so they feel pressure.
  4. D. Set identical goals for the whole class to keep things simple.
  5. E. Discourage journaling so members rely on you to remember their goals.
Show answer

Answer: B — Amundson recommends public goal setting (building trust and accountability) and public recognition of met goals, plus written goals on a whiteboard and in personal journals. A removes the accountability/community benefit; C is punitive and demoralizing; D ignores individualization; E contradicts the recommendation to have athletes write their goals.

Scenario 8. Which athlete-stated goal best satisfies all three of Amundson's points of performance?

  1. A. 'I don't want to fail the rope climb anymore.'
  2. B. 'I want to get better at everything someday.'
  3. C. 'I want to perform 10 unbroken kipping pull-ups within eight weeks.'
  4. D. 'I want to not have a bad squat.'
  5. E. 'I want to be elite as fast as humanly possible.'
Show answer

Answer: C — Option C is specific (10 unbroken kipping pull-ups), positive tense (perform, not 'don't fail'), and has a challenging-yet-realistic time frame (eight weeks). A and D are negatively framed; B lacks specificity and a real time frame; E is vague and sets an unrealistic, undefined horizon.

D1 · Screening & Ongoing Assessment 8% of exam Confidence tier: ___

CFJ_Log_Harrison.pdf

Open the PDF on Google Drive →

Why this is on the reading list

This article makes the case that a purposeful training log is a coach's primary instrument for quantifying performance, tracking progress over time, and reconstructing the chain of stressors that precedes a chronic injury. It backs Domain 1 most directly — quantifying/tracking performance (1.2.6), monitoring for over-/under-training and injury warning signs (1.2.4), benchmarking work capacity (1.2.2), goal identification and progression (1.2.3, 1.2.5), and using logged history to flag injury risk for referral (1.1.2). The reading also reinforces benchmark-based program evaluation (Domain 2) and goal-setting/accountability leadership (Domain 5). For a CCFT candidate, the takeaway is not the author's specific journal product but the coaching habit of capturing objective, longitudinal data and acting on it.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 1.2.6 Quantify and track performance
  • 1.2.2 Evaluate athlete's work capacity
  • 1.2.3 Identify athlete's fitness goals
  • 1.2.4 Monitor athlete for signs of over- or under-training
  • 1.2.5 Identify when athlete is ready to progress to another goal/skill
  • 1.1.2 Recognize conditions/injuries outside CCFT Scope of Practice that require referral (risk factors)
  • 2.3.2 Use benchmarks to assess effectiveness of programming
  • 2.3.3 Adjust programming based on performance and goals
  • 2.3.4 Evaluate athlete progress relative to CrossFit's definition of fitness and their personal goal
  • 5.1.1 Provide athletes with goal setting
  • 7.1.1 Self-assess sessions according to the foundations of effective training

What to focus on while reading

  • The six-plus stated reasons to keep a log and which coaching task each maps to: Injury Diagnosis & Treatment (1.1.2, 1.2.4), Setting PRs (1.2.6, 2.3.3), Celebrating Success (1.2.6, 5.1), Goal Setting (1.2.3, 5.1.1), Planning (programming/lesson logistics), Accountability (5.1), Benchmarking (1.2.2, 2.3.2), Nostalgia (motivation).
  • The distinction between ACUTE injuries (obvious cause) and CHRONIC injuries (accumulation of many stressors over time, hardest to diagnose and recover from) — and why a log is most valuable for the chronic kind.
  • The specific data fields the author recommends logging beyond WOD time: training volume, weekly volume, strength vs. met-con balance, time domains, time of day trained, mobility/stretching practice, recovery/rest days, eating-habit ratings, sleep, and how a movement felt before/during/after.
  • The 'quick tip' to jot a note any time anything hurt or didn't feel right before, during, or after training — 'no matter how insignificant it might feel at the time.' This is the injury-clue / warning-sign behavior.
  • The idea of isolating variables: with many inputs affecting performance, the log lets you isolate what conditions produced a PR so you can replicate them — a controlled, data-driven approach to programming adjustments.
  • Benchmarking protocol: pick a measure for each of the 10 General Physical Skills, record an initial benchmark, schedule quarterly re-tests, and track all results on one page — this is objective, scheduled re-assessment of fitness over time.
  • Goal-setting mechanics: specific, measurable, with a target date (the deadlift-plus-50-lb-by-Aug-31 example); a dedicated goals page reviewed frequently; scheduled 3/6/9/12-month reviews to 'close the loop' and ensure accountability.
  • The Ben Smith anecdote: writing goals down makes them real and increases probability of achieving them — work ethic AND the written goal together. Note this is motivation/adherence, not a guarantee.
  • The 'at-a-glance' monthly-or-longer planning page (days on/off, strength vs. met-con, time domains) as a high-level programming/planning view.
  • Planning uses: scheduling training and recovery days in advance, scheduling 'goat work'/skill sessions with specifics, and protecting training time from competing demands.
  • The line 'constantly varied does not mean random' (photo caption) — the log supports purposeful, planned variance rather than chaos.
  • Accountability framing: the affiliate (coach + community) is the strongest accountability; a log is a partial substitute for athletes without affiliate access — note the author does NOT claim the log replaces coaching.
  • Author's honest framing in 'What Now?': start small (just write something down), build the habit, then add variables (warm-ups, mobility, skill work); the value of the data is personal and individual.
  • What the article does NOT claim: it offers no clinical diagnostic procedure, no rhabdo screening protocol, no medical thresholds — it is about the coaching HABIT of data capture, not medical assessment.

Concepts to understand

  • A training log is the coach's tool for quantifying and tracking performance objectively over time — turning subjective impressions ('I think I'm getting stronger') into longitudinal evidence you can act on (1.2.6).
  • Chronic injuries accumulate from many stressors over time and are the hardest to diagnose; a detailed log reconstructs that stressor history (volume spikes, new loads, movements that nagged) so a coach can spot risk and a clinician can diagnose — understand this as an EARLY-WARNING and REFERRAL-support function, not as the coach diagnosing (1.1.2, 1.2.4).
  • Logging how a movement felt before/during/after training surfaces small warning signs early; an experienced coach treats a recurring 'didn't feel right' note as a trigger to scale, deload, or refer — not to push through (1.2.4, 1.1.2).
  • Performance has many inputs (volume, recovery, nutrition, sleep, time of day, mobility). The log lets you isolate which conditions coincided with PRs so you can deliberately replicate them — this is the logic behind data-driven programming adjustments (2.3.3, 1.2.6).
  • Benchmarking against the 10 General Physical Skills with scheduled quarterly re-tests gives an objective, repeatable evaluation of work capacity and fitness over time — the same logic CrossFit uses to evaluate programming effectiveness (1.2.2, 2.3.2, 2.3.4).
  • Effective goals are specific, measurable, and time-bound, with scheduled review checkpoints to close the loop — the coach's role is to help the athlete set and revisit these, which drives both progression decisions and adherence (1.2.3, 1.2.5, 5.1.1).
  • Writing goals down and reviewing them frequently increases follow-through; this is a motivation/accountability mechanism (work ethic + written goal together), useful for athletes who lack affiliate-level accountability (5.1.1, 5.1.2).
  • A log doubles as a planning tool: scheduling training, recovery, and skill/'goat' days in advance enforces purposeful variance ('constantly varied is not random') and protects training time — supporting deliberate program design over random workouts (2.1, 5.2.4).
  • Celebrating logged progress (the 100-lb-to-185-lb back-squat example) sustains long-term motivation by making real, relative progress visible — relevant to keeping athletes engaged and progressing (5.1).
  • Self-assessment for the coach: the same disciplined recording habit underlies a coach reviewing their own sessions and decisions against the foundations of effective training (7.1.1).
  • Scope awareness: a log informs and supports medical diagnosis but does not replace it — the coach gathers and hands off data, the clinician diagnoses and treats (1.1.2, scope of practice).

How the exam applies this

Expect scenario items where an athlete reports a vague recurring ache, a stalled or sudden drop in performance, or a desire to set/progress goals, and you must choose the coach action that uses objective logged data — reviewing training history, flagging a stressor pattern, scheduling a benchmark re-test, or referring out when notes suggest a developing injury (1.1.2, 1.2.4, 1.2.6). Other items will frame the log as a programming-evaluation tool (re-test the benchmark, compare to baseline, adjust load/volume per the data — 2.3.2, 2.3.3) or as a goal-setting/accountability tool (help the athlete write a specific, time-bound goal and schedule reviews — 1.2.3, 5.1.1). The exam rewards the answer that gathers and acts on data and respects scope, over answers that guess, push through pain, or diagnose.

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Training log
A purposeful, ongoing record of workout details and surrounding variables (loads, times, volume, recovery, nutrition, how movements felt) kept to provide historical data a coach and athlete can analyze and act on — not just a list of WOD times.
Acute injury
An injury with a clear, single, immediate cause (e.g., a sudden strain), so the cause is rarely in doubt.
Chronic injury
An injury that develops gradually from the accumulation of many stressors over time; hardest to diagnose and slowest to recover from, which is exactly why a detailed log is valuable for reconstructing its cause.
Training volume
The total amount of work performed (e.g., sets, reps, load, and frequency), often tracked weekly; spikes in volume are a common precursor to overuse/chronic injury and are worth logging.
PR (personal record)
An athlete's best performance on a movement or workout; the log helps isolate the conditions that produced a PR so they can be replicated.
Benchmark
A fixed, repeatable measure of fitness recorded as a baseline and re-tested on a schedule (the author suggests quarterly) to objectively evaluate change over time.
10 General Physical Skills
CrossFit's ten components of fitness (cardiovascular/respiratory endurance, stamina, strength, flexibility, power, speed, coordination, agility, balance, accuracy); the article recommends selecting a measurable benchmark for each.
Goat
An athlete's weak movement or skill that needs dedicated, deliberate practice; the article recommends scheduling 'goat work' sessions in advance with specific prescriptions.
Met-con (metabolic conditioning)
Conditioning-style work emphasizing metabolic demand; tracked alongside strength work in a high-level 'at a glance' plan to balance training emphasis.
Time domain
The duration/energy-system window a workout targets (short/medium/long); logging time domains helps ensure varied, balanced programming.
Constantly varied (not random)
A core CrossFit programming principle that variance is intentional and planned, not haphazard; the log supports purposeful planning of that variance.
Accountability
The external pressure to follow through; strongest from an affiliate (coach + community), with a log serving as a partial substitute for athletes who train without that support.
Closing the loop
Returning to written goals on a scheduled cadence (3/6/9/12 months) to review progress, judge success, and reset — turning goal-setting into an accountable cycle.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • A logged note that a movement 'hurt' or 'didn't feel right' — recurring or worsening — is a warning sign: scale or deload, investigate the root cause, and refer to a medical professional if it persists or escalates. Do not coach the athlete to push through (1.1.2, 1.2.4).
  • A clear pattern of rising training volume/load in the log preceding pain or performance decline points to overuse/over-training; act on it by adjusting programming, not ignoring it (1.2.4, 2.3.3).
  • Scope of practice: the log SUPPORTS medical diagnosis but the coach does not diagnose or treat injuries — hand the history to a physician/therapist and stay in the coaching lane (1.1.2).
  • A log/journal product is a tool, not a guarantee of safety or results, and it does not replace a coach's in-person observation, medical screening (e.g., health questionnaire), informed consent, or an Emergency Action Plan.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. A long-time member tells you her right knee has 'felt off' for several weeks but isn't sharply painful. She keeps a detailed training log. What is the best coach action?

  1. A. Tell her it's minor and to push through the next few WODs to test it
  2. B. Review her log with her for recent spikes in volume, new loads, or movements she noted bothered the knee, scale accordingly, and refer her to a medical professional if it persists or worsens
  3. C. Diagnose it as patellar tendinitis based on the description and prescribe a rehab protocol
  4. D. Program around it indefinitely without further follow-up and say nothing about a referral
  5. E. Stop all of her training until the knee is completely pain-free
Show answer

Answer: B — The log's diagnostic value is reconstructing the stressor history of a chronic, gradually developing complaint; the coach uses it to spot a pattern, scale, and refer — staying in scope (1.1.2, 1.2.4). A pushes through pain (unsafe). C diagnoses and prescribes rehab, which is outside the coach's scope. D ignores the warning sign and the referral duty. E is an overreaction that abandons the athlete rather than managing the issue with data and referral.

Scenario 2. An athlete wants to 'get stronger' but has no concrete target. Using the article's approach, what should you help him set up?

  1. A. A vague intention to 'lift more often' with no metric or date
  2. B. A specific, measurable, time-bound goal (e.g., 'add 50 lb to deadlift by Aug 31'), recorded on a dedicated goals page with scheduled review checkpoints
  3. C. A promise to attend more classes, tracked only in his memory
  4. D. A single max-effort test today with no follow-up plan
  5. E. A goal to simply 'beat the other members' on the whiteboard
Show answer

Answer: B — The article defines effective goals as specific, measurable, and time-bound, written down and reviewed on a schedule to close the loop (1.2.3, 5.1.1). A and C lack any measurable target or accountability cadence. D captures a baseline but provides no goal or progression plan. E is competitive comparison rather than an individualized, trackable goal.

Scenario 3. You want an objective way to judge whether your athlete's fitness is actually improving over a year, independent of how any single WOD feels. Which approach best fits the article?

  1. A. Ask the athlete each month whether they feel fitter
  2. B. Select a measurable benchmark for each of the 10 General Physical Skills, record an initial baseline, and schedule quarterly re-tests tracked on one page
  3. C. Compare the athlete's WOD times to the box's top performers
  4. D. Re-test only when the athlete asks to
  5. E. Rely on body-weight changes alone as the fitness measure
Show answer

Answer: B — The article's benchmarking protocol — a measure per General Physical Skill, an initial benchmark, and scheduled quarterly re-tests — gives objective, repeatable evaluation of fitness/work capacity over time (1.2.2, 2.3.2, 2.3.4). A is subjective. C compares against others rather than the athlete's own trajectory. D and E are unscheduled or too narrow to evaluate broad fitness.

Scenario 4. An athlete recently hit several PRs and asks how to 'keep the magic going.' How does the article suggest the log helps?

  1. A. It guarantees continued PRs if she trains harder
  2. B. It lets her isolate the conditions that coincided with the PRs — volume, recovery, nutrition, sleep, time of day — so those conditions can be deliberately replicated
  3. C. It proves which single exercise caused all the gains
  4. D. It replaces the need for any coaching or programming going forward
  5. E. It tells her exactly how much she will lift next month
Show answer

Answer: B — With many variables affecting performance, the log's value is isolating which conditions accompanied success so they can be replicated and programming adjusted accordingly (1.2.6, 2.3.3). A and E overclaim certainty the article explicitly avoids. C oversimplifies multifactorial progress to one cause. D contradicts the article, which positions the log as a supplement to, not a replacement for, coaching.

Scenario 5. A remote/virtual athlete without access to an affiliate struggles to stay consistent. Per the article, what is the most accurate framing of how a training log helps?

  1. A. The log fully replaces a coach and community for accountability
  2. B. The log provides a partial measure of accountability and planning structure, though affiliate membership (coach plus community) remains the stronger source
  3. C. Accountability doesn't matter as long as the athlete is motivated
  4. D. The athlete should stop training until they can join an affiliate
  5. E. Only competition can create real accountability
Show answer

Answer: B — The article calls affiliate membership the most notable accountability source and presents the log as a partial substitute for those who lack it — not a full replacement (5.1.1, 5.1.2). A overstates the log's role. C dismisses accountability the article emphasizes. D and E are not supported and ignore the practical value of self-logging for a virtual athlete.

Scenario 6. When planning a member's week, an athlete says 'constantly varied means I should just do something random every day.' Using the article's planning section, how should you respond?

  1. A. Agree — randomness is the point of CrossFit
  2. B. Clarify that constantly varied is not random; use the log to schedule training, recovery, and skill/'goat' days in advance so variance is purposeful and recovery is protected
  3. C. Tell him planning is unnecessary because variety handles everything
  4. D. Have him max out on a different lift daily with no rest days
  5. E. Tell him to copy whatever the most advanced member does each day
Show answer

Answer: B — The article explicitly states 'constantly varied does not mean random' and recommends using the log to plan training, recovery, and skill/goat sessions in advance — purposeful variance with protected recovery (planning supports 2.1 and 5.2.4). A, C, and D conflate variance with chaos and omit recovery, raising overtraining/injury risk. E substitutes imitation for individualized planning.

Scenario 7. Which statement best captures the limit of what a training log can do, consistent with CCFT scope of practice?

  1. A. The log lets a coach diagnose and treat chronic injuries without involving a clinician
  2. B. The log supplies detailed history that supports a physician's or therapist's diagnosis, but the coach gathers and refers — they do not diagnose or treat
  3. C. The log makes medical screening, informed consent, and an Emergency Action Plan unnecessary
  4. D. The log guarantees an athlete will avoid injury if kept consistently
  5. E. The log is only useful for elite athletes chasing the Games leaderboard
Show answer

Answer: B — The article frames the log as making diagnosis and recovery easier by providing history ('how much more helpful... than “my knee hurts”'), which supports the clinician — the coach stays in scope by gathering and referring (1.1.2). A and D overstate the log into diagnosis/guarantee. C wrongly treats the log as a substitute for screening, consent, and an EAP. E contradicts the article's point that the log benefits every athlete, including the non-elite celebrating relative progress.

D1 · Screening & Ongoing Assessment 8% of exam Confidence tier: ___

CFJ_Pregnant_Perkins.pdf

Open the PDF on Google Drive →

Why this is on the reading list

This article is on the CCFT reading list because pregnant athletes are a named special population the exam expects a trainer to screen, scale, and monitor competently. It backs Domain 1's readiness-screening and referral concepts and connects directly to Domain 2's special-population scaling: the trainer must recognize warning signs that require stopping or referral, understand which movements to modify as pregnancy progresses, and stay inside the CCFT Scope of Practice rather than acting as a medical authority. The piece reinforces that exercise (including resistance and functional training) is generally beneficial in pregnancy, but that individual readiness, medical clearance, and ongoing monitoring govern what a coach actually does.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 1.1.1 Screen athlete for medical issues (e.g., health questionnaire)
  • 1.1.2 Recognize conditions/injuries outside CCFT Scope of Practice that require referral (risk factors)
  • 1.1.4 Assess psychological tolerance for training
  • 1.2.4 Monitor athlete for signs of over- or under-training
  • 1.2.6 Quantify and track performance
  • 2.2.2 Scale for special populations (e.g., pregnant, adaptive)
  • 5.2.3 Manage risk for the athlete
  • 5.2.6 Recognize warning signs for possible injury or overexertion

What to focus on while reading

  • Table 3 — the explicit list of warning signs to STOP exercising during pregnancy (vaginal bleeding, dizziness, chest pain, calf pain or swelling, decreased fetal movement, dyspnea/shortness of breath, headache, muscle weakness, preterm labor, amniotic fluid leakage). Treat this as a referral/stop checklist a coach must act on.
  • The repeated cautionary framing: two healthy case studies do NOT prove CrossFit during pregnancy is advised for any pregnant woman — preliminary, encouraging, not sufficient evidence. Hunt for every place the authors hedge.
  • RPE (rating of perceived exertion) as the monitoring tool — the 6-20 scale, 'light' = 11-12, the CrossFit sample workout sat at ~15-18 ('hard' to 'very hard'). Note RPE is how intensity is quantified and tracked here.
  • The volume/intensity comparison (Table 4): the sample CrossFit WOD was ~3x the prescribed exercise volume and ~5x the prescribed intensity of standard pregnancy resistance-training guidelines — the gap between what guidelines prescribe and what these athletes did.
  • Specificity of training — the principle that programs should be built around the demands of the target 'event.' Note the authors' framing of pregnancy/labor/motherhood as an athletic event requiring functional strength and power, not just aerobic fitness.
  • Which movements got modified and WHEN, by trimester (Tables 5/6): sit-ups/GHD sit-ups (supine) early, push-ups/burpees/pull-ups scaled to box/band versions mid-pregnancy, running stopped in 3rd trimester. Note that neither woman modified the Olympic lifts and both set PRs in them.
  • Why supine (lying-on-back) exercises are generally not recommended in pregnancy, and the qualifier (short duration, well-informed athlete may do some) — footnote under Table 6.
  • Braxton Hicks contractions — what they are (relatively painless, pre-due-date), and the coaching response: stop the activity that appears to be causing them and consult a medical doctor. Note there is no consistent established link between specific exercises and Braxton Hicks.
  • The Valsalva maneuver definition (inhale, hold breath to brace and lift more) and that guidelines advise LIMITING it, plus limiting large pressor-effect and heavy/repetitive isometric work in pregnancy.
  • Environmental and self-management guidance for any pregnant exerciser: hydrate heavily, avoid hot/humid conditions, rise slowly after sitting/lying, and if feeling sick/hot or any warning sign appears — stop, sit, keep head above heart, seek medical attention for persistent illness or injury.
  • Postpartum return-to-training caution: experts advise caution in the first 4-6 weeks after delivery because pregnancy's physiological/morphological changes persist; the two subjects resumed at ~1.7 and ~2.7 weeks (faster than the cautious guidance).
  • ACOG's role — the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists is the cited medical authority for resistance-training guidelines in pregnancy; recognize that the medical guidance comes from physicians, not the trainer.
  • The two best predictors of newborn health named in the article: birth weight and gestational age (full term = 37-41 weeks). Note both babies were normal weight and full term.
  • The 1985 origin and conservative nature of early pregnancy-exercise guidelines, and how aerobic 'guidelines' evolved into stronger 'recommendations' over 25 years — context for why resistance/high-intensity guidance is still cautious.

Concepts to understand

  • Pregnancy is a special population that a CrossFit trainer scales FOR, not a contraindication to training — but the trainer's job is to screen, refer for medical clearance, monitor, and modify, never to medically clear the athlete or override a physician.
  • Stop-and-refer judgment: a coach must recognize the pregnancy-specific warning signs in Table 3 in real time and respond by stopping the athlete and directing her to medical care — this is risk management (5.2.3) and warning-sign recognition (5.2.6), not diagnosis.
  • Scope of practice: anything medical (clearing a pregnancy for high intensity, interpreting bleeding/contractions, deciding postpartum return timing) belongs to the physician/ACOG; the trainer applies their guidance and the athlete's clearance.
  • RPE as a monitoring and intensity-quantifying tool you can use with any athlete, especially when objective load isn't the constraint — understand 'light' (11-12) vs 'hard/very hard' (15-18) on the 6-20 scale and how to read it across a session and across weeks (1.2.6, 1.2.4).
  • Relative intensity / scaling for the individual: the pregnant athlete's appropriate intensity is relative to her, her training history, her trimester, and her physician's guidance — a well-trained athlete continuing her program differs from a novice starting one.
  • Trimester-progressive modification: scaling needs change as pregnancy advances (e.g., growing abdomen makes supine work, jumping, and high-impact movements problematic) — the coach adjusts the SAME stimulus to keep it safe and effective rather than removing training.
  • Specificity of training: design around the demands of the goal. For pregnancy/motherhood the relevant demands are functional strength and power (squatting, lifting, carrying a growing child, protecting the low back), not just aerobic capacity — this justifies functional, varied training over isolation 'toning.'
  • Functional movement carries over to motherhood: proper squat/deadlift/carry mechanics map onto lifting a baby, climbing stairs with a child, and loading car seats — coaching mechanics has a direct quality-of-life payoff for this population.
  • Evidence humility: the article is two case studies plus a small body of conservative studies; encouraging but not proof. Understand that a coach should not generalize 'these two were fine' into 'CrossFit is safe for every pregnant athlete' — individualize and defer to medical clearance.
  • Psychological tolerance and athlete autonomy: these were experienced, motivated athletes who chose to continue; assessing an athlete's training history, comfort, and willingness (1.1.4) is part of deciding how aggressively to program for a pregnant member.
  • Postpartum is still a special-population window: the body has not reverted at delivery, so return-to-training should be cautious and medically guided in the first 4-6 weeks regardless of how fit the athlete was.
  • Environmental risk amplifies in pregnancy: heat, dehydration, and rapid position changes raise risk; managing the training environment (hydration, temperature, pacing position changes) is part of managing risk for this athlete.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenario questions where a pregnant member presents a symptom or a coaching decision and you must choose the safe, in-scope action — recognizing a Table 3 warning sign and stopping/referring (1.1.2, 5.2.6), modifying a movement appropriately for her trimester (2.2.2), or declining to make a medical call that belongs to her physician (1.1.1, scope). Other items test monitoring judgment: reading RPE to gauge whether intensity is appropriate and tracking it across sessions (1.2.6, 1.2.4), and managing environmental/positional risk (5.2.3). The exam rewards the coach who individualizes, defers medical decisions, and modifies-rather-than-excludes, and who does not over-generalize two encouraging case studies into blanket advice.

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Specificity of training
The principle that a training program should be designed around the specific demands of the goal or 'event' (e.g., the strength, power, or energy systems it requires). For pregnancy/motherhood, that means functional strength and power, not aerobic work alone.
RPE (Rating of Perceived Exertion)
A subjective 6-20 scale an athlete uses to rate how hard effort feels. 'Light' is roughly 11-12; 'hard' to 'very hard' is roughly 15-18. Used here to quantify and monitor pregnancy training intensity when objective load isn't the limiting factor.
Valsalva maneuver
Inhaling and holding the breath to brace the trunk and exert more force during a lift. Pregnancy guidelines advise LIMITING it because of the pressor (blood-pressure) effect it produces.
Pressor effect
A rise in blood pressure produced by certain efforts (e.g., heavy isometrics, Valsalva). Pregnancy resistance-training guidance recommends limiting exercises that cause a large pressor effect.
ACOG
American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists — the medical body whose guidelines the article uses for resistance/aerobic exercise during pregnancy. The authoritative medical source the trainer defers to.
Braxton Hicks contractions
Relatively painless 'practice' contractions that can occur before the due date. Coaching response: stop the activity that appears to be triggering them and consult a physician; no consistent link to specific exercises is established.
Supine (position)
Lying on the back. Exercises performed supine are generally not recommended in pregnancy; some may be acceptable only briefly and for a well-informed athlete, due to physiological contraindications.
Gestational age
How far along a pregnancy is, measured in weeks. Full term is 37-41 weeks. With birth weight, it is one of the two best predictors of newborn health cited here.
Birth weight
The newborn's weight at delivery; with gestational age, one of the two best predictors of a newborn's health. Normal-weight, full-term deliveries in this article were the key safety outcome.
Apgar score
A quick newborn health assessment scored shortly after birth; one of the outcome measures tracked in pregnancy-exercise research summarized in the article.
Light resistance training
The conservative intensity (roughly RPE 11-12, ~3 kg, 1 set of 8-12 reps, HR <140 bpm in older studies) used in most pregnancy resistance-training research — far below the intensity these CrossFit athletes trained at.
Exercise volume
Total work performed, here counted as total repetitions in a session. The sample CrossFit WOD (255 reps) was about three times the prescribed pregnancy resistance-training volume (80 reps).
Modification / scaling (in pregnancy)
Adjusting a movement to keep it safe and effective as pregnancy progresses (e.g., GHD sit-ups to AbMat, regular push-ups to box push-ups, pull-ups to banded pull-ups, dropping running in the 3rd trimester) rather than stopping training.
Postpartum
The period after delivery. Pregnancy's physiological and morphological changes persist into it, so medical experts advise caution returning to training in the first 4-6 weeks.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • Table 3 STOP-and-seek-care signs in a pregnant athlete: vaginal bleeding, dizziness, chest pain, calf pain or swelling, decreased fetal movement, dyspnea (shortness of breath), headache, muscle weakness, preterm labor, amniotic fluid leakage — any of these means stop, sit down (head above heart), and refer to medical care.
  • Braxton Hicks contractions during activity — stop the suspected activity and direct the athlete to consult her physician.
  • Interpreting any of these symptoms, clearing a pregnant athlete for high intensity, or deciding when she may return postpartum is OUTSIDE the trainer's scope — refer to and defer to her physician/ACOG guidance.
  • Supine (lying-on-back) exercises are generally contraindicated in pregnancy — avoid or strictly limit them.
  • Heavy/repetitive isometrics, large pressor-effect movements, and the Valsalva maneuver should be limited for pregnant athletes.
  • Postpartum return-to-training inside the first 4-6 weeks warrants caution and medical guidance, regardless of prior fitness.
  • Environmental risk: do not let a pregnant athlete train in hot/humid conditions or under-hydrated; watch for overheating and have her rise slowly after lying or sitting.
  • Do not generalize: two healthy outcomes are not evidence that high-intensity training is safe for every pregnant athlete — individualize and require medical clearance.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. A 3rd-trimester athlete with physician clearance is mid-WOD when she tells you she's noticed some vaginal bleeding but feels otherwise fine and wants to finish. What is the best coaching action?

  1. A. Let her finish since she feels fine, then suggest she mention it to her doctor later
  2. B. Scale the remaining movements to lower intensity and continue
  3. C. Stop her immediately, have her sit with her head above heart level, and direct her to seek medical attention
  4. D. Tell her bleeding is normal in late pregnancy and reassure her
  5. E. Substitute the Olympic lifts, which she has set PRs in, for the rest of the workout
Show answer

Answer: C — Vaginal bleeding is an explicit Table 3 warning sign to stop exercising and seek care; continuing (A, B, E) ignores a stop signal, and reassuring/interpreting it (D) is a medical judgment outside the trainer's scope. The in-scope action is to stop and refer.

Scenario 2. A well-trained CrossFit member is 18 weeks pregnant and cleared by her OB to keep training. She asks how to handle GHD sit-ups and push-ups, which are getting awkward. Which response best reflects the article's approach to scaling this population?

  1. A. Remove all core and pressing work for the rest of the pregnancy to be safe
  2. B. Keep everything as prescribed; modifying signals weakness
  3. C. Substitute AbMat sit-ups for GHD sit-ups and box/incline push-ups for floor push-ups, adjusting further as her belly grows
  4. D. Have her switch entirely to walking and swimming for the duration
  5. E. Tell her you can't advise her because pregnancy is outside your scope
Show answer

Answer: C — The case studies modified exactly this way (GHD to AbMat, regular to box push-ups) as pregnancy progressed — modify to keep training safe and effective rather than removing it (A, D) or refusing to scale (B). Scaling movements is squarely within a trainer's scope, so E is wrong; medical clearance has already been obtained.

Scenario 3. A pregnant member asks you point-blank: 'Is it safe for me to keep doing high-intensity CrossFit through my whole pregnancy? Those two women in the CrossFit Journal did great.' What is the most appropriate response?

  1. A. 'Yes — the evidence shows high-intensity CrossFit is safe for pregnant women.'
  2. B. 'Those are only two encouraging case studies, not proof for everyone. Let's follow your physician's clearance and guidance, scale as needed, and watch for warning signs.'
  3. C. 'No — pregnant women should only do light toning exercises.'
  4. D. 'It depends on your max lifts; if you're strong enough you'll be fine.'
  5. E. 'I can't talk about exercise and pregnancy at all.'
Show answer

Answer: B — The article explicitly cautions readers not to generalize two healthy outcomes into broad safety claims (rules out A) while noting exercise is generally beneficial and individualized (rules out C). Safety isn't a function of strength (D), and scaling/monitoring within physician guidance is in scope (rules out E).

Scenario 4. You're monitoring a pregnant athlete's training. Which approach best fits how the article quantifies and tracks appropriate intensity for this population?

  1. A. Require her to hit the same barbell loads she used before pregnancy every session
  2. B. Use only heart rate, capping every session at 140 bpm regardless of how she feels
  3. C. Use Rating of Perceived Exertion (RPE) to gauge effort and track it across sessions and trimesters, adjusting based on how she's responding
  4. D. Ignore intensity entirely as long as she finishes the workout
  5. E. Match her intensity to whatever the rest of the class is doing
Show answer

Answer: C — The article uses RPE (6-20 scale) as the tool to quantify and compare intensity, supporting ongoing monitoring (1.2.6, 1.2.4). A rigid load mandate (A) or class-matching (E) ignores her individual state; the 140-bpm figure was from older conservative studies, not a universal cap (B); and ignoring intensity (D) abandons monitoring.

Scenario 5. A pregnant athlete in her second trimester wants to do a workout with several sets of weighted sit-ups and bench-style pressing while lying on her back. What is the best programming adjustment?

  1. A. Program it as written; supine work is fine throughout pregnancy
  2. B. Avoid or strictly limit the supine (lying-on-back) work and substitute movements she can perform upright or inclined
  3. C. Allow it only if she uses the Valsalva maneuver to brace hard
  4. D. Replace the whole session with a max-effort deadlift test
  5. E. Cancel her session and send her home
Show answer

Answer: B — Supine exercises are generally not recommended in pregnancy (Table 6 footnote), so avoiding/limiting and substituting upright variations is correct. Programming it as written (A) ignores the contraindication; the Valsalva maneuver should be limited, not encouraged (C); a max-effort test (D) and sending her home (E) are both inappropriate overreactions/contradictions to sound scaling.

Scenario 6. Mid-session, a pregnant athlete reports she's started having mild, relatively painless contractions that seem to coincide with her box jumps. What should you do?

  1. A. Keep going — painless contractions are harmless and unrelated to exercise
  2. B. Diagnose them as Braxton Hicks and reassure her she's in no danger
  3. C. Stop the activity that appears to be causing them and advise her to consult her physician
  4. D. Increase intensity to 'push through' and see if they stop
  5. E. Tell her she is in preterm labor and call an ambulance immediately
Show answer

Answer: C — The article's guidance for the described contractions (consistent with Braxton Hicks) is to stop the suspected activity and consult a doctor. Continuing or escalating (A, D) ignores the signal; the trainer should not diagnose (B) or declare a medical emergency like preterm labor (E) — both are medical judgments. Stopping and referring is the in-scope action.

Scenario 7. A member who delivered her baby 10 days ago messages that she feels great and wants to jump back into full-intensity CrossFit tomorrow. Best response?

  1. A. 'Great — come in tomorrow and pick up right where you left off.'
  2. B. 'Let's be cautious in the first 4-6 weeks postpartum and follow your doctor's guidance before ramping intensity back up.'
  3. C. 'You should wait at least a full year before training again.'
  4. D. 'As long as you set a PR your first day back, you're recovered.'
  5. E. 'Postpartum isn't something I need to consider; pregnancy is over.'
Show answer

Answer: B — Experts advise caution in the first 4-6 weeks postpartum because pregnancy's physiological changes persist, and medical guidance governs the return. Jumping straight back to full intensity (A, D) ignores that; a year-long blanket wait (C) overstates it; and treating postpartum as irrelevant (E) ignores that it is still a special-population window.

Scenario 8. When deciding how to program for a pregnant athlete preparing for 'labor and motherhood,' which emphasis best reflects the article's specificity-of-training argument?

  1. A. Almost entirely long, slow aerobic work like distance running, since endurance matters most
  2. B. Functional strength and power (squatting, deadlifting, carrying) that transfer to accommodating the growing abdomen and later lifting and carrying the baby — without excluding aerobic work
  3. C. Isolation 'toning' machines for one light set each, as in the standard pregnancy resistance protocol
  4. D. Maximal one-rep-max testing across all lifts every week
  5. E. Whatever minimizes any movement, to avoid all risk
Show answer

Answer: B — Specificity of training means building around the actual demands — for motherhood those are functional strength and power (squat, lift, carry) plus protecting the low back, with aerobic work included but not the sole focus. Pure aerobic emphasis (A) and light isolation toning (C) miss those demands; weekly max testing (D) is unnecessary and risky; and minimizing all movement (E) contradicts the article's case that functional training is beneficial.
