Why this is on the reading list

This article is on the CCFT reading list because it operationalizes the psychological dimension of fitness — the one element that does not appear among the 10 physical/neurological components but determines whether an athlete can actually demonstrate work capacity on demand. For the exam it directly backs Domain 1's requirement to assess an athlete's psychological tolerance for training (1.1.4), and it supplies the coaching toolkit (positive beliefs, mental preparation, mental toughness) a trainer uses to build that tolerance, manage fear, and progress athletes — which is why it also reaches into Educating, Training cueing, and Leadership tasks.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 1.1.4 Assess psychological tolerance for training
  • 1.2.4 Monitor athlete for signs of over- or under-training
  • 1.2.5 Identify when athlete is ready to progress to another goal/skill
  • 5.1.1 Provide athletes with goal setting
  • 5.1.3 Establish rapport and adapt approach based on athlete response
  • 5.2.2 Apply scaling to meet current physical and psychological needs of each athlete
  • 4.2.2 Use multiple cueing strategies (visual, tactile, verbal)
  • 4.2.3 Utilize effective cues (short, specific, actionable)
  • 3.1.7 Teach importance of movements that produce little/no power (e.g., L-sit, back lever)

What to focus on while reading

  • The article's central claim: fitness is the demonstration of work capacity, so the mind is a performance variable on the same footing as rest and nutrition — not a 'soft' add-on.
  • The three components of psychological readiness and their precise definitions: positive beliefs (programming the mind to expect success), mental preparation (focusing the mind on the challenge ahead), mental toughness (overcoming fear, pressure, and adversity).
  • WHY these three were chosen — they are the aspects elite, highest-honor athletes consistently cite when explaining their success. Note the appeal to expert/champion consensus, not theory.
  • The Roger Bannister sub-four-minute-mile story and the rapid record-breaking that followed: the function it serves is illustrating that belief, not just physiology, gates performance ('realize' vs. 'think/feel/hope').
  • The pre-conscious-mind-as-spam-filter analogy and the 'drivers wearing hats' exercise: give the mind a target and it finds it everywhere. Beliefs are prime filters that decide what we attend to and deem important; they are self-reinforcing.
  • How negative beliefs become physically and emotionally self-fulfilling in the box — the handstand-is-scary athlete, the dread before Fran/Murph manifesting as butterflies, sickness, hyper-awareness of aches.
  • That the article grounds belief-work in Cognitive Behavior Therapy (CBT): the belief sits between the trigger/event and the emotional/physical consequence.
  • The 6-step CBT-style reframing protocol for performance-limiting beliefs — and especially the FIVE distortion patterns to recognize: all-or-nothing thinking, generalizing, selective focus, jumping to conclusions, selective memory. Be able to recognize each by example in an athlete's self-talk.
  • The emphasis on WRITING self-talk down and reading it ALOUD — externalizing distorted thoughts is what exposes them, and reframes must be spoken to be heard.
  • The reframing example with the resistance-band progression (green to blue to red band): a concrete, evidence-anchored positive reframe tied to measurable progress.
  • The definition and purpose of mental preparation: aligning mindset, focus, and mood; protecting the mind from drifting to negatives by anchoring on the next action.
  • The pre-movement / pre-lift routine concept (linking a physical cue — gripping the bar, settling the feet, breathing — to a thought or image): why it builds consistency, confidence, and trust, and prevents over-thinking.
  • The split application: max-effort/strength days need a routine for 100% effort and technique with concentration; met-con days need pre-game prep to reduce nerves and focus on maximal effort.
  • The 7-step mental-preparation protocol — note the role of identifying the right MOOD (relaxed, focused, angry — individual), attaching a PHYSICAL CUE to that state, mentally rehearsing success, and selecting POSITIVE technique cues ('head and chest forward', 'jump to full extension').
  • The definition of mental toughness for CrossFit specifically: maintaining confidence-enhancing positive beliefs and laser focus on the immediate task WHILE being physically overwhelmed.
  • T-CUP — Thinking Correctly Under Pressure (Sir Clive Woodward / 2003 Rugby World Cup, derived from Yehuda Shinar): concentration on the task survives huge physical and psychological pressure; under pressure the inner voice gets louder and tells you to quit, slow down, or cheat range of motion.
  • The three mental-toughness strategies and how they DIFFER: dissociation (focus AWAY from pain — counting reps, music, technique cues), association (focus INTO body sensations — breathing, fatigue, tension, lactic acid — to find 'again, faster' moments and to check mechanics like locked-out abs in a press), and self-talk (repeating positive beliefs, encouragement, counting, positive technique cues).
  • The 21-15-9 / dissociation-by-counting insight: breaking reps into manageable chunks divisible into threes is more palatable than counting in sevens — a practical coaching tool.
  • The caution about music: it can mask the breathing/heart-rate biofeedback the mind uses to gauge fatigue (a double-edged tool the coach should understand).
  • The repeated line 'the best dissociative technique is to listen to your coach' — the coach IS an external focus tool during a workout.
  • The closing application to NEW athletes: belief-building helps people get over fears (the box jump), maintain motivation, progress faster, and carries over into life — tying psychological readiness back to coaching beginners and special cases.
  • The framing that psychological readiness, like the 10 fitness components, can be TRAINED and DEVELOPED — it is a coachable skill, not a fixed trait.
  • The cross-reference to Wendy Swift's 'Performance Psychology: Taming Your Inner Voice' for self-talk — signaling self-talk is a deeper topic the exam may treat across articles.

Concepts to understand

  • Performance as the test of fitness: work capacity only counts if it can be demonstrated, so psychological readiness is a legitimate, trainable performance variable — apply by treating a confident, focused athlete and a fearful, distracted one as having different effective fitness on the same day.
  • Psychological tolerance is assessable and coachable: a CCFT must read whether an athlete is mentally ready (1.1.4) and intervene — recognizing dread, avoidance, catastrophizing, or fear as signals, not character flaws.
  • Beliefs are self-fulfilling filters: what an athlete expects, their pre-conscious mind selects for and amplifies — so a coach changes outcomes by changing what the athlete focuses on and expects, not only by changing the programming.
  • Negative beliefs reliably degrade performance ('screw you over every time'): catastrophic or absolute self-talk before a lift or WOD predicts failure and produces real emotional/physical symptoms — the coach intercepts this before it compounds.
  • The CBT chain (trigger → belief → emotional/physical consequence): the leverage point is the BELIEF in the middle; change the interpretation and you change the felt experience and the behavior.
  • Recognizing the five cognitive distortions in athlete self-talk so you can name and reframe them: all-or-nothing thinking, overgeneralizing ('always/never/can't'), selective focus, jumping to conclusions, and selective memory (shrinking wins, magnifying misses).
  • The reframing method as a coaching conversation: surface the self-talk, voice it aloud, test it for realism ('what would you say to a friend who said this?'), and replace it with a positive statement anchored to real, measured progress (band colors, PR history).
  • Mental preparation = aligning mindset, focus, and mood and anchoring attention on the NEXT action so the mind cannot drift to fear — apply as a pre-WOD/pre-lift routine you can teach an athlete to self-administer.
  • Pre-performance routines link a physical cue to a thought/image: they create consistency, confidence, and trust in preparation and stop over-thinking — the coach can install simple, repeatable routines for the bar approach, the first pull, the breath.
  • Differentiating preparation by workout type: max-effort/strength demands concentration on 100% effort and technique; met-con demands nerve-reduction and a focus on sustained maximal effort — scaling the mental approach to the stimulus parallels scaling the load.
  • Mental toughness (CrossFit-specific) = holding positive belief and task-focus while physically overwhelmed; it is the trait that decides the last rounds of a met-con and 'last-gasp' finishes.
  • T-CUP / Thinking Correctly Under Pressure: concentration is the underpinning skill; when pressure spikes the inner voice gets louder and pushes quitting, slowing, and cutting range of motion — naming this lets the coach pre-arm the athlete against it.
  • Dissociation vs. association as deliberate, situational attention strategies: dissociate (count reps, music, technique cue, listen to coach) to escape pain when the goal is to keep moving; associate (read breathing, fatigue, tension, lactate) to self-regulate pacing ('again, faster') and to audit mechanics (e.g., abs locked in a press). The coach prescribes the right one for the moment.
  • Self-talk as a mental-toughness tool: positive repetition, self-encouragement, counting, and positive technique cues sustain focus and 'go faster for longer' — and crucially, cues must be framed toward what TO do, not what to avoid.
  • Cue framing principle that connects directly to Training: short, specific, positive technique cues ('head and chest forward', 'jump to full extension', 'hip thrust') serve double duty as both movement correction and dissociative focus — keep cues actionable and positively worded.
  • Belief-building as the on-ramp for beginners and fearful clients: reframing fear (past injury, no athletic background, box-jump anxiety) and developing toughness drives motivation, faster progress, and life carry-over — central to onboarding and goal-setting.
  • Psychological readiness is trainable like any fitness component — so it belongs in goal-setting, progression decisions, and ongoing coaching, not treated as a fixed personality limit.
  • The motivational link to little/no-power, fear-inducing skills (handstands, getting inverted): mental work is often the gate to skills that aren't limited by strength — apply by coaching the belief, not just the movement, when fear blocks progress (relates to 3.1.7).

How the exam applies this

Expect scenario items where an athlete shows fear, dread, catastrophic self-talk, or freezing before a lift or skill, and you must choose the best coaching response — that is 1.1.4 (assess psychological tolerance) and 5.2.2 (scale to the athlete's psychological needs) in action, and the reframing/preparation protocols supply the right answers. Other items will hinge on choosing the correct attention strategy for the moment (dissociation to push through pain vs. association to self-pace or check mechanics), or on framing a cue positively and actionably (4.2.3), or on using belief-building and goal-setting to onboard a fearful beginner (5.1.1, 5.1.3). Because the article frames the mind as trainable, watch for questions that test whether you treat psychological barriers as coachable skills rather than fixed traits or reasons to dismiss the athlete.

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Psychological readiness
The state of being mentally prepared to perform, made up of positive beliefs, mental preparation, and mental toughness; assessable and trainable like the physical components of fitness.
Positive beliefs
Programming the mind to expect success — confidence-level expectations that bias attention and behavior toward a good outcome.
Negative beliefs
Self-defeating expectations (e.g., 'there's no way this goes up') that reliably degrade performance and produce real emotional and physical symptoms.
Mental preparation
Aligning mindset, focus, and mood before performance and anchoring attention on the immediate next action so the mind cannot drift to negative thoughts.
Mental toughness
In CrossFit terms, the capacity to maintain confidence-enhancing positive beliefs and laser focus on the immediate task while being physically overwhelmed by the workout.
Pre-movement (pre-performance) routine
A consistent sequence linking a physical cue (grip, foot placement, breath) to a thought or image, used to build confidence, ensure consistency, and prevent over-thinking before a lift or effort.
Cognitive Behavior Therapy (CBT)
An approach to emotional and behavioral issues that works on how people think; here it frames beliefs as the link between a trigger and its emotional/physical consequences, making the belief the point of intervention.
All-or-nothing thinking
Black-or-white self-talk with no middle ground — e.g., a single mistake means complete failure.
Generalizing
Distorted thinking marked by absolute words like 'always,' 'never,' and 'can't' (e.g., 'I can't resist bread').
Selective focus
Fixating on one unpleasant detail and letting it color the whole experience (e.g., 'my hands hurt on pull-ups, so I hate pull-ups').
Jumping to conclusions
Anticipating the worst outcome and treating the prediction as established fact (e.g., 'that lift was hard, so I'm not strong enough to deadlift my body weight').
Selective memory
Exaggerating insignificant setbacks (a missed snatch) while shrinking genuine achievements (a first kipping pull-up).
Reframing
Restating a distorted, performance-limiting thought as a positive statement anchored to real, measurable progress, then saying it aloud to internalize it.
T-CUP (Thinking Correctly Under Pressure)
A performance model from Sir Clive Woodward's 2003 Rugby World Cup side (derived from Yehuda Shinar) emphasizing sustained concentration on the task despite intense physical and psychological pressure.
Concentration / focus
The underpinning skill of T-CUP — keeping attention on the task when distractions (clock, crowd, fatigue, fear) and a louder inner voice push the athlete to quit, slow down, or cheat range of motion.
Dissociation
Deliberately focusing attention AWAY from pain or discomfort onto something else — counting reps, music, a technique cue, or the coach's voice — to keep moving.
Association
Deliberately focusing attention INTO the body's sensations (breathing rhythm, muscle fatigue, tension, lactic-acid build-up) to self-regulate pacing and audit mechanics.
Self-talk
The internal (or spoken) commentary an athlete runs; a mental-toughness tool when it repeats positive beliefs, encouragement, counts reps, and gives positive technique cues.
Pre-conscious filter ('spam filter')
The mind's tendency to let through and amplify whatever it has been told to value — give it a target (a belief) and it finds confirming evidence everywhere.
Work capacity (demonstrated)
Fitness as the actual demonstration of work across broad time and modal domains — performance you can show, not just possess, which is why the mental game matters.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • Persistent dread, panic, or catastrophic self-talk before training that does not respond to reframing or routine may signal anxiety beyond coaching — recognize the boundary and refer to an appropriate professional rather than 'coaching through' a mental-health condition (psychological coaching here is performance-focused, not therapy).
  • Using music loud enough to mask breathing and heart-rate biofeedback can blunt an athlete's perception of fatigue/exertion and mask warning signs of overexertion — apply with awareness, and keep volume below hearing-damage levels.
  • Inner-voice pressure that pushes an athlete to 'cheat the range of motion' or slow technique under fatigue is a cue to protect mechanics and safety — do not let mental 'toughness' override sound movement.
  • Author is an organizational psychologist, not the athlete's clinician — the CCFT applies these as motivation/performance tools within scope; diagnosing or treating psychological conditions is outside CCFT scope of practice.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. A normally strong athlete sets up under a near-max clean and you hear him mutter, 'There's no way this is going up.' He misses the lift. On the next attempt, what is the best coaching action grounded in this article?

  1. A. Add weight to force him to rise to the challenge
  2. B. Tell him to stop talking and just lift
  3. C. Have him reset with a brief routine and a single positive technique cue ('jump to full extension') to refocus on the next action
  4. D. Reduce the load two plates and end his strength work for the day
  5. E. Explain the neurophysiology of the central nervous system before he lifts again
Show answer

Answer: C — C applies both mental preparation (a pre-lift routine anchoring attention on the immediate action) and positive, actionable self-talk/cueing, directly countering the negative belief that preceded the miss. A risks safety and reinforces dread. B dismisses the problem without redirecting focus. D over-scales for a psychological, not physical, limiter. E floods the athlete with information at exactly the moment he should be focusing on the next action — the article warns against over-thinking.

Scenario 2. An athlete two rounds into Fight Gone Bad is gassed and you can see him about to break. Which attention strategy does the article suggest to help him keep moving through the pain in a high-rep met-con?

  1. A. Association — have him focus intently on the burning in his muscles
  2. B. Dissociation — give him something to focus on away from the discomfort, such as counting reps in small chunks or a technique cue, and tell him to listen to your voice
  3. C. Tell him to stop and analyze why he feels tired
  4. D. Have him visualize a future competition to distract himself
  5. E. Increase the pace immediately regardless of how he feels
Show answer

Answer: B — B is dissociation — deliberately drawing attention away from pain via rep-counting, technique cues, and the coach's voice (the article explicitly calls the coach the best dissociative tool). A is association, which focuses INTO the pain and is better for pacing/mechanics checks, not for pushing through when overwhelmed. C breaks task-focus. D is unfocused and not tied to the immediate task. E ignores his state and risks form breakdown/overexertion.

Scenario 3. During a heavy strength session, an athlete keeps under-bracing on the press. You want to use an attention strategy that helps him FEEL whether his midline is tight. Which approach fits the article's description?

  1. A. Dissociation — play loud music to take his mind off it
  2. B. Association — have him focus on the physical sensation of locking out his abs and bracing during the press
  3. C. Have him count reps backward to stay distracted
  4. D. Tell him to think about anything except the lift
  5. E. Tape over the mirror so he can't watch himself
Show answer

Answer: B — B is association: focusing into body sensations (the article's exact example is discerning whether the abs were locked out during a press) to audit and correct mechanics. A, C, and D are all dissociative — they draw attention AWAY from the body, which is the opposite of what's needed to feel and fix bracing. E removes visual feedback without engaging proprioception.

Scenario 4. A new client tells you, 'I'll never be able to do a real pull-up without the bands.' Following the article's reframing method, what is the best response?

  1. A. Agree that pull-ups are very hard and move on
  2. B. Tell her bands don't count and she needs to try harder
  3. C. Have her say it aloud, then help her reframe it against her actual progress: 'I've moved from the green band to blue to red — I'm getting stronger and will get a dead-hang soon'
  4. D. Ignore the comment to avoid drawing attention to it
  5. E. Assign her max-effort strict pull-up attempts until she succeeds
Show answer

Answer: C — C follows the article's CBT-style protocol: externalize the self-talk by voicing it, test its realism, and replace it with a positive statement anchored to measurable progress (the band-color example from the text). A and B reinforce or dismiss the limiting belief. D leaves the distortion ('never') unchallenged. E pushes physical intensity without addressing the belief that is the actual limiter and risks failure that confirms the negative belief.

Scenario 5. You read a new member's self-talk after a tough session: 'I missed one snatch today, so I'm clearly hopeless at the barbell — I never get these.' Which cognitive distortions from the article are most clearly present, and what should you do?

  1. A. None — this is realistic self-assessment, so leave it alone
  2. B. Selective memory and generalizing ('never') — help her reframe by listing her real recent wins and replacing the absolute language
  3. C. Only all-or-nothing thinking — tell her to be more positive
  4. D. This is outside coaching entirely; refer her to a psychologist immediately
  5. E. Jumping to conclusions only — add more snatch volume next session
Show answer

Answer: B — B correctly identifies selective memory (magnifying one miss while shrinking achievements) and generalizing (the absolute 'never'), and pairs them with the article's reframing remedy anchored to real progress. A mistakes distortion for accuracy. C names only one pattern and offers no method. D over-escalates a normal coachable belief to referral (referral is reserved for issues beyond performance coaching). E ignores the belief work and just adds volume.

Scenario 6. It's a max-effort back squat day. An athlete asks how to 'get her head right' before her heaviest attempt. Which guidance best reflects the article's mental-preparation steps for a strength day?

  1. A. Keep her mind blank and approach the bar without any routine
  2. B. Have her establish a consistent routine, get into her best performance mood, attach a physical cue, mentally rehearse a successful rep, and pick one positive technique cue to fire on the lift
  3. C. Have her focus on how nervous she is so she respects the weight
  4. D. Tell her to think about everything that could go wrong so she's prepared
  5. E. Distract her with conversation right up until she unracks the bar
Show answer

Answer: B — B is the article's mental-preparation protocol applied to a max-effort day: a routine for 100% effort and technique, the right mood, a physical anchor cue, mental rehearsal of success, and a positive technique cue. A discards the routine that builds confidence and consistency. C and D deliberately prime negative beliefs and nerves, which the article says undermine performance. E breaks the focus on the immediate task that preparation is meant to protect.

Scenario 7. A beginner freezes at the bottom of a box-jump progression, visibly afraid, even though he clearly has the leg strength to clear the box. What does this article suggest is the highest-leverage coaching priority?

  1. A. Add height to the box to build confidence faster
  2. B. Treat it as a strength deficit and program more squats
  3. C. Address the belief and fear directly — reframe it, build a small success, and develop his mental toughness, since the limiter is psychological, not physical
  4. D. Tell him box jumps aren't important and skip them permanently
  5. E. Have him watch advanced athletes until he feels ready
Show answer

Answer: C — C matches the article's closing point that belief-building helps new athletes get over fears (the box-jump example is named) and that psychological readiness is the gate when strength is not the limiter. A increases the threat. B misdiagnoses a mental barrier as a physical one. D abandons the skill instead of coaching the athlete through a coachable fear. E is passive and doesn't build the belief or a graded success experience.

Scenario 8. Which statement best captures why this article treats the 'mind game' as part of fitness rather than an optional extra — and how that should shape your coaching?

  1. A. Fitness is purely the 10 physical/neurological components, so mental work is just motivation and doesn't change performance
  2. B. Because fitness is the demonstrated work capacity, and psychological readiness — like the physical components — is trainable and directly affects whether an athlete can show that capacity, so it belongs in assessment, goal-setting, and daily coaching
  3. C. Because mental skills replace the need for technique and intensity
  4. D. Because only elite competitors need psychological readiness; regular members do not
  5. E. Because the mind cannot be trained, so coaches should select only mentally tough athletes
Show answer

Answer: B — B reflects the article's thesis: fitness is demonstrated work capacity, psychological readiness is a trainable component on par with the others, and it shapes performance — so it belongs in assessment (1.1.4), goal-setting (5.1.1), and ongoing coaching. A denies the article's central claim. C wrongly substitutes mental work for technique/intensity. D contradicts the explicit application to new and fearful clients. E contradicts the article's repeated point that psychological readiness can be trained and developed.
