Why this is on the reading list

This article gives the coach the physiological 'why' behind muscle soreness, which directly supports two D1 assessment tasks: distinguishing normal training adaptation (DOMS) from danger signals (rhabdomyolysis), and reading chronic soreness as a marker of overtraining/under-recovery. It explains why CrossFit's constantly-varied, full-range, high-rep, fast-eccentric movements reliably produce soreness, why gradual progression prevents harm, and why most popular 'recovery' interventions (static stretching, massage, ice, NSAIDs) don't reduce DOMS. The coach needs this to make ready-to-train calls, manage risk, and educate athletes without overstepping scope.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 1.1.1 Screen athlete for medical issues (e.g., health questionnaire)
  • 1.1.2 Recognize conditions/injuries outside CCFT Scope of Practice that require referral (risk factors)
  • 1.1.3 Assess for rhabdomyolysis ('rhabdo') risk
  • 1.1.4 Assess psychological tolerance for training
  • 1.2.4 Monitor athlete for signs of over- or under-training
  • 1.2.2 Evaluate athlete's work capacity
  • 1.2.5 Identify when athlete is ready to progress to another goal/skill
  • 1.2.6 Quantify and track performance
  • 2.2.4 Design programming for injured athletes to maintain fitness and restore functionality
  • 5.2.3 Manage risk for the athlete
  • 5.2.6 Recognize warning signs for possible injury or overexertion
  • 6.2.1 Identify additional lifestyle goals (sleep/recovery, stress)
  • 6.2.4 Recognize scope-of-practice limitations

What to focus on while reading

  • The definition of DOMS (delayed onset muscle soreness) and its time course: first appears ~8 hours post-exercise, peaks at 24-48 hours, mostly gone in 4-5 days but can linger longer. Highlight this timeline — it lets you predict and explain soreness to athletes.
  • The distinction between DOMS and 'immediate' soreness from injury — the article flags this explicitly. A coach must not treat acute injury pain as if it were normal training soreness.
  • The mechanical hypothesis vs. the disproven metabolic (lactic acid) hypothesis. Lock in that lactic acid does NOT cause muscle damage or DOMS — eccentric actions cause less lactic acid yet more damage. This is a common myth the exam may test.
  • The three muscle ACTIONS (not just 'contractions'): concentric (shortening, the lift/up phase), isometric (tension, no length change), eccentric (lengthening under tension, the lowering/down phase). Know which phase each is in a squat or press.
  • Why eccentric actions cause the most damage — weak links in the muscle microstructure 'pop'/tear (visible as Z-disc streaming under microscope). Eccentric loading is also what drives the most strength/size adaptation.
  • The specific CrossFit movement variables that amplify soreness: high total reps/volume, high SPEED of eccentric (explosive/jumping movements), and full range of motion with the muscle loaded near its fully stretched/lengthened position (e.g., quads/glutes/adductors at the bottom of a wall ball or full squat).
  • Why high-rep bodyweight workouts (Cindy) often cause MORE soreness than heavy strength days (1-1-1 or 3-3-3) — fewer total heavy reps performed more slowly = less intramuscular strain; high-rep fast bodyweight = more strain.
  • The full list of consequences of muscle damage beyond pain: temporary swelling, reduced strength/power (lagging behind soreness — muscle can feel fine but still be weak), reduced range of motion / contracted muscles at rest, altered gait, decreased sprint and endurance performance, reduced insulin sensitivity (slower glycogen replenishment), tremor, impaired fine motor control, and loss of proprioception/force sense.
  • The KEY safety passage on rhabdomyolysis: compromised muscle-fiber membranes leak creatine kinase, myoglobin, and potassium into the blood; usually normal and reversible, but rare excessive spillage can cause cardiac arrhythmias (electrolyte imbalance) and/or kidney failure (myoglobin clogging kidneys). Cola-colored urine in hours/days after a hard workout = go to the ER immediately.
  • The stated key to AVOIDING rhabdo: 'judicious and gradual introduction to intensity for athletes who are unaccustomed to training that involves significant eccentric muscular stress.' This is the coaching action item.
  • The 'repeated bout effect' — a second similar bout causes less damage and soreness; this is what training and adaptation are. Note it disappears after a few weeks of detraining ('couch potato').
  • The strength/recovery dissociation: do NOT assume a muscle is fully recovered just because soreness is gone — force capability can lag several more days. Bears directly on readiness-to-train decisions.
  • Chronic/lingering soreness PLUS feeling unenthusiastic about training = a sign of overtraining / under-recovery; prescribe rest. Highlight this as a monitoring cue.
  • The 'should I train sore?' answer = 'it depends.' Mild-to-moderate DOMS is usually fine; severe soreness in a muscle group warrants relative rest for THAT body part. Train a DIFFERENT movement pattern instead (sore legs from squatting Cindy → don't load heavy back squats the next day; running is OK because the pattern differs, though performance may suffer).
  • Soreness as delayed feedback / a coaching diagnostic: unexpected soreness in an UNUSUAL place after a known movement (e.g., excessive soreness somewhere other than the low back after heavy deadlifts) may signal a technique fault. Logging where you got sore informs technique work.
  • What does NOT reliably reduce DOMS: post-exercise static stretching, massage, cryotherapy (ice), and pre-workout warm-up. Note the article is honest that evidence is weak/absent for all of these against DOMS specifically.
  • Why NSAIDs (ibuprofen) are NOT recommended for DOMS: (a) soreness is protective feedback and masking it risks further injury, and (b) anti-inflammatories can slow the muscle's adaptive processes.
  • The legitimate reasons to still warm up and to still stretch — performance improvement, injury (strain) prevention, and improved extensibility/flexibility — even though they don't prevent DOMS. Don't overclaim the benefit.
  • Stretching nuance: dynamic stretching before explosive/powerful work; prolonged static stretching BEFORE exercise reduces explosive output (do it after); ballistic stretching is least effective and may predispose to injury.
  • The programming bottom line: progress gradually in weight and reps; reel in the ego ('don't ski a double-black-diamond as a green skier'); avoid long layoffs; favor fewer WODs done consistently over bingeing then breaking; bodyweight WODs (squats, push-ups, pull-ups, sit-ups) at intensity keep muscles from de-adapting when away from the gym.

Concepts to understand

  • DOMS is a normal, expected, and largely UNAVOIDABLE byproduct of effective training — it signals adaptation, not failure. A coach should normalize mild-to-moderate soreness rather than treat all soreness as 'overdoing it.'
  • Muscle damage is mechanical (driven by eccentric loading), not metabolic — lactic acid is not the cause of DOMS. The coach should not perpetuate the lactic-acid myth when educating athletes.
  • Eccentric muscle action (lengthening under tension) is both the primary CAUSE of damage/soreness AND a primary DRIVER of strength and hypertrophy adaptation — the same mechanism that makes you sore makes you stronger.
  • Soreness magnitude scales with three controllable program variables — total volume (reps/work), eccentric SPEED (explosive/jumping/fast movements), and range of motion under stretch (full-depth loading) — so a coach can predict and modulate soreness by adjusting these.
  • Unaccustomed, novel, or post-layoff stimulus is the trigger for the worst soreness; because CrossFit is constantly varied and hits diverse muscle groups, soreness will recur — gradual on-ramping and consistency blunt it via the repeated bout effect.
  • Recovery of FORCE/strength lags behind the disappearance of soreness; readiness to train at full output cannot be judged by soreness alone.
  • Most marketed recovery modalities (static stretching, massage, ice, anti-inflammatories) do not measurably reduce DOMS, and NSAIDs may actively blunt adaptation — the coach should set honest expectations and not recommend NSAIDs to mask training soreness.
  • Rhabdomyolysis is the dangerous tail of normal muscle-damage physiology: it is a medical emergency outside the coach's scope, and the coach's job is prevention (gradual intensity for the unaccustomed), recognition (cola-colored urine, disproportionate pain/swelling), and referral (ER), not diagnosis or treatment.
  • Chronic, lingering, or unusually placed soreness is a SIGNAL to be read — either overtraining/under-recovery (prescribe rest) or a technique fault (cue/correct), not something to push through indiscriminately.
  • Training a sore body part again with the SAME movement pattern compounds risk; train a different pattern or give that part relative rest — this is how to keep an athlete moving without overloading damaged tissue.
  • Warming up and stretching have real value (performance, strain-injury prevention, flexibility) independent of DOMS; the coach should program them for the right reasons and not promise soreness relief they don't deliver.
  • Reframing soreness positively (permission to rest, evidence of adaptation, delayed performance feedback) is a leadership/psychology tool for keeping athletes engaged and managing their tolerance for hard training.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenario items where an athlete reports soreness and you must choose the safest, most appropriate coaching action: telling the difference between normal DOMS and a referral-worthy red flag (cola-colored urine, disproportionate swelling/pain → rhabdo → ER, supporting 1.1.2/1.1.3/5.2.3/5.2.6), deciding whether and how to train a sore athlete (relative rest, change the movement pattern, supporting 1.2.4/2.2.4), and reading chronic soreness plus low motivation as overtraining requiring rest (1.2.4/6.2.1). Other items test myth-busting judgment — declining to recommend NSAIDs, static stretching, massage, or ice as DOMS cures (6.2.3/6.2.4), correctly programming gradual progression to prevent rhabdo in unaccustomed/de-trained athletes (5.2.3), and using unexpected soreness as a technique-fault diagnostic (1.2.6). Because the exam tests applied judgment, the right answer usually balances safety, gradual progression, and honest education over aggressive intervention.

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

DOMS (Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness)
Muscle soreness that begins about 8 hours after a workout, peaks at 24-48 hours, and usually fades within 4-5 days. It is the normal, expected soreness of training adaptation, distinct from the immediate pain of an acute injury.
Concentric action
A muscle SHORTENING while generating tension — the true 'contraction.' This is the lifting/'up' phase of a movement, e.g., standing up out of a squat or pressing a bar overhead. Less damaging and less anabolic than eccentric work.
Isometric action
A muscle generating tension with NO change in length — e.g., holding a handstand or pulling on a deadlift too heavy to budge. Tension without movement.
Eccentric action
A muscle LENGTHENING while still under tension — the lowering/'down' or deceleration phase, e.g., descending into a squat. The most structurally stressful action for muscle fibers; it causes the most damage/soreness AND drives the most strength and size adaptation.
Mechanical hypothesis
The now-accepted explanation that muscle damage is initiated by mechanical stress — physical micro-tearing of muscle fibers during eccentric loading — rather than by metabolic byproducts.
Metabolic hypothesis (lactic acid myth)
The older, disproven idea that muscle damage/soreness is caused by metabolic byproducts such as lactic acid. Eccentric actions produce LESS lactic acid yet MORE damage, which helped disprove it. Lactic acid does not cause DOMS.
Z-disc streaming
The disruption of the normally regular, repeating banding pattern (Z discs) inside muscle fibers, visible under an electron microscope after severe eccentric exercise — physical evidence of mechanical muscle damage.
Creatine kinase / myoglobin
Muscle proteins that leak from damaged muscle-fiber membranes into the bloodstream after exercise. Usually a normal, reversible sign of muscle damage; in excess (rhabdo) myoglobin can clog the kidneys.
Exertional rhabdomyolysis ('rhabdo')
A rare, serious breakdown of muscle that spills excessive proteins and electrolytes (e.g., potassium) into the blood, potentially causing cardiac arrhythmias and/or kidney failure. Cola/Coca-Cola-colored urine after a hard workout is a warning sign — go to the ER immediately. A medical emergency outside coaching scope.
Repeated bout effect
The protective adaptation whereby a second, similar bout of exercise causes much less damage and soreness than the first. It is the essence of training and recovery improvement, and it fades after a few weeks of detraining.
Length-dependent damage
The finding that muscles stressed eccentrically while near their fully stretched/lengthened position (e.g., quads and glutes at the bottom of a full squat or wall ball) are more prone to damage than when the eccentric load occurs only in mid-range or short positions.
Relative rest
Resting a specific severely sore muscle group while still training — typically by switching to a different movement pattern that doesn't reload the damaged tissue (e.g., running instead of heavy back squats when the quads are wrecked).
Proprioception
The body's sense of where a limb is in space and how much force a muscle is producing. Damaged, sore muscles temporarily lose proprioceptive precision, contributing to shakiness and impaired fine motor control after hard training.
Dynamic / static / ballistic stretching
Dynamic = controlled movements through a range of motion (best before explosive work). Static = holding a stretch (best AFTER a workout; done before, it reduces explosive output). Ballistic = repetitive bouncing at end range (least effective, may predispose to injury). None reliably reduce DOMS.
Overtraining / under-recovery
A state signaled by chronic, lingering muscle soreness combined with unusual lack of enthusiasm for training; the indicated response is appropriate rest until body and mind recover.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • Cola/Coca-Cola-colored (dark brown/red) urine in the hours or days after a hard workout is a potential sign of exertional rhabdomyolysis — direct the athlete to the ER immediately; this is outside coaching scope (referral required).
  • Disproportionate, severe pain and swelling in a muscle after intense eccentric work (especially in an athlete new to training or returning from a layoff) can indicate rhabdo — escalate to medical care rather than treating it as ordinary DOMS.
  • Prevention is the coach's lane: introduce intensity judiciously and gradually for athletes who are unaccustomed to (or de-trained from) significant eccentric/high-volume stress; aggressive early intensity is the primary rhabdo risk factor.
  • Chronic soreness that lingers beyond the usual 4-5 days, paired with low motivation, points to overtraining/under-recovery — prescribe rest; do not push the athlete through it.
  • Do NOT recommend NSAIDs (ibuprofen) to mask training soreness — it can hide protective feedback (risking further injury) and may blunt muscle adaptation. Recommending or directing medication is outside coaching scope of practice; defer to a medical professional.
  • Immediate sharp soreness/pain (as opposed to delayed DOMS) may indicate an acute injury, not normal adaptation — assess and refer rather than coaching through it.
  • Reduced strength/force can persist for days AFTER soreness disappears — do not green-light maximal/heavy loading on a recently damaged muscle group based on the absence of soreness alone.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. An athlete texts you the morning after their first high-intensity workout: their legs are extremely sore and their urine is dark brown, 'like Coca-Cola.' What is the best course of action?

  1. A. Reassure them this is normal DOMS, tell them to hydrate, foam roll, and come to class tomorrow
  2. B. Recommend an ibuprofen and a hot bath to reduce the soreness
  3. C. Advise them to go to the emergency room immediately, as cola-colored urine can indicate rhabdomyolysis
  4. D. Tell them to take static stretching breaks throughout the day to flush out the lactic acid
  5. E. Schedule a light recovery row session to promote blood flow to the legs
Show answer

Answer: C — Cola/Coca-Cola-colored urine after a hard workout is a classic warning sign of exertional rhabdomyolysis, which can cause kidney failure and cardiac arrhythmias — a medical emergency outside coaching scope requiring immediate ER referral (1.1.3, 5.2.6). A and E dangerously treat it as ordinary soreness; B recommends medication (out of scope) and masks a danger signal; D is based on the disproven lactic-acid myth and ignores the emergency.

Scenario 2. A member did 'Cindy' (high-rep pull-ups/push-ups/squats) yesterday and reports severe leg soreness. Today's class WOD features heavy back squats. What is the most appropriate coaching guidance?

  1. A. Have them squat heavy as programmed — training through soreness builds resilience fastest
  2. B. Tell them to skip the gym entirely until all soreness is completely gone
  3. C. Scale them to a different movement pattern (e.g., row or run) and give the sore quads relative rest, rather than reloading the same pattern with heavy squats
  4. D. Recommend a pre-workout ibuprofen so they can squat heavy without feeling the soreness
  5. E. Have them perform prolonged static stretching of the quads before squatting to eliminate the soreness
Show answer

Answer: C — Severe soreness in a muscle group calls for relative rest of THAT body part; loading heavy back squats repeats the same pattern that caused the damage and compounds risk. Switching to a different pattern keeps the athlete training safely (1.2.4, 2.2.4, 5.2.3). A ignores the danger; B over-restricts (mild-moderate DOMS is fine and a different pattern is workable); D masks protective feedback and is out of scope; E won't remove the damage and static stretching before lifting reduces output.

Scenario 3. A new athlete asks why they get so sore and whether lactic acid buildup is to blame. What is the most accurate explanation to give?

  1. A. Yes — lactic acid accumulates and causes the soreness, so cooling down clears it out
  2. B. Soreness is caused by mechanical micro-damage from eccentric (lengthening-under-tension) muscle actions; lactic acid is not the cause of DOMS
  3. C. Soreness means they are overtraining and should reduce all intensity going forward
  4. D. Soreness comes from dehydration and poor electrolyte intake during the workout
  5. E. Soreness is purely psychological and disappears once they get fitter
Show answer

Answer: B — The accepted (mechanical) explanation is that DOMS results from physical micro-tearing during eccentric actions; eccentric work produces less lactic acid yet more damage, which disproved the metabolic/lactic-acid theory (supports educating accurately, 6.2.3). A perpetuates the myth; C wrongly equates normal adaptation soreness with overtraining; D and E are not the mechanism.

Scenario 4. An athlete's quads feel completely recovered — no soreness — two days after a brutal squat session, and they want to attempt a 1-rep-max back squat today. What is the best guidance?

  1. A. Go for the max — if the soreness is gone, the muscle is fully recovered and ready
  2. B. Be cautious: muscle force/strength can stay reduced for several days after soreness disappears, so a max attempt may be premature and underperform
  3. C. They can never max within the same week as a hard squat session under any circumstance
  4. D. Have them take ibuprofen first to ensure no residual soreness interferes
  5. E. Soreness and strength recover at exactly the same rate, so the absence of soreness guarantees full power
Show answer

Answer: B — The article stresses that the time course of soreness and strength loss are not tightly linked — a muscle can feel fine yet not have regained full force capability for a few more days. Judging readiness by soreness alone is unreliable (1.1.4 readiness, 1.2.4, 5.2.3). A and E assume a false equivalence; C is an overly rigid absolute; D is out of scope and irrelevant to recovered force.

Scenario 5. Over the past two weeks an experienced athlete reports muscle soreness that lingers longer than usual and admits they feel unusually unmotivated and flat about training. What does this most likely indicate, and what should you do?

  1. A. They are simply not warming up enough; add more warm-up and continue normal volume
  2. B. They need more protein and creatine; recommend supplements and keep training hard
  3. C. It likely signals overtraining/under-recovery; advise appropriate rest until body and mind recover
  4. D. They are detraining; immediately increase training frequency and intensity
  5. E. It is normal DOMS; tell them to push through it every session
Show answer

Answer: C — Chronic, lingering soreness combined with low enthusiasm is the article's described signature of overtraining/under-recovery, for which the prescribed response is appropriate rest (1.2.4, 6.2.1, 5.2.3). A and E mis-read a recovery problem; B is out of scope and counterproductive; D would worsen the over-reaching.

Scenario 6. A member asks which recovery methods will actually reduce their day-after muscle soreness. Based on the evidence in the article, what is the most honest answer?

  1. A. Post-workout static stretching, massage, and ice will each significantly reduce DOMS
  2. B. Taking ibuprofen after every workout is the most effective way to prevent DOMS
  3. C. None of these reliably reduce DOMS; warm-ups and stretching are worth doing for performance, flexibility, and strain-injury prevention, but won't prevent soreness, and NSAIDs may even blunt adaptation
  4. D. A thorough warm-up beforehand fully protects against DOMS
  5. E. Ballistic bouncing stretches are the best way to both improve flexibility and cut soreness
Show answer

Answer: C — The article reports weak or absent evidence that static stretching, massage, cryotherapy, or warm-ups reduce DOMS, and notes NSAIDs may slow adaptation while masking protective feedback. The honest coach sets expectations and still programs warm-ups/stretching for their real benefits (6.2.3, 6.2.4). A, B, D over-promise; E is wrong — ballistic stretching is least effective and may predispose to injury.

Scenario 7. A coach is on-ramping someone who has been completely sedentary for a year but used to be very fit. To minimize the risk of rhabdomyolysis, the best approach is to:

  1. A. Start at full prescribed intensity since they were once fit and 'muscle memory' will protect them
  2. B. Introduce intensity and volume judiciously and gradually because they are currently unaccustomed to significant eccentric stress
  3. C. Have them do only maximal eccentric (negative) lowering reps to rebuild strength fastest
  4. D. Skip any progression and test them with a high-rep benchmark on day one to gauge fitness
  5. E. Rely on post-workout ice baths to prevent any muscle damage from heavy first sessions
Show answer

Answer: B — The article names the key to avoiding rhabdo as judicious, gradual introduction to intensity for athletes unaccustomed to significant eccentric stress — and a year of detraining erases prior adaptation (repeated bout effect fades). Gradual progression is the coach's risk-management lane (5.2.3, 5.2.6, 2.2.4). A overestimates residual protection; C and D maximize eccentric/volume stress on an unprepared athlete; E cannot prevent the underlying damage.

Scenario 8. After a heavy deadlift session (3-3-3-3-3), an athlete reports the expected low-back soreness but ALSO unusually intense soreness in one hamstring and the opposite trap. How should a coach interpret and use this information?

  1. A. Ignore it — soreness location is random and tells you nothing useful
  2. B. Treat the unexpected, asymmetric soreness as delayed feedback that may point to a technique fault or compensation worth reviewing and logging
  3. C. Conclude the athlete has rhabdo and send them to the ER
  4. D. Tell them lactic acid simply pooled in those areas and it is meaningless
  5. E. Increase their deadlift load next session to 'even out' the soreness
Show answer

Answer: B — The article frames DOMS as delayed feedback: soreness in an unusual place after a known movement can flag a technique issue, and logging where you got sore informs future technique work (1.2.6, supports fault-finding). A and D dismiss a useful signal; C overreacts (no rhabdo red flags like cola-colored urine are described); E would reinforce a possible faulty pattern under heavier load.

Scenario 9. A member who hates being sore is considering quitting CrossFit, or alternatively training hard for two weeks and then taking a month off to 'recover fully' before bingeing again. What is the soundest guidance?

  1. A. The binge-then-long-layoff plan is ideal because full recovery between blocks prevents soreness
  2. B. Some muscle damage and soreness are essential, largely unavoidable prerequisites for adaptation; progress gradually and train consistently rather than taking long layoffs, because layoffs erase adaptation and bring the soreness right back
  3. C. They should only ever lift heavy singles, since heavy strength work never causes soreness
  4. D. Quitting is the only way to avoid soreness, so support that decision
  5. E. They should take daily NSAIDs so they can train hard continuously without any soreness
Show answer

Answer: B — Muscle damage/soreness are essential, largely unavoidable prerequisites for adaptation; consistency builds the repeated-bout protection, while long layoffs let adaptation disappear and reintroduce severe soreness on return (1.2.5 progression, 1.2.4, 5.1 engagement/psychology). A is exactly backwards; C is false (heavy work still causes some soreness and avoids volume adaptation); D is unnecessary; E masks protective feedback and may blunt adaptation.

D1 · Screening & Ongoing Assessment 8% of exam Confidence tier: ___

amjcaserep-19-145.pdf

Open the PDF on Google Drive →

Why this is on the reading list

This case report documents a previously healthy 17-year-old athlete who, the day after a single strenuous off-season workout, developed exertional rhabdomyolysis severe enough to trigger acute compartment syndrome (a surgical emergency), losing 80% of one leg muscle. It is on the CCFT reading list to build a coach's instinct for the two highest-stakes screening duties in Domain 1: recognizing when post-workout 'soreness' is actually rhabdomyolysis (1.1.3) and recognizing when a presentation is outside CCFT scope and demands immediate medical referral (1.1.2). It also reinforces that the danger lives at the intersection of an unaccustomed athlete, novel high-volume work, and a delay in recognizing warning signs (1.1.1, 1.2.4, 5.2.6).

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 1.1.3 Assess for rhabdomyolysis ('rhabdo') risk
  • 1.1.2 Recognize conditions/injuries outside CCFT Scope of Practice that require referral (risk factors)
  • 1.1.1 Screen athlete for medical issues (e.g., health questionnaire)
  • 1.2.4 Monitor athlete for signs of over- or under-training
  • 5.2.6 Recognize warning signs for possible injury or overexertion
  • 5.2.3 Manage risk for the athlete
  • 7.3.1 Create and follow an Emergency Action Plan (EAP)
  • 7.4.1 Work within CCFT Scope of Practice

What to focus on while reading

  • The trigger: a previously healthy, fit athlete developed this after ONE strenuous workout during an off-season training camp — note that prior fitness did not protect him, and the inciting event was a single bout of unaccustomed, high-volume exertion.
  • The deceptive early presentation: the night of the workout the pain was 'relatively mild' and he assumed it was 'typical post-exercise muscle soreness' and went to bed — highlight this, because it is exactly the misread a coach must guard against.
  • The timeline of deterioration: mild soreness that evening → woke the next morning with WORSENING pain plus a new inability to dorsiflex (lift) his foot ('foot drop'). Symptoms that get worse overnight and add neurological signs are the alarm.
  • The CK number: creatine kinase was 19,011 U/mL against a normal reference of 24-170 U/mL — over 100x normal. Note CK is the lab marker of muscle breakdown; you don't order it, but you should know what it signals.
  • The classic rhabdo triad to anchor in memory: muscle pain, muscle weakness, and dark ('tea-' or 'cola-colored') urine — the article centers pain and weakness; the dark-urine sign is the one most associated with rhabdo in coaching contexts.
  • Pain 'out of proportion to examination' and 'not relieved by rest' as the hallmark distinguishing a true emergency from ordinary soreness, which DOES improve with rest.
  • Swelling and a tense/tight feeling in the muscle compartment, plus pain on passive stretch of the muscle — tangible signs a coach could observe or that an athlete would report.
  • The downstream danger of rhabdo beyond the muscle: kidney damage (from myoglobin), electrolyte imbalances, and cardiac rhythm abnormalities — this is WHY rhabdo is an emergency, not just a sore-muscle problem.
  • Treatment was emergent and hospital-level: aggressive IV fluids, four surgeries (fasciotomies + debridement), and six months of rehab — underscore that nothing here is within a coach's scope to manage.
  • The role of TIME: athletes diagnosed within 24 hours had no long-term complications; delays (driven by the athlete dismissing symptoms and by initial misdiagnosis) drove the catastrophic outcomes in the literature review. Early recognition and referral is the entire game.
  • The two named NCAA football rhabdo OUTBREAKS (13 players at Iowa in 2011 during off-season workouts) — note these were group events tied to off-season conditioning, which is the closest parallel to a CrossFit class doing novel high-volume work.
  • The risk-factor list the article cites for non-fracture cases (metabolic conditions, sickle cell trait, blood disorders, illicit drug use) — relevant to what a health questionnaire should surface before training.

Concepts to understand

  • Rhabdomyolysis is muscle-cell death that spills the cells' contents into the bloodstream; the danger is not the sore muscle itself but the released contents (myoglobin, potassium) damaging the kidneys and disrupting heart rhythm — understand it as a systemic medical emergency, not a localized soreness.
  • The single biggest rhabdo risk factor a coach controls is the mismatch between an athlete's current conditioning and the workout's volume/novelty: deconditioned, returning, or brand-new athletes hit with high-rep eccentric work (and the heat/dehydration of a camp setting) are the classic setup, even if they were 'athletic' before.
  • Prior fitness is NOT protection. This patient was a high-level athlete; rhabdo struck after one unfamiliar workout. A coach must scale novel high-volume sessions for EVERY athlete returning from a layoff, not just obvious beginners.
  • How to distinguish ordinary DOMS (delayed-onset muscle soreness) from a red-flag presentation: DOMS is bilateral, proportional to the work, peaks at 24-72h, and eases with light movement and rest. Rhabdo/compartment signs are disproportionate pain, pain that worsens (especially overnight) rather than eases, marked swelling/tightness, weakness, neurological changes (numbness, can't move a joint), and dark urine.
  • The coach's job is recognize-and-refer, NOT diagnose-and-treat. Spotting a possible rhabdo or compartment-syndrome picture means activating the EAP and sending the athlete for emergency medical evaluation — measuring compartment pressures, ordering CK, and giving IV fluids are all outside CCFT scope.
  • Why urgency matters: outcomes are time-dependent. Athletes evaluated within 24 hours did well; every hour of an athlete 'toughing it out' or being told to rest raises the risk of permanent muscle/nerve loss or kidney failure. 'Wait and see' is the dangerous default a coach must override.
  • Compartment syndrome as the worst-case escalation of localized rhabdo: swelling inside a muscle's fixed fascial sheath raises pressure until blood can't perfuse the muscle, killing it. A coach won't diagnose it, but should know that a tight, severely swollen, disproportionately painful limb with numbness or loss of movement is a do-not-wait emergency.
  • Hydration, environment, and recovery as modifiable risk levers: off-season camps and outbreaks cluster around heat, dehydration, and back-to-back novel sessions — the same conditions a coach manages through scaling, work:rest, hydration, and not piling unaccustomed volume on returning athletes.
  • Pre-participation screening (the health questionnaire) exists partly to surface rhabdo predispositions — sickle cell trait, metabolic muscle disorders, recent illness, certain medications/supplements, and substance use — so that programming and monitoring can account for elevated risk.
  • Post-workout monitoring is an ongoing assessment duty, not a one-time intake task: checking in after an unusually hard or novel session, and educating athletes to report worsening pain, swelling, weakness, or discolored urine rather than dismiss it, is how early cases get caught.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenario questions that hand you an athlete with symptoms after a hard or first-back-from-layoff workout and ask for the BEST coaching action — the safe answer keys on recognizing red flags (disproportionate or worsening pain, dark urine, swelling, weakness) and choosing immediate medical referral / EAP activation over 'rest and ice,' 'push through,' or self-treatment (tasks 1.1.3, 1.1.2, 5.2.6, 7.3.1). Other items test prevention: how to scale and monitor returning or novel athletes facing high-volume work to keep rhabdo risk low (1.2.4, 5.2.3, 2.2.x), and what a pre-participation questionnaire should flag (1.1.1). Scope-of-practice items will reward the coach who refers and refuses to diagnose or manage the medical condition (7.4.1).

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Rhabdomyolysis ('rhabdo')
Breakdown of skeletal muscle that releases the muscle cells' contents (including myoglobin and potassium) into the blood; can poison the kidneys and disrupt heart rhythm, making it a medical emergency rather than ordinary soreness.
Exertional rhabdomyolysis
Rhabdo caused by exercise — typically intense, high-volume, or unaccustomed activity in someone not conditioned for that specific load; the form most relevant to coaching.
Creatine kinase (CK)
An enzyme released when muscle cells break down; blood CK is the standard lab marker of muscle damage. Here it was ~19,000 vs a normal of 24-170, signaling massive muscle injury. Coaches don't order it but should know what it indicates.
Myoglobin
A muscle protein released during rhabdo; in large amounts it can clog and damage the kidneys, and it can turn urine dark brown ('tea-' or 'cola-colored'), one of rhabdo's tell-tale signs.
DOMS (delayed-onset muscle soreness)
Normal, bilateral, self-limiting muscle soreness that peaks 24-72 hours after unaccustomed exercise and eases with rest and light movement — the benign condition that rhabdo is dangerously easy to mistake for.
Acute compartment syndrome
A surgical emergency in which swelling inside a muscle's rigid fascial compartment raises pressure enough to cut off blood flow, causing muscle and nerve death if not released quickly. The catastrophic escalation seen in this case.
Exertional (atraumatic) compartment syndrome
Compartment syndrome triggered by exercise rather than a fracture or blow; rare and easily missed because there is no obvious injury, which is why awareness matters.
Fasciotomy
Emergency surgery that cuts open the fascia to relieve compartment pressure and restore blood flow. Cited here only to underscore that this is a hospital problem, never a coaching one.
Foot drop
Inability to lift (dorsiflex) the foot due to nerve or muscle damage; a neurological warning sign that something far more serious than soreness is happening.
Pain out of proportion
Pain markedly more severe than the apparent injury would explain, and not relieved by rest — a classic red flag separating a true emergency from ordinary post-workout discomfort.
Pain on passive stretch
Sharp pain when the muscle is stretched without the athlete contracting it; a sign of compartment/muscle injury, distinct from the general tightness of normal soreness.
Scope of practice
The boundary of what a CrossFit trainer is qualified and permitted to do; diagnosing or treating rhabdo/compartment syndrome falls outside it — the coach's role is to recognize warning signs and refer for medical care.
Emergency Action Plan (EAP)
A facility's written, rehearsed plan for medical emergencies — who calls 911, where the AED is, how EMS reaches the athlete. The mechanism a coach uses to act when a rhabdo/compartment emergency is suspected.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • Disproportionate or worsening muscle pain — especially pain that intensifies overnight or after rest rather than easing — following an intense or unaccustomed workout. STOP assuming it's DOMS; treat as possible rhabdo and refer for medical evaluation.
  • Dark, brown, or cola/tea-colored urine after hard training: a hallmark of rhabdomyolysis. Refer for emergency medical care immediately; this signals possible kidney involvement.
  • Marked, persistent swelling and a tense/tight feeling in a muscle, with pain on passive stretch — possible compartment syndrome. Do not wait, ice, or 'monitor at home'; activate the EAP and get emergency care.
  • Any new neurological sign — numbness, tingling, or inability to move a joint or lift the foot — after exercise. This is beyond soreness and beyond coaching scope; emergency referral.
  • Setup conditions that raise the index of suspicion: a deconditioned, returning, or brand-new athlete; the first session of a camp or 'on-ramp'; high-rep eccentric work; heat and dehydration; back-to-back novel high-volume days. Scale aggressively and monitor afterward.
  • Pre-participation questionnaire findings that elevate rhabdo risk — sickle cell trait, metabolic muscle disorders, recent viral illness, certain medications/stimulants, or substance use — warrant extra caution in programming and may require medical clearance (outside scope to evaluate; refer).
  • Scope-of-practice line: a coach NEVER diagnoses rhabdo or compartment syndrome, measures compartment pressure, orders labs, or manages fluids. Recognize, refer, document, and follow up — that is the whole coaching responsibility.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. Two days after his first class back from a six-week layoff (a high-rep dumbbell and pull-up couplet), an athlete texts you that his arms are 'killing him,' he can barely straighten his elbows, they look swollen, and his urine this morning was 'really dark, almost brown.' What is the BEST action?

  1. A. Reassure him this is normal DOMS after time off and recommend rest, hydration, and a light recovery walk.
  2. B. Tell him to take ibuprofen and ice his arms, and check back in a couple of days.
  3. C. Advise him to seek emergency medical evaluation now for possible rhabdomyolysis, and follow up to confirm he went.
  4. D. Schedule a deload week and have him come in for some easy rowing to flush the muscles.
  5. E. Have him do gentle stretching and foam rolling and message you if it isn't better by the weekend.
Show answer

Answer: C — The triad of severe disproportionate pain, weakness/swelling, and dark ('cola-colored') urine after unaccustomed high-volume work is a classic rhabdomyolysis red flag — a medical emergency with kidney risk. The coach's duty is immediate referral (1.1.3, 1.1.2, 5.2.6). A, B, D, and E all treat it as ordinary soreness and dangerously delay care; rest, NSAIDs (which can worsen kidney injury), stretching, or more exercise are not the coach's call and waste the time-sensitive window.

Scenario 2. An athlete from yesterday's leg-heavy workout reports anterior shin pain that is 'way worse than it should be,' isn't helped by rest, and his lower leg feels tight and swollen; he also says his foot feels a bit numb. What does this presentation most require from you?

  1. A. Cue him to stretch the calves and quads and ice for 20 minutes every few hours.
  2. B. Recognize possible acute compartment syndrome, activate the EAP, and arrange emergency medical care without delay.
  3. C. Tell him it's likely shin splints from the volume and to skip leg day next week.
  4. D. Measure the firmness of the compartment yourself and decide whether it warrants a referral.
  5. E. Recommend an over-the-counter anti-inflammatory and a follow-up in 48 hours if it persists.
Show answer

Answer: B — Pain out of proportion, not relieved by rest, with a tense swollen compartment and a neurological sign (numbness) is the textbook compartment-syndrome emergency from this case — outcomes hinge on getting decompression within hours. Refer immediately (5.2.6, 7.3.1, 1.1.2). A, C, and E mistake it for a benign overuse problem and lose critical time; D is outside scope — a coach never measures compartment pressure or self-clears an emergency.

Scenario 3. You are programming the first week of a beginner 'on-ramp' that overlaps with a July heat wave. Several athletes are returning after long layoffs. Which approach BEST manages rhabdomyolysis risk?

  1. A. Run the standard class as written so newcomers experience real intensity from day one.
  2. B. Scale volume and intensity down, cap eccentric/high-rep work, emphasize hydration and work-to-rest, and educate athletes to report unusual pain, swelling, or dark urine.
  3. C. Push hard early to build a fitness base quickly, then back off once they adapt.
  4. D. Skip warm-ups to save time and get more working sets in while motivation is high.
  5. E. Have everyone go for a max-effort benchmark on day one to establish a baseline score.
Show answer

Answer: B — Rhabdo clusters where novel high-volume (especially eccentric) work, deconditioned athletes, heat, and dehydration meet — exactly this scenario, and the same pattern as the off-season football outbreaks the article cites. Scaling load, capping volume, managing hydration and rest, and teaching athletes the warning signs is sound risk management (1.2.4, 5.2.3, 2.2.x). A, C, D, and E all increase the unaccustomed load or remove safeguards, raising risk.

Scenario 4. A genuinely fit, competitive athlete returns from two weeks off and is annoyed when you scale her back into a high-volume session. She argues, 'I'm in great shape — rhabdo is a beginner problem.' What is the most accurate and appropriate coaching response?

  1. A. Agree, and let her do the workout as prescribed since she is clearly conditioned.
  2. B. Explain that prior fitness does not prevent exertional rhabdo after unaccustomed work — the case literature includes high-level athletes — so a smart re-entry protects her, then keep the scale in place and monitor her afterward.
  3. C. Tell her rhabdo only happens in extreme heat, so as long as the gym is air-conditioned she's fine at full volume.
  4. D. Let her self-select her scaling since she knows her body best.
  5. E. Have her do more volume than prescribed to prove the point that she can handle it.
Show answer

Answer: B — The case patient was a high-level athlete who developed rhabdo and compartment syndrome after a single unfamiliar workout — prior fitness is not protection, and the inciting factor is unaccustomed load, not the athlete's baseline. The coach educates, holds the appropriate scale, and monitors (1.2.4, 5.2.3, 1.1.3). A, C, D, and E either remove the safeguard or rely on a false reassurance, exposing her to risk.

Scenario 5. A new member's intake questionnaire notes that he carries sickle cell trait. He's eager to jump into your hardest classes immediately. What is the most appropriate coaching action?

  1. A. Disregard it, since he feels healthy and wants to train hard.
  2. B. Recognize sickle cell trait as a factor that can elevate exertional risk, encourage him to obtain medical clearance, and introduce intensity and volume gradually with attentive monitoring.
  3. C. Diagnose how his trait will affect training and prescribe a specific medical management plan yourself.
  4. D. Tell him he cannot train at your gym because of his condition.
  5. E. Put him straight into the most intense conditioning to see how his body responds under load.
Show answer

Answer: B — Pre-participation screening exists to surface conditions like sickle cell trait that the article lists among non-fracture/exertional risk factors; the coach's role is to flag it, refer for clearance, and program conservatively with monitoring (1.1.1, 1.1.2, 5.2.3). C is outside scope (coaches don't diagnose or write medical plans), D is an inappropriate blanket exclusion rather than a clearance-and-scale approach, and A/E ignore a documented risk and court an emergency.

Scenario 6. Which set of features BEST helps you distinguish ordinary delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) from a presentation that should prompt emergency referral?

  1. A. DOMS causes severe one-sided pain with numbness; rhabdo causes mild, even soreness on both sides.
  2. B. DOMS is bilateral, proportional to the work, peaks at 24-72h and eases with light movement and rest; refer when pain is disproportionate or worsening, the limb is very swollen/tight or weak, there is numbness/loss of movement, or urine is dark.
  3. C. Any soreness lasting more than one day is rhabdo and requires the ER.
  4. D. If the athlete can still walk and talk, no presentation needs referral regardless of other signs.
  5. E. Dark urine and disproportionate pain are normal after any hard workout and can be ignored.
Show answer

Answer: B — B states the real decision rule: benign DOMS is bilateral, proportional, time-limited, and improves with rest, whereas disproportionate/worsening pain, marked swelling or weakness, neurological signs, or dark urine are red flags warranting emergency referral (1.1.3, 5.2.6). A inverts the signs, C over-refers on a false rule, and D and E dangerously dismiss genuine emergencies — note this patient walked in unassisted yet had lost most of a leg muscle, so 'can still walk' is no reassurance.

D1 · Screening & Ongoing Assessment 8% of exam Confidence tier: ___

nihms639095.pdf

Open the PDF on Google Drive →

Why this is on the reading list

This commentary deconstructs the unloaded back squat and presents the Back Squat Assessment (BSA) — a 10-criterion, three-domain (Upper Body, Lower Body, Movement Mechanics) movement-screening tool a coach can run with nothing but a dowel and eyes. For CCFT, it is the clearest worked example of using a fundamental movement (the squat) to screen an athlete's neuromuscular control, strength/stability, and mobility before adding load. It directly backs Domain 1's assessment-of-readiness and capacity-to-perform-functional-movements tasks, and supplies the 'demonstrate proficiency before you load' logic (mechanics → consistency → intensity) that recurs across the CrossFit methodology.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 1.1.1 Screen athlete for medical issues (use the squat screen; refer on pain/discomfort)
  • 1.1.2 Recognize conditions/injuries outside CCFT Scope of Practice that require referral
  • 1.2.1 Assess capacity/capability to perform functional movements (the back squat screen)
  • 1.2.5 Identify when athlete is ready to progress to another goal/skill (proficiency before load)
  • 1.2.6 Quantify and track performance (BSA scoring: 0 = perfect; deficit if fault on 2+ of 10 reps)
  • 1.1.4 Assess psychological/training tolerance — establish movement competency before vigorous loading
  • 4.1.1 Identify points of performance (criterion-by-criterion 'desired technique')
  • 4.1.3 Identify faults in movement (the 10 common deficits)
  • 4.1.6 Identify root cause of faults (neuromuscular vs strength vs mobility)
  • 4.2.6 Apply basic principles of anatomy and biomechanics
  • 4.2.7 Address the most egregious fault first (triage the limiting deficit)
  • 5.2.1 Apply mechanics-consistency-intensity to programming for safety and performance
  • 5.2.6 Recognize warning signs for possible injury or overexertion

What to focus on while reading

  • The mechanics → consistency → intensity logic stated plainly: an athlete should demonstrate consistent, proficient bodyweight back squat technique BEFORE adding external load or progressing to plyometrics/loaded variations. Highlight every sentence that says 'do not increase intensity until form is consistent.'
  • The single biggest referral trigger: refer the athlete to a licensed healthcare professional if they report PAIN or DISCOMFORT during ANY phase of the squat assessment. Note this also applies to the pre-screen of neck range of motion.
  • The structure of the BSA: 10 criteria grouped into 3 domains — Upper Body (head, thoracic, trunk), Lower Body (hip, frontal-plane knee, tibial translation, foot), Movement Mechanics (descent, depth, ascent). Memorize the grouping, not the table verbatim.
  • The three deficit categories every fault gets sorted into: Neuromuscular (control/recruitment/awareness), Strength/Stability (weakness/asymmetry/instability), Mobility (joint immobility/tissue tightness). This is the article's root-cause framework.
  • Scoring rules: a perfect score is 0 (ten flawless reps); mark a deficit only if the athlete fails the standard on 2 OR MORE of the 10 reps. The screen is 10 continuous reps at a controlled, moderate pace.
  • Why three viewing angles matter: anterior, posterior, and lateral. Note WHICH faults are seen from WHICH view (e.g., knee valgus/hip drop from anterior/posterior; trunk angle, tibial translation, descent/ascent tempo, depth from lateral).
  • Standardization for reliability: dowel held pronated slightly wider than shoulder width, resting across posterior delts just below C7; forearms parallel to torso; 'bend the bar' to engage lats/retractors and stiffen the torso. Heels ~shoulder-width, toes forward to ≤10° out. The standardized verbal script.
  • Head vs gaze are RELATED BUT INDEPENDENT — head stays neutral (to slight extension); gaze can be straight ahead or slightly up. Downward gaze tends to drive hip/trunk flexion. Athletes tend to move in the direction of their gaze.
  • Trunk standard: maintain a neutral, slightly LORDOTIC lumbar spine and keep the line of the trunk PARALLEL to the line of the tibias (lateral view). A rounded/kyphotic spine under load raises disc-herniation risk.
  • Knee tracking standard (frontal plane): knees track over toes; the LATERAL aspect of the knee should not cross the vertical plane of the MEDIAL malleolus (valgus check), and the medial knee should not cross the lateral malleolus (varus check). Valgus is far more common than varus.
  • The evidence-based myth-busting the article does: there is NO known evidence that squatting below parallel increases injury risk to cruciate/collateral ligaments or menisci; and there is NO defined point at which knees-past-toes becomes harmful — restricting forward translation actually shifts load to hip/spine via increased forward trunk lean. Note this contradicts common gym lore.
  • Tibial translation: keep heels down and let the tibia translate freely with hip ROM; aim to match shin angle to torso angle; initiate by 'breaking the hips back.' Restricting the shins forces forward trunk lean and loads the spine.
  • Foot standard: whole foot stays on the ground; weight shifts to heel and lateral foot ('L' loading) on descent; toes stay down. Heels rising = lost base of support and compensatory torques up the chain; loading lateral foot improves glute recruitment.
  • Descent standard: hip-hinge (break the hips, sit back 'as if into a chair slightly too far away'), keep shoulder-to-hip vertical distance constant, controlled eccentric tempo of 2:1 up to 4:1 (descent:ascent). The classic fault: 'knee-loading' strategy (load drops onto the knees).
  • Depth standard: tops of thighs at LEAST parallel to ground; the common deficit is squatting too SHALLOW (which limits posterior-chain loading and feeds quad-dominance). Excessive depth is rarely harmful unless contraindicated by existing pathology.
  • Ascent standard: hips and shoulders rise at the SAME pace (constant shoulder-hip distance); hip-drive leads. The classic early-learner fault is hips rising faster than shoulders ('stripper/good-morning' fault), which dumps the athlete into trunk flexion — dangerous under load.
  • Valsalva / bracing: inhale ~80% of max and hold to raise intra-abdominal pressure and create 'proximal stiffness'; amount of air scales with load. Connect this to torso stiffness and force output.
  • Anatomical variation limits the 'ideal': hip socket depth and torso-to-leg-length ratio change achievable depth and shin angle — a deep hip socket can BONILY block depth (cannot be stretched away); the kneeling 'pelvic rock' test estimates an individual's safe depth and ideal stance/knee width. Long-femur athletes sit hips back; long-torso athletes share hip/knee load with more shin travel.
  • The screen is unloaded and uses only a dowel — it is positioned as a low-cost alternative to lab testing, NOT a clinical diagnosis. Keep the coach inside scope: screen, refer on pain, correct what's coachable.

Concepts to understand

  • Screening as a coaching act: the unloaded back squat is a single compound movement sensitive enough to expose neuromuscular, strength, and mobility limitations — so a coach can use it to judge readiness to load (Tasks 1.2.1, 1.2.5) without lab equipment.
  • Mechanics → Consistency → Intensity as a gate, not a slogan: proficiency at bodyweight must precede external load and plyometrics; loading a faulty pattern only imprints compensations and raises injury risk. This is the article's core programming/progression principle (Tasks 1.2.5, 5.2.1).
  • Root-cause classification: every observed fault should be attributed to a neuromuscular (control/awareness/recruitment), strength/stability (weakness/asymmetry), or mobility (joint/tissue restriction) cause — because the corrective is different for each. Coaching the symptom without the cause wastes reps (Task 4.1.6).
  • Triage of faults: identify and correct the MOST egregious limiting deficit first; one spinal/positional fault cascades into others (e.g., poor head position drives spinal flexion; restricted ankle/shin drives forward trunk lean; lost hip mobility drives compensatory trunk flexion) (Task 4.2.7).
  • The spine behaves as one unit: a change in one segment forces compensation elsewhere. Cervical hyperextension can compensate for missing thoracic extension; cervical flexion drives lumbar extension/compression — so head position is a torso-stability issue, not a cosmetic one.
  • Bracing and proximal stability: a stiffened torso (erector spinae isometric + abdominal wall tension + Valsalva to ~80% inhalation) turns the flexible spine into a load-bearing rod and enables more force at the hips/shoulders. Stability is built before the descent, not recovered mid-rep.
  • Posterior-chain loading via the hip hinge: breaking the hips back migrates load to glutes/hamstrings (safer for knees and lumbar spine); a 'knee-loading' strategy is the failure mode and usually co-occurs with excessive shin travel and/or heels lifting.
  • Knee valgus is usually ACTIVE and correctable: dynamic medial knee collapse is most often a faulty neuromuscular pattern (hip adduction + knee abduction) driven by weak hip abductors/external rotators, overactive adductors, weak posterior chain, and/or limited ankle dorsiflexion — i.e., often coachable, sometimes a mobility/strength fix.
  • Evidence over gym lore: below-parallel depth is not shown to harm healthy knee ligaments/menisci, and there is no proven 'knees-must-not-pass-toes' threshold — artificially restricting shin travel shifts and increases load on the hip and spine. A coach should cue from evidence, not folklore (relevant to teaching relative intensity and sound mechanics).
  • Depth has a training purpose: squatting to at least parallel adequately challenges the glutes/hamstrings and trains motor-control positions used in sport; chronically shallow squatting reinforces quad-dominance that limits performance and is associated with injury risk.
  • Constant shoulder-to-hip distance is the master tell for both descent and ascent: if that vertical gap changes (hips shoot up on the ascent, or athlete pitches forward on descent), the trunk is flexing and the pattern is unsafe to load.
  • Anatomy individualizes the 'ideal': hip socket geometry and torso:leg ratios mean the textbook positions are targets, not absolutes — bony hip restriction caps depth and cannot be stretched open, so a coach scales depth/stance to the athlete rather than forcing a template (connects screening to scaling, Tasks 5.2.2, 1.2.1).
  • Scope of practice and referral: the coach screens and corrects movement; pain or discomfort in any phase, or suspected pathology a mobility/strength routine doesn't resolve, triggers referral to a licensed healthcare professional (Tasks 1.1.1, 1.1.2, 7.4.1).
  • Standardization buys reliability: fixed arm position, stance, script, viewing angles, rep count, and a clear pass/fail rule (fault on ≥2 of 10 reps) make the assessment repeatable and comparable over time, which is what lets a coach 'quantify and track performance' (Task 1.2.6).
  • Cueing strategy follows cause: positional/awareness (neuromuscular) faults usually respond to verbal/visual/tactile cues; strength and mobility faults need targeted training or mobilization — knowing which it is tells the coach whether a cue will even work.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenarios where you observe a single squat fault and must pick the BEST next action: classify its likely root cause (neuromuscular vs strength vs mobility), choose which fault to address first (triage), decide whether to cue/scale/refer, or judge readiness to add load (Tasks 4.1.3, 4.1.6, 4.2.7, 1.2.1, 1.2.5). Pain-in-any-phase items test referral and scope (Tasks 1.1.1, 1.1.2, 7.4.1). Knees-past-toes and below-parallel items test whether you coach from evidence rather than myth (relative intensity / sound mechanics). 'When is the athlete ready to load?' items test the mechanics-consistency-intensity gate (Tasks 1.2.5, 5.2.1).

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Back Squat Assessment (BSA)
The article's proposed screening tool: 10 scored criteria grouped into three domains (Upper Body, Lower Body, Movement Mechanics), observed over 10 continuous unloaded reps to flag functional deficits before loading.
Functional deficit
An observable movement limitation during the squat caused by inefficient neuromuscular control, muscle weakness/asymmetry/instability, or joint/tissue immobility — flags elevated injury risk and sub-optimal performance.
Neuromuscular deficit
A fault rooted in poor motor control, recruitment, or positional awareness (not strength or mobility) — e.g., active knee valgus or losing neutral head position; usually responsive to cueing and motor practice.
Strength/Stability deficit
A fault from inadequate or asymmetrical force production or joint stability — e.g., not holding chest up (weak erectors/rhomboids) or losing depth (weak posterior chain); needs targeted strengthening.
Mobility deficit
A fault from restricted joint range or tissue tightness — e.g., heels rising from limited ankle dorsiflexion, or capped depth from tight posterior chain/adductors; needs mobilization (and, if bony, may be uncorrectable).
Mechanics → Consistency → Intensity
The progression principle the article operationalizes: establish correct mechanics, prove they are consistent at bodyweight, and only then add intensity/load — so technique survives heavier loading.
Hip hinge (break the hips)
Initiating the descent by sending the hips back ('sit into a chair slightly too far away') to load the posterior chain — the safe alternative to a knee-dominant descent.
Knee-loading strategy
A descent fault where load drops onto the anterior knees instead of the hips; typically co-occurs with excessive shin travel and/or heels lifting and reduces posterior-chain recruitment.
Dynamic (active) knee valgus
Medial collapse of the knee during the squat (hip adduction + knee abduction); identified when the medial knee crosses the vertical plane of the medial malleolus; most often a correctable neuromuscular pattern.
Knee varus
Outward (bow-legged) movement of the knee during the squat — less common than valgus, sometimes a compensation in athletes with flat feet.
Tibial (anterior) translation angle
How far the shin travels forward as the knees move; should be unrestricted with heels down, matched to torso angle — restricting it forces forward trunk lean and loads the hip/spine.
Positive shin angle
The forward inclination of the tibia during the squat; the goal is to achieve it through proper hip kinematics, with shin angle roughly matching torso angle (lateral view).
'L' foot loading
The intended center-of-pressure path: from mid-foot at stance toward the heel and lateral foot during descent, keeping toes down — improves balance and glute recruitment.
Neutral / lordotic lumbar spine
The slight natural inward curve of the low back maintained throughout the squat; preserving it lets the spine bear load safely — losing it (flexion/kyphosis) raises compressive/shear and disc-herniation risk under load.
Valsalva maneuver
Inhaling ~80% of max and briefly holding the breath to raise intra-abdominal pressure, stiffen the spine, and create 'proximal stiffness' for greater limb force; air volume scales with load.
Triple extension
Simultaneous extension of the ankles, knees, and hips that drives the ascent and underlies explosive sport actions like jumping and running.
Constant shoulder-to-hip distance
The vertical gap between shoulders and hips that should stay fixed through descent and ascent; if it shrinks (hips rise first), the trunk is flexing — an unsafe pattern to load.
Closed kinetic chain exercise
Movement with the foot fixed to the ground (like the squat); loads joints in a way that protects the ACL, making it favorable for rehab and for active knee stabilization.
Pelvic rock test
A kneeling self-assessment that estimates an individual's safe squat depth and ideal foot/knee width by rocking the pelvis back until the neutral lumbar curve begins to flex, at progressively wider knee positions.
Anatomical variation
Individual differences — mainly hip socket geometry and torso-to-leg-length ratio — that legitimately alter achievable depth and shin angle; deep hip sockets can bonily block depth and cannot be stretched open.
Upper crossed syndrome
A postural pattern of internally rotated, rounded shoulders with tight/short pectorals that makes it hard to open the chest and retract the scapulae during the squat (a mobility-side cause of a chest-down fault).

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • REFER to a licensed healthcare professional if the athlete reports pain or discomfort during ANY phase of the squat assessment — this is the article's explicit stop-and-refer rule (Tasks 1.1.1, 1.1.2, 7.4.1).
  • Refer on neck pain/discomfort or inability to achieve normal physiological neck range of motion during the pre-screen — abstain from training that athlete until cleared.
  • Excessive cervical hyperextension under load is flagged as dangerous (and is often a compensation for missing thoracic extension) — do not load it.
  • Spinal flexion / rounded (kyphotic) lumbar spine under heavy load raises disc-herniation and shear risk — treat a coach's inability to restore a neutral spine as a stop-loading signal, not a 'push through' moment.
  • Suspected bony/anatomical hip restriction or any fault a sound mobility/strength routine fails to improve warrants evaluation by a licensed healthcare provider — outside CCFT scope to diagnose or treat.
  • Scope boundary: the BSA is a coaching screen and a low-cost alternative to lab testing — it is NOT a medical diagnosis; the coach screens, cues, scales, and refers, but does not diagnose pathology.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. During a bodyweight squat screen, an athlete reports a sharp pinch in the front of the hip at the bottom of every rep. The athlete has full ankle mobility and otherwise clean mechanics. What is the BEST coaching action?

  1. A. Add a banded distraction and have the athlete squat deeper to 'work through' the pinch
  2. B. Load a barbell to see if the pinch changes under tension
  3. C. Stop the movement and refer the athlete to a licensed healthcare professional
  4. D. Cue the athlete to widen stance and continue to full depth
  5. E. Tell the athlete the pinch is normal hip impingement and ignore it
Show answer

Answer: C — Pain or discomfort during ANY phase of the squat assessment is the article's explicit referral trigger and is outside CCFT scope to diagnose or treat. A and D push through pain (and a deep bony hip restriction cannot be stretched away); B adds load to a painful pattern; E dismisses a flagged symptom. Only C respects the stop-and-refer rule.

Scenario 2. An athlete's knees collapse inward (medial knee crosses the medial malleolus) during the bottom of the squat. There is no pain, ankle dorsiflexion is adequate, and the collapse appears when they speed up. What is the MOST likely root cause to address first?

  1. A. A mobility deficit — tight Achilles limiting dorsiflexion
  2. B. A neuromuscular deficit — active valgus from a faulty hip-adduction/knee-abduction pattern with insufficient posterior-chain control
  3. C. A structural deficit requiring orthopedic referral
  4. D. A footwear problem — switch to lifters and retest
  5. E. Insufficient squat depth pulling the knees in
Show answer

Answer: B — The article identifies active dynamic valgus (hip adduction + knee abduction from muscular contraction) as the most common driver, typically tied to weak hip abductors/external rotators and inadequate posterior-chain recruitment — a neuromuscular/strength issue that usually responds to cueing and training. A is ruled out (dorsiflexion is adequate); C is premature with no pain; D/E are not the primary mechanism the article cites.

Scenario 3. A coach wants to decide whether a new athlete is ready to start adding load to the back squat. Which standard best reflects the article's guidance?

  1. A. Add load immediately; loading reveals faults faster than bodyweight reps
  2. B. The athlete may load once they can demonstrate consistent, proficient bodyweight back squat technique across the screen
  3. C. Readiness is based purely on the athlete's training goal, not their mechanics
  4. D. Any athlete who can reach parallel once is ready for a 1RM test
  5. E. Load when the athlete reports they 'feel ready,' regardless of observed mechanics
Show answer

Answer: B — The mechanics → consistency → intensity principle is explicit: demonstrate consistent, proper bodyweight technique BEFORE adding external resistance or progressing to plyometrics. Loading a faulty pattern (A, D) imprints compensations and raises injury risk; C and E ignore the movement standard the gate is built on.

Scenario 4. An athlete asks you to stop them from letting their knees travel past their toes because they read it 'destroys the knees.' They are a long-femur athlete and forcing vertical shins makes them pitch their chest toward the floor. Best response?

  1. A. Agree and place a board to physically block the knees from moving forward
  2. B. Explain there is no proven point where knees-past-toes becomes harmful; restricting shin travel actually shifts and increases load on the hip and spine via forward trunk lean — let the shins track naturally with heels down
  3. C. Tell them to squat only to a quarter-depth so the knees never pass the toes
  4. D. Switch them to leg extensions to avoid the squat entirely
  5. E. Have them squat on their toes so the knees can travel freely
Show answer

Answer: B — The article directly refutes the knees-behind-toes rule: with feet fixed, anterior tibial translation should be unrestricted, and consciously restricting it increases forward trunk lean and raises hip/spine forces. A and C reproduce the harmful restriction (and waste the squat's benefit); D abandons the movement; E violates the heels-down/whole-foot standard.

Scenario 5. On the ascent out of the bottom of the squat, an athlete's hips shoot up faster than their shoulders, dumping the chest forward. There is no pain. What does this most likely indicate, and what is the priority?

  1. A. Excellent hip drive — reinforce it and add load
  2. B. The shoulder-to-hip distance is collapsing, indicating a posterior-chain/hip-extension control fault; prioritize correcting it before loading because it is dangerous to the low back under resistance
  3. C. A pure ankle mobility problem — mobilize ankles and retest
  4. D. A breathing error — have them exhale at the bottom
  5. E. An equipment issue — give them a weight belt and proceed
Show answer

Answer: B — Hips rising faster than shoulders shrinks the constant shoulder-to-hip vertical distance and forces trunk flexion — an incorrect pattern the article calls dangerous to the lumbar spine under progressive load, often tied to weak/under-recruited posterior chain and hip extensors. It is a fault to fix, not reinforce (A); ankle mobility (C), breath timing (D), and a belt (E) don't address the root pattern. The article also advises exhaling only after the ascent is complete, so D is wrong on its face.

Scenario 6. A coach can only watch the squat from one angle for a quick check of dynamic knee valgus and a unilateral hip drop. Which viewing perspective is MOST appropriate?

  1. A. Lateral (side) view
  2. B. Anterior (or posterior) view
  3. C. A 45-degree oblique view only
  4. D. Overhead view
  5. E. Any view works equally for these faults
Show answer

Answer: B — Frontal-plane knee alignment (valgus/varus) and hip-line symmetry/unilateral dropping are assessed from the anterior or posterior perspective. The lateral view (A) is for trunk angle, tibial translation, descent/ascent tempo, and depth. The article specifies multi-angle screening precisely because faults are angle-specific; for valgus and hip drop, frontal-plane viewing is required, so E is incorrect.

Scenario 7. An athlete consistently squats only to a quarter-depth and is very quad-dominant. They have no pain and adequate mobility. According to the article, why does depth matter and what should the coach do?

  1. A. Shallow squatting is safer and should be preserved to protect the knees
  2. B. Shallow depth under-loads the glutes/hamstrings and reinforces quad-dominance that limits performance and is linked to injury risk; cue/scale toward at-least-parallel depth
  3. C. Depth is irrelevant as long as the athlete moves load
  4. D. Force the athlete to a deep ATG squat immediately regardless of control
  5. E. Refer the athlete for imaging because shallow squatting is a medical red flag
Show answer

Answer: B — The article states squatting to at least parallel is needed to adequately challenge the posterior chain and train sport-relevant motor control, and that shallow training feeds quad-dominance associated with injury risk. A and C contradict the text; D ignores the need for control and individual anatomy; E misapplies referral (no pain/pathology is present) — shallow depth here is a coaching/scaling issue, not a medical emergency.

Scenario 8. During the screen an athlete keeps losing a neutral spine, and you notice their head is dropping into a downward gaze on every rep. Best first cue, and why?

  1. A. Cue a downward gaze to 'protect the neck' — head and gaze are the same thing
  2. B. Cue gaze straight ahead or slightly up while keeping the head neutral, because athletes tend to move in the direction of their gaze and a downward gaze drives hip/trunk flexion
  3. C. Ignore the head and only cue the lumbar spine
  4. D. Cue maximal cervical hyperextension to force the chest up
  5. E. Add load so the athlete 'tightens up' automatically
Show answer

Answer: B — The article treats head and gaze as related but independent: keep the head neutral (to slight extension) while gaze stays forward or slightly up, since downward gaze increases hip/trunk flexion and athletes drift toward their gaze. A conflates head and gaze; C ignores how the head cascades into spinal position; D introduces a flagged-dangerous cervical hyperextension; E loads a faulty pattern.

Scenario 9. An athlete's heels rise off the floor at the bottom of the squat, the shins travel far forward, and the load visibly shifts onto the knees. No pain. How should the coach interpret and prioritize this?

  1. A. It's a harmless style choice — leave it alone
  2. B. It's a clustered 'knee-loading' pattern often tied to limited ankle dorsiflexion (mobility) and/or weak posterior chain; restore a whole-foot/heels-down base and hip-hinge loading, and consider a heel block as a temporary aid
  3. C. Immediately refer for surgery
  4. D. Tell the athlete to squat faster to power through the sticking point
  5. E. Cue the athlete to push the knees even further forward
Show answer

Answer: B — Heels lifting reduces the base of support and creates compensatory torques; it commonly co-occurs with excessive tibial translation and a knee-loading descent, with root causes in ankle dorsiflexion mobility and/or posterior-chain strength. The article suggests a heel block as an interim aid while mobility improves. A dismisses a real fault; C misapplies referral with no pain; D and E worsen the pattern.

Scenario 10. Two athletes get a 'shallow depth' deficit. Athlete X is tight in the posterior chain and adductors; Athlete Y has a deep hip socket that bonily blocks further depth (confirmed by limited range with no soft-tissue give). What is the BEST coaching distinction?

  1. A. Treat both identically with aggressive stretching to force parallel
  2. B. Stretch/mobilize Athlete X toward greater depth, but scale Athlete Y's depth to their anatomy because a bony hip restriction cannot be stretched open
  3. C. Refer both immediately; shallow depth always indicates pathology
  4. D. Load both heavily so the extra weight drives them deeper
  5. E. Tell both to squat to whatever depth feels good with no standard
Show answer

Answer: B — The article distinguishes mobility-driven limits (Athlete X — tight posterior chain/adductors, improvable) from anatomical/bony limits (Athlete Y — hip socket geometry that cannot be stretched away, so scale depth to the individual). A and D try to force past a bony block; C over-refers a non-painful coaching issue; E abandons the standard entirely. Matching the corrective to the root cause is the article's central logic.

D2 · Programming
