D2 · Programming 14% of exam Confidence tier: ___

06_03_CF_Template.pdf

PDF link not yet available

Why this is on the reading list

This is the foundational programming article on the CCFT reading list: it is the explicit bridge from CrossFit's philosophy of fitness ('What is Fitness?') to the construction of actual workouts. It supplies the template a coach uses to design single workouts and to sequence them into a GPP-building cycle that crosses all three modalities and hits all three metabolic pathways while preserving constant variance. It directly backs Domain 2 (Programming) tasks 2.1.1 and 2.1.2, and underpins how mechanics-consistency-intensity is applied to programming in Domain 5 (5.2.1).

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 2.1.1 Design single workouts using the CrossFit methodology
  • 2.1.2 Design a sequence of workouts that improves general physical preparedness (GPP)
  • 2.3.2 Use benchmarks to assess effectiveness of programming
  • 2.3.4 Evaluate athlete progress relative to CrossFit's definition of fitness and their personal goal
  • 5.2.1 Apply mechanics-consistency-intensity to programming for safety and performance
  • 5.2.10 Manage logistics (ratio, equipment demands, duration, space)
  • 3.1.9 Teach the goals of CrossFit programming and how goals are met (programming with variance)

What to focus on while reading

  • The central tension the template is built to resolve: structure vs. variance. Note Glassman's line 'What your regimen needs is to not become routine' and that the template is 'as much descriptive as prescriptive' — it is NOT a fixed routine to copy.
  • The seven variables the template intentionally leaves open to variance: mode, exercise, metabolic pathway, rest, intensity, sets, and reps. Be able to list these.
  • The two macro patterns: 3-days-on / 1-day-off (the primary one discussed) and 5-days-on / 2-days-off (the accommodation for normal work/school/family weeks).
  • WHY the 3-on/1-off pattern exists: it allows a higher volume of high-intensity work; by day 4 neuromuscular function and anatomy are 'hammered' so continued work is less effective without dropping intensity. The 4th day off is recovery, not arbitrary.
  • The honest trade-off Glassman makes: the 3-on/1-off does not sync with the 7-day week; the 5-on/2-off is slightly less effective but convenience, attitude, exercise selection, and pacing can overshadow that gap. Coaching judgment, not dogma.
  • The three MODALITIES and the PRIMARY ADAPTATION each targets: M (monostructural/'cardio' = cardiorespiratory capacity & stamina), G (gymnastics/bodyweight = body control, the neurological skills — coordination, balance, agility, accuracy — plus upper-body and trunk capacity), W (weightlifting = strength, power, hip/leg capacity).
  • The selection criteria for which exercises populate each modality: functionality, neuroendocrine (neuroendocrine/neuroendocrine) response, and broad/dramatic impact on the body. Know example exercises in each column of Table 2.
  • The workout STRUCTURE by element count — this is the heart of the article:
  • Single-element days (1, 5, 9) = PRIORITY ELEMENT / single effort. M = long slow distance; G = a single high-skill movement practiced (often too complex to time yet); W = a single heavy lift, low rep. Recovery is NOT a limiting factor; rest is long and deliberate; focus is the element, not metabolic effect.
  • Two-element days (2, 6, 10) = TASK PRIORITY couplet, typically 3-5 rounds (most often 5) for time. Task is fixed, time varies. Moderate-to-high intensity. Work/rest interval management is CRITICAL. Calibration cue: round 1 should be 'hard but possible'; if round 2 is easy, the elements are too light.
  • Three-element days (3, 7, 11) = TIME PRIORITY triplet, typically 20 minutes, scored by rounds/rotations completed (AMRAP). Athlete kept moving for a set time; elements are individually light-to-moderate and only become a challenge through repeated cycles. Work/rest management is a MARGINAL factor here.
  • The unifying principle stated near the end: as element count rises from 1 to 2 to 3, the workout's effect depends LESS on the individual element chosen and MORE on the effect of repeated efforts.
  • The worked examples in Table 4 — map each to its structure (e.g., 'Run 10K' = single M; '(5 HSPU / 225x5 deadlift +20lb/round) x5 for time' = two-element couplet; 'Run 400m/10 pull-ups/Thruster 50%BW x15 for 20 min' = three-element AMRAP).
  • Three scoring/quantification methods embedded here: single-effort load/distance, time-to-complete (task priority), and rounds-in-time (time priority) — these are how you benchmark and track (2.3.2, 1.2.6).
  • The closing 'Application' framing: the template was reverse-engineered FROM the qualities of 1/2/3-element WODs, not the other way around; good workouts have 'composition, symmetry, balance, theme, and character' — programming as a craft, not a formula.

Concepts to understand

  • Theory-to-practice bridge: the template's job is to operationalize the 'What is Fitness?' definition of fitness into concrete daily workouts. Understand it as the connective tissue between philosophy and the WOD, not as a workout calendar to memorize.
  • Structured variance: a coach must hold structure (a defensible framework of modalities, pathways, and day-types) and flexibility (constant variation of the open variables) at the same time. Apply by designing a cycle that is systematic in its coverage yet unpredictable in its specifics.
  • The three modalities as coverage, not preference: M, G, and W together force broad adaptation. Programming that over-weights one modality (e.g., all 'W' because the coach likes barbells) violates the template's intent and produces narrow fitness.
  • Modality-to-adaptation mapping: be able to justify WHY a given workout is on the calendar by naming the adaptation it drives (e.g., a single heavy-lift day develops strength/power; a long row develops cardiorespiratory endurance/stamina).
  • Hitting all three metabolic pathways across the cycle: the template is engineered so that, over a 3-day block, programming touches phosphagen, glycolytic, and oxidative pathways — single heavy/skill efforts, short hard couplets, and longer AMRAPs respectively. Apply by checking a week for pathway balance, not just movement variety.
  • Priority type drives stimulus — the most exam-relevant distinction: 'Priority Element' (focus the movement/effort), 'Task Priority' (fixed work, time floats — couplets for time), 'Time Priority' (fixed time, work floats — triplets as AMRAPs). Choosing the priority type IS choosing the stimulus.
  • Inverse relationship between element count and intensity-per-element: 1 element = highest intensity/skill on that single thing; 2 elements = high intensity, manage work/rest; 3 elements = lower per-element intensity, the volume/repetition is the stressor. Apply when you want a specific physiological effect.
  • Calibration of difficulty by feel: 'first round hard but possible; if round two is easy it's too light' is a concrete loading heuristic the coach uses to scale loads, reps, and pace so the intended stimulus actually lands.
  • Recovery as a programmed variable: the 4th day off and the long deliberate rests on single-element days are deliberate recovery decisions tied to intensity, not afterthoughts. Programming intensity and programming recovery are the same decision.
  • Macro-pattern selection is a coaching judgment for the athlete's life context: pick 3-on/1-off for maximal stimulus when scheduling allows, or 5-on/2-off when work/school/family demand a 7-day-week rhythm — accepting a small effectiveness trade for adherence.
  • Programming as craft/art: 'choreography of exertion' built from physiological knowledge, the limits of human performance, effective elements, experimentation, and luck. Understand that the template aids the art but does not replace coaching judgment and observation.
  • Descriptive vs. prescriptive: the template describes the shape of good CrossFit programming more than it dictates exact workouts; real WODs do not fit it 'neatly and cleanly.' Apply it as a lens for analyzing/auditing a program, not a rigid cookie-cutter.
  • Feedback-driven evaluation: Glassman built and validated the model from athlete feedback and gym observation. The coach should likewise evaluate programming by tracking results and adjusting — connecting to using benchmarks and progress evaluation.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenario questions that hand you a workout (or a week of them) and ask you to classify its structure, name the priority type, predict its stimulus, or spot what is missing from a cycle — these map to 2.1.1 (design single workouts) and 2.1.2 (sequence for GPP). You will likely face items where an athlete's program over-emphasizes one modality or one priority type and you must choose the correction that restores variance and pathway/modality balance (2.1.2, 3.1.9). Other items test the inverse element-count/intensity relationship and the difficulty-calibration cue ('round one hard but possible'), asking what to adjust when a couplet or AMRAP is mis-loaded (2.1.1, 5.2.1). Scoring-method questions (load/distance vs. time-to-complete vs. rounds-in-time) surface as benchmarking and tracking choices (2.3.2, 2.3.4, 1.2.6), and logistics/scheduling questions test choosing 3-on/1-off vs. 5-on/2-off for a given athlete's life (5.2.10).

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Theoretical template
A structured-but-flexible model for building CrossFit workouts that defines programming objectives (modalities, day-types, priority) while leaving mode, exercise, pathway, rest, intensity, sets, and reps open to variance. It is descriptive as much as prescriptive.
Constant variance / 'not become routine'
The CrossFit programming requirement that workouts stay unpredictable so they mimic the random demands of sport, combat, and survival. The template formalizes coverage without freezing the specifics.
3-on / 1-off
The primary training cycle: three consecutive high-intensity training days followed by one rest day. Maximizes volume of high-intensity work; by day 4 the body is too taxed to keep intensity high, so it rests.
5-on / 2-off
A slightly less effective but life-friendly weekly cycle (train five days, rest two) that syncs with the standard work/school week. Used when scheduling and adherence outweigh the small loss in effectiveness.
Modality
One of the three movement categories the template programs across — M, G, W. Each is represented in a workout by a single exercise.
Monostructural metabolic conditioning (M)
'Cardio' — single-structure activities like run, row, bike, jump rope. Primary aim: improve cardiorespiratory capacity and stamina.
Gymnastics (G)
Bodyweight/calisthenic movements (air squat, pull-up, push-up, dip, HSPU, rope climb, muscle-up, sit-up, jumps). Primary aim: body control via the neurological skills (coordination, balance, agility, accuracy) plus upper-body and trunk capacity.
Weightlifting (W)
Olympic lifts and powerlifting basics (deadlift, clean, press, snatch, clean & jerk, KB swing, med-ball drills). Primary aim: strength, power, and hip/leg capacity.
Single-element day (Priority: Element)
Days 1, 5, 9 — one modality, one exercise, single effort. M = long slow distance; G = practice one high-skill movement; W = one heavy low-rep lift. Recovery is not a limiting factor; rest is long and deliberate.
Two-element day / couplet (Task Priority)
Days 2, 6, 10 — two alternating exercises, typically 3-5 (usually 5) rounds for time. Task is fixed and time varies; moderate-to-high intensity; work/rest interval management is critical.
Three-element day / triplet (Time Priority)
Days 3, 7, 11 — three exercises cycled for a set time (typically 20 min), scored by rounds/rotations completed (AMRAP). Time is fixed and work varies; individually light-to-moderate elements made hard by repetition; work/rest management is a marginal factor.
Task priority
A scoring/structure approach where the amount of work is fixed and the time to finish is the score (e.g., 5 rounds for time). The athlete races a set task.
Time priority
A scoring/structure approach where the duration is fixed and the amount of work completed is the score (e.g., AMRAP in 20 minutes). The athlete accumulates as many rounds as possible.
Neuroendocrine response
The hormonal/nervous-system reaction to training; one of the criteria (with functionality and broad bodily impact) used to select the exercises that populate each modality.
GPP (General Physical Preparedness)
Broad, general fitness across all capacities. Sequencing the template's day-types and modalities over a cycle is how a coach builds GPP rather than narrow specialization.
Choreography of exertion
Glassman's framing of well-composed programming as a craft — built from physiological knowledge, the limits of human performance, effective elements, experimentation, and luck; marked by composition, symmetry, balance, theme, and character.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • Treating the template as a fixed routine to copy verbatim contradicts its purpose — programming that stops varying ('becomes routine') violates the constant-variance requirement and narrows fitness.
  • The article is a programming model, not a safety or medical document. Intensity is built into every day-type, so the coach must still apply mechanics-consistency-intensity ordering and scale load/reps/pace to the athlete; do not push a novice into prescribed RX loads to 'match the template.'
  • Single heavy-lift days (W) and high-intensity couplets carry injury and (with very high-rep, novel, or eccentric-heavy efforts) rhabdomyolysis risk — the template does not address screening or scaling, so those judgments come from the coach and other articles.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. An athlete shows you a 'Run 400m / 10 pull-ups / Thruster at 50% bodyweight x15, AMRAP 20 minutes' workout and asks how to attack it. Using the template's logic, what is your best coaching guidance?

  1. A. Treat it like a couplet: go all-out on round one and expect to fade — the elements are meant to be very high intensity.
  2. B. Recognize it as a three-element time-priority workout where the elements are individually light-to-moderate; settle into a sustainable 'blistering but repeatable' pace because the challenge comes from accumulated rounds, not any single element.
  3. C. Rest long and deliberately between movements and prioritize perfecting each rep, since recovery is not a limiting factor on this day.
  4. D. Stop at five rounds for time, since triplets are scored by time to complete five rounds.
  5. E. Drop the thruster load to a single heavy rep because three-element days are about strength.
Show answer

Answer: B — Three-element days (3, 7, 11) are time-priority AMRAPs: fixed time, score = rounds completed, elements individually light-to-moderate and made hard only by repeated cycles, so pacing for sustainability maximizes rotations. A describes the two-element/couplet character (high intensity), not triplets. C describes single-element days where recovery isn't limiting. D applies couplet scoring (rounds for time) to a time-priority piece. E confuses it with a single heavy-lift day.

Scenario 2. A coach has programmed the last three weeks almost entirely as heavy single-lift days and barbell couplets because 'strength is king.' Athletes are getting stronger but gassing out on anything longer than five minutes and their pull-up and handstand skills have stalled. What is the best programming fix per the template?

  1. A. Add even more weightlifting volume; the conditioning will follow strength.
  2. B. Switch entirely to long monostructural cardio for a few weeks to rebuild the engine.
  3. C. Restore variance by rotating across all three modalities (M, G, W) and all three day-types — including gymnastics-skill days and longer time-priority triplets — so the cycle again builds broad GPP across all metabolic pathways.
  4. D. Keep the modalities the same but just randomize the loads each day.
  5. E. Drop rest days to a 6-on/1-off pattern so there's more time to fit everything in.
Show answer

Answer: C — The template builds GPP by crossing all three modalities and all three day-types so the program hits all metabolic pathways and the full skill set. The symptoms (poor stamina, stalled gymnastics) signal lost variance and modality imbalance, fixed by restoring the full rotation (2.1.2). A and B each over-weight one modality — the same mistake in a new direction. D leaves the imbalance intact. E adds volume without recovery and ignores the actual gap (modality/day-type coverage); Glassman notes the body is hammered by day four.

Scenario 3. You program a two-element couplet — '(5 handstand push-ups / 5 deadlifts) x 5 rounds for time' — and your fittest athlete cruises through round two with no breaks and finishes barely winded. According to the template, what should you conclude and do?

  1. A. Perfect — task-priority workouts are supposed to feel comfortable after the first round.
  2. B. The elements are too easy; increase load, reps, or pace so round one is 'hard but possible' and later rounds force pacing, rest, and breaking the work into manageable chunks.
  3. C. Convert it to a 20-minute AMRAP, since couplets should always be time-priority.
  4. D. Add a third element on the spot to make it a single-element day.
  5. E. Tell the athlete to slow down so the workout lasts longer.
Show answer

Answer: B — Glassman gives an explicit calibration cue for couplets: the first round should be hard but possible, and 'if the second round can be completed without trouble, the elements are too easy.' The remedy is to raise intensity via load, reps, or pace. A inverts the intent. C and D misclassify the workout (a 20-min AMRAP is a triplet/time-priority structure; adding/removing elements changes the day-type entirely). E manipulates the athlete instead of correcting the programming.

Scenario 4. A client works a standard Monday-Friday job with weekends reserved for family, and is frustrated trying to follow the 3-on/1-off cycle because the rest day keeps landing on workdays. What does the template say you should do?

  1. A. Insist on 3-on/1-off regardless — it's the only correct CrossFit pattern and the difference is too large to give up.
  2. B. Have them skip the off day whenever it falls on a workday so they always train Monday-Friday.
  3. C. Move them to the 5-on/2-off pattern; it's slightly less effective in theory, but convenience, attitude, exercise selection, and pacing can overshadow that gap, and adherence matters more.
  4. D. Tell them to train twice a day on weekends to make up the volume.
  5. E. Abandon structured programming and just do random workouts whenever they have time.
Show answer

Answer: C — Glassman explicitly devised the 5-on/2-off pattern for people whose work/school/family scheduling needs a 7-day-week rhythm, and says the potential difference 'may not warrant restructuring your entire life,' since convenience, attitude, exercise selection, and pacing can overshadow it. A is dogmatic and contradicts the text. B removes recovery the cycle depends on. D piles on volume without addressing the scheduling reality. E throws out the structure the template exists to provide (5.2.10, 2.1.2).

Scenario 5. Day 5 of a cycle is a single-element gymnastics day and you have programmed handstand practice. A newer athlete asks why it isn't 'for time' like the other days. What is the best, template-accurate answer?

  1. A. It was an oversight; everything in CrossFit should be timed for intensity.
  2. B. Single-element gymnastics days are for practicing a complex, high-skill movement where recovery isn't the limiter and the focus is improving the skill itself — it may not yet be good enough to include efficiently in a timed workout.
  3. C. Gymnastics never counts as real training, so timing it would be pointless.
  4. D. We time it; you'll do max handstand hold and we'll score the seconds as your metcon.
  5. E. Skip it and do a heavy deadlift instead, since strength transfers to gymnastics.
Show answer

Answer: B — On single-element days (1, 5, 9) the focus is the element, not metabolic effect: the G day is practice of a single complex skill, rest is long and deliberate, recovery is not a limiting factor, and the skill 'may not be yet suitable for inclusion in a timed workout because performance is not yet adequate for efficient inclusion.' A and D force a metcon frame onto a skill day. C dismisses a core modality. E swaps modality and abandons the programmed skill development the cycle needs (2.1.1, 3.1.9).

Scenario 6. Across a single 3-day block you want to confirm your programming is hitting the breadth the template intends. Which week best reflects the model's design?

  1. A. Day 1: heavy back squat singles; Day 2: heavy deadlift couplet; Day 3: heavy clean triplet — all barbell, all heavy.
  2. B. Day 1: long slow row (single M, oxidative); Day 2: a moderate-to-high-intensity couplet for time (mixed, glycolytic); Day 3: a 20-minute triplet AMRAP crossing modalities (sustained, oxidative/mixed) — varying day-type, modality mix, and metabolic pathway.
  3. C. Three identical 20-minute AMRAPs of the same triplet to drive consistency.
  4. D. Day 1: max-effort sprints; Day 2: more sprints; Day 3: even more sprints — to specialize the engine.
  5. E. Three rest days, because the body is hammered by the fourth day anyway.
Show answer

Answer: B — The template's intent is breadth: differing day-types (priority-element, task-priority, time-priority), a mix of modalities, and coverage of multiple metabolic pathways across the block to build GPP. B demonstrates that breadth. A, C, and D each collapse the variance into one modality, one day-type, or one pathway — narrow specialization the template is built to avoid. E misreads the recovery logic: the 4th day is the rest day, not days 1-3 (2.1.2, 2.1.1).

Scenario 7. You want a benchmark you can re-test to track an athlete's progress on a task-priority workout. Which scoring method matches that day-type, and how is improvement read?

  1. A. Score by rounds completed in a fixed time; more rounds next time means improvement.
  2. B. Score by the load lifted for a single rep; a heavier single means improvement.
  3. C. Score by the time required to complete the set task (e.g., 5 rounds); a faster time on a future re-test, at the same work, means improvement.
  4. D. Score by total calories burned as shown on a monitor.
  5. E. Task-priority workouts can't be scored, so use perceived exertion only.
Show answer

Answer: C — Task priority fixes the work and lets time vary, so the score is time-to-complete and a faster time on the same task indicates improved capacity — a clean re-testable benchmark (2.3.2, 2.3.4, 1.2.6). A is the time-priority (AMRAP) scoring method. B is the single-element heavy-lift scoring method. D is not the template's scoring construct for couplets. E is false — the workout is explicitly 'scored by the time required to complete five rounds.'

PDF link not yet available

Why this is on the reading list

This Glassman article introduces 'The Girls' (Angie, Barbara, Chelsea, Diane, Elizabeth, Fran) and explains WHY a coach repeats fixed, named workouts: only by repeating an identical workout can you measure progress objectively. It is the conceptual backbone for using benchmarks to evaluate programming effectiveness (Task 2.3.2) and to track work capacity over time (1.2.6, 1.2.2). It also exposes the design logic behind these couplets and calisthenic triplets — varied metabolic demand, the centrality of the pull-up, and how the same workout exposes different weaknesses in different athletes — which directly informs single-workout design (2.1.1) and scaling decisions (2.2.x).

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 2.3.2 Use benchmarks to assess effectiveness of programming
  • 2.3.1 Evaluate program success relative to athlete goals and needs
  • 2.3.3 Adjust programming based on performance and goals
  • 2.3.4 Evaluate athlete progress relative to CrossFit's definition of fitness and their personal goal
  • 2.1.1 Design single workouts using the CrossFit methodology
  • 2.1.2 Design a sequence of workouts that improves general physical preparedness (GPP)
  • 2.2.5 Scale by skill level
  • 2.2.3 Scale for athletes with sport-specific goals
  • 1.2.2 Evaluate athlete's work capacity
  • 1.2.6 Quantify and track performance
  • 1.2.5 Identify when athlete is ready to progress to another goal/skill

What to focus on while reading

  • The exact composition of all six benchmarks: Angie (100 pull-ups, 100 push-ups, 100 sit-ups, 100 squats, one exercise fully completed before the next, for time); Barbara (5 rounds of 20 pull-ups / 30 push-ups / 40 sit-ups / 50 squats, 3 min rest between rounds, for time); Chelsea (5 pull-ups / 10 push-ups / 15 squats every minute on the minute for 30 minutes); Diane (21-15-9 deadlift 225 lb + handstand push-ups); Elizabeth (21-15-9 clean 135 lb + ring dips); Fran (21-15-9 thruster 95 lb + pull-ups).
  • The naming convention itself: benchmarks get a female given name so they are instantly recognizable in the WOD stream — note the National Weather Service rationale Glassman cites (short distinctive names reduce error).
  • The two thematic groups: Group 1 (Angie, Barbara, Chelsea) = pure calisthenics emphasizing the pull-up; Group 2 (Diane, Elizabeth, Fran) = weightlifting-plus-gymnastics couplets.
  • The varied metabolic stimulus across Group 1 — Angie ~20 min steady, aerobic flavor increasing throughout; Barbara ~3 min work / 3 min rest x5 = aerobic interval at ~1:1 with strong anaerobic character; Chelsea ~40 sec on / 20 sec off = anaerobic interval with abbreviated rest giving an aerobic flavor (a hybrid like Tabata).
  • How the stimulus SHIFTS within each Group 1 workout: Angie gets steadier as it progresses; Barbara's rounds lengthen while rest stays fixed, raising aerobic demand; Chelsea's rest shrinks as rounds lengthen but rest can never exceed 1 minute.
  • The 'exploiting weakness' theme in Group 2: larger athletes typically find the loads easy but fail the gymnastics (HSPU, ring dips, pull-ups); smaller athletes breeze the gymnastics but struggle with the loads and reps; middleweights suffer at both ends.
  • The repeatability-for-measurement thesis: 'Only by repeating workouts can we confidently measure our progress' — and the instruction to complete a posted Girl within three days and log results to build a performance database.
  • The non-negotiable rule of execution: complete the full prescribed reps of one exercise before moving on; you may break any set into subsets but cannot 'roll on' early.
  • The explicit scaling permission: if the loads exceed your capacity even at a few reps you have 'no choice but to amend the workout with lighter loads' — Rx is not mandatory.
  • The pacing/strategy guidance for Group 2: chop sets into manageable subsets (e.g., 7x3 round one, 5x3 round two, 3x3 round three); elite times ~4 minutes, but 'no shame' in 60 minutes.
  • Why the pull-up is treated as sacrosanct and 'everyone needs more' — and the lat/rear-delt/biceps soreness athletes report.
  • The portability/practicality angle: Group 1 needs only a pull-up bar and ~15 sq ft — relevant to programming for travel or constrained equipment.
  • Glassman's framing of workout design as 'the choreography of exertion' — symmetry, theme, character — i.e., these are deliberately engineered exemplars, not random.
  • The skill-gate movements singled out for development: handstand push-up (a 'gateway movement') and ring dip ('the ring dip is to the bar dip as squats are to leg press').

Concepts to understand

  • Benchmarks measure programming AND the athlete: a repeated, standardized, fixed-prescription workout is the measuring stick. Because the stimulus is held constant, a faster time (or more rounds) is a clean signal that fitness improved — this is the practical mechanism behind Task 2.3.2 and 1.2.6.
  • Why repeatability is required for valid measurement: if you never repeat an identical task you cannot separate 'the athlete got fitter' from 'this workout was just easier.' Constant test = interpretable result.
  • Same modalities can yield different metabolic stimuli: Angie, Barbara, and Chelsea share the same movements yet train different energy pathways because of structure (continuous vs. fixed-rest intervals vs. EMOM with shrinking rest). Structure — not just movement selection — drives the training effect.
  • Work-to-rest ratio and interval length determine the dominant energy system: ~3 min on / 3 min off (Barbara) sits at the aerobic/anaerobic border; ~40 on / 20 off (Chelsea) is anaerobic with an aerobic overlay; continuous effort (Angie) is aerobic-dominant. Understand how to read a workout's structure and predict its stimulus.
  • Couplet design (Group 2) pairs a heavy/structural weightlifting movement with a demanding gymnastics movement to produce a whole-body stimulus across functional hip, push, and pull patterns — the essence of constantly varied functional movement at high intensity.
  • Benchmarks expose individual weaknesses by design: the same workout punishes the big/strong athlete's gymnastics and the small/skilled athlete's strength. A coach uses this diagnostic value to identify the limiting modality and direct future programming and skill work (1.2.5, 2.3.3).
  • Scaling preserves the intended stimulus: amend loads/reps so the athlete can still hit the metabolic and movement target. Lighter loads or subset strategies keep the workout 'the same workout' for that athlete while protecting mechanics and safety (2.2.5, 2.2.3).
  • Rep-completion discipline defines the workout: the prescribed structure (finish all reps of a movement before advancing; break into subsets as needed) is part of the test — changing the order or rolling on early invalidates the comparison.
  • GPP is built by repeated, broad, varied exposure: 'doing the WOD' IS training for the Girls — general training transfers to performance on these standardized tests, which is the GPP thesis (2.1.2).
  • Tracking and database-building: logging benchmark results over time creates the longitudinal data a coach needs to quantify progress, set goals, and adjust programming — connect this to 1.2.6 and 2.3.3/2.3.4.
  • Movement development as programming input: identifying a benchmark-exposed deficiency (e.g., no HSPU, no ring dip) tells the coach what progressions and skill practice to program next, and when an athlete is ready to attempt the Rx version (1.2.5).
  • Design intent vs. randomness: 'best' CrossFit workouts are deliberately engineered for impact, balance, and stimulus — the coach should be able to articulate WHY a workout is built the way it is, not just run it (2.1.1).

How the exam applies this

Expect scenarios that ask you to pick the right benchmark to RE-TEST a specific quality (e.g., choosing Fran to reassess high-intensity anaerobic capacity, or Angie to gauge aerobic-leaning bodyweight endurance), or to interpret a result — a faster Fran after a training block is evidence the program is working (2.3.2, 2.3.4). Other items will give an athlete profile (large/strong vs. small/skilled) and ask how to scale a Girl while preserving its stimulus (2.2.3, 2.2.5), or ask you to predict/explain a workout's metabolic demand from its work-to-rest structure (2.1.1, 1.2.2). You may also be asked how to use a benchmark diagnostically to decide what to program next or whether an athlete is ready to progress to the Rx movement (2.3.3, 1.2.5).

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Benchmark workout
A standardized, fixed-prescription workout that is repeated periodically so an athlete's performance can be measured and compared over time. Because the task is constant, changes in score reflect changes in fitness.
The Girls
CrossFit's original named benchmark workouts (Angie, Barbara, Chelsea, Diane, Elizabeth, Fran), each given a female name so it is instantly recognizable in the daily WOD stream.
Angie
For time: 100 pull-ups, then 100 push-ups, then 100 sit-ups, then 100 squats — all reps of one movement completed before the next. ~20 minutes of largely steady work with a growing aerobic flavor.
Barbara
5 rounds for time of 20 pull-ups, 30 push-ups, 40 sit-ups, 50 squats, with a fixed 3-minute rest between rounds. ~3 min work / 3 min rest = an aerobic interval (~1:1) with strong anaerobic character.
Chelsea
Every minute on the minute for 30 minutes: 5 pull-ups, 10 push-ups, 15 squats. About 40 sec work / 20 sec rest — an anaerobic interval with abbreviated rest that gives it an aerobic flavor (a hybrid, like Tabata).
Diane
3 rounds of 21-15-9 reps: deadlift 225 lb and handstand push-ups, for time. A heavy-hinge + gymnastics-push couplet.
Elizabeth
3 rounds of 21-15-9 reps: clean 135 lb (hang clean) and ring dips, for time. A pull/front-rack + gymnastics-push couplet on rings.
Fran
3 rounds of 21-15-9 reps: thruster 95 lb and pull-ups, for time. The signature short, brutally intense weightlifting-plus-gymnastics couplet.
Couplet
A workout built from two movements alternated for rounds — here a weightlifting element paired with a calisthenic/gymnastic element to drive a whole-body stimulus.
Metabolic stimulus / pathway
The energy-system demand a workout imposes (phosphagen, glycolytic/anaerobic, oxidative/aerobic). The same movements can target different pathways depending on workout structure and work-to-rest ratio.
Work-to-rest ratio
The proportion of working time to resting time in an interval. It strongly influences which energy system dominates — e.g., 1:1 at ~3 min (Barbara) vs. ~2:1 at ~40/20 (Chelsea).
EMOM (every minute on the minute)
An interval format (used in Chelsea) where a fixed amount of work starts at the top of each minute; the remaining time in that minute is rest, so faster work earns more rest.
21-15-9 rep scheme
A descending three-round rep ladder (21, then 15, then 9) used in Diane, Elizabeth, and Fran — front-loads volume and produces a fast, high-intensity finish.
Choreography of exertion
Glassman's phrase for deliberate workout design — engineering impact, balance, theme, and character into a workout rather than assembling movements at random.
Handstand push-up (HSPU)
An inverted vertical press described as a 'gateway movement' to advanced upper-body gymnastics; a common deficiency the benchmarks expose and a target for progression work.
Ring dip
A dip performed on gymnastic rings, far harder than a bar dip due to instability ('the ring dip is to the bar dip as squats are to leg press').
GPP (general physical preparedness)
Broad, non-specialized fitness across many tasks and modalities. Doing the daily WOD builds GPP, which is what prepares an athlete to perform well on the benchmarks.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • Rhabdomyolysis risk: high-volume, eccentric-heavy bodyweight work (especially the 100 push-ups/sit-ups and the high-rep pull-ups in Angie/Barbara, or repeated deadlifts) in deconditioned, returning, or first-time athletes can provoke exertional rhabdo. Scale volume, and refer/seek medical care for dark urine, disproportionate swelling, or severe persistent soreness (relates to 1.1.3).
  • Rx is not the goal for everyone: prescribing the as-written loads/reps to an athlete who cannot maintain sound mechanics is a safety and coaching error. The article explicitly endorses amending loads — scale to preserve mechanics and the intended stimulus before chasing the leaderboard.
  • Skill-gated movements (HSPU, ring dips, kipping pull-ups) carry fall and overuse risk if forced before competence; develop them with progressions rather than letting an unready athlete grind reps.
  • Pull-up volume frequently drives significant lat/rear-delt/biceps soreness — counsel athletes so this is expected, not alarming, and monitor for overtraining when benchmarks are repeated too aggressively.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. A coach wants to objectively prove that an athlete's 'engine' (high-intensity anaerobic capacity) has improved after an eight-week training block. Which approach gives the cleanest evidence?

  1. A. Have the athlete try a brand-new, never-before-done couplet and judge effort by how hard it looked
  2. B. Re-test a previously recorded benchmark like Fran under identical prescription and compare the times
  3. C. Add 10 lb to the athlete's thruster and see if they can finish
  4. D. Ask the athlete how fit they feel compared to two months ago
  5. E. Switch the athlete to a different gym program and compare general impressions
Show answer

Answer: B — B isolates the variable: because the benchmark is run at an identical prescription, a faster time is a clean signal the athlete got fitter (Task 2.3.2/1.2.6). A and E introduce new, non-comparable tasks; C changes the prescription so it is no longer the same test; D is subjective, not measured.

Scenario 2. Three workouts — Angie, Barbara, and Chelsea — use almost the same movements. A new coach assumes they all train the same thing. What is the best correction?

  1. A. They are effectively interchangeable, so pick whichever fits the clock
  2. B. They differ only in total reps, which doesn't change the training effect
  3. C. Their differing structures (continuous, fixed-rest interval, and EMOM with shrinking rest) produce distinctly different metabolic stimuli
  4. D. Only the movement selection matters for stimulus, and the movements are the same
  5. E. Chelsea is hardest, so it trains everything the other two do plus more
Show answer

Answer: C — The article's core point is that identical modalities yield different stimuli because of structure: Angie is steady/aerobic-leaning, Barbara is a ~1:1 aerobic interval with anaerobic character, and Chelsea is an anaerobic interval with abbreviated, shrinking rest (Task 2.1.1). A, B, and D ignore that workout structure drives the energy-system demand; E misstates the relationship.

Scenario 3. A large, very strong athlete cruises through the deadlifts in Diane but cannot perform a single strict handstand push-up. The coach wants to preserve Diane's intended stimulus while keeping mechanics sound. Best action?

  1. A. Tell the athlete to skip the HSPU and just do extra deadlifts to keep moving
  2. B. Insist on Rx HSPU and let the athlete grind out partial reps however they can
  3. C. Scale the HSPU to an appropriate progression (e.g., pike push-ups or box HSPU) so the athlete still trains the vertical press and metabolic demand
  4. D. Replace Diane entirely with a strength-only deadlift session
  5. E. Have the athlete go home until they can do an Rx handstand push-up
Show answer

Answer: C — Scaling the deficient movement preserves the couplet's whole-body, push-dominant stimulus while protecting mechanics and safety (Tasks 2.2.5, 5.2.2). A drops the pressing stimulus that is the point of Diane; B is a mechanics/safety failure; D and E abandon the workout and the athlete's training opportunity.

Scenario 4. Glassman notes Diane, Elizabeth, and Fran 'root out weaknesses.' A coach observes a small, gymnastics-strong athlete flying through pull-ups but stalling badly on the 95 lb thrusters in Fran. How should the coach USE this information?

  1. A. Conclude the athlete is simply unfit and needs an easier program overall
  2. B. Treat the thruster as the limiting modality and program strength/loading work to address the exposed weakness
  3. C. Remove thrusters from the athlete's training so Fran feels easier next time
  4. D. Tell the athlete to focus more on pull-ups since that's their strength
  5. E. Conclude the workout is poorly designed because it isn't balanced for this athlete
Show answer

Answer: B — Benchmarks are diagnostic by design: the exposed weakness (loading/strength) is exactly what future programming should target (Tasks 2.3.3, 1.2.5). A misreads a specific deficiency as global unfitness; C avoids the weakness instead of training it; D doubles down on an existing strength; E blames the tool for doing its job.

Scenario 5. An athlete asks why CrossFit bothers repeating the exact same named workouts instead of always doing something new. What is the most accurate explanation grounded in the article?

  1. A. Repeating workouts is mainly for nostalgia and tradition
  2. B. Only by repeating an identical workout can progress be confidently measured, so the most formative, expressive workouts are repeated as standardized tests
  3. C. New workouts are too hard to program, so coaches recycle old ones
  4. D. Repetition is meant to let athletes memorize movements they already know
  5. E. The Girls are repeated because they require the least equipment
Show answer

Answer: B — The article states 'only by repeating workouts can we confidently measure our progress,' and the Girls were chosen as the most challenging, formative, and expressive of the fitness ideal (Tasks 2.3.2, 2.3.4). A, C, and D miss the measurement rationale; E is a side benefit of Group 1, not the reason benchmarks exist.

Scenario 6. A coach is selecting a benchmark to gauge an athlete's aerobic-leaning bodyweight endurance with minimal equipment while the athlete is traveling. Which choice and rationale best fit the article?

  1. A. Fran, because its 21-15-9 couplet is the fastest test of all-around fitness
  2. B. Angie, because it is ~20 minutes of largely steady work with a growing aerobic flavor and needs only a pull-up bar and ~15 sq ft
  3. C. Elizabeth, because ring dips and cleans are easy to set up in a hotel room
  4. D. Diane, because deadlifts at 225 lb travel well
  5. E. Barbara, because its rest periods make it a pure strength test
Show answer

Answer: B — Angie fits the goal (aerobic-leaning, steady bodyweight endurance) and the constraint (Group 1 needs only a pull-up bar and ~15 sq ft, ideal for travel) per the article (Tasks 2.1.1, 2.2.3). A targets short high-intensity, not aerobic endurance; C and D require loaded/ring equipment that is impractical while traveling; E mischaracterizes Barbara, which is an aerobic interval, not a pure strength test.

Scenario 7. During Barbara, an athlete proposes shortening the 3-minute rest to 'make it harder' and rolling into the next movement before finishing all reps to save time. Why should the coach decline if the goal is a valid benchmark result?

  1. A. There is no harm; any modification still counts as Barbara
  2. B. Changing the prescribed rest and rep-completion structure alters the test, so the score is no longer comparable to standard Barbara
  3. C. Shorter rest is dangerous and always causes injury
  4. D. The athlete should instead add reps to each round to make it official
  5. E. Rolling on early is fine as long as the total reps are eventually completed in any order
Show answer

Answer: B — The fixed 3-minute rest and the rule to complete all reps of a movement before advancing are part of Barbara's standard; altering them invalidates comparison to prior results and others' scores (Tasks 2.3.2, programming integrity). A and D change the workout; E violates the explicit rule not to roll on until the prescribed reps are done; C overstates a safety claim that isn't the core reason here.

Why this is on the reading list

This 2003 Glassman article is the CCFT reading list's primary case study in adapting CrossFit programming to a GROUP/TEAM context under real-world logistical constraints (limited equipment, mixed-ability rosters, even/odd headcounts). Domain 2 (Programming) tests whether a coach can design workouts at a group level (2.1) and scale across categories of athletes (2.2), and this article shows how to preserve 'the physiological character of CrossFit' while solving the structure/timing/equipment problems that defeat naive group programming. It also feeds Domain 5 (Leadership and Management) heavily — logistics, ratios, equipment demands, organizing athletes/space/time, and building a culture of camaraderie — because the article's central claim is that teamwork dynamics add a stimulus 'no equivalent in the solo effort.'

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 2.1.1 Design single workouts using the CrossFit methodology
  • 2.1.2 Design a sequence of workouts that improves general physical preparedness (GPP)
  • 2.2.1 Scale by age group
  • 2.2.3 Scale for athletes with sport-specific goals
  • 2.2.5 Scale by skill level
  • 2.3.2 Use benchmarks to assess effectiveness of programming
  • 2.3.3 Adjust programming based on performance and goals
  • 5.1.2 Create a culture/community of excellence and camaraderie
  • 5.2.4 Plan lessons for a class period (warm-up, skill development, workout, cool-down)
  • 5.2.10 Manage logistics (ratio, equipment demands, duration, space)
  • 5.2.11 Organize athletes, space, equipment, time to achieve workout objectives
  • 1.2.6 Quantify and track performance
  • 3.1.9 Teach the goals of CrossFit programming and how goals are met (programming with variance)
  • 3.1.10 Teach the relationship between technique and intensity (threshold training)

What to focus on while reading

  • The six explicit design criteria Glassman lists (accommodate wide variance incl. male/female; ultimately tax elite AND novice; motivate/amplify camaraderie; work with odd OR even numbers; preserve CrossFit's physiological character; modest equipment demands) — these ARE the rubric for evaluating any group workout on the exam.
  • The second list of design goals: inspire creative programming in PT leaders; rely largely on low-skill movements while simultaneously developing complex ones; be doable outside; ready athletes AND instructors for more sophisticated programming; motivate continued exploration after graduation; guarantee athletes can follow the WOD by course end; be teachable by experienced PT instructors after a 3-day course + 2 weeks prep.
  • The structural problem the article exists to solve: most individual WODs DON'T scale to a team logistically (running 10 people simultaneously could require 10 rowers, 10 ropes, 10 kettlebells one day; 10 sets of rings, 10 racks, 10 GHDs the next; sending 1–2 at a time can take hours).
  • The 'magic of teamwork' thesis: when well-constructed, the physiological effect EQUALS the individual workout, but teamwork/competition dynamics add a stimulus with no solo equivalent. Note that the chief obstacles are LOGISTICAL (structure, planning, timing, equipment) and 'can readily be overcome.'
  • The 'throwing numbers on the board' mechanism — a chalkboard/whiteboard as an indispensable motivational tool; 29 of 30 workouts are perfectly quantifiable; quantification creates a climate where everyone gives their all (this is performance tracking AND culture-building at once).
  • The handicapped-start system across the recurring 5K (mass start to capture baseline → compute time gaps between placings → next week start in reverse finishing order separated by those gaps so equal effort = dead-even finish → ranking now reflects relative IMPROVEMENT, letting slower athletes win foot races for the first time). Understand WHY this design choice serves motivation and how it lets you rank improvement instead of raw ability.
  • The two-five-man-team structure: split the crew between the two BEST athletes as captains; captains selected for 'instinctive nurturing manner and team spirit'; elite athletes genuinely celebrating lesser athletes is the payoff.
  • How team-completion penalties build in self-pacing and accountability (Run/Rope/Ring race: a missed rope ascent adds 2 to the team's required ascents, a missed dip set adds 10 to required dips) — note how the SCORING design forces athletes to manage work/rest and contributes only what they can.
  • The roster-equalizing mechanism in Hoover Ball and Tug-of-War (form teams of roughly EQUAL combined body weight / strength, then make substitutions you suspect favor the losing side and test by re-running) — a live, iterative way to balance mixed-ability groups.
  • The 'stick work' / broomstick (1" x 6-ft dowel) thread that runs through the whole 6 weeks: introducing the Olympic and squat movements under near-zero load to build accuracy/coordination/balance/flexibility BEFORE adding load; warm-ups preview the week's coming movements; the deliberate sequencing of squat → press progression → clean → press-and-jerk → clean & jerk → snatch across the 6 weeks.
  • The threshold-training / zero-tolerance-on-technique theme: 'cheating range of motion is completely unacceptable'; remediation protocol for bad form (segregate the athlete, send back to broomstick → 65 lb → 95 lb with great technique, then 'rehabilitate' back to the team; deadlift remediation = practice with the last load they can lift beautifully for 10 reps).
  • Specific ROM standards stated for Chelsea: kipping/kicking ALLOWED on pull-ups (highly functional) but require Adam's-apple-to-bar and FULL extension at bottom; squats below parallel to full hip/leg extension; rigid-body push-ups.
  • How named benchmarks are deployed inside a group course (Chelsea: 5 pull-ups/10 push-ups/15 squats EMOM for 30 min, scored as rounds-on-the-minute / additional rounds to 30 min, e.g. '12/9'; Tabata squats scored as the LEAST reps in any of the 8 intervals; team Tabata score = average of all five members).
  • The 5-on / 2-off weekly template (Mon–Fri work, weekends rest) and the fixed weekly anchor: every week opens with a 5K plus stick work, trunk work, calisthenics, and stretching, and reviews performance trends — i.e., the warm-up/skill/workout structure of a class.
  • The deliberately MODEST equipment list (2 Olympic bars, 5 sets of 40-lb dumbbells, rubber plates, pull-up/dip station, 2 truck tires, 10 dowels, racks, bench, 25-ft rope, medicine balls, rings, a box, a truck, two 1.5-pood kettlebells) — proof that 'CrossFit for 10' runs on minimal kit, much of it improvised (stations built with inmate labor).
  • Scoring/ranking mechanics across formats — how the article makes nearly every workout quantifiable and rankable (time to completion, rounds completed, wins, fewest faults/least visits to the ground, composite scores like Tabata-average × sum of pull-ups+dips).
  • The honest caveat that loads/reps/sets/rest are 'but a suggestion' calibrated to large metropolitan SWAT teams and 'may have to be tempered' for regional academies — i.e., the prescribed numbers are a starting point to be scaled to the population in front of you.
  • The teaching-time investment baked into the design: 20–30 minutes to introduce/practice new movements before racing; 'don't start the race until nearly everyone can perform a reasonable approximation'; 'if it takes 30 minutes to get everyone's form right, that's O.K.' — technique gates intensity.
  • Examples of low-skill / improvised functional formats that need almost no equipment and build camaraderie (Tug-of-War, Hoover Ball, Pushed Truck Races, Tire Flip Races, Fallen Comrade carry drills, Medicine-ball Throw, conga lines).

Concepts to understand

  • Group-level workout design vs. individual design: a workout that is sound for one athlete may be logistically unworkable for ten; designing at the group level means choosing formats (relays, conga lines, two-team competitions, partner movements) that share scarce equipment and keep everyone working while preserving the intended metabolic/structural stimulus (2.1.1, 5.2.10, 5.2.11).
  • Preserving 'the physiological character of CrossFit' under constraint — a well-built team workout delivers a physiological effect EQUAL to the individual version; the team format is a packaging/logistics solution, not a dilution of the stimulus. You must be able to judge whether a proposed group format keeps mechanics-consistency-intensity intact or quietly waters it down.
  • Teamwork/competition as an additional stimulus: the dynamics of teams and competition add intensity and engagement that has 'no equivalent in the solo effort,' which is WHY group programming can be more effective for motivation even when the physical work is matched (5.1.2).
  • Quantification as the engine of intensity and culture: making results measurable and visible ('numbers on the board') is both a performance-tracking practice (1.2.6) and a motivational/cultural tool (5.1.2). Understand that nearly every CrossFit workout should be observable, measurable, repeatable so it can be scored, ranked, and re-tested.
  • Handicapping to rank IMPROVEMENT, not raw ability: by staggering starts according to prior performance gaps, the coach engineers situations where less-fit athletes can win, surfacing relative improvement and protecting motivation — a scaling-by-result technique for mixed-ability groups (2.2.5, 2.3.3, 5.1.2).
  • Roster balancing for fair competition: building teams of roughly equal combined bodyweight/strength, and iteratively swapping members to balance outcomes, is how you keep two-team formats competitive across a wide ability spread (2.2.5, 5.2.11).
  • Scaling by skill level through load and movement complexity: introducing high-skill lifts under near-zero load (broomstick/dowel) develops coordination/balance/accuracy first, then load is added only once technique holds — load is a scaling variable layered on top of competence, not a substitute for it (2.2.5, 3.1.10).
  • Threshold training / technique gating intensity in a GROUP setting: zero tolerance for cheated range of motion; athletes with intractable faults are pulled, regressed to lighter loads or the dowel, then reintroduced. Intensity is earned by mechanics and consistency, and the group does not get to trade ROM for a better score (3.1.10, 5.2.1).
  • Programming a SEQUENCE for GPP: the 6-week course is a progression — early weeks build foundational squats and presses with sticks, later weeks layer the clean, press-and-jerk, clean & jerk, and snatch — so that by graduation athletes (and their instructors) are ready for more sophisticated programming and can follow the daily WOD (2.1.2).
  • Benchmarking and re-testing inside a program: recurring fixed tests (the weekly 5K, Chelsea, Tabata squats) let the coach measure trends and prove the program is working; the repeated 5K with trend review is a built-in benchmark loop (2.3.2, 2.3.3, 1.2.6).
  • Scaling by population / sport-specific goals: the prescribed loads were calibrated to metropolitan SWAT teams and are explicitly meant to be tempered for less-conditioned groups — the published numbers are a template to adjust to the athletes and their goals (military/LEO tactical fitness), not absolutes (2.2.1, 2.2.3, 2.3.3).
  • Class-period architecture as the unit of delivery: every session follows a warm-up (stretching, stick work, trunk/calisthenic work) → skill development (introduce/practice the day's new movement) → workout (the scored event) pattern, and the weekly 5K previews the coming week's movements — a concrete model of lesson planning (5.2.4).
  • Self-pacing and personal responsibility engineered through scoring: penalty rules and 'you're not expected to complete all reps in one set' coaching teach athletes to manage work/rest intervals and contribute appropriately — survival depends on skilled management of effort, a transferable skill the workout design forces athletes to practice (5.2.8, 5.2.6).
  • Format toolbox for equipment-poor, mixed-ability groups: relays/team races (one team on ropes, one on rings), conga lines (single station cycled through the whole line), partner/assisted movements (two-man pull-up, two-man squat), and low-skill primal formats (tug-of-war, tire flip, truck push, fallen-comrade carry, Hoover Ball) — each solves the 'one piece of equipment, many athletes' problem while keeping intensity and camaraderie high (2.1.1, 5.2.10, 5.2.11).
  • Designing for the INSTRUCTOR, not just the athlete: a stated goal is that experienced PT leaders can be trained to run the course confidently after a short clinic, and that athletes graduate able to explore fitness independently — programming should be transmissible and should build coaching capacity, not just one-off results (3.1.9, 7.1.2 context).

How the exam applies this

Expect Domain 2 scenarios that hand you a class of 8–12 athletes, a sparse equipment inventory, and an even/odd headcount, then ask for the BEST way to run a given stimulus as a group — the right answer keeps everyone working and preserves the intended metabolic/structural demand (relay, conga line, partner format) rather than buying ten of everything or running athletes one-at-a-time for hours (2.1.1, 5.2.10, 5.2.11). Mixed-ability questions test whether you scale by skill via load/movement complexity and use handicapping or balanced teams so both elite and novice are 'ultimately taxed' and the slower athlete can still win/improve (2.2.5, 2.3.3). Benchmark/evaluation items use the recurring 5K, Chelsea, or Tabata to ask how you'd measure whether the program is working and adjust it (2.3.2, 2.3.3, 1.2.6). Leadership items lean on 'numbers on the board,' captain selection, and celebrating improvement to build camaraderie (5.1.2), and lesson-planning items test the warm-up → skill → workout structure (5.2.4). Watch for distractors that sacrifice range of motion or technique to make a group format 'fairer' or faster — the article's zero-tolerance stance means those are wrong (3.1.10, 5.2.1).

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Team / group workout
A workout structured so multiple athletes train together — via relays, partner work, conga lines, or two-team competition — sharing limited equipment while preserving CrossFit's intended physiological stimulus. The format adds a teamwork/competition stimulus with no solo equivalent.
'6 Weeks of CrossFit for 10'
The article's packaged 30-workout, six-week PT course built for ~10 athletes (typically two five-man teams), designed for institutional clients (military, law enforcement, SWAT) running on existing/minimal equipment.
WOD (Workout of the Day)
The single prescribed daily workout. The article notes most individual WODs don't scale logistically to a team, which is the problem these team workouts solve.
Preserve the physiological character
The design requirement that a team workout deliver a physiological effect equal to the individual version — the team format changes the logistics, not the training stimulus.
'Throwing numbers on the board'
Posting quantified results on a chalkboard/whiteboard. 29 of the 30 workouts are perfectly quantifiable; making results visible creates a climate where everyone gives maximal effort. Functions as both performance tracking and culture-building.
Handicapped start
Staggering athletes' start times by the time gaps recorded in a prior effort (started in reverse finishing order). If everyone repeats their prior effort they finish dead-even, so the new finishing order reflects relative IMPROVEMENT rather than raw ability — letting slower athletes win and stay motivated.
Mass start
All athletes begin simultaneously, used to capture a clean baseline (e.g., the first 5K of each cycle) before computing handicaps for the next staggered run.
Stick work / broomstick (dowel)
Practicing Olympic and squat-family movements with a 1"×6-ft dowel under near-zero load to build accuracy, coordination, balance, and flexibility before adding load — a skill-development and scaling-by-skill tool woven through the whole course.
Conga line
A format where the whole team cycles single-file through one station (e.g., bench press then immediately a pull-up bar; or rope climb then rings), so a single piece of equipment keeps everyone working with minimal idle time — solves the equipment-scarcity problem.
Two-man pull-up
An assisted pull-up where one partner drives the other up with a squat-like push-press, contacting only at the hands/fingers (ribs/butt). A partner-scaling movement that lets athletes accumulate volume and use all major muscle groups.
Chelsea
Benchmark WOD: 5 pull-ups, 10 push-ups, 15 squats every minute on the minute for 30 minutes. Scored as rounds completed on the minute / additional rounds completed up to 30 min (e.g., '12/9'); the first number ranks, the second breaks ties.
Tabata squat
An interval protocol of 20 s work / 10 s rest × 8, scored as the LEAST squats in any single interval; a team's score is the average of all five members. CrossFit's application of Izumi Tabata's interval research.
Threshold training (zero-tolerance ROM)
Holding intensity to the point where technique/range of motion stays sound. 'Cheating range of motion is completely unacceptable'; faulty athletes are pulled and regressed until form holds, then reintroduced — technique gates intensity.
Remediation / 'rehabilitation'
The protocol for an athlete with bad technique: segregate them, regress to the dowel/lighter load, rebuild great form, then return them to the team (for the deadlift, the last load they can lift beautifully for 10 reps).
Five-on / two-off
The weekly training rhythm (Mon–Fri work, weekends rest) the course is built on, fitting the standard workweek.
Pood
A Russian unit of mass used for kettlebells; the course uses 1.5-pood (≈50-lb) kettlebells for swings.
Team captain
The two best athletes, chosen to split and lead the crew, selected for instinctive nurturing manner and team spirit; the payoff is elite athletes genuinely celebrating the achievements of lesser athletes.
GPP (General Physical Preparedness)
Broad, non-specialized fitness across many capacities — the target the six-week sequence is built to develop, progressing from low-skill to complex movements.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • Loads/reps/sets/rest in this article are explicitly a SUGGESTION calibrated to large metropolitan SWAT teams and 'may have to be tempered' for regional academies or less-conditioned groups — do not treat the prescribed numbers as universal Rx; scale to the population in front of you.
  • High-volume upper-body workouts like Chelsea ('high volume pull-up workout… abundantly clear the following day') and heavy repeated deadlift/clean sessions carry real overtraining and tissue-overload risk in novice or deconditioned athletes; manage volume, recovery, and exertion warning signs (relevant to Domain 1 readiness and Domain 5 risk management, though this article does not address rhabdomyolysis directly).
  • Heavy near-maximal lifting is built in (e.g., Deadlift III climbing to 305 lb, 'how to safely attempt post-maximal lifts'); the article assumes athletes have been trained for five weeks and demands abort-the-lift-on-loss-of-lumbar-extension supervision. Loading novices to maximal/near-maximal without that supervision is outside safe practice — technique must gate load.
  • Improvised/heavy implements (650–800 lb truck tire flips, pushing a real pickup truck, fallen-comrade carries, tug-of-war) introduce crush, strain, and footing hazards; arrange equipment/space and coach mechanics (drive the chest into the tire, don't deadlift it) to manage risk (Domain 5).
  • Always teach and groove movement before racing — 'don't start the race until nearly everyone can perform a reasonable approximation'; starting a timed/competitive team event before technique is adequate trades safety and the training stimulus for speed.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. You coach 10 tactical athletes (a police unit) of widely mixed fitness. You have only 2 Olympic bars, one pull-up/dip station, a 25-ft rope, two kettlebells, and a field. You want to run a hard met-con that keeps everyone working AND preserves a CrossFit-quality stimulus. Which approach best reflects the design principles in 'Team Workouts'?

  1. A. Run the athletes through the WOD one or two at a time so each gets the exact individual prescription, even if the session takes a few hours.
  2. B. Tell the unit's command you must buy ten rowers, ten ropes, and ten kettlebells before you can program for the group.
  3. C. Build two five-person teams and run a relay/competition format (e.g., 800 m run, then one team to the rope for ascents and one to the rings for dips), using shared stations so everyone stays working while the metabolic demand is preserved.
  4. D. Replace the conditioning entirely with a long steady group jog so no equipment is needed and nobody is left out.
  5. E. Cancel met-con for the day and do individual one-rep-max testing instead.
Show answer

Answer: C — The article's whole point is solving the team-logistics problem WITHOUT diluting the stimulus or buying ten of everything: two-team relays and shared-station formats keep all athletes working with minimal equipment while preserving CrossFit's physiological character. A (one-at-a-time, hours) and B (wholesale equipment purchase) are the exact failure modes Glassman calls out. D abandons the intended stimulus; E doesn't deliver conditioning at all.

Scenario 2. Each week your group repeats a 5K. Week 1 you used a mass start and recorded the time gap between every placing. For Week 2, the article has you start athletes in reverse order of last week's finish, separated by those exact gaps. What is the PRIMARY programming/coaching purpose of this handicapped start?

  1. A. To make the workout shorter so it fits the class period.
  2. B. So the finishing order now reflects each athlete's relative IMPROVEMENT rather than raw ability, letting slower athletes win and stay motivated.
  3. C. To reduce congestion at equipment stations during the run.
  4. D. To force the fastest athletes to do extra distance as a penalty.
  5. E. To randomize results so no one can be ranked.
Show answer

Answer: B — If every athlete repeats their prior effort they finish dead-even, so any change in finishing order reflects improvement, not baseline fitness. This lets less-fit athletes 'win foot races for the first time' and surfaces relative progress — a scaling-and-motivation device for mixed-ability groups (2.2.5, 2.3.3, 5.1.2). It does not shorten the workout (A), manage congestion (C), penalize the fast (D), or randomize (E).

Scenario 3. During a team deadlift session at 135 lb, one athlete's lumbar spine repeatedly rounds and he can't correct it, even though his teammates are moving well and the clock is running. Based on the article's standards, what is the best action?

  1. A. Let him finish his sets at 135 lb to keep the team's timing intact and fix it next week.
  2. B. Add load to challenge him into bracing harder.
  3. C. Pull him from the group and regress him to the dowel/65–95 lb (or the last load he can lift beautifully for 10 reps), rebuild sound form, then reintroduce him.
  4. D. Tell him to use a little less range of motion so his back stays flatter.
  5. E. Switch him to max-effort singles so he spends less total time under load.
Show answer

Answer: C — The article is explicit: nothing other than perfect form can be tolerated; athletes with intractable faults are segregated and 'rehabilitated' through the dowel and lighter loads before returning to the team, and for the deadlift specifically you regress to the last load they can lift beautifully for 10 reps (3.1.10, 5.2.1). Continuing at load (A), adding load (B), reducing ROM (D), or going maximal (E) all trade safety/technique for speed or score — the opposite of the zero-tolerance standard.

Scenario 4. You're packaging a six-week group course for novices and want to introduce the Olympic and squat-family lifts safely. The article repeatedly programs 'stick work' with a 1"×6-ft dowel and warns against the argument that the movements 'would be easier with a load.' Why introduce these lifts under near-zero load first?

  1. A. Because light implements let athletes lift more total weight over the session.
  2. B. Because near-zero load exposes and forces development of accuracy, coordination, balance, and flexibility, whereas load masks a lack of coordination and limits learning the basics.
  3. C. Because dowels are the only equipment most institutional clients own.
  4. D. Because the dowel work counts as the conditioning stimulus for the day.
  5. E. Because beginners should never progress to loaded barbell lifts.
Show answer

Answer: B — Glassman states that introducing essential movements under near-zero load 'places enormous demands on accuracy, coordination, balance, and flexibility,' and that a load 'will only serve to mask a lack of coordination and ultimately limit the athletes' ability to learn these essential basics.' This is scaling-by-skill: build competence, then add load (2.2.5, 3.1.10). The other options misstate the purpose.

Scenario 5. A skeptical PT director asks why you spend so much effort posting every athlete's time and score on a whiteboard instead of just running the workouts. Which answer best captures the article's reasoning?

  1. A. It's required record-keeping for liability and has no training effect.
  2. B. Posting quantified results ('throwing numbers on the board') creates a climate where everyone gives their all and builds camaraderie, and nearly every workout is designed to be quantifiable precisely so it can be scored and tracked.
  3. C. It lets you skip warm-ups because athletes are already motivated.
  4. D. Numbers on the board replace the need to coach movement quality.
  5. E. It is mainly to identify athletes to cut from the program.
Show answer

Answer: B — The article calls the board 'an indispensable tool,' notes 29 of 30 workouts are perfectly quantifiable, and says 'throwing numbers on the board creates a climate where everyone gives their all.' Quantification is simultaneously performance tracking (1.2.6) and a motivational/cultural lever (5.1.2). It does not replace warm-ups (C) or coaching (D), and the purpose is motivation/measurement, not cutting athletes (E).

Scenario 6. The published loads in 'Team Workouts' (e.g., specific bench, deadlift, and clean weights) were calibrated to large metropolitan SWAT teams. You're about to run the course with a regional academy of less-conditioned recruits, including several beginners. What is the most defensible programming decision?

  1. A. Use the exact prescribed loads and reps because they are the validated CrossFit standard.
  2. B. Treat the prescribed loads/reps/sets/rest as a starting suggestion and temper them to the recruits' demonstrated capacity, scaling load and volume to maintain sound mechanics.
  3. C. Increase the loads because academy recruits need to be challenged harder than SWAT.
  4. D. Drop all barbell work and only do bodyweight movements for six weeks.
  5. E. Keep the loads but remove all coaching of technique to save time.
Show answer

Answer: B — The article explicitly states the specifics of 'load and reps, sets and rest, are but a suggestion,' designed around SWAT capacities, and 'some of the workouts may have to be tempered a bit to accommodate regional police academies or departments.' That is scaling to the population and their goals (2.2.1, 2.2.3, 2.3.3). Treating the numbers as fixed Rx (A), loading heavier (C), gutting the program (D), or removing technique coaching (E) all ignore the article's guidance.

Scenario 7. You want to keep a two-team competition genuinely competitive across a wide ability spread, and to make sure both the elite AND the novice members are taxed and engaged. Which combination of tactics is most consistent with the article?

  1. A. Stack all the strongest athletes on one team so the workout finishes faster.
  2. B. Form teams of roughly equal combined bodyweight/strength, appoint nurturing captains, use scoring penalties that require each athlete to contribute, and iteratively swap members to balance outcomes.
  3. C. Let athletes self-select teams with friends and don't track results.
  4. D. Have only the fittest athletes compete while the rest watch and learn.
  5. E. Remove all scoring so no one feels pressure.
Show answer

Answer: B — The article balances teams by equal combined bodyweight/strength (Hoover Ball, Tug-of-War), selects captains for nurturing manner and team spirit, builds penalties so each athlete must contribute (e.g., missed rope/ring attempts add to the team's requirement), and tests/adjusts team makeup to keep contests close. This 'ultimately taxes elite and novice' and amplifies camaraderie (2.2.5, 5.1.2, 5.2.11). Stacking (A), untracked self-selection (C), benching most athletes (D), and removing scoring (E) all undercut those design criteria.

Scenario 8. Mid-workout in the Run/KBS/Pull-up race, a newer athlete is anxious because he can't do all 30 pull-ups or all 50 kettlebell swings unbroken. According to the article, what is the best coaching response and its rationale?

  1. A. Tell him he must complete each movement unbroken or he fails the workout.
  2. B. Remind him he isn't expected to do all reps in a single set; surviving these workouts depends on skilled management of work/rest intervals, which this workout is designed to teach.
  3. C. Cut his reps in half permanently so he never has to break a set.
  4. D. Pull him from the workout for the day.
  5. E. Tell him to drop the kettlebell weight to the lightest available and ignore the pull-ups.
Show answer

Answer: B — The article explicitly says athletes 'will need to be reminded that they are not necessarily expected to complete all 30 pull-ups or even all 50 Kettlebell swings in a single set' and that 'survival is often dependent on skilled management of work & rest intervals… a great workout on which to hone that skill' (5.2.8, 5.2.6). Demanding unbroken sets (A), permanently halving reps (C), pulling him (D), or abandoning movements (E) all miss the intended pacing lesson.
