Why this is on the reading list

This article is Glassman's deep analysis of the benchmark workout Fran, using it to teach the physics of work and power, the inverse relationship between time-to-completion and intensity, and how structural variations of the same workload produce radically different demands. It backs the Programming domain directly: understanding why a workout is structured the way it is (2.1.1), how rep schemes drive a strength-to-metabolic continuum, how to use benchmarks to evaluate programming and athletes (2.3.2), and the foundational CrossFit thesis that intensity is power and power is fundamental to results. For a CCFT candidate it converts 'Fran' from a workout to memorize into a model for reasoning about how any couplet's load, rep count, and split design shape the training stimulus.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 2.1.1 Design single workouts using the CrossFit methodology
  • 2.1.2 Design a sequence of workouts that improves general physical preparedness (GPP)
  • 2.2.5 Scale by skill level
  • 2.3.2 Use benchmarks to assess effectiveness of programming
  • 2.3.3 Adjust programming based on performance and goals
  • 2.3.4 Evaluate athlete progress relative to CrossFit's definition of fitness and their personal goal
  • 1.2.2 Evaluate athlete's work capacity
  • 1.2.6 Quantify and track performance
  • 3.1.10 Teach the relationship between technique and intensity (threshold training)
  • 3.1.11 Teach relative intensity

What to focus on while reading

  • The exact structure of Fran: 21-15-9 reps of thrusters and pull-ups, scored by time to completion; note the standard notation Glassman uses ('Three rounds, 21-15-9 reps, for time, of 95-pound thrusters and pull-ups').
  • Why the thruster + pull-up pairing is described as 'perfectly complementary' — each movement contains exactly what the other lacks (push/squat vs. pull), and together they hit all major muscle groups using three superfunctional core movements (squat, push press, pull-up).
  • The physicist's definition of work and its practical reduction: Work = Force x Distance; measure work as weight lifted multiplied by the distance it travels.
  • That work for any given athlete in Fran is FIXED regardless of how fast or slow they finish — capacity and performance do not change the total work, only the time.
  • The method for estimating bodyweight work: travel of the center of mass (presumed between pubic bone and navel, in the frontal plane) multiplied by the athlete's bodyweight, for both the thruster and the pull-up.
  • The honest admission that these are 'zero-order' approximations (no dynamics), and WHY they overestimate (much of the leg/arm doesn't travel as far as the center of mass) and why the pull-up overestimation is smaller than the squat overestimation (arms are lighter than legs).
  • The worked Greg Amundson example (6 ft, 200 lb): center of mass travels 24 in on the pull-up, 26 in on the thruster, bar travels 47 in.
  • The derived numbers: each pull-up = 400 ft-lbs; each thruster = 805 ft-lbs (433 ft-lbs to move the body + 372 ft-lbs to move the 95-lb load); total Fran = 45 x (805+400) = 54,225 ft-lbs.
  • The two 'counterintuitive' observations: (1) the unweighted squat-to-overhead and the pull-up are nearly equal in work per rep — the squat and pull-up are 'metabolic equals'; (2) for a 200-lb athlete, bodyweight is about two-thirds of Fran's total demand.
  • The conclusion that Fran selects for athletes LIGHTER than 200 pounds (because bodyweight dominates the workload).
  • The central power equation: Average Power = Work / Time; because work is fixed, average power (and therefore intensity) varies INVERSELY with time — faster time = greater average power.
  • The load-vs-power experiment: standard 95 lb = 315 ft-lbs/sec; 'Fat Fran' at 115 lb DROPS power ~20% (to 253 ft-lbs/sec); 'Anorexic Fran' at 75 lb RAISES power ~7% (to 338 ft-lbs/sec).
  • The diminishing-returns ceiling: Fran 'maximally compresses' to ~2:20-2:25 (empty-handed, no load on thrusters, simulated pull-ups); below ~75 lb further load reduction only DECREASES power; Greg's max power lies between 75 and 95 lb.
  • The 'isomers' concept (borrowed from chemistry): 1x45, 3x15, 5x9, 9x5 are EXACTLY equal in mechanical work but very different in feel, effect, and resulting time.
  • The predicted time ranking fastest-to-slowest: 9x5, 5x9, 3x15, 1x45 — and that standard Fran's 21-15-9 split falls between 3x15 and 1x45 for most people.
  • WHY more fractured splits (9x5) are faster for weaker athletes: numerous transitions provide 8 breaks/relief that let the athlete shift effort before bogging down or stalling — but any work is harder than rest, so cardiorespiratory demand can spike.
  • The strength-to-metabolic continuum: the LESS fractured isomer (1x45) demands more strength and stamina; the MORE fractured isomer (9x5) is the metabolic 'wallop' that rewards rest.
  • The developmental prediction: as athletes get fitter, their best times should migrate from the 9x5 (fractured) side toward the 1x45 side, and the advantage of fracturing should DISAPPEAR — 'an athlete rests to recover from weakness.'
  • Glassman's prescription for improving Greg: spend more time with Fran's HEAVIER sisters (because going heavier hurt his power 20%, that's his weak link), not endless repeats at standard load.
  • The closing methodological creed: 'measure, think, and experiment'; the value of measurement is knowing what you are doing so you can do something different — and Richard Burton's caution that human movement resists simple lever arithmetic.

Concepts to understand

  • Work is fixed, power is variable: a benchmark workout represents a constant quantity of mechanical work for a given athlete; the only variable the athlete controls is time, and time inversely determines average power. Apply this when explaining to an athlete why a faster Fran is a 'fitter' Fran even though they moved the same total load.
  • Power = intensity, and intensity drives results: the CrossFit creed that the faster effort expresses greater average power, and power/intensity is the fundamental driver of adaptation. Apply this when justifying time-priority scoring and when pushing an athlete to sustain output rather than coast.
  • Bodyweight dominates bodyweight-heavy couplets: in Fran, roughly two-thirds of the work is moving the athlete, so lighter athletes are favored. Apply this to set realistic expectations across athletes of different body sizes and to understand why a benchmark 'selects for' certain body types — not as a reason to despair, but as context for relative performance.
  • The squat and pull-up are metabolic equals: per-rep work of the unweighted squat-to-overhead and the pull-up is nearly identical. Apply this when balancing pushing/pulling/squatting volume in programming and when estimating the relative demand of mixing these movements.
  • Complementary movement pairing: the best couplets pair movements that supply what the other lacks (push vs. pull) so that together they cover all major muscle groups. Apply this when designing your own couplets — pick movements that complement rather than compound the same fatigue.
  • Isomers — same work, different structure, different stimulus: identical total reps and load can be arranged into different splits (1x45, 3x15, 5x9, 9x5) that produce different times and dramatically different physiological experiences. Apply this to deliberately bias a workout toward strength/stamina (fewer, larger sets) or toward metabolic conditioning (many small sets).
  • The strength-to-metabolic continuum via degree of fracture: less fracturing = more strength/stamina demand; more fracturing = more metabolic demand and more reliance on rest. Apply this to diagnose what a given rep scheme is actually training and to match the scheme to the athlete's goal.
  • Rest is a confession of weakness: athletes break sets to recover from a limiting factor (muscular or metabolic). The fracturing that helps a weaker athlete loses its advantage as fitness improves. Apply this to read an athlete's set-break pattern as a diagnostic of their weak link, and to track progress by watching breaks shrink over time.
  • Load tuning has an optimum, not a monotonic trend: lowering load raises power only up to a point (Fran's ~2:20-2:25 floor), then further reductions decrease power; adding load can crater power if it exceeds the athlete's strength. Apply this when scaling load — the goal is the load that maximizes sustainable power for that athlete, not simply 'lighter is easier/faster.'
  • Train the limiter, not the lift you're already good at: because going heavier cost Greg the most power, the heavier variant exposes and addresses his weak link. Apply this principle generally — the variation that most degrades an athlete's output points to what they should train.
  • Benchmarks as measurement instruments: Fran is a repeatable, standardized test that holds work constant so power becomes a clean, comparable signal of fitness over time. Apply this to use named benchmarks to evaluate program effectiveness (2.3.2) and track an individual's progress (1.2.6).
  • Measure, think, experiment: analysis is not the goal of coaching, but quantification reveals what you're actually doing and lets you change it deliberately. Apply this as a coaching/programming discipline — test, interpret, adjust, retest — rather than guessing.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenario items that hand you an athlete profile or a goal and ask you to choose or modify a workout's structure. A heavier, strong athlete who stalls on Fran versus a light, gymnastics-strong athlete who flies through it tests whether you understand that bodyweight dominates the workload and that load/scaling should target the limiter (2.2.5, 2.3.3). Items may give you the same total reps in different splits and ask which arrangement trains strength versus metabolic conditioning, or which an under-developed athlete will finish fastest (2.1.1, 2.1.2). Others may show an athlete's Fran time improving and ask what it proves about programming or fitness (2.3.2, 2.3.4, 1.2.6), or test the core principle that for fixed work, intensity is governed by time, so faster = more powerful = the CrossFit goal (3.1.10, 3.1.11).

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Fran
A benchmark CrossFit workout: three rounds of 21-15-9 reps of barbell thrusters (95 lb for men) and pull-ups, scored by time to completion. Used as a standardized fitness test.
Thruster
A combination movement: a front squat flowing directly into a push-press, driving the barbell from the bottom of the squat to fully locked out overhead in one continuous effort.
Couplet
A workout built from two movements paired together. Fran is a couplet of thrusters and pull-ups.
Work (mechanical)
Force multiplied by the distance the point of application moves. Practically, weight lifted multiplied by how high it is lifted; measured here in foot-pounds. For a given athlete in a given workout, total work is fixed regardless of speed.
Power
The rate of doing work — work divided by time. In Fran, expressed in foot-pounds per second. Because work is constant, power rises as time falls.
Intensity
In CrossFit, operationally equal to average power — how much work is done per unit time. Intensity is treated as the fundamental driver of fitness adaptation.
Foot-pound (ft-lb)
A unit of work equal to the work of moving one pound a distance of one foot. Greg's full Fran totals 54,225 ft-lbs at 95 lb.
Center of mass travel
The vertical distance the body's center of mass (approximated between pubic bone and navel) moves during a rep; multiplied by bodyweight to estimate the work of moving the body itself.
Zero-order approximation
A simplified estimate that ignores complicating factors (here, dynamics and the differing travel of individual limb segments). Useful for insight but acknowledged to overestimate the true work.
Isomer (of a workout)
A term borrowed from chemistry for a variant with the same parts but different structure: same total reps and load arranged in a different split (e.g., 1x45, 3x15, 5x9, 9x5). Equal in mechanical work, different in time, feel, and effect.
Fracture / degree of fracture
How finely a workout's reps are broken into rounds. More fracture (e.g., 9x5) means more transitions and built-in rest, shifting demand toward metabolic conditioning; less fracture (1x45) shifts demand toward strength and stamina.
Strength-to-metabolic continuum
The spectrum along which a workout's stimulus shifts based on its structure: unfractured arrangements stress strength/stamina, heavily fractured arrangements deliver a metabolic 'wallop' that relies on rest.
Fat Fran
Glassman's nickname for a heavier Fran variant (115 lb), which raised total work but dropped Greg's average power about 20%.
Anorexic Fran
Glassman's nickname for a lighter Fran variant (75 lb), which lowered total work and raised Greg's average power about 7%.
Maximal compression
The theoretical fastest time for a workout — for Fran, about 2:20-2:25 performed empty-handed; below the load that hits this floor, removing load only decreases power.
Benchmark workout
A named, standardized, repeatable workout used as a fitness yardstick. Because its work is fixed, it isolates time/power as a clean measure of progress and program effectiveness.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • The article models a maximal-intensity, time-priority workout; in practice a novice attempting prescribed (Rx) Fran at 95 lb with kipping pull-ups before earning mechanics and consistency is a mechanics-consistency-intensity violation and an injury/rhabdo risk — intensity is earned, not assumed.
  • Thrusters and pull-ups taken to high-rep failure for time are a recognized rhabdomyolysis-risk pattern, especially in deconditioned, returning, or first-time athletes; scale volume and load before chasing a fast time.
  • 'Lighter athletes are favored' and the body-type observations are programming insight, not a judgment of an athlete's worth — do not let benchmark math discourage heavier athletes; coach to their personal goals and relative intensity.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. Two athletes run standard Fran (21-15-9, 95 lb thrusters and pull-ups). Athlete A weighs 145 lb with strong gymnastics; Athlete B weighs 215 lb and is a strong powerlifter. Both attack it hard, yet A finishes well ahead of B. Based on the article's analysis, what is the most accurate explanation to give B?

  1. A simply tried harder and expressed more intensity than B
  2. Roughly two-thirds of Fran's work is moving bodyweight, so the workout inherently favors lighter athletes; B's heavier body is doing substantially more total work
  3. The 95-lb load is too light to challenge B, so B was under-stimulated and coasted
  4. B's powerlifting strength is irrelevant to Fran because the barbell load is trivial for everyone
  5. A's faster time proves A did less total work than B
Show answer

Answer: B — The article shows bodyweight accounts for about two-thirds of Fran's demand for a 200-lb athlete, so it 'selects for athletes lighter than 200 pounds.' B's larger bodyweight means more total work per rep. A is wrong (effort isn't the structural cause), C misreads the data (the load isn't the dominant term, bodyweight is), D ignores that load still contributes about a third, and E is false — work per rep depends on bodyweight and load, not on who finishes faster; faster time means more power, not less work.

Scenario 2. You want to bias a conditioning session toward a heavy metabolic stimulus that lets a moderately-conditioned class keep moving, rather than toward maximal strength-stamina. Using the article's isomer logic with the same total reps and load, which structure best fits that intent?

  1. 1 round of 45 thrusters then 45 pull-ups (1x45)
  2. 3 rounds of 15 and 15 (3x15)
  3. 9 rounds of 5 and 5 (9x5)
  4. A single unbroken set of all reps with no transitions
  5. Whichever has the fewest transitions, to save time
Show answer

Answer: C — Glassman places 9x5 at the metabolic end of the continuum: numerous transitions give relief (8 breaks), keep weaker athletes moving, and drive cardiorespiratory demand 'through the roof.' 1x45 (A) and the unbroken set (D) sit at the strength-and-stamina end. E inverts the logic — fewer transitions push toward strength demand, not metabolic. B is intermediate. The more fractured the split, the more metabolic the wallop, which matches the stated intent.

Scenario 3. An athlete has done Fran at 95 lb several times. They ask how to lower their time. Their power dropped sharply when they tried it heavier and barely moved when they tried it lighter. Per Glassman's reasoning with Greg Amundson, what is the most efficacious recommendation?

  1. Keep repeating standard 95-lb Fran as often as possible until the time drops
  2. Spend more time training with the heavier variants, because going heavier is where their power collapsed and that exposes the limiter
  3. Only train the lighter variant, since lighter loads produced their highest power
  4. Switch entirely to long slow cardio to build an aerobic base
  5. Add bodyweight so their two-thirds bodyweight work increases
Show answer

Answer: B — Glassman predicts the most efficacious route to a better Fran is time with the heavier sisters, because going 20 lb heavier cost Greg about 20% of his power while going lighter only added about 7% and then plateaued — the heavy end is the weak link. A (just repeating) doesn't target the limiter; C trains an already-strong quality and lighter loads hit a power floor; D abandons the specific demand; E is nonsensical for performance. Train where output degrades most.

Scenario 4. A coaching colleague claims that since Fran is 'the same workout,' an athlete's 95-lb time and a 115-lb time should be directly comparable measures of fitness. How should you correct this using the article's framework?

  1. They are comparable because total work is identical at both loads
  2. They are not directly comparable: changing the load changes the total work, so the two efforts represent different workloads and different average power outputs — only a fixed-work benchmark holds the standard constant
  3. They are comparable because time is the only thing that matters in CrossFit
  4. Neither time means anything because the approximations are only zero-order
  5. The 115-lb time is always the better fitness measure because it is heavier
Show answer

Answer: B — The article shows 95-lb Fran is 54,225 ft-lbs while 115-lb Fran is 57,735 ft-lbs — different total work, and Greg's average power fell from 315 to 253 ft-lbs/sec. A benchmark works as a measuring stick precisely because work is held constant; change the load and you've changed the test. A is factually wrong on the work totals; C oversimplifies (time only indexes power when work is fixed); D throws out a useful instrument over an honest caveat; E has no basis.

Scenario 5. Over three months an athlete's recorded set-breaks in Fran shrink — they used to need many small sets (a 9x5-like pattern) and now string together large unbroken sets, and their time has dropped. What does this best indicate about their development, per the article?

  1. They are overtraining and should deload immediately
  2. Their strength, stamina, and metabolic conditioning have advanced, so the advantage of fracturing is disappearing and their performance is migrating toward the less-fractured (1x45) end of the continuum
  3. They have simply memorized the workout
  4. Their total work has increased, proving they are doing more
  5. The change is meaningless because rest schemes are personal preference
Show answer

Answer: B — Glassman states that as athletes develop, best times migrate from the 9x5 side toward the 1x45 side, and the advantage of the more fractured split disappears — because 'an athlete rests to recover from weakness.' Fewer breaks means the limiting weakness has receded. A has no support (improving performance, not overtraining signs); C ignores the physiological signal of fewer breaks; D is false — total work at a fixed load is constant; E contradicts the article's point that breaks are a confession of a limiter, not arbitrary preference.

Scenario 6. A first-time member asks to do Rx Fran (95 lb, kipping pull-ups) on day one because they saw it online. Applying CrossFit methodology and risk management, what is the best response?

  1. Let them do it Rx, since Fran is just two basic movements and time-priority builds intensity fastest
  2. Scale load and volume and establish mechanics and consistency first; intensity (a fast time) is earned, and high-rep thrusters/pull-ups to failure carry rhabdo and injury risk for a novice
  3. Have them do the empty-handed ~2:20 version to set a baseline, then immediately retest at 115 lb
  4. Refuse to let them ever attempt Fran until they can do 20 strict pull-ups
  5. Tell them Fran is only for athletes under 200 lb so they shouldn't bother
Show answer

Answer: B — Mechanics-consistency-intensity means intensity is added only after sound, repeatable movement; pushing maximal-intensity high-rep thrusters and kipping pull-ups on a novice invites injury and rhabdomyolysis. A ignores that intensity is earned and that 'basic' movements at high rep/load are demanding. C jumps a beginner straight to load testing. D is an arbitrary, overly rigid gate. E misuses the body-type observation as a reason to exclude an athlete rather than to scale and coach them to their own goals.
