Why this is on the reading list

This article argues that CrossFit's benchmark workouts (Fran, Linda, Grace, Fight Gone Bad, a repeated 5k) are valid, repeatable, sport-specific fitness tests that out-perform expensive lab tests like VO2 max and Wingate for tracking real-world work capacity. For the CCFT exam it backs Domain 2's core idea that programming is evaluated by re-testable benchmarks measured against the athlete's goals, and that testing must mirror the demands the athlete actually faces. It also reinforces why CrossFit defines and quantifies fitness through repeatable, observable, measurable performance rather than isolated physiological markers.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 2.3.2 Use benchmarks to assess effectiveness of programming
  • 2.3.1 Evaluate program success relative to athlete goals and needs
  • 2.3.3 Adjust programming based on performance and goals
  • 2.3.4 Evaluate athlete progress relative to CrossFit's definition of fitness and their personal goal
  • 2.2.3 Scale for athletes with sport-specific goals
  • 1.2.6 Quantify and track performance
  • 1.2.2 Evaluate athlete's work capacity
  • 1.2.3 Identify athlete's fitness goals
  • 3.1.9 Teach the goals of CrossFit programming and how goals are met (programming with variance)

What to focus on while reading

  • The central claim: there is NO single, movement-agnostic VO2 max — there is a running VO2 max, cycling VO2 max, thruster VO2 max, wall-ball VO2 max, etc. VO2 max is specific to the movement being performed.
  • WHY a treadmill/bike VO2 max test fails the wrestler: it does not mirror the multi-line-of-action demands (pushes, pulls, static grips, arms and legs) of his actual sport.
  • The four physiological determinants of VO2 max at sea level: (1) heart's ability to pump blood, (2) oxygen-carrying capacity of blood (hemoglobin), (3) muscles' ability to accept a large blood supply (capillarization), (4) muscle cells' ability to extract and use oxygen (mitochondria + aerobic enzymes).
  • Why lung/oxygen delivery is NOT the limiting factor at sea level — most people get adequate air in.
  • The distinction between SYSTEMIC (central, e.g., stroke volume) adaptations and PERIPHERAL (local muscle) adaptations — and how a runner and a cyclist can have equal stroke volumes but different VO2 max readings depending on the test modality.
  • Daily physiological variation: resting and max heart rate fluctuate day to day; VO2 max can vary up to ~8% from natural daily variation alone — so a single test cannot establish change.
  • Why even TWO tests aren't ideal — the difference can be driven by hydration, nutrition, and environmental temperature rather than real fitness change.
  • The remedy: cheap, repeatable tests done many times a year (5k run 6-7+ times) so that non-training variation cancels out and the TREND becomes the signal.
  • How CrossFit benchmark workouts function as standardized, repeatable tests — 'the benchmark workouts become the standardized tests.'
  • Concrete benchmark-as-test designs the author proposes: three 2-min rounds of thrusters + pull-ups (Fran-like), three 2-min sets of clean and jerks (Grace-like), a continuous 6-min Fight Gone Bad-style test.
  • How to test single energy systems if you want them isolated: phosphagen = max 60m sprint, vertical jump, or clean and jerk; glycolytic = something maximal for ~90 seconds; aerobic = sustained 6+ minute effort.
  • The requirement that a movement used to test VO2 max must be sustainable CONTINUOUSLY for ~6 minutes or more — if you have to break sets and rest (e.g., 20-lb wall ball overloading the arms), it's not measuring aerobic capacity; lighten the load so work is continuous.
  • The free numeric-estimate options: 1.5-mile run (6 laps of a 400m track) or a 12-minute max-distance run, plugged into a VO2 max calculator.
  • The honest acknowledgement that field estimates have prediction error vs. true gas-exchange measurement — but they are free and repeatable.
  • The 150 wall-ball-for-time example for non-runners and the rule that improving time = improving wall-ball VO2 max.
  • The opening epistemology point: coaches' field-tested trial-and-error often leads the science; scientists later study why it works.
  • The cross-country skier example — highest recorded VO2 maxes because they use the most muscle tissue — connecting muscle mass recruited to aerobic capacity expressed.

Concepts to understand

  • Test specificity / sport-specificity: a valid assessment must replicate the energy-system AND movement demands of the athlete's actual sport or goal. Choosing a test that doesn't mirror the demand produces data that doesn't answer the question being asked.
  • VO2 max is movement-specific, not a universal number: because peripheral muscle adaptations (capillarization, mitochondria) are local, an athlete expresses different VO2 max values depending on which muscles the test loads. A coach cannot treat one lab number as a global fitness verdict.
  • Systemic vs. peripheral adaptation: training drives both a central/cardiac response (stroke volume, blood volume) and local muscular responses (capillary density, enzyme/mitochondrial content). Understanding this explains why modality changes the score and why cross-training transfers imperfectly.
  • Benchmarks as standardized, repeatable tests: CrossFit's named workouts (Fran, Grace, Linda, Fight Gone Bad) are reproducible protocols whose scores are directly comparable over time — they ARE the gym's fitness lab. Re-testing the same benchmark is how programming effectiveness is evaluated.
  • Trend over single data point: because of daily biological variation (~8% for VO2 max) plus hydration/nutrition/temperature noise, change must be inferred from many repetitions over a year, not one or two tests. The slope of the trend, not any single result, is the signal.
  • Quantifying and tracking performance with low-cost, high-frequency measurement: cheap repeatable tests beat expensive infrequent ones for monitoring progress because frequency lets noise average out and lets the coach adjust quickly.
  • Designing a test that exposes the targeted energy system: aerobic tests require continuous effort of ~6+ minutes; if local muscular fatigue forces rest breaks, the test stops measuring aerobic capacity and starts measuring local muscular endurance — load and rep selection must keep the effort continuous.
  • Energy-system targeting for isolation when desired: phosphagen (≤~10 s maximal — sprint, jump, single C&J), glycolytic (~30-90 s maximal), oxidative/aerobic (sustained multi-minute). A coach should match test duration and intensity to the pathway in question.
  • Evaluating progress against CrossFit's definition of fitness and the athlete's personal goal: the right test is the one tied to what the athlete is trying to accomplish; for a wrestler, that's a multi-modal capacity test resembling a match, not an isolated treadmill number.
  • Cost/access/control as practical programming criteria: tests the coach can administer on demand, repeat frequently, and run without external labs are more useful for ongoing monitoring — practicality is part of test validity in the field.
  • Coaching-leads-science epistemology: hands-on, field-tested observation frequently precedes scientific validation; this underwrites CrossFit's empirical, observe-measure-repeat approach to programming rather than deferring to conventional lab standards.
  • Muscle mass recruited drives expressed aerobic capacity: the more muscle tissue an event uses (cross-country skiing, thrusters), the higher the VO2 max expressed — favoring whole-body, multi-joint testing and programming.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenarios where an athlete or another coach wants to spend money on a lab VO2 max or body-composition test, or where you must pick the best way to measure whether your programming is working (2.3.2, 1.2.6). The exam-correct move is almost always to re-test a relevant, repeatable benchmark that mirrors the athlete's goal and demands, track the trend over multiple attempts, and interpret single-test swings cautiously because of daily variation (2.3.1, 2.3.3). Sport-specific cases (a wrestler, a rower, a runner) test whether you choose a movement- and energy-system-appropriate assessment rather than a generic one (2.2.3, 1.2.2), and conceptual items test whether you can explain why CrossFit relies on benchmark workouts to quantify fitness (3.1.9, 2.3.4).

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

VO2 max
The maximum rate at which the body can take up and use oxygen, measured by comparing the oxygen content of inspired vs. expired air during work to exhaustion; the conventional lab measure of aerobic fitness, expressed in ml of O2 per kg of body weight per minute.
Gold standard (of testing)
The reference test considered most accurate for a measurement — here, the lab gas-exchange VO2 max test. The article challenges whether being the 'gold standard' makes it the most USEFUL test for a coach tracking real performance.
Wingate test
A 30-second maximal-output stationary-bike test used to assess the anaerobic (phosphagen and glycolytic) energy pathways.
Stroke volume
The amount of blood pumped by the heart per beat. A central/systemic factor in VO2 max; two athletes can share a large stroke volume yet test differently because of peripheral muscle differences.
Systemic (central) adaptation
Whole-body training adaptations centered on the cardiovascular system, such as increased stroke volume and blood volume; they benefit performance across many activities.
Peripheral adaptation
Local adaptations within the specific muscles trained — more capillaries (capillarization), more mitochondria, and more aerobic enzymes — which improve oxygen delivery to and extraction by those particular muscles.
Capillarization
The density of capillaries within a muscle, determining how large a blood supply that muscle can accept; a key peripheral determinant of VO2 max.
Mitochondria / aerobic enzymes
The cellular machinery that extracts oxygen from blood and uses it to produce energy aerobically; their quantity in a muscle determines how effectively that muscle uses delivered oxygen.
Hemoglobin content (oxygen-carrying capacity)
The blood's capacity to carry oxygen, set largely by hemoglobin; one of the four sea-level determinants of VO2 max.
Movement-specific VO2 max
The principle that VO2 max is not one fixed number but varies by the movement tested — a 'running VO2 max,' 'cycling VO2 max,' 'thruster VO2 max,' etc. — because the limiting peripheral adaptations are local to the muscles used.
Daily (biological) variation
Normal day-to-day fluctuation in physiological measures; VO2 max can vary up to ~8% from this alone, so a single test cannot reliably establish whether fitness has changed.
Benchmark workout
A named, standardized CrossFit workout (e.g., Fran, Grace, Linda, Fight Gone Bad) performed under fixed conditions so that scores are comparable over time — functioning as a repeatable field test of work capacity.
Phosphagen system
The energy pathway powering very short, maximal efforts (roughly ≤10 seconds); tested with a max sprint, vertical jump, or single clean and jerk.
Glycolytic system
The energy pathway powering high-intensity efforts lasting roughly 30-90 seconds before fatigue forces a stop; tested with an all-out effort sustainable for about 90 seconds.
Oxidative (aerobic) system
The energy pathway powering sustained efforts of several minutes or more; tested with continuous work of about 6 minutes or longer.
Work capacity
The athlete's ability to do real work across modalities and durations; CrossFit measures it through repeatable benchmark performance rather than isolated lab markers.
1.5-mile / 12-minute run test
Field tests (6 laps of a 400m track, or max distance run in 12 minutes) that estimate a numeric VO2 max via published calculators — free and repeatable, with some prediction error vs. true gas-exchange measurement.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • This article is educational/programming theory and contains no medical-emergency content, but note one real-world safety thread: the wrestler is cutting >11% body weight (62 kg to 55 kg) before testing — rapid weight-cutting/dehydration is a genuine athlete-safety and (potentially) referral concern, and dehydration is explicitly named as a factor that distorts test results.
  • Recommending or interpreting expensive lab tests (VO2 max, body composition) for a client is outside what a CCFT needs to do and the article advises against it — keep guidance within scope by using gym-based benchmarks rather than positioning yourself as a clinical exercise physiologist.
  • Do not draw fitness conclusions from a single test result; acting on one data point (e.g., changing a program because of one 'down' VO2 max or benchmark day) ignores daily variation and is a judgment error.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. A competitive rower asks you to help track whether her conditioning program is improving her race fitness. A nearby university offers a treadmill VO2 max test for $200. What is the best coaching recommendation?

  1. A. Book the treadmill VO2 max test because it is the gold standard and gives a precise number.
  2. B. Re-test a repeatable, rowing-specific benchmark (e.g., a 2k row or a fixed-time max-meters piece) several times across the season and track the trend.
  3. C. Run one treadmill VO2 max test now and one at season's end, then compare the two numbers.
  4. D. Have her do a Wingate test to capture her anaerobic power instead.
  5. E. Use a single body-composition scan as the primary measure of her conditioning.
Show answer

Answer: B — B applies test specificity and the trend-over-single-point principle: a rowing-specific, repeatable benchmark mirrors her sport's demands and, done frequently, lets daily variation average out. A and C fail because a treadmill test isn't rowing-specific and, per the article, one or even two tests can't separate real change from ~8% daily variation plus hydration/nutrition/temperature noise. D measures the wrong thing for endurance race fitness. E measures body composition, not conditioning.

Scenario 2. You program 'Karen' (150 wall-ball shots for time) as a way to monitor an athlete's aerobic capacity. With a 20-lb ball, his arms fatigue and he must stop and rest in long sets. Based on the article, what should you change so the test better reflects his VO2 max?

  1. A. Keep the 20-lb ball but allow unlimited rest, since total time still reflects aerobics.
  2. B. Increase the ball weight so the test is harder and more discriminating.
  3. C. Use a lighter ball (and possibly add reps) so he can work continuously for 6 minutes or more.
  4. D. Replace it with a single all-out 30-second effort to capture his anaerobic power.
  5. E. Stop testing aerobic capacity with wall ball entirely; only a lab test can measure VO2 max.
Show answer

Answer: C — The article states a movement used to test VO2 max must be sustainable continuously for ~6 minutes or more; if local muscular fatigue forces rest breaks, you're measuring muscular endurance, not aerobic capacity. Lightening the load (and adding reps) restores continuous work. A is wrong because the rest breaks are exactly the problem. B worsens it. D tests the wrong energy system. E ignores the article's whole point that repeatable field/benchmark tests are valid measures.

Scenario 3. Coaches of a 62 kg wrestler want a treadmill VO2 max test plus a Wingate test to evaluate his fitness for competition. Why does the author consider these poor choices, and what does he propose instead?

  1. A. They are too easy; he proposes adding a heavier treadmill protocol.
  2. B. They don't mirror wrestling's multi-line-of-action demands; he proposes a multi-modal benchmark like 2-min rounds of thrusters/pull-ups or a Fight Gone Bad-style test.
  3. C. They are unsafe; he proposes skipping testing altogether.
  4. D. They overestimate VO2 max; he proposes only a body-fat measurement.
  5. E. They are fine as designed; he only objects to the cost.
Show answer

Answer: B — Wrestling uses pushes, pulls, and static grips with arms and legs over three 2-minute rounds; a treadmill/bike test and an isolated 30-second Wingate don't reproduce those combined cardiovascular-plus-muscular demands. The author proposes multi-modal benchmark tests (Fran-like thruster/pull-up rounds, Grace-like clean-and-jerk sets, or a 6-minute Fight Gone Bad-style test) that tax the relevant systems together. Cost is a secondary benefit, not the main objection (so E is wrong); the other options misstate his reasoning.

Scenario 4. An athlete is discouraged because his benchmark Fran time was 12 seconds slower this week than three weeks ago and concludes his programming isn't working. How should you, as the coach, interpret and respond?

  1. A. Agree the program failed and overhaul it immediately.
  2. B. Explain that single-session swings reflect daily variation, hydration, sleep, and conditions; judge progress from the trend across many re-tests, not one result.
  3. C. Tell him benchmark times are unreliable and switch to a lab VO2 max test.
  4. D. Add more volume right away to force a faster time next week.
  5. E. Stop re-testing Fran because the number is demoralizing.
Show answer

Answer: B — The article emphasizes that physiological parameters vary day to day (up to ~8% for VO2 max) and that hydration, nutrition, and temperature can move a single result more than real fitness change does. The coaching-correct response is to read the trend over multiple re-tests rather than react to one data point. A and D overreact to noise; C abandons a valid repeatable benchmark for an expensive, less practical test; E discards the very tool that reveals the trend over time.

Scenario 5. Which test design best isolates an athlete's PHOSPHAGEN energy system, consistent with the article's examples?

  1. A. A continuous 6-minute Fight Gone Bad-style effort.
  2. B. A 5k run repeated several times across the year.
  3. C. A maximal 60-meter sprint, a vertical jump, or a single clean and jerk.
  4. D. An all-out effort sustained for about 90 seconds until collapse.
  5. E. A treadmill ramp test to exhaustion.
Show answer

Answer: C — The article maps the phosphagen system to very short, maximal efforts: a max sprint (~60m), a vertical jump, or a single clean and jerk. A and E target the aerobic/oxidative system (sustained effort), B is an aerobic field test, and D describes a glycolytic-system effort (~90 seconds). Matching test duration and intensity to the target pathway is the underlying skill.

Scenario 6. A runner and a cyclist have nearly identical stroke volumes, yet the runner scores a higher VO2 max on a treadmill and the cyclist scores higher on a bike. What concept best explains this, and why does it matter for how you assess athletes?

  1. A. Lung oxygen delivery differs between them, so you should test breathing capacity.
  2. B. One simply has a higher 'true' VO2 max, so always use the higher number.
  3. C. Peripheral (local muscle) adaptations are movement-specific, so VO2 max is movement-specific — assess athletes with tests that match the movements relevant to their goal.
  4. D. Daily variation explains the gap, so a single test on either modality is fine.
  5. E. Stroke volume is irrelevant to VO2 max, so ignore cardiovascular factors entirely.
Show answer

Answer: C — Equal stroke volumes (a central factor) but different modality scores point to peripheral adaptations — the trained muscles' capillarization and mitochondrial/enzyme content are local, making VO2 max movement-specific ('running VO2 max,' 'cycling VO2 max'). The coaching implication is to test with movements that match the athlete's goal. A is wrong because at sea level lung delivery isn't limiting; B and D misread the cause; E contradicts the article, which lists stroke volume as a genuine determinant.

Scenario 7. A general-fitness member wants the most useful, sustainable way to confirm over the next year that her aerobic conditioning is trending upward, without lab costs. What do you recommend?

  1. A. One professionally administered VO2 max test now, treated as her baseline for life.
  2. B. A repeatable field/benchmark test (e.g., a 5k run, a 12-minute run, or a continuous 6-minute benchmark) performed many times across the year, watching the trend.
  3. C. Whichever single test produces the highest number so she stays motivated.
  4. D. A 30-second Wingate test repeated monthly.
  5. E. Monthly body-fat percentage measurements as a proxy for aerobic fitness.
Show answer

Answer: B — The article's core practical recommendation is cheap, repeatable tests done frequently so non-training variation cancels out and the trend becomes visible — a 5k, 12-minute run, or sustained 6-minute benchmark fits. A single baseline (A) can't show change and ignores daily variation; C cherry-picks noise; D tests the anaerobic system, not aerobic conditioning; E measures body composition, not aerobic capacity.

D2 · Programming 14% of exam Confidence tier: ___

69_08_dissecting_fish.pdf

Open the PDF on Google Drive →

Why this is on the reading list

This article gives you the conceptual engine behind why CrossFit programs the way it does: the 'fish diagram' explains the inverse relationship between an athlete's proximity to genetic potential and the program complexity required to keep progressing, and it argues that CrossFit develops overall fitness as a single entity rather than a stack of separately periodized components. For Domain 2 (Programming, 14%), it directly supports designing GPP sequences, deciding when and how much to bias a training stimulus toward a single element (e.g., strength), and explaining why constantly varied, broad-spectrum training sustains progress longer than single-modality specialization. It also underpins the 'trust the program / don't make unacceptable modifications' judgment a trainer needs when athletes want to cherry-pick their favorite domains.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 2.1.1 Design single workouts using the CrossFit methodology
  • 2.1.2 Design a sequence of workouts that improves general physical preparedness (GPP)
  • 2.2.3 Scale for athletes with sport-specific goals
  • 2.2.5 Scale by skill level
  • 2.3.3 Adjust programming based on performance and goals
  • 2.3.4 Evaluate athlete progress relative to CrossFit's definition of fitness and their personal goal
  • 3.1.9 Teach the goals of CrossFit programming and how goals are met (programming with variance)
  • 3.1.12 Teach the principles of scaling

What to focus on while reading

  • The core claim of the fish diagram: as fitness/performance rises toward genetic potential, the NEED for training complexity rises with it (the two are positively linked), while the RATE of adaptation falls — note these are two different relationships moving in opposite directions.
  • The beginner-to-advanced programming progression for a single element: linear progression (load up every workout) -> weekly load increases -> monthly load increases. Each step = a more complex program organization. Tie this to scaling by skill level (2.2.5).
  • Figure 2's key point: each fitness component (strength, endurance, mobility) has its OWN independent plot on the diagram, so one athlete can be advanced in one element and beginner in another at the same time — programming complexity should match each element's level.
  • The 'least-developed element improves fastest' rule under CrossFit's even-handed approach, and that as elements converge toward similar proximity to genetic potential, their rates of gain even out.
  • The conceptual breakthrough: don't dissect fitness into components — RECONSTRUCT it as a single entity. The 'performance improvement' line on the diagram represents OVERALL FITNESS, not any one derived component.
  • Figure 3's finite-recovery model: a fixed pool of recoverable work units (the example uses 100 units / 72 hours) gets distributed across elements. Total fitness gain is roughly the same regardless of distribution; only the PROFILE/bias changes.
  • The 80/20 strength/endurance example vs. the ~33/33/33 strength/endurance/mobility example — same total fitness gain, different element-by-element magnitudes. Understand the trade-off, not the numbers.
  • The counterintuitive complexity rule: every time you ADD a fitness element to the training, the complexity line for each individual element FLATTENS — i.e., the more elements you train concurrently, the SIMPLER the program organization you can run and still progress.
  • Why this is the punchline: this flattening is the reason the basic CrossFit model sustains steady fitness increases LONGER than any single-element model before requiring elaborate periodization.
  • The three integration principles at the end: (1) teach/learn every barbell lift correctly, (2) trust the program, (3) think about and apply what you learn with patient, progressive effort ('invisible work time').
  • What counts as an UNACCEPTABLE modification vs. an acceptable 'tweak': ignoring your least-favorite element, or training an element at less than capacity (running geeks scaling down WOD weight, lifters refusing to run) = unacceptable; small evidence-based tweaks to a sound system = OK.
  • The honest limit Kilgore concedes: the 'black box' / emergent magic of mixed-modal training produces a bonus that this math model cannot fully account for — note this so you don't over-trust the tidy numbers.
  • The framing that all of this is a trainer's analytical/judgment work ('invisible work time' / Think-Learn-Apply) — programming decisions are reasoned, not formulaic.

Concepts to understand

  • Inverse relationship between adaptation rate and required complexity: a novice gets fast results from simple programming; an advanced athlete near genetic potential needs increasingly complex programming to extract small additional gains. Apply this to choose program complexity by where the athlete sits, not by what looks impressive.
  • Each fitness element progresses independently: design or scale the stimulus for an element based on THAT element's developmental level for THAT athlete (e.g., simple, frequent strength loading for a strength-novice who is endurance-advanced).
  • Fitness as a single entity: CrossFit develops overall fitness; strength, endurance, and mobility are derivative inputs. Evaluate program success against broad fitness and the athlete's goal (2.3.4), not against maximal gain in any one isolated component.
  • Finite recoverable work capacity: an athlete can only recover from a bounded amount of training stress per unit time, so programming is an allocation problem — biasing toward one element necessarily takes 'work units' from others.
  • Bias vs. total gain: changing the distribution of training across elements changes the PROFILE of adaptation (which element grows fastest) but leaves total fitness gain roughly constant — useful when an athlete has a legitimate sport-specific need (2.2.3).
  • Least-developed-element-improves-fastest: under even-handed CrossFit programming, the weakest element gains fastest and rates converge over time — a rationale for general, varied programming and for attacking weaknesses (consistent with CrossFit's goal of no holes).
  • Concurrent training flattens complexity: training multiple elements at once lets you keep program organization simple while still progressing, which is why constantly varied GPP outruns single-element programs on duration of progress (2.1.2, 3.1.9).
  • Integrating focused strength work into CrossFit: it is permissible to bias toward strength to accelerate strength gains, but only with eyes open to the cost to other elements and without abandoning broad-spectrum intent — a scaling/bias decision, not a methodology change (2.2.3, 2.3.3).
  • Acceptable tweaks vs. unacceptable modifications: small, justified adjustments to a sound, varied program are fine; selectively avoiding weak domains or sandbagging effort guts the result. Apply this when an athlete pressures you to drop their weak movements.
  • Programming requires trainer judgment ('Think. Learn. Apply.'): sound programming comes from continual study, observation, and reasoning applied to the individual — the exam rewards reasoned application over memorized templates.
  • Limits of the model (the black box): the emergent benefit of mixed-modal variance exceeds what any additive component math predicts, so trust the methodology even where the arithmetic is incomplete.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenario questions that hand you an athlete profile (e.g., strong but poor engine, or a masters athlete with a sport-specific goal) and ask what programming or scaling decision best serves CrossFit's broad-fitness goal — testing 2.2.3, 2.2.5, 2.3.3, and 2.3.4. Others will probe whether you can justify constantly varied GPP over single-element specialization (2.1.2, 3.1.9) or recognize when an athlete's requested change (skipping their weak domain, scaling weight to stay in their comfort zone) is an unacceptable modification rather than legitimate scaling (3.1.12). The 'finite recovery / bias-the-stimulus' idea typically appears as a trade-off question: bias toward strength and accept slower conditioning gains, or keep balance for overall fitness.

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Fish diagram
Kilgore and Rippetoe's graph (named because its lines resemble a fish) showing how fitness/performance improvement, rate of adaptation, and required training complexity relate across an athlete's career. Its central message: the closer you get to genetic potential, the more complex your program must become.
Genetic potential
The ceiling of adaptation an individual can reach. The nearer an athlete is to it, the slower the gains and the more sophisticated the programming needed to keep progressing.
Training complexity (program organization)
How elaborate a program's structure is — e.g., simple linear progression (add load every session) for novices vs. weekly or monthly load progressions and periodization for advanced athletes.
Linear progression
The simplest program organization: increasing the load (or stimulus) every workout. It works best and only for as long as a relative beginner can keep adding load; gains from it eventually max out and require a more complex scheme.
Fitness as a single entity
The idea that CrossFit's target is overall fitness itself, with strength, endurance, and mobility as derivative inputs — so the 'performance improvement' line on the fish diagram represents total fitness, not any one component.
Recoverable work tolerance / work units
The finite amount of training stress an athlete can recover from in a given window (Kilgore's example: 100 work units per 72 hours). Programming distributes this limited pool across fitness elements.
Training bias
Skewing the distribution of training toward one element (e.g., 80% strength / 20% endurance). It speeds gains in the favored element and slows the others, but total fitness gain stays roughly constant — only the adaptation profile shifts.
Profile bias
The characteristic shape of an athlete's development across elements that results from how training was distributed — the same total fitness expressed as different strength/endurance/mobility balances.
Complexity flattening
The principle that adding more fitness elements to concurrent training flattens the complexity line for each element, so you can run a simpler overall program and still progress — the mechanism behind CrossFit's durability of gains.
Broad-spectrum fitness
Capacity developed evenly across all elements/domains; the non-negotiable focus of CrossFit programming that tweaks must not compromise.
Unacceptable modification
A change that undermines broad-spectrum intent — ignoring a least-favorite element, or training an element below one's capacity (e.g., habitually scaling WOD weights down to avoid hard lifting, or a lifter refusing to run).
Invisible work time
The unbilled mental labor of a trainer — reading, observing, reasoning, and planning — that Kilgore argues is essential to good programming. Captured in his 'Think. Learn. Apply.' framing.
The black box / mixed-modal magic
The emergent, hard-to-measure performance bonus that arises from the interplay of varied training elements, exceeding what additive component math predicts.
GPP (general physical preparedness)
Broad, non-specialized fitness across all elements — the outcome CrossFit programming is built to develop and sustain (Content Outline task 2.1.2).

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. A relatively new athlete has been adding weight to their main lifts every single session for months and is still setting PRs each week. They ask whether they should switch to a more elaborate, periodized strength template like the advanced athletes use. Based on the fish-diagram concept, what is the best coaching response?

  1. A. Switch them to a complex monthly-periodized program now so they learn good habits early
  2. B. Keep them on simple linear progression (adding load each session) for as long as it keeps producing gains, and add complexity only when those gains stall
  3. C. Stop progressing load and focus exclusively on technique until they plateau naturally
  4. D. Have them bias 80% of training to strength to maximize their newbie gains
  5. E. Move them straight to weekly load increases to slow the progression down on purpose
Show answer

Answer: B — The fish diagram says required complexity rises only as an athlete approaches genetic potential; a novice still gaining from the simplest scheme should stay on it until it stops working (B). A is premature complexity. C abandons a working stimulus. D narrows their program against broad-fitness intent and isn't what the situation calls for. E deliberately handicaps a progression that is still productive.

Scenario 2. An athlete is advanced in endurance, intermediate in mobility, and a near-beginner in strength. Using the principle that each fitness element has its own plot on the fish diagram, how should you organize their training?

  1. A. Use a single uniform complexity level across all three elements since they train together
  2. B. Program the most complex organization for strength because it's the weakest element
  3. C. Match program complexity to each element's level: simple, frequent loading for strength; moderate for mobility; the most complex organization reserved for the advanced endurance element
  4. D. Drop strength work until endurance and mobility catch down to it
  5. E. Treat all three as advanced and periodize everything heavily
Show answer

Answer: C — Each element progresses independently, so complexity should track each element's developmental level (C): the advanced element needs the most complex programming, the novice element the simplest. A and E ignore the independent-plots concept. B inverts the relationship (beginners need simple, not complex, programming). D wastes the opportunity for the weak element to improve fastest.

Scenario 3. A masters athlete trains roughly equal thirds of strength, endurance, and mobility and is frustrated that their squat isn't climbing as fast as a friend who does a dedicated strength block. They ask whether the balanced approach is 'wasting' their training. What is the most accurate explanation grounded in the article?

  1. A. Balanced training wastes effort; switch fully to strength to stop leaving gains on the table
  2. B. Recoverable work capacity is finite, so balanced thirds yield the same total fitness gain but a different profile — slower strength gain offset by greater endurance and mobility gains; biasing toward strength would speed the squat but cost the other elements
  3. C. The friend must be using performance enhancers, because balanced training should produce equal strength gains
  4. D. Strength is unaffected by how training is distributed, so the balance is irrelevant to the squat
  5. E. They should add more total volume so every element gains at the maximum rate simultaneously
Show answer

Answer: B — With a finite recoverable work pool, distribution shifts the profile of adaptation while keeping total fitness gain roughly constant (B): even thirds buy broad fitness at the cost of slower single-element gains. A abandons broad-spectrum intent. C is a non-sequitur. D contradicts the bias-affects-magnitude point. E ignores that recovery capacity is bounded — you can't max every element at once.

Scenario 4. A member who hates rowing and the assault bike asks you to let them substitute extra lifting for every conditioning piece because 'strength is what matters for me.' How should you handle this within the article's principles?

  1. A. Agree — biasing toward their goal is exactly what the fish diagram endorses
  2. B. Refuse to coach them further until they commit to conditioning
  3. C. Explain that systematically ignoring their least-developed element is an unacceptable modification that undercuts broad fitness; keep them training conditioning at full effort while you can still legitimately bias some emphasis toward strength
  4. D. Let them skip conditioning for now and revisit it in a few months
  5. E. Tell them total fitness is identical regardless, so it doesn't matter what they skip
Show answer

Answer: C — Ignoring a least-favorite element is precisely the 'unacceptable modification' the article warns against; the fix is to preserve broad-spectrum work at real effort while reasoned emphasis is fine (C). A confuses acceptable bias with abandoning an element. B is needlessly punitive. D normalizes dropping the weakness. E misuses the total-fitness claim — total gain is similar across distributions, but eliminating an element entirely (and sandbagging effort) is what's prohibited.

Scenario 5. A newer coach argues that to build the broadest, longest-lasting fitness, athletes should run highly complex, separately periodized blocks for strength, then endurance, then mobility in sequence. Using the article's 'complexity flattening' point, what is the better-supported programming approach?

  1. A. The coach is right; sequential single-element blocks are the most durable way to build fitness
  2. B. Concurrently training multiple elements flattens the complexity needed per element, so a simpler, constantly varied program sustains fitness gains longer than sequential single-element specialization
  3. C. Athletes should only ever train one element at a time to avoid interference
  4. D. Program complexity has no effect on how long progress can be sustained
  5. E. Maximal complexity in every element at all times is what produces the longest progress
Show answer

Answer: B — The article's punchline is that adding elements flattens each element's complexity line, letting a simpler concurrent program keep producing gains longer than any single-element model (B). A and C describe the specialization the article argues is less durable. D contradicts the central adaptation/complexity relationship. E is the opposite of the flattening insight — concurrency reduces, not maximizes, the complexity required.

Scenario 6. You're explaining to a new trainer why CrossFit programs constantly varied, broad work instead of just chasing one number. Which statement best captures the article's 'fitness as a single entity' reasoning?

  1. A. CrossFit develops overall fitness as the entity; strength, endurance, and mobility are derivative inputs, so we program and evaluate against broad fitness and the athlete's goal rather than maxing any one component
  2. B. CrossFit develops three separate fitnesses that should each be periodized independently and judged on their own
  3. C. Only the single best component an athlete has should drive programming decisions
  4. D. Overall fitness is just the sum of three numbers with nothing emergent beyond them
  5. E. Component development is irrelevant; only the daily WOD score matters
Show answer

Answer: A — The article's reframe is that overall fitness itself is what CrossFit develops, with the components as derivative (A) — which is why progress is judged against broad fitness and the athlete's goal (task 2.3.4). B is the dissect-it view Kilgore explicitly abandons. C and E distort the evaluation basis. D ignores the 'black box' emergent bonus he concedes exists beyond the additive math.

D2 · Programming 14% of exam Confidence tier: ___

71_08_Human_Power_Output.pdf

Open the PDF on Google Drive →

Why this is on the reading list

This article supplies the exercise-physiology reasoning behind why CrossFit programs the way it does: mixed-modal metabolic conditioning ('metcon') workouts that span the entire human power spectrum and tax all three energy systems, all muscle fiber types, the cardiovascular system, and the CNS at once. For a CCFT candidate, it backs Domain 2 (Programming) directly because it explains, mechanistically, why constantly varied, full-body, high-power workouts build broad work capacity while specialized training (pure strength or pure aerobic) does not. The exam never asks you to recite watts or fiber names; it asks you to make programming and scaling decisions that reflect this 'why,' and to teach athletes the goal of variance. Understanding this article lets you defend a workout's stimulus, scale it without losing the intended training effect, and explain to an athlete why their pure-strength or pure-cardio background leaves gaps CrossFit fills.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 2.1.1 Design single workouts using the CrossFit methodology
  • 2.1.2 Design a sequence of workouts that improves general physical preparedness (GPP)
  • 2.2.5 Scale by skill level
  • 2.2.3 Scale for athletes with sport-specific goals
  • 2.3.4 Evaluate athlete progress relative to CrossFit's definition of fitness and their personal goal
  • 3.1.9 Teach the goals of CrossFit programming and how goals are met (programming with variance)
  • 3.1.8 Teach the CrossFit definition of fitness and health and the four models illustrating it
  • 3.1.11 Teach relative intensity
  • 1.2.2 Evaluate athlete's work capacity
  • 1.2.4 Monitor athlete for signs of over- or under-training

What to focus on while reading

  • Glassman's directive to 'blur distinctions between cardio and strength training' — note this is the thesis the whole article defends, and it maps to CrossFit's definition of fitness (work capacity across broad time and modal domains).
  • Table 1: the inverse relationship between power output and time to exhaustion (6,000 W metabolic / 1 sec for an Olympic lift down to 1,000 W / 2 hours for a 40-mile bike). Understand the SHAPE of the curve, not the exact numbers.
  • The three predominant energy systems mapped to power: phosphagen (highest power, seconds), glycolytic (high power, ~14 sec to minutes), oxidative (low power, minutes to hours).
  • The note that only the PREDOMINANT system is listed — every effort uses all three; even a 14-sec sprint draws ~10% from oxidative, and a 6-min effort draws ~20% from anaerobic. This kills any exam answer that treats a workout as purely one system.
  • Figure 1: activities expressed as a PERCENTAGE of an individual's max power output — this is the bridge to relative intensity and scaling (a load is light or heavy relative to THIS athlete).
  • Three muscle fiber types and their roles: Type IIb/IIx (max bursts, fatigue fast), Type IIa (sustained power, more fatigue-resistant), Type I (low intensity, endurance).
  • The orderly recruitment principle: Type I recruited first (low threshold), then Type IIa (~20% of max demand), then Type IIb at the highest demand. Recruitment is driven by demand for force/power via CNS excitation.
  • Only TRAINED athletes can recruit all available motor units — this explains fast early strength gains in novices ('learning' to recruit fibers), a scaling/progression insight.
  • How a continuous metcon recruits fibers over TIME: as early-recruited fibers fatigue, the athlete must send stronger waves of excitation and pull in higher-threshold fibers — so a sustained metcon ends up taxing the whole fiber pool even at submaximal loads.
  • The 'capillary dilution' concept: pure heavy/low-rep strength training enlarges Type II fibers and spreads capillaries farther apart, hurting oxygen delivery — why strong-only athletes gas out on metcons.
  • Aerobic training does the opposite: increases capillary density and the capillary-to-fiber ratio, improving oxygen extraction.
  • What conventional strength training does NOT do: improve cardiac output, blood volume, or blood composition — a key limitation the exam may test as a programming gap.
  • What steady aerobic training does NOT do: build force/power or Type II size — the opposite gap.
  • The relative-load example: an athlete with a 270 lb clean & jerk does 'Grace' (135 lb) at ~50% of max and starts with mostly Type I/IIa; an athlete with a 150 lb C&J must recruit everything from rep one and fatigues far faster. Same workout, completely different relative intensity and stimulus.
  • Body-size effects: lighter athletes have an advantage in bodyweight-heavy WODs (Angie, Cindy, Murph) because there is less total work; taller athletes do more work on squats and floor-to-overhead. This is a real scaling consideration.
  • CNS / neural fatigue: repeated intense efforts deplete neurotransmitters and reduce both physical AND cognitive performance — relevant to monitoring overtraining and managing intensity.
  • The 'instant switching' demand (e.g., Helen's run-to-kettlebell-to-pull-up): blood must be redistributed between muscle beds, which is itself a trainable stress unique to mixed-modal work.
  • Hormonal response factors that strength-style metcons satisfy: large-muscle-group exercises, heavy loads, moderate-to-high volume, short rest, and 2+ years of training — and that only fibers ACTIVATED by resistance work get the hormonal adaptation.
  • Chronic long-slow-distance can LOWER testosterone (males) and estrogen (females) — supports 'train hard and smart, not just long,' and CrossFit's success with endurance athletes on lower mileage.
  • Which athletes transfer best into CrossFit at the outset: those from anaerobic-based sports with long match durations (rugby, soccer, MMA) that already demand varied power outputs — vs. pure strength or pure aerobic specialists who struggle.
  • The specific benchmark WODs and their stimulus character: Grace (heavy/short), Fran (high-power couplet), Linda (three-bar strength-biased but still for time), Helen/Angie/Cindy/Murph (more bodyweight, more aerobic flavor) — note which lean strength vs. which lean aerobic.
  • Leyland's honest limit: even after dissecting the mechanisms, he admits research has NOT explained 'why the whole is greater than the sum of the parts' — so treat this as a supporting rationale, not settled proof.
  • The 'Ferrari engine with a lawnmower fuel pump' framing — the muscles are the engine, but delivery/recovery systems are the fuel pump; broad fitness needs both.

Concepts to understand

  • The human power spectrum: maximal power can only be sustained for seconds, and as duration lengthens, sustainable power drops sharply. Where a movement or workout sits on this curve predicts which energy system dominates and how it should be programmed and paced.
  • Energy systems are a continuum, not switches: phosphagen, glycolytic, and oxidative all contribute at every intensity; the question is which PREDOMINATES. Programming a 'pure' energy-system day is an oversimplification — be skeptical of exam answers that label a metcon as exclusively one system.
  • Relative intensity / relative load: the same absolute load is light or heavy depending on the individual's max. This is the physiological basis for scaling by load and for the CrossFit principle of relative intensity (task 3.1.11) — you scale to keep an athlete in the intended stimulus.
  • Orderly motor-unit recruitment: the body recruits fibers in order of demand (Type I → IIa → IIb). Higher power demand = more and higher-threshold fibers. This explains why heavier/more-explosive work trains Type II and why light long work trains Type I.
  • Recruitment over the course of a workout: in a sustained metcon, fatigue of early fibers forces recruitment of the whole fiber pool over time, so even a moderate-load metcon ends up working strength fibers AND endurance fibers — the mechanism behind metcon's broad stimulus.
  • Why specialists fail at metcons: pure strength athletes suffer capillary dilution and have untrained delivery/recovery systems; pure aerobic athletes lack force and Type II development; bodybuilders get gassed. CrossFit's mixed-modal demand trains the gaps both leave.
  • Cardiovascular and circulatory adaptations are trainable and largely separate from raw strength: cardiac output, blood volume, capillary density, and hemoglobin matter most at lower intensities and are NOT built by conventional strength training — so a complete program must include work that develops them.
  • Mixed-modal 'switching' is its own trainable stress: rapidly redirecting blood flow between muscle groups (run → pull-up) is a demand classic single-modality training never imposes, and CrossFit's couplets/triplets train it.
  • CNS / neural fatigue is real and limits performance: intense repeated efforts deplete neurotransmitters and degrade physical and cognitive output. This informs how you sequence intensity, manage volume, and watch for overtraining (task 1.2.4).
  • Hormonal adaptation is stimulus-specific: large-muscle, heavy, short-rest, higher-volume work (which metcons embody) acutely elevates anabolic hormones, but only fibers actually recruited by resistance work adapt — so movement selection and load matter for the adaptive payoff.
  • Long-slow-distance has costs: chronic excessive endurance work can suppress anabolic hormones, supporting CrossFit's preference for shorter, intense, varied training to drive adaptation efficiently — including for endurance athletes.
  • Work capacity is the target output: CrossFit's whole rationale here is increasing work capacity across broad time and modal domains, which is exactly the definition of fitness the exam expects you to teach and program toward (tasks 3.1.8, 3.1.9, 1.2.2, 2.3.4).
  • Body dimensions and bodyweight change the actual work done: lighter athletes do less work in bodyweight WODs; taller athletes do more in full-range movements. A coach accounts for this when comparing scores, scaling, and setting expectations.
  • Variance as the mechanism, not just a slogan: constantly varied, full-body, high-power movements are what force the body across the entire power range and tax every system — variance is the programming tool that produces broad GPP (tasks 2.1.2, 3.1.9).

How the exam applies this

Expect scenario questions that hand you an athlete's background (powerlifter, marathoner, bodybuilder, rugby player) or a specific benchmark and ask what stimulus the workout delivers, why a given athlete will struggle, or how to scale to preserve the intended training effect — that's tasks 2.1.1, 2.2.5, and 2.2.3. You may be asked to justify constantly varied, mixed-modal programming over isolated strength or steady cardio (tasks 2.1.2, 3.1.9) or to explain relative intensity when two athletes lift the same bar but at very different percentages of their max (task 3.1.11). Monitoring items may probe recognizing fatigue, including CNS/neural fatigue, and avoiding the over-training a single-modality, high-volume bias can cause (tasks 1.2.4, 1.2.2). The right answer almost always reflects applied coaching judgment about stimulus and the athlete in front of you — not a memorized number from Table 1.

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Power output
The rate of doing work (work per unit time, measured in watts). Higher power can only be produced for a short time; the article ranks activities by how much of an athlete's max power they demand and how long that can be held.
Metcon (metabolic conditioning)
A workout that combines full-body, multi-joint, high-power movements performed for time with little or no rest, taxing multiple energy systems and fiber types at once — the mixed-modal workouts most particular to CrossFit (e.g., Fran, Helen, Grace).
Metabolic power vs. mechanical power
Metabolic power is the chemical energy the muscle burns; mechanical power is the useful external output. Only ~23% of metabolic power becomes mechanical output — the rest is lost as heat.
Phosphagen (ATP/CP) system
The energy system that fuels the highest-power, shortest-duration efforts (seconds) such as a max lift or short sprint, using high-energy phosphates stored in the muscle. No oxygen delivery required.
Glycolytic system
The energy system that predominates in high-power efforts lasting roughly 15 seconds to a couple of minutes; produces lactate. Dominant in efforts like a 200–400 m run and much of a hard metcon.
Oxidative (aerobic) system
The energy system that predominates in lower-power, longer-duration work (minutes to hours), relying on oxygen delivery; supplies ~99% of marathon energy and aids recovery between bursts in metcons.
Type I (slow-twitch) fibers
Low-threshold, fatigue-resistant muscle fibers recruited first and used for low-intensity, endurance work. Improve via oxidative enzyme and mitochondrial increases rather than large size gains.
Type IIa (fast-twitch) fibers
Intermediate fast-twitch fibers — more fatigue-resistant than IIb but slower to produce force; recruited for sustained power such as a 400 m sprint or repeated sub-max lifts.
Type IIb / IIx (fast-twitch) fibers
Highest-threshold, highest-force, fastest-fatiguing fibers; recruited for maximal and near-maximal bursts. Require the largest CNS waves of excitation to activate.
Motor unit
A single motor neuron and all the muscle fibers it controls; every fiber in one motor unit is the same type. Force is increased by recruiting more (and higher-threshold) motor units.
Motor-unit recruitment (size/threshold principle)
The orderly activation of fibers by demand: low-threshold Type I first, then Type IIa near ~20% of max demand, then Type IIb at the highest demand. Only trained athletes can recruit all available units.
Neural / CNS fatigue
Reduced performance caused by depletion of neurotransmitters during intense, repeated effort; degrades both physical output and cognitive function and is an integral part of fatigue in metcons.
Capillary dilution (dilation)
When heavy, low-rep strength training enlarges Type II fibers without adding capillaries, the existing capillaries spread farther apart — worsening oxygen delivery and partly explaining why strength-only athletes gas out on metcons.
Capillary density / capillary-to-fiber ratio
A measure of oxygen-delivery capacity that aerobic-style training improves, enhancing the muscle's ability to extract oxygen — the opposite effect of capillary dilution.
Relative intensity (relative load)
A load or effort expressed as a percentage of a given athlete's maximum rather than an absolute number; the same bar can be ~50% for one athlete and near-max for another, which is why scaling preserves the intended stimulus.
Work capacity across broad time and modal domains
CrossFit's definition of fitness — the ability to do work across many durations and movement types. Metcons aim to expand it, and it is the yardstick for evaluating programming and progress.
Anabolic hormones
Tissue-building hormones (insulin, IGF, testosterone, growth hormone) acutely elevated by large-muscle, heavy, short-rest, higher-volume training; only recruited fibers benefit from their effects.
GPP (general physical preparedness)
Broad, non-specialized fitness across all capacities — the goal of a well-sequenced CrossFit program, achieved through constant variance across the power spectrum.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. A new member is a competitive powerlifter with an elite squat, bench, and deadlift but says he 'has no engine.' He gets completely gassed and has to rest constantly during 'Helen' (3 rounds: 400 m run, 21 KB swings, 12 pull-ups). Based on the physiology in this article, what is the best explanation to give him and the soundest programming response?

  1. A. His Type I fibers are genetically absent, so he should avoid all conditioning and stick to lifting.
  2. B. Years of heavy, low-rep training enlarged his Type II fibers and spread his capillaries apart (capillary dilution), and never trained his cardiac output or oxygen delivery; scale Helen to keep him moving and progressively build the conditioning side he's missing.
  3. C. He simply isn't trying hard enough; tell him to push harder and he'll be fine next time with no changes.
  4. D. Helen is an aerobic workout and powerlifters can't do aerobic work, so substitute a pure strength day instead.
  5. E. His glycolytic system is fully developed from lifting, so the only fix is more maximal singles.
Show answer

Answer: B — B reflects the article's mechanism: heavy low-rep training increases Type II fiber size, causing capillary dilution and poor oxygen delivery, and conventional strength training does not improve cardiac output, blood volume, or capillarization — exactly the systems Helen demands. The coaching response is to scale to preserve the stimulus and build the missing capacity. A is false (fiber types aren't 'absent'). C ignores a real physiological gap and the coach's job to scale. D is wrong because Helen is predominantly anaerobic/mixed and avoiding conditioning perpetuates the gap. E misidentifies the limitation.

Scenario 2. Two athletes do 'Grace' (30 clean-and-jerks at 135 lb for time). Athlete A has a 270 lb clean-and-jerk; Athlete B has a 155 lb clean-and-jerk. How should a coach think about the stimulus and scaling for each, per this article?

  1. A. The workout is identical for both because the load and reps are the same, so no scaling thought is needed.
  2. B. For Athlete A, 135 lb is ~50% of max — she can start with mostly Type I/IIa fibers and recruit more as they fatigue; for Athlete B, 135 lb is near-max, forcing maximal recruitment and rapid fatigue from rep one, so B likely needs a load reduction to keep the intended fast, powerful stimulus.
  3. C. Athlete B will do better because lighter athletes always have the advantage in every CrossFit workout.
  4. D. Athlete A should add weight to 'make it fair' since the workout is too easy at 50% for everyone.
  5. E. Relative intensity is irrelevant for barbell cycling; only absolute load determines the stimulus.
Show answer

Answer: B — B applies relative intensity and orderly recruitment directly from the text: at ~50% of max, Athlete A starts with lower-threshold fibers and progressively recruits higher-threshold ones as fatigue sets in, while Athlete B must recruit everything immediately and fatigues fast. Scaling load for B preserves the intended stimulus. A and E deny relative intensity. C overgeneralizes the bodyweight advantage (which applies to bodyweight-heavy WODs, not a fixed external barbell load). D misreads scaling as 'making it fair' rather than matching stimulus.

Scenario 3. A coach is defending CrossFit's constantly-varied, mixed-modal metcon programming to a skeptical endurance athlete who believes 'more long-slow-distance miles is always better.' Which response is best supported by this article?

  1. A. Long-slow-distance is the most complete training that exists, so the athlete is correct and CrossFit adds nothing.
  2. B. Chronic long-slow-distance can lower anabolic hormone levels and only trains a narrow slice of the power spectrum; mixed-modal metcons train all fiber types, all energy systems, the cardiovascular and CNS demands, and have improved endurance athletes on less mileage.
  3. C. Endurance training is useless and should be eliminated entirely from any program.
  4. D. The only benefit of metcons is that they are shorter, so the athlete just saves time with no performance difference.
  5. E. Metcons are purely anaerobic and therefore can't help an endurance athlete at all.
Show answer

Answer: B — B captures several of the article's points: chronic LSD can suppress testosterone/estrogen, single-modality work trains a narrow power band, and CrossFit has produced good endurance results with less mileage by training the whole spectrum and recovery-from-bursts. A and C are extremes the article doesn't support (it values both ends of the spectrum). D undersells the physiological breadth. E is wrong — the article notes the aerobic system aids recovery within metcons and that varied training improves aerobic capacity too.

Scenario 4. During a class, an experienced athlete late in a long, heavy metcon starts missing reps he normally makes, looks mentally foggy, and his coordination on the barbell deteriorates. Using this article's concepts, what is the most accurate read and the best in-the-moment coaching action?

  1. A. This is purely peripheral muscle fatigue with no nervous-system component, so push him to finish at the same load regardless.
  2. B. Intense repeated effort can cause CNS/neural fatigue that depletes neurotransmitters and degrades both physical AND cognitive performance; reduce load or scale reps to maintain mechanics and intensity safely rather than letting form collapse.
  3. C. He is faking fatigue to get out of the workout; ignore it.
  4. D. Fogginess and missed reps mean he is dehydrated only, so the sole fix is water with no load change.
  5. E. This proves he needs heavier singles next time to 'toughen up' his nervous system.
Show answer

Answer: B — B matches the text: neural/CNS fatigue from repeated intense bouts depletes neurotransmitters and reduces both physical and cognitive performance, so the right move protects mechanics by scaling load/reps while keeping the intended intensity. A denies the CNS component the article emphasizes. C dismisses a real warning sign. D fixates on one possible factor and ignores the demonstrated neural mechanism. E is the opposite of sound risk management for an athlete already showing fatigue-driven breakdown.

Scenario 5. A coach claims, 'Fran is a pure glycolytic workout and Murph is a pure aerobic workout, so I'll program them as single-energy-system days.' How should this be assessed against the article?

  1. A. Correct — each CrossFit workout trains exactly one energy system, so labeling them this way is accurate.
  2. B. Flawed — the article stresses that only the PREDOMINANT system can be named; all three contribute at every intensity, and sustained metcons recruit the whole fiber pool over time, so treating any metcon as single-system oversimplifies the stimulus.
  3. C. Correct for Fran but Murph uses no energy system at all because it is bodyweight.
  4. D. Flawed only because Fran is actually aerobic and Murph is actually glycolytic — the labels are just swapped.
  5. E. Correct, because energy systems operate as on/off switches selected by the athlete before the workout.
Show answer

Answer: B — B reflects the article's explicit caution: tables list only the predominant system, but every effort uses all three (e.g., even a 14-sec sprint draws ~10% oxidative; a 6-min effort ~20% anaerobic), and in a sustained metcon early fibers fatigue and force recruitment across the full pool. So no metcon is cleanly single-system. A and E treat energy systems as discrete switches, which the article rejects. C is nonsense (all work needs energy). D just swaps incorrect labels rather than fixing the underlying oversimplification.

Scenario 6. Two athletes weigh the same, but Athlete X is much taller. In 'Murph' (lots of squats, run, bodyweight movements) and in floor-to-overhead lifting, how should a coach interpret their relative outputs and scores per this article?

  1. A. Height is irrelevant to work done; identical bodyweight means identical work in every movement.
  2. B. The taller athlete performs more mechanical work in full-range movements like squats and floor-to-overhead lifts, so the coach should account for that when comparing scores and setting expectations, while remembering lighter athletes are advantaged in bodyweight-dominant WODs.
  3. C. The shorter athlete is automatically less fit because a slower Murph time always means worse conditioning.
  4. D. The taller athlete should always scale down because being tall is a disability in CrossFit.
  5. E. Body dimensions only affect Olympic lifting and have no bearing on bodyweight workouts.
Show answer

Answer: B — B applies the article's note that range of motion and body dimensions change actual work done — taller athletes do more work on squats and floor-to-overhead movements — and that lower bodyweight is an advantage in bodyweight-heavy WODs. A coach uses this to interpret scores fairly, not to penalize anyone. A and E deny the dimension effect. C wrongly equates a raw time with fitness without accounting for the work performed. D mislabels a physical characteristic as a disability and applies blanket scaling with no rationale.

Scenario 7. A gym owner asks why the program rotates across heavy lifting days, interval days, longer aerobic pieces, and mixed-modal metcons instead of just running a dedicated strength cycle. Which justification best matches this article and the goal of GPP?

  1. A. Variety is only for keeping members entertained and has no physiological purpose.
  2. B. Constantly varied work across the full power spectrum is the mechanism that develops broad work capacity — it trains all fiber types, all three energy systems, cardiovascular delivery/recovery, and the CNS coordination of switching modalities, which a single-modality cycle cannot.
  3. C. A dedicated strength cycle alone produces identical broad fitness, so the variety is unnecessary.
  4. D. Aerobic-only programming would achieve the same GPP with less effort.
  5. E. Mixing modalities is dangerous and should be avoided in favor of isolating one capacity at a time.
Show answer

Answer: B — B states the article's core programming rationale: it is the mixed-modal, full-spectrum variance that taxes every fiber type, every energy system, the circulatory delivery/recovery machinery, and the CNS — producing the broad work capacity (GPP) that specialized training leaves incomplete. A trivializes variance, which the article treats as a mechanism. C and D are exactly the specialization traps the article argues against (strength-only and aerobic-only each leave gaps). E contradicts the article, which presents mixed-modal training as CrossFit's central, effective method.
