Open the PDF on Google Drive →

Why this is on the reading list

This article is the CCFT reading list's most complete treatise on the mechanics of scaling, which is the heart of Domain 2 (Programming, 14% of the exam) and recurs in Domains 3 and 5. It directly backs the cluster of tasks under 2.2 (create scaling options for categories of athletes) and 3.1.12 (teach the principles of scaling) by giving you a usable system: scale to preserve the intended stimulus (time domain/metabolic pathway, movement pattern, complexity) using the elements of volume, load, and range of motion. It also connects scaling to rhabdo risk (1.1.3), to relative intensity (3.1.11), and to managing risk and group cohesion in a class (5.2.2, 5.2.3). Master the WHY and the decision logic here, not the specific workouts.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 2.2 Create scaling options to optimize results for categories of athletes
  • 2.2.1 Scale by age group
  • 2.2.2 Scale for special populations (e.g., pregnant, adaptive)
  • 2.2.3 Scale for athletes with sport-specific goals
  • 2.2.4 Design programming for injured athletes to maintain fitness and restore functionality
  • 2.2.5 Scale by skill level
  • 2.1.1 Design single workouts using the CrossFit methodology
  • 2.3.3 Adjust programming based on performance and goals
  • 1.1.3 Assess for rhabdomyolysis ('rhabdo') risk
  • 1.2.5 Identify when athlete is ready to progress to another goal/skill
  • 3.1.11 Teach relative intensity
  • 3.1.12 Teach the principles of scaling
  • 3.1.10 Teach the relationship between technique and intensity (threshold training)
  • 4.1.6 Identify root cause of faults
  • 5.2.2 Apply scaling to meet current physical and psychological needs of each athlete
  • 5.2.3 Manage risk for the athlete
  • 5.2.9 Balance attention across individuals while maintaining group cohesion

What to focus on while reading

  • The thesis sentence: we scale to PRESERVE THE INTENDED STIMULUS despite limitations (experience, injury, illness, range of motion) — highlight it; nearly every exam scaling question hinges on this 'preserve the stimulus' logic.
  • The Glassman frame: 'Ahead of efficacy is safety' — note that safety outranks getting the perfect stimulus when the two conflict.
  • The definition of a properly scaled workout: one that 'safely maximizes relative intensity (load, speed, range of motion)' to keep building work capacity despite limitations — tie this to the term 'relative intensity'.
  • The long-term GOAL of scaling: build toward being able to do workouts 'as prescribed' (Rx) — scaling is a bridge, not a permanent destination.
  • The THREE stimuli to preserve, in order of treatment: (1) Time Domain / metabolic pathway, (2) General Movement Patterns, (3) Complexity. Be able to name and apply each.
  • How workout DURATION maps to metabolic pathway: longer = more aerobic; shorter/intense = ATP-CP and glycolytic. Note the nuance that heavy loads in volume slow output, shifting a short workout toward ATP-CP/aerobic.
  • The deadlift+row example: scaling load too light keeps a heavy-DL workout in the glycolytic pathway and destroys the intended ATP-CP/aerobic stimulus — heavy load is the stimulus, so don't scale it away.
  • The duration-of-effort diagnostic: ~21 reps at 235 lb for an experienced affiliate female ≈ 75–100 sec; if a scaled athlete finishes 21 deadlifts in 35 sec she's lifting too light. Understand the PRINCIPLE (use time-per-set to audit your scale), not the numbers.
  • The handstand-push-up+row example: an athlete needing a minute of rest per HSPU will miss the glycolytic stimulus — scale the movement so she can move fast and stay mostly glycolytic, even if she doesn't finish at the same time as Rx athletes.
  • The class-cohesion error: if most of the class spends 6 minutes on a set while scaled athletes finish in 90 seconds, that's a scaling error that costs both stimulus AND the athlete's sense of belonging — note the dual cost.
  • The 'no significant outliers' principle: keep the whole class working together (don't let one person finish in 3 min while everyone else works 20).
  • Weightlifting-day handling: time domain and metabolic pathway are expressed as REP SCHEME and RELATIVE LOADING — scaling a 20-rep-max back squat to a strict press should still be a higher-volume lift (e.g., 10-rep max), not a 1-rep max.
  • The risk-reduction caveat for novices: increasing the rep scheme on lifting days forces lower loads and creates coaching opportunities (e.g., a 1-month athlete does sets of 5 submaximal instead of a 1-RM overhead squat).
  • The 'completion window' forecasting tool: estimate a time window (task-priority) or round/rep count (time-priority) from the programmed movements/reps/loads so you know the target pathway and can scale to hit it (Appendix 1 worked example).
  • Table 1 — the SIX general movement patterns: upper-body pressing & static holds; upper-body pulling & static hangs; lower-body pressing; lower-body pulling; accessory core; combined patterns. Be able to bucket a movement into the right pattern.
  • The 'compound yet irreducible' rationale: to develop a movement you must practice that movement (even at reduced ROM) — mobility work alone won't develop the squat if you never squat.
  • The 'never skip the pattern entirely' rule: completely avoiding a movement or its scaled variants (e.g., always skipping ring dips and their progressions) means the athlete never develops it safely.
  • Plane of motion (usually sagittal or frontal/coronal) is a SECONDARY consideration when preserving patterns.
  • Table 2 — go-to progressions that preserve the pattern: pull-up → ring row/negative/jumping; back squat → box/air/goblet; power clean → elevated start/high pull/DB clean; HSPU → handstand hold/push-up/negatives/reduced ROM; double-under → single-under/bar hop/low box; toes-to-bar → knee raise/AbMat/V-up. Understand the logic of matching the pattern, not memorizing the table.
  • The injury workflow: begin every class by asking about injuries/illness, then use pre-built progressions to build the scaling plan — connect to screening (1.1) and class management (5.2).
  • The honest limit: sometimes (injury, permanent disability) you CAN'T preserve every pattern, and that's acceptable because pattern is only one of many stimuli — you can still deliver quality training.
  • Complexity as a sub-stimulus: Olympic lifts and gymnastics are most complex, but even a double-under scaled wrong wrecks the stimulus.
  • The key distinction: TRAINING to develop a complex movement (do this in dedicated skill work, off the clock) vs. APPLYING an already-owned complex movement in a timed workout (scale complexity during the WOD to preserve the metabolic response).
  • The decision rule for load vs. complexity: if the athlete can do the complex movement CONSISTENTLY with all points of performance, scale LOAD instead of complexity; if it's not consistently SAFE, scale COMPLEXITY.
  • The progression mandate: the ultimate goal is continual progress in complexity — don't let athletes stagnate in simplified scales; guide them upward (1.2.5).
  • The example of scaling complexity for mobility: push jerk → push press for an athlete who can't receive the jerk in the re-dip due to shoulder mobility; receiving snatch in power position vs. squat.
  • THE ELEMENTS OF SCALING (the levers you pull): (1) Volume/total reps, (2) Load, (3) Range of Motion. Know what each controls.
  • Volume = function of experience (how long they've trained) and recency (how recently they've trained); 'Be impressed by intensity, not volume.'
  • RHABDO LINK: controlling volume addresses rhabdo risk in less-experienced athletes and returning athletes; increased volume of ECCENTRIC movement (plus experience/age) correlates with rhabdo risk — 'the poison is in the dose.'
  • Methods of scaling volume: reduce rep scheme; reduce the time protocol to control reps (prefer scaling reps; only cut time when inexperience meets a long workout).
  • The over-scaling trap: if you scale reps/load/complexity so much that the scaled athlete accumulates MORE reps than an Rx athlete, you've defeated the purpose — keep round pacing similar to Rx.
  • The 'don't add volume to compensate' rule: when you simplify a movement (e.g., ring dips → box dips), do NOT increase reps just because it feels easier — total rep volume still matters.
  • Load is usually the FIRST thing coaches reach for but is rarely the only or most important lever — its job is to preserve the desired stimulus while watching ROM and total rep volume.
  • Load priorities: generally prioritize ROM over load (while keeping the original stimulus and long-term progression in mind); scale load to avoid losing points of performance; appropriate load can vary day to day; beware loads so light the athlete piles up too many reps.
  • The goblet-squat example: warm up adding load until points of performance break down at full ROM; for a 'train-wreck' squat or injury, get creative — load closer to the frontal plane (DBs on shoulders), shift to posterior load (back squat), or use a depth target/box to slow each rep when no load is tolerable.
  • ROM and the power equation: Power = (Force x Distance) / Time — ROM is the 'distance' term, so more ROM = more power output = more intensity; limited ROM reduces work capacity and signals a missing component of fitness (Figure 1).
  • The definition of SAFE ROM: the range in which the athlete can maintain points of performance for that movement; it varies day to day; exceeding it raises injury risk and lowers efficiency.
  • The cumulative-damage point: a tiny fault (small hip tuck in an air squat, internal shoulder roll in an overhead squat) is harmless in one rep but structurally damaging across speed/volume/load (e.g., 100 wall-ball shots) — coaches must intervene, not watch passively.
  • The overhead-squat as the 'yellow highlighter of mobility': a few reps assess shoulder, hip, knee, and ankle ROM at once — a screening tool (links to 1.2.1).
  • Root-cause logic for ROM limits: use tactile/visual/verbal cues to determine whether the limit is poor MOTOR CONTROL, a MOBILITY restriction, or both (links to 4.1.6).
  • The long-term ROM plan (Figure 2): scale ROM DURING workouts to build intensity within current safe ROM, while applying mobility + motor-control work OUTSIDE workouts to expand safe ROM — the two converge at full ROM with greater work capacity.
  • ROM-scaling checklist (Figure 3): during warm-up find today's safe ROM (where points of performance consistently break despite cues); scale ROM at the START position (raise the deadlift) and/or FINISH position (stop the kettlebell swing at eye level); use objects as tactile cues (depth target for a squat).
  • The Travis case (34-yo, just finished 3-week intro, rounds his lumbar in squats/deadlifts): assess safe ROM in CONTROLLED reps (not under workout duress), use a squat target as a tactile cue, and if he can't hold position with the med ball, lighten it (or go to a PVC thruster) or raise the target — don't rely on the same scaling method every time.
  • Concentric vs. eccentric end-range limits: Travis shows the eccentric end (bottom of a squat); the overhead position is the often-neglected concentric end — full shoulder flexion, hands at/inside shoulder width, elbows straight, neutral midline.
  • How specific movements expose shoulder-flexion limits: kettlebell swing and kipping pull-up reveal them (bent/flared elbows = internal rotation; 'broken' midline = lumbar/thoracic overextension); a wider barbell grip can MASK a flexion limit, but the narrow KB-swing grip highlights it.
  • Definitive-limit cueing for poor body awareness: give a hard stop the athlete can feel ('Stop with the kettlebell at eye level') set BEFORE the workout starts; for kipping pull-ups, scale to strict pull-ups or a progression step while addressing mobility separately.
  • The EXPERIENCE-LEVEL definitions and timelines — Beginner (<18 months; needs guidance scaling most elements; submaximal loads), Intermediate (~18–36 months; full-ROM pain-free nine foundational movements, knows maxes, can often self-scale), Experienced (>36 months; refining maxes, advanced gymnastics, no daily scaling when healthy), Returning Athlete (intermediate/experienced who took ≥1 month off volume eccentric training; needs ≥2 weeks of scaled volume for rhabdo risk).
  • The naming-convention caveat: the beginner/intermediate/experienced labels do NOT dictate who uses which scaled version — you may mix elements across levels (e.g., an injured experienced athlete gets beginner movement patterns + intermediate rep scheme), and age matters (intermediate loads/reps may fit an experienced masters athlete).
  • Pre-scaled workouts: pre-writing intermediate and beginner versions of the daily WOD to expedite class scaling — a class-management efficiency tool (links to 5.2.10/5.2.11).
  • Tables 3 and 4 — two athletes, same 12-min thruster/pull-up/burpee AMRAP: injured Athlete 1 (elbow epicondylitis) gets single-arm and plank-style modifications to spare elbow flexion; inexperienced Athlete 2 (limited squat ROM) gets controlled-depth thrusters to a target, ring rows, and step-in burpees to protect the midline. Understand WHY each modification preserves the pattern while respecting the limitation.
  • Competition-scaling errors: (1) reducing load/time/complexity but NOT adjusting total or potential rep count raises risk for less-experienced athletes — always consider total rep exposure in chippers/AMRAPs; the 30–75 upper-body / 50–100 lower-body cumulative-rep figures are EXAMPLES of boundaries, explicitly NOT recommendations; (2) ignoring the cumulative effect of multiple WODs across an event — for scaled divisions, rep count and loads should DECREASE over an event; ending with a long chipper is irresponsible for less-experienced athletes.
  • Appendix 1 method (not the numbers): estimate per-rep/per-movement times, add transitions, account for fatigue breaks, and sum to a completion window; the sample window 5:50–11:30 means if an athlete finishes in <3 min or >~15 min, you likely scaled reps/load/ROM wrong.

Concepts to understand

  • Scaling exists to PRESERVE THE INTENDED STIMULUS, not merely to make a workout 'easier' — the coach must first know what adaptation the workout targets, then choose modifications that keep that adaptation intact despite the athlete's limitations.
  • Safety outranks the perfect stimulus: 'Ahead of efficacy is safety.' When a scale that would best preserve the stimulus conflicts with the athlete's safety, choose safety.
  • Relative intensity is the target of a good scale: safely maximize load, speed, and range of motion relative to THIS athlete's current capacity so work capacity keeps increasing — being scaled does not mean being un-intense.
  • Scaling is a temporary bridge toward Rx, not a permanent ceiling; a coach must actively progress athletes (load, complexity, ROM) rather than leave them parked in an easy variant (ties to 'identify when ready to progress').
  • The three stimuli to protect — time domain/metabolic pathway, movement pattern, and complexity — give you a diagnostic checklist: ask which stimulus a workout is built around before you change anything.
  • Workout duration (with the athlete's training level) sets the primary metabolic pathway; heavy loading in a short workout shifts emphasis from glycolytic toward ATP-CP and aerobic, so the load itself can BE the stimulus and must not be scaled away.
  • Time-per-task is a feedback signal: if a scaled athlete's set duration is far shorter (or longer) than the class's, the scale is wrong — use observed effort time to audit and correct scaling in real time.
  • Class cohesion is a programming-and-scaling concern, not just a vibe: scaling that produces big time outliers undermines both the training stimulus AND the athlete's sense of belonging, so aim to keep the class finishing in a similar window.
  • On weightlifting days, 'time domain' translates into rep scheme and relative loading — preserve the volume character of the lift when you substitute movements (a high-rep-max stays high-rep, not 1-RM).
  • Forecasting a completion window before class lets you choose scales that land athletes in the intended pathway; it's a planning tool that turns 'preserve the stimulus' into a concrete time/round target.
  • Functional movements are 'compound yet irreducible': you can only develop a movement by performing it (even at reduced ROM or as a scaled variant) — so the worst scaling habit is letting an athlete skip a pattern entirely, because that pattern never develops.
  • Movement patterns can be substituted within a shared bucket (the six patterns) so the athlete keeps training the pattern even when the exact prescribed movement is off the table; plane of motion is a secondary nicety.
  • Pre-built 'go-to' progressions are the coach's scaling vocabulary: having them ready makes on-the-spot scaling (especially for injuries) fast and pattern-preserving.
  • Complexity must be handled differently depending on context: develop complex skills in dedicated skill sessions off the clock; during timed WODs, scale complexity down to protect the metabolic response.
  • The load-vs-complexity decision: keep complexity and scale LOAD when the movement is consistently sound with all points of performance; scale COMPLEXITY when the movement isn't consistently safe — never scale complexity out of habit when load would do.
  • Volume is governed by experience and recency, and is the primary lever for managing rhabdo risk; eccentric volume in under-trained or returning athletes is the danger — 'the poison is in the dose.'
  • Over-scaling is a real failure mode: if a scaled athlete accumulates more reps or finishes far faster than Rx athletes, the scale defeats its own purpose — match round pacing, and never add volume to 'compensate' for a simpler movement.
  • Load is the most over-relied-upon lever and rarely the most important one; its purpose is to preserve stimulus while protecting points of performance, and the right load can change day to day.
  • Range of motion is the 'distance' in Power = (F x D)/T, so ROM directly drives power and intensity; restricting ROM below capability wastes work capacity, but exceeding SAFE ROM injures the athlete.
  • Safe ROM is athlete- and day-specific: it's the range in which points of performance hold, and the coach establishes it in controlled warm-up reps, not under the duress of the workout.
  • ROM development is a two-front, long-term campaign: build intensity WITHIN today's safe ROM during workouts, and expand safe ROM with mobility + motor-control work OUTSIDE workouts; the two converge at full-ROM with greater capacity.
  • Root-cause analysis precedes the right ROM fix: determine via cues whether a limitation is mobility, motor control, or both, because the off-the-clock remedy differs.
  • Tactile targets and definitive limits (a squat target, 'stop at eye level') let athletes with poor body awareness stay inside safe ROM without having to self-detect the fault under fatigue.
  • Experience level is just ONE of many scaling inputs (alongside injury, age, recency, ROM, body awareness); the beginner/intermediate/experienced labels guide but do not dictate the scale, and elements can be mixed across levels for one athlete.
  • Age modifies scaling independent of skill: a masters athlete who is technically experienced may still warrant intermediate-level loads and reps.
  • The returning athlete is a distinct, high-risk category: prior ability plus recent absence from eccentric volume demands a deliberate ramp (≥2 weeks of scaled volume) regardless of the athlete's protests — a rhabdo-prevention rule.
  • Pre-scaled class versions are a logistics tool that lets a coach scale a full class quickly while still individualizing by pulling elements across levels.
  • Competition programming for scaled divisions must control TOTAL and POTENTIAL rep exposure and the cumulative load of multiple events; rep counts and loads should taper across an event, and big finishing chippers are inappropriate for less-experienced fields.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenario items that hand you a workout plus an athlete profile (months of experience, an injury, a mobility limit, returning from a layoff, a masters athlete) and ask for the BEST scaling decision — these map to 2.2.1–2.2.5 and 5.2.2. The reliable test-taking move is to first identify the intended stimulus (which metabolic pathway / movement pattern / complexity the workout targets) and then choose the option that preserves it while respecting the limitation, rather than the option that just lowers the number. Other items probe judgment: load vs. complexity decisions (scale load if the movement is consistently sound, complexity if it's unsafe — 2.2.5, 3.1.12), ROM scaling via safe ROM and tactile targets (5.2.3), rhabdo prevention through volume control for novices and returning athletes (1.1.3), recognizing over-scaling when a scaled athlete out-reps or out-paces Rx athletes (2.3.3), and competition rep-exposure errors (2.2.3). Watch for the 'preserve the stimulus' and 'safety ahead of efficacy' principles as the discriminators between a tempting wrong answer and the best one.

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Intended stimulus
The specific adaptation a workout is designed to produce (e.g., a particular metabolic pathway, a movement pattern, a skill). Scaling decisions are judged by whether they keep this adaptation intact.
Relative intensity
Intensity measured against an individual athlete's current capacity (load, speed, ROM) rather than an absolute standard. A good scale safely maximizes relative intensity so work capacity keeps rising even for limited athletes.
As prescribed (Rx)
Doing a workout exactly as written, with no scaling. Becoming able to perform workouts Rx is the long-term goal that scaling builds toward.
Time domain
The duration of a workout's effort. Combined with the athlete's training level, it largely determines which metabolic pathway is trained.
Metabolic pathways (ATP-CP, glycolytic, aerobic/oxidative)
The three energy systems the body uses. Short, intense efforts rely on ATP-CP and glycolytic; longer efforts rely on the aerobic pathway. Heavy loading can shift a short workout toward ATP-CP and aerobic by slowing output.
Completion window
An estimated time range (for task-priority workouts) or total round/rep count (for time-priority workouts) forecast from the programmed movements, reps, and loads. It tells the coach the target pathway so scaling can hit it.
Task-priority workout
A workout with a fixed amount of work where the variable is time (e.g., 'for time'). Its completion forecast is a time window.
Time-priority workout
A workout with a fixed time where the variable is work completed (e.g., an AMRAP). Its forecast is a round/rep count.
Six general movement patterns
Gordon's buckets for preserving movement when scaling: upper-body pressing & static holds; upper-body pulling & static hangs; lower-body pressing; lower-body pulling; accessory core; and combined patterns. Substitute within the same bucket to keep training the pattern.
Compound yet irreducible
A defining property of functional movements: they are made of multiple joint actions but cannot be broken into simpler pieces without losing what they train. Practically, you must perform a movement (even reduced) to develop it.
Plane of motion
The geometric plane a movement travels in (commonly sagittal or frontal/coronal). Preserving it is a secondary consideration when scaling, behind preserving the pattern itself.
Movement complexity
How much neurologic and skill demand a movement carries (Olympic lifts and gymnastics are most complex). Even simple-seeming movements like double-unders have complexity that, if mishandled, changes the stimulus.
Volume (total reps)
The total repetitions an athlete performs. Driven by experience and recency, it's the primary lever for managing rhabdo risk and must be tracked even when movements are simplified.
Eccentric loading
The lengthening phase of a muscle contraction (e.g., lowering in a pull-up or squat). High eccentric volume in under-trained or returning athletes correlates with rhabdomyolysis risk.
Rhabdomyolysis (rhabdo)
A serious condition in which damaged muscle releases contents into the bloodstream, threatening the kidneys. Risk rises with excessive (especially eccentric) volume in inexperienced or recently inactive athletes — 'the poison is in the dose.'
Points of performance
The defined positional and movement standards that make a rep sound and safe (e.g., neutral spine, full lockout). Maintaining them defines whether a load, ROM, or complexity is appropriate.
Range of motion (ROM)
The distance through which a movement travels. It is the 'distance' term in Power = (F x D)/T, so larger ROM yields more power and intensity; restricting it below capability reduces work capacity.
Safe ROM
The range in which an athlete can consistently maintain a movement's points of performance. It varies day to day and is established in controlled warm-up reps; exceeding it raises injury risk.
Tactile cue / target
A physical object (a box or ball as a squat-depth target, 'stop the kettlebell at eye level') that gives an athlete with poor body awareness a definitive, feelable limit to stay within safe ROM.
Train-wreck squat
Gordon's term for a squat with extremely poor motor control where the athlete can't tolerate even sub-Rx anterior loading without faulting — requiring creative load placement or unloaded depth challenges.
Yellow highlighter of mobility
Gordon's nickname for the overhead squat, because a few reps simultaneously reveal an athlete's shoulder, hip, knee, and ankle ROM — a quick mobility screen.
Pre-scaled workout
A pre-written intermediate and beginner version of the day's workout, prepared in advance to let a coach scale a whole class efficiently while still mixing elements for individuals.
Beginner
An athlete consistently doing CrossFit fewer than ~18 months; still developing ROM, body awareness, and consistency in the nine foundational movements; needs guidance scaling most elements and typically uses submaximal loads.
Intermediate
An athlete with roughly 18–36 months of consistent CrossFit; performs the nine foundational movements pain-free at full ROM with all points of performance, knows their maxes, and can often self-scale.
Experienced
An athlete with more than ~36 months of consistent CrossFit; refining maxes and advanced gymnastics, and not requiring scaling for daily workouts when healthy.
Returning athlete
A formerly intermediate/experienced athlete who has taken a month or more off from volume eccentric training. High rhabdo risk; needs a deliberate ramp (about two weeks or more) of scaled volume.
Technique-versus-intensity (threshold training)
CrossFit's principle that intensity is added only as technique allows. In scaling, it means building load/speed/volume within current safe ROM and sound mechanics, not beyond them.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • Rhabdomyolysis risk is the central safety thread: excessive volume — especially eccentric volume — in inexperienced athletes and in returning athletes (off ≥1 month) can cause rhabdo. Control volume deliberately; returning athletes need ~2+ weeks of scaled volume regardless of their protests.
  • Exceeding an athlete's safe ROM under speed, load, or volume (e.g., repeated reps with a lost neutral spine, internally rotated shoulder, or hip tuck) causes cumulative structural damage even when a single rep looks harmless — the coach must intervene, not watch passively.
  • Scaling load/complexity/time without controlling TOTAL rep exposure increases injury risk, particularly in competition chippers and AMRAPs for less-experienced athletes — always check total and potential rep counts.
  • Letting athletes do dedicated skill development (e.g., near-max HSPU or complex-lift practice) under the clock during a metcon increases risk and misses the stimulus — develop complexity off the clock.
  • Stagnation in over-simplified scales is its own failure: never leave an athlete parked in an easy variant; progress them, and recognize when they are ready to advance.
  • Injuries and illness must be surfaced BEFORE the workout (ask at the start of every class) so the coach can build a safe, pattern-preserving scaling plan — note that this is the boundary where some conditions require referral and fall outside coaching scope.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. The programmed workout is 21-15-9 reps of deadlifts (355/235 lb) and rowing for calories; the intended stimulus is heavy ATP-CP/aerobic work with the heavy deadlift slowing output. A newer female athlete can't safely pull 235 lb. You watch her finish the set of 21 deadlifts at a reduced load in about 35 seconds while the rest of the class takes 75–100 seconds per set. What is the BEST conclusion and action?

  1. A. The scale is appropriate because she is moving efficiently and staying with the class.
  2. B. She is lifting too light — the load no longer preserves the heavy ATP-CP/aerobic stimulus, so increase her load (still sub-Rx) until her set time and effort align with the class and points of performance hold.
  3. C. Reduce her reps further so she finishes even faster and avoids fatigue.
  4. D. Add rounds to her workout to make up for the lighter load.
  5. E. Switch her to a long, light, high-rep deadlift set to maximize volume.
Show answer

Answer: B — Set duration is a real-time audit of scaling: 35 seconds versus the class's 75–100 indicates the load is too light and has shifted her into the glycolytic pathway, defeating the heavy ATP-CP/aerobic stimulus the workout was built around. The fix is to raise her load (kept sub-Rx and within sound mechanics) so her effort time matches the class. A is wrong because pace alone doesn't confirm stimulus. C and E worsen the mismatch or convert it into a high-volume rhabdo risk. D adds volume to 'compensate,' which the article explicitly warns against.

Scenario 2. A 24-year-old with two months of experience and limited squat ROM (tight hips and ankles) is doing a wall-ball workout. During controlled warm-up squats you find she consistently loses her neutral spine below a certain depth despite cues. What is the BEST way to scale her ROM for the workout?

  1. A. Have her squat to full depth anyway so she develops mobility under the workout load.
  2. B. Remove the squatting element entirely and substitute an unrelated movement.
  3. C. Set a squat target (a box or stacked ball) at her current safe depth as a tactile cue so she stays within safe ROM, and plan separate mobility/motor-control work outside the workout to expand that ROM over time.
  4. D. Tell her to 'just be careful' and watch her closely during the metcon.
  5. E. Increase her wall-ball reps since a shallower squat is easier.
Show answer

Answer: C — Safe ROM is established in controlled reps and protected during the workout with a definitive tactile limit; intensity is built within that range while mobility and motor control are developed off the clock to expand it (Figures 2–3). A drives her past safe ROM under fatigue and load (cumulative injury risk). B abandons the 'compound yet irreducible' need to keep squatting to develop the squat. D leaves an athlete with poor body awareness to self-detect a fault she can't reliably catch. E adds volume to compensate for a simpler movement, which is prohibited.

Scenario 3. An experienced athlete returns after taking two months completely off from CrossFit. He is frustrated and wants to do today's high-volume metcon fully as prescribed. What is the BEST coaching decision?

  1. A. Let him do it Rx — he has the prior skill and capacity to handle it.
  2. B. Treat him as a returning athlete and scale his volume for a period of about two weeks or more to reduce rhabdomyolysis risk, even though he objects.
  3. C. Keep the Rx volume but tell him to go at 50% effort.
  4. D. Scale only the complexity of the movements and keep the full rep count.
  5. E. Have him sit out entirely until he completes a new intro course.
Show answer

Answer: B — A returning athlete combines prior ability with a recent absence from eccentric volume, which is exactly the rhabdo-risk profile; the article prescribes ~2+ weeks of scaled volume regardless of the athlete's protests. A ignores the risk. C is unrealistic and unmonitorable under a clock. D keeps the dangerous variable (total/eccentric volume) untouched. E over-restricts an athlete who only needs a volume ramp, not a full re-onboarding.

Scenario 4. An athlete can consistently perform the programmed power snatch with all points of performance, but the prescribed load is too heavy for him to keep sound mechanics. According to the article's decision logic, what should you scale?

  1. A. Scale the complexity by switching him to a much simpler movement pattern.
  2. B. Scale the load (keep the power snatch) since the movement itself is consistently safe and sound.
  3. C. Reduce his reps drastically and keep the heavy load.
  4. D. Increase his reps at the heavy load to build tolerance.
  5. E. Remove the snatch and add an unrelated accessory movement.
Show answer

Answer: B — The rule is: if the athlete can do the complex movement consistently with all points of performance, scale LOAD rather than complexity; scale complexity only when the movement isn't consistently safe. Here the snatch is sound, so reduce load and preserve the movement and its development. A and E needlessly strip a movement he can safely train (stagnation risk). C keeps an unsafe load. D adds volume at an unsafe load — compounding risk.

Scenario 5. You are writing pre-scaled options for a 25-minute AMRAP of 7 push-ups, 12 deadlifts, and 15 box jumps for a class that includes several beginners. Which approach best preserves the intended stimulus while managing risk?

  1. A. Keep the 25-minute time domain for everyone and only lower the loads for beginners.
  2. B. For beginners, reduce the time domain (e.g., a 10–12-minute AMRAP) AND scale load, reps, and complexity so their round pacing stays similar to Rx athletes and total rep exposure stays appropriate.
  3. C. Keep all reps and time identical and tell beginners to rest whenever needed.
  4. D. Cut only the reps in half but keep the full 25 minutes so beginners accumulate more rounds.
  5. E. Increase the beginners' reps because their scaled movements are easier.
Show answer

Answer: B — When inexperience meets a long workout, the article allows reducing the time domain, and stresses scaling reps/load/complexity together so the scaled athlete's round pacing matches Rx athletes and total rep exposure stays controlled (a rhabdo and over-scaling safeguard). A leaves a long, high-exposure workout intact for beginners. C and D let beginners accumulate excessive total volume. E violates the rule against adding volume to compensate for simpler movements.

Scenario 6. A coach is designing the final event of a scaled-division local competition. Which programming choice best reflects responsible scaling for less-experienced athletes across a multi-event day?

  1. A. End with a long chipper to test who has the most grit.
  2. B. Decrease rep counts and loads as the event progresses, ending on a shorter, lower-volume workout, because cumulative fatigue compromises recovery and motor control for less-experienced athletes.
  3. C. Keep every workout at identical volume so all events are 'fair.'
  4. D. Reduce loads on the final event but raise the rep counts to keep it challenging.
  5. E. Program the highest total rep count of the day in the final event to crown the winner decisively.
Show answer

Answer: B — The article warns that multiple workouts compound stress on recovery and motor control for beginner/intermediate athletes, so rep counts and loads should DECREASE over an event, and a long finishing chipper is explicitly called irresponsible for less-experienced fields. A and E maximize exactly the cumulative exposure the article cautions against. C ignores accumulating fatigue. D trades load for rep volume — still raising total exposure when it should fall.

Scenario 7. The programmed workout is 21-15-9 handstand push-ups and rowing for calories, intended to keep athletes mostly in the glycolytic pathway by moving fast. An athlete needs roughly a minute of rest before every HSPU. What is the BEST scaling decision?

  1. A. Have her do the HSPU as prescribed so she accumulates the full 45 reps for strength.
  2. B. Assign an HSPU scale (e.g., a pattern-preserving progression) that lets her move quickly and stay mostly glycolytic, accepting that she won't finish at the same time as experienced athletes.
  3. C. Remove all pressing from her workout and have her only row.
  4. D. Keep the HSPU but give her unlimited time so she completes every prescribed rep.
  5. E. Increase her row distance to make up for easier pressing.
Show answer

Answer: B — The intended stimulus is fast, glycolytic work; an athlete resting a minute per rep would be doing repeated near-max efforts and miss that stimulus entirely. The fix is a pressing scale within the same movement pattern that lets her move quickly. A turns a metcon into max-effort skill work under a clock (wrong context, higher risk). C abandons the pressing pattern she still needs to develop. D preserves reps but destroys the metabolic stimulus. E adds compensatory volume the article warns against.

Scenario 8. A 1-rep-max overhead squat is programmed. A CrossFit athlete with one month of experience is in class. What is the most appropriate scale?

  1. A. Have him attempt a true 1-rep max so you can establish his number.
  2. B. Have him perform sets of about 5 reps at submaximal loading, which forces lower loads, reduces risk, and creates more coaching opportunities while still training the pattern.
  3. C. Skip the overhead squat entirely and have him do air squats only.
  4. D. Keep the 1-rep-max format but spot him heavily through failed reps.
  5. E. Give him the heaviest load he can move once, regardless of position breakdown.
Show answer

Answer: B — The article specifically recommends increasing the rep scheme (e.g., sets of 5 submaximal) for less-experienced athletes on lifting days: it forces lower, safer loads and opens coaching opportunities while preserving the movement pattern and its development. A and E push a novice to maximal load with immature mechanics. C abandons the pattern he needs to practice. D treats spotting through failure as a substitute for appropriate loading, which it is not.

Scenario 9. Scaling for a missing overhead position: during a kettlebell-swing-to-overhead workout, an athlete's elbows bend and flare as the bell nears the top, and cues don't fix it. What does this most likely indicate, and what is the best response?

  1. A. It indicates laziness; cue louder and keep the full overhead ROM.
  2. B. It indicates a likely shoulder-flexion (overhead ROM) limitation; cap the swing height at a definitive limit such as eye level set before the workout, and address shoulder mobility separately.
  3. C. It indicates a grip problem; have her use a wider grip to fix it.
  4. D. It indicates she needs more load to stabilize the bell overhead.
  5. E. It indicates she should switch to an unrelated lower-body movement.
Show answer

Answer: B — Flared, bent elbows (internal rotation) at the top of a narrow-grip KB swing highlight a shoulder-flexion limitation; when cues don't correct it, reduce swing-height ROM with a definitive pre-set limit ('stop at eye level') and work mobility off the clock. A misreads a mobility limit as effort. C is impossible with a kettlebell's fixed narrow grip (and a wider grip merely masks the limit on a barbell). D adds load to an unsafe overhead position. E abandons the pressing/overhead pattern she needs to develop.

Scenario 10. An 'experienced' athlete is recovering from a wrist injury and normally does all movements Rx. For today's workout you find the prescribed movements aggravate the wrist. How does the article say you should build her scale?

  1. A. Use the beginner pre-scaled version wholesale, since any scaling means she's effectively a beginner today.
  2. B. Mix elements across levels — for instance, take movement patterns from the beginner version (to spare the wrist) while keeping a rep scheme from the intermediate version — because experience level is only one input and the labels don't dictate the scale.
  3. C. Keep her Rx and tell her to push through the discomfort.
  4. D. Send her home until the wrist fully heals.
  5. E. Cut her workout time in half and keep all Rx movements.
Show answer

Answer: B — The article stresses that the beginner/intermediate/experienced labels guide but do not dictate the scale, and that a coach may pull elements from multiple levels for one athlete — e.g., an injured experienced athlete getting beginner movement patterns with an intermediate rep scheme. A over-scales a capable athlete. C ignores the injury and risk management. D needlessly removes an athlete who can train around the injury to maintain fitness. E keeps the aggravating Rx movements while only cutting time.

Scenario 11. A coach reasons: 'I scaled ring dips to box dips because they're easier, so I'll bump the reps from 10 to 18 to keep it hard.' What is the problem with this reasoning?

  1. A. Nothing — harder movements should always be matched by fewer reps and easier ones by more.
  2. B. Increasing volume to 'compensate' for a simpler movement violates the rule to control total rep volume regardless of how the movement was scaled, and can push the athlete into excessive exposure.
  3. C. Box dips don't preserve the pressing pattern, so the substitution itself is invalid.
  4. D. The reps should have been increased even more to truly match the difficulty.
  5. E. Ring dips can never be scaled, so no rep change matters.
Show answer

Answer: B — The article explicitly says not to increase volume just because a coach perceives the movement or load as simpler — total rep volume must be respected to manage risk (including rhabdo) and preserve the intended stimulus. A states the opposite of the article's guidance. C is false: box dips are a valid pressing-pattern scale. D compounds the error. E is incorrect — ring dips have a defined progression.

D2 · Programming 14% of exam Confidence tier: ___

CFJ_2016_02_Volume_Hobart.pdf

PDF link not yet available

Why this is on the reading list

This article is the CCFT reading list's definitive treatment of when, why, and how to add training volume to a CrossFit program without sacrificing intensity and variance. It directly backs Domain 2 (Programming) by teaching that intensity (not volume) drives fitness, that volume is reserved for a narrow population of advanced competitors with an unshakable mechanics-and-consistency foundation, and that any added volume must replicate competition demands while being matched by recovery. The exam will test whether a coach can correctly decide who gets volume, how to sequence it, and how to monitor for overtraining — not whether they can recite Hobart's tables.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 2.1.1 Design single workouts using the CrossFit methodology
  • 2.1.2 Design a sequence of workouts that improves general physical preparedness (GPP)
  • 2.2.3 Scale for athletes with sport-specific goals
  • 2.2.5 Scale by skill level
  • 2.3.1 Evaluate program success relative to athlete goals and needs
  • 2.3.3 Adjust programming based on performance and goals
  • 2.3.4 Evaluate athlete progress relative to CrossFit's definition of fitness and their personal goal
  • 1.2.4 Monitor athlete for signs of over- or under-training
  • 1.2.1 Assess capacity/capability to perform functional movements
  • 1.2.3 Identify athlete's fitness goals
  • 5.2.1 Apply mechanics-consistency-intensity to programming for safety and performance
  • 3.1.10 Teach the relationship between technique and intensity (threshold training)
  • 3.1.11 Teach relative intensity

What to focus on while reading

  • The core thesis stated up front: CrossFit programming thrives upon intensity, NOT volume — highlight every restatement ('Be impressed by intensity, not volume'; 'Past one hour, more is not better'; 'Volume is no substitute').
  • The exact prerequisites an athlete must meet BEFORE adding volume: rarely needs to scale, can post competitive times on all workouts, has no issues making mechanics and consistency corrections, performs ~99% of programmed workouts as prescribed.
  • Who volume is NOT for: anyone who requires frequent scaling, anyone who struggles with mechanics — for them volume just ingrains bad movement patterns ('a loser's gambit').
  • The mechanics-consistency-intensity hierarchy as the gatekeeper: volume sits on top of an 'unshakable foundation of mechanics and consistency' linked to intensity — tie this to the CrossFit charter triangle.
  • Who the audience for added volume actually is: almost exclusively the competitive CrossFit athlete (Open/Regionals/Games), NOT the general 'training for life' population.
  • The single most repeated coaching takeaway: 'every athlete will continue to improve with a single CrossFit workout per day — volume is not the cure-all; effective coaching is.'
  • The general-population prescription: training once a day, 4–5 times per week, is enough for a lifetime of fitness; an occasional two-a-day can be fun but is never required.
  • The frequency baseline CrossFit already delivers: one 60-minute session (warm-up, one workout, cool-down) 3–6 times per week addresses general health and fitness.
  • The three distinct reasons volume is a PROBLEM, not a solution: (1) it's unnecessary for getting fitter and can be counterproductive or harmful when misapplied; (2) intensity and effective variance must be maintained as volume rises — volume cannot replace variance for GPP; (3) fitting multiple workouts into the one-hour class is impractical and degrades the coach's ability to cue, correct, and keep athletes safe.
  • The cost side of volume: harder to maintain intensity, harder to hit PRs, requires extra rest; too much volume without ample recovery causes over-reaching/overtraining that pushes athletes backward.
  • Hobart's own evidence: every fall since 2009 he takes time off high-volume training, plays other sports, and still sees personal bests with LESS volume — use this as the 'volume isn't necessary' proof point.
  • Glassman's 'blur the distinction between strength training and metabolic conditioning' — why max-effort lifts are tested right after conditioning, and what that implies for how to program volume.
  • Competition data used as a programming guide — note the structure, not the exact numbers: Regionals commonly run two events/day (three ~25% of the time), ~six events across three days; Games average ~three events/day across ~13 events over five days with at least one rest day; single-modality tests appear most at the Games.
  • Common competition combinations to train for: chipper + couplet/triplet/chipper (~60% of two-event days), and single-modality effort + couplet/triplet/chipper; chippers run ~6–25 min, averaging ~19 min; time domains above 20 min are a staple at the Games.
  • The actual volume-progression method: start with just TWO two-a-day sessions per eight-day block, then build toward six workouts placed across Day 1–Day 3 to replicate a regional/Games weekend (~six or seven events in three days).
  • Table 1 vs Table 2 logic — Table 1 introduces two double-sessions in an 8-day block; Table 2 stacks a double, single, then triple in the first three days to mimic competition density, then fills the rest with single sessions, rest days, and skill work.
  • How skill work is treated: NOT for time or intensity; tucked into warm-ups, cool-downs, or before/after/between strength and conditioning sessions to keep technical improvement going.
  • The instruction to VARY where single, double, and triple sessions fall — never fall into the same weekly pattern, and never always 'strength then a met-con,' because competition won't follow a predictable script (athletes may be asked to lift heavy after a conditioning test).
  • The recovery-monitoring checklist Hobart spells out: enough sleep? eating enough to support performance but not excess body fat? enjoying it or cranky/worn out? intensity/performance maintained or improving? aggravating nagging injuries? fresh on arrival or unreasonably sore? honestly communicating or ignoring signs of over-reaching/overtraining?
  • The role of training partners/rivals: 'find someone you hate losing to' — a rival drives intensity higher than you'd reach alone; 'It's not what you do but who you do it with that matters' — community/atmosphere as a programming-adjacent lever.
  • The Hinshaw running principle: no point adding running volume if you slow down — 'then you are just spending more time practicing running slow' — and generalize it to all training (junk volume ingrains slow/sloppy execution).
  • Hackenbruck's line as the practical summary: 'You don't need harder workouts, you need to go harder in your workouts.'
  • The exit criteria / failure response: if added volume produces results POORER than they would have been without it, retool the approach — back off and start again; volume must never come at the cost of intensity and variance.

Concepts to understand

  • Intensity is the independent variable most commonly associated with maximizing favorable adaptation — a coach should default to protecting intensity and treat volume as secondary, optional, and conditional.
  • Volume is a tool with a very narrow indication: it applies almost exclusively to advanced competitors who already own mechanics, consistency, and the ability to express intensity — prescribing it to a developing athlete is a programming error.
  • The mechanics → consistency → intensity hierarchy is the prerequisite gate for volume; volume layered on poor mechanics simply rehearses faults and ingrains bad habits, so it harms rather than helps that athlete.
  • For general-population members ('training for life'), one quality session a day, 4–5x/week, delivers a lifetime of fitness; the coach's job is to resist the urge to cram more and instead improve the quality of each session.
  • Adding volume without protecting variance undermines GPP — volume cannot substitute for constantly varied training; any fitness domain trained without intensity will regress.
  • Recovery is a programming variable, not an afterthought: increased volume mandates increased rest, sleep, and nutrition, or the athlete slides into over-reaching/overtraining and moves backward.
  • Volume should be reverse-engineered from competition demands — use the known structure of Regionals/Games (events per day, common couplet/triplet/chipper combinations, time domains, single-modality after conditioning) to shape what and when you program.
  • Effective volume progression is incremental and periodized: begin with minimal added sessions (e.g., two doubles in an 8-day block) and build only as the athlete demonstrably maintains intensity, ultimately replicating a competition weekend's physiological stress.
  • Variability of placement matters: rotating single/double/triple sessions and refusing a fixed 'strength-then-metcon' template prepares athletes for the unpredictable sequencing of real competition.
  • Skill work is distinct from conditioning volume — it is low-intensity, not-for-time technical practice that can be woven into warm-ups/cool-downs and does not count as the kind of high-intensity volume that demands extra recovery.
  • Class-management reality constrains volume: stacking multiple workouts into a 60-minute group class degrades a coach's ability to cue, correct, and keep athletes safe — a programming decision that creates a coaching and safety problem.
  • Continuous evaluation governs whether volume stays: if performance, intensity, PRs, mood, soreness, or injury trends worsen, the volume experiment has failed and must be dialed back — program based on observed results, not on a fixed plan.
  • Community, rivalry, and training partners are intensity multipliers; a coach can sometimes raise effective intensity (and delay any need for volume) through the social environment rather than by adding work.
  • 'More work for more's sake' is junk volume — practicing a movement slowly or sloppily just makes the athlete better at moving slowly or sloppily; quality of execution gates the value of any added volume.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenario questions that hand you an athlete profile and ask for the best programming decision. The classic stem describes a member who still scales frequently or has movement faults and 'wants to do two-a-days' — the correct answer protects mechanics/consistency and intensity (tasks 2.2.5, 5.2.1, 2.1.1) by declining or deferring volume, not by adding sessions. Other stems test whether you reserve volume for competitors who rarely scale and post competitive times (2.2.3), whether you reverse-engineer volume from competition structure while preserving variance for GPP (2.1.2), and whether you recognize over-reaching/overtraining signs and adjust the program in response (1.2.4, 2.3.3). Watch for distractors that equate 'more volume' with 'more fitness' — they will be wrong because they sacrifice intensity, variance, or recovery.

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Volume
The total amount of work performed — typically the number of sessions/workouts (e.g., two-a-days) added beyond the standard one-workout-per-day. In this article, the thing a coach is tempted to add but should mostly resist.
Intensity
The rate of doing work (power output); the variable CrossFit prioritizes because it drives the greatest favorable adaptation. 'Be impressed by intensity, not volume.'
Variance / Constantly varied
Programming across broad time and modal domains so no aspect of fitness is neglected. Volume cannot replace variance when training for GPP.
General Physical Preparedness (GPP)
Broad, general, and inclusive fitness — work capacity across broad time and modal domains — which CrossFit develops and which requires intensity and variance, not just volume.
Mechanics, Consistency, Intensity
CrossFit's developmental hierarchy: master technique (mechanics), repeat it reliably (consistency), then add speed/load (intensity). Volume is only appropriate after this foundation is solid.
Two-a-day (double session)
Two separate training sessions in one day; the basic unit of added volume. Fun occasionally for general athletes, but a deliberate, sparing tool for competitors.
Triple session
Three sessions in one day, used in higher-volume blocks (e.g., Table 2) to replicate the density of a competition day.
Over-reaching / Overtraining
The result of too much volume without adequate recovery — declining performance, persistent soreness, fatigue, crankiness, aggravated injuries — that pushes an athlete backward instead of forward.
Single-modality (max-effort) event
A test of one capacity (e.g., a 1-rep-max jerk, heavy sandbag carry, short sprint), often programmed right after or later than a conditioning piece to 'blur the distinction' between strength and met-con.
Chipper
A long, multi-movement workout done once through (you 'chip away' at the tasks); ranges ~6–25 min, averages ~19 min, and is the most common building block paired with couplets/triplets at Regionals.
Couplet / Triplet
Workouts built from two (couplet) or three (triplet) movements; the most frequently tested formats for time at competition, often paired with a chipper on two-event days.
Skill work
Technical practice that is NOT for time or intensity; can be folded into warm-ups, cool-downs, or between strength/conditioning sessions to keep improving technique without adding recovery-demanding volume.
Threshold training
Training at the highest intensity an athlete can sustain with sound mechanics; relevant because adding volume must never push an athlete past the point where technique holds.
Deload / Off-season
A planned reduction in volume (Hobart's annual fall break) during which athletes recover, cross-train, and often still set PRs — evidence that less volume can yield more fitness.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • Prescribing extra volume to an athlete who still requires frequent scaling or has unresolved movement faults — this ingrains bad mechanics and raises injury risk; the correct action is to fix mechanics/consistency first.
  • Increasing volume without a corresponding increase in recovery (sleep, nutrition, rest days) — a direct path to over-reaching/overtraining.
  • Ignoring warning signs of overtraining: declining performance, unreasonable or persistent soreness, athletes arriving unfresh, aggravated nagging injuries, crankiness/burnout, or athletes hiding how worn out they are.
  • Cramming multiple workouts into a single 60-minute group class — it degrades the coach's ability to cue, correct, and supervise, creating a safety and quality problem for the whole group.
  • Continuing a volume increase that is producing results poorer than the athlete would achieve without it — this signals the program must be backed off and retooled.
  • Confusing long, low-intensity training ('90 minutes at 60 percent') with productive work — chasing volume at the expense of intensity is a coaching error.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. A 35-year-old general-population member trains 4x/week, enjoys CrossFit, and tells you she wants to start doing two-a-days because she sees competitors doing them online. She still scales most metcons and gets corrections on her squat and kipping mechanics. What is the best coaching response?

  1. A. Add a second daily session immediately so she doesn't fall behind her goals.
  2. B. Decline the added volume for now, explain that one quality session 4–5x/week delivers a lifetime of fitness, and focus her training on mechanics, consistency, and intensity.
  3. C. Have her do two-a-days but make both sessions long and light to limit fatigue.
  4. D. Tell her two-a-days are only for the Games and that she should never train more than once a day.
  5. E. Add volume but skip skill work to save time in the hour.
Show answer

Answer: B — Volume is reserved for advanced athletes who rarely scale and have solid mechanics; for a developing general member, more volume just rehearses faults and isn't needed — 'every athlete will continue to improve with a single CrossFit workout per day.' B fixes the foundation and matches her actual goal (fitness for life). A and C add volume she isn't ready for; C also trades intensity for junk volume. D is false — occasional two-a-days can be fine, and volume isn't exclusive to the Games. E removes the very technical practice she needs.

Scenario 2. A competitive athlete who performs ~99% of programmed workouts as prescribed, rarely scales, and posts competitive times is ready to add volume for the upcoming Regionals season. Which approach best reflects the article's method?

  1. A. Immediately program three-a-days every training day to maximize total work.
  2. B. Start with about two two-a-day sessions in an eight-day block, monitor that intensity is maintained, then progressively build toward replicating a competition weekend's density.
  3. C. Add a fixed daily 'strength then metcon' template and repeat it identically every week.
  4. D. Double every workout's reps so each single session becomes twice as long.
  5. E. Add long, easy aerobic volume daily regardless of pace.
Show answer

Answer: B — Hobart prescribes incremental, periodized progression: begin with minimal added volume (two doubles in an 8-day block) and build only while intensity holds, ultimately mimicking the ~6–7 events over three days of a competition weekend. A jumps to unsustainable volume with no recovery. C violates the explicit instruction to vary placement and avoid a predictable strength-then-metcon pattern. D and E are junk volume that sacrifice intensity; E specifically ignores the 'practicing running slow' warning.

Scenario 3. Three weeks into a higher-volume block, your competitor's metcon times are slowing, he's unusually sore on arrival, he's been short-tempered, and an old shoulder niggle is flaring. What should you do?

  1. A. Push through — declining performance is normal and will rebound if he just trains harder.
  2. B. Add another session to break through the plateau.
  3. C. Recognize these as signs of over-reaching/overtraining, back off the volume, and prioritize recovery (sleep, nutrition, rest) before reintroducing load.
  4. D. Keep the volume identical but tell him to stop complaining.
  5. E. Switch entirely to long, low-intensity cardio to 'flush' the fatigue.
Show answer

Answer: C — The article lists exactly these as red flags — declining performance, unreasonable soreness, crankiness, aggravated injuries — and says too much volume without recovery pushes athletes backward. The correct response is to dial back and restore recovery (task 1.2.4 / 2.3.3). A, B, and D worsen the overtraining. E abandons intensity and variance and still doesn't address the recovery deficit.

Scenario 4. You coach a busy 6 a.m. class of 14 athletes in a single 60-minute hour. A competitive member asks you to program a second workout for him to do during the same class so he can get his volume in. What's the best decision?

  1. A. Yes — run him through two workouts in the hour; group classes are the right place for volume.
  2. B. No — stacking multiple workouts in the group hour degrades your ability to cue, correct, and keep everyone safe; have him do his second session outside class time.
  3. C. Yes, but stop coaching the other 13 athletes so you can supervise his two workouts.
  4. D. Tell him volume is pointless and he should never train more than the class.
  5. E. Let him self-coach both workouts unsupervised in the corner.
Show answer

Answer: B — Hobart names class management as a core reason volume is impractical in the standard hour: it impedes the trainer's ability to cue, correct, maximize safety, and attend to athletes. The competitor's extra volume belongs outside the group class (task 5.2.1 / 5.2.10). A and C sacrifice the group's coaching and safety; E removes supervision entirely; D wrongly dismisses volume's legitimate (if narrow) role.

Scenario 5. An advanced athlete adds volume for two training cycles, but his competition-relevant scores come out worse than they were before he added the extra work. What does the article recommend?

  1. A. Add even more volume — the gains are just delayed.
  2. B. Keep the volume the same and wait several more months.
  3. C. Retool the approach: back off the volume and start again, because volume must not come at the cost of intensity and variance.
  4. D. Conclude the athlete has reached his genetic ceiling and stop competing.
  5. E. Remove all skill work to free up energy for more conditioning volume.
Show answer

Answer: C — Hobart is explicit: if added volume produces results poorer than they would have been without it, you need to retool — perhaps back off and start again — because volume benefits an athlete only when intensity and variance are preserved (task 2.3.1 / 2.3.3). A and B double down on a failing experiment. D is an unsupported leap. E strips out useful technical work and still doesn't fix the intensity problem.

Scenario 6. When programming volume for a Regionals-bound athlete, why does the article advise varying where you place single, double, and triple sessions rather than repeating the same weekly layout?

  1. A. Because varying the layout reduces the total amount of work the athlete has to do.
  2. B. Because competition sequencing is unpredictable — athletes may be asked to lift heavy after a conditioning test — so training must prepare them for varied event order, not a fixed pattern.
  3. C. Because athletes get bored with repetition and need novelty for its own sake.
  4. D. Because varying placement removes the need for rest days.
  5. E. Because it lets the coach avoid ever programming heavy lifting.
Show answer

Answer: B — The article ties varied placement directly to competition reality: 'always doing the same thing — often strength and then a met-con — will lead you astray, as there's no guarantee competition will follow the same pattern.' Preparing for heavy-after-conditioning and other combinations is the point (task 2.1.2 / 2.2.3). A and D are false — varying layout doesn't cut total work or remove rest needs. C trivializes the rationale; E contradicts the 'blur the distinction' principle that includes heavy lifting after conditioning.

Scenario 7. A coach claims, 'The way to get my members fitter is to keep adding more workouts each week.' Which statement best reflects the article's correction of this belief?

  1. A. Correct — more volume reliably equals more fitness for everyone.
  2. B. Volume is secondary; intensity and variance are the keys, and for nearly all members one quality session a day with effective coaching produces a lifetime of fitness.
  3. C. Members should add volume only by lengthening every workout to 90 minutes.
  4. D. Fitness comes from volume as long as recovery is ignored.
  5. E. Adding workouts is fine because intensity takes care of itself at higher volume.
Show answer

Answer: B — The article's thesis is 'Be impressed by intensity, not volume' — volume is secondary and can even be counterproductive or harmful when misapplied, while intensity and variance drive results and effective coaching beats more workouts (tasks 2.3.4, 3.1.10). A and E are exactly the misconception being corrected; in fact maintaining intensity gets HARDER as volume rises. C describes junk volume (90 min at low intensity). D inverts the recovery requirement.

CFJ_Cochran_Diabetes.pdf

Open the PDF on Google Drive →

Why this is on the reading list

This first-person account by a Type 1 diabetic CrossFitter is on the reading list to make the special-populations side of programming concrete: how a coach scales, monitors, and manages risk for an athlete with a chronic medical condition without lowering the standard of fitness. It directly backs Domain 2's tasks on scaling for special populations (2.2.2), designing for athletes whose condition must be managed (2.2.4), and tracking/adjusting programming from recorded data (2.3.3) — while reinforcing that scaling, not exclusion, is the answer. It also reaches into screening/referral (1.1.x), performance tracking (1.2.6), lifestyle health markers (6.1.4), and scope of practice (7.4.1).

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 2.2.2 Scale for special populations (e.g., pregnant, adaptive)
  • 2.2.4 Design programming for injured athletes to maintain fitness and restore functionality (here: an athlete with a chronic medical condition to manage)
  • 2.1.1 Design single workouts using the CrossFit methodology (manipulating duration/metabolic pathway)
  • 2.3.3 Adjust programming based on performance and goals
  • 2.3.2 Use benchmarks to assess effectiveness of programming (Fran retested over time)
  • 1.1.1 Screen athlete for medical issues (e.g., health questionnaire)
  • 1.1.2 Recognize conditions/injuries outside CCFT Scope of Practice that require referral
  • 1.2.6 Quantify and track performance
  • 1.2.4 Monitor athlete for signs of over- or under-training
  • 6.1.4 Review basic health markers (HDL, triglycerides, A1C, body fat %, lean mass, BP, bone density)
  • 5.2.3 Manage risk for the athlete
  • 5.2.6 Recognize warning signs for possible injury or overexertion
  • 5.2.8 Educate athletes on personal responsibility in a workout setting
  • 7.4.1 Work within CCFT Scope of Practice

What to focus on while reading

  • The core programming lever she discovered: workout DURATION drives her glucose response — intense WODs over ~20 min spiked her blood glucose to unsafe levels (>250 mg/dl), while the same intensity under ~20 min did not. Note this is a duration/metabolic-pathway effect, not an intensity-reduction effect.
  • How she scales: she scales the WOD so it can be COMPLETED in under 20 minutes, and explicitly notes 'there is nothing wrong with scaling a WOD midway through.' Flag scaling as a real-time, in-workout decision, not just a pre-workout plan.
  • The opposite glucose reaction by workout type: long aerobic efforts (5K), short-interval work (800m intervals), and a 1-rep-max day make her glucose DROP (toward hypoglycemia), while long mixed-modal grinders (Filthy Fifty, Murph) make it SPIKE. Map this to the three metabolic pathways.
  • Her concrete management actions on pump therapy: LOWER basal rate to 30% ~30 min before workouts that drop her glucose; INCREASE basal rate by 20% ~30 min before workouts that spike it. (These are HER medical decisions, not the coach's — see scope.)
  • The data habit that made everything work: 'Record your WODs and record your blood sugar before and after.' She found her pattern only by tracking results over time — tie this to quantifying/tracking performance and adjusting programming from data.
  • The benchmark thread: Fran as a repeated test — her first attempt (25 lb thrusters, band pull-ups, goal = completion) vs. later Rx'd attempts under 10 minutes. Note how a benchmark reveals both fitness progress and changing physiology.
  • The compounding-stressors lesson: the SAME workout (Fran) that normally doesn't spike her glucose DID spike it (>300 mg/dl) when stacked with travel, hours of sitting/classroom, a Tabata, and a diet change. Highlight that stress is cumulative and the athlete's response is 'not static or linear.'
  • Concrete glucose numbers and what they mean: non-diabetic ~85 mg/dl; her normal range 70–120 mg/dl; post-WOD spike >300 mg/dl; later hypo drop to ~50 mg/dl; HbA1c of 7.6% ≈ ~190 mg/dl average. Understand the directions (high = hyperglycemia, low = hypoglycemia), not the numbers as memorized cutoffs.
  • The acute danger statements: acute hyperglycemia can cause death; untreated hypoglycemia can progress to insulin shock and death; her husband has had to 'act quickly... to save my life.' These are the red-flag stakes that justify an EAP and athlete self-management.
  • Why she got fitter AND needed less insulin: improved body composition (more muscle, less fat) made insulin work more efficiently, lowering her daily insulin and bolus ratio. Connect training adaptation → health-marker improvement (HbA1c) → medication reduction.
  • The coaching mandate she states plainly: 'if you are coaching Type 1 diabetics, make sure they learn how to take care of themselves.' The coach's job is to enable self-management and safe scaling, not to manage the disease.
  • The Type 1 vs Type 2 distinction she draws: Type 1 (juvenile/insulin-dependent, produces NO insulin, must inject) vs Type 2 — 'similar but in most respects completely different.' Note the relevance to why HER glucose responses differ.
  • The athlete-autonomy theme: her doctor initially said CrossFit was 'too intense'; she pushed back, learned to manage it, and her A1c results improved. Watch how informed self-management changed the medical picture rather than confirming the doctor's caution.

Concepts to understand

  • Scaling is the answer for special populations, not exclusion. A chronic medical condition (here, Type 1 diabetes) is managed by scaling and monitoring — 'CrossFit is safe for everyone... diabetics have to know how to be safe' — the same logic a coach applies to an athlete with a chronic injury (2.2.2, 2.2.4).
  • Workout duration and metabolic pathway are programming variables a coach can deliberately manipulate. For this athlete, capping duration (sub-20-minute) controlled an unsafe physiological response while preserving intensity — understand duration/pathway as a scaling dial, distinct from load or reps (2.1.1, 2.2.2).
  • Different metabolic demands produce opposite physiological responses in the same athlete. Long aerobic and maximal-effort work dropped her glucose; long glycolytic grinders spiked it. A coach scaling a special-population athlete must understand that the TYPE of workout, not just its difficulty, changes the risk (2.2.2).
  • Programming for special populations is data-driven and iterative. The athlete recorded WODs and pre/post blood glucose, found a pattern, and adjusted — then kept adjusting as conditions changed. This is 'evaluate results → adjust programming' in action, and it is never finished (2.3.2, 2.3.3, 1.2.6).
  • Stressors are cumulative and the response is non-linear. Travel, sleep loss, sitting, diet changes, and prior workouts stack with the WOD's stress — the same benchmark can produce a very different physiological result on a different day. A coach must read the whole athlete on the day, not just the workout on paper (1.2.4, 5.2.6).
  • Benchmarks reveal both fitness progress and physiological change. Re-testing Fran over time showed performance improvement (band-assisted/scaled → Rx'd, sub-10-minute) and exposed how external stress alters her response. Use repeatable benchmarks to evaluate programming effectiveness (2.3.2).
  • Training adaptations change health markers and even medication needs. Improved body composition (more lean mass) improved insulin efficiency, lowering her HbA1c trend and daily insulin/bolus ratio — a concrete example of fitness improving a measurable health marker (6.1.4, 2.3.4).
  • Recognize hyperglycemia vs hypoglycemia as bidirectional risks. High glucose (hyperglycemia) and low glucose (hypoglycemia/insulin shock) are BOTH potentially fatal and can occur hours after a workout. A coach must recognize warning signs and have an emergency plan, even though treatment is the athlete's/medical responsibility (5.2.6, 1.1.2).
  • Screening and referral set the stage. A medical condition like Type 1 diabetes should surface in intake screening; the coach recognizes it as outside scope to treat, defers diabetes management to the athlete and her physician, and focuses on safe training (1.1.1, 1.1.2, 7.4.1).
  • Scope of practice: the coach coaches fitness; the athlete and her doctor manage the disease. Insulin dosing, basal-rate changes, and bolus ratios are explicitly the athlete's medical decisions — the coach's lane is scaling, monitoring, education, and emergency readiness, never prescribing or adjusting medication (7.4.1, 5.2.3, 5.2.8).
  • Athlete personal responsibility is part of the safety system. The athlete must know her own condition, track her own data, carry her own supplies, and make her own in-workout decisions; the coach's job is to require and enable that self-management (5.2.8, 5.2.3).

How the exam applies this

Expect scenario questions that drop you into coaching an athlete who discloses a chronic medical condition (diabetes is a classic stand-in for 'special population') and ask what the coach should do: scale appropriately and keep training (2.2.2, 2.2.4), refer disease management to the athlete and physician rather than advising on medication (7.4.1, 1.1.2), watch for warning signs and have an EAP (5.2.6, 7.3.1), and use recorded data to adjust programming over time (2.3.3, 1.2.6). Other items test whether you recognize that duration/metabolic-pathway choices are legitimate scaling tools (2.1.1), that benchmarks like Fran measure progress and changing physiology (2.3.2), and that fitness gains improve health markers such as A1c (6.1.4). The trap answers will be excluding the athlete from training, or stepping outside scope by recommending insulin or dietary medical changes.

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Type 1 diabetes
An insulin-dependent form of diabetes (often called 'juvenile diabetes') in which the body produces NO insulin, so the person must inject insulin daily to survive. In the article, this is the chronic condition the athlete manages while training.
Type 2 diabetes
The more common form of diabetes; the author notes it is 'similar but in most respects completely different' from Type 1. Unlike Type 1, Type 2 diabetics still produce insulin. Relevant because the two types respond differently to exercise.
Insulin
A hormone that carries glucose (sugar) from the blood into the body's cells. Without it, blood glucose rises dangerously. Type 1 diabetics must supply it externally via injection or a pump.
Glucose (blood sugar)
The sugar that all carbohydrates break down into and that the liver also produces, especially under stress. Measured in mg/dl; the athlete's coaching-relevant variable to keep in a safe range.
Hyperglycemia
Blood glucose that is too HIGH. In the article, intense long workouts spiked her glucose above 300 mg/dl; acute hyperglycemia can cause death and chronic high glucose damages kidneys, nerves, and the cardiovascular system.
Hypoglycemia
Blood glucose that is too LOW. The author dropped to ~50 mg/dl hours after a workout; if untreated it can progress to insulin shock and death. A bidirectional risk the coach must be aware of.
Insulin shock
A severe, potentially fatal state resulting from dangerously low blood glucose if hypoglycemia is left untreated. One of the acute emergencies that justifies an emergency action plan.
HbA1c (A1c) test
A blood test that measures average blood glucose over roughly the prior three months. Her 7.6% corresponded to about 190 mg/dl average. It is one of the basic health markers a coach may review (6.1.4) and a way to see whether training is improving health.
Basal rate
The continuous background insulin drip delivered by an insulin pump. The athlete adjusts it before workouts — lowering it to 30% before glucose-dropping workouts, raising it 20% before glucose-spiking ones. This is HER medical decision, outside the coach's scope.
Bolus ratio
The dosing ratio for the extra insulin taken to cover food/carbohydrate intake. Her bolus ratio dropped as her body composition improved, because insulin worked more efficiently with more muscle.
Pump therapy
Insulin delivery via a pump providing a constant insulin drip (basal) plus on-demand doses (bolus), as opposed to manual syringe injections. It let her fine-tune insulin around specific workouts.
Three metabolic pathways
The body's three energy systems (phosphagen, glycolytic, and oxidative). The author learned which workout types tax which pathway and how each affects her glucose — long mixed-modal work spiked it; aerobic and maximal-effort work dropped it. Understanding these lets a coach predict an athlete's physiological response.
Scaling
Adjusting a workout (here, by capping its duration to under 20 minutes, or scaling mid-workout) so the athlete can train safely at appropriate intensity. The article's central message: 'CrossFit is scalable,' and scaling — not exclusion — keeps a special-population athlete training.
Body composition
The proportion of lean mass to fat. Her shift toward more muscle improved insulin efficiency, lowered her required insulin, and improved her A1c — a measurable health benefit of training.
Fran (benchmark WOD)
A short benchmark workout (21-15-9 thrusters and pull-ups). Used here as a repeated test that tracked both her fitness progress (band-assisted/scaled to Rx'd, sub-10-minute) and her changing physiological response under different conditions.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • Diabetes management (insulin dosing, basal-rate and bolus changes, dietary medical adjustments) is OUTSIDE the CCFT scope of practice. The coach does not prescribe, adjust, or advise on medication — that belongs to the athlete and her physician (7.4.1, 1.1.2).
