  • A chronic medical condition disclosed at intake is a referral/medical-clearance trigger, not a reason to exclude the athlete. Screen for it, ensure the athlete is managing it with her doctor, and scale rather than turn her away (1.1.1, 1.1.2).
  • Both hyperglycemia (high) and hypoglycemia (low) can be life-threatening and can strike HOURS after the workout. The coach must recognize warning signs (confusion, collapse, abnormal behavior) and have an Emergency Action Plan ready (5.2.6, 7.3.1).
  • Require and enable athlete self-management: the diabetic athlete should monitor her own glucose before/after training, carry her own supplies/fast-acting glucose, and be cleared to make her own in-workout decisions. Coaching such an athlete means making sure 'they learn how to take care of themselves' (5.2.8, 5.2.3).
  • Cumulative stress (poor sleep, travel, illness, diet changes) can turn a normally safe workout into an unsafe one for a special-population athlete — read the whole athlete on the day before assuming a benchmark will behave as usual (1.2.4, 5.2.6).
  • Do NOT give medical, insulin, or therapeutic-dietary advice. A coach may discuss general fitness scaling and basic health markers, but must defer disease treatment to qualified medical professionals (7.4.1).

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. A new athlete discloses on her intake form that she has Type 1 diabetes and is insulin-dependent. She is eager to start and is already managing her condition with an endocrinologist. What is the BEST coaching action?

  1. A. Decline to train her because intense workouts are too dangerous for diabetics
  2. B. Welcome her, confirm she is managing her condition with her physician, and plan to scale and monitor her training like any special-population athlete
  3. C. Tell her to lower her insulin before every workout so her blood sugar doesn't crash
  4. D. Have her sign up but program her exactly like everyone else with no special monitoring
  5. E. Refer her out permanently and suggest she find a medically supervised program instead
Show answer

Answer: B — Special populations are scaled and monitored, not excluded (2.2.2, 2.2.4), and disclosed medical conditions are confirmed/cleared with the athlete's physician (1.1.1, 1.1.2). A and E wrongly exclude her. C is outside scope — the coach never advises on insulin dosing (7.4.1). D ignores the heightened monitoring and scaling a special-population athlete warrants.

Scenario 2. A Type 1 diabetic athlete tells you she has noticed her blood glucose spikes to unsafe levels only on intense workouts lasting longer than about 20 minutes, but not on shorter ones. She wants to keep training hard. As her coach, the MOST appropriate programming response is to:

  1. A. Reduce the intensity of all her workouts so she never works near her limit
  2. B. Scale longer workouts so she can complete them in under ~20 minutes, preserving intensity while controlling duration
  3. C. Recommend she increase her insulin dose before long workouts so she can do them as prescribed
  4. D. Stop programming any metabolic conditioning for her
  5. E. Tell her the spikes are normal and she should ignore them
Show answer

Answer: B — Duration is a legitimate scaling/programming variable; capping it to sub-20-minute controlled her physiological risk while keeping intensity (2.1.1, 2.2.2) — exactly what the article describes. A needlessly sacrifices intensity. C is a medical/insulin recommendation outside scope (7.4.1). D over-restricts. E ignores a genuine safety signal (5.2.6).

Scenario 3. Over several weeks, a special-population athlete brings you a log showing her workout times alongside a physiological marker she records before and after each session. A clear pattern emerges. What does this BEST illustrate about programming for her?

  1. A. Programming for special populations should be fixed once and left unchanged
  2. B. Recorded data should be used to find patterns and iteratively adjust programming to the individual
  3. C. The coach should take over recording and interpreting all of the athlete's medical data
  4. D. Logs are only useful for tracking PRs, not for guiding programming
  5. E. Once a pattern appears, monitoring can stop
Show answer

Answer: B — The article's method is record results, find the pattern, adjust, and keep adjusting (2.3.3, 1.2.6, 2.3.2). A and E are wrong because the athlete's response is 'not static or linear' — monitoring continues. C oversteps scope into medical-data management (7.4.1). D undersells data as a programming tool.

Scenario 4. A diabetic athlete who normally tolerates a benchmark workout fine arrives having driven six hours overnight, slept poorly, sat through hours of class, and changed her usual diet. She wants to hit the same benchmark Rx'd. What is the MOST important coaching consideration?

  1. A. Past tolerance guarantees she'll be fine today, so proceed as normal
  2. B. Cumulative stressors can change her physiological response, so adjust expectations, monitor closely, and be ready to scale
  3. C. Tell her to take extra insulin to offset the added stress
  4. D. Cancel her session entirely because any deviation is unsafe
  5. E. Ignore the lifestyle factors since they aren't part of the workout
Show answer

Answer: B — Stress is cumulative and the response is non-linear — the same benchmark spiked her glucose past 300 mg/dl under stacked stressors (1.2.4, 5.2.6). The coach reads the whole athlete and is ready to scale. A and E dismiss real risk. C is a medication recommendation outside scope (7.4.1). D over-restricts when monitoring and scaling suffice.

Scenario 5. Mid-workout, a Type 1 diabetic athlete starts showing confusion and unsteadiness and tells you she feels 'off.' She is carrying her own glucose supplies. What is the BEST immediate coaching response?

  1. A. Push her to finish the WOD since she's almost done
  2. B. Have her stop, help her access her own supplies and check her glucose, and activate the Emergency Action Plan if she does not quickly stabilize
  3. C. Administer insulin to her yourself to bring her levels down
  4. D. Tell her to walk it off and keep moving
  5. E. Do nothing because managing her diabetes is entirely her responsibility
Show answer

Answer: B — Confusion/unsteadiness are warning signs of a glucose emergency that can be fatal (hypo- or hyperglycemia); the coach recognizes the signs, stops the athlete, lets her self-manage, and is ready to activate the EAP (5.2.6, 7.3.1, 5.2.3). A and D ignore danger. C is both medically wrong and outside scope (7.4.1). E abdicates the coach's duty to recognize and respond to an emergency.

Scenario 6. After months of training, a diabetic athlete reports her A1c has improved and her doctor reduced her daily insulin. She asks why. Which explanation is the BEST and stays within a coach's lane?

  1. A. The workouts cured her diabetes
  2. B. Improved body composition (more lean mass) made her insulin work more efficiently, which can improve health markers like A1c — while her physician continues to manage her medication
  3. C. She can now stop monitoring her blood glucose
  4. D. The coach should advise her on exactly how much to lower her insulin going forward
  5. E. A1c improvements mean she no longer needs her doctor
Show answer

Answer: B — Training improved body composition and insulin efficiency, improving her A1c and lowering required insulin — a measurable health-marker benefit a coach can speak to in general terms (6.1.4, 2.3.4). A overstates (diabetes isn't cured). C and E are unsafe. D crosses into prescribing medication, outside scope (7.4.1).

Scenario 7. An experienced coach is explaining to a diabetic athlete why certain workouts drop her blood glucose (a long run, 800m intervals, a 1-RM day) while others spike it (Filthy Fifty, Murph). The BEST framing for this difference is:

  1. A. The workouts that spike glucose are simply harder than the ones that drop it
  2. B. Different workouts tax different metabolic pathways, and the energy-system demand — not just difficulty — drives her physiological response
  3. C. It's random and can't be anticipated
  4. D. Only the total amount of weight lifted determines the glucose response
  5. E. Glucose always rises with any kind of exercise
Show answer

Answer: B — The article ties the opposite responses to the three metabolic pathways — understanding the energy-system demand of a workout lets a coach anticipate the effect (2.2.2). A is wrong because maximal-effort and long aerobic work (very 'hard' in different ways) dropped her glucose. C ignores a learnable pattern. D and E are oversimplifications contradicted by the article.

D2 · Programming 14% of exam Confidence tier: ___

CFJ_Kilgore_Adaptations.pdf

PDF link not yet available

Why this is on the reading list

Kilgore's 'Adaptation for Fitness' supplies the physiological 'why' beneath CrossFit programming: Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (alarm-resistance-exhaustion) and super-compensation explain how a workout drives a fitness gain and why progression, recovery, and load management are non-negotiable. For a CCFT candidate this is core Domain 2 reasoning — it justifies designing workouts that disrupt homeostasis, sequencing them for GPP, dosing volume/intensity, and reading over- and under-training. It also connects to Domain 1 (over/under-training signs) and Domain 6 (sleep and nutrition as recovery levers), but the exam will test it as applied programming judgment, not as a biology recall quiz.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 2.1.1 Design single workouts using the CrossFit methodology
  • 2.1.2 Design a sequence of workouts that improves general physical preparedness (GPP)
  • 2.3.1 Evaluate program success relative to athlete goals and needs
  • 2.3.2 Use benchmarks to assess effectiveness of programming
  • 2.3.3 Adjust programming based on performance and goals
  • 2.3.4 Evaluate athlete progress relative to CrossFit's definition of fitness and their personal goal
  • 1.2.4 Monitor athlete for signs of over- or under-training
  • 1.2.5 Identify when athlete is ready to progress to another goal/skill
  • 1.2.6 Quantify and track performance
  • 6.2.1 Identify additional lifestyle goals (sleep/recovery, stress) that support adaptation
  • 6.2.3 Provide additional lifestyle guidance (recovery, sleep, nutrition for adaptation)

What to focus on while reading

  • The three GAS stages in order — alarm, resistance, exhaustion — and which two are positive (alarm + resistance) versus which signals failure (exhaustion).
  • What actually triggers the alarm stage: a NOVEL stress, or a previously experienced stress applied at greater magnitude or frequency than before. Note this is the physiological argument for progressive overload and for variance.
  • The cause-and-effect chain stated explicitly: alarm stage is the STIMULUS for adaptation; resistance stage is WHERE the fitness gain actually occurs. Kilgore even proposes renaming resistance the 'adaptation phase.'
  • The hard programming rule: 'No increased load leads to no improvement in fitness.' Highlight it — it is the single most testable sentence for designing a sequence of workouts.
  • Selye's recovery window for return to homeostasis after the alarm stage: roughly 6 to 48 hours.
  • Variable duration of the resistance stage (days to months) and the factors that change it: magnitude of homeostatic disruption, single vs. cumulative overload, and whether the trainee is fit or unfit.
  • The specificity principle worked through the 10K-running example: a specific stress produces a specific set of adaptations; long slow distance running won't appreciably improve sprint speed or squat strength.
  • How exhaustion stage maps to exercise in practice: rarely death, usually OVERTRAINING — caused by excessive volume (duration, frequency, or both) and/or intensity, marked by inability to train/compete at expected levels (fitness has decayed).
  • The molecular flow: DNA makes RNA makes protein makes function — and how a novel stress down-regulates normal genes and up-regulates 'survival' genes during alarm, then reverses during resistance to build more/efficient architectural (actin, myosin) and metabolic (enzyme) proteins.
  • Super-compensation defined and the TWO conditions required for it: (1) training hard enough to disrupt homeostasis, AND (2) adequate rest afterward. If either is missing, super-compensation cannot occur.
  • The timing argument behind super-compensation: it is NOT the return of fitness to baseline that produces a gain — it is the RELATIVE TIMING of fatigue decay vs. fitness-restoration decay. Gain happens only when fatigue dissipates faster than fitness-restoration processes decay.
  • What happens when recovery is too slow: fatigue reduction slower than fitness restoration yields no gain or a retained Stage-1 performance decrement — the practical picture of under-recovery.
  • Figure 1 (super-compensation curve): work capacity dips below baseline during disruption, climbs back during recovery, and overshoots baseline transiently if adequate time is allowed. Be able to point to where on the curve the next workout should land.
  • Recovery methodologies that maximize super-compensation and speed fatigue reduction: adequate nutrition and sleep; their neglect both blunts the gain AND pushes the athlete toward overtraining (Stage 3).
  • The fatigue definition: a REDUCTION in the ability to do work — explicitly framed as the opposite of fitness.
  • The genetic-ceiling idea: proper application of stress raises performance until a genetic ceiling is reached, which few athletes ever approach (use to temper expectations and keep progressing).
  • Selye's historical framing — 1936 'A Syndrome Produced by Diverse Nocuous Agents,' exercise treated as a 'nocuous' (harmful) stress — and the analogy to Nietzsche ('what does not kill us makes us stronger') and Milo of Croton (progression for ~2 millennia).
  • The author's closing caution: experimental literature on programming is sparse/questionable, so coaches must learn anatomy/physiology AND apprentice under successful practitioners to apply it.

Concepts to understand

  • General Adaptation Syndrome as the master model: every training adaptation follows alarm -> resistance -> (avoidable) exhaustion regardless of stress type; the coach's job is to keep athletes cycling through alarm and resistance without tipping into exhaustion.
  • Progressive overload is the practical translation of the alarm stage: because only a stress that EXCEEDS prior magnitude/frequency triggers adaptation, a static training load eventually stops producing fitness — so a workout sequence must continually advance load/stimulus.
  • Variance as a stimulus engine: novel stress reliably triggers the alarm stage, so constantly varied programming keeps presenting the body with something to adapt to (connects GAS to CrossFit's 'constantly varied').
  • Adaptation happens during recovery, not during the workout: the workout is only the trigger; the measurable fitness change is laid down in the resistance/recovery phase — so rest and the inter-workout interval are programming variables, not afterthoughts.
  • Super-compensation as the dosing principle: schedule the next hard exposure to land near the top of the super-compensation overshoot — train too soon (under-recovered) and you stack fatigue or stall; train too late and the overshoot decays back to baseline.
  • The fatigue-vs-fitness timing model: a session creates both fatigue and a fitness-restoration response; a net gain requires fatigue to dissipate faster than the fitness-restoration process decays — this is why recovery quality literally determines whether a workout 'counts.'
  • Specificity: adaptations are specific to the stress imposed, so program selection must match the athlete's goal (and a broad GPP goal demands broad, varied stimuli rather than one modality).
  • Magnitude vs. cumulative effect: a single bout's adaptation may be immeasurable, but cumulative homeostatically disruptive sessions sum to measurable strength or endurance gains — justifying patience, consistency, and longitudinal tracking over chasing single-session PRs.
  • Overtraining as the practical exhaustion stage: driven by too much volume and/or intensity plus inadequate recovery; recognized as decayed performance and inability to train/compete at expected levels — the failure mode the coach must prevent and detect.
  • Recovery inputs are programming inputs: sleep and nutrition determine the size of the super-compensation and the speed of fatigue clearance, so lifestyle coaching is inseparable from whether the program produces results.
  • Homeostatic disruption is the deliberate goal of a hard session: feeling tired, sore, or sluggish afterward is the expected, even desired, signal that the alarm stage was reached — distinguishing productive disruption from injury or true overtraining.
  • Genetic ceiling and the long runway: performance can keep rising with correct stress because almost no athlete reaches their genetic ceiling — supports continued, intelligent progression rather than premature plateaus.
  • The molecular rationale (DNA->RNA->protein->function): you don't need the biochemistry to coach, but understanding that adaptation = changed gene expression building new contractile/metabolic proteins reinforces why stimulus must be specific, repeated, and recovered-from.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenarios that hand you an athlete's recent training, results, and recovery habits and ask for the best programming decision. A plateau after weeks of identical workouts tests progressive overload and the 'no increased load = no improvement' rule (2.1.2, 2.3.3). An athlete who is always sore, performing below baseline, and sleeping poorly tests recognizing the exhaustion/overtraining stage and prescribing recovery or deload (1.2.4, 2.3.3, 6.2.3). Questions about WHEN to load again, or why a hard-charging member isn't improving, test super-compensation timing and the fatigue-vs-fitness model (2.1.1, 2.1.2). A sport-specific request (e.g., a runner who wants a bigger squat) tests specificity and goal-matched program design (2.3.1, 2.3.4). The right answer is almost always the experienced coach's judgment call — manipulate stimulus or recovery to keep the athlete adapting — not a textbook definition.

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS)
Selye's model that any organism, faced with a sufficient stress, passes through three stages — alarm, resistance, exhaustion — as it adapts or fails to adapt. The conceptual foundation for all of exercise physiology and CrossFit programming.
Alarm stage (Stage 1)
The body's emergency response to a novel or larger-than-before stress; it diverts resources to survival, temporarily depresses performance, and acts as the STIMULUS that triggers adaptation. Return to homeostasis takes roughly 6-48 hours after the stress is removed.
Resistance stage (Stage 2)
The phase where the body builds more metabolic and structural elements to better withstand the same stress next time — i.e., where the fitness gain actually occurs. Kilgore suggests calling it the 'adaptation phase.' Lasts days to months depending on the disruption.
Exhaustion stage (Stage 3)
The failure state where adaptive capacity is overwhelmed; in extreme stress it can mean death, but in exercise it usually shows up as overtraining — decayed fitness and inability to train or compete at expected levels.
Overtraining
The exercise-world expression of Selye's exhaustion stage, caused by excessive volume (duration, frequency, or both) and/or intensity without adequate recovery; diverse and destructive in its effects but generally marked by an inability to perform at expected levels.
Super-compensation
The transient rise in work capacity ABOVE baseline that follows a hard, homeostasis-disrupting session plus adequate rest. Requires both conditions; if training isn't hard enough or rest isn't sufficient, it cannot occur.
Homeostasis / homeostatic disruption
Homeostasis is the body's internal equilibrium; disrupting it (through hard training) is the deliberate goal that sets off the alarm stage. Adequate disruption is necessary to trigger adaptation.
Fatigue
A reduction in the ability to do work — the opposite of fitness. Exists not just as tiredness but as biochemical and structural changes in cells and tissues; its timing relative to fitness-restoration determines whether a workout yields a gain.
Progressive overload (progression)
The principle that training load must continually increase to keep driving adaptation, because only a stress exceeding prior magnitude/frequency triggers the alarm stage. 'No increased load leads to no improvement in fitness.'
Specificity
Adaptations are specific to the stress imposed: a given stimulus produces a particular set of changes (e.g., 10K running improves distance running but not sprint speed or squat strength). Program selection must match the desired adaptation.
Genetic ceiling
The theoretical upper limit of performance set by one's genetics. Proper stress keeps raising performance toward it, but few athletes ever approach this limit — so there is almost always room to keep improving.
Nocuous stress
A harmful stress (Selye's term); exercise is classified as one. It is the sub-lethal application of such stress that drives beneficial adaptation.
DNA -> RNA -> protein -> function
The molecular information flow behind adaptation: training changes which genes are active, altering the proteins a cell makes (e.g., actin, myosin, enzymes) and therefore its function and performance.
Cumulative overload
Fitness gain that accrues from a SERIES of homeostatically disruptive sessions rather than any single bout; one workout's adaptation may be immeasurable, but the sum is measurable strength or endurance.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • Signs of the exhaustion/overtraining stage — persistent performance decline, chronic soreness/fatigue, inability to train or compete at expected levels — are a programming warning, not a cue to push harder; reduce volume/intensity and prioritize recovery (1.2.4, 2.3.3).
  • Stacking hard sessions on an under-recovered athlete (training before the super-compensation window, with poor sleep/nutrition) actively moves them toward overtraining — recovery is part of the prescription, not optional.
  • Normal post-workout tiredness, mild soreness, and a transient performance dip are EXPECTED signs of homeostatic disruption — do not confuse them with injury or true overtraining; the distinction is a judgment the coach must make.
  • This article is exercise physiology, not medicine: it does not address rhabdomyolysis, medical screening, or referral. Overtraining management here stays within coaching scope; escalate anything that looks medical (e.g., dark urine, severe persistent pain) per scope-of-practice rules.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. A 9-month member has done the same five workouts at the same loads on a fixed weekly rotation. Her benchmark times and lifts have not improved in two months, though she trains hard and recovers well. Using the General Adaptation Syndrome, what is the best programming adjustment?

  1. A. Keep the program identical and wait longer, since adaptation can take months
  2. B. Progressively increase the load/stimulus and introduce variety so workouts again exceed her prior magnitude or frequency
  3. C. Cut her training volume in half to force super-compensation
  4. D. Add an extra rest day each week without changing the workouts
  5. E. Switch her entirely to long, slow distance running to build a new base
Show answer

Answer: B — Only a stress that exceeds previously experienced magnitude or frequency triggers the alarm stage and drives adaptation — Kilgore's 'no increased load leads to no improvement in fitness.' A repeated, unchanging stimulus stops producing gains. (A) waiting won't help an already-adapted stimulus; (C) and (D) reduce stress when she's recovering well, removing the very stimulus she needs; (E) violates specificity and abandons her broad fitness for a single modality.

Scenario 2. An athlete training twice a day, six days a week, reports he is constantly sore, his Fran and back squat have both regressed, and he's been sleeping five hours a night under work stress. He wants to add more volume to 'break through.' What is the best coaching response?

  1. A. Add the extra volume he requested; more stimulus means more adaptation
  2. B. Hold load constant but add a third daily session to increase frequency
  3. C. Reduce volume and intensity, build in recovery, and address sleep/nutrition before progressing again
  4. D. Tell him the soreness is normal disruption and to keep training as is
  5. E. Refer him immediately to a physician for the soreness
Show answer

Answer: C — Declining performance plus chronic soreness and poor sleep is the exercise expression of Selye's exhaustion stage — overtraining from excess volume/intensity and inadequate recovery. The fix is less stress and better recovery; sleep and nutrition determine the size of super-compensation and speed of fatigue clearance. (A) and (B) add stress and deepen the hole; (D) ignores objectively decayed fitness; (E) overreaches scope — this is a coaching/recovery problem, not yet a medical one.

Scenario 3. A coach asks why two athletes who do an identical hard workout can have opposite outcomes — one gets fitter, the other stalls. Based on the super-compensation model, what best explains the difference?

  1. A. The workout itself was too easy for the one who stalled
  2. B. Genetics alone determine the result regardless of recovery
  3. C. Whether fatigue dissipated faster than the fitness-restoration process decayed, which depends on adequate rest, sleep, and nutrition between sessions
  4. D. Specificity — they were training different qualities
  5. E. The one who stalled simply needs to train more frequently
Show answer

Answer: C — Super-compensation requires BOTH sufficient disruption AND adequate recovery. The fitness gain comes from the relative timing of fatigue decay versus fitness-restoration decay; if fatigue reduction is slower than fitness restoration, the net result is no gain (or a retained performance decrement). Recovery quality is the decisive variable here. (A) and (E) assume the stimulus/frequency is the problem when the same workout was done; (B) ignores that the article says few approach their genetic ceiling and recovery still governs the outcome; (D) doesn't apply — same workout, same quality.

Scenario 4. A recreational runner who comfortably runs 10K three times a week complains that her back squat and 100m sprint haven't improved at all. She asks why her running isn't making her stronger and faster. What principle best explains this, and what should you program?

  1. A. Progressive overload — she just needs to run farther
  2. B. Specificity — long slow distance running produces distance-running adaptations, not strength or sprint adaptations, so program strength and short high-intensity work for those goals
  3. C. Super-compensation — she isn't resting enough between runs
  4. D. Overtraining — she should stop running entirely
  5. E. Genetic ceiling — she has maxed out her strength potential
Show answer

Answer: B — Kilgore uses almost this exact example: a specific stress yields a specific set of adaptations, and long slow distance running will not appreciably improve sprint speed or squat strength. To improve those qualities you must impose the specific stresses that drive them. (A) more running deepens the same specific adaptation; (C) and (D) misdiagnose recovery/overtraining when the issue is stimulus type; (E) is unsupported — few athletes approach their genetic ceiling.

Scenario 5. After a brutal benchmark workout, a new member feels tired, a little sore, and sluggish the next day and worries she did something wrong. How should the coach interpret and respond to this, per the adaptation model?

  1. A. This is overtraining; she should take a full week off
  2. B. This is a likely injury; refer her out before her next session
  3. C. This is the expected, even desired, sign that homeostasis was disrupted and the alarm stage reached; reassure her and ensure she recovers (sleep, nutrition) before the next hard exposure
  4. D. This means the workout was too easy and should be made harder immediately
  5. E. This is irrelevant noise; tell her to ignore how she feels entirely
Show answer

Answer: C — Kilgore explicitly calls the Stage-1 dip in capacity and the feelings of tiredness/soreness normal, expected, and even desired — they confirm homeostasis was disrupted, the training goal at that point. The coach reassures and protects recovery so super-compensation can occur. (A) and (B) overreact to a normal training signal (no red-flag symptoms described); (D) ignores that the disruption already occurred; (E) discards useful feedback the model says to read.

Scenario 6. A coach is convinced a single great workout should produce a visible jump in a beginner's strength and is frustrated when one session changes nothing measurable. What does the adaptation model say, and how should it shape the program?

  1. A. The adaptation from a single bout may be immeasurable; gains come from the cumulative effect of many homeostatically disruptive sessions, so program for consistent, progressive exposure and track over time
  2. B. If one session doesn't move the needle, the program is wrong and should be scrapped
  3. C. Beginners can't adapt and need months of rest first
  4. D. Strength only improves from maximal singles, not workouts
  5. E. The athlete has hit their genetic ceiling already
Show answer

Answer: A — The article states the magnitude of change from a single bout is small and may be immeasurable in practice, but the cumulative result of a series of disruptive sessions is measurable as strength or endurance. That argues for consistency, progression, and longitudinal tracking rather than chasing single-session results. (B) overreacts to expected single-session variability; (C) is false — beginners adapt readily; (D) is unsupported; (E) contradicts the article's note that few approach the genetic ceiling.

Scenario 7. Two athletes both need 48 hours less to recover. One is a deconditioned beginner who just did a single moderate overload; the other is a fit veteran who absorbed a heavy cumulative week. Why might the LENGTH of their resistance/adaptation phase differ, and what does that mean for programming the next hard session?

  1. A. The resistance phase is fixed at 48 hours for everyone, so program identically
  2. B. Phase duration varies with the magnitude of homeostatic disruption, single vs. cumulative overload, and training status — so individualize the recovery interval before the next hard exposure
  3. C. Only nutrition changes phase length, so feed them the same and proceed
  4. D. The veteran always recovers slower because he is older
  5. E. Beginners never reach the resistance phase, so it doesn't apply to them
Show answer

Answer: B — Kilgore says the resistance stage ranges from days to months depending on the magnitude of disruption, whether the overload was single or cumulative, and whether the trainee is fit or unfit. That variability means the inter-session recovery interval — and therefore where the next hard workout lands on the super-compensation curve — must be individualized. (A) misreads the 6-48h figure (that's return toward homeostasis after alarm, not a universal adaptation length); (C) ignores the multiple stated factors; (D) and (E) are unsupported generalizations.

D2 · Programming 14% of exam Confidence tier: ___

CFJ_Mason_Conjugate.pdf

PDF link not yet available

Why this is on the reading list

This article sits on the CCFT reading list because it is a concrete, worked example of designing a multi-week sequence of workouts to develop a specific component of fitness (absolute strength) while preserving general physical preparedness (GPP) — the core of Domain 2 Programming. It illustrates how a coach reasons about training intensity vs. volume to avoid overtraining, how exercise variation drives adaptation, and how a strength block is blended with met-cons rather than replacing them. The exam will not ask you to recite Mason's nine-week template; it will ask you to apply the underlying programming logic — intensity/volume trade-offs, variance, overtraining risk, and matching a program to an athlete's weakness and goals.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 2.1.2 Design a sequence of workouts that improves general physical preparedness (GPP)
  • 2.1.1 Design single workouts using the CrossFit methodology
  • 2.2.3 Scale for athletes with sport-specific goals
  • 2.2.5 Scale by skill level
  • 2.3.1 Evaluate program success relative to athlete goals and needs
  • 2.3.3 Adjust programming based on performance and goals
  • 2.3.4 Evaluate athlete progress relative to CrossFit's definition of fitness and their personal goal
  • 1.2.4 Monitor athlete for signs of over- or under-training
  • 1.2.5 Identify when athlete is ready to progress to another goal/skill
  • 5.2.1 Apply mechanics-consistency-intensity to programming for safety and performance
  • 3.1.9 Teach the goals of CrossFit programming and how goals are met (programming with variance)
  • 3.1.11 Teach relative intensity

What to focus on while reading

  • The author's central thesis: that improving a CrossFitter's absolute strength makes them a better CrossFitter ONLY IF it does not add large body weight or detrain endurance/strength endurance — note the qualifier, it is the whole point.
  • The definition of the conjugate system: frequent rotation of exercises and exercise variations (different bar, stance, hand placement, range of motion, bands/chains) to work weaknesses and prevent neural overtraining.
  • The second, less obvious function of conjugate variation: it creates a 'chaotic' periodization of VOLUME, because different exercises (back squat vs. front squat) force different loads and therefore different total training volume.
  • What max-effort (ME) work is: a progressive warm-up to a single maximal attempt (1RM), allowing training at ~100% intensity year-round.
  • How the article defines intensity here: a PERCENTAGE of one's 1RM (load-based / absolute-strength definition) — contrast this with CrossFit's power-output definition of intensity.
  • The intensity-vs-volume relationship for overtraining: higher intensity requires LOWER volume to avoid neural overtraining; high volume even at low-to-moderate intensity causes muscular overtraining.
  • Why combining the FULL Westside system with FULL CrossFit is a mistake — both are highly taxing, and stacking them leads to stagnation, neural and muscular overtraining, and regression.
  • Why the author DROPS dynamic-effort (speed) work: he values it mainly as active recovery, believes its carryover to absolute strength is minimal, and argues CrossFit met-cons already serve a similar supportive/conditioning role.
  • The actual hybrid template structure: 2 ME days per week (one upper, one lower) separated by 72 hours, plus 3 standard CrossFit met-con days.
  • The single caveat on the met-con days: AVOID met-cons that use heavy loads or low repetitions during this program (so you do not double up heavy work and trigger overtraining).
  • The warning to keep total met-con volume reasonable — choose WODs carefully, train them hard, but do NOT add extra work on top.
  • Why isolation/assistance work is included even though CrossFit normally avoids it: every athlete has a limiting muscle (e.g., triceps in the press) that caps a compound lift, and isolation work both addresses that weak link and allows greater targeted overload.
  • The rotation rule for the PRIMARY ME exercise: changed every fourth week (NOT weekly as in true Westside) — note WHY: weekly rotation would be excessive for athletes at this strength level and would block the neural adaptations (motor-unit recruitment, firing sequence) that come from repeating a movement.
  • Why the switch happens specifically at week four: after ~3 weeks of the same movement at 100% intensity, overtraining risk on that lift becomes real even for less-developed athletes.
  • How assistance exercises are handled differently: varied but not as rigidly, because they are done at much lower intensity (8-20+ reps), often taken to or near concentric failure (1-2 reps shy).
  • The author's repeated instruction to use the exercise lists to build a UNIQUE program that targets the individual's OWN weaknesses — the template is a starting point, not a prescription.
  • The framing that this block should be run at least once per year by any CrossFitter — absolute strength is a real component of fitness, not an 'also-ran,' and it supports quality of life into later years.

Concepts to understand

  • Specializing vs. not specializing: CrossFit's goal is broad, general fitness ('our specialty is not specializing'), so any strength-focused block must be bounded in time and must not erode the other capacities — a coach borrows tools from a specialist system without converting the athlete into a specialist.
  • Absolute strength as a component of fitness: understand WHY raising a CrossFitter's 1RMs improves general performance (a given workout load becomes a lower relative intensity, so it is more sustainable/repeatable) and the conditions under which it backfires (excess body mass, lost endurance).
  • The conjugate principle = variance applied to strength: rotating exercises and variations attacks weaknesses, prevents accommodation/neural overtraining, and — crucially — automatically varies training volume. This is the same 'constantly varied' logic CrossFit already uses, applied to the strength domain.
  • Intensity defined two ways: this article uses intensity = % of 1RM (load). CrossFit defines intensity = average power (force x distance / time). A coach must know which definition is in play when reading or writing a program, because the overtraining math here is built on the load-based definition.
  • The intensity-volume inverse relationship as a programming governor: as intensity rises toward 1RM, volume must fall; as volume rises, intensity must stay moderate — violating this in either direction is the mechanism of overtraining (neural at high intensity, muscular at high volume).
  • Overtraining as an additive-stress problem: two individually safe systems can become unsafe when stacked. The applied lesson is that a coach budgets total systemic stress across ALL training, not per-session — adding a heavy strength block means removing heavy/low-rep met-cons.
  • Max-effort method: building strength by repeatedly working up to a true 1RM, which lets the athlete train at maximal intensity frequently — paired with conjugate variety so the same movement is not maxed week after week.
  • Why dynamic-effort work can be substituted by met-cons in a CrossFit context: understand the reasoning (DE's main practical value is active recovery and explosiveness; met-cons supply recovery-level stimulus PLUS conditioning), and be able to evaluate that trade-off rather than treat it as dogma.
  • Assistance / isolation work as targeted weakness correction: the limiting-muscle concept — a compound lift is capped by its weakest contributor, so isolating and overloading that muscle raises the ceiling on the compound movement. This is individualization in action.
  • Movement rotation timing as a balance between adaptation and overtraining: hold a primary lift long enough (3 weeks) to get neural efficiency gains, but rotate (week 4) before chronic 100% loading causes overtraining. Frequency of variation is itself a programmable variable, tuned to the athlete's development level.
  • Scaling the source system to the audience: Mason deliberately deviates from true Westside (4-week rotation instead of weekly, no DE days) because the target population's strength level and recovery capacity differ. The transferable skill is adapting any borrowed program to the athlete in front of you, not copying it.
  • Program individualization and self-direction: the template is explicitly a skeleton; full benefit requires selecting exercises that address the specific athlete's weaknesses — connecting back to assessing the athlete and matching programming to identified gaps and goals.
  • Evaluating program success: success is judged against the athlete's goal (more absolute strength) AND against CrossFit's definition of fitness (the other capacities must hold) — a strength block that tanks conditioning has failed even if 1RMs went up.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenario questions where an athlete or a coach proposes stacking a full strength program on top of full CrossFit, or adds heavy/low-rep met-cons during a strength block, and you must recognize the overtraining risk and the correct adjustment (2.3.3, 1.2.4, 5.2.1). Expect questions framing an athlete whose 1RMs have plateaued or who is the 'strong-but-not-strong-enough' CrossFitter, asking which programming approach best fits a sport-specific or skill-level need (2.2.3, 2.2.5, 2.1.2). You may be asked to explain why variance/conjugate rotation drives adaptation and why a primary lift is held then rotated, mapping to teaching the goals of programming and relative intensity (3.1.9, 3.1.11, 2.1.1). Questions may also test whether you evaluate a strength block correctly — judging it against both the athlete's strength goal and the preservation of overall fitness (2.3.1, 2.3.4).

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Conjugate system
A training method that frequently rotates exercises and exercise variations (changing bar, stance, grip, range of motion, or adding bands/chains) to attack weaknesses, prevent the nervous system from over-adapting, and — as a side effect — vary total training volume.
Max-effort (ME) method
Strength work in which the athlete warms up progressively to a single maximal lift (a 1RM), enabling training at roughly 100% intensity on a regular basis.
Dynamic-effort (DE) / speed work
Lifting relatively light loads (typically 50-60% of 1RM) for 2-3 reps as fast as possible to train the nervous system to be explosive. Mason omits it from his hybrid, valuing it mainly as active recovery and arguing met-cons cover that role.
Absolute strength
The maximum force an athlete can produce regardless of body weight or time — measured by 1RM lifts. Distinct from strength endurance and from CrossFit's power-output sense of 'intensity.'
Intensity (as used here)
In this article, intensity = the load lifted expressed as a percentage of the athlete's 1RM. (Note: CrossFit's primary definition of intensity is average power output — force x distance / time — so always check which meaning applies.)
Training volume
The total amount of work performed (roughly sets x reps x load). Because different exercises allow different loads, rotating them automatically changes volume even at similar set/rep schemes.
Neural (nervous-system) overtraining
Breakdown driven primarily by training too intensely (too close to 1RM) too often; the corrective lever is to reduce volume or rotate the maximal movement.
Skeletal-muscular overtraining
Breakdown driven primarily by too much total volume, which can occur even at low-to-moderate intensity; the corrective lever is to cap total work.
Assistance / isolation work
Lower-intensity, higher-rep (8-20+) accessory exercises (often single-muscle) taken to or near concentric failure, used to strengthen the specific muscle that limits a compound lift and to overload it directly.
Limiting muscle
The weakest contributing muscle in a compound lift (e.g., the triceps in a max press) that caps how much the athlete can lift until it is specifically strengthened.
Met-con (metabolic conditioning)
Conditioning-focused CrossFit workouts. In this program they replace dynamic-effort days and supply general conditioning, with the rule that heavy/low-rep met-cons are avoided during the strength block.
Periodization
Planned variation of training variables over time. The conjugate system produces a 'chaotic' volume-based periodization through constant exercise rotation rather than rigid linear phases.
Concentric failure
The point in a set where the muscle can no longer complete the lifting (shortening) phase of a rep; assistance sets here are taken to or within 1-2 reps of it.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • Combining a full high-intensity strength program with full CrossFit volume is an explicit recipe for overtraining and regression — recognize this as a programming/risk error a coach must prevent (1.2.4, 5.2.1).
  • Running heavy, low-repetition met-cons during a max-effort strength block stacks heavy loading on heavy loading and drives overtraining — the program specifically forbids it.
  • Adding extra work 'above and beyond' the prescribed WODs (uncontrolled total volume) is flagged as a caution; monitor athletes who chronically do more than programmed for over-training signs.
  • Adding large amounts of absolute strength is only beneficial if it does NOT add significant body weight or detrain endurance/strength endurance — uncontrolled bulking or lost conditioning would defeat the purpose for a CrossFitter.
  • Max-effort 1RM work is high-risk loading: it must be built up to with a progressive warm-up and managed with sound mechanics before maximal intensity — implicit application of mechanics-consistency-intensity (5.2.1).

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. A competitive CrossFitter tells you their conditioning is strong but their 1RM lifts lag, and they want to run a dedicated strength block. They propose keeping their normal full CrossFit schedule AND adding a complete Westside program (two ME days, two DE days, all assistance work) on top. What is the best coaching response?

  1. A. Approve it — more training stimulus always produces faster results.
  2. B. Approve it but add extra accessory volume so no muscle is undertrained.
  3. C. Decline the full stack; explain that two highly taxing programs run in entirety lead to neural and muscular overtraining, and instead blend a limited strength block (e.g., 2 ME days) into the existing CrossFit week.
  4. D. Replace all CrossFit with the full Westside program until the lifts catch up, then return to CrossFit.
  5. E. Keep full CrossFit and add only the DE (speed) days, since those are the lightest.
Show answer

Answer: C — C reflects the article's core programming logic: both systems are extremely taxing, so running both in full stacks systemic stress and causes overtraining/regression — the fix is a bounded hybrid (a couple of ME days folded into CrossFit). A and B ignore the intensity/volume governor and worsen overtraining. D abandons CrossFit's general-fitness goal and turns the athlete into a specialist. E still combines two full programs and adds load the author considers low-value for absolute strength.

Scenario 2. You are building a strength-focused sequence for an intermediate athlete using a conjugate approach. On the three non-strength days you normally program standard met-cons. Which adjustment best fits the method's intent?

  1. A. Program the heaviest, lowest-rep met-cons you can on those days to reinforce the strength stimulus.
  2. B. Keep met-cons but avoid those with heavy loads or low repetitions, and keep total volume reasonable.
  3. C. Add a second strength session on each met-con day to maximize strength exposure.
  4. D. Remove met-cons entirely so all recovery goes to the strength work.
  5. E. Make every met-con a max-effort 1RM test to track strength daily.
Show answer

Answer: B — B is the explicit caveat in the article: during the strength block, met-cons continue (they supply conditioning and serve a recovery/support role replacing DE work) but heavy/low-rep met-cons are avoided and total volume is kept reasonable. A and C double up heavy loading or volume and invite overtraining. D removes the conditioning the program relies on and abandons GPP. E turns conditioning days into maximal-intensity days, exactly the overtraining trap.

Scenario 3. An athlete on the hybrid program asks why the primary max-effort lift is rotated every fourth week instead of every week like in the original Westside system. What is the soundest explanation to give?

  1. A. Weekly rotation is illegal under CrossFit rules.
  2. B. Holding a lift for about three weeks lets neural adaptations (better motor-unit recruitment and firing) develop, but rotating by week four avoids overtraining from repeated 100% efforts; weekly change would be excessive for this athlete's strength level.
  3. C. Rotating weekly costs too much equipment, so monthly is cheaper.
  4. D. The lift should never be rotated at all; consistency on one movement is best.
  5. E. Rotation timing is random and has no physiological basis.
Show answer

Answer: B — B captures the article's reasoning: weekly rotation (true Westside) is unnecessary for athletes at this strength level and would prevent the neural efficiency gains that come from repeating a movement, yet after ~3 weeks of maxing the same lift overtraining risk rises, so week four is the switch point. A and C are fabrications. D ignores that some rotation is needed to attack weaknesses and avoid overtraining. E contradicts the explicit adaptation-vs-overtraining rationale.

Scenario 4. A coach insists CrossFit never uses isolation movements, so the assistance/isolation exercises in this program (e.g., triceps pressdowns, glute-ham raises) should be cut. Why does the program include them anyway?

  1. A. To inflate workout time so the session feels harder.
  2. B. Because every athlete has a limiting muscle that caps a compound lift, and isolating plus overloading that muscle raises the ceiling on the main movement.
  3. C. Because isolation work replaces the need for any compound lifting.
  4. D. Because isolation work is the primary driver of metabolic conditioning.
  5. E. Because CrossFit requires bodybuilding-style training for all athletes.
Show answer

Answer: B — B is the article's stated rationale: a compound lift is limited by its weakest contributor (e.g., triceps in the press), and assistance/isolation work both addresses that weak link and permits greater targeted overload — a deliberate, individualized exception to CrossFit's usual preference for compound movements. A is nonsense. C and E overstate the role of isolation work. D confuses low-intensity strength accessory work with conditioning.

Scenario 5. Mid-block, an athlete reports stalled progress, persistent fatigue, and declining performance after weeks of maxing the same lift while also doing heavy, low-rep met-cons most days. Which programming variable should you adjust first, and how?

  1. A. Increase intensity further — push heavier 1RMs to break the plateau.
  2. B. Add more total training days to force adaptation.
  3. C. Reduce the stacked high-intensity load — rotate the ME lift and remove the heavy/low-rep met-cons — because the symptoms point to overtraining from too much high-intensity volume.
  4. D. Switch entirely to dynamic-effort speed days at 50-60% for the rest of the block.
  5. E. Keep everything the same; plateaus resolve on their own with time.
Show answer

Answer: C — C applies the intensity/volume-overtraining relationship and the monitoring task (1.2.4, 2.3.3): the athlete has stacked maximal-intensity strength work with heavy/low-rep met-cons, the classic overtraining setup the article warns against. The corrective levers are to rotate the maxed movement and strip out the redundant heavy met-cons. A and B add the very stress causing the problem. D over-corrects toward a method the author already judged low-value for strength and ignores the real cause. E neglects clear over-training warning signs.

Scenario 6. Two athletes both increase their back-squat 1RM by 40 lb over a strength block. Athlete X gained 18 lb of body weight and their benchmark met-con times got noticeably slower; Athlete Y's body weight and conditioning held steady. Evaluating against the program's intent for a CrossFitter, which statement is most accurate?

  1. A. Both succeeded equally because both added 40 lb to their squat.
  2. B. Athlete X succeeded more because more body weight means more strength.
  3. C. Athlete Y's outcome best fits the goal, because added absolute strength benefits a CrossFitter only if it does not bring large body-weight gain or detrain conditioning.
  4. D. Neither succeeded because absolute strength is irrelevant to CrossFit.
  5. E. Success can't be judged without a new 1RM test next year.
Show answer

Answer: C — C reflects the article's explicit qualifier and the evaluation tasks (2.3.1, 2.3.4): more absolute strength helps a CrossFitter only when it isn't accompanied by a big body-weight increase or a detraining effect on endurance/strength endurance. Athlete X gained strength but lost conditioning and added mass, so for a CrossFitter the block underperformed its purpose. A and B ignore the qualifier. D wrongly dismisses strength as a fitness component. E delays an evaluation the available data already supports.

D2 · Programming 14% of exam Confidence tier: ___

CFJ_Mason_Linear.pdf

PDF link not yet available

Why this is on the reading list

This 2010 CrossFit Journal article by Chris Mason argues that pure linear progression (steadily adding load to the same lifts every session) eventually stalls for any athlete training at real intensity, and proposes a conjugate-variation model (Westside Barbell) as a more durable strength-development strategy. For the CCFT exam it is a Programming (Domain 2) reading: it backs your ability to design a sequence of workouts that drives general physical preparedness over time (2.1.2), to recognize when a program has stopped producing results and adjust it (2.3.3), and to evaluate program success against an athlete's goals and progress (2.3.1, 2.3.4). It also reinforces the core CrossFit programming idea that variance, not monotony, is what keeps adaptation coming. Read it for the reasoning about WHY progress stalls and WHAT to change, not to memorize Westside templates.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 2.1.1 Design single workouts using the CrossFit methodology
  • 2.1.2 Design a sequence of workouts that improves general physical preparedness (GPP)
  • 2.2.5 Scale by skill level (beginner vs. experienced/advanced strength athlete)
  • 2.3.1 Evaluate program success relative to athlete goals and needs
  • 2.3.2 Use benchmarks to assess effectiveness of programming (e.g., 1RM, 5x5 loads)
  • 2.3.3 Adjust programming based on performance and goals
  • 2.3.4 Evaluate athlete progress relative to CrossFit's definition of fitness and their personal goal
  • 1.2.4 Monitor athlete for signs of over- or under-training
  • 1.2.5 Identify when athlete is ready to progress to another goal/skill
  • 3.1.9 Teach the goals of CrossFit programming and how goals are met (programming with variance)

What to focus on while reading

  • The author's definition of linear progression: progressively adding small load increments (5-10 lb) to the same exercise at a fixed set/rep scheme (e.g., 5x5) every session until you can no longer add weight.
  • The author's definition of 'intensity' here — note it is the WEIGHTLIFTING definition (percentage of 1-rep max), NOT CrossFit's power-output definition. This distinction matters because the exam uses 'intensity' in the CrossFit sense elsewhere.
  • Why linear progression works at first: rapid early adaptation via contractile myofibril hypertrophy AND neural adaptation ('beginner's gains').
  • The central claim: neural adaptation becomes the LIMITING factor because the trainee works at high intensity on the same movements every session, and the nervous system has a ceiling on how much high-intensity work it can keep adapting to.
  • The two 'fixes' the linear-progression camp prescribes for stalls — eat more, or take time off — and why the author says each fails (excess calories add body fat/health risk and only delay the stall; time off causes detraining and muscular atrophy).
  • The yo-yo / negative-return mechanism: muscular recovery is faster than neural recovery, so time off lets muscle atrophy, leaving the athlete weaker and forcing the nervous system to work even harder on return.
  • Conjugate variation (Westside Barbell, Louie Simmons): CONSTANT variation of the exercises used to train a given movement/body part, so high-intensity training can continue without neural overtraining.
  • The max-effort (ME) rotation example: floor press > board press > reverse-band press > full-range bench across a four-week cycle; squat bar swaps (straight bar > Buffalo Bar) with the same box-squat/band setup.
  • The motor-learning principle the argument rests on: movements that LOOK nearly identical have very little skill (neural) transfer — fastest straight-line runner isn't the fastest in a circle; a great tennis player can be a poor badminton player.
  • How conjugate variation addresses WEAK POINTS two ways: (1) rotating ME exercises inherently hits weaknesses (weak bench lockout > board/floor press; weak squat from hamstrings/glutes > good mornings), and (2) assistance/'special' exercises deliberately target individual weaknesses, yielding an athlete who is stronger and less injury-prone.
  • The author's structure of a conjugate week per major lift: one dynamic-effort (DE / speed) day and one max-effort (ME) day for bench and squat, with the ME exercise switched each week; DE percentages cited as roughly 50-55% of max.
  • The author's rebuttal to 'conjugate is too complicated/dangerous for beginners' — that the scheme is simple, percentages are easy, and Simmons built teenage world-champion powerlifters from Day 1.
  • Note what the article does NOT cover: it is a strength-bias powerlifting argument and does not address conditioning, metcons, the full CrossFit definition of fitness, or how to integrate this with daily WODs. Hold its claims as one perspective on the GPP/variance principle, not as CrossFit doctrine.
  • The author is the co-owner of a nutrition company and a Westside team member — note the perspective/source so you weigh the claims as an informed opinion piece, not a peer-reviewed study.

Concepts to understand

  • Why a beginner-friendly progression eventually stops working: the body adapts fast at first (hypertrophy + neural), then adaptation slows, so the same stimulus stops producing the same result — the practical cue that it is time to CHANGE the program, not just push harder.
  • Diminishing returns and the difference between under-training and over-reaching: at some point MORE of the same high-intensity work yields zero or negative returns; an experienced coach recognizes a true plateau versus a temporary dip and adjusts the variable that is actually limiting.
  • Neural fatigue vs. muscular fatigue as separate recovery systems: the nervous system recovers more slowly than muscle, so a program that hammers the CNS every session can stall an athlete even when the muscles feel ready — relevant to monitoring over-training signs.
  • Variance as the engine of continued adaptation: this is the bridge to CrossFit's own programming philosophy — constantly varied stimulus keeps the body adapting; monotonous, identical sessions invite stagnation. Be able to connect 'conjugate variation' to CrossFit's 'constantly varied.'
  • Specificity / limited skill transfer from motor learning: small changes to a lift (different bar, different range, bands) are experienced as a meaningfully different skill by the nervous system — which is exactly what lets you keep intensity high while giving the CNS variety.
  • Programming to address weak points: rotating movements and adding targeted assistance work fixes the limiting links in a lift (lockout, posterior chain) and reduces injury risk — an application of evaluating an athlete's needs and adjusting the plan accordingly.
  • Matching the strength approach to athlete training age (skill level): linear progression is genuinely effective and appropriate for novices; experienced athletes generally need more structured variation. Choosing the right tool for the athlete in front of you IS the coaching judgment the exam tests.
  • Evaluating a program by results, not by faith: the article warns that a program 'working for a while' creates false confidence; a coach must judge effectiveness against the athlete's actual progress toward their goal and be willing to abandon what has stopped working.
  • Why the prescribed 'fixes' (eat more / rest) can be the wrong lever: they treat symptoms while ignoring the structural cause (no variation), and rest can backfire via detraining — understand the reasoning so you pick the correct intervention, not the popular one.
  • Reading the source critically: this is one coach's argument for a strength bias, framed in powerlifting terms. Understand the mechanism it teaches (variance defeats neural overtraining) while recognizing the exam wants applied programming judgment, not adoption of any single template.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenario items where an athlete who progressed well on a fixed linear program (e.g., 5x5 adding 5 lb weekly) has stalled, and you must choose the best coaching response — recognizing the plateau and introducing variation (2.3.3, 1.2.4) rather than simply telling them to add more weight, eat more, or quit. Other items may ask which strength approach fits a given athlete's training age (linear for a true novice vs. more varied work for an experienced lifter — 2.2.5), or how to evaluate whether a program is succeeding against the athlete's goal (2.3.1, 2.3.4). The deeper, transferable idea — that constantly varied stimulus drives continued adaptation while monotony stalls it — supports questions about why CrossFit programs are built on variance (2.1.2, 3.1.9).

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Linear progression
A strength method where you add a small, steady load increment to the same exercise at a fixed set/rep scheme every session (e.g., 5x5) for as long as you can keep adding weight. Simple and effective for beginners; stalls once neural adaptation maxes out.
Intensity (weightlifting definition)
As used in THIS article, the load on the bar expressed as a percentage of your 1-rep max. Note this differs from CrossFit's definition of intensity as power output (force x distance / time) — don't conflate the two on the exam.
1-rep maximum (1RM)
The most weight you can lift for a single repetition of a given exercise. Used as the reference point for 'intensity' percentages and as a benchmark for tracking strength progress.
5x5
Five working sets of five repetitions — a common linear-progression set/rep scheme. The athlete repeats it with the same load until all 5x5 is achieved, then adds weight next session.
Beginner's gains
The rapid early strength and size increases a new trainee experiences because the body adapts quickly to a novel stimulus. These slow markedly as the athlete becomes trained, signaling the need to change the program.
Contractile myofibril hypertrophy
Growth of the force-producing protein structures (myofibrils) inside muscle fibers — the kind of muscle growth that actually increases strength, as opposed to fluid/sarcoplasmic swelling.
Neural adaptation
Improvements in how efficiently the nervous system recruits and coordinates muscle to perform a specific movement. A major source of early strength gains and, per the article, the factor that limits continued progress on linear programs.
Neural (CNS) overtraining
A state where the nervous system can no longer keep adapting to repeated high-intensity work on the same movements, causing stalled or declining performance even when muscles feel recovered.
Detraining / atrophy
Loss of strength and muscle size from a reduction or break in training. The article notes muscle recovers faster than the nervous system, so time off can cause muscular atrophy and leave the athlete weaker on return.
Conjugate variation (conjugate method)
A strength system (popularized by Louie Simmons / Westside Barbell) built on constantly rotating the exercises used to train a movement, allowing repeated high-intensity training without neural overtraining.
Max-effort (ME) day
A training day where the lifter works up to a near-maximal single (1RM attempt) on a chosen variation of a main lift. In the conjugate system the ME exercise is swapped each week.
Dynamic-effort (DE / speed) day
A training day focused on moving submaximal loads (cited as roughly 50-55% of max) as fast as possible to develop speed and power, complementing the heavy ME day for the same lift.
Assistance / special exercises
Supplemental movements (good mornings, board/floor presses, etc.) chosen to strengthen an individual athlete's specific weak points; described as the 'mortar' that supports the conjugate system and reduces injury risk.
Skill transfer (motor learning)
The degree to which practicing one movement improves performance of another. The article's key point: even very similar-looking movements can transfer little, so small lift variations feel like new skills to the nervous system.
Weak-point training
Programming deliberately aimed at the limiting link in a lift (e.g., a weak bench lockout or weak posterior chain in the squat) by selecting exercises and assistance work that target that specific weakness.
General physical preparedness (GPP)
Broad, all-around fitness and a foundation of work capacity across many domains — the goal a coach builds toward when sequencing workouts over time; the lens through which the exam asks you to judge a strength program's place in the bigger plan.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • This is a single-author opinion piece arguing a strength bias in powerlifting terms — it is NOT CrossFit programming doctrine. Do not treat 'switch everyone to Westside conjugate' as a default exam answer; the best answer is usually to match the approach to the individual athlete and their goals.
  • Scope of practice: the article's 'eat more' fix touches nutrition. A CCFT trainer gives general nutrition guidance only; detailed dietary prescription and managing health problems from excess intake fall outside scope and warrant referral when relevant.
  • Over-training is a monitoring/safety concern: persistent plateaus, performance decline, and inability to recover can signal over-reaching or non-functional overreaching. Recognize these signs (1.2.4) and adjust load/variation/recovery rather than simply pushing more intensity.
  • The piece downplays the idea that varied/heavier strength work could be risky for beginners. A coach must still apply mechanics-consistency-intensity in order: novices earn intensity (including near-max singles) only after sound, consistent mechanics — safety governs progression regardless of which strength model you choose.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. An experienced member has run a 5x5 back-squat linear progression for eight months, adding 5 lb per session. For the last three weeks she has failed to complete 5x5 at the same weight, feels run-down, and is frustrated. What is the best coaching response, consistent with this article?

  1. A. Tell her to keep the same program and simply try harder next session.
  2. B. Tell her to add even more weight to force an adaptation.
  3. C. Recognize the plateau as neural fatigue from monotonous high-intensity work and introduce variation (e.g., rotate squat variations / vary loading) to restore progress.
  4. D. Tell her to stop strength training for a month and rest completely.
  5. E. Tell her the problem is purely diet and prescribe a specific high-calorie meal plan.
Show answer

Answer: C — The article's core thesis is that linear progression stalls when the nervous system can no longer adapt to repeated high-intensity work on the same movement; the fix is variation, not more of the same. C applies that reasoning (and tasks 2.3.3, 1.2.4). A and B ignore the plateau and risk deeper overtraining. D causes detraining/atrophy (the article's explicit warning) and can leave her weaker. E oversteps nutrition scope of practice and, per the article, treats a symptom rather than the structural cause.

Scenario 2. A brand-new trainee with sound, consistent squat and press mechanics wants to get stronger. Based on this article's view of training age, which strength approach is most appropriate to start with?

  1. A. A full Westside conjugate template with weekly max-effort exercise rotations from Day 1.
  2. B. A simple linear progression, because it is effective and easy for novices, while monitoring for the eventual stall.
  3. C. No strength work until the athlete has competed in a sanctioned meet.
  4. D. Only dynamic-effort speed days at 50-55% with no heavy lifting.
  5. E. Random, never-repeated loading with no progression scheme at all.
Show answer

Answer: B — The article concedes linear progression is 'very simple and quite effective for beginners' — it just gets exhausted later. For a novice with sound mechanics, B is the right tool and reflects matching method to skill level (2.2.5) plus watching for the plateau (1.2.4/1.2.5). A is more complexity than a novice needs at the outset (though the article argues it CAN work, B is the better-matched starting point). C and D are unjustified restrictions; E abandons the progressive overload a beginner needs.

Scenario 3. While explaining to a class why CrossFit programming constantly varies its stimulus, you want to borrow the strongest supporting idea from this article. Which concept best reinforces the value of variance?

  1. A. Muscle is metabolically cheap, so the body adds it freely.
  2. B. Repeating identical high-intensity sessions eventually overwhelms the nervous system's capacity to adapt, whereas varying the stimulus lets high-intensity training continue.
  3. C. Only total weekly calories determine strength progress.
  4. D. Skill transfers fully between any similar-looking movements, so variation is unnecessary.
  5. E. Time off from training is the primary driver of long-term strength.
Show answer

Answer: B — B is the article's central mechanism and maps directly to teaching the goals of CrossFit programming through variance (3.1.9) and sequencing for GPP (2.1.2). A inverts the article (muscle is described as physiologically expensive). C is the simplistic 'just eat more' fix the article rejects. D contradicts the motor-learning point that similar movements have LITTLE transfer. E is the detraining trap the article warns against.

Scenario 4. A lifter's bench press always fails at lockout. Applying the weak-point logic the article describes with the conjugate system, what is the most appropriate programming adjustment?

  1. A. Drop the bench press entirely and only do more cardio.
  2. B. Keep benching the exact same way every session until the lockout improves on its own.
  3. C. Add targeted variations/assistance that train the lockout range (e.g., board press or floor press) and select assistance exercises for the limiting muscles.
  4. D. Increase calories and assume the lockout will resolve.
  5. E. Tell the lifter the sticking point is genetic and cannot be trained.
Show answer

Answer: C — The article explicitly says rotating ME exercises and using assistance/'special' exercises address weak points — a weak bench lockout is helped by board or floor presses. C applies that and reflects adjusting programming to the athlete's needs (2.3.3, 2.3.1). A throws out the trained lift; B is the monotony the article blames for stalls; D is the rejected nutrition-only fix; E is defeatist and contradicts the article's claim that weaknesses are trainable.

Scenario 5. A coach reads this article and decides to immediately convert every member at the gym to a Westside conjugate strength template, regardless of experience, goals, or whether they came to CrossFit for conditioning. What is the best critique of this decision?

  1. A. It is ideal — one optimal strength system should be applied to everyone identically.
  2. B. Programming should be evaluated against each athlete's individual goals and needs; this is one strength-biased perspective, and a coach should match the approach to the athlete rather than apply a single template universally.
  3. C. Conjugate training is unsafe for everyone and should never be used.
  4. D. Linear progression is always superior, so the change is simply wrong.
  5. E. Strength training has no place in CrossFit, so no template should be used.
Show answer

Answer: B — The exam rewards individualized programming judgment (2.3.1, 2.3.4). The article is a persuasive opinion piece favoring a strength bias; B correctly frames the takeaway — understand the variance principle, but fit the method to the athlete's training age, goals, and needs. A ignores individualization. C and E are overstatements the article does not support. D simply inverts the same one-size-fits-all error.

D2 · Programming 14% of exam Confidence tier: ___

CFJ_Nitz_PerformancePregnancy.pdf

Open the PDF on Google Drive →

Why this is on the reading list

This article is the CCFT reading list's concrete worked example of scaling CrossFit programming for a pregnant athlete, which is an explicitly named special population in the Content Outline (2.2.2). It backs the broader programming-and-scaling cluster (2.1, 2.2, 2.3) by showing how a coach modifies load, volume, intensity, movement selection, and time domains in response to a changing physiology while preserving the methodology (constantly varied functional movement). It also carries direct risk-management and scope-of-practice weight: relaxin-driven joint laxity, supine vena cava compression, core-temperature limits, rhabdo risk in beginners, and deferral to a physician for high-risk pregnancy all surface in Domains 1, 5, and 7. The exam will not ask you to recite Nitz's no-go list; it will hand you a pregnant athlete in a class and ask what you do next.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 2.2.2 Scale for special populations (e.g., pregnant, adaptive)
  • 2.2.1 Scale by age group (general scaling-by-category reasoning the article models)
  • 2.2.5 Scale by skill level (beginner-vs-veteran CrossFitter divergence in programming)
  • 2.1.1 Design single workouts using the CrossFit methodology (Baby Nancy as a scaled benchmark)
  • 2.1.2 Design a sequence of workouts that improves GPP (maintain strength/stamina/flexibility across trimesters)
  • 2.3.1 Evaluate program success relative to athlete goals and needs (goal shifts from PRs to maintenance/birth prep)
  • 2.3.3 Adjust programming based on performance and goals (progressive de-load as pregnancy advances)
  • 1.1.1 Screen athlete for medical issues (recognize pregnancy and high-risk status)
  • 1.1.2 Recognize conditions outside CCFT Scope of Practice that require referral (high-risk pregnancy to physician)
  • 1.1.3 Assess for rhabdomyolysis risk (beginner + pregnancy is a high-risk combination)
  • 5.2.2 Apply scaling to meet current physical and psychological needs of each athlete
  • 5.2.3 Manage risk for the athlete
  • 5.2.6 Recognize warning signs for possible injury or overexertion (dizziness, talk-test failure)
  • 6.2.1 Identify additional lifestyle goals (hydration, heat exposure, recovery as risk factors)
  • 7.4.1 Work within CCFT Scope of Practice (medical decisions belong to the physician)

What to focus on while reading

  • Hunt for the three physiological changes Nitz names and WHY each one changes your programming: shifting center of gravity (balance/agility loss), the ~10-fold rise in relaxin (ligament/joint laxity), and increased blood volume + cardiac output + heart rate (cardio-respiratory load).
  • Note that the coaching prescription splits on training history: a brand-new CrossFitter who is or is about to be pregnant proceeds with 'extreme caution,' light weights, low reps, no intensity ramp; a long-time CrossFitter can keep doing most workouts roughly 4–6 months in. Capture this as a scale-by-skill-level decision, not a one-size rule.
  • Mark the explicit goal shift: the pregnant athlete's objective is no longer PRs — it is maintain strength/stamina/flexibility, gain only necessary weight, and prepare for childbirth. This is the 'evaluate program success relative to goals' pivot.
  • Highlight the 'talk test' / rate of perceived exertion as the primary intensity governor, and understand exactly why it replaces a heart-rate cap.
  • Capture the True/False trio precisely, because the exam loves the half-true and false items: (1) TRUE — don't lie on your back after ~first trimester/4 months (vena cava compression → reduced blood/oxygen to baby, dizziness); (2) HALF-TRUE — inversion isn't proven harmful but raised blood volume means you could get dizzy and fall; (3) FALSE — the >140 bpm rule is outdated (ACOG dropped it in 1994; no correlation between HR and core temperature).
  • Understand the real risk mechanism: high intensity → maternal hypoxia → insufficient oxygen to the baby (baby draws oxygen from maternal blood) → possible brain damage. Heart rate is a poor proxy because pregnancy elevates resting and working HR via increased blood volume.
  • Lock in the core-temperature ceiling: do not let core temp exceed ~102°F — risk of central nervous system abnormalities in the baby. Hydration and avoiding overheating are programming constraints, not afterthoughts.
  • Record the relaxin-driven movement cautions: beware ballistic and quick lateral movements and squatting below parallel (note 'squat to parallel' is reinforced in the Baby Nancy notes).
  • Capture the 'no-go until after birth' list and the reasoning ('too many things can go wrong,' 'not worth the risk of falling'): rope climbs and handstand push-ups (sub beginner rope climbs / rope pull-ups), heavy or max-effort lifts, GHD sit-ups (back/hip extensions are okay for a few months), and box jumps (first to self-select out due to balance/weight redistribution).
  • Note the general-strategy edits: remove 'for time' (rushing → tripping), do not work to exhaustion (protects baby's oxygen supply), keep running and rowing as the safer cardio engines, and de-scale by swapping movements (squat-to-box for squats, ring rows for pull-ups, knees-to-elbows for sit-ups, elevated/incline push-ups, dumbbells for barbells as the belly grows).
  • Catch the rhabdo warning aimed specifically at newbie CrossFitters — pregnancy is a 'really bad time to induce rhabdo,' which can affect any beginner. Tie this to screening/readiness, not just programming.
  • Read the scope-of-practice boundary at the end: a high-risk pregnancy means the physician may forbid exercise; the coach defers and offers safe options within whatever the doctor allows (e.g., bed-rest-compatible activity).
  • Study the 'Baby Nancy' sample as a scaled benchmark: Advanced 5 rounds (run/row 400m + 15 OHS @ 45 lb), Intermediate 4 rounds (run/row/walk 400m + 15 OHS @ 25 lb), Beginner 3 rounds (row/walk 200m + 10 OHS @ 10 lb or PVC), all squatting only to parallel. Notice the three scaling levers moved together: rounds (volume), distance + modality (run→row→walk), and load.
  • Notice the article is a 2008 trainer's field experience with anecdotal/observational claims ('data I have collected,' 'studies show') — treat the physiological mechanisms and scaling logic as exam-relevant, and treat the baby-outcome claims as motivational context, not testable physiology.
