Concepts to understand

  • Pregnancy is a special population requiring scaling, not exclusion: the default coaching posture is to keep the athlete training while modifying intensity, load, volume, movement selection, and time domain — 'downshift, don't get off the highway.'
  • Scaling for pregnancy is individualized and history-dependent: a beginner gets the most conservative prescription (light, low-rep, no intensity ramp), while an experienced CrossFitter can sustain most workouts for several months — the same diagnosis does not yield the same program.
  • The athlete's goal changes, so the definition of program success changes: you are now optimizing for maintained capacity, controlled weight gain, flexibility, and birth preparation — progress is measured against those needs, not against a one-rep max or a faster Fran.
  • Intensity is the true risk variable, governed by perceived exertion (the talk test), not by a heart-rate number: if she can hold a conversation she is in a safe zone, even above 140 bpm; if she's gasping, back off — and never push into a hypoxic state.
  • Why heart-rate caps fail in pregnancy: increased blood volume raises relative bpm at rest and in all activity, so 140 (or even 150) bpm can occur without high exertion; ACOG retired the 140 rule in 1994 after finding no HR–core-temperature correlation.
  • The maternal-fetal oxygen link drives the safety logic: the baby gets oxygen from maternal blood, so maternal hypoxia from over-exertion can deprive the baby and risk brain damage — this is the mechanistic reason to cap intensity and avoid working to exhaustion.
  • Relaxin biomechanics: the ~10-fold rise in relaxin softens ligaments to open the pelvis, which increases joint instability — so you remove ballistic loading, quick lateral movement, and below-parallel squatting that exploit lax joints.
  • Center-of-gravity shift compromises balance and agility, which is why falling-risk movements (box jumps, rope climbs, HSPU) come off the menu first and why 'for time' is removed to stop rushing.
  • Supine-position risk after ~first trimester: a grown uterus compresses the vena cava when lying on the back, reducing venous return and fetal oxygenation and causing dizziness — so reprogram away from prolonged supine work as pregnancy advances.
  • Thermoregulation as a programming constraint: keep core temperature under ~102°F (CNS-abnormality risk to the baby), which makes hydration, environment, and work density real variables in workout design.
  • Movement substitution as the practical scaling toolkit: squat-to-box for squats, ring rows for pull-ups, knees-to-elbows for sit-ups, elevated push-ups, dumbbells for barbells, beginner rope climbs/rope pull-ups for rope climbs — substitute, don't simply delete, to preserve the stimulus.
  • Volume/time-domain management: prefer running and rowing as scalable aerobic engines, cut total volume and 'for time' pressure, and avoid working to exhaustion — preserving aerobic stimulus without spiking intensity.
  • Progressive de-load across the pregnancy: workouts that are fine early self-select out as the belly grows and discomfort rises ('if it feels weird, painful, or uncomfortable, don't do it') — programming is continuously re-adjusted, the article's expression of 'adjust based on performance and goals.'
  • Rhabdo risk is elevated for a pregnant beginner: unaccustomed eccentric load on a deconditioned athlete is the classic rhabdo setup, and pregnancy is a especially bad time to trigger it — screen and throttle accordingly.
  • Scope of practice and medical deferral: high-risk pregnancy is a physician's call; the coach does not override medical restriction and instead programs only within the limits the doctor sets, including bed-rest-safe options.
  • Maintenance minimum: aim for at least three training days per week to retain fitness — enough to preserve adaptation without chasing performance gains.
  • Distinguishing testable mechanism from motivational claim: the physiological constraints and scaling rules are coaching-relevant; the anecdotal baby-outcome benefits are context, and an exam answer should rest on the safety mechanism, not the marketing.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenario items that drop a pregnant athlete into your class and ask for the next coaching action — which movement to substitute, how to govern intensity, what to pull from a benchmark, or when to refer (tasks 2.2.2, 5.2.2, 5.2.3, 1.1.2). The classic distractors are the outdated 140-bpm cap (wrong: use the talk test / RPE) and 'tell her to stop exercising' (wrong unless a physician has restricted a high-risk pregnancy). You may also see screening/readiness items where the right move is recognizing rhabdo risk in a pregnant beginner (1.1.3) or deferring a medical decision to the doctor (7.4.1), and programming-evaluation items where success is redefined as maintenance and birth prep rather than PRs (2.3.1, 2.3.3). Treat every option through the lens of the experienced coach managing risk while keeping the athlete training.

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Relaxin
A pregnancy hormone that rises roughly ten-fold to soften and loosen pelvic ligaments so the baby can pass through the birth canal; the side effect is increased joint laxity throughout the body, which makes ballistic, deep-range, and quick lateral movements riskier.
Vena cava compression (supine hypotension)
After about the first trimester, lying on the back lets the enlarged uterus press on the vena cava (the major veins returning blood to the heart), reducing blood return and fetal oxygen and causing dizziness/lightheadedness — the reason to avoid prolonged supine work later in pregnancy.
Talk test / Rate of Perceived Exertion (RPE)
A self-paced intensity gauge: if the athlete can carry on a conversation, intensity is in a safe range; if she's breathing too hard to talk, she backs off. For pregnancy it replaces a fixed heart-rate cap as the primary intensity governor.
Hypoxia
Insufficient oxygen in the blood. Because the baby draws oxygen from the mother's blood, pushing the mother into a hypoxic state can deprive the baby of oxygen and risk brain damage — the mechanistic basis for capping intensity and avoiding work to exhaustion.
Cardiac output / blood volume increase
Pregnancy raises blood volume and cardiac output, which elevates resting and working heart rate. This is why a heart-rate number (like 140 bpm) is a poor intensity limit — the same bpm now reflects less actual exertion.
ACOG 140-bpm guideline (retired 1994)
The American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology once advised keeping exercise heart rate at or below 140 bpm to protect core temperature, then dropped it in 1994 after finding no correlation between heart rate and core temperature. The cap is outdated; use perceived exertion instead.
Core temperature ceiling (~102°F)
An upper limit on maternal core body temperature during exercise; exceeding it can increase the risk of central nervous system abnormalities in the baby. Drives hydration and heat-management constraints in programming.
Rhabdomyolysis (rhabdo)
Breakdown of muscle tissue that releases contents into the bloodstream, potentially damaging the kidneys; it can affect any beginner subjected to excessive, unfamiliar load. Pregnancy is an especially bad time to induce it, so beginners must be throttled.
Center of gravity shift
As the baby grows, the mother's center of gravity moves forward and up, degrading balance and agility — the reason fall-risk movements (box jumps, rope climbs, HSPU) are removed early and 'for time' urgency is cut.
GHD sit-up
A glute-ham-developer sit-up involving a large supine trunk extension/flexion range; specifically placed on the no-go list during pregnancy even though milder back/hip extensions are tolerated for a few months.
Movement substitution (de-scaling)
Replacing a contraindicated or too-difficult movement with a safer one that preserves the intended stimulus — e.g., squat-to-box for squats, ring rows for pull-ups, knees-to-elbows for sit-ups, dumbbells for barbells — rather than deleting the element entirely.
Baby Nancy
The article's sample scaled benchmark (a pregnancy-modified 'Nancy') prescribed at Advanced/Intermediate/Beginner levels by adjusting rounds, run-row-walk modality/distance, and overhead-squat load, always squatting only to parallel — a model of moving multiple scaling levers together.
High-risk pregnancy
A pregnancy a physician judges to need activity restriction (up to full bed rest). It is a medical determination outside the coach's scope; the coach programs only within the doctor's limits.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • High-risk pregnancy is a physician's decision, not the coach's — if a doctor has restricted activity, do not override it; program only within those limits and defer the medical call (scope of practice).
  • Dizziness, lightheadedness, or feeling faint (e.g., from supine vena cava compression or raised blood volume) is a stop-and-modify signal, not something to push through.
  • Failing the talk test (gasping, can't hold a conversation) means intensity is too high — back off immediately to protect maternal/fetal oxygenation.
  • Beginner + pregnant is an elevated rhabdomyolysis-risk combination; cap load, reps, and intensity and avoid unfamiliar high-volume eccentric work.
  • Core temperature above ~102°F risks CNS abnormalities in the baby — enforce hydration and avoid overheating/heat plus heavy work density.
  • Do not rely on a heart-rate cap (e.g., 140 bpm) as the safety limit — it is outdated for pregnancy; use perceived exertion.
  • Remove fall-risk and high-instability movements (box jumps, rope climbs, handstand push-ups, heavy/max-effort lifts, GHD sit-ups) given balance loss and relaxin-driven joint laxity.
  • Never program the pregnant athlete to work to exhaustion — it limits the baby's oxygen supply.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. A long-time CrossFitter who is 18 weeks pregnant tells you her doctor has cleared her to keep exercising and she feels great. Mid-WOD she's working hard but says she can still talk in short sentences, and her wrist monitor reads 148 bpm. What is the best coaching action?

  1. A. Stop her immediately — any heart rate above 140 bpm is unsafe in pregnancy.
  2. B. Let her continue at this effort, monitoring the talk test, since she can still hold a conversation and isn't gasping.
  3. C. Tell her to lie on her back and rest until her heart rate drops below 140.
  4. D. Switch her to max-effort lifting to get the work done faster before fatigue sets in.
  5. E. End her training for the day and advise she only walk for the rest of the pregnancy.
Show answer

Answer: B — The 140-bpm cap is outdated (ACOG retired it in 1994; no HR–core-temp correlation), and pregnancy raises bpm via increased blood volume, so a number alone is a poor limit. The talk test / perceived exertion is the correct governor — if she can converse and isn't hypoxic, the intensity is acceptable (B). A and C act on the obsolete HR rule; C also puts her supine, risking vena cava compression. D raises injury and rhabdo/intensity risk. E needlessly removes safe, beneficial training.

Scenario 2. A brand-new member who just started CrossFit three weeks ago tells you she is six weeks pregnant and is excited to 'go all in.' What is the most appropriate programming decision?

  1. A. Program her like any other beginner and ramp intensity normally over the next month.
  2. B. Have her sit out entirely until after delivery to avoid any liability.
  3. C. Proceed with extreme caution: light weights, low reps, no intensity ramp, with heightened attention to rhabdo risk.
  4. D. Put her straight into 'Baby Nancy' at the Advanced level to build a base quickly.
  5. E. Tell her to keep her heart rate under 140 bpm and otherwise train at full effort.
Show answer

Answer: C — A pregnant true beginner is the article's most conservative case: light weights, low reps, no intensity ramp, and explicit rhabdo vigilance because pregnancy is a bad time to induce it in a deconditioned athlete (C). A ramps intensity she shouldn't have. B over-restricts a low-risk, cleared athlete and isn't required. D prescribes an advanced dose to a beginner. E repeats the outdated HR cap and contradicts 'no intensity ramp.'

Scenario 3. You're scaling 'Nancy' (5 rounds: 400m run + 15 overhead squats) for a pregnant athlete who is a solid intermediate. Which modification best fits the article's approach?

  1. A. Keep 5 rounds and the 400m run, but load the barbell heavier to keep it challenging.
  2. B. Reduce to ~4 rounds, allow run/row/walk for the 400m, lighten the overhead-squat load, and squat only to parallel.
  3. C. Add a strict 'for time' cap so she finishes faster and spends less time training.
  4. D. Replace overhead squats with GHD sit-ups to reduce the load on her legs.
  5. E. Keep everything identical to the prescribed workout since she is an experienced athlete.
Show answer

Answer: B — The Baby Nancy model moves several scaling levers together — fewer rounds (volume), run/row/walk modality choice, lighter load, and squatting only to parallel to respect relaxin-driven joint laxity (B). A increases load against guidance. C reintroduces 'for time,' which the article removes to prevent rushing/tripping. D swaps in a no-go movement (GHD sit-ups). E ignores that even experienced athletes need pregnancy-specific scaling.

Scenario 4. During a workout a 30-week-pregnant athlete becomes dizzy and lightheaded after a set that had her lying on her back for tempo work. What should you do first?

  1. A. Have her push through one more round to see if it passes.
  2. B. Get her off her back, reposition her, check on her, and substitute a non-supine movement — supine pressure on the vena cava can reduce blood flow and oxygen.
  3. C. Tell her dizziness is normal in pregnancy and continue as programmed.
  4. D. Increase her intensity to raise her heart rate and 'wake her up.'
  5. E. Send her home and tell her she should not train again while pregnant.
Show answer

Answer: B — After roughly the first trimester, lying supine lets the uterus compress the vena cava, cutting venous return and fetal oxygenation and causing dizziness. The first action is to get her off her back, check her, and reprogram to a non-supine option (B). A and D push through or escalate a clear warning sign. C dismisses a meaningful symptom. E over-restricts based on a single, manageable position issue.

Scenario 5. A pregnant client asks why you've crossed box jumps and rope climbs off her workouts but kept rowing and running. What's the best explanation grounded in the article?

  1. A. Rowing and running burn more calories, which is the priority now.
  2. B. Box jumps and rope climbs carry a high fall risk given her shifted center of gravity, while running and rowing are scalable, lower-fall-risk aerobic options.
  3. C. Box jumps and rope climbs raise the heart rate above 140 bpm and the others don't.
  4. D. Rope climbs and box jumps are banned by ACOG for all pregnant women.
  5. E. Running and rowing are the only movements that are completely safe in pregnancy.
Show answer

Answer: B — The center-of-gravity shift degrades balance, making fall-prone movements (box jumps, rope climbs, HSPU) the first to come off the list, while run/row remain useful scalable aerobic engines (B). A misstates the priority (maintenance, not calorie burn). C reverts to the outdated HR rationale. D invents a blanket ACOG ban. E overstates safety — even run/row are dosed and de-scaled, not unconditionally 'safe.'

Scenario 6. A pregnant athlete's chart and conversation reveal her physician has classified her pregnancy as high-risk and told her not to do strenuous exercise. She still wants to train with you. What is the correct response?

  1. A. Override the doctor and design a light CrossFit program since exercise is generally good in pregnancy.
  2. B. Respect the physician's restriction, keep her within whatever the doctor allows, and offer safe options (e.g., bed-rest-compatible activity) rather than strenuous training.
  3. C. Tell her CrossFit is safe for everyone and to ignore the doctor.
  4. D. Refuse to interact with her at all until after delivery.
  5. E. Have her sign a waiver and then run her through a normal scaled class.
Show answer

Answer: B — High-risk status is a medical determination outside the coach's scope; the coach defers to the physician and programs only within the allowed limits, offering safe alternatives (B). A, C, and E all override or work around a medical restriction. D needlessly abandons the client when safe, doctor-permitted options may exist. A signed waiver (E) does not authorize ignoring a physician's restriction.

Scenario 7. An experienced pregnant athlete is frustrated that her workouts are 'too easy' and wants to chase a new back-squat PR before she gets too far along. How should you frame the conversation?

  1. A. Agree and program a heavy 1RM attempt this week while she still feels strong.
  2. B. Reframe the goal: during pregnancy success is maintaining strength, stamina, and flexibility, controlling weight gain, and preparing for childbirth — not setting PRs — and keep heavy/max-effort lifts off the list.
  3. C. Tell her goals don't matter and just have her do whatever she feels like.
  4. D. Switch her entirely to walking so there's no chance of any hard effort.
  5. E. Tell her to keep her heart rate under 140 and otherwise max out.
Show answer

Answer: B — The article explicitly redefines the goal during pregnancy toward maintenance and birth prep and removes heavy or max-effort lifts ('too many things can go wrong'), so the coach resets expectations accordingly (B). A programs a contraindicated max attempt. C abandons coaching. D over-restricts a capable, cleared athlete. E mixes the outdated HR cap with a max-out instruction that contradicts the no-max-effort guidance.

Scenario 8. While de-scaling a workout for a mid-pregnancy athlete whose belly is now large, which set of substitutions best matches the article's toolkit?

  1. A. Sit-ups → GHD sit-ups; pull-ups → kipping pull-ups; squats → below-parallel squats.
  2. B. Squats → squat-to-box (sit to a box and stand); pull-ups → ring rows; sit-ups → knees-to-elbows; push-ups → elevated/incline push-ups; barbells → dumbbells.
  3. C. Add 'for time' scoring to every workout and keep all barbell movements as prescribed.
  4. D. Replace running and rowing with box jumps and rope climbs to keep variety.
  5. E. Remove all aerobic work and program only heavy singles.
Show answer

Answer: B — These are the article's exact substitutions — squat-to-box, ring rows, knees-to-elbows, elevated push-ups, and dumbbells for barbells as the belly grows — preserving stimulus while reducing risk (B). A reintroduces GHD sit-ups and below-parallel squatting, both contraindicated. C adds the 'for time' pressure the article removes. D swaps safe engines for fall-risk movements. E eliminates beneficial aerobic work and adds heavy singles.

Scenario 9. It's a hot summer day and a pregnant athlete is grinding through a long metcon and sweating heavily. What is the most important coaching priority specific to her?

  1. A. Push her to finish fast so she's done before she overheats.
  2. B. Keep her well hydrated and prevent her core temperature from getting too high (above ~102°F), since overheating risks CNS abnormalities in the baby; slow the pace and reduce density as needed.
  3. C. Tell her to keep her heart rate over 150 to maximize the training effect.
  4. D. Have her lie on her back to cool down between rounds.
  5. E. Ignore the heat since heart rate, not temperature, is the only real concern.
Show answer

Answer: B — Core temperature above ~102°F can cause CNS abnormalities in the baby, so hydration and heat management are real programming constraints — slow down and reduce density (B). A trades one risk (overheating) for another (rushing/over-exertion). C pushes intensity that risks hypoxia. D puts her supine, risking vena cava compression. E is backwards — the article flags core temperature, not a heart-rate number, as the heat-related concern.

D2 · Programming 14% of exam Confidence tier: ___

CFJ_Platek_IWCABTAMD_March2011.pdf

PDF link not yet available

Why this is on the reading list

This article is the empirical backstop for CrossFit's operational definition of fitness — 'increased work capacity across broad time and modal domains' (IWCABTAMD) — the exact phrase the exam expects you to use when defining fitness and evaluating whether a program is working. Platek et al. analyze repeat-posted scores on four benchmark WODs (Fran, Angie, Cindy, CrossFit Total) and show statistically significant improvement over time, independent of age, sex, and how often the athlete saw the specific workout. For a CCFT, the value is not the statistics; it is the logic of using benchmark retests as objective, quantified evidence that programming is producing GPP — which is exactly what Domain 2's evaluation tasks (2.3.1–2.3.4) and quantify-and-track task (1.2.6) ask you to do.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 2.1.2 Design a sequence of workouts that improves general physical preparedness (GPP)
  • 2.3.1 Evaluate program success relative to athlete goals and needs
  • 2.3.2 Use benchmarks to assess effectiveness of programming
  • 2.3.3 Adjust programming based on performance and goals
  • 2.3.4 Evaluate athlete progress relative to CrossFit's definition of fitness and their personal goal
  • 1.2.2 Evaluate athlete's work capacity
  • 1.2.6 Quantify and track performance
  • 1.2.5 Identify when athlete is ready to progress to another goal/skill
  • 3.1.8 Teach the CrossFit definition of fitness and health and the four models illustrating it
  • 3.1.9 Teach the goals of CrossFit programming and how goals are met (programming with variance)

What to focus on while reading

  • The expansion and exact meaning of IWCABTAMD: 'increased work capacity across broad time and modal domains' — note this IS the operational definition of fitness, and 'work capacity' is the measurable variable the whole study tracks.
  • Why anecdote is insufficient: the 'he ran 1.6 miles after six weeks' story is contrasted with the need for tracked progress over time across many athletes. Highlight the move from N=1 anecdote to a larger data-driven demonstration.
  • The four benchmark WODs used as the measuring stick and exactly what each measures: Fran (21-15-9 thrusters + pull-ups, scored as time), Angie (scored as time), Cindy (scored as rounds/reps in a fixed time, an AMRAP), CrossFit Total (scored as total load — back squat + press + deadlift).
  • How each benchmark's score is the metric: faster time = more work capacity for Fran/Angie; more rounds = more work capacity for Cindy; heavier total load = more capacity for CrossFit Total. Different modal/time domains, same underlying construct.
  • The headline finding: performance improved significantly over repeated time points for all four benchmarks (Fran times dropped, Angie improved, Cindy rounds increased, CrossFit Total loads went up).
  • The three 'independent of' claims and why they matter for a coach: improvement was NOT correlated with (1) the athlete's age, (2) how frequently they encountered that specific WOD, and largely not (3) sex (only CrossFit Total showed the expected large sex gap in absolute load). Variance, not WOD-specific practice, drove the gains.
  • The honest limitations the authors flag: small effect sizes (time accounted for only ~8–15% of variance), no scientific control, no nutrition tracking, no movement correction, reliance on self-reported scores, possible false posts (self-serving attribution bias), possible non-CrossFitters in the sample, and attrition (data limited to first 3–4 posts).
  • What the authors say accounts for the OTHER ~85–92% of variance: pre-CrossFit fitness, sex, age, nutrition, and dedication — plus a hypothesized hormonal mechanism (upregulation of the HPA and HPG axes).
  • Their stated next step: collaborate with affiliates running Paleo/Zone nutrition challenges, using pre/post benchmark WODs and morphological measurements (weight, waist, body-fat %) and photos — a real-world template for how a coach documents program effectiveness.
  • The repeated-measures design logic in plain terms: the SAME athletes were retested across time, so improvement reflects within-person change — exactly the model a coach uses when re-running a benchmark on the same client months later.

Concepts to understand

  • Fitness operationally defined as work capacity across broad time and modal domains — and that 'increased work capacity' is the thing you are trying to produce and the thing you measure to prove the program worked.
  • Benchmark (named) WODs function as standardized, repeatable tests: because the workout is fixed, re-running it later isolates the athlete's change in fitness, making it a valid before/after measuring stick for program evaluation.
  • The difference between a result that feels real (anecdote, N=1) and a result demonstrated across many athletes over time — and why a coach should ground claims of progress in tracked, retested data rather than a single good day.
  • Reading a score correctly per benchmark: for time-based WODs lower is better; for AMRAPs more rounds/reps is better; for load tests heavier is better. Improvement direction depends on how the WOD is scored.
  • Variance over many time/modal domains is the point: gains showed up across a sprint-couplet (Fran), a longer monostructural+gymnastics test (Angie), a bodyweight AMRAP (Cindy), and a max-strength test (CrossFit Total) — evidence of GPP, not specialization.
  • Improvement independent of WOD frequency means the broad, constantly varied program — not drilling the test itself — produced the gains; 'training the test' is not what made athletes better, supporting CrossFit's anti-specialization programming logic.
  • Improvement independent of age (within this adult sample) and largely independent of sex supports scaling the SAME program across a mixed class rather than fundamentally different programs by demographic.
  • Effect size literacy for coaches: a statistically significant result can still be small (here ~8–15% of variance), so 'it works' and 'it explains most of the outcome' are different claims; nutrition, sleep, baseline fitness, and adherence carry much of the rest.
  • Confounders and why uncontrolled real-world data is weak evidence: no control group, self-reported scores, possible dishonest or non-CrossFitter posts, and attrition all limit how strongly you can attribute change to the program.
  • The practical evaluation loop this models: establish baseline on benchmarks → run the program → retest the same benchmarks → compare → attribute improvement to the program only after accounting for obvious confounders → adjust programming accordingly.
  • Why a coach pairs performance retests with health/morphological markers (weight, waist, body-fat %) — performance data alone misses body-composition and health change, so good program documentation tracks both.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenarios where an athlete or skeptic asks 'how do we know this is working?' and you must choose the answer grounded in re-testing benchmark WODs and tracking quantified scores over time (2.3.2, 1.2.6) rather than relying on feel or a single PR. You may be asked to pick the best evidence that a program is producing fitness as CrossFit defines it — increased work capacity across broad time and modal domains (2.3.4, 3.1.8) — or to recognize that improvement on a broad, varied program (not drilling one test) is what demonstrates GPP (2.1.2, 3.1.9). Other items test judgment about limitations: distinguishing 'statistically improved' from 'fully explained,' or recognizing that nutrition, sleep, and adherence — not just training time — drive results, so the coaching response is to address those too (2.3.3).

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

IWCABTAMD
'Increased Work Capacity Across Broad Time And Modal Domains' — CrossFit's operational, measurable definition of fitness; the more work you can do, faster, across many movement types and workout durations, the fitter you are.
Work capacity
The total amount of work (force x distance, or load moved) an athlete can perform in a given time; the core variable CrossFit programming aims to increase and that benchmark retests measure.
Broad time and modal domains
Across many workout durations (short sprints to long efforts) and many movement modalities (weightlifting, gymnastics, monostructural/cardio); fitness shows up everywhere, not in one specialty.
Benchmark WOD
A named, standardized workout (e.g., Fran, Angie, Cindy, CrossFit Total) repeated periodically so an athlete's change in score over time is an objective measure of changing fitness.
Fran
21-15-9 reps of 95-lb thrusters and pull-ups, for time; a short, high-intensity benchmark scored by completion time (lower = fitter).
Cindy
An AMRAP (as many rounds as possible) in a fixed time of 5 pull-ups, 10 push-ups, 15 air squats; scored by number of rounds/reps (more = fitter).
CrossFit Total
A max-strength benchmark scored as the combined best single lift of the back squat, shoulder press, and deadlift; total load (heavier = stronger/fitter).
General physical preparedness (GPP)
Broad, non-specialized fitness across all capacities; improvement on several different benchmarks at once is evidence that a program is building GPP rather than one narrow skill.
Repeated-measures (within-subject) design
Testing the same athletes at multiple time points so observed change reflects each person's own improvement; the logic behind re-running a benchmark on the same client later.
Statistical significance
A result unlikely to be due to chance (here p < .05); it indicates a real difference exists but says nothing about how large or meaningful that difference is.
Effect size
How much of the outcome a factor actually explains; here training time explained only ~8–15% of the variance in performance, meaning the effect was real but small.
Variance
The spread in outcomes across athletes; the study could attribute only a small share of performance variance to time, leaving most to factors like nutrition, baseline fitness, and adherence.
Confounding variable
An untracked factor (nutrition, sleep, pre-CrossFit fitness, movement quality) that influences the outcome and clouds whether the program alone caused the change.
Self-serving attribution bias
The tendency to report flatteringly — here, athletes possibly posting falsely fast times — a data-honesty threat in self-reported performance logs.
Attrition
Drop-off in participants over time; here posting fell sharply after the first few entries, limiting the analyzable data to athletes' first three to four posts.
HPA / HPG axes
Hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal and -gonadal hormonal systems; the authors hypothesize training upregulates these as a partial physiological mechanism behind improved capacity (unproven here).
Morphological measurements
Body measurements such as weight, waist circumference, and body-fat percentage, taken alongside benchmark scores to document body-composition change, not just performance change.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. A member who has trained consistently for four months says, 'I feel fitter, but how do we actually know your program works?' Which response best reflects how CrossFit defines and demonstrates fitness?

  1. A. 'Trust the process — everyone here gets results, so you will too.'
  2. B. 'Let's re-run a couple of benchmarks you did at the start — your Fran time and your CrossFit Total — and compare. Improvement across different tests is objective evidence your work capacity went up.'
  3. C. 'Step on the scale; if your weight dropped, the program is working.'
  4. D. 'Just check whether you can do the most recent WOD faster than the people next to you.'
  5. E. 'Fitness is subjective, so feeling better is really the only measure that matters.'
Show answer

Answer: B — B operationalizes fitness as increased work capacity across broad time and modal domains and uses repeated benchmark testing on the SAME athlete to demonstrate it objectively (2.3.2, 2.3.4, 1.2.6) — exactly the article's method. A is faith, not evidence. C tracks one body-composition marker, which misses performance/work-capacity entirely. D compares to other athletes rather than the athlete's own baseline. E abandons CrossFit's measurable definition of fitness.

Scenario 2. You want to show a new athlete's progress with the strongest possible evidence using benchmarks. Which approach best mirrors the study's design logic?

  1. A. Compare her current Fran time to the gym's all-time fastest Fran.
  2. B. Record her scores on Fran, Cindy, and the CrossFit Total now as a baseline, then retest the same benchmarks after a block of training and compare her own before/after.
  3. C. Ask her at the end of each class whether she felt the workout was hard.
  4. D. Only retest the one workout she practices most, since that is where she will improve fastest.
  5. E. Average everyone's scores in class today and tell her where she ranks.
Show answer

Answer: B — B is a within-subject (repeated-measures) before/after across multiple modal domains — the article's exact method and the soundest way to attribute change to the program (1.2.6, 2.3.1). A and E benchmark against other people, not her own baseline. C is subjective, not quantified. D 'trains the test'; the study specifically found improvement was independent of WOD frequency, so isolating one practiced workout is both weaker evidence and not how GPP is demonstrated.

Scenario 3. The article reports improvement was statistically significant but that training time explained only about 8–15% of the variance in performance. A coach should take this to mean:

  1. A. The program does not actually work and the gains were random.
  2. B. The program produces real, measurable gains, but most of the outcome is driven by other factors — nutrition, sleep, baseline fitness, and adherence — so a coach should address those too.
  3. C. Effect size is irrelevant as long as the result is statistically significant.
  4. D. Athletes should drill the benchmark workouts more often to raise the effect size.
  5. E. Only elite athletes will see any benefit from the program.
Show answer

Answer: B — B correctly separates 'statistically real' from 'fully explanatory': a small effect size means the training effect is genuine but modest, with much of performance owed to confounders the authors name (nutrition, sex, age, pre-CrossFit fitness, dedication). This is the coaching cue to manage lifestyle factors, not just programming (2.3.3, Domain 6 lifestyle). A misreads significance. C dismisses effect size, which is exactly what tells you how much the program explains. D again confuses test-practice with fitness. E is unsupported.

Scenario 4. A skeptic argues 'these athletes only got faster at Fran because they kept doing Fran over and over.' Based on the study's findings, the best evidence-based counterpoint is:

  1. A. 'You're right — repetition of the specific workout is the main driver, which is why we test it often.'
  2. B. 'Improvement was independent of how frequently athletes encountered that specific WOD and showed up across four different benchmarks, which points to broad, constantly varied training building general fitness — not drilling one test.'
  3. C. 'It doesn't matter why they improved as long as the numbers went up.'
  4. D. 'The sample was all elite athletes, so the result can't be questioned.'
  5. E. 'Age and sex fully explain the differences, not the training.'
Show answer

Answer: B — B uses the article's specific finding — no correlation between WOD frequency and performance gains, and improvement across Fran, Angie, Cindy, and CrossFit Total — to argue the broad varied program produced GPP rather than test-specific practice (2.1.2, 3.1.9, 2.3.4). A concedes the opposite of what the data showed. C dodges the question. D is false (mixed adult sample, not elite). E contradicts the finding that gains were largely independent of age and sex.

Scenario 5. You're designing how your affiliate will document the results of an upcoming 8-week nutrition challenge so you can honestly claim it worked. Which plan best follows the article's recommended template and accounts for confounders?

  1. A. Take a single 'after' Fran time at the end and post it as proof.
  2. B. Before and after the challenge, record benchmark WOD scores plus morphological measurements (weight, waist, body-fat %), keep the training program consistent so nutrition is the main thing that changed, and compare each athlete to their own baseline.
  3. C. Ask members to self-report whether they think they got fitter.
  4. D. Only measure body weight before and after, since nutrition mainly affects weight.
  5. E. Compare this year's challenge group to a different group of members from two years ago.
Show answer

Answer: B — B mirrors exactly what the authors describe for affiliate nutrition challenges — pre/post benchmark WODs plus morphological measurements, same-subject comparison — and improves attribution by holding the training program constant so the nutrition variable is isolated (2.3.1, 2.3.3, 1.2.6, plus Domain 6). A is a single uncontrolled data point. C is subjective. D captures only one marker and ignores performance/work capacity. E introduces a non-equivalent historical comparison group, a classic confound.

Scenario 6. An athlete improved her Cindy from 14 to 17 rounds but her Fran time got slower over the same period. How should a coach interpret this for evaluating the program against CrossFit's definition of fitness?

  1. A. The program failed because one benchmark got worse.
  2. B. Look at the pattern across multiple modal/time domains and context (sleep, the workout preceding the test, recovery); a single slower benchmark does not by itself overturn broad evidence of rising work capacity, but it flags something to investigate and possibly adjust.
  3. C. Ignore the Fran result entirely since Cindy improved.
  4. D. Conclude she should stop doing Fran so it can't drag down her data.
  5. E. Switch her to a specialized program for whichever benchmark she likes most.
Show answer

Answer: B — B reflects the article's multi-domain logic (the authors even noted the workout preceding a Fran can affect the score) and the coaching tasks of evaluating progress across broad domains and adjusting programming (2.3.3, 2.3.4, 1.2.2). One down-data-point among several up-data-points is a prompt to investigate confounders (fatigue, what preceded the test, recovery), not a verdict. A overreacts to a single test; C cherry-picks; D and E abandon broad GPP for test-management or specialization, the opposite of CrossFit's model.

D2 · Programming 14% of exam Confidence tier: ___

CFJ_Pregnancy_Christensen_Table_5.pdf

PDF link not yet available

Why this is on the reading list

The CCFT Content Outline explicitly names pregnant athletes as a special population a trainer must be able to scale for (2.2.2). This article is a movement-by-movement scaling table that shows the reasoning behind each modification — preserving the metabolic/stimulus intent of a workout while protecting the pregnant athlete from movements that become unsafe or uncomfortable as pregnancy advances. The exam will not ask you to recall a specific substitution from memory; it will give you a coaching scenario (a pregnant athlete at month X, a given workout) and ask for the best scaling decision, which is exactly the applied judgment this article trains.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 2.2.2 Scale for special populations (e.g., pregnant, adaptive)
  • 2.2.5 Scale by skill level
  • 2.1.1 Design single workouts using the CrossFit methodology (preserve intended stimulus when scaling)
  • 5.2.2 Apply scaling to meet current physical and psychological needs of each athlete
  • 5.2.3 Manage risk for the athlete
  • 1.1.2 Recognize conditions outside CCFT scope that require referral (e.g., medical clearance for pregnancy)
  • 6.2.4 Recognize scope-of-practice limitations

What to focus on while reading

  • The governing principle stated repeatedly: scale to PRESERVE the intended stimulus (tax the same metabolic pathway / reproduce the same breathing pattern), not just to make the movement easier.
  • For running: the three low-impact substitutes (sled drag/push, row 500 m, AirBike 0.4-0.6 mi) and the instruction to adjust weight/distance so she works for ABOUT THE SAME TIME as the run would take.
  • For double-unders: jumping is often the FIRST thing to become uncomfortable; substitutes (singles, 8-kg KB swings for half the reps, AirBike 15 s per 15 DUs) are chosen to reproduce the BREATHING pattern.
  • For rowing: by ~7 months, limited ROM/stroke length kills the metabolic response — note the cues (shorten catch, knees out, raise damper to 7+) and the option to substitute sled or running.
  • For kettlebell swings: increased pulling on the front of the body/pelvis as the belly grows; reduce with Russian swings to eye level + a major focus on contracting the abdominals; scale to KB deadlifts or GHD hip extensions/good mornings if dynamic movement bothers her.
  • The squat and deadlift LOAD GUIDELINE: no more than 70% of pre-pregnancy 1-rep max for all loading past 3-5 months; the athlete should not be straining excessively; sub rep schemes (e.g., 5x5 instead of a 1RM attempt).
  • Deadlift-specific cue: use a sumo stance once the belly interferes with the thighs.
  • Olympic lifts: scale load, scale ROM (lift from the hang), use dumbbells, switch to the POWER version and add a squat (power clean + front squat instead of squat clean) if a dynamic squat reception is uncomfortable — and that some athletes simply won't pass a barbell by the belly (personal comfort).
  • Pull-ups: kipping creates a 'tug' on the stomach and, past 3-4 months, raises the risk of DIASTASIS RECTI — sub strict pull-ups (1 strict for every 3 kipping), ring rows, seated/low-bar rows; note ring rows are described as potent and not to be underestimated.
  • The hard rule on midline FLEXION: eliminate sit-ups, GHD sit-ups, toes-to-bars, knees-to-elbows after the first trimester, and ANY similar midline-flexion movement once 'coning' of the stomach is seen.
  • The visual sign 'coning' (the middle of the stomach forms a little mountaintop) as the trigger to stop flexion work — the goal is to let the abdominals separate at a natural pace and favor midline STABILIZATION over flexion.
  • Flexion substitutes that stabilize instead of flex: plank hold, sideways walking plank (~20 ft per 20 sit-ups), side planks.
  • Box jumps are 'similar to running' — jarring/uncomfortable; scale box height, step-ups, or weighted step-ups to a lower height with reps cut in half.
  • Handstand push-ups: largely personal choice (some are fine inverted); substitutes are strict HSPU, seated DB press, barbell strict/push press, and a single-leg eyes-closed DB press for balance and full-body tension while pressing overhead.
  • The recurring theme that pregnancy scaling is INDIVIDUAL and comfort-driven: phrases like 'personal choice,' 'modify according to the athlete's preference,' 'bothers some while others experience no discomfort' appear throughout — there is no one-size answer.
  • The progression of WHEN things change: first trimester (eliminate midline flexion), 3-4 months (diastasis risk, drop kipping), 3-5 months (70% 1RM cap), ~7 months (rowing loses stimulus) — note the timeline because scenarios will specify a month.

Concepts to understand

  • Scaling preserves stimulus, not just safety: the right substitution keeps the same energy-system demand or movement intent (same work time for a run, same breathing for double-unders) while removing the unsafe/uncomfortable element.
  • Pregnancy is a 'special population' under 2.2.2 — the trainer must be able to modify any movement on demand, and the decision is driven by the stage of pregnancy AND the individual athlete's comfort, not a fixed rulebook.
  • Midline flexion is the central contraindication: once coning appears (typically after the first trimester), flexion movements (sit-ups, T2B, K2E, GHD sit-ups) are replaced with stabilization holds (planks) to protect the linea alba and allow natural abdominal separation.
  • Diastasis recti risk is the reason kipping and heavy flexion are removed past ~3-4 months; the coach manages this risk proactively rather than waiting for a problem.
  • Impact and 'jarring' movements (running, box jumps, double-unders/jumping) become uncomfortable and are swapped for low-impact equivalents (sled, erg, AirBike, step-ups) that keep the metabolic demand.
  • Load is capped, not eliminated: ~70% of pre-pregnancy 1RM past 3-5 months, with 'no excessive straining' as the felt cue — and rep schemes are adjusted (sub a 5x5 for a 1RM) rather than chasing maxes.
  • Range-of-motion accommodations (sumo deadlift once belly interferes, lifting from the hang, shortened row stroke with knees out) let a movement continue as the body geometry changes.
  • When a scaled movement no longer delivers its purpose (e.g., rowing produces no metabolic response by 7 months), abandon it for one that does (sled/run) — keep the GOAL, change the tool.
  • Athlete preference and psychological comfort are legitimate programming inputs: some women pass a barbell by the belly with no issue, others won't — the coach modifies to the individual, which is the heart of 5.2.2.
  • Knowing common scale targets per movement: run -> sled/row/AirBike; DUs -> singles/KB/AirBike; KB swing -> Russian swing/KB deadlift/GHD hip ext; pull-up -> strict/ring row; flexion -> planks; box jump -> step-up; HSPU -> seated/standing press.
  • Recognize the boundary between coaching and medicine: monitoring comfort and scaling movements is in scope; clearing a pregnancy for exercise, diagnosing diastasis, or overriding a physician's guidance is not.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenario items that name a pregnant athlete at a specific stage and a specific movement or workout, then ask for the best scaling action — these test 2.2.2 and 5.2.2 directly. Some items will hinge on a single trigger (coning seen -> stop flexion; past 3-4 months -> drop kipping due to diastasis risk; load capped at ~70% 1RM past 3-5 months), while others test the deeper principle of preserving stimulus (choosing a sled drag for the same work-time as a run, picking the substitute that reproduces double-under breathing). A few may probe risk management and scope (1.1.2, 6.2.4): the best answer keeps the athlete training while deferring medical decisions to her physician.

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Coning (doming)
A visible ridge or 'mountaintop' that forms down the midline of the belly during effort — the trigger to STOP sit-ups, toes-to-bars, GHD sit-ups and other midline-flexion work so the abdominals can separate naturally.
Diastasis recti
Separation of the two halves of the rectus abdominis (the 'six-pack' muscle) along the midline; the risk of worsening it is why kipping and heavy flexion are removed past about 3-4 months of pregnancy.
Midline flexion vs. midline stabilization
Flexion bends the trunk forward (sit-up, T2B, K2E); stabilization holds the trunk rigid (plank). During pregnancy, replace flexion with stabilization.
Preserving the stimulus
Scaling so the modified movement still hits the workout's intended demand — same metabolic pathway, same work duration, or same breathing pattern — rather than just making it easier.
70% 1RM guideline
A loading cap used past 3-5 months of pregnancy: keep working loads at no more than ~70% of the athlete's pre-pregnancy one-rep max, with no excessive straining.
Russian swing (to eye level)
A kettlebell swing finished at about eye height rather than overhead; reduces front-of-body/pelvic pull while keeping the hip-hinge stimulus.
Sumo deadlift stance
A wide stance with hands inside the knees; used in pregnancy once the belly interferes with the thighs in a conventional pull.
Power version (Olympic lift)
Catching the bar above a full squat (power clean/power snatch); used when a dynamic deep-squat reception is uncomfortable, optionally adding a separate front squat to keep the squat work.
Ring row
A horizontal body-row on gymnastic rings — described as a potent, often underestimated scale for pull-ups during pregnancy.
Sideways walking plank
Travelling horizontally in a plank position (about 20 ft per 20 sit-ups) as a challenging, flexion-free substitute for sit-ups.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • 'Coning'/doming of the belly during any movement = immediate signal to eliminate that movement and all midline flexion; do not push through it.
  • Past ~3-4 months, kipping movements raise diastasis recti risk — switch to strict; do not let a pregnant athlete keep kipping just to keep the rep count.
  • Past 3-5 months, do not program working loads above ~70% of pre-pregnancy 1RM, and an athlete straining excessively under load is a stop signal.
  • Clearing a pregnancy for exercise, diagnosing diastasis recti, or overriding a physician is OUTSIDE CCFT scope (1.1.2, 6.2.4) — require/respect medical clearance and defer medical questions to her doctor.
  • Pain, a 'tug' on the stomach, or any new discomfort is the athlete's cue and the coach's cue to modify immediately — pregnancy scaling is comfort-driven and individual, never forced.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. A 5-months-pregnant athlete is cleared to train. Today's workout has '5 rounds for time: 400-m run.' She says running now feels jarring and uncomfortable. What is the best scaling decision?

  1. A. Tell her to run anyway since she's cleared, just at an easy pace
  2. B. Replace each run with a sled drag (or row/AirBike), adjusting weight/distance so each effort takes about the same time the 400-m run would
  3. C. Cut the workout to 2 rounds and keep the runs
  4. D. Replace the runs with max-effort sit-ups to keep the metabolic demand
  5. E. Have her sit out the metcon entirely
Show answer

Answer: B — The goal is to preserve the metabolic stimulus while removing the impact: a sled/row/AirBike taxes the same pathway, and matching the work TIME keeps the intended dose. A ignores her discomfort and the impact concern. C needlessly cuts volume instead of substituting. D introduces midline flexion, which is the opposite of what pregnancy scaling wants. E removes her from training unnecessarily.

Scenario 2. During a workout, you notice the middle of a pregnant athlete's belly forms a visible ridge or 'mountaintop' as she does toes-to-bars. What should you do?

  1. A. Nothing — coning is normal and harmless during exercise
  2. B. Add weight to make her brace harder
  3. C. Stop the toes-to-bars and replace midline-flexion work with stabilization holds such as planks or side planks
  4. D. Switch her to GHD sit-ups for a fuller range of motion
  5. E. Tell her to finish the set but slow down
Show answer

Answer: C — 'Coning' is the article's explicit trigger to eliminate sit-ups, toes-to-bars, GHD sit-ups and any similar midline FLEXION, replacing them with stabilization (planks) so the abdominals separate at a natural pace and to limit diastasis risk. A is false — coning is the warning sign. B and E push through the exact movement to avoid. D is also a flexion movement and is specifically to be eliminated.

Scenario 3. A pregnant athlete at about 4 months has been doing kipping pull-ups and reports a 'tug' on her stomach. What is the most appropriate scale?

  1. A. Keep kipping but reduce the total reps by half
  2. B. Move to strict pull-ups (banded if needed, ~1 strict for every 3 kipping) or ring rows
  3. C. Switch to GHD sit-ups to train the same muscles
  4. D. Have her do butterfly pull-ups since they are more efficient
  5. E. Tell her pull-ups are now unsafe and remove all pulling
Show answer

Answer: B — Past ~3-4 months, kipping raises diastasis recti risk and the 'tug' is a clear signal; the article prescribes strict pull-ups (1 strict per 3 kipping) or potent horizontal options like ring rows. A keeps the kipping that's causing the problem. C is flexion work, not pulling, and is contraindicated. D is still a kip. E over-restricts — strict pulling is encouraged, not banned.

Scenario 4. A 5-rep-max back squat day is programmed. Your pregnant athlete is in her second trimester (about 4-5 months) and cleared to lift. How should you guide her loading?

  1. A. Let her chase a true 1-rep max since squatting under load is fine
  2. B. Remove all squatting and substitute air squats only
  3. C. Keep her loaded but cap working weight around 70% of her pre-pregnancy 1RM, adjust depth/load for comfort, and avoid excessive straining
  4. D. Have her squat to a fixed competition depth regardless of comfort
  5. E. Replace squats with heavy sit-ups for core strength
Show answer

Answer: C — The article allows loaded squats but uses a guide of no more than ~70% of pre-pregnancy 1RM past 3-5 months, adjusts depth and load for comfort, and avoids excessive straining (subbing a 5x5 for a max). A ignores the load cap and the no-straining cue. B over-restricts when loading is permitted. D forces depth against comfort. E adds contraindicated flexion.

Scenario 5. Squat-clean triplet is on the board. Your pregnant athlete enjoys barbell cycling but says receiving the clean in a deep squat now feels uncomfortable with her belly. Best modification?

  1. A. Tell her to keep doing squat cleans to maintain her skill
  2. B. Switch her to power cleans (catch above the squat) and, if needed, add a front squat so she keeps the squat work — e.g., power clean + front squat
  3. C. Remove the barbell and give her toes-to-bars instead
  4. D. Have her clean from the hang at her usual heavy load to a full squat
  5. E. Skip the lifting portion and send her to the rower for the whole session
Show answer

Answer: B — The article's Olympic-lift guidance is to scale the dynamic squat reception by going to the POWER version and optionally adding a squat (power clean + front squat) when a deep dynamic catch is uncomfortable. A ignores her stated discomfort. C drops the lift for a contraindicated flexion movement. D keeps the deep catch that's the problem. E needlessly removes the lifting stimulus when a clean modification exists.

Scenario 6. An athlete who is about 7 months pregnant is assigned a 500-m row for metcon. She reports she can row but gets 'no metabolic response' because her stroke is so short. What is the best coaching move?

  1. A. Tell her rowing is the prescribed movement, so keep rowing as written
  2. B. Have her row 1,000 m instead to compensate
  3. C. Cue a shorter catch with knees pushed out and raise the damper, and if she still can't get a response, substitute a sled pull/push or running (if she's still running)
  4. D. Replace the row with GHD sit-ups
  5. E. Give her a max-load deadlift set instead
Show answer

Answer: C — The article notes that by ~7 months limited ROM/stroke length kills the metabolic response; the fixes are technical (shorten catch, knees out, raise damper to 7+) and, if those fail, substitute a sled or running so the stimulus is actually delivered. A keeps a movement that no longer works. B just adds volume to an ineffective movement. D introduces contraindicated flexion. E abandons the metabolic intent for a heavy lift.

Scenario 7. A new member tells you she is 8 weeks pregnant and wants to start CrossFit at your gym. Which response best fits a CCFT trainer's scope and the article's spirit?

  1. A. Tell her exercise is unsafe during pregnancy and she should wait until after delivery
  2. B. Diagnose whether she has diastasis recti before letting her train
  3. C. Welcome her, confirm she has (or obtains) medical clearance, then individualize scaling by stage and comfort — substituting impact and midline-flexion work as pregnancy progresses
  4. D. Put her through the standard prescribed class with no modifications to see how she handles it
  5. E. Prescribe specific prenatal medical guidelines and supplement dosages
Show answer

Answer: C — The in-scope move is to keep her training with individualized, stage-appropriate scaling driven by comfort, while deferring medical clearance and diagnoses to her physician. A is false and over-restrictive. B and E cross into medical practice (diagnosis, prenatal medical/supplement guidance) outside CCFT scope. D ignores the need to scale impact and flexion for a pregnant athlete.

Scenario 8. A workout calls for 50 double-unders. Your pregnant athlete finds jumping uncomfortable. Which substitution best preserves the intended stimulus?

  1. A. Have her rest until the jumping portion passes
  2. B. Replace double-unders with sit-ups for the same rep count
  3. C. Use singles, or 8-kg kettlebell swings for half the reps, or AirBike (~15 s per 15 double-unders) to reproduce the breathing pattern
  4. D. Add a weighted vest so fewer reps are needed
  5. E. Switch her to a 1-rep-max snatch
Show answer

Answer: C — Jumping is often the first thing to become uncomfortable; the article's substitutes (singles, 8-kg KB swings for half the reps, or AirBike intervals) are chosen specifically to reproduce the breathing/metabolic pattern of double-unders. A removes the stimulus. B swaps in contraindicated flexion. D adds load and impact, the opposite of the intent. E abandons the metabolic piece for a heavy lift.

D2 · Programming 14% of exam Confidence tier: ___

CFJ_Simmons_Conjugate.pdf

Open the PDF on Google Drive →

Why this is on the reading list

This article is on the CCFT reading list as a primary source on programming theory: it explains the conjugate system, the principle of accommodation, and the use of varied stimuli to drive continuous adaptation — ideas that directly underpin CrossFit's own commitment to constant variation and to designing sequences of workouts that build general physical preparedness. It backs Domain 2 (Programming), especially the design of GPP-developing sequences (2.1.2), the management of accommodation through variance, and the use of intensity-zone control (Prilepin-style volume regulation). A CCFT candidate is not expected to coach powerlifting or implement Westside; the value is understanding WHY variance defeats staleness and HOW to regulate volume and intensity so adaptation continues, then applying that judgment to CrossFit class programming.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 2.1.2 Design a sequence of workouts that improves general physical preparedness (GPP)
  • 2.1.1 Design single workouts using the CrossFit methodology
  • 2.3.2 Use benchmarks to assess effectiveness of programming
  • 2.3.3 Adjust programming based on performance and goals
  • 2.3.1 Evaluate program success relative to athlete goals and needs
  • 1.2.4 Monitor athlete for signs of over- or under-training
  • 2.2.3 Scale for athletes with sport-specific goals
  • 3.1.9 Teach the goals of CrossFit programming and how goals are met (programming with variance)
  • 3.1.10 Teach the relationship between technique and intensity (threshold training)

What to focus on while reading

  • The definition of 'accommodation' — Simmons states it plainly: when you use the same routine over and over, you fail to make progress. Highlight this; it is the conceptual spine of the whole article and the bridge to CrossFit's constant variation.
  • The remedy for accommodation: a planned ROTATION of exercises, both small (assistance) and large (core lifts), cycled in and out of the plan. Note that variance here is deliberate and structured, not random.
  • The two parent systems Westside fuses: the Soviet system (many special exercises to advance superior athletes) and the Bulgarian system (near-max lifts performed every workout). Note Westside takes the variety from one and the daily-max philosophy from the other.
  • The contrast Simmons draws with the 'progressive gradual overload' / block periodization model — divided into time blocks, each working a single element. He calls it a 'dead-end street' and observes he peaked a week or two BEFORE or AFTER a meet but seldom ON meet day. Capture WHY a single-element block model under-delivers.
  • The science claim: training at 90% or above for 3 weeks causes physical and mental fatigue. This is the rationale for switching the core barbell exercise each week — note the link between sustained high intensity and accumulated fatigue.
  • The role of the pendulum wave (credited to Verkhoshansky, 1964) — waving volume and intensity in cycles (3 weeks for speed/explosive strength, 2 weeks for strength-speed) rather than holding a constant load.
  • Prilepin's contribution: regulating the NUMBER of reps and sets at a given intensity zone — i.e., calculating volume per intensity zone, and recognizing it is wasteful to do too many reps at a given intensity. This is the quantitative core of intelligent loading.
  • The max-effort method vs. the dynamic (speed/explosive) method — two distinct stimuli. Max-effort works to a top single 'according to level of preparedness'; the dynamic method develops explosive strength.
  • The 72-hour recovery spacing: a severe workout can be repeated every 72 hours, and 72 hours separate a speed day from a max-effort day for the same lift. Highlight this as a concrete recovery-management rule.
  • The 'level of preparedness' / autoregulation idea: a Westside max effort is the MOST one is capable of THAT day — it may not be an all-time record. This is daily readiness-based loading, not a fixed percentage off a 1RM.
  • The Bulgarian volume contrast: ~4,000 max lifts/year based on the day's strength vs. Westside/Soviet ~600 all-time-record lifts/year. Note the tradeoff and Simmons' judgment that the Westside frequency is 'more practical.'
  • That special bars (front squat, safety-squat bar, max squat) each produce a DIFFERENT max, so the same %/reps/sets yields the same bar speed but different absolute volume each week — variety built into the loading itself to avoid overusing one loading pattern.
  • The results list at the end (elite totals, big squats/benches/deadlifts) — read it as the BENCHMARK evidence Simmons offers that the system works; note he explicitly invites comparison of outcomes between gyms.
  • The required-reading list (Bompa, Zatsiorsky, Siff/Supertraining, Verkhoshansky, etc.) — signals this is a theory-grounded methodology, not anecdote; useful for the professional-development mindset.

Concepts to understand

  • Accommodation: the biological law that a constant stimulus produces a diminishing response. Understand it well enough to explain to a member why repeating the same workout stalls progress and why CrossFit's constant variation exists to prevent exactly this.
  • Variance as the antidote to accommodation: progress is sustained by rotating the stimulus (movements, loads, modalities, time domains). Be able to apply this to designing a sequence of CrossFit workouts that keeps adaptation moving rather than letting the body settle.
  • Conjugate / concurrent development: training multiple qualities (e.g., maximal strength AND explosive strength) in parallel within the same training period, rather than isolating one quality per block. Connect this to CrossFit's goal of broad, general, inclusive fitness developed simultaneously across capacities.
  • Periodization models compared: block/linear 'progressive gradual overload' (one element per block) vs. wave/pendulum periodization (oscillating volume and intensity). Understand the practical failure mode Simmons describes — peaking off-schedule and stalling — and why varied loading addresses it.
  • Intensity-zone volume management (Prilepin's table, in principle): there is an optimal amount of work at each intensity zone; too little under-stimulates and too much wastes the athlete. Apply the judgment — match reps/sets to the intensity used.
  • Maximal-effort method: working to a top single based on the day's preparedness to develop absolute strength and the ability to recruit. Recognize it as one specific high-intensity stimulus.
  • Dynamic / speed-strength method: moving submaximal loads with maximal speed to develop rate of force development and explosive strength — a different stimulus serving a different quality.
  • Autoregulation / 'level of preparedness': loading the day's session to what the athlete can actually do today, not to a rigid percentage. Connect to CrossFit's relative-intensity and scaling logic — meet the athlete where they are on a given day.
  • Recovery spacing as a programming variable: the 72-hour rule shows that frequency, not just content, is programmed. Apply to how often a class re-loads the same movement pattern or energy system.
  • Benchmarking to validate programming: Simmons uses measured competitive results to prove the system works. Connect to CrossFit's use of benchmark workouts (named WODs, retests) to evaluate whether programming is producing adaptation.
  • Specificity within variety: assistance/special exercises are chosen to eliminate specific weaknesses while the rotation keeps the overall stimulus fresh — variance is purposeful, targeted at gaps, not arbitrary.
  • Transfer of principle, not protocol: the candidate's job is to extract the underlying training laws (accommodation, variance, intensity-zone volume, autoregulation) and apply them to CrossFit programming — NOT to import a powerlifting template into a CrossFit class.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenario questions that hand you a coaching/programming situation and ask for the best decision. A member who has plateaued after running the same lifts/WODs for weeks tests whether you recognize accommodation and prescribe variance (2.1.2, 2.3.3). A question about why CrossFit programs with constant variation tests the conjugate/accommodation rationale (3.1.9). Items may probe volume-at-intensity judgment — recognizing that piling reps at a high percentage wastes the athlete — and the difference between max-effort and speed-strength stimuli. Autoregulation ('train to today's capacity') maps onto relative intensity and readiness monitoring (1.2.4, 3.1.10), and using measured results to judge a program maps onto benchmarking (2.3.1, 2.3.2). The throughline: apply the principle, do not memorize Westside specifics.

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Conjugate system
A training approach that develops several qualities at once by rotating many exercises (large core lifts plus smaller special/assistance exercises) within the same period, rather than training one element at a time.
Accommodation
The drop-off in results that happens when the body is exposed to the same training stimulus repeatedly; the same routine done over and over stops producing progress.
Special (assistance) exercises
Supplemental movements rotated in and out of the plan to target and eliminate specific weaknesses while keeping the overall stimulus varied.
Unidirectional loading
Selecting a rotation of exercises all aimed at advancing one main outcome (e.g., a bigger squat); variety in the movements, single direction in the goal.
Progressive gradual overload (block/linear periodization)
The older model that divides training into time blocks, each devoted to a single element; Simmons criticizes it as a 'dead-end' that often leaves the athlete peaking before or after — not on — the target day.
Pendulum / wave periodization
A plan that oscillates (waves) volume and intensity across short cycles instead of holding load constant; credited to Verkhoshansky and used at Westside in roughly 3-week (speed/explosive) and 2-week (strength-speed) cycles.
Maximal-effort (max-effort) method
Working up to the heaviest single you can manage that day, based on current preparedness, to build absolute strength; at Westside it need not be an all-time record, just the day's best.
Dynamic (speed-strength) method
Lifting submaximal loads as fast as possible to develop explosive strength and rate of force development; the second stimulus paired with the max-effort method.
Prilepin's recommendations
Guidelines for how many reps and sets to perform at a given intensity zone, so volume is matched to intensity and the athlete isn't worked uselessly hard at a percentage.
Level of preparedness (autoregulation)
Loading the session to what the athlete is actually capable of on that specific day rather than to a fixed percentage of a one-rep max.
GPP (General Physical Preparedness)
The broad base of fitness — a wide range of physical capacities — that a varied program builds; in CrossFit, the explicit goal of programming across modalities and time domains.
Soviet system
Training model using many special exercises to advance the development of superior athletes; one of the two parents of Westside conjugate.
Bulgarian system
Training model in which near-maximal lifts are performed in nearly every session, based on the day's strength rather than fixed percentages; the other parent of Westside conjugate.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • This is a competitive powerlifting methodology built for advanced lifters maxing repeatedly; do NOT prescribe near-daily maximal singles or a Westside template to general CrossFit members — that mismatch raises injury and overtraining risk. Take the PRINCIPLE (variance, intensity-zone volume, autoregulation), not the protocol.
  • Sustained training at 90%+ for ~3 weeks is stated to cause physical and mental fatigue — recognize this as an over-training warning sign and a cue to vary or deload (ties to 1.2.4).
  • Maxing 'to the day's preparedness' still requires sound mechanics first; high intensity layered on poor technique is a safety problem (mechanics-consistency-intensity), not a programming nuance.
  • Programming heavy loading and high frequency must respect recovery (the 72-hour spacing) and individual readiness; ignoring recovery to chase the system's volume is a risk-management failure.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. A 35-year-old member who has done the exact same strength session — 5x5 back squat at the same load — three days a week for two months tells you her squat hasn't moved in weeks and she feels flat. Based on the principle Simmons emphasizes, what is the BEST programming response?

  1. A. Keep the program identical but tell her to try harder and add more sets at the same weight.
  2. B. Recognize accommodation to a constant stimulus and introduce planned variance — rotate movements (e.g., front squat, tempo squat, box squat), vary loads and rep schemes, and add targeted accessory work.
  3. C. Have her max out a heavy single every session for the next month to force progress.
  4. D. Tell her plateaus are normal and no change is needed.
  5. E. Switch her entirely to a single-element block focused only on high-rep squatting for eight weeks.
Show answer

Answer: B — Her stalled progress under an unchanging stimulus is textbook accommodation; the remedy Simmons describes is a planned rotation of varied stimuli. A doesn't change the stimulus. C imports near-daily maxing — an advanced-lifter protocol that is inappropriate and risky here. D ignores a solvable problem. E is the single-element block model Simmons criticizes as a 'dead-end' and abandons variance.

Scenario 2. A member asks, 'Why does CrossFit keep changing the workouts every day instead of letting me master one program?' Which explanation best reflects the training principle this article supports?

  1. A. Variety keeps classes entertaining so members don't get bored.
  2. B. Constantly varied stimuli prevent accommodation — the body stops adapting to a stimulus it sees repeatedly — so variance is what keeps adaptation and broad fitness (GPP) progressing.
  3. C. Changing workouts daily guarantees every member hits a personal record every day.
  4. D. Variety means technique never has to be refined because no movement repeats.
  5. E. Frequent change lets the coach avoid having to program intensity or recovery.
Show answer

Answer: B — The article's core law is accommodation: a repeated stimulus yields diminishing returns, so deliberate variance sustains adaptation and builds general physical preparedness. A is a side benefit, not the mechanism. C overstates outcomes. D is false — movements do recur and technique is continually refined. E misframes variance as an excuse to skip programming fundamentals.

Scenario 3. While programming a strength piece, you're deciding how much work to do at a heavy intensity. A newer coach suggests, 'Just have them keep doing sets at 90% until they're exhausted.' Drawing on Prilepin's contribution as Simmons describes it, what is the soundest approach?

  1. A. Match the number of reps and sets to the intensity zone, because there is an optimal volume at each intensity and piling on reps at a high percentage is wasteful and fatiguing.
  2. B. Always do the maximum possible reps at every intensity to maximize volume.
  3. C. Ignore intensity zones entirely and program purely by how the athlete feels.
  4. D. Only ever train at low intensity to be safe.
  5. E. Keep load and reps identical every single session indefinitely.
Show answer

Answer: A — Simmons credits Prilepin with regulating reps and sets per intensity zone and explicitly notes it is a waste of time to do too many reps at a given intensity — volume should be matched to intensity. B is the exact error being corrected. C discards a useful quantitative guide. D needlessly forfeits the strength stimulus. E reintroduces the constant loading that drives accommodation.

Scenario 4. An advanced member wants to keep working a heavy squat but you notice that after three weeks of consistently heavy (90%+) work she's irritable, sleeping poorly, and her bar speed has dropped. Consistent with the article, what should you do?

  1. A. Read these as accumulated physical and mental fatigue from sustained high intensity, vary the stimulus and reduce load, and manage recovery before pushing again.
  2. B. Add a fourth and fifth heavy day to break through.
  3. C. Tell her to keep grinding the same heavy work; fatigue means it's working.
  4. D. Have her test an all-time-record max immediately to see where she stands.
  5. E. Conclude she's simply undertrained and double the weekly volume at 90%+.
Show answer

Answer: A — Simmons states that training at 90%+ for about three weeks causes physical and mental fatigue — the signs described. The response is to vary the stimulus, back off the load, and protect recovery (over-training monitoring, 1.2.4). B, C, D, and E all add high-intensity load on top of an already fatigued athlete, escalating injury and burnout risk.

Scenario 5. Two athletes show up for a heavy day. One slept well and feels strong; the other is run down from a hard week. Using Westside's 'level of preparedness' idea, how should you handle the day's top set?

  1. A. Require both to hit the same fixed percentage of their one-rep max regardless of how they feel.
  2. B. Let each work up to the most they can handle WELL today — the day's best for that athlete — which may differ from an all-time record, while holding mechanics standards.
  3. C. Make both attempt an all-time personal record because that's the only number worth counting.
  4. D. Cancel the heavy work for both since one is tired.
  5. E. Have the tired athlete go heaviest to 'toughen up.'
Show answer

Answer: B — A Westside max effort is the most the athlete can do that day according to preparedness — daily autoregulation, not a rigid percentage. That lets the fresh athlete push and the fatigued athlete train appropriately, with sound mechanics as the gate. A ignores readiness. C and E court injury by forcing maximal loads onto a tired lifter. D needlessly scraps training the prepared athlete could do safely.

Scenario 6. You want to know whether your eight-week strength cycle actually worked. Which approach is most consistent with how Simmons judges the conjugate system's success?

  1. A. Re-test relevant benchmarks (e.g., a known strength lift or named workout) and compare measured results before and after to see if performance improved.
  2. B. Assume it worked because the athletes showed up and seemed to enjoy it.
  3. C. Judge success only by how sore the athletes got each session.
  4. D. Decide it worked if the programming looked varied on paper.
  5. E. Avoid measuring anything so athletes don't feel pressured.
Show answer

Answer: A — Simmons validates Westside with measured competitive outcomes and explicitly invites comparison of results between gyms — i.e., benchmarking. Re-testing and comparing objective performance is the same logic applied to CrossFit (2.3.1, 2.3.2). B, C, and D rely on proxies that don't establish adaptation, and E removes the measurement needed to evaluate the program at all.

Scenario 7. A coach proposes building the gym's whole quarter as a strict linear block: four weeks of only endurance, then four weeks of only strength, then four weeks of only power, each quality in isolation. What concern from this article should you raise?

  1. A. None — isolating one quality per block is exactly what Simmons recommends.
  2. B. Simmons criticizes the single-element block model as a 'dead-end' and favors developing qualities concurrently with waved, varied loading; isolating one element per block risks detraining the others and the off-schedule peaking he describes.
  3. C. The only problem is that the blocks are too short; make each one twelve weeks.
  4. D. Strict isolation blocks are required by CrossFit's definition of fitness.
  5. E. The blocks should all be run at 90%+ intensity the entire time.
Show answer

Answer: B — Simmons explicitly rejects the 'progressive gradual overload' block approach (one element per block) as a dead-end and builds Westside on concurrent, conjugate development with waved loading — which aligns with CrossFit's broad, simultaneous development of capacities. A and D misstate his position. C doesn't fix the isolation problem and lengthens detraining of the neglected qualities. E ignores his own warning that sustained 90%+ work for three weeks breeds fatigue.

D2 · Programming 14% of exam Confidence tier: ___

ijspt-12-697.pdf

Open the PDF on Google Drive →

Why this is on the reading list

This clinical commentary gives the CCFT candidate the physiological and programming backbone for two things the exam tests hard in Domain 2: how to bias a workout toward a specific energy system using duration, intensity, and work-to-rest ratios, and how to keep an injured athlete fit while progressively rebuilding capacity without re-injuring them. It backs 2.1.1 (designing single workouts), 2.2.4 (programming for injured athletes to maintain fitness and restore functionality), and 2.3.2 (using benchmarks/monitoring to assess programming effectiveness). The acute:chronic workload ratio it teaches is the single most exam-relevant tool here: it is a concrete, low-cost way to quantify whether an athlete has trained enough to handle the next jump in load — directly the logic a coach uses to decide when and how fast to progress.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 2.1.1 Design single workouts using the CrossFit methodology
  • 2.1.2 Design a sequence of workouts that improves general physical preparedness (GPP)
  • 2.2.3 Scale for athletes with sport-specific goals
  • 2.2.4 Design programming for injured athletes to maintain fitness and restore functionality
