  • 2.3.2 Use benchmarks to assess effectiveness of programming
  • 2.3.3 Adjust programming based on performance and goals
  • 1.2.2 Evaluate athlete's work capacity
  • 1.2.4 Monitor athlete for signs of over- or under-training
  • 1.2.5 Identify when athlete is ready to progress to another goal/skill
  • 1.2.6 Quantify and track performance
  • 5.2.3 Manage risk for the athlete
  • 5.2.6 Recognize warning signs for possible injury or overexertion
  • 7.4.1 Work within CCFT Scope of Practice

What to focus on while reading

  • The three metabolic pathways named explicitly: phosphagen (ATP-PCr), glycolytic (anaerobic glycolysis), and oxidative (aerobic). Note WHICH one dominates at WHICH duration/intensity — this is the core of Table 1.
  • Table 1 (Energy System Demands): memorize the duration-to-system map as a CONCEPT, not numbers to recite — 0–6 s maximal = phosphagen; 6–30 s near-maximal = phosphagen + anaerobic glycolysis; 30–120 s high = anaerobic glycolysis; 2–3 min moderate = anaerobic + aerobic glycolysis; >3 min low = oxidative.
  • Why pure endpoint sports (Olympic lifting, 100 m sprint, marathon) are EASY to classify but team sports are HARD — because real activity spans all three systems and uses intermittent on/off effort.
  • The principle that energy systems are NOT on/off switches — all three contribute simultaneously; only their RELATIVE contribution shifts with task. This is the single most testable conceptual point.
  • Repeated Sprint Ability (RSA): the ability to repeat near-maximal efforts with limited fatigue. Note that the aerobic system, which supplies <10% of a single sprint, can supply up to ~49% across repeated sprints — i.e., aerobic fitness drives recovery between hard efforts.
  • Table 2 (Chamari & Padulo classification): three practical buckets — Explosive Efforts (up to 6 s, e.g., 3–5 s work : 60–120 s rest), High-Intensity Efforts (6 s to 1 min, e.g., 30 s : 30 s), Endurance Efforts (>1 min, e.g., 3 min : 3 min). This is a coach-friendly alternative to physiology jargon.
  • The nine manipulable training variables (Table 3): work-interval intensity, work-interval duration, modality, recovery intensity, recovery duration, number of series, series duration, time between series, between-series recovery intensity. Understand that changing any one of these changes the training stimulus.
  • Modality substitution logic: bike/row can replace running when running is contraindicated by injury — you keep the energy-system stimulus while protecting the healing tissue. This is the heart of 'train around the injury.'
  • The RTP progression sequence for modality and intensity: bike → linear running → change-of-direction running → open-environment skill work; and longer rest intervals → sport-specific (shorter) rest intervals. Note that intensity, modality, AND rest all progress.
  • RPE / CR-10 scale (Table 7): 0 = rest up to 10 = maximal; this is the low-cost intensity-prescription and monitoring tool when HR/GPS isn't available.
  • Session RPE (sRPE) = CR-10 rating × session duration in minutes = an arbitrary internal training-load number. This is the affordable load-quantification method to actually remember and apply.
  • Timing of sRPE collection: classically 20–30 min post-session, but newer evidence (boxers at 10 vs 30 min; resistance training at 15 vs 30 min) shows little difference — so it's practically usable even when you can't keep the athlete around.
  • External vs internal load: EXTERNAL = what the athlete DID (distance, weight lifted, total volume, work:rest you prescribed); INTERNAL = how they RESPONDED (HR, RPE). A coach plans external and monitors internal.
  • The acute:chronic workload ratio: acute = most recent week's load; chronic = rolling 4-week average; ratio = acute ÷ chronic. >1 means this week exceeded recent norms.
  • The risk thresholds: rugby athletes exceeding an acute:chronic ratio of 2.11 had ~3.4x greater injury risk. In the worked example, ratio is flagged YELLOW above 1 and RED above 2.
  • The paradox worth understanding: high CHRONIC workload can be protective (it builds tolerance), but SPIKES in acute load (a high acute:chronic ratio) are what drive injury risk. Fitness is built by loading; injury comes from loading too fast.
  • Task-based vs time-based RTP: Herrington's argument that clearing an athlete on defined PERFORMANCE goals beats clearing them on healing TIMEFRAMES alone. Connect this to CrossFit's measurable-performance ethos.
  • Where the coach's authority ends: 'medically cleared,' StARRT risk assessment, and the multi-disciplinary RTP team (physician, PT, ATC) — these are referral/scope boundaries, not the trainer's call.

Concepts to understand

  • Energy-system specificity by duration and intensity: given a target adaptation, you choose work duration, intensity, and rest to bias the dominant pathway — short maximal efforts with long rest train the phosphagen system; 30–120 s hard efforts with incomplete rest tax glycolysis; sustained >3 min low-intensity work trains the oxidative system.
  • All three energy systems run concurrently — you never train 'only' one. Programming shifts the RELATIVE contribution. A coach who treats them as isolated switches will mis-prescribe.
  • Work-to-rest ratio as the primary programming lever: the SAME exercise becomes a different stimulus depending on rest. 5 s sprint : 2 min rest = phosphagen/power; 30 s : 30 s = glycolytic/'high-intensity'; 3 min : 3 min = mixed/endurance. This is exactly how CrossFit varies interval pieces.
  • Aerobic base supports anaerobic output: better aerobic fitness speeds recovery (PCr resynthesis, lactate clearance) BETWEEN hard efforts, so even power/team athletes need some oxidative conditioning to sustain repeated intensity. Don't over-program long slow distance for power athletes, but don't neglect aerobic capacity either.
  • Repeated Sprint Ability as a model for CrossFit conditioning: most CrossFit metcons ARE intermittent near-maximal efforts — RSA logic (repeat hard efforts with limited fatigue) maps directly onto 'increased work capacity across broad time and modal domains.'
  • Training the injured athlete to MAINTAIN fitness: rehabilitation is not detraining. You substitute modalities to preserve the energy-system stimulus and biomotor abilities the athlete will lose if they simply rest, then re-develop what was lost — directly task 2.2.4.
  • Progressive, planned loading: you advance modality (low-impact → sport-specific), intensity (sub-maximal → maximal), and rest (long → sport-specific) in a deliberate sequence rather than all at once — the applied version of mechanics → consistency → intensity for a returning athlete.
  • Quantifying load cheaply with sRPE: when you lack HR/GPS, RPE × duration gives a single number per session you can chart over time — this is how a real gym tracks whether an athlete is doing more or less work week to week.
  • Acute:chronic workload ratio as a progression-and-safety gauge: it operationalizes 'has this athlete trained enough to handle what's next?' Keep the ratio in a moderate range; flag spikes; build chronic load gradually so the athlete tolerates future demand.
  • Monitoring distinguishes under- from over-training: tracking load lets you increase OR decrease daily stress deliberately, so the athlete improves consistently without being over- or under-exposed — directly tasks 1.2.4 and 2.3.3.
  • Benchmarks/measurement drive program adjustment: charting load and performance over time turns programming from guesswork into a feedback loop — the data is the discussion point for whether to push or pull back (task 2.3.2/2.3.3).
  • Needs analysis precedes prescription: you match the conditioning to the demands the athlete will actually face (the sport, position, level) — in CrossFit terms, to the athlete's goals and the demands of life/competition — before selecting durations, intensities, and modalities.
  • Task-based readiness over calendar-based readiness: progress and clearance should hinge on demonstrated performance/capacity, not merely elapsed time — reinforcing CrossFit's measurable, repeatable, observable standard for deciding when to progress.
  • Internal vs external load distinction: plan the external load (modality, volume, intensity, work:rest), then read the internal response (RPE/HR) to confirm the athlete absorbed it as intended; a mismatch (high RPE for planned-easy work) is a signal to adjust.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenario items that hand you an athlete goal or a piece of a workout and ask you to pick the work-to-rest structure that trains the intended energy system — e.g., 'to develop maximal-power repeatability, which interval is best?' tests Table 1/Table 2 logic under task 2.1.1. Injured-athlete vignettes (running contraindicated, athlete bored/detraining) will test 2.2.4: the best answer substitutes a modality that preserves the stimulus, not 'rest until healed.' Monitoring vignettes will give you a load trend or an acute:chronic spike and ask whether to progress, hold, or deload — mapping to 1.2.4, 2.3.3, and risk management 5.2.3/5.2.6, where the safe answer recognizes that a sharp load spike, not high overall fitness, is the injury driver. Watch for scope items where 'medically cleared' or RTP decisions belong to the medical team, not the trainer (7.4.1).

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Phosphagen system (ATP-PCr)
The fastest energy pathway; uses stored ATP and phosphocreatine to fuel all-out efforts of roughly 0–6 seconds. Very high power output but very limited capacity — it fuels a heavy single lift or a short sprint, then needs rest to recharge.
Glycolytic system (anaerobic glycolysis)
The intermediate pathway; breaks down glucose/glycogen without oxygen to fuel hard efforts of about 30 seconds to 2 minutes. Higher capacity than the phosphagen system but produces fatiguing by-products that limit how long it can run.
Oxidative (aerobic) system
The endurance pathway; uses oxygen to produce ATP for efforts longer than ~3 minutes and to recover between hard bouts. Lowest rate of energy supply but essentially unlimited capacity.
Repeated Sprint Ability (RSA)
The capacity to perform repeated maximal or near-maximal efforts with brief recovery and minimal drop-off in performance — the on/off effort pattern that characterizes team sports and most CrossFit metcons.
Work-to-rest ratio
The relationship between effort duration and recovery duration in an interval (e.g., 30 s work : 30 s rest). Adjusting it changes which energy system a workout trains even if the exercise stays the same.
Rating of Perceived Exertion (RPE) / CR-10 scale
A 0–10 self-report scale (0 = rest, 10 = maximal) used to prescribe and monitor how hard an effort feels — an affordable substitute for heart-rate or power measurement.
Session RPE (sRPE)
A single internal-load number for a whole session, calculated as the CR-10 rating multiplied by session duration in minutes. Charted over time, it tracks how an athlete's training load rises and falls.
External training load
What the athlete actually did — distance run, weight lifted, total volume, prescribed work:rest. It is what the coach PLANS for a session.
Internal training load
How the athlete responded to the work — measured by heart-rate response or RPE. It is what the coach MONITORS to confirm the session landed as intended.
Acute load
The athlete's most recent week of training load — a snapshot of current stress.
Chronic load
The rolling four-week average of training load — a measure of the fitness/tolerance the athlete has built up over time.
Acute:chronic workload ratio
Acute load divided by chronic load. Around or below 1 means this week is in line with recent training; well above 1 signals a spike that raises injury risk (flagged 'red' above 2 in the article's example).
Return-to-play (RTP) continuum
The staged transition from injury to full competition, generally moving through protecting tissue, guiding healing, and restoring strength/energy-system capacity — a multi-disciplinary process.
StARRT framework
Strategic Assessment of Risk and Risk Tolerance — a return-to-play decision model that weighs health risk, activity risk, and the athlete's risk tolerance to decide readiness.
Task-based vs time-based RTP
Two ways to decide readiness: time-based clears an athlete after a healing timeframe; task-based clears them after they meet defined performance goals. Task-based is argued to be superior because it is measurable and performance-driven.
Needs analysis
An assessment of the specific physical demands an athlete must meet (sport, position, level of play) used to target the right energy systems, modalities, intensities, and work:rest in their program.
Detraining
The loss of fitness adaptations that occurs when training stops or drops too far — the outcome conditioning during rehab is designed to prevent.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • Energy-system training is within a trainer's lane, but 'medical clearance' and return-to-play decisions are not — those belong to the physician/PT/athletic-trainer team. A coach who 'clears' an injured athlete to return is acting outside CCFT scope of practice (7.4.1).
  • Diagnosing, treating, or rehabilitating an injury is outside scope — the trainer's role is to train AROUND a known, professionally-managed injury (maintain fitness via safe modalities), not to rehab the injured tissue itself. Refer out (1.1.2).
  • A spiking acute:chronic workload ratio (and especially the ~2.11 threshold tied to ~3.4x injury risk) is a programming warning sign to slow down and deload — ignoring a load spike and pushing intensity is a risk-management failure (5.2.3, 5.2.6).
  • Reading a returning or progressing athlete's high RPE for planned-easy work, or a sudden jump in session load, as a cue to back off — over-exposing an athlete to load they aren't prepared to tolerate invites injury (1.2.4).

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. An athlete's goal is to repeat short, maximal-power efforts (think heavy sled pushes or short sprints) with full power each time. Based on the energy-system and work-to-rest logic in this article, which interval structure best targets that quality?

  1. A. 5 seconds of all-out work followed by 5 seconds of rest, repeated continuously
  2. B. 5 seconds of all-out work followed by 60–120 seconds of rest, for several sets
  3. C. 3 minutes of hard work followed by 3 minutes of rest
  4. D. 20 minutes of continuous moderate-pace work
  5. E. 30 seconds of hard work followed by 30 seconds of rest
Show answer

Answer: B — Maximal-power repeatability relies on the phosphagen (ATP-PCr) system, which is fast but has limited capacity and needs long recovery (~60–120 s) to fully resynthesize PCr — matching the article's 'Explosive Efforts' bucket (up to 6 s work : 60–120 s rest). A is too little rest, so power collapses after the first effort. C and E shift the stimulus toward glycolytic/mixed work. D trains the oxidative system. Only B preserves full-power output across repeats.

Scenario 2. A recreational athlete in your gym tears a calf muscle; their physical therapist says running is contraindicated for now but cleared them for low-impact cross-training. The athlete is anxious about losing the conditioning they built. What is the best programming response within your scope?

  1. A. Have them fully rest until the PT clears running, to avoid any risk
  2. B. Keep their running intervals but cut the intensity in half
  3. C. Substitute a low-impact modality such as the bike or rower at matched work-to-rest ratios to preserve the energy-system stimulus while protecting the healing tissue
  4. D. Begin a rehab protocol for the calf so they heal faster
  5. E. Tell them conditioning can't be maintained during injury and to focus only on upper-body lifting
Show answer

Answer: C — Task 2.2.4 is exactly this: program for the injured athlete to MAINTAIN fitness without aggravating the injury. The article's core move is modality substitution — bike/row replaces running when running is contraindicated, keeping the conditioning stimulus while the tissue heals. A causes needless detraining. B still loads the contraindicated movement. D is outside the trainer's scope (rehab belongs to the PT). E is false — conditioning CAN be maintained via substitution.

Scenario 3. You are tracking a returning athlete's training with session RPE (RPE × minutes). Their four-week average (chronic) load is about 3,300, and this week's (acute) load jumps to roughly 6,900 — an acute:chronic ratio above 2. What is the most appropriate action?

  1. A. Keep increasing load — a high number means high fitness, which protects against injury
  2. B. Pull back and plan lower-load sessions to let the load spike dissipate before progressing further
  3. C. Ignore it; sRPE is too subjective to base decisions on
  4. D. Immediately stop all training for two weeks
  5. E. Add a maximal-effort test day to confirm they can handle the load
Show answer

Answer: B — An acute:chronic ratio above 2 is the article's 'red' flag — a load SPIKE associated with sharply higher injury (and re-injury) risk (rugby athletes above 2.11 had ~3.4x the risk). The correct response is the one modeled in the paper's example: notice the spike and schedule lower-load weeks so accrued fatigue dissipates before pushing again. A confuses chronic fitness (protective when built gradually) with an acute spike (the actual risk). C dismisses a validated low-cost tool. D over-reacts and causes detraining. E adds MORE load at exactly the wrong moment.

Scenario 4. A coach wants to monitor whether athletes are doing more or less work week to week but the gym has no heart-rate straps or GPS units. Which approach is both affordable and supported by this article?

  1. A. Estimate load from how the athletes look at the end of class
  2. B. Require everyone to buy GPS units for accurate external-load data
  3. C. Multiply each athlete's CR-10 session RPE by the session duration in minutes and chart that number over time
  4. D. Use only the prescribed weights on the whiteboard as the load measure
  5. E. Skip monitoring — it requires expertise most coaches don't have
Show answer

Answer: C — Session RPE (CR-10 rating × duration in minutes) is the article's headline low-cost method for quantifying internal training load and charting it over time — it requires no expensive technology and is validated against heart-rate-based TRIMP measures. A is too vague to track trends. B is the costly option the article explicitly works to avoid. D captures only one slice of external load (and not the conditioning response). E is wrong — the whole point is that sRPE makes monitoring accessible to any coach.

Scenario 5. Which statement best reflects how the three energy systems should inform your CrossFit programming?

  1. A. Each system is an on/off switch — you train one system per workout and the others shut off
  2. B. Only the phosphagen and glycolytic systems matter for CrossFit; the aerobic system is irrelevant
  3. C. All three systems contribute simultaneously, but their relative contribution shifts with the effort's duration and intensity — so you bias the dominant system through your choice of duration, intensity, and rest
  4. D. The aerobic system is only relevant to marathoners and has no role in high-intensity training
  5. E. Energy-system demands are fixed by the exercise, so changing rest periods doesn't change the training effect
Show answer

Answer: C — The article stresses that the systems work in concert with no distinct on/off switch; only their RELATIVE contributions change with task. You program by biasing the dominant system through duration, intensity, and work-to-rest. A and E contradict this directly. B and D wrongly dismiss the aerobic system — the paper shows aerobic metabolism, while <10% of a single sprint, can supply up to ~49% across repeated sprints and is essential for recovery between hard efforts, which is central to broad CrossFit work capacity.

Scenario 6. An injured athlete is several weeks into return-to-play and has been doing straight-ahead bike and linear running intervals well. The sport (basketball) demands repeated cutting and reactive sprinting. What is the most appropriate next progression?

  1. A. Return them straight to full-contact play since their straight-line conditioning is good
  2. B. Keep them on the bike indefinitely to stay completely safe
  3. C. Progress modality toward change-of-direction running and open-environment skill work, and shift rest intervals toward sport-specific (shorter) ratios
  4. D. Max out their straight-line sprint volume before adding any new movement
  5. E. Hand the decision entirely to the athlete since they know how they feel
Show answer

Answer: C — The article lays out a deliberate progression: bike → linear running → change-of-direction running → open-environment skill work, while rest intervals move from long toward sport-specific. The athlete has earned the next rung — introducing change-of-direction and reactive demands that mirror basketball — not a jump to full play (A, which skips needed steps and is also a medical-clearance decision beyond the trainer's scope). B causes stagnation. D over-loads one quality instead of advancing specificity. E abdicates the coach's programming responsibility.

Scenario 7. Two athletes both perform a workout that, on paper, is the same prescribed external load. Athlete X reports an RPE of 4 (somewhat hard); Athlete Y reports a 9 (almost maximal). How should you interpret this using the internal/external load distinction?

  1. A. The data is contradictory and should be discarded
  2. B. External load is what they did and is identical, but internal load (their response) differs sharply — Y is under more relative stress, a cue to monitor and possibly adjust Y's programming
  3. C. Athlete Y simply has a worse attitude and should be pushed harder
  4. D. RPE is meaningless when the external load is matched
  5. E. Both athletes should be progressed identically next session because the prescription was the same
Show answer

Answer: B — The article separates external load (what the athlete did — the planned modality, volume, intensity, work:rest) from internal load (how they responded — RPE/HR). Identical external load can produce very different internal responses; Y's RPE of 9 signals far greater relative stress, which is a monitoring and adjustment cue (tasks 1.2.4, 2.3.3). A and D dismiss valid signal. C misreads a physiological response as attitude. E ignores that matched prescriptions don't guarantee matched recovery or readiness to progress.
