12_03_Anatomy_Physiology.pdf

Open the PDF on Google Drive →

Why this is on the reading list

This article is on the CCFT reading list because it gives the coach the minimal shared vocabulary needed to teach movement and communicate corrections precisely: four body parts (spine, pelvis, femur, tibia), three joints (knee, hip, SI joint), two motions (flexion/extension), and three biomechanics rules. Effective coaching depends on coach and athlete sharing this terminology, which is the backbone of Domain 3 (Educating) tasks 3.1.1, 3.1.2, 3.1.6, and 3.2.x. It also underpins Domain 4's requirement to apply basic principles of anatomy and biomechanics (4.2.6) and to find the root cause of faults (4.1.6), because it defines 'muted/frozen hip' and the 'pelvis chasing the femur' error that drives many faults.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 3.1.1 Teach proper execution of movements
  • 3.1.2 Layer instruction to meet athlete capability
  • 3.1.3 Use progressions to teach complex moves
  • 3.1.6 Teach descriptive/defining characteristics of functional movements
  • 3.2.1 Demonstrate proper movements
  • 3.2.2 Demonstrate movement faults
  • 4.1.6 Identify root cause of faults
  • 4.2.1 Communicate cues to correct unsound mechanics
  • 4.2.2 Use multiple cueing strategies (visual, tactile, verbal)
  • 4.2.3 Utilize effective cues (short, specific, actionable)
  • 4.2.6 Apply basic principles of anatomy and biomechanics

What to focus on while reading

  • The exact roster the coach asks athletes to learn: FOUR body parts (spine, pelvis, femur, tibia), THREE joints (knee, hip, SI joint), TWO motions (flexion, extension), and THREE biomechanics rules — memorize the counts as an organizing frame, but focus on why each grouping aids communication.
  • Which two parts make up 'the leg' (femur + tibia) and which two make up 'the trunk' (pelvis + spine) — this naming lets a coach cue a whole segment with one word.
  • Each joint and what it connects: knee connects tibia to femur; hip connects femur to pelvis; SI joint connects pelvis to spine. Note the spine is itself 'a whole bunch of joints.'
  • The plain definitions of the two motions: flexion = reducing (closing) a joint angle; extension = increasing (opening) a joint angle. Be able to apply these at any of the four joints.
  • How the coach tests understanding before moving on: athletes must flex/extend leg, hip, spine, and SI joint on cue, then perform combinations ('flex one leg and trunk but not your hip') — this is a teaching-checkpoint method, not trivia.
  • Rule 1 — functional movement 'weds the spine to the pelvis'; the trunk should stay tight and solid (small-range SI/spine movement only) for running, jumping, squatting, throwing, cycling, etc.
  • Rule 2 — the dynamics/power of those movements come from the HIP, primarily hip extension; 'powerful hip extension is necessary and nearly sufficient for elite athletic capacity.'
  • Rule 3 — 'do not let the pelvis chase the femur instead of the spine'; this is the fault called 'muted hip function' / 'frozen hip,' where the hip angle stays open and is powerless to extend.
  • Why the author frames the whole lesson around COACHABILITY — the payoff of a shared lexicon is that athletes become more correctable, faster.
  • The intentional simplicity: spine is shown with a normal 'S' shape; iconography is deliberately basic so any athlete can grasp it (relevant to layering instruction, 3.1.2).

Concepts to understand

  • A shared movement vocabulary is a coaching tool, not academic anatomy: the value of the four-parts/three-joints/two-motions/three-rules system is that it makes communication efficient and athletes more coachable — understand it as the foundation for every cue you will give.
  • Segment naming ('the leg' = femur + tibia; 'the trunk' = pelvis + spine) lets a coach correct a whole region with one short word, supporting the 'short, specific, actionable' cueing standard (4.2.3).
  • Flexion vs. extension as an applied skill: you must be able to instantly classify what a joint is doing and cue the opposite — e.g., recognizing that a rounding lower back is trunk flexion when you want a neutral/tight trunk.
  • The 'trunk stays solid' principle: in functional movements the spine and pelvis move together as one rigid unit; the SI joint and spine are built only for small, multi-directional range — understand this to explain WHY you cue a braced midline.
  • Power originates at the hip via hip extension: understand that strong hip extension is the engine of athletic movement, so faults that block hip extension are the ones that most reduce power and performance.
  • 'Muted hip function' / 'frozen hip' / 'pelvis chasing the femur': understand this as a root-cause fault — when the pelvis follows the thigh instead of staying tied to the spine, the hip angle never closes and then cannot powerfully open (extend). Many visible faults trace back to this.
  • Teaching by checkpoint: confirm an athlete can demonstrate each isolated motion on cue, then combine cues, before progressing — a model for layering instruction (3.1.2) and using progressions (3.1.3).
  • Demonstration of faults as a teaching device: the article models showing both the correct pattern (pelvis and spine together, power from the hip) and the fault (pelvis chasing femur), supporting 3.2.1 and 3.2.2.
  • Anatomy-to-cue translation: understanding the parts/joints lets you diagnose a root cause (4.1.6) and then deliver the matching cue (4.2.1) rather than just naming a symptom.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenario questions where an athlete shows a midline or hip fault and you must pick the correct anatomical interpretation or the best short cue — e.g., identifying that 'pelvis chasing the femur' (muted/frozen hip) is the root cause of a powerless deadlift or jump and choosing to restore hip extension (4.1.6, 4.2.6). Other items test whether you can use the simple lexicon to communicate (3.1.1, 4.2.3): given a beginner who doesn't understand a complex cue, the best answer layers instruction using the trunk/leg, flexion/extension vocabulary (3.1.2). Some questions probe the three rules directly — recognizing that the trunk should stay tight while power comes from hip extension (4.2.6) — framed as judgments an experienced coach makes on the floor, not definitions to recite.

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Trunk
The combined unit of the pelvis and spine; in functional movement it is kept tight and solid so it moves as one piece.
Leg
The combined unit of the femur (thigh bone) and tibia (shin bone).
Spine
The vertebral column, shown with a normal 'S' curve; functionally it is many joints designed for small-range movement in multiple directions.
Pelvis
The hip bone structure connecting the spine (via the SI joint) to the femurs (via the hip joints); part of the 'trunk.'
Femur
The thigh bone; the upper bone of 'the leg,' connecting at the hip above and the knee below.
Tibia
The shin bone; the lower bone of 'the leg,' connecting at the knee.
Knee joint
The joint connecting the tibia and femur.
Hip joint
The joint connecting the femur to the pelvis; the primary source of athletic power through its extension.
Sacroiliac (SI) joint
The joint connecting the pelvis to the spine; built for small range of motion, it should stay stable so the trunk moves as a unit.
Flexion
Reducing (closing) the angle of a joint — e.g., bending the knee or rounding the trunk forward.
Extension
Increasing (opening) the angle of a joint — e.g., straightening the knee or driving the hips open.
Hip extension
Opening the hip angle by driving the pelvis and femur apart; described as necessary and nearly sufficient for elite athletic capacity.
Muted hip function (frozen hip)
A fault in which the pelvis 'chases the femur' instead of staying tied to the spine; the hip angle stays open and is therefore powerless to extend.
Coachability
The intended payoff of the shared lexicon — athletes who know the terms can be corrected more accurately and quickly.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. During a deadlift, a new athlete's hips shoot up first and the bar stalls; on review you see the pelvis tipping and 'following' the thighs while the lower back rounds, and the lockout is weak. Using this article's framework, what is the most accurate root-cause description and your best first correction?

  1. A. The knees are flexing too much; cue 'straighten the legs sooner.'
  2. B. 'Muted/frozen hip' — the pelvis is chasing the femur, so the hip angle stays open and can't powerfully extend; cue to tie the pelvis to the spine and drive hip extension.
  3. C. The athlete lacks grip strength; switch to a lighter bar.
  4. D. The spine is extending too much; cue more trunk flexion.
  5. E. The SI joint is moving through too large a range; cue to mobilize the SI joint.
Show answer

Answer: B — The pelvis following the thigh instead of staying wed to the spine is exactly the 'muted hip function / frozen hip' fault: the hip never closes, so it cannot powerfully extend, killing the lockout. The fix is to keep the trunk (pelvis + spine) solid and restore hip extension. A and C address symptoms unrelated to the described root cause; D is backwards (you want a neutral/solid trunk, not more flexion); E misreads the SI joint, which should stay small-range and stable, not be mobilized.

Scenario 2. A beginner doesn't understand the cue 'maintain a neutral trunk' during squats. Per this article's teaching method, what is the best way to layer the instruction?

  1. A. Repeat the same cue louder until it lands.
  2. B. Skip the concept and just let them squat with whatever back position happens.
  3. C. Teach the simple lexicon first — define 'trunk' as pelvis + spine and demonstrate flexion vs. extension at the trunk — then test that they can flex and extend it on cue before squatting.
  4. D. Give a detailed lecture on vertebral anatomy and intervertebral discs.
  5. E. Cue several corrections at once so they fix everything in one rep.
Show answer

Answer: C — The article's whole point is building a shared, simple vocabulary and confirming understanding before progressing: define the part, demonstrate the motion, test it on cue, then apply it. C does exactly that. A and B abandon teaching; D over-complicates (the lesson is intentionally simple); E violates the layer-and-test approach and overloads the athlete.

Scenario 3. An athlete asks why you keep telling them to 'stay tight through the middle' for running, jumping, and throwing. Which explanation best reflects the article's three biomechanics rules?

  1. A. A tight midline burns more calories during the workout.
  2. B. Functional movement weds the spine to the pelvis; the trunk should stay solid (the SI joint/spine are built only for small-range movement) so that power can be delivered from the hip.
  3. C. A tight trunk increases knee flexion, which is where power comes from.
  4. D. The spine should move through a large range to generate force.
  5. E. Keeping the trunk loose lets the pelvis chase the femur, which is desirable.
Show answer

Answer: B — Rules 1 and 2 together: the trunk (pelvis + spine) stays solid because the SI joint and spine are designed for small range, and the dynamic power comes from the hip. B states this directly. C misattributes power to the knee; D contradicts the small-range principle; E describes the muted/frozen hip fault the article warns against, not a goal.

Scenario 4. You cue an athlete: 'Flex your leg and your trunk, but do not flex your hip.' This combination cue is being used to accomplish what, according to the article?

  1. A. To warm up the cardiovascular system.
  2. B. To confirm the athlete truly understands flexion/extension at each named joint and can control them independently before progressing.
  3. C. To diagnose a torn ligament.
  4. D. To test grip endurance.
  5. E. To measure VO2 max.
Show answer

Answer: B — The article describes giving combination cues like 'flex one leg and trunk but not your hip' specifically as a checkpoint to verify the athlete understands and can control flexion vs. extension at each joint before moving on. The other options are unrelated to the lexicon-comprehension test.

Scenario 5. Two athletes show the same visible deadlift fault. Coach A names anatomy precisely ('your pelvis is chasing your femur — tie it to your spine and open the hip'); Coach B says only 'that looked off, do it better.' Why does the article favor Coach A's approach?

  1. A. Longer cues are always better than short ones.
  2. B. A shared, precise vocabulary makes the athlete more coachable — it lets the coach communicate the exact root cause and the matching correction efficiently.
  3. C. Naming bones intimidates athletes into compliance.
  4. D. Coach A's approach replaces the need for the athlete to ever reach intensity.
  5. E. There is no meaningful difference; both are equally effective.
Show answer

Answer: B — The article's thesis is that a shared terminology renders athletes 'more coachable' by enabling accurate, precise communication of both the fault and the fix. B captures this. A is false (the article values simple, short cues); C and D are not claims the article makes; E ignores the article's central point that vague feedback is far less useful than precise, vocabulary-grounded feedback.

D3 · Educating 19% of exam Confidence tier: ___

41_06_Scoop_Second_Pull.pdf

Open the PDF on Google Drive →

Why this is on the reading list

This article dissects the single most power-dense piece of the Olympic lifts — the scoop (double knee bend) and the second pull — and explains both the mechanics that make it work and the teaching progression CrossFit uses to install the feel. For a domain about Educating, it is a model of how to teach a complex move: reduce the lift to its critical instant, anchor a new posture to one the athlete already owns (the dip of the push-press), and explain WHY the posture matters (compressive vs. shear spinal loading, maximal hip-leg extension). It directly backs teaching proper execution, using progressions to teach complex moves, layering instruction, teaching the defining characteristics of functional movement (a wave of contraction core-to-extremity), and the technique-intensity relationship.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 3.1.1 Teach proper execution of movements
  • 3.1.3 Use progressions to teach complex moves
  • 3.1.2 Layer instruction to meet athlete capability
  • 3.1.6 Teach descriptive/defining characteristics of functional movements
  • 3.1.10 Teach the relationship between technique and intensity (threshold training)
  • 3.2.1 Demonstrate proper movements
  • 3.2.3 Demonstrate movement progressions
  • 4.1.1 Identify points of performance
  • 4.1.6 Identify root cause of faults
  • 4.2.6 Apply basic principles of anatomy and biomechanics
  • 2.2.3 Scale for athletes with sport-specific goals

What to focus on while reading

  • The opening claim: Olympic weightlifters out-leap and out-sprint high-jumpers and sprinters — highlight that the carryover is to ALL explosive sport, not just lifting.
  • The definition of speed-strength as the combination of starting strength (fire many motor units instantaneously) AND explosive strength (keep them firing once on).
  • The sequence of the clean's first pull: a deadlift with shoulders forward of the bar; bar travels along the shin; torso angle of inclination stays CONSTANT off the floor.
  • The trigger for the scoop: it happens 'as the bar passes the knees' — note the cue is positional, not a count.
  • What the scoop actually is: torso rotates to perpendicular WITHOUT elevating the bar, which re-bends the knees — i.e., the 'double knee bend.'
  • The exact launch point of the second pull: 'at the instant the torso is perfectly erect, the hips and legs are violently extended.'
  • The biomechanics payoff: when the torso is perpendicular, spinal forces are ENTIRELY compressive with essentially NO shear — this is the safety argument for the posture.
  • The danger statement: a second pull initiated with the torso forward-inclined could exceed the spine's tolerance to shear — 'It is that powerful.'
  • Why the hook grip exists: the second pull is so forceful that grip cannot be maintained without the thumb trapped by the fingers.
  • The KEY teaching identity: the setup for the second pull (readied by the scoop) is IDENTICAL to the bottom of the dip in the dip-drive-press of the push-press / jerk.
  • The actual progression drill: find the bottom of the push-press dip, then — moving NOTHING but the arms — lower the bar to the hang and back several times to feel the shared hip/leg/torso position.
  • How dip depth is determined: where the athlete can maximally accelerate the bar WITHOUT dropping the chest going up or down — generally about six to eight inches.
  • Glassman's split of CrossFit's 10 fitness components by HOW they're developed: explosiveness/coordination/accuracy/agility/balance via practice (neurological); cardiorespiratory endurance/stamina/flexibility/strength via training (organic) — speed-strength sits in the practice/training overlap.
  • Two coaching implications stated explicitly: (1) when the scoop and second pull 'click,' the performance return can be IMMEDIATE; (2) without the precise neurological stimulus, speed-strength won't fully express.
  • The kettlebell argument: KB snatch/swing/clean are 'first pulls to full extension' — no scoop, no second pull, limited power, because the torso only becomes upright AFTER the hips and legs are already extended.
  • The trajectory point illustrated by Annie's hip trace: in a swing the hip never travels directly upward; in the scoop-and-second-pull it does — the horizontal sweep IS the scoop, the vertical components are the 1st and 2nd pulls.
  • Glassman's prescription for developing the three qualities: lift heavy (dead/squat/bench) for limit strength, kettlebells for aerobic/anaerobic strength endurance, Olympic lifts for explosiveness — different tools, different adaptations.

Concepts to understand

  • WHY the Olympic lifts are the gold standard for developing power: they uniquely train speed-strength via the second pull, and that explosiveness has high carryover to all explosive sport — you should be able to justify programming the lifts for an athlete whose goal is jumping/sprinting/contact-sport power.
  • Speed-strength = starting strength + explosive strength; understand it as a NEUROLOGICAL skill (rate and persistence of motor-unit recruitment), which is why it is a 'learned phenomenon' developed by practice plus training, not by load alone.
  • The mechanical sequence first pull → scoop → second pull as a single chain, and the ability to name what changes at each stage (constant torso angle → torso rotates to vertical while knees re-bend → violent triple extension straight up).
  • The scoop / double knee bend as a repositioning move, not a power move — its job is to deliver the athlete to the correct launch posture (torso vertical) without raising the bar.
  • The vertical-torso requirement as the central safety AND performance principle: vertical = compressive-only spinal loading + maximal available hip-leg extension; forward-inclined at launch = shear risk + leaked power. This is a 'why,' not just a 'what,' and is the kind of biomechanical rationale a coach must be able to explain.
  • Triple extension (ankle, knee, hip) directed vertically as the defining output of the second pull — connect this to the functional-movement idea of explosive, core-to-extremity power production.
  • The teaching transfer principle: anchor a hard-to-feel position (second-pull launch) to a position the athlete already owns (push-press dip). Understand this as a general progression strategy — build the unfamiliar from the familiar.
  • The hang-pull-from-the-dip drill as a concrete progression you could run with a class today, and what specifically it teaches (the shared hip/leg/torso geometry of the dip and the second pull).
  • How to set dip depth by OUTPUT (max bar acceleration with no chest drop) rather than by a fixed number — the ~6–8 inches is a typical result, not a prescription; this is athlete-specific coaching by feel and observation.
  • The development map: which adaptations come from practice (neurological — explosiveness, coordination, accuracy, agility, balance) vs. training (organic — endurance, stamina, flexibility, strength), and why that means you must PRACTICE the Olympic lifts, not just grind them as conditioning.
  • The 'click' and immediacy: motor-learning breakthroughs can yield sudden performance jumps, which shapes how you coach patience and how you recognize readiness to progress.
  • Why kettlebell ballistics (and Swiss ball / Pilates) do NOT substitute for the Olympic lifts for power: the KB line of action makes the torso vertical only after extension, so there is no scoop and no second pull — understand the distinction so you can pick the right tool for a stated goal.
  • Tool-to-goal matching as a programming judgment: heavy slow lifts for limit strength, KB ballistics for strength endurance, Olympic lifts for explosiveness — each develops a different quality and they are not interchangeable.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenarios that ask you to TEACH or PROGRESS the Olympic-lift power positions rather than recite them. A common form: an athlete starts the second pull with the chest forward / bar drifting — the best answer names the root cause (failure to finish the scoop and reach a vertical torso) and gives the correct progression (use the push-press dip to install the launch posture), tying to tasks 3.1.1, 3.1.3, and 4.1.6. Others test the WHY — choosing the explanation that the vertical torso keeps spinal forces compressive and unlocks maximal hip-leg extension (4.2.6) — or test tool selection: which modality to program for an athlete whose goal is vertical jump or sprint speed (2.2.3), where the Olympic lifts, not kettlebell swings, are correct because only the second pull develops speed-strength.

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Speed-strength
The blend of starting strength (firing many muscle units instantly) and explosive strength (keeping them firing once on). It is the neurological quality that lets an athlete produce force FAST, and it is what the second pull develops.
Starting strength
The ability to recruit a large number of motor units instantaneously at the very onset of a movement — the 'off-the-line' component of speed-strength.
Explosive strength
The ability to keep motor units firing once they have been switched on, sustaining force production through the movement.
First pull
The opening phase of the clean — essentially a deadlift with the shoulders set forward of the bar; the bar travels up the shin while the torso's angle of inclination stays constant.
Scoop (double knee bend)
As the bar passes the knees, the athlete rotates the torso to perpendicular WITHOUT raising the bar, which re-bends the knees. It repositions the body into the launch posture for the second pull; it does not itself generate the lift's power.
Second pull
The violent extension of the hips and legs initiated at the instant the torso is perfectly erect, driving athlete and bar directly upward. It is the most powerful and power-dense piece of the Olympic lifts.
Triple extension
Simultaneous extension of the ankles, knees, and hips. In the second pull it is directed vertically, producing the explosive upward power that carries over to jumping and sprinting.
Compressive force vs. shear force
With the torso vertical, spinal loading is purely compressive (along the spine, well tolerated). With the torso forward-inclined under a violent extension, dangerous shear (across the spine) appears — the reason the second pull must launch from a vertical torso.
Dip-drive-press cycle
The mechanics of the push-press / jerk: a short vertical dip, an explosive leg drive, then the press. The bottom of the dip is the SAME hip/leg/torso position as the launch of the second pull — the bridge CrossFit uses to teach it.
Hook grip
A grip in which the thumb is pinned against the bar by the fingers. Because the second pull is so forceful, an ordinary grip slips; the hook grip keeps the bar secured.
Limit strength
Maximal force capacity, developed largely through heavy slow lifting (deadlift, squat, bench). Distinct from speed-strength, which the Olympic lifts develop.
Practice vs. training (development modes)
Glassman's distinction: neurological qualities (explosiveness, coordination, accuracy, agility, balance) are honed by PRACTICE; organic qualities (cardiorespiratory endurance, stamina, flexibility, strength) are built by TRAINING. Speed-strength requires both — so the Olympic lifts must be practiced for skill, not just used as conditioning.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • Initiating the second pull with the torso still forward-inclined creates spinal SHEAR under a very high force — the article explicitly warns the spine may not withstand it. Coaching the vertical-torso launch is a risk-management requirement, not a style preference.
  • Loading the Olympic lifts heavy before the scoop-and-second-pull posture is sound stacks intensity on top of a faulty, shear-loaded position — prioritize the mechanics (vertical torso, finished scoop) before adding load or speed.
  • Treating Olympic lifts purely as metcon fodder ignores that speed-strength is a learned, practiced skill; grinding them fatigued degrades the precise neurological stimulus and the power positions — a movement-quality and injury concern.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. A developing athlete cleans with a chest that pitches forward as he begins the upward drive; the bar swings out and he finishes with hips back. You judge his first pull off the floor as acceptable. What is the BEST coaching priority and tool?

  1. A. Tell him to pull the bar higher and faster off the floor to build momentum into the catch
  2. B. Cue and drill a fully finished scoop so the torso reaches vertical before extension, using the push-press dip to install the launch posture
  3. C. Add load to force a more aggressive hip drive and 'teach' the finish under heavier weight
  4. D. Switch him to kettlebell swings to develop the same explosive hip extension with less complexity
  5. E. Have him widen his grip to reduce the distance the bar must travel
Show answer

Answer: B — The fault is launching the second pull before the torso is vertical — an unfinished scoop. The article's own teaching method is to borrow the push-press dip (an identical hip/leg/torso position the athlete already owns) to install the correct vertical-torso launch (3.1.3, 4.1.6, 4.2.6). A pulls harder on the wrong position; C adds intensity to a shear-loaded fault (a safety error); D abandons the lift — KB swings cannot develop the second pull because the torso only becomes vertical after extension; E does not address the posture.

Scenario 2. An athlete asks WHY you insist the torso be perpendicular to the ground at the moment of explosion in the clean. Which explanation is most accurate and complete?

  1. A. A vertical torso looks more athletic and is what judges score in competition
  2. B. A vertical torso keeps spinal loading purely compressive (essentially no shear) and is the only posture from which maximal hip-leg extension power can be produced
  3. C. A vertical torso shortens the distance the bar travels, which is why it is faster
  4. D. A vertical torso keeps the bar closer to the body so the hook grip can be released earlier
  5. E. A vertical torso reduces how much the knees have to re-bend during the scoop
Show answer

Answer: B — The article makes both points explicitly: at perpendicular torso the spine sees only compressive force (no meaningful shear), and ONLY from that posture can maximum hip-leg extension power be effected. This couples safety and performance (4.2.6, 3.1.10). A is cosmetic; C and D are not the article's rationale; E reverses cause and effect — the scoop's re-bend is what delivers the vertical torso, not the other way around.

Scenario 3. A masters athlete's goal is to improve his standing vertical jump and short-sprint speed for recreational basketball. He currently does only kettlebell swings and steady rowing for 'power.' What programming change is best supported by this article?

  1. A. Keep kettlebell swings as the primary power tool — they train the same explosive hip extension as the Olympic lifts
  2. B. Add Olympic-lift practice (clean/snatch variants) to develop speed-strength via the second pull, since that quality carries over directly to jumping and sprinting
  3. C. Replace everything with heavy deadlifts and back squats, because limit strength is what produces explosiveness
  4. D. Add more steady-state rowing volume to build the aerobic base that underlies jumping power
  5. E. Add Pilates and Swiss-ball work to improve the core stability that limits his jump
Show answer

Answer: B — The article opens with weightlifters out-jumping and out-sprinting other athletes precisely because of the second pull's speed-strength, and states this carries over to all explosive sport (2.2.3, 3.1.6). A is the error the article rebuts — KB swings are 'first pulls to full extension' with no second pull. C develops limit strength, a different quality. D and E target endurance/stability, not explosiveness. Only the Olympic lifts develop the targeted power.

Scenario 4. While teaching the launch position for the second pull to a group, which progression best matches the method described in the article?

  1. A. Have athletes perform several maximal cleans and correct the posture rep by rep as they fatigue
  2. B. Have each athlete find the bottom of the push-press dip, then — moving nothing but the arms — lower the bar to the hang and back repeatedly to feel the shared hip/leg/torso position
  3. C. Have athletes hold a forward-inclined deadlift position and explosively shrug from there
  4. D. Have athletes practice the catch (rack) position first, then work backward to the pull
  5. E. Have athletes jump vertically without a bar until the timing feels explosive, then add the barbell at full weight
Show answer

Answer: B — This is verbatim the article's teaching drill: find the push-press dip, hold the hips/legs/torso fixed, and shuttle the bar between hang and shoulders using only the arms to feel that the dip and the second-pull launch are the same position (3.1.3, 3.2.3). A loads a fault under fatigue; C rehearses the shear-loaded forward position the article warns against; D and E omit the core teaching point — anchoring the launch posture to the already-owned dip.

Scenario 5. A coach claims, 'Explosiveness is just raw strength — if my athletes squat and deadlift heavy enough, the speed-strength will come.' Based on the article's distinction between how qualities develop, what is the best response?

  1. A. Agree — limit strength and speed-strength are the same adaptation under different names
  2. B. Explosiveness is a learned, neurological quality developed through practice plus training; without the precise stimulus of the second pull it won't fully express, so the Olympic lifts must be practiced, not just heavy lifting performed
  3. C. Disagree — explosiveness comes only from cardiorespiratory training, so add more conditioning
  4. D. Agree in part — heavy squats build explosiveness, but only if performed for very high reps to fatigue
  5. E. Explosiveness is purely genetic and cannot be trained, so programming choice is irrelevant
Show answer

Answer: B — The article explicitly calls explosiveness a 'learned phenomenon' and speed-strength a compilation of speed and power developed through training AND practice; absent the precise neurological stimulus of the second pull, it won't fully express. So heavy slow lifting builds limit strength but not speed-strength (3.1.10, 2.2.3). A and D conflate distinct qualities; C miscategorizes it as organic/aerobic; E denies trainability the article affirms.

Scenario 6. An athlete demonstrates a smooth dumbbell swing and asks why it can't be his main exercise to build the same upward power as the clean. Using the hip-trajectory point from Annie's traces, what is the most accurate coaching explanation?

  1. A. The swing IS equivalent; he can use it as his primary power builder
  2. B. In the swing the hip never travels directly upward and the torso becomes vertical only after the hips and legs have already extended, so there is no scoop and no second pull — the upward power is comparatively low no matter how hard he thrusts
  3. C. The swing is too light to build any power and should be dropped entirely from training
  4. D. The swing is dangerous to the spine and should never be programmed for any athlete
  5. E. The swing builds more vertical power than the clean but is harder to learn, so the clean is only a beginner substitute
Show answer

Answer: B — The trace of Annie's hip shows the swing's hip path is never directly upward, and the article explains the KB line of action makes the torso vertical only after full extension — precluding the scoop and second pull and capping the power (3.1.6, 4.2.6). A and E invert the relationship; C overstates — KB ballistics are valuable for aerobic/anaerobic strength endurance, just not speed-strength; D is an unsupported blanket safety claim.

D3 · Educating 19% of exam Confidence tier: ___

52_06_Aerobic_Paradox.pdf

Open the PDF on Google Drive →

Why this is on the reading list

Kilgore dismantles the conventional belief that long-slow-distance aerobic work is the path to aerobic fitness, arguing that VO2max and metabolic adaptation are driven by Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome — you must disrupt homeostasis in a system to improve that system. This is foundational support for teaching the CrossFit definition of fitness, the role of intensity (and its relationship to technique), the metabolic pathways/energy systems model, and why CrossFit produces 'aerobic' results without 'aerobic' training. It directly backs Domain 3 tasks on teaching CrossFit's definition of fitness, the four fitness models, relative intensity, and the technique-intensity (threshold training) relationship.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 3.1.5 Teach the definition of CrossFit
  • 3.1.8 Teach the CrossFit definition of fitness and health and the four models illustrating it
  • 3.1.9 Teach the goals of CrossFit programming and how goals are met (programming with variance)
  • 3.1.10 Teach the relationship between technique and intensity (threshold training)
  • 3.1.11 Teach relative intensity
  • 3.1.12 Teach the principles of scaling
  • 2.1.2 Design a sequence of workouts that improves general physical preparedness (GPP)
  • 2.3.4 Evaluate athlete progress relative to CrossFit's definition of fitness and their personal goal
  • 1.2.2 Evaluate athlete's work capacity
  • 1.2.4 Monitor athlete for signs of over- or under-training

What to focus on while reading

  • The central thesis: a disruption of homeostasis in a physiological system is REQUIRED for adaptation/improvement in that same system — this is Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome applied correctly.
  • Hunt for the definition Kilgore gives for 'aerobic' (in the presence of oxygen) and why, by definition, low-to-moderate continuous work CANNOT disrupt oxygen homeostasis — so it cannot drive a VO2max gain.
  • The distinction between ENDURANCE improving and VO2max improving — they are NOT the same thing. LSD improves substrate storage/utilization (endurance) but not VO2max.
  • VO2max definition: the MAXIMUM amount of oxygen the body can CONSUME at maximal effort. Note the emphasis on CONSUMPTION (at the muscle), not DELIVERY (heart/lungs/vasculature).
  • Kilgore's 'heresy': consumption does not relate strongly to delivery — VO2max gains come from adaptations AT and IN the muscle (enzymes, glucose transporters, myoglobin), not from cardiovascular development.
  • The beginner vs. trained-athlete distinction: beginners adapt to ANY non-specific stress above sedentary life; intermediate/advanced/elite athletes require SPECIFIC, higher-intensity stress. (This is the SAID/specificity principle and directly parallels scaling by skill level.)
  • The 3-to-9-month window after which LSD stops being a sufficiently specific stimulus for oxygen-handling adaptation in a consistently training athlete.
  • Table 1 — read it carefully. Note which methods show 'None' for actual VO2 disturbance (Recovery, LSD, Tempo) vs. small (Interval) vs. large (Reps), and what each method ACTUALLY trains vs. what it is conventionally INTENDED to train.
  • The 70% VO2max prescription: why it is a RECOVERY workload (easy enough to recover without losing neuromuscular condition), NOT an effective fitness-building stimulus — and the note that 20-60 min of aerobic activity is a workout, not a warm-up/cool-down.
  • Lactate myth-busting: lactate is an essential hydrogen-ion acceptor in glycolytic metabolism, not a villain; its accumulation is a CONSEQUENCE that COINCIDES with oxygen-homeostasis disruption, not the cause of adaptation. Correlation is not causation.
  • Oxygen saturation as the marker of the driving force of VO2max gain: rest/LSD ~98% (insignificant drop); beginners adapt to a drop of ~1% (to 97%); intermediate/advanced/elite need drops to ~91% or lower — only achievable via high-intensity intervals.
  • Productive interval intensities: Kilgore argues 150-250% of VO2max, far above the conventional 85-105% race-pace range, and that intervals should be a much larger share of training than the traditional ~5% of mileage.
  • The flawed-research point: most VO2max research is done on BEGINNERS, whose non-specific responsiveness makes the data misleading when applied to trained athletes — a 'progress-retarding mistake.'
  • The CrossFit tie-in: why CrossFitters get aerobically fit WITHOUT training in a conventionally 'aerobic' manner — because high-intensity work disrupts oxygen homeostasis and drives the muscle-level adaptations that actually raise VO2max.
  • Kilgore's closing proposition: the power of training to improve aerobic fitness (and reduce mortality) likely lies toward the ANAEROBIC end of the metabolic spectrum — the conceptual bridge to CrossFit's 'intensity' thesis.

Concepts to understand

  • General Adaptation Syndrome (Selye) applied to training: no homeostatic disruption in a system means no adaptation in that system. Be able to use this to justify WHY a coach programs intensity and variance rather than steady-state cardio.
  • Homeostatic disruption as the trigger for adaptation — and that the disruption must be GREATER than what the trainee has previously experienced (progressive overload). Partial glycogen depletion counts only if it exceeds prior experience.
  • Specificity / SAID principle: a specific adaptation results from a specific stress. LSD produces a metabolic (substrate) adaptation; high-intensity intervals produce an oxygen-handling (VO2max) adaptation. Match the stimulus to the desired result.
  • Beginner non-specific responsiveness vs. trained-athlete specificity: a beginner improves on almost anything; an intermediate/advanced athlete needs targeted intensity. This is the physiological basis for scaling by skill level and for why benchmarks must be interpreted by training age.
  • VO2max is defined by oxygen CONSUMPTION at the working muscle, not oxygen DELIVERY by the heart and lungs. The rate-limiter for trained athletes is extraction/utilization, not pumping capacity.
  • Endurance is multi-faceted (energy substrate handling AND oxygen handling) — improving 'endurance' does not necessarily mean VO2max improved. Coaches must not conflate 'can go longer' with 'aerobically more powerful.'
  • Intensity is the independent variable most responsible for driving adaptation: the level of exertion that exceeds oxygen-consumption capacity (and incidentally produces lactate) is the level that forces VO2max improvement. This is the foundation for CrossFit's emphasis on relative intensity.
  • Relative intensity: the same workload is recovery for an elite athlete and homeostasis-disrupting for a beginner. Intensity must be judged relative to the individual's current capacity — a 70% effort means different things to different athletes.
  • Threshold / technique-intensity relationship (CrossFit): intensity is the key to results, but intensity is only safely and effectively expressed once mechanics are sound and consistent. Kilgore's physiology explains WHY intensity matters; CrossFit constrains HOW it is pursued (mechanics, then consistency, then intensity).
  • Lactate is not the enemy and not the mechanism: it is an inevitable byproduct of high-intensity glycolysis whose accumulation merely coincides with the oxygen-homeostasis disruption that actually drives adaptation. Don't program 'to make lactate'; program to exceed oxygen-consumption capacity.
  • The recovery role of low-intensity work: 70% VO2max steady-state has a legitimate place — active recovery — but should not be mistaken for fitness-building work. Useful for programming easy days and understanding why a 'cardio day' isn't necessarily progress.
  • Constantly varied, high-intensity functional movement produces broad metabolic adaptation (GPP): because intensity disrupts homeostasis across energy systems, CrossFit-style training drives aerobic AND anaerobic adaptation simultaneously — resolving the 'paradox' in the title.
  • Evidence literacy for coaches: be skeptical of recommendations (even from authoritative bodies like ACSM) when the underlying data is drawn from beginners or measures the wrong variable. Prioritize observed, real-world performance results over entrenched convention.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenario questions in which an athlete or another coach claims that long, slow cardio is the way to build 'aerobic fitness,' and you must explain — in CrossFit terms — why intensity and variance, not steady-state distance, drive broad adaptation (3.1.5, 3.1.8, 3.1.9). Items will test whether you can teach relative intensity (the same effort means different things to different athletes) and the technique-then-intensity sequence (3.1.10, 3.1.11), and whether you correctly distinguish 'endurance improved' from 'VO2max/work capacity improved' when evaluating progress against CrossFit's definition of fitness (2.3.4, 1.2.2). You may also see programming items where the right answer applies specificity and progressive homeostatic disruption rather than non-specific volume (2.1.2), and recovery-day reasoning where low-intensity work is correctly identified as recovery, not a fitness stimulus (1.2.4).

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS)
Selye's model of how the body responds to stress through a programmed series of responses; correctly applied, it means a system only adapts (gets fitter) after its homeostasis is disrupted by a sufficient stressor.
Homeostasis
The body's stable internal balance. Adaptation requires DISRUPTING it; if a workload is comfortably within current capacity (no disruption), no fitness gain follows.
VO2max
The maximum amount of oxygen the body can CONSUME at maximal effort — the benchmark marker of aerobic fitness. Defined by the ability to consume (extract and use) oxygen at the muscle, not the ability of the heart and lungs to deliver it.
Aerobic
Literally 'in the presence of oxygen.' By definition, aerobic (oxygen-met) work cannot disrupt oxygen homeostasis, so it cannot, on its own, drive a VO2max improvement in a trained athlete.
Anaerobic
'Without sufficient oxygen' — high-intensity effort where oxygen demand at the muscle outpaces supply. This shortfall is the stimulus that forces oxygen-handling adaptation and VO2max gains.
Long-slow-distance (LSD)
Continuous low-to-moderate intensity work (e.g., 60-120 min at ~70% VO2max). Depletes energy substrates and improves substrate storage/utilization (endurance) but does NOT raise VO2max in trained athletes.
Interval training
Shorter, more intense bouts with brief rest. When intense enough to exceed oxygen-consumption capacity, it depresses oxygen saturation and drives the muscle-level adaptations that raise VO2max.
Specificity (SAID)
Specific Adaptation to Imposed Demand — the body adapts precisely to the kind of stress applied. The desired result dictates the required stimulus; this is why trained athletes need targeted intensity, not generic volume.
Relative intensity
Intensity measured against an individual's current capacity rather than an absolute number. The same workload (e.g., 70% effort) can be hard for one athlete and easy recovery for another.
Oxygen saturation (SpO2)
The percent of hemoglobin carrying oxygen (~98% at rest). A meaningful DROP (to ~91% or lower in trained athletes) signals the oxygen-homeostasis disruption that drives VO2max gains; LSD barely moves it.
Glycogen depletion
Using up stored carbohydrate in muscle/liver. Significant or progressively greater depletion is a metabolic homeostatic disruption that drives improved substrate storage and utilization.
Lactate / lactic acid
A byproduct of glycolysis and an essential hydrogen-ion acceptor — not a toxin. Its accumulation COINCIDES with intense, oxygen-deficit work but is a consequence, not the cause, of adaptation.
Oxidative metabolism
Energy production using oxygen (fat and carbohydrate). The dominant pathway during LSD work.
Glycolytic metabolism
Energy production from breaking down carbohydrate (glucose/glycogen), prominent during higher-intensity interval and rep work; anaerobic glycolysis dominates when oxygen can't keep up.
Recovery workload
Low-intensity effort (~70% VO2max) easy enough to permit physiological recovery without losing neuromuscular condition — useful, but not a fitness-building stimulus.
General Physical Preparedness (GPP)
Broad, non-specialized fitness across many capacities — the goal of CrossFit programming, achieved by constantly varied, high-intensity functional movement that disrupts homeostasis across energy systems.
ACSM aerobic prescription
The conventional recommendation of 20-60 minutes of continuous low-to-moderate aerobic activity. Kilgore argues this trains substrate handling/recovery, not VO2max, in anyone past the beginner stage.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • Recovery/active-recovery work is legitimate, but do not confuse a low-intensity 'cardio day' with fitness-building progress — misreading it can mask under-training when an athlete's results stall (relates to 1.2.4).
  • Article-specific intensity figures (e.g., '150-250% of VO2max,' specific saturation percentages) are illustrative of the argument, not prescriptions to chase in a class setting; pursue intensity only after mechanics and consistency are established, and within each athlete's safe, scaled capacity.
  • This is an exercise-physiology argument, not medical guidance — programming maximal-intensity work for untrained, deconditioned, or at-risk athletes without screening and scaling raises injury and overexertion risk (defer to screening, scaling, and Scope of Practice).

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. A member who runs 5+ miles at an easy, conversational pace three times a week tells you she's frustrated that her Fran and rowing benchmark times haven't improved in months. She asks why all that 'cardio' isn't making her more fit. Based on Kilgore's reasoning, what is the BEST coaching explanation and adjustment?

  1. A. Her easy continuous running keeps oxygen supply matched to demand, so it never disrupts homeostasis enough to drive new adaptation; add higher-intensity, varied work that exceeds her current capacity.
  2. B. She simply isn't running far enough — increasing her weekly mileage at the same pace will eventually raise her work capacity.
  3. C. Her benchmarks are stalled because lactic acid is accumulating and poisoning her muscles; she needs more rest, not more intensity.
  4. D. Steady running is the gold standard for aerobic fitness, so her benchmarks should be ignored as long as she can run longer.
  5. E. She needs to run at exactly 70% of VO2max in every session to maximize aerobic development.
Show answer

Answer: A — A applies Selye/GAS and specificity correctly: easy continuous work keeps oxygen demand met by supply, so it can't disrupt oxygen homeostasis and won't drive further adaptation in a trained athlete — the fix is intensity and variance above current capacity. B repeats the non-specific-volume mistake the article criticizes. C misattributes the cause to lactate, which Kilgore explicitly debunks as a coincident byproduct, not a poison. D wrongly conflates 'can run longer' with improved fitness/VO2max. E describes a recovery workload, which the article says induces no improvement.

Scenario 2. While teaching a class the CrossFit definition of fitness, an athlete pushes back: 'Real aerobic fitness only comes from long runs — how can short, intense CrossFit workouts make me aerobically fit?' Which response best teaches the concept Kilgore explains?

  1. A. 'You're right that long runs are technically superior for the aerobic system; CrossFit just makes you anaerobically fit.'
  2. B. 'VO2max is about how much oxygen your muscles can CONSUME. High intensity makes demand outstrip supply, which forces your muscles to adapt and extract more oxygen — that's what actually raises aerobic fitness.'
  3. C. 'Aerobic fitness is mostly genetic, so the type of training doesn't really matter.'
  4. D. 'Long runs and CrossFit are completely interchangeable; pick whichever you enjoy.'
  5. E. 'Aerobic fitness comes from building a bigger, stronger heart, which only long slow distance can do.'
Show answer

Answer: B — B captures Kilgore's core 'heresy': VO2max is defined by oxygen consumption at the muscle, and the homeostatic disruption from high intensity drives the muscle-level adaptations that raise it. A concedes a false premise (that LSD is superior for the aerobic system in trained athletes). C is false and dismissive of training effect. D ignores specificity and the differing adaptations each method produces. E states the delivery-based view the article explicitly rejects ('consumption does not relate strongly to delivery').

Scenario 3. A brand-new, previously sedentary client starts CrossFit. A 12-year competitive athlete in the same class is plateaued. Applying Kilgore's beginner-vs-trained distinction, how should you think about the stimulus each needs?

  1. A. Both need identical programming because the physiology of adaptation is the same for everyone.
  2. B. The beginner will improve on almost any work above sedentary life, while the trained athlete needs a specific, higher-intensity stress to disrupt homeostasis and progress.
  3. C. The trained athlete should switch entirely to long slow distance, since that's what advanced athletes respond to best.
  4. D. The beginner needs maximal-intensity intervals immediately to avoid wasting time.
  5. E. Neither will improve without first maximizing weekly training volume.
Show answer

Answer: B — B is the specificity point: beginners respond to non-specific stress (anything beyond sedentary life), whereas intermediate/advanced/elite athletes require specific, higher-intensity stimulus — which also underpins scaling by skill level. A ignores training age. C inverts the article (LSD becomes insufficient for trained athletes after ~3-9 months). D is unsafe and ignores the need to establish mechanics/consistency first. E repeats the volume fallacy the article criticizes.

Scenario 4. In programming an easy/recovery day, a newer coach writes '45 minutes continuous jog at ~70% effort' and labels it 'aerobic base building to raise the class's VO2max.' What is the most accurate critique using this article?

  1. A. The session is fine and correctly labeled — 70% continuous work is the most effective way to raise VO2max.
  2. B. The workload is appropriate for active recovery, but it should not be labeled a VO2max/fitness-building stimulus, because a 70% effort doesn't disrupt oxygen homeostasis.
  3. C. The session should be removed entirely; recovery work has no place in a program.
  4. D. The intensity should be raised to 70% for everyone so it becomes a true VO2max workout.
  5. E. It will raise VO2max as long as athletes accumulate lactate during the jog.
Show answer

Answer: B — B matches the article: ~70% steady work is a legitimate recovery workload (easy enough to recover without losing neuromuscular condition) but cannot disrupt oxygen homeostasis, so calling it a VO2max stimulus is wrong. A and D misstate the physiology. C overcorrects — recovery work is valuable, just not for the labeled purpose. E is false; at recovery intensity little lactate is produced, and lactate is a coincident byproduct, not the driver of VO2max gains.

Scenario 5. An athlete with sound mechanics asks how to get the most fitness benefit from a metcon. A teammate insists the goal is to 'feel the lactic burn as long as possible.' How should you frame the actual driver of adaptation per Kilgore, while honoring CrossFit's coaching priorities?

  1. A. Chase the lactic burn directly — maximizing lactate is the mechanism that raises fitness.
  2. B. Once mechanics and consistency are in place, pursue intensity that pushes oxygen demand past supply; the resulting adaptation — not the lactate itself — drives the fitness gain.
  3. C. Keep the effort easy and continuous to stay 'aerobic' and protect the heart.
  4. D. Avoid intensity altogether until VO2max has already improved through long slow distance.
  5. E. Intensity is irrelevant; only total volume of work determines fitness improvement.
Show answer

Answer: B — B integrates the physiology (intensity that exceeds oxygen-consumption capacity is the driver; lactate is a coincident byproduct) with CrossFit's mechanics-consistency-intensity sequence and relative-intensity principle. A confuses correlation with causation — the article explicitly rejects 'making lactate' as the goal. C keeps demand met by supply, so no homeostatic disruption and no gain in a trained athlete. D inverts the LSD-vs-intensity relationship. E denies the central role of intensity the article establishes.

Scenario 6. Two athletes finish the same benchmark workout. Athlete X improved her time; Athlete Y did not improve his time but reports he can now 'keep going much longer' at an easy pace after months of jogging. Using Kilgore's framing, how should you interpret each result relative to CrossFit's definition of fitness and work capacity?

  1. A. Both improved their aerobic power equally, since both feel more endurance.
  2. B. X demonstrated improved work capacity on the test; Y improved substrate-handling endurance, which is real but is not the same as improved VO2max/work capacity at intensity.
  3. C. Y is clearly fitter because endurance at an easy pace is the truest measure of fitness.
  4. D. Neither result tells you anything useful about fitness.
  5. E. X's faster time must be a measurement error, because only long slow distance improves benchmark performance.
Show answer

Answer: B — B applies the endurance-vs-VO2max distinction and CrossFit's measurable work-capacity standard: a faster benchmark reflects improved work capacity, whereas 'can go longer easy' reflects substrate adaptation, which the article warns is wrongly equated with raised VO2max. A conflates the two adaptations. C elevates easy-pace endurance over measurable output, contrary to CrossFit's definition. D ignores the diagnostic value of benchmarks (2.3.4). E denies the legitimate intensity-driven improvement.

D3 · Educating 19% of exam Confidence tier: ___

57_07_Support_on_Rings.pdf

Open the PDF on Google Drive →

Why this is on the reading list

This article is on the CCFT reading list because it models how a single foundational gymnastics position (the ring support) branches into a family of progressions and how a staple CrossFit movement (the ring dip) is taught, scaled, and standardized. It directly backs Domain 3 (Educating): using progressions to teach complex moves (3.1.3), teaching proper execution (3.1.1), layering instruction to athlete capability (3.1.2), and teaching the value of low/no-power strength holds like the L-sit and levers (3.1.7). It also reinforces the technique-before-intensity logic (3.1.10) by insisting the support be mastered before ring dips are loaded, and it gives concrete teaching points, depth/lockout standards, and a scaling method (adjustable-height rings) a coach must be able to deploy.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 3.1.1 Teach proper execution of movements
  • 3.1.2 Layer instruction to meet athlete capability
  • 3.1.3 Use progressions to teach complex moves
  • 3.1.7 Teach importance of movements that produce little/no power (e.g., L-sit, back lever)
  • 3.1.10 Teach the relationship between technique and intensity (threshold training)
  • 3.1.12 Teach the principles of scaling
  • 3.2.1 Demonstrate proper movements
  • 3.2.2 Demonstrate movement faults
  • 3.2.3 Demonstrate movement progressions
  • 4.1.3 Identify faults in movement
  • 4.1.4 Identify refinements of sound mechanics to optimize performance
  • 4.2.4 Reinforce sound mechanics
  • 2.2.5 Scale by skill level
  • 5.2.3 Manage risk for the athlete
  • 5.2.7 Arrange equipment, athletes, instructors to maximize safety

What to focus on while reading

  • The ring-spacing standard: 50 cm apart is the official distance; the practical gymnast shortcut is one forearm length (back of elbow to fingertips), usually placing rings just outside the shoulders. Note this is a setup/coaching detail you would cue, not a number to brute-memorize.
  • The prerequisite logic: a perfect 1-minute support hold should be attained BEFORE training ring dips. Highlight this as the article's explicit progression gate.
  • Two methods of adding load to a weighted support: (1) hip belt or weight vest, (2) holding a dumbbell/kettlebell/plate with the feet. Note WHY the author prefers the feet method: you can dump the load instantly and continue unweighted, or abort the movement safely.
  • Benchmark goals offered: hold a perfect support for a full minute; then hold a support plus added load equal to half body weight for a minute. These are concrete progress markers a coach can set.
  • How body lean changes muscular recruitment in a support: leaning FORWARD shifts emphasis to pecs, front delts, biceps (builds toward the maltese); leaning BACK shifts load to back, lats, triceps (builds toward the Victorian).
  • Definitions of the advanced holds referenced: maltese (advanced ring strength hold); Victorian (described as the hardest ring strength move, basically an upside-down maltese / a front lever with the body level with the arms; noted that no one has yet performed it perfectly).
  • The swing-in-support teaching cues: start slow, keep the body relatively straight, gain amplitude by leaning into the swing and pushing down on the rings, and use a soft surface underneath for safety. All standard support rules still apply.
  • The three persistent support rules repeated throughout: keep arms locked, don't 'ride the straps,' keep shoulders active (pushing down on the rings).
  • Ring dip difficulty vs bar dip: most people do only one-third to one-half as many dips on rings as on bars; the ratio improves as support strength improves. Understand the WHY (instability) rather than the exact ratio.
  • The counterintuitive point: the ring dip gets HARDER as technique matures, because correct technique removes the strap support that beginners lean on.
  • The three maturity levels of the ring dip and how to tell them apart: (1) Immature — rings held tight to the body and turned inward (backs of hands forward), arms pushing out against the straps, strap angle changes; tell-tale sign is RED MARKS on the forearms. (2) Intermediate — straps clear of the body or only lightly touching the arms; described as 'quite functional.' (3) Mature — rings stay turned OUTWARD (palms forward) the entire rep, forearms never contact the rings/straps; required in competitive gymnastics and develops the most strength, skill, and body control.
  • The diagnostic cue for readiness: if an athlete has to brace on the straps during a dip, send them back to build the support position first.
  • The CrossFit ring-dip DEPTH standard: 'hands to your armpits,' which is below 90 degrees (parallel) — explicitly analogized to a full-depth squat.
  • The objective depth-gauge scaling trick: set height-adjustable rings so the toes just barely touch the ground at the bottom of each rep, giving an objective per-rep depth check; raise the rings in small increments over time toward full range of motion.
  • The TOP-of-rep standard: full lockout is required; the article warns about an athlete being criticized for failing to lock out at the top.
  • The closing principle: an enormous amount of gymnastics capacity develops from a small handful of foundational movements — from the simple support, dozens of exercises branch out.

Concepts to understand

  • Progression gating: complex/loaded ring work is built on a mastered foundation. A coach should not advance an athlete to ring dips (or weighted/leaning/swinging variations) until the static support is solid for time. Apply this as a decision rule, not a memorized sequence.
  • Position dictates recruitment: changing body alignment inside an isometric hold changes which muscles bear the load and the difficulty. Understand that leaning forward vs back is a deliberate programming lever to bias development toward specific advanced skills (maltese vs Victorian).
  • Low/no-power strength holds matter: supports, the L-sit, the maltese, levers, and the Victorian produce little or no measurable external power yet build essential strength, midline stability, and body control. Be able to explain to an athlete WHY you program a movement that 'isn't going anywhere.'
  • Technique vs intensity (threshold training) in a static skill: better ring-dip technique is HARDER, not easier, because correctness removes the assistive strap contact. A coach must therefore expect rep counts to drop as quality rises and must not let athletes chase volume by reverting to the immature, strap-riding pattern.
  • Reading the same movement at multiple skill levels: the immature/intermediate/mature ring dip is a continuum a coach must be able to identify on sight and use to place each athlete and prescribe the next refinement.
  • Fault recognition by tell-tale sign: red marks on the forearms after ring dips reveal a strap-riding, arms-in fault even if the coach didn't watch every rep — an example of inferring a root cause from evidence after the fact.
  • Scaling depth objectively: using ring height so the toes graze the floor at the bottom converts a subjective 'go lower' into an objective per-rep standard, and lets the coach progressively restore full range of motion for athletes with shoulder limitations.
  • Defining the rep standards: a valid CrossFit ring dip requires depth (hands to armpits, below parallel) AND full lockout at the top. A coach must judge both ends of the range, exactly as with a squat.
  • Loading a hold safely: when adding external load to a support, prefer methods that allow instant release (holding weight with the feet) so the athlete can dump the load and abort safely — a risk-management choice a coach builds into setup.
  • Equipment setup as coaching: correct ring spacing (~one forearm, just outside the shoulders) and a soft landing surface for swings are setup decisions that protect mechanics and safety before the first rep.
  • Foundational economy: mastery of a few basics multiplies into many skills — the rationale for spending coaching time perfecting the support rather than rushing to flashy variations.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenario items that hand you an athlete struggling with ring dips and ask for the best coaching response — the strongest answers usually route back to building the support first (3.1.3, 3.1.10) rather than adding reps or load. You may be asked to identify a fault from a described symptom (red forearms, no lockout, partial depth) and name the refinement (4.1.3, 4.1.4, 4.2.4), to select an objective scaling method for an athlete who can't reach depth (the toe-touch ring height; 2.2.5, 3.1.12), or to choose the safest way to load or set up a hold (feet-held weight, soft surface, ring spacing; 5.2.3, 5.2.7). Conceptual items may test why a coach programs a 'no-power' hold like an L-sit or lever and why correct ring-dip technique reduces rep count (3.1.7, 3.1.10).

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Support (on rings)
A static, arms-locked hold at the top of the rings with shoulders pushed down (active) and bodyweight stabilized above the rings; the foundational position from which most other ring skills branch.
Riding the straps
A fault where the athlete braces or pushes against the support straps for assistance instead of holding the position with their own strength; a sign the support is not yet solid and a cue to regress to support work.
Active shoulders
Keeping the shoulders depressed and pushing down on the rings throughout a hold, rather than letting the body sag into the joints; one of the three core support rules (locked arms, no strap-riding, active shoulders).
Weighted support
A support hold performed with added external load — via hip belt/vest or by gripping a dumbbell, kettlebell, or plate with the feet — used to build greater static pressing strength; a benchmark goal is half-bodyweight added for one minute.
Leaning support
A support performed with the torso tilted forward or back to deliberately shift muscular emphasis and difficulty — forward biases pecs/front delts/biceps (toward the maltese), backward biases back/lats/triceps (toward the Victorian).
Maltese
An advanced ring strength hold in which the body is held roughly level with the rings; developed in part through forward-leaning support work.
Victorian
Described as the hardest ring strength move — essentially an upside-down maltese or a front lever with the body level with the arms; noted as not yet performed perfectly by anyone; approached via backward-leaning support work.
Swing in support
Generating controlled back-and-forth amplitude while staying in a support, body kept relatively straight, gaining swing by leaning into it and pushing down on the rings; started slowly and performed over a soft surface for safety.
Ring dip
A staple CrossFit dip performed on rings rather than bars; far harder than a bar dip due to ring instability, and progressively harder as technique matures and strap assistance is removed.
Immature ring dip
A faulty/early pattern with rings held tight to the body and turned inward (backs of hands forward), arms pushing out against the straps; identifiable afterward by red marks on the forearms.
Intermediate ring dip
A functional dip in which the straps are clear of the body or only lightly touching the arms — a usable competence level on the way to mature technique.
Mature ring dip
A dip in which the rings stay turned outward (palms forward) through the whole rep so the forearms never contact the rings or straps; the hardest version, required in competitive gymnastics, and the one that builds the most strength, skill, and body control.
Depth standard ('hands to armpits')
The CrossFit ring-dip bottom standard — descending until the hands reach the armpits, which is below 90 degrees (below parallel), analogous to a full-depth squat.
Lockout
Full extension of the arms at the top of the rep; required for a valid ring dip — finishing short of lockout is a no-rep fault.
Toe-touch depth gauge
A scaling/standard-setting method using height-adjustable rings set so the toes just graze the floor at the bottom of each rep, giving an objective depth check that can be progressively raised toward full range of motion.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • Athletes with shoulder issues should approach full ring-dip depth slowly and work up to it — a coach must scale depth (e.g., the toe-touch height method) rather than force range of motion on a limited shoulder.
  • Strap-riding and arms-pushed-out positions cause forearm abrasion/red marks; persistent bracing on the straps signals inadequate support strength and is a cue to regress, not to add load or reps.
  • Swinging in support can quickly get out of control; require a soft landing surface and start slowly to manage fall risk (risk management / equipment-and-space setup).
  • When adding external load to a support, favor a setup the athlete can release instantly (weight held by the feet) so they can dump the load and abort safely if the position fails.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. A newer athlete asks you to add ring dips to today's workout. You watch a few reps and see her rings pulled tight to her body and turned inward, her arms shoving outward against the straps, and afterward you notice red marks on her forearms. What is the best coaching action?

  1. A. Add a light dumbbell held between her feet to build dip strength faster
  2. B. Tell her to do more reps so the pattern becomes automatic
  3. C. Regress her to building a solid support hold first, since bracing on the straps shows her support isn't yet strong enough
  4. D. Increase the ring height so she gets a longer range of motion
  5. E. Switch her to bar dips permanently because ring dips aren't appropriate for her
Show answer

Answer: C — The strap-riding, arms-out pattern and the red forearm marks are the article's classic signs of an immature ring dip built on an inadequate support. The author explicitly says if an athlete has to brace on the straps, send them back to the support position first (3.1.3, 3.1.10, 4.1.3). A and B add load/volume to a broken pattern; D makes it harder, not safer; E abandons a trainable progression rather than coaching it.

Scenario 2. An athlete with a cranky shoulder can't yet hit the 'hands-to-armpits' ring-dip depth without pain. Which scaling approach best matches the article's method for restoring full range of motion over time?

  1. A. Let him stop at 90 degrees and count those as full reps
  2. B. Set height-adjustable rings so his toes just barely touch the floor at the bottom, giving an objective depth gauge, then raise the rings in small increments over time
  3. C. Add a weight vest so he develops strength through the partial range
  4. D. Have him perform bar dips instead and never return to rings
  5. E. Tell him to push through the pain to full depth on every rep
Show answer

Answer: B — The article's specific solution is height-adjustable rings set so the toes just graze the ground at the bottom — an objective per-rep depth check — then raising the rings incrementally toward full ROM (2.2.5, 3.1.12). A redefines the standard and stalls progress; C loads a limited shoulder; D abandons the goal; E ignores the explicit guidance to work up to depth slowly for shoulder issues (red flag / 5.2.3).

Scenario 3. A strong athlete brags that he can crank out 30 ring dips. When you watch, he keeps the rings turned inward and lets his forearms rest on the straps to save energy, and he doesn't fully lock out at the top. He asks why you'd want him to do the 'harder' version where the rings stay turned out. What is the best explanation to give him?

  1. A. The turned-out (mature) dip is harder precisely because it removes the strap assistance, and it builds greater strength, skill, and body control — plus a valid rep still requires full lockout
  2. B. The turned-in version is fine; rep count is all that matters
  3. C. Turning the rings out is purely a competition aesthetic with no training benefit
  4. D. He should add weight first and worry about technique later
  5. E. Locking out at the top is optional as long as he hits depth
Show answer

Answer: A — This tests technique-vs-intensity on a skill (3.1.10) plus the rep standards. The mature ring dip keeps the rings turned outward so the forearms never touch the straps; it's tougher but develops more strength, skill, and control, and a valid dip also requires lockout at the top (3.1.1, 4.1.4). B and E accept faults; C denies the documented training benefit; D inverts the correct order of mechanics before load/volume.

Scenario 4. You're setting up a station for weighted supports for a member who is new to loading the hold. Which setup best reflects the article's safety-minded loading choice?

  1. A. Have her hold a dumbbell between her feet so she can dump the load and abort instantly if the position fails
  2. B. Strap a barbell across her thighs so it can't move
  3. C. Have a partner hold extra plates on her shoulders during the hold
  4. D. Load a heavy hip belt she cannot remove without help
  5. E. Skip the support entirely and load ring dips instead
Show answer

Answer: A — The author prefers holding the weight with the feet specifically because the athlete can dump the load at any time and continue unweighted or abort the movement safely (5.2.3, 5.2.7). B, C, and D all trap the athlete under load with no quick release; E skips the foundational hold the article says should precede loaded/advanced work.

Scenario 5. A coach wants to bias an athlete's ring-support training toward eventually developing a maltese. According to the article, which variation shifts the emphasis appropriately?

  1. A. Leaning forward in the support, which shifts emphasis to the pecs, front delts, and biceps
  2. B. Leaning back in the support, which shifts load to the back, lats, and triceps
  3. C. Adding a swing in support
  4. D. Holding a strict, perfectly vertical support with no lean
  5. E. Doing more bar dips to build pressing strength
Show answer

Answer: A — The article states that leaning forward from a mature support shifts emphasis to the pecs, front delts, and biceps and is a great step toward the maltese; leaning back biases the back/lats/triceps toward the Victorian (B). This tests understanding that body alignment is a deliberate recruitment/programming lever (3.1.2, 4.1.4). C, D, and E don't target the maltese's specific demands.

Scenario 6. During a beginner class, an athlete asks why you keep prioritizing static holds like the support and L-sit when they 'don't go anywhere' and don't seem like real exercise. Which response best reflects the reasoning in the article?

  1. A. They're warm-up filler; you do them because there's nothing better early on
  2. B. These low/no-power holds build the foundational strength, midline stability, and body control that dozens of more advanced ring skills branch out from
  3. C. They're only included because they look impressive
  4. D. They burn the most calories of any gymnastics movement
  5. E. They're a substitute for ever needing to dip, press, or lift
Show answer

Answer: B — The article closes on the principle that an enormous amount of gymnastics capacity develops from a small handful of foundational movements — from the simple support, dozens of exercises branch out (3.1.7, 3.1.3). Coaches must be able to justify programming 'no-power' holds. A and C dismiss their value; D is an unsupported calorie claim; E overstates their role as a replacement for other training.

Scenario 7. You're about to teach ring swings to an intermediate group for the first time. Which setup and cueing choice best manages risk per the article?

  1. A. Start at maximum amplitude immediately so they feel the full movement
  2. B. Start slowly, keep the body relatively straight, gain amplitude by leaning into the swing and pushing down on the rings, and place a soft surface underneath
  3. C. Let them bend at the hips aggressively to generate speed
  4. D. Remove the support rules (locked arms, active shoulders) since the body is now moving
  5. E. Tell them to grab the straps for extra control if they start to lose it
Show answer

Answer: B — The article warns swings can quickly get out of control, so start slowly, stay relatively straight, build amplitude by leaning in and pushing down on the rings, and use a soft surface underneath (5.2.3, 5.2.7, 3.1.1). All normal support rules still apply, which rules out D and E (strap-riding is still a fault); A and C invite loss of control.

Why this is on the reading list

This article gives the trainer the biomechanical 'why' behind the single most repeated coaching point in CrossFit lifting: maintain a flat back with natural lumbar curvature. It backs Domain 3 (Educating) directly — teaching proper execution and the technique-intensity relationship — because it equips the coach to explain to athletes, in concrete and even quantitative terms, why a rounded spine under load is dangerous and why a flat back is not the same as an upright back. It also feeds Domain 4 (applying anatomy and biomechanics to correct movement) and Domain 5 (managing risk), but its primary value is making the coach a credible educator who can justify a cue rather than just bark it.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 3.1.1 Teach proper execution of movements
  • 3.1.6 Teach descriptive/defining characteristics of functional movements
  • 3.1.10 Teach the relationship between technique and intensity (threshold training)
  • 4.2.6 Apply basic principles of anatomy and biomechanics
  • 4.1.3 Identify faults in movement
  • 4.1.6 Identify root cause of faults
  • 4.2.1 Communicate cues to correct unsound mechanics
  • 5.2.1 Apply mechanics-consistency-intensity to programming for safety and performance
  • 5.2.3 Manage risk for the athlete
  • 5.2.6 Recognize warning signs for possible injury or overexertion

What to focus on while reading

  • The three directions force is applied to tissue: compression, tension, shear — and which two matter for the spine (compression and shear).
  • The definition of shear: a force acting parallel to a surface that can slide one vertebra relative to another.
  • Why the deadlift creates a 'huge torque' about the lumbar spine — the load and upper-body center of mass sit far from the vertebrae (long moment arm).
  • That the L4-L5 disc is treated as the center of rotation, and that 85–95% of disc herniations occur at L4/L5 or L5/S1.
  • The very short moment arm of the spinal erectors (2.4–2.8 inches), which forces those muscles to pull with hundreds to thousands of pounds of force.
  • That erector muscle force does TWO things: it pulls vertebrae together (compression) AND a component of it counteracts (neutralizes) the forward shear.
  • McGill's two kinds of shear: REACTION shear (from gravity on load + upper body) vs JOINT shear (the true, net shear = reaction shear + muscle/ligament shear). Joint shear is what determines injury risk.
  • The Rippetoe quote and why it's biomechanically correct: 'shear on the back doesn't occur if the back is rigid' — because a rigid, neutral back keeps muscles engaged to offset shear.
  • What happens when the spine FULLY FLEXES (rounds): erectors switch off, passive ligaments take the load, and the interspinous ligaments' line of pull ADDS to shear instead of opposing it.
  • The critical coaching distinction: a FLAT back is NOT the same as an UPRIGHT/vertical back. A vertical-but-rounded back produces MORE joint shear than a horizontal-but-flat back.
  • That correct trunk angle is dictated by the athlete's anthropometry (limb and torso proportions), not by trying to be vertical.
