  • The model used (4D WATBAK), that it is STATIC (no acceleration), 2-D in the sagittal/fore-aft plane — and why that means it fits the slow deadlift but NOT Olympic lifts or anything with rotation.
  • Why load weight (not body weight) is the dominant variable in the force calculations.
  • The published thresholds: NIOSH compression safe limit ~760 lb (3,433 N), max permissible 6,376 N; Waterloo shear safe limit ~500 N (~100 lb), max permissible 1,000 N (~200 lb).
  • The headline numbers at 300 lb: compression ~10,000 N in BOTH postures (compression barely changes), but joint shear = 699 N (correct) vs 3,799 N (flexed).
  • The numbers at 600 lb: correct form shear only ~1,200 N (just 20% over the industrial upper limit), but flexed-spine shear ~6,700 N — 'off the chart.'
  • WHY compression hardly changes between postures (moment arm of muscle/ligament is about the same) while shear changes enormously.
  • The point that elite powerlifters tolerate 20,000+ N of compression with no ill effect — i.e., the spine is built for compression; shear is the real danger.
  • The summary mechanism: full flexion inactivates extensors, loads posterior passive tissues, and produces high shear; a neutral-to-slightly-extended lumbar posture disables the interspinous ligaments and reduces joint shear.
  • The final generalization: the deadlift is the example, but 'the concept carries over to all lifts' and the WHOLE spine should be rigid and neutral.

Concepts to understand

  • Spine is strong in compression, weak in shear. The coaching priority is managing shear, and rigid neutral posture is the lever that controls it — be able to explain this trade-off to an athlete.
  • Moment arm drives force. Because the load sits far from the spine (long arm) but the erectors attach close to the joint (short ~2.4–2.8 in arm), the muscles must generate forces many times the bar weight. Understand this to explain why 'small' loads still load the spine heavily and why bar-to-body distance matters.
  • A rigid, neutral spine keeps the erectors active, and a component of their force cancels the shear — so the back is self-protecting only while it stays braced. Apply this when teaching bracing and 'set the back before you pull.'
  • Full flexion is a switch, not a gradient endpoint to fear vaguely: it turns OFF the muscles and hands the load to ligaments whose line of pull ADDS to shear. This is the mechanistic reason a rounded deadlift is dangerous.
  • Reaction shear vs joint shear: the shear an athlete intuitively worries about (from the load) is not the full story; the true joint shear depends on whether muscle or ligament is bearing the load. Understand this so you can debunk the 'stay vertical to reduce shear' myth.
  • Flat ≠ upright. The fault to hunt is loss of neutral curvature (rounding), NOT a forward torso angle. A coach who chases 'chest up / stay vertical' instead of 'flat back' can actually increase shear. This is the article's single most exam-relevant coaching insight.
  • Anthropometry sets the back angle. The correct torso angle differs per athlete by limb/torso length, so 'sound mechanics' is a flat spine at the angle the athlete's body dictates — not one universal silhouette.
  • Mechanics before intensity (threshold training): the article quantifies WHY — load is the dominant driver of spinal force, so adding intensity (weight) to a flexed spine multiplies shear into clearly injurious ranges. Use this to justify never loading a fault.
  • Model literacy: a static, 2-D sagittal-plane model approximates a slow lift well but cannot be trusted for accelerating or rotational movements. Understand the limits so you don't over-claim these exact numbers for cleans, snatches, or twisting.
  • The danger scales nonlinearly with bad form: at 300 lb the flexed shear (3,799 N) is already far past the 1,000 N max permissible limit; at 600 lb it reaches ~6,700 N. Understand that heavier + rounded is not a little worse, it is dramatically worse.
  • Generalization to all lifting: the L4-L5/L5-S1 region is the example because most herniations happen there and torques are greatest, but the rigid-neutral principle protects the entire spine across every loaded movement (squats, presses, cleans, kettlebell work).

How the exam applies this

Expect scenario questions where an athlete or even a 'rule of thumb' is wrong and you must pick the action that protects the spine for the right reason. The classic trap maps to the flat-vs-upright distinction (3.1.1, 4.2.1): an athlete rounds the back trying to 'stay upright' and the best answer is to cue a flat/neutral spine at a more horizontal angle, not to push them more vertical. Others test technique-before-intensity (3.1.10, 5.2.1): when a lifter loses lumbar position under load, the correct move is to reduce load and restore mechanics rather than coach through it. Anatomy/biomechanics items (4.2.6) may ask you to identify shear (not compression) as the injurious force in a rounded deadlift, or to explain why a light load can still be risky (moment arm / load is the dominant variable). Root-cause and risk items (4.1.6, 5.2.3, 5.2.6) reward recognizing lumbar flexion under load as a stop-or-scale warning sign.

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Compression
A force that squeezes a structure together along its length. In the lumbar spine it presses adjacent vertebrae toward each other; the spine tolerates this very well (powerlifters survive 20,000+ N).
Tension
A force that pulls a tissue apart (stretching). Noted in the article but set aside because it is not the relevant loading mode for this lumbar discussion.
Shear
A force acting parallel to a surface; in the spine it tends to slide one vertebra forward/backward relative to the next. This is the force that most endangers the lumbar discs.
Torque (moment of force)
A rotational force; here, the tendency of the load and upper body to rotate the lifter forward about the lumbar spine. Larger when the load is farther from the spine.
Moment arm
The perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation to the line of a force. A long moment arm (the bar far from the spine) creates large torque; the erectors' tiny ~2.4–2.8 in arm forces them to produce huge counter-forces.
Lumbar lordosis
The natural inward (slightly extended) curve of the lower spine. Maintaining it is the goal — it keeps the extensor muscles engaged and minimizes joint shear under load.
Lumbar flexion (rounding)
Loss of the natural lumbar curve as the low back rounds forward. Under load it shuts off the erectors and shifts support to passive ligaments, spiking shear.
Spinal erectors / erector spinae
The muscles running alongside the spine that extend the trunk. Their force both compresses the vertebrae and, importantly, counteracts forward shear when the spine is held neutral and rigid.
Interspinous ligaments
Passive connective tissues linking the spinous processes of adjacent vertebrae. They engage when the spine fully flexes — but their line of pull ADDS to joint shear rather than reducing it.
Reaction shear
The shear at L4-L5 produced purely by gravity acting on the load and upper-body mass. It grows as the trunk approaches horizontal — but it is not the whole picture.
Joint shear (true shear)
The net, actual shear experienced at the L4-L5 joint = reaction shear plus muscle/ligament shear. This resultant value, not reaction shear alone, determines whether loading is safe or injurious.
L4-L5 / L5-S1
The lowest lumbar joints/discs where torques are greatest; 85–95% of disc herniations occur here, which is why the model focuses on this region.
Anthropometry
An individual's body and limb proportions (torso and leg length, etc.). It dictates the correct torso angle in the pull, so sound mechanics looks different across athletes.
Static biomechanical model (4D WATBAK)
A non-dynamic, 2-D sagittal-plane computer model that calculates joint torques and forces in a fixed posture with no acceleration. Accurate for slow lifts like the deadlift; not valid for Olympic lifts or rotational movement.
NIOSH compression limit
An occupational guideline: ~760 lb-force (3,433 N) suggested safe spinal compression, with 6,376 N as a maximal permissible limit, set for general workers — conditioned athletes far exceed it safely.
Waterloo shear limits
Ergonomic guidelines of ~500 N (~100 lb) as a safe joint-shear limit and 1,000 N (~200 lb) as the maximal permissible limit — useful reference points for how far a flexed-spine lift exceeds 'safe.'
Threshold training (technique–intensity relationship)
The CrossFit principle that intensity should be added only up to the point sound mechanics can be maintained. This article quantifies the cost of violating it: adding load to a flexed spine multiplies shear into injurious ranges.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • Lumbar flexion (rounding) under load is a stop-or-scale signal — at 300 lb a flexed deadlift already produces ~3,799 N of joint shear, nearly 4x the 1,000 N maximal permissible limit. Reduce load and restore neutral spine before adding intensity.
  • Chasing an 'upright/vertical' back can increase injury risk: cueing an athlete more vertical when they are rounding is the wrong correction. Cue a FLAT/neutral spine at the angle their anthropometry allows.
  • Heavier load with poor form is dramatically (not marginally) more dangerous — shear roughly doubles to ~6,700 N going from 300 to 600 lb in flexion. Never coach an athlete 'through' one more rep on a rounded back.
  • These exact numbers apply to a slow, sagittal-plane deadlift only. Do NOT cite them as safety limits for cleans, snatches, or any twisting/accelerating movement — the static 2-D model does not model those.
  • Persistent inability to hold a neutral lumbar spine (especially with pain) is a mechanics root-cause issue and may exceed coaching scope — consider scaling, position/mobility work, and referral if pain is present (within CCFT scope-of-practice limits).

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. A new athlete sets up for a deadlift with a rounded lower back, telling you he keeps his back rounded so he can 'stay more upright and reduce shear on his spine.' What is the best coaching response?

  1. A. Agree — a more vertical torso does reduce shear, so just have him brace harder while staying upright.
  2. B. Cue a flat, neutral spine and let the torso angle be more horizontal as his proportions dictate, explaining that a flat back — not an upright back — is what controls shear.
  3. C. Tell him to round slightly more to engage the ligaments, which are strong in CrossFitters.
  4. D. Add weight so his body is forced into a better position under load.
  5. E. Leave it; rounding the back is fine for a slow lift like the deadlift.
Show answer

Answer: B — B is correct: the article's core point is that a flat back is NOT the same as an upright back, and a vertical-but-rounded spine produces MORE joint shear than a horizontal-but-flat one. A and E repeat the exact myth the article debunks (and rounding switches the erectors off). C is dangerous — flexion shifts load to ligaments whose pull ADDS to shear. D loads a fault, multiplying shear.

Scenario 2. An athlete asks why you stress spinal position so much on the deadlift when 'the bar isn't even that heavy.' Which explanation is biomechanically accurate?

  1. A. The spine is weak in compression, so even light loads crush the discs.
  2. B. Because the load sits far from the spine while the erectors attach very close to it, the muscles must pull with forces many times the bar weight; load is the dominant driver of spinal force, so position matters even at moderate weights.
  3. C. Tension forces in the discs increase sharply with any load.
  4. D. The danger is only about how heavy the bar feels, not about geometry.
  5. E. Body weight, not load, dominates the forces, so a light bar is automatically safe.
Show answer

Answer: B — B is correct: the long moment arm of the load and the tiny ~2.4–2.8 in moment arm of the erectors mean muscle forces reach hundreds-to-thousands of pounds, and the article states load weight is the dominant factor. A is wrong — the spine is strong in compression. C names the wrong force (tension is irrelevant here). E inverts the stated relationship; D ignores the geometry that the whole article is about.

Scenario 3. During a heavy deadlift, you see an experienced lifter's lumbar spine flex (round) on the last two reps of a set. What is the most appropriate action and rationale?

  1. A. Say nothing — experienced lifters can flex safely because their ligaments are strong.
  2. B. Cue louder to 'chest up' and let them finish the heavier set to build resilience.
  3. C. Stop the set or reduce the load to restore a neutral spine, because lumbar flexion under load shuts off the erectors and lets ligament pull spike joint shear into injurious ranges.
  4. D. Add a belt and continue at the same load, since a belt removes shear.
  5. E. Switch them to a more vertical torso position to eliminate the shear.
Show answer

Answer: C — C is correct: flexion inactivates the extensors and loads passive tissue, and the model shows joint shear far exceeding safe limits in a flexed spine (e.g., 3,799 N at 300 lb). A is false — ligaments add to shear, not protect. B coaches through a fault. D overstates a belt (it does not 'remove shear,' and the issue is spinal position). E repeats the flat-vs-upright error.

Scenario 4. Which statement best captures why a fully flexed lumbar spine is dangerous under load, according to the article?

  1. A. It increases compression far beyond what the spine can tolerate while leaving shear unchanged.
  2. B. It inactivates the back extensors and loads the posterior ligaments, whose line of pull adds to joint shear — so shear rises dramatically while compression changes little.
  3. C. It eliminates torque about the spine, so the lifter loses control of the bar.
  4. D. It converts shear into harmless tension.
  5. E. It engages the erectors more strongly, overheating the muscle.
Show answer

Answer: B — B is correct and matches the summary: flexion switches off extensors, loads ligaments that add to shear, and the data show shear spiking while compression is nearly the same in both postures (because the moment arms are about equal). A is backwards (compression is barely affected, and the spine handles it well). C and D are fabricated; E contradicts the finding that flexion shuts the erectors OFF.

Scenario 5. A coach wants to use the article's 4D WATBAK shear numbers to argue that a particular power clean is 'within safe limits.' What is the correct caution?

  1. A. The numbers apply to any barbell lift, so the comparison is valid.
  2. B. The model is static and 2-D in the sagittal plane and is accurate only for slow, fore-aft lifts like the deadlift — it is not valid for an accelerating or rotational movement like the power clean.
  3. C. The model overstates shear, so any real lift is safer than reported.
  4. D. The numbers only apply to lifters over 6 feet and 200 pounds.
  5. E. The model already accounts for acceleration, so it works for Olympic lifts too.
Show answer

Answer: B — B is correct: the article explicitly says the static 2-D model cannot be used for loads accelerating at a reasonable rate or for movements with a rotational component, so it suits the slow deadlift but not the power clean. A and E contradict the stated model limits. C invents a claim. D is wrong — the model assumes that subject but notes load (not body size) dominates the values.

Scenario 6. You are explaining the technique-before-intensity (threshold training) principle using this article's data. Which point most directly supports it?

  1. A. Compression is the same in good and bad form, so intensity does not matter for safety.
  2. B. Because load is the dominant driver of spinal force, adding weight to a flexed spine multiplies joint shear into clearly injurious ranges (e.g., ~3,799 N at 300 lb rising to ~6,700 N at 600 lb), so intensity must be added only while a neutral spine can be held.
  3. C. Heavier loads automatically force better positions, so just keep adding weight.
  4. D. The safe shear limit rises as load rises, so heavier lifting is self-correcting.
  5. E. Shear is irrelevant; only the athlete's perceived effort should govern load.
Show answer

Answer: B — B is correct: the data show that stacking intensity on a flexed spine drives shear far past the maximal permissible limit, which is exactly why mechanics must precede intensity. A misuses the compression finding to dismiss the real (shear) danger. C is the dangerous myth the article rejects. D and E invent claims with no support in the text.

Scenario 7. An athlete maintains a flat, neutral spine but pulls with a fairly horizontal torso, and a bystander says he is 'doing it wrong because he isn't upright.' How should you respond?

  1. A. The bystander is right; cue the athlete to raise his chest until he is nearly vertical.
  2. B. The torso angle should be set by the athlete's anthropometry; a flat, neutral spine at a more horizontal angle is sound and produces less joint shear than forcing a vertical, rounded position.
  3. C. Have him round slightly to get more upright, since being vertical is the priority.
  4. D. Stop the lift entirely; a horizontal torso always means injury.
  5. E. It does not matter how he positions his spine as long as he finishes the rep.
Show answer

Answer: B — B is correct: trunk alignment is dictated by limb and torso proportions, and a flat back at a more horizontal angle is preferable to a vertical rounded back, which yields more shear. A and C chase 'upright' at the expense of neutral position — the precise error the article warns against. D is an overreaction (a flat horizontal pull is sound). E ignores that spinal position is the safety-critical variable.

D3 · Educating 19% of exam Confidence tier: ___

CFJ_Anatomy_Physiology_Primer.pdf

Open the PDF on Google Drive →

Why this is on the reading list

Anatomy and physiology are the trainer's working vocabulary and the foundation of every cue, scaling decision, and safety call. CrossFit defines its coaching on 'mechanics' and the bone-muscle-joint lever system, so a trainer must understand structure (form) to explain and improve function. This primer directly backs the Educating domain's requirement to teach functional movement characteristics and apply basic anatomy and biomechanics (3.1.6, 4.2.6), and its cardiorespiratory and kidney/hydration sections support lifestyle, recovery, and risk-management judgment (6.2.x, 5.2.3). The exam never tests memorized bone lists; it tests whether you can use this knowledge to coach, communicate professionally, and keep athletes safe.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 3.1.6 Teach descriptive/defining characteristics of functional movements (joints, levers, ranges of motion)
  • 3.1.1 Teach proper execution of movements (form equals function; small anatomical errors degrade performance)
  • 4.2.6 Apply basic principles of anatomy and biomechanics when facilitating correct movement
  • 4.1.1 Identify points of performance (anatomical landmarks that define sound positions)
  • 4.1.6 Identify root cause of faults (structure/biomechanics behind a fault)
  • 4.2.1 Communicate cues to correct unsound mechanics using correct anatomical language
  • 6.2.1 Identify additional lifestyle goals — sleep/recovery context; hydration as recovery/lifestyle
  • 6.2.3 Provide additional lifestyle guidance (drink-to-thirst hydration practice)
  • 6.2.4 Recognize scope-of-practice limitations (hydration/medical guidance boundaries)
  • 6.1.4 Review basic health markers (cardiac adaptation, blood pressure physiology context)
  • 5.2.3 Manage risk for the athlete (dehydration, hyponatremia, heat injury awareness)
  • 5.2.6 Recognize warning signs for possible injury or overexertion (fatigue, anaerobic transition, heat)
  • 1.1.2 Recognize conditions outside CCFT scope that require referral (e.g., cardiac symptoms, hyponatremia)
  • 1.1.3 Assess for rhabdomyolysis risk (kidney filtration of muscle breakdown products — supporting physiology)

What to focus on while reading

  • The opening thesis: trainers create fitness by stressing STRUCTURES to drive FUNCTIONAL change — 'form equals function.' Highlight this; it is the reason the whole article exists and the lens for every exam application.
  • Concrete examples of small anatomical errors that wreck performance: too-narrow a bench-press grip, starting a pull with the bar too far from the shins, running with elbows held away from the body. These are exactly the kind of fault/cue items the Training domain tests.
  • Why anatomy is also a COMMUNICATION tool — the 'pulled his thyroid' and 'ver-tee-byou-lar' examples. Professional credibility and a common language with therapists/clinicians is an exam-relevant point (professionalism, referral handoffs).
  • Bones form LEVERS at moveable joints, making the body a biological machine. Note that adding muscle mass moves the angle of pull toward the optimal ~90 degrees for force; losing mass reduces force-producing protein interactions.
  • Long-bone structure: epiphysis (the two ends), epiphyseal/growth plate, diaphysis (shaft), cancellous (spongy) bone near the ends absorbs stress, compact bone in the shaft, cartilage at joint surfaces, medullary cavity (marrow/blood-cell production), periosteum.
  • MYTH-BUSTER to flag: weighted exercise does NOT harm growth plates. This is a classic 'parent/athlete misconception' the exam can frame as a coaching-communication scenario.
  • Cartilage gets THICKER with appropriate loading — systematically loading bones in exercise is HEALTHY for bone and joint. This refutes the 'lifting wears out your joints' myth.
  • Axial vs. appendicular skeleton: axial = vertical core (skull, vertebral column, ribs, sternum, clavicles); appendicular = the appendages (arms, legs, hands, feet, shoulder girdle, hip bones).
  • Vertebral column notation: C = cervical (7), T = thoracic (12, all attach to ribs), L = lumbar (5), then sacrum and coccyx. Know C/T/L numbering convention (e.g., L1 sits just below T12).
  • The radius is on the THUMB side of the forearm in all orientations — a fixed landmark useful for cueing grip/forearm position.
  • Hip anatomy: ilium, ischium, and pubis fuse to form the acetabulum, the socket where the femur articulates. Hips-knees-ankles are 'the basis of almost all functional exercises.'
  • Muscle micro-structure: actin (thin) and myosin (thick) are the two contractile proteins; one Z-line to the next Z-line = a sarcomere. Contraction shortens sarcomeres, pulling the ends toward the midpoint.
  • The contraction trigger sequence: nerve impulse hits the cell, calcium/sodium/potassium ions shift to spread the impulse, actin and myosin bind and shorten. Calcium is stored in/released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
  • Sarcoplasm = the cell's site of ANAEROBIC metabolism (high-intensity work); mitochondria = AEROBIC metabolism (lower-intensity, long-duration). This anaerobic/aerobic distinction recurs in the lung section.
  • Muscle-tendon continuity: connective tissue (collagen) runs THROUGH the muscle belly, not just tacked on the ends. At the belly the muscle-to-connective ratio is high; toward the ends muscle cells taper and the ratio flips until a tendon proper exists.
  • WHY we want non-stretchy tendons and ligaments: a rope transfers force better than a bungee cord. Stretchy tendons would waste force; stretchy ligaments would invite dislocation.
  • Flexibility/ROM comes mostly from MUSCLE's ability to stretch — not from stretchy tendons or ligaments. Ligaments LIMIT joint travel and guard against dislocation; normal full-ROM exercise carries low ligament/dislocation risk.
  • Joint definition: the bones joined + the tendons of crossing muscles + the ligaments connecting bone to bone. Know what makes up a joint.
  • Movement vocabulary you must be able to USE in cues: flexion (close the book/angle), extension (open the book/angle), abduction/adduction, internal/external rotation, circumduction, protraction/retraction, elevation/depression, opposition, dorsiflexion (toes up) vs. plantar flexion (toes down/heel up).
  • Heart structure: mostly muscle wrapping chambers. Atria (upper, thin-walled) RECEIVE blood and push it down; ventricles (lower, thick-walled) PUMP it out. Left ventricle wall is thickest because it drives systemic circulation against ~100 mmHg vs. ~25 mmHg pulmonary side.
  • Right side = pulmonary side (sends deoxygenated blood to lungs); left side = systemic side (sends oxygenated blood to the body). Ventricular septum is the shared wall.
  • The pulmonary EXCEPTION to the artery/vein rule: pulmonary artery carries DEoxygenated blood, pulmonary vein carries OXYGENATED blood. The generic rule (arteries carry oxygenated away, veins carry deoxygenated toward the heart) has this one reversal.
  • Electrical conduction order: sinoatrial (SA) node is the pacemaker that starts the beat → atrioventricular (AV) node acts as a timer (lets atria finish before ventricles fire) → bundle of His → right/left bundle branches → Purkinje fibers spread the impulse so ventricles contract as one unit. Electrical activity must PRECEDE contraction.
  • THREE hypertrophy types — the highest-yield cardiac concept: (1) PATHOLOGICAL = chamber enlarges, walls THIN (balloon analogy), pumping efficiency corrupted, BAD; (2) ECCENTRIC ('runner's heart') = chamber enlarges AND muscle is added to keep wall thickness normal, pumps high VOLUMES, GOOD; (3) CONCENTRIC = chamber stays same, walls THICKEN to pump against high PRESSURE/resistance (heavy/high-intensity work), GOOD.
  • ANGIOGENESIS: low-oxygen (hypoxic) stress drives growth of new capillaries and arterioles in heart and skeletal muscle — an endurance-friendly adaptation that improves O2 delivery and creates collateral 'detour' vessels (traffic-detour analogy). Helps explain why fit people have fewer heart attacks, though it does NOT prevent disease (atherosclerosis still progresses).
  • Vasculature size order: arteries → arterioles → capillaries (one red blood cell wide) → venules → veins. Veins are larger-diameter and lower-pressure than their paired arteries; the right atrium is the lowest-pressure point, so blood flows down the gradient back to it.
  • Lungs: left has 2 lobes, right has 3. Air path: mouth/nose → larynx → trachea → right/left primary bronchi → branching tree → alveoli. The diaphragm (floor of the thoracic cavity) and the rigid ribcage enable breathing.
  • Alveoli are the gas-exchange engine (~300 million, tennis-court surface area, ~0.3 micron blood-gas barrier). 90% of gas exchange happens at alveoli. Oxygen diffuses in, carbon dioxide diffuses out across this thin barrier.
  • Ventilation responses: aerobic exercise can raise breathing rate 300–400%; near-sprint effort can exceed baseline by >500%, but even that can't keep up — so the body shifts to ANAEROBIC metabolism, which is short-lived, then fatigue forces a slowdown. This is the physiological basis of the technique-intensity threshold and 'redline' fatigue you coach around.
  • Respiratory adaptation: increased VITAL CAPACITY (max air moved in/out per cycle) from nearly every training modality; residual volume drops. There is an anatomical ceiling — training reaches the plateau sooner, it doesn't move the ceiling.
  • Kidney functions (4): eliminate nitrogenous wastes (urea, ammonia, creatinine, uric acid), reabsorb glucose/amino acids, produce hormones (erythropoietin → red cells; renin → blood pressure; calcitriol → vitamin D), and maintain water/electrolyte/acid-base balance.
  • Nephron filtration chain: glomerulus (filters) → Bowman's capsule → proximal convoluted tubule (reabsorption) → loop of Henle (sodium/water balance) → distal convoluted tubule (secretion). Filtration is passive, driven by hydrostatic pressure; big items (red/white cells, platelets, plasma proteins) stay in circulation.
  • Exercise effect on the kidney: exercise-induced hypertension raises filtration rate UNLESS heavy sweat loss causes dehydration, which slows filtration; sustained heavy training can lower resting glomerular filtration rate.
  • Water balance hormone: arginine vasopressin (AVP / ADH). Hypothalamus senses concentrated blood → releases AVP → reabsorbs water. Big returning fluid load → AVP inhibited → water removed.
  • Sodium is the largest extracellular solute and sets osmolarity; dehydration loses proportionally MORE water than sodium, raising sodium concentration, so the kidney conserves water as a survival response.
  • The DEHYDRATION CONTINUUM and its thresholds: thirst kicks in around ~2% body-weight loss; ~5% is where performance losses and symptoms begin; death risk around ~16% (a 200-lb male losing ~32 lb / ~4 gallons). A gallon of water weighs ~8.3 lb / 3.8 kg.
  • Practical time-to-dehydration math: severe exercise in severe heat/humidity can cost up to 1.5 L/hr; reaching 5% loss requires avoiding fluids and near-max effort in high heat for roughly 80–210 minutes. Sessions under 30–60 minutes carry no dehydration danger and no benefit from drinking.
  • HEAT INJURY vs. hydration: in normal training even in heat, hydration status does NOT strongly correlate with heat injury. Adding water to a heat-injured person does not cure them — LOWERING body temperature does. (Dousing with water to cool can beat drinking it.)
  • HYPONATREMIA: low blood sodium from OVER-drinking (hyper-hydration). Most common in SLOW marathon runners who sweat less yet drink heavily before/during/after. Following one-size-fits-all pre/during/after guidelines without individualization can over-hydrate ~half of runners.
  • The article's coaching bottom line on hydration: trust THIRST. Make drinks available when athletes are thirsty — that avoids both under- and over-hydration. This is the applied takeaway most likely to appear as a scenario.

Concepts to understand

  • Form equals function: you cannot reliably improve or correct a movement without understanding the structure producing it. Use anatomy to diagnose WHY a fault happens (root cause) and to craft the cue that fixes it — not to recite names.
  • The body as a system of levers: bones are levers, joints are fulcrums, muscles apply force. Mechanical efficiency depends on positions and angles of pull (toward ~90 degrees), which is why 'small' setup errors (grip width, bar distance from shins, elbow position) meaningfully change force and performance.
  • Anatomical/physiological language as professional currency: precise terms (vertebral not 'ver-tee-byou-lar') build credibility, enable clean handoffs to clinicians/therapists, and underpin clear cueing. Sloppy anatomy signals incompetence and can erode athlete trust.
  • Bone and joint loading is health-PROMOTING: appropriate load thickens cartilage and strengthens bone; weighted exercise does not damage growth plates. Be able to correct the common 'lifting wears out joints / stunts growth' myths confidently and accurately.
  • Axial vs. appendicular organization, and the C/T/L vertebral notation — enough to communicate about regions (e.g., 'lumbar' vs. 'thoracic') and understand spinal positioning cues, not to itemize every bone.
  • Muscle contraction mechanics at a usable level: actin and myosin slide within sarcomeres on a calcium-triggered, ion-mediated signal. Understand that contraction = sarcomere shortening transmitted through connective tissue to bone — this is how a cue ('pull the bar to the body') translates to force on a lever.
  • Muscle-tendon-ligament force transfer and the 'rope vs. bungee' principle: stiff tendons transmit force efficiently; ligaments cap joint range to prevent dislocation. ROM is primarily a muscle-stretch property — informs mobility coaching and why full-ROM training is generally safe.
  • Joint anatomy and movement vocabulary as the basis for points of performance and cues: flexion/extension, ab-/adduction, internal/external rotation, dorsiflexion/plantar flexion, etc. You must be able to NAME the movement you want and translate it into a short, actionable cue.
  • Heart as an adaptable pump: chamber/wall structure follows the workload (atria receive, ventricles pump; left side is high-pressure systemic). Structure changes with training (or detraining), with performance and health consequences.
  • The three hypertrophy types and what training drives each: endurance/volume work → eccentric ('runner's heart'); high-intensity/high-resistance work → concentric; disease (not training) → pathological wall-thinning. Distinguishing 'good' adaptive hypertrophy from pathological is the key conceptual discrimination here and reinforces that varied CrossFit programming drives broad cardiac adaptation.
  • Angiogenesis as an endurance and survival adaptation: hypoxic training stimulus builds new capillaries/collateral vessels, improving oxygen delivery and providing 'detour' routes — part of why fitness lowers cardiac-event frequency, even though it doesn't make anyone immune to disease.
  • Aerobic vs. anaerobic transition and ventilation: there is a point where breathing can't supply enough oxygen, metabolism goes anaerobic, and fatigue forces a slowdown. This physiology underlies pacing, the technique-breaks-down-at-high-intensity reality, and recognizing overexertion.
  • Respiratory trainability and its ceiling: training raises vital capacity and breathing efficiency up to an individual anatomical limit. Manage athlete expectations — conditioning improves how fast and how fully you use your lungs, not the size of the lungs themselves.
  • Kidney/fluid homeostasis basics: the nephron filters by pressure and reabsorbs what the body needs; AVP/ADH and sodium balance regulate how much water is kept or excreted. Sodium sets osmolarity, which is why both dehydration and over-hydration are sodium-concentration problems.
  • The rhabdomyolysis link (supporting physiology): intense/novel/eccentric muscle work can break down muscle and dump products (like myoglobin and creatinine) into the blood that the kidneys must filter. Understanding kidney filtration explains why rhabdo is a medical emergency and a referral, even though the primer doesn't name rhabdo directly.
  • Evidence-based hydration practice: drink-to-thirst beats rigid pre/during/after volume rules for typical training. Under-hydration impairs but is rarely dangerous in short sessions; over-hydration can cause hyponatremia. The coach's job is to make fluids available and let thirst guide intake.
  • Heat injury is a TEMPERATURE problem, not primarily a hydration problem: cooling the athlete is the priority response; drinking water does not fix heat illness. This reframes a very common coaching misconception and is a safety-critical distinction.
  • Scope-of-practice and referral judgment around physiology: cardiac symptoms, suspected hyponatremia, suspected rhabdo, or heat illness are medical events — the trainer manages immediate risk (cool, summon help, stop activity) and refers, rather than diagnosing or treating.

How the exam applies this

Expect these concepts as coaching scenarios, not recall. A 'why does this fault happen / what cue fixes it' item tests form-equals-function and lever mechanics (4.1.6, 4.2.6, 4.2.1); a parent worried that lifting will stunt a teen's growth or 'wear out' joints tests the growth-plate and cartilage-loading facts as a communication problem (3.1.6, 5.1.3). Hydration and heat scenarios are highly likely: an athlete asking how much water to drink, a long hot session, a slow marathoner who over-drinks, or an athlete showing heat-illness signs — all test drink-to-thirst guidance, the dehydration continuum, hyponatremia awareness, cooling-over-drinking for heat injury, and knowing when to refer (6.2.1, 6.2.3, 6.2.4, 5.2.3, 5.2.6, 1.1.2). Cardiac-adaptation items may ask you to identify good (eccentric/concentric) versus pathological hypertrophy or explain why a fit athlete adapts, reinforcing that varied programming builds broad cardiorespiratory fitness (6.1.4, 3.1.9).

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Form equals function
The principle that an anatomical structure's shape determines what it can do; to improve or correct a movement you must understand the structure producing it.
Lever (biological machine)
A bone acting as a rigid bar that rotates around a joint (fulcrum) when a muscle applies force; the bone-muscle-joint assembly produces all movement.
Angle of pull
The angle at which a muscle pulls on a bone; force application is most effective near 90 degrees, and added muscle mass can shift the angle toward that optimum.
Epiphysis
The end of a long bone (there are two per long bone).
Epiphyseal plate (growth plate)
Cartilage layer between epiphysis and diaphysis where bone grows in length; it fuses at maturity. Weighted exercise does not harm it.
Diaphysis
The shaft (long middle portion) of a long bone.
Cancellous (spongy) bone
Porous bone found nearer the bone ends that helps absorb mechanical stress.
Compact bone
Dense mineralized bone in the shaft that provides support and protection.
Cartilage
Fibrous tissue lining joint surfaces; it thickens with appropriate loading, so systematic loading is healthy for joints.
Medullary cavity
The central hollow of a long bone housing marrow, which produces blood cells.
Periosteum
The fibrous sheath covering the outer surface of a bone.
Axial skeleton
The body's vertical core: skull, vertebral column, ribs, sternum, and collarbones.
Appendicular skeleton
The appendages and their girdles: arms, legs, hands, feet, shoulder, and hip bones.
Vertebral notation (C/T/L)
Cervical (C, 7), thoracic (T, 12 — all attach to ribs), and lumbar (L, 5) vertebrae numbered top-down (e.g., L1 sits just below T12).
Acetabulum
The hip socket formed where the ilium, ischium, and pubis fuse; the femur articulates here.
Actin
The thin contractile protein (thin filament) of muscle that interacts with myosin to produce contraction.
Myosin
The thick contractile protein (thick filament) of muscle that binds actin to shorten the sarcomere.
Sarcomere
The basic contractile unit of muscle, spanning one Z-line to the next; it shortens during contraction.
Sarcoplasm
Muscle-cell cytoplasm and the site of anaerobic (non-oxygen) metabolism supporting high-intensity work.
Mitochondria
Cell 'powerhouses' that run aerobic (oxygen-requiring) metabolism (Krebs cycle, electron transport) for lower-intensity, longer-duration work.
Sarcoplasmic reticulum
The muscle cell's calcium store; rapid calcium release into the sarcoplasm initiates contraction.
Tendon
Connective tissue that transmits muscle force to bone; its collagen network actually runs through the muscle belly, becoming a discrete tendon where muscle cells run out.
Ligament
Dense collagen band connecting bone to bone that limits joint range and guards against dislocation; not meant to be stretchy.
Joint
The functional unit made of the bones joined, the tendons of muscles crossing it, and the ligaments connecting the bones.
Range of motion (ROM)/flexibility
How far a joint can move, governed mostly by muscle's ability to stretch (not by stretchy tendons or ligaments).
Flexion / Extension
Flexion closes a joint angle (like closing a book); extension opens it (like opening a book).
Abduction / Adduction
Abduction moves a limb away from the body's midline; adduction moves it toward the midline.
Dorsiflexion / Plantar flexion
Dorsiflexion lifts the toes/foot toward the shin; plantar flexion points the foot down (heel up), as in pushing on a shovel.
Circumduction
Circular movement of a limb combining flexion, extension, abduction, and adduction (e.g., arm circles).
Atrium (plural atria)
Thin-walled upper heart chambers that receive incoming blood and push it into the ventricles.
Ventricle
Thick-walled lower heart chambers that pump blood out; the left ventricle is thickest because it drives systemic circulation.
Ventricular septum
The shared muscular wall dividing the right and left ventricles.
Pulmonary (right) side
Right atrium and ventricle; receive deoxygenated blood from the body and send it to the lungs (low pressure, ~25 mmHg).
Systemic (left) side
Left atrium and ventricle; receive oxygenated blood from the lungs and deliver it to the body (high pressure, ~100 mmHg).
Pulmonary exception
The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood and the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood — the reverse of the usual artery/vein rule.
Sinoatrial (SA) node
The heart's natural pacemaker that initiates each heartbeat in the atria.
Atrioventricular (AV) node
The conduction relay/timer that delays the impulse so the atria finish contracting before the ventricles fire.
Bundle of His / bundle branches / Purkinje fibers
The conduction pathway from the AV node that spreads the impulse so both ventricles contract as a single coordinated unit.
Pathological hypertrophy
Disease-driven heart enlargement where the chamber grows but walls thin (no added muscle), corrupting pumping efficiency — a bad adaptation.
Eccentric hypertrophy ('runner's heart')
Beneficial adaptation where the ventricular chamber enlarges AND muscle is added to keep wall thickness normal, enabling higher blood volumes (endurance training).
Concentric hypertrophy
Beneficial adaptation where chamber size stays the same but ventricular walls thicken to pump against high pressure/resistance (high-intensity/heavy work).
Angiogenesis
Growth of new capillaries and arterioles in response to low-oxygen stress, improving oxygen delivery and creating collateral 'detour' vessels in heart and muscle.
Artery / Arteriole / Capillary / Venule / Vein
The vessel size sequence; capillaries are one red-blood-cell wide and the site of exchange; veins are larger and lower-pressure than their paired arteries.
Alveoli
The ~300 million tiny lung air sacs (tennis-court surface area) where ~90% of oxygen/carbon-dioxide exchange occurs across a very thin blood-gas barrier.
Blood-gas barrier
The ~0.3-micron membrane between alveolar air and capillary blood across which oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse.
Aerobic vs. anaerobic metabolism
Aerobic = oxygen-using energy production for lower-intensity/longer work (mitochondria); anaerobic = non-oxygen, high-intensity, short-lived energy production (sarcoplasm).
Vital capacity
The maximum volume of air moved in and then out in one respiratory cycle; improves with training up to an individual anatomical ceiling.
Nephron / Glomerulus / Bowman's capsule
The kidney's filtering unit: the glomerulus (capillary tuft) filters blood by pressure into Bowman's capsule to begin urine formation.
Loop of Henle
The nephron segment central to sodium and water balance via differential permeability to sodium and water along its descending and ascending limbs.
Glomerular filtration
Passive, pressure-driven filtering of water and small solutes from blood; rises with higher blood pressure and slows with dehydration.
Arginine vasopressin (AVP / ADH)
The anti-diuretic hormone released when blood is too concentrated; it drives water reabsorption to restore balance.
Osmolarity
Solute concentration of body fluids (largely set by sodium); dehydration raises it by losing proportionally more water than sodium.
Dehydration continuum
The progression of effects by percent body-weight water loss: thirst ~2%, performance loss/symptoms begin ~5%, death risk ~16%.
Hyponatremia
Dangerously low blood sodium caused by over-drinking; most common in slow marathon runners who sweat little yet drink heavily.
Drink-to-thirst
Evidence-based hydration practice of making fluids available and letting thirst guide intake, avoiding both under- and over-hydration.
Heat injury
Heat-related illness driven by elevated body temperature; treated by cooling the athlete, not by adding water — hydration status correlates weakly with it in normal training.
Erythropoietin / Renin / Calcitriol
Kidney-produced hormones regulating red-blood-cell production, blood pressure, and vitamin D metabolism, respectively.
Nitrogenous wastes
Protein/nucleic-acid breakdown products (urea, ammonia, creatinine, uric acid) the kidneys eliminate; their presence is a marker of metabolic load.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • Cardiac warning signs (chest pain, unusual shortness of breath, fainting, palpitations) are outside the trainer's scope — stop activity and refer for medical evaluation; do not attempt to diagnose hypertrophy or any cardiac condition.
  • Heat illness is a temperature emergency: the correct response is to COOL the athlete by any means (shade, water dousing, ice, fanning) and summon medical help — drinking water does NOT treat heat injury. Misremembering this can be life-threatening.
  • Hyponatremia (over-hydration): an athlete in a long event who has been drinking heavily and shows confusion, nausea, headache, or swelling may be over-hydrated — this is a medical emergency requiring referral, NOT more water.
  • Rhabdomyolysis risk (supporting physiology): intense, novel, or heavily eccentric workloads can break down muscle and overload kidney filtration; dark/cola-colored urine, severe disproportionate muscle pain, and swelling are red flags requiring immediate medical referral (links to tasks 1.1.3 and 1.1.2).
  • Avoid rigid one-size-fits-all hydration mandates (forced pre/during/after volumes): they can push athletes into over-hydration and hyponatremia; coach drink-to-thirst and keep fluids available instead.
  • Do not give clinical or medical-nutrition diagnoses about fluids, electrolytes, kidney function, or cardiac adaptation — recognize scope-of-practice limits (6.2.4) and refer to qualified professionals when an athlete presents symptoms or asks for medical advice.
  • Correct, don't reinforce, dangerous myths: weighted exercise does not damage growth plates and appropriate loading is good for bone/joint health — but always defer to a physician for any athlete with a known orthopedic condition or injury.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. A parent of a 14-year-old worries that letting their child do weighted squats and deadlifts will 'stunt his growth' by damaging the growth plates. What is the best response?

  1. A. Agree and keep the teen to bodyweight movements only until skeletal maturity to be safe.
  2. B. Explain that properly coached weighted exercise does not harm growth plates, and that appropriate loading actually supports healthy bone and joint development.
  3. C. Tell the parent growth plates are irrelevant to exercise and dismiss the concern.
  4. D. Refer the family to an endocrinologist before allowing any loaded movement.
  5. E. Recommend the teen avoid all squatting until age 18.
Show answer

Answer: B — The primer explicitly states weighted exercise does nothing to harm the epiphyseal (growth) plates and that systematic loading thickens cartilage and benefits bone/joint health (3.1.6, 5.1.3). B corrects the myth accurately while keeping a professional tone. A and E act on a false belief; C is dismissive and erodes trust; D is an unnecessary referral with no symptoms.

Scenario 2. It's a hot, humid day and an athlete collapses near the end of a 12-minute outdoor metcon — flushed, disoriented, and very hot to the touch. What is your priority action?

  1. A. Immediately have them drink as much water as possible to rehydrate.
  2. B. Give an electrolyte/sodium drink to correct presumed hyponatremia.
  3. C. Begin cooling them by any means available (shade, dousing with water, ice, fanning) and activate medical help.
  4. D. Walk them around to keep blood flowing until they feel better.
  5. E. Have them sit and finish the workout once they catch their breath.
Show answer

Answer: C — The article states that for a heat-injured person, getting body temperature DOWN — not adding water to the gut — is what helps; hydration status correlates weakly with heat injury (5.2.3, 5.2.6, 1.1.2). C cools and escalates appropriately. A and B assume a fluid problem and could worsen outcomes; D and E delay treatment of a temperature emergency.

Scenario 3. A member asks how much water she should force herself to drink during a typical 45-minute class to perform her best. What is the most evidence-aligned guidance?

  1. A. Drink a fixed large volume every 15 minutes regardless of thirst to stay ahead of dehydration.
  2. B. Drink to thirst and keep water available; a session under about 30–60 minutes carries no dehydration danger and no performance benefit from forced drinking.
  3. C. Avoid all fluids during training because drinking impairs performance.
  4. D. Pre-load 1–2 liters right before class and avoid drinking during it.
  5. E. Weigh herself before and after every class and replace exactly that weight in water mid-session.
Show answer

Answer: B — Per the primer, the average training session isn't long enough to cause meaningful dehydration, thirst is a reliable safeguard (~2% loss), and forcing fluids risks over-hydration/hyponatremia (6.2.1, 6.2.3, 6.2.4). B is the drink-to-thirst recommendation the article endorses. A and D promote over-hydration; C is false (severe dehydration does impair); E is impractical and unnecessary for a short session.

Scenario 4. An experienced endurance athlete's physical shows an enlarged heart with an enlarged left-ventricular chamber and NORMAL wall thickness, and her physician calls it a benign training adaptation. Which concept best explains this?

  1. A. Pathological hypertrophy — the chamber enlarged and walls thinned.
  2. B. Concentric hypertrophy — walls thickened against high pressure.
  3. C. Eccentric hypertrophy ('runner's heart') — chamber enlarged with added muscle keeping wall thickness normal, improving high-volume pumping.
  4. D. Angiogenesis — growth of new capillaries reduced wall thickness.
  5. E. Atrophy — the heart shrank from detraining.
Show answer

Answer: C — Eccentric hypertrophy enlarges the ventricular chamber and ADDS muscle to keep the wall at normal thickness, enabling higher blood volumes — the classic endurance ('runner's heart') adaptation (6.1.4). A is the disease pattern (chamber up, walls thin). B describes thickened walls from high-resistance work, which doesn't match a normal-thickness wall. D is a vascular adaptation, not chamber remodeling. E is the opposite of enlargement.

Scenario 5. A coach cues an athlete to bring the elbows in close while running and to start the deadlift with the bar against the shins, explaining that these 'small' positions matter. What anatomical principle is the coach applying?

  1. A. Stretchier tendons transfer force better, so tighter positions stretch the tendons.
  2. B. Form equals function — small anatomical/positional errors (e.g., elbows held away, bar too far from shins) change the lever mechanics and meaningfully reduce force and performance.
  3. C. Ligament laxity increases range of motion and thus power.
  4. D. Anaerobic metabolism only works when limbs are close to the body.
  5. E. Cartilage thins under load, so positions must minimize joint contact.
Show answer

Answer: B — The primer opens with form-equals-function and gives these exact examples (elbows away when running, bar too far from shins) as small anatomical errors that significantly reduce performance via altered lever mechanics (4.2.6, 4.1.6, 4.2.1). A is false — we want stiff, rope-like tendons. C is false and dangerous (ligament laxity invites dislocation). D and E are unrelated/incorrect physiology.

Scenario 6. During a long, hot competition workout, a slower-paced athlete who has been sipping water steadily for hours becomes nauseated, confused, and has a headache, with no signs of being overheated. What should the coach suspect and do?

  1. A. Severe dehydration — have him drink several more cups of water quickly.
  2. B. Possible hyponatremia from over-drinking — stop giving plain water, stop the athlete, and get medical help.
  3. C. Normal fatigue — tell him to push through the last round.
  4. D. Low blood sugar — give a large bolus of water with the meal.
  5. E. Muscle cramp — stretch and continue.
Show answer

Answer: B — Hyponatremia (low blood sodium) is most common in slow runners who sweat little yet drink heavily before/during/after; symptoms like nausea, confusion, and headache without overheating fit, and MORE plain water makes it worse (5.2.3, 6.2.4, 1.1.2). B halts water, stops activity, and refers. A directly worsens the condition; C and E ignore a medical emergency; D misattributes the cause and still pushes fluid.

Scenario 7. An athlete who did an unusually high-volume, eccentric-heavy session two days ago now has severe, disproportionate muscle soreness, swelling, and dark cola-colored urine. What is the appropriate coaching action?

  1. A. Program a light recovery workout and tell him to hydrate and stretch.
  2. B. Reassure him it's normal delayed-onset soreness and to train through it.
  3. C. Treat it as a possible medical emergency (rhabdomyolysis) and refer him for immediate medical evaluation.
  4. D. Recommend a sauna session to flush it out.
  5. E. Give him salt tablets to fix the dark urine.
Show answer

Answer: C — Dark urine, swelling, and severe disproportionate pain after intense/novel/eccentric work are classic rhabdomyolysis red flags; the kidney must filter muscle-breakdown products, making this a medical emergency well outside trainer scope (1.1.3, 1.1.2, 5.2.6). C refers immediately. A, B, D, and E delay care, mask the problem, or risk worsening it — none address a potentially organ-threatening condition.

Scenario 8. When teaching the difference between flexion and extension at the elbow, which explanation is both accurate and most usable as a cue framework?

  1. A. Flexion opens the joint angle; extension closes it.
  2. B. Flexion closes the joint angle (like closing a book); extension opens it (like opening a book).
  3. C. Flexion and extension both describe rotation around the long axis of the bone.
  4. D. Flexion is movement away from the midline; extension is movement toward it.
  5. E. Flexion only occurs in the lower body; extension only in the upper body.
Show answer

Answer: B — The primer defines extension as opening the joint angle like opening a book and flexion as closing it like closing a book (3.1.6, 4.2.1). B is correct and gives an intuitive coaching analogy. A reverses the definitions; C describes rotation, not flexion/extension; D describes adduction/abduction; E is simply false.

Scenario 9. A new coach wants to know why CrossFit requires trainers to learn anatomy and physiology if the exam doesn't ask them to memorize every bone. What is the best rationale to give?

  1. A. So they can perform medical diagnoses on athletes during class.
  2. B. So they understand the structures they're stressing to drive functional change, can find root causes of faults, cue precisely, and communicate professionally with athletes and clinicians.
  3. C. Mostly to pass licensing boards required to open a gym.
  4. D. Because clients expect trainers to recite Latin bone names on demand.
  5. E. It isn't really necessary; cueing can be learned without any anatomy.
Show answer

Answer: B — The article frames anatomy/physiology as the means to understand the materials you work with (form equals function), to diagnose and correct movement, and as a shared professional language with therapists and clinicians (4.2.6, 4.1.6, 3.1.6). B captures the applied purpose. A exceeds scope; C and D miss the point; E contradicts the article's central thesis.

Scenario 10. Which statement correctly applies the 'pulmonary exception' that a coach might reference when explaining circulation to a curious athlete?

  1. A. All arteries carry oxygenated blood and all veins carry deoxygenated blood, with no exceptions.
  2. B. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs and the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood back to the heart — the reverse of the usual rule.
  3. C. The pulmonary vein carries deoxygenated blood, like all other veins.
  4. D. The aorta carries deoxygenated blood to the body.
  5. E. The right ventricle pumps oxygenated blood into systemic circulation.
Show answer

Answer: B — The primer notes the pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein are exceptions: the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood and the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood. B states this correctly. A ignores the exception; C and D state the wrong oxygenation; E confuses the pulmonary (right) side with systemic (left)-side function.

D3 · Educating 19% of exam Confidence tier: ___

CFJ_Coaching_Bergeron.pdf

Open the PDF on Google Drive →

Why this is on the reading list

Bergeron's article reframes coaching as more than fault-correction: a great coach builds a relationship through awareness, trust, and intentional language, and that relationship is what unlocks an athlete's willingness to be taught and pushed. For the CCFT exam this backs the 'Educating' domain's relational tasks (layering instruction to the athlete in front of you, teaching concepts in a way they actually absorb) and bleeds heavily into communication, rapport, and motivation. The exam tests whether a candidate can read an individual athlete, choose the right communication strategy, and frame cues so they help rather than hurt performance.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 3.1.2 Layer instruction to meet athlete capability
  • 3.1.1 Teach proper execution of movements
  • 4.2.1 Communicate cues to correct unsound mechanics
  • 4.2.2 Use multiple cueing strategies (visual, tactile, verbal)
  • 4.2.3 Utilize effective cues (short, specific, actionable)
  • 4.2.4 Reinforce sound mechanics
  • 4.2.8 Balance relentlessness with acknowledgement of improvement
  • 5.1.2 Create a culture/community of excellence and camaraderie
  • 5.1.3 Establish rapport and adapt approach based on athlete response
  • 5.1.4 Lead by example
  • 1.1.4 Assess psychological tolerance for training
  • 1.2.3 Identify athlete's fitness goals

What to focus on while reading

  • The distinction Bergeron draws between a 'good coach' (sees and corrects faults, gets athletes to move better) and a 'great coach' (connects with athletes beyond the movement) — note this is a both/and, not a replacement for mechanics.
  • The definition of 'the deeper side of coaching': developing awareness of an athlete's potential, building trust, and creating an atmosphere of success.
  • The stated true goal of coaching: to improve the lives, health, and happiness of clients — not just to improve a Fran time.
  • The three pillars the article is organized around: Awareness, Trust, and Coach the Positive. Be able to define each and give a coaching example.
  • The 'Awareness' concept: reading individual athletes — what motivates them, what they can/can't do, whether they learn visually or verbally, whether competition fires them up or turns them off, their mood and focus that day.
  • The Coach's Prep Course term 'presence and attitude' and its definition: interpersonal skills; the trainer's responsibility to determine how to relate to and motivate each individual because each person has different needs.
  • The contrast between 'treat others as you want to be treated' (good) and 'treat athletes the way THEY want to be treated' (great) — the failure mode of coaching everyone the way YOU like to be coached.
  • Trust as the foundation of the athlete-coach relationship and the claim that athletes who trust their coach will do anything asked of them.
  • The counterintuitive point that great coaches build trust by LISTENING, not by showing how knowledgeable they are. Note the limit of over-explaining the 'whys' — it helps but doesn't by itself create deep trust.
  • The Covey quote 'True influence comes as others sense that you are being influenced by them' and what it implies about really listening vs. waiting for your turn to talk.
  • The concrete trust-building practice at CrossFit New England: deliberately scheduling down time so coaches spend ~5 minutes after class talking with (listening to) newer athletes.
  • The second key to trust: character, conduct, and leading by example — living with integrity, and specifically being 'loyal to those who are not present' (defending absent members vs. gossiping).
  • The mechanism of 'Coach the Positive': what a coach says gets replayed in the athlete's mind and can become a self-fulfilling prophecy, for better or worse.
  • The specific reframes: 'you need to work on your gymnastics' vs. 'with your work ethic you'll get better at gymnastics'; 'I can't believe how fast you did that' vs. 'Wow, you were so fast today — keep it up.'
  • The subconscious-mind claim: the mind ignores the negation and focuses on the action — 'Don't put the bar down' is heard as 'put the bar down'; 'Don't slow down' makes the athlete hear 'slow.'
  • The positive replacement cues Bergeron offers: 'Big set,' 'Get one more,' instead of 'Don't put the bar down.'
  • The progression of habit: words lead to actions, actions to habits, habits to destiny — and the responsibility this places on a coach's language.
  • The implementation guidance: don't try to apply all the drills at once — pick one, gauge the reaction, reflect on what worked, and adjust.
  • The note that these relationship tools scale: start one-on-one, then use them with small groups, teams, and classes (and even outside the gym).
  • The author's credibility context: Ben Bergeron, 15+ years coaching, Level 1 Seminar Staff, coached CrossFit New England's affiliate team to a 2011 Games win — i.e., this is a high-level practitioner's view of coaching, not theory.

Concepts to understand

  • Coaching is fault-correction PLUS relationship: seeing and fixing mechanics makes you good; connecting with and understanding the individual athlete is what makes coaching great and durable. On the exam, the 'best' answer usually integrates both, not one at the expense of the other.
  • Individualization of approach (presence and attitude): the same instruction must be delivered differently to different athletes. The coach's job is to determine how to relate to and motivate THIS person — by personality, learning style, mood, and goal — rather than applying a single style to everyone.
  • Reading the athlete in real time: a coach continuously assesses whether the message is landing (absorbing vs. lost), which cue types work, whether the athlete is energized or shut down by competition or the spotlight, and adjusts on the spot. This is the relational side of layering instruction (3.1.2) and adapting approach (5.1.3).
  • Goal individualization: not every athlete is chasing a faster benchmark; some train for health, stress relief, community, or longevity. Identifying the real goal (1.2.3) changes how you coach and motivate them.
  • Trust is earned and it yields compliance and effort: when an athlete trusts the coach, they buy into hard or unglamorous instruction. Trust is built over months/years, so coaching is a long game, not a single session.
  • Listening builds trust more than expertise display: deep, sincere listening (being visibly influenced by the athlete) creates trust; lecturing the 'whys' demonstrates competence but does not, by itself, create connection. Knowing the science is necessary but not sufficient.
  • Lead-by-example and integrity as trust drivers: a coach's conduct — including loyalty to people who aren't in the room (no gossip) — signals trustworthiness to everyone present. This is 5.1.4 and feeds gym culture (5.1.2).
  • Language shapes performance and self-belief: coaching statements are replayed and can become self-fulfilling. Framing matters — affirming effort and capability ('with your work ethic...') builds athletes up; labeling weakness or expressing disbelief tears them down.
  • Positive cueing / phrasing cues as actions, not negations: cue the action you WANT, not the one you fear, because the mind focuses on the named action and drops the 'don't.' Replace 'Don't put the bar down' with 'Big set'; replace 'Don't slow down' with 'Finish strong.' This is the practical core of effective cueing (4.2.3).
  • Acknowledging improvement alongside correction: positive, sincere reinforcement ('Keep it up!') is part of coaching, not flattery — it balances relentless fault-correction with recognition so athletes stay motivated (4.2.8, 4.2.4).
  • Deliberate systems for relationship-building: trust isn't left to chance — Bergeron engineers it (scheduled down time, a five-minute post-class conversation with newer members). A coach/affiliate can structure the environment to produce connection.
  • Skill-building progression for coaching itself: master one relational tool at a time, observe the athlete's reaction, reflect, and adjust — the same iterative, feedback-driven approach used to teach movement applies to developing your own coaching.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenario questions that put you with a specific athlete and ask for the BEST coaching response: an athlete who shuts down under competitive pressure, a newer member who isn't bonding with the gym, an athlete repeatedly told 'don't put the bar down' who keeps dropping it, or a coach deciding how to build buy-in. The strongest answers individualize the approach (presence and attitude, 5.1.3), use short positive action cues instead of negations (4.2.3), build trust by listening rather than lecturing, and pair correction with sincere acknowledgement of progress (4.2.8). Watch for distractors that are technically true but relationship-blind — e.g., delivering accurate biomechanics in a way that ignores the athlete's mood, goal, or learning style.

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

The deeper side of coaching
Bergeron's term for coaching beyond movement correction: developing awareness of an athlete's potential, building trust, and creating an atmosphere of success — i.e., the athlete-coach relationship.
Good coach vs. great coach
A good coach reliably sees and corrects faults so athletes move better; a great coach does that AND connects with, reads, and understands each athlete as an individual.
Awareness
Reading an athlete to learn what motivates them, what they can and can't do, how they learn, and how they're responding in the moment, then tailoring coaching to that person.
Presence and attitude
A Coach's Prep Course term for a trainer's interpersonal skills — recognizing that each person has different needs and that it is the trainer's responsibility to figure out how to relate to and motivate each individual.
Trust (athlete-coach)
The foundation of the relationship; when present, athletes will buy into and execute even hard or unglamorous instruction. Built over time, primarily through listening and consistent character.
Listening to build trust
Building trust by deeply and sincerely understanding the athlete (letting yourself be influenced by them) rather than by demonstrating how much you know.
Loyalty to those not present
Defending absent members instead of gossiping about them; a visible display of integrity that builds trust with everyone who is present.
Coach the positive
Framing coaching language to set athletes up for success, because what a coach says is replayed and can become a self-fulfilling prophecy.
Self-fulfilling prophecy (in coaching)
The idea that a coach's repeated words become an athlete's belief and then their behavior — affirming words build the athlete up; doubting or labeling words tear them down.
Positive (action) cueing
Cueing the action you want rather than negating the one you don't, because the mind focuses on the named action and ignores the 'don't' — e.g., 'Big set' instead of 'Don't put the bar down.'
Lead by example
Earning influence through your own character and conduct so athletes feel confident following you; one of the two keys (with listening) to building trust.
Atmosphere of success
An environment a coach intentionally creates — through connection, trust, and positive language — in which athletes expect to improve; scalable from one athlete to a whole class.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • The article is about the relational and communication side of coaching, not medical screening — it does not cover injury referral, rhabdo, or scope-of-practice limits. Don't import safety content the text doesn't contain.
  • 'Athletes who trust their coach will do anything the coach asks' is a point about buy-in, NOT a license to push past safe limits — a great coach's authority is still bounded by sound mechanics, appropriate scaling, and the athlete's physical and psychological tolerance.
  • Reading an athlete's mood, focus, and psychological state connects to assessing psychological tolerance for training (1.1.4); a coach who senses an athlete is checked out or overwhelmed should adjust the session, not simply push harder.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. During 'Grace,' you keep telling an athlete 'Don't put the bar down,' yet she keeps dropping it after nearly every rep. Based on Bergeron's view of coaching language, what is the BEST adjustment?

  1. A. Say it louder and more often so the instruction sticks
  2. B. Switch to a positive action cue like 'Big set' or 'Get one more'
  3. C. Stop cueing entirely and let her self-regulate
  4. D. Tell her she's not strong enough yet and should scale the load
  5. E. Explain the physiology of why touch-and-go is more efficient
Show answer

Answer: B — Bergeron argues the mind focuses on the named action and ignores the negation, so 'Don't put the bar down' is heard as 'put the bar down.' Cue the action you want instead — 'Big set,' 'Get one more.' A just amplifies the counterproductive cue; C abandons coaching; D is a discouraging label and an unprompted scaling assumption; E shows knowledge but doesn't fix the framing problem and adds noise mid-effort.

Scenario 2. A new member is technically competent but hasn't connected with the gym and seems likely to quit. Drawing on Bergeron's 'Trust' section, what is the MOST effective coach action?

  1. A. Give her a detailed written breakdown of her movement faults to show you're invested
  2. B. Pair her with the fittest athlete so she's motivated to keep up
  3. C. Spend about five minutes after class genuinely listening to and talking with her
  4. D. Publicly praise her in front of the class to make her feel included
  5. E. Send her extra programming so she has homework between sessions
Show answer

Answer: C — Bergeron describes deliberately using post-class down time to spend ~5 minutes with newer athletes, building trust primarily through listening. A and E lead with information/output rather than connection; B can backfire for an athlete turned off by competition; D may embarrass someone who prefers the shadows — the article warns coaches to read individual preferences.

Scenario 3. Two athletes need the same correction (staying on their heels in the squat), but one loves competition and the spotlight while the other is quiet and easily discouraged. What does Bergeron's concept of 'presence and attitude' suggest?

  1. A. Deliver the identical cue to both — consistency is fairness
  2. B. Coach each athlete the way YOU personally prefer to be coached
  3. C. Adapt how you deliver and frame the correction to each athlete's personality and response
  4. D. Only correct the competitive athlete, since the quiet one will be discouraged
  5. E. Skip the correction for both to protect morale
Show answer

Answer: C — 'Presence and attitude' is the trainer's responsibility to determine how to relate to and motivate each individual; great coaches treat athletes the way THEY want to be treated, not identically and not the way the coach prefers. A and B are the exact failure modes Bergeron names; D and E abandon coaching the movement, which is still the job — only the delivery should differ.

Scenario 4. An athlete finishes a tough workout with a surprisingly fast time. Which response best reflects Bergeron's 'coach the positive' principle?

  1. A. 'I can't believe how fast you did that.'
  2. B. 'Did you count all your reps? That seems too fast.'
  3. C. 'Wow, you were so fast today — keep it up!'
  4. D. 'That was fast, but your form broke down at the end.'
  5. E. 'Most people can't hit that time, so don't expect to repeat it.'
Show answer

Answer: C — Bergeron specifically contrasts 'I can't believe how fast you did that' (which the athlete may hear as disbelief or an accusation of cheating) with 'Wow, you were so fast today — keep it up!', which affirms and reinforces. A and B express doubt; D buries the win under criticism in a moment meant for acknowledgement; E plants a ceiling. The point is that sincere positive reinforcement is part of coaching, not flattery.

Scenario 5. Before class, a coach jokes with a few members about another member who isn't there. According to Bergeron, what is the likely effect on trust?

  1. A. It builds camaraderie among the people present and strengthens trust
  2. B. It's neutral as long as it's lighthearted
  3. C. It erodes trust, because those present sense you'll talk about them when they're absent
  4. D. It only matters if the absent member finds out
  5. E. It improves the coach's authority by showing confidence
Show answer

Answer: C — Bergeron states that being loyal to those who are not present builds trust in those who are present, and that gossip — however lighthearted — signals you'll talk behind people's backs and tears down trust. So A, B, D, and E all miss the mechanism: the damage is to the watching athletes' trust, regardless of whether the absent member ever hears about it.

Scenario 6. A coach is excellent at explaining the biomechanical 'why' behind every cue, yet several athletes still don't seem to fully trust him. What does Bergeron suggest is the missing ingredient?

  1. A. He should explain the 'whys' in even greater technical depth
  2. B. He should listen deeply and sincerely, letting athletes feel he's influenced by them
  3. C. He should require athletes to prove they understand the science before progressing
  4. D. He should rely on his competition résumé to establish authority
  5. E. He should reduce all communication to avoid over-coaching
Show answer

Answer: B — Bergeron says great coaches build trust by doing the opposite of showcasing knowledge — they listen, citing Covey: 'True influence comes as others sense that you are being influenced by them.' Explaining the whys is useful but doesn't by itself create deep trust, so A and C double down on the wrong lever; D substitutes credentials for connection; E overcorrects — the fix is better listening, not silence.

Scenario 7. A coach wants to start applying 'the deeper side of coaching' but is excited to overhaul everything at once — new listening habits, all-positive cueing, and post-class conversations starting tomorrow. What does Bergeron actually recommend?

  1. A. Implement every drill simultaneously for maximum impact
  2. B. Focus on one drill at a time, gauge the reaction, reflect, and adjust
  3. C. Only use these tools with advanced athletes, never beginners
  4. D. Master them privately before ever using them with real athletes
  5. E. Abandon mechanics coaching to make room for the relational work
Show answer

Answer: B — Bergeron explicitly says not to implement all the drills at once — pick one, gauge the reaction, reflect on what worked, and adjust, then later scale from one-on-one to groups. A contradicts that guidance; C and D invent restrictions the article doesn't make (he says to start one-on-one, then progress to groups, teams, classes, and even family); E is a false trade-off — the deeper side adds to fault-correction, it doesn't replace it.

Scenario 8. A coach notices an athlete is unusually quiet, moving slower than normal, and seems mentally elsewhere during the warm-up. Consistent with Bergeron's 'Awareness' and sound coaching judgment, what is the best first move?

  1. A. Ignore it and run the programmed workout exactly as written at full intensity
  2. B. Read the athlete, check in, and adjust the approach or session to where she actually is today
  3. C. Call her out in front of the group to snap her into focus
  4. D. Assume she's being lazy and program extra accessory work as a consequence
  5. E. Tell her to push through because intensity will fix her mood
Show answer

Answer: B — Awareness is about reading whether an athlete is dialed in, energized, in a good mood, or somewhere else, and adjusting to that person — which also overlaps with assessing psychological tolerance for training. B reads and adapts; A ignores clear signals; C may embarrass an athlete who prefers the shadows and damages trust; D and E assume the worst and push intensity onto someone who may not be ready, which is poor judgment.

D3 · Educating 19% of exam Confidence tier: ___

CFJ_Hollingsworth_Hip.pdf

Open the PDF on Google Drive →

Why this is on the reading list

Dan Hollingsworth's "The Athletic Hip" gives the trainer the anatomical and biomechanical literacy needed to TEACH hip-driven movements (squat, deadlift, snatch, running, pistols) and to EXPLAIN why faults happen rather than just naming them. It is on the CCFT reading list because Domain 3 (Educating) asks the coach to teach proper execution, layer instruction, use progressions, teach functional-movement characteristics, and apply anatomy/biomechanics so cues land with athletes. The hip is framed as the body's power-generation and transfer station that initiates nearly all complex movement — so understanding it underpins teaching the core-to-extremity, hip-extension-driven nature of CrossFit's functional movements. It also feeds Domain 4 (root cause of faults) and gives the coach plain-English explanations for neutral spine, knees-out, and lateral-hip stability.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 3.1.1 Teach proper execution of movements
  • 3.1.2 Layer instruction to meet athlete capability
  • 3.1.3 Use progressions to teach complex moves
  • 3.1.6 Teach descriptive/defining characteristics of functional movements
  • 3.1.7 Teach the importance of movements that produce little/no power (e.g., L-sit, back lever)
  • 3.1.10 Teach the relationship between technique and intensity (threshold training)
  • 4.2.6 Apply basic principles of anatomy and biomechanics
  • 4.1.6 Identify root cause of faults
  • 4.2.1 Communicate cues to correct unsound mechanics
  • 4.1.3 Identify faults in movement
  • 1.1.2 Recognize conditions/injuries outside CCFT Scope of Practice that require referral

What to focus on while reading

  • The thesis sentence: the hip is the 'power-generation and transfer station that initiates and directs nearly all complex human movements' — anchor every teaching point to this idea.
  • Coxofemoral joint = true ball-and-socket between the femoral head and the acetabulum of the pelvis; note it is far MORE stable but LESS mobile than the shoulder, and why that stability-for-mobility tradeoff is what lets the hip be strong and powerful (the snatch-landing analogy).
  • Why hip stability matters: thick ligamentous capsule (thickest anterosuperior), the acetabular labrum acting like a 'wheel chock' deepening the socket — understand these as the reason you can load the hip aggressively.
  • The femoral neck is the weakest link in the femur and is susceptible to stress fracture — highlight the referral cue: a new athlete with hip pain on high-impact work should be evaluated to rule out stress fracture (scope-of-practice red flag).
