  • The six primary hip actions: flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, internal rotation, external rotation — know what each looks like, NOT the exact degree numbers (the author explicitly says memorizing ROM averages is not the point; recognizing deviation from normal is).
  • How two-joint muscles make hip ROM depend on neighboring joints: hamstrings cap hip flexion at ~90° with the knee straight but allow ~120–135° with the knee bent; rectus femoris limits hip extension when the knee is flexed — this explains warm-up and stretching positions.
  • Anterior vs. posterior pelvic tilt: anterior tilt = hip flexion = increased lumbar lordosis (arch); posterior tilt = hip extension = flattened lordosis. Note the explicit coaching instruction that new athletes often must be TAUGHT pelvic tilt BEFORE they can understand a 'neutral spine' cue.
  • Lateral pelvic tilt and single-leg stance: a hip dropping on the non-stance side (Trendelenburg pattern) during a pistol, lunge, or running stance signals lateral hip (abductor) weakness — a root-cause observation.
  • Lumbo-pelvic rhythm: coordinated motion of hip + sacrum + lumbar spine produces more total range than any single joint; the seated toe-touch example shows ~90° from the hip plus lumbar flexion to finish — relevant for teaching forward-flexion mechanics and recognizing flexibility limits.
  • Hip flexors (iliopsoas as prime mover, plus rectus femoris, sartorius, TFL): note iliopsoas = iliacus (off ilium) + psoas major (off lumbar spine) joining a common tendon; sedentary people can become hip-flexor-dominant.
  • Tight hip flexors as a ROOT CAUSE of multiple faults: they cause anterior pelvic tilt, which pre-lengthens the hamstrings (so 'tight hamstrings' may actually be tight hip flexors), and which inhibits the glutes (anterior tilt = hip flexion = blunted glute force) — the deadlift-plateau explanation.
  • The glute-squeeze demonstration: stand tall, squeeze glutes, then bend forward at the hips — you cannot hold the contraction once flexed; this teaches WHY hip position governs glute force production.
  • Hip extensors (gluteus maximus + hamstrings) produce the 'violent opening of the hip' required in nearly every explosive athletic movement — this is the biomechanical basis for hip extension being central to CrossFit's powerful functional movements.
  • Glute max is most active in neutral/extended hip; at ~35° of hip flexion the hamstrings take over as primary hip extensor — helps explain torso angle and where power comes from in a lift.
  • Glute max also externally rotates the femur, so glute-max weakness can contribute to KNEES ROLLING IN at the bottom of the squat — a direct fault-to-anatomy link.
  • Hip abductors (gluteus medius and minimus): in a closed chain (squat) they PREVENT the knees from caving and keep knees-in-line-with-toes; in open chain (single-leg stance) they keep the pelvis level. Their weakness is implicated in chronic knee pain and lower-back issues.
  • Hip external rotators — the six deep rotators (obturator internus/externus, gemellus superior/inferior, quadratus femoris, piriformis); tightness/weakness here limits squat depth, causes knees to buckle in the catch of Olympic lifts, and blocks 'bouncing out of the hole.'
  • Piriformis and the sciatic nerve: the sciatic nerve passes just inferior to the piriformis (occasionally pierces it); piriformis tightness/spasm can compress it and refer pain down the leg ('piriformis syndrome'/sciatica) — note the author flags this as often over-diagnosed.
  • The author's stated purpose: not memorization, but a working understanding of hip structure/function so you can engage the hip fully and spot inefficiencies limiting performance.
  • Author credibility/scope: Hollingsworth is a board-certified orthopedic PT and certified athletic trainer — note where his clinical observations cross from coaching into diagnosis/treatment (a coach educates and cues; diagnosis and rehab are referrals).

Concepts to understand

  • The hip as the body's primary power generator and transfer station — understand that teaching any explosive movement is largely teaching the athlete to open the hip forcefully, which connects directly to CrossFit's emphasis on core-to-extremity, hip-driven functional movement.
  • The stability-vs-mobility tradeoff: the coxofemoral joint sacrifices range of motion (vs. the shoulder) for stability, and that stability (capsule + labrum + deep socket) is precisely what permits high force and load — use this to reassure and educate athletes about loading the hip.
  • Two-joint muscle behavior: because muscles like the hamstrings and rectus femoris cross two joints, the position of one joint changes the muscle's length and force at the other — understand this to explain why ROM and power change with stance, and to choose effective stretching/warm-up positions.
  • Pelvic tilt as the gateway to 'neutral spine': anterior tilt produces hip flexion and lumbar arch; posterior tilt produces hip extension and a flattened low back. The athlete must be able to FEEL and CONTROL pelvic tilt before a 'flat/neutral back' cue is meaningful — a layering-of-instruction principle (3.1.2).
  • Root-cause reasoning from anatomy: a visible fault (knees caving, lumbar flexion under load, anterior tilt, a dropping hip in single-leg stance) traces back to a specific muscular cause (glute/abductor/external-rotator weakness or hip-flexor tightness) — understand the chain so you correct the cause, not just the symptom (4.1.6).
  • The hip-flexor-tightness cascade: tight hip flexors → anterior pelvic tilt → hamstrings pre-lengthened (appear 'tight') AND glutes inhibited (weak extension) → limited deadlift/squat performance and possible back/knee/hip pain. This single mechanism explains several common athlete complaints at once.
  • Closed-chain vs. open-chain function of the same muscles: hip abductors keep knees tracking over toes when the foot is planted (squat) but level the pelvis when standing on one leg (run/pistol) — understand context to predict what their weakness will look like.
  • Where power lives across the range: glute max dominates extension near neutral/extension; hamstrings take over as the hip flexes past ~35° — understand this to explain torso angle, the 'hips first' sequence, and why posture at the start of a pull matters.
  • External rotation and knee tracking: the glute max and the deep six external rotators help roll the femur out, keeping knees in line with toes; their weakness/tightness shows up as knees buckling in Olympic-lift catches and shallow, sticky squats.
  • Lumbo-pelvic rhythm as coordinated multi-segment motion: total flexibility/ROM is shared across hip, sacrum, and lumbar spine; understanding this helps you coach forward flexion and recognize when an athlete's limitation forces compensatory lumbar motion under load.
  • Recognizing 'deviation from the norm' over memorizing numbers: the coaching skill is to see normal-looking vs. abnormal hip motion and respond, not to recite degree ranges — this matches the exam's understand-and-apply, not-rote, design.
  • Scope of practice at the hip: the coach educates, cues, mobilizes within general fitness, and refers; pain patterns suggesting stress fracture (femoral neck), nerve compression (sciatic/piriformis), or persistent dysfunction belong to a qualified medical professional — understand the line between coaching and clinical care.
  • Teaching movements that produce little/no power still trains hip control: even isometric/stability demands (single-leg balance, holds) reveal and build the pelvic stabilizers — relevant to 3.1.7 and to programming for lateral-hip strength.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenario questions where you observe a fault and must pick the BEST root-cause explanation or cue: knees caving in a squat (glute-max/abductor or external-rotator weakness, tasks 4.1.6, 4.2.1), a lumbar round under a deadlift or an athlete who can't find a 'flat back' (teach anterior/posterior pelvic tilt first, tasks 3.1.2, 3.1.10), a deadlift plateau or 'tight hamstrings' that is actually tight hip flexors and anterior tilt (apply anatomy/biomechanics, task 4.2.6), or a hip that drops during a pistol/run (lateral-hip/abductor weakness, task 4.1.6). Other items test how you LAYER and SEQUENCE teaching (progress mobility/awareness before loaded complexity, tasks 3.1.2–3.1.3) and how you explain WHY hip extension drives CrossFit's powerful functional movements (tasks 3.1.1, 3.1.6). A subset will test scope of practice: hip pain suggesting a femoral-neck stress fracture or sciatic/piriformis nerve symptoms must be referred, not diagnosed or 'treated' by the coach (task 1.1.2).

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Coxofemoral joint
The true hip joint — the ball-and-socket articulation between the head of the femur and the acetabulum of the pelvis; the body's main power-generation and transfer station for complex movement.
Acetabulum
The cup-shaped socket of the pelvis (formed by all three pelvic bones) that receives the femoral head; only its upper, weight-bearing portion is lined with smooth articular cartilage.
Femoral neck
The angled segment connecting the femoral head to the shaft; the weakest link in the femur and prone to stress fracture — hip pain in a new athlete on high-impact work warrants medical evaluation.
Acetabular labrum
A wedge-shaped cartilage ring around the acetabulum that deepens the socket and adds stability, working like a 'wheel chock' that keeps the femoral head seated.
Joint capsule (hip)
The thick, strong sleeve of ligaments enclosing the hip (thickest anterosuperiorly) that is a major source of the joint's stability under load.
Anterior pelvic tilt
Tipping the top of the pelvis forward; produces hip flexion and increases lumbar arch (lordosis). Tight hip flexors drive this and it inhibits the glutes.
Posterior pelvic tilt
Tipping the top of the pelvis backward; produces hip extension and flattens the normal lumbar lordosis.
Lateral pelvic tilt
Dropping or raising one side of the pelvis in the frontal plane over a single planted hip; excessive drop on the non-stance side during single-leg stance signals lateral hip (abductor) weakness.
Neutral spine
A controlled mid-range spinal position used as the safe standard for loaded movement; athletes typically must first learn to feel and control pelvic tilt before this cue is meaningful.
Lumbo-pelvic rhythm
The coordinated movement of the hip, sacrum, and lumbar spine that together produce more range than any single joint alone (e.g., a seated toe-touch needs hip flexion plus lumbar flexion).
Two-joint (biarticular) muscle
A muscle crossing two joints (e.g., hamstrings, rectus femoris) whose length and force at one joint depend on the position of the other — the reason hip ROM changes with knee position.
Iliopsoas
The prime hip flexor, made of the iliacus (origin on the ilium) and psoas major (origin on the lumbar spine) joining a common tendon onto the proximal femur; can become dominant in sedentary athletes.
Rectus femoris
The only two-joint muscle of the quadriceps; crosses hip and knee, assists hip flexion (most when the knee is slightly flexed), and limits hip extension when the knee is bent.
Gluteus maximus
A primary hip extensor and lateral (external) rotator of the femur; most powerful near neutral/extension, inhibited in hip flexion; weakness can let the knees roll in at the bottom of a squat.
Hamstrings
Two-joint extensors of the hip and flexors of the knee (origin on the ischial tuberosities/'sit bones'); become the primary hip extensor past about 35° of hip flexion.
Hip abductors (gluteus medius and minimus)
Prime movers that keep the knees tracking over the toes in a closed chain (squat) and keep the pelvis level in single-leg stance; weakness is linked to chronic knee, hip, and low-back pain.
Hip external rotators (deep six)
Obturator internus/externus, gemellus superior/inferior, quadratus femoris, and piriformis — deep muscles that rotate the femur outward; tightness/weakness limits squat depth and lets knees buckle in Olympic-lift catches.
Piriformis
A deep external rotator lying near the sciatic nerve; tightness or spasm can compress the nerve and refer pain down the leg ('piriformis syndrome'/sciatica) — noted as often over-diagnosed.
Sciatic nerve
The largest, longest nerve in the body, supplying much of the lower limb; passes just below (occasionally through) the piriformis, so hip-rotator tightness can produce radiating leg pain.
Hip flexion / extension / abduction / adduction / internal rotation / external rotation
The six primary hip actions; for coaching, recognizing normal vs. abnormal motion matters more than memorizing degree ranges.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • A new athlete reporting hip pain, especially with high-impact activity, must be referred for medical evaluation to rule out a femoral-neck stress fracture — the femoral neck is the femur's weakest link and outside CCFT scope to diagnose (task 1.1.2).
  • Buttock pain radiating down the leg (possible sciatic-nerve compression / 'piriformis syndrome'/sciatica) is a neurological symptom requiring medical referral, not coach diagnosis or treatment — the article also notes it is frequently over-diagnosed, so avoid labeling it yourself.
  • Persistent or recurring knee, hip, or low-back pain linked to hip dysfunction is a coaching cue to scale and refer for assessment, not to 'rehab' the athlete; the coach corrects mechanics within scope and defers diagnosis/treatment to a qualified medical professional.
  • The article's clinical claims come from a board-certified orthopedic PT/athletic trainer — use them to inform CUEING and PROGRAMMING, but do not adopt the diagnostic/clinical role; teaching anatomy to athletes is in scope, diagnosing pathology is not.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. During a back squat, an athlete's knees consistently cave inward at the bottom even at light loads, and the movement looks otherwise controlled. Based on hip anatomy, what is the BEST coaching response?

  1. A. Tell the athlete the knee joint is unstable and refer for an MRI before training continues
  2. B. Treat it as a glute-max / hip-abductor / external-rotator strength and activation issue — cue 'knees out / spread the floor,' reinforce when corrected, and program lateral-hip and external-rotation work
  3. C. Add load so the athlete is forced to brace harder and the knees straighten out
  4. D. Conclude the hamstrings are too tight and prescribe static hamstring stretching only
  5. E. Switch the athlete to leg-press machines indefinitely to avoid the fault
Show answer

Answer: B — Knees caving traces to the muscles that externally rotate the femur and abduct the hip — gluteus maximus (external rotation) plus gluteus medius/minimus (keeping knees over toes in a closed chain). The fix is a cue plus targeted strengthening (root cause, tasks 4.1.6 and 4.2.1). A and E over-react and don't address the cause; the article calls piriformis/clinical labels over-diagnosed and a planted-foot squat fault is not an automatic medical referral. C adds intensity on top of a broken position (violates mechanics-before-intensity). D blames the wrong muscle group — hamstrings don't cause valgus knees.

Scenario 2. A brand-new athlete cannot hold a flat/neutral back in the deadlift setup — the low back rounds. Cueing 'flat back' and 'chest up' isn't working. What is the most appropriate teaching step?

  1. A. Keep repeating 'flat back, chest up' louder until it clicks
  2. B. First teach the athlete to feel and control anterior and posterior pelvic tilt, then connect that awareness to finding neutral spine before loading
  3. C. Load the bar heavier so the weight pulls them into position
  4. D. Stop deadlifting permanently because their spine isn't built for it
  5. E. Tell them to arch as hard as possible at all times
Show answer

Answer: B — The article states new athletes often must be taught anterior/posterior pelvic tilt BEFORE they can understand a 'neutral spine' cue — anterior tilt produces lumbar arch, posterior tilt flattens it, so 'neutral' has no meaning until they can move the pelvis on purpose. This is layering instruction to capability (tasks 3.1.2, 3.1.10). A just repeats a cue they can't yet execute; C adds load to a broken position; D is unwarranted; E over-corrects into excessive lordosis.

Scenario 3. An experienced athlete is stuck on their deadlift, says their hamstrings 'always feel tight,' and stretching the hamstrings hasn't helped. Their pelvis sits in a noticeable forward (anterior) tilt at setup. What explanation and action best fit hip biomechanics?

  1. A. The hamstrings are simply genetically short — increase hamstring stretching volume
  2. B. Tight hip flexors are tilting the pelvis forward, which pre-lengthens the hamstrings (so they feel 'tight') and inhibits the glutes — address hip-flexor mobility and posterior tilt / glute engagement
  3. C. The athlete needs more total spinal flexion to reach the bar
  4. D. The plateau is purely a grip-strength problem
  5. E. Refer immediately for suspected femoral-neck stress fracture
Show answer

Answer: B — The article describes the cascade directly: tight hip flexors cause anterior pelvic tilt, which places the hamstrings in a lengthened (pre-loaded) state so further lengthening 'appears' limited, and the same anterior tilt/hip-flexion inhibits the gluteus maximus — a plausible cause of a deadlift plateau (apply anatomy/biomechanics, task 4.2.6). A treats the symptom and misidentifies the cause; C would add dangerous lumbar flexion; D ignores the postural finding; E is a referral cue for unexplained hip PAIN on impact, which isn't described here.

Scenario 4. While coaching pistols (single-leg squats), you notice one athlete's pelvis dips down on the non-standing side and they lose balance on that leg. What does this most likely indicate and how should you respond?

  1. A. Lateral hip (abductor: gluteus medius/minimus) weakness on the stance leg — scale to a supported single-leg progression and add lateral-hip strengthening
  2. B. A short leg that requires orthotics and a referral before any single-leg work
  3. C. Weak grip causing the imbalance
  4. D. Excellent stability — no change needed
  5. E. Tight hamstrings preventing the descent
Show answer

Answer: A — The article specifies that the hip abductors level the pelvis in single-leg stance and that a downward dip of the opposite hip signals lateral hip weakness (root cause, task 4.1.6); single-leg-stance activities like pistols and running are the named examples. The coach scales the progression and strengthens the abductors (tasks 2.2.5, 3.1.3). B over-medicalizes a strength deficit; C and E name unrelated muscles; D ignores a clear instability.

Scenario 5. In the catch (landing) of a snatch, an athlete's knees buckle inward and they get stuck in a shallow squat, unable to 'bounce out of the hole.' Which understanding best guides your coaching?

  1. A. The shoulder joint is too mobile and is destabilizing the squat
  2. B. Weakness/tightness in the hip external rotators (the deep six, incl. piriformis) and glute max limits squat depth and lets the knees buckle — cue knees out and program external-rotation strength and hip mobility
  3. C. The athlete simply isn't trying hard enough — add intensity
  4. D. This is definitely piriformis syndrome — stop training and refer for nerve testing
  5. E. The adductors are the prime cause and should be heavily strengthened
Show answer

Answer: B — The article links limited squat depth, knees buckling in the landing of Olympic lifts, and inability to bounce out of the hole to weakness/tightness in the hip external-rotation group (and glute-max external-rotation function), tasks 4.1.6 and 4.2.6. A misattributes to the shoulder; C ignores the mechanical cause; D over-diagnoses (the article calls piriformis syndrome over-diagnosed, and there's no radiating nerve pain described); E is wrong — the article says the adductors' role is unclear and may relate to internal rotation, not the knees-out function.

Scenario 6. You're warming up athletes for heavy deadlifts and want to improve usable hip flexion in the setup. Knowing the hamstrings are two-joint muscles, which approach reflects correct hip biomechanics?

  1. A. Only stretch with the knees locked straight, since that's the strongest position
  2. B. Recognize that with the knee straight, hamstring tension caps hip flexion near 90°, but bending the knee releases the hamstrings and allows ~120–135° — use knee-bent positions to access greater hip flexion during warm-up/mobility
  3. C. Hip flexion is fixed and unaffected by knee position, so stance doesn't matter
  4. D. Maximize lumbar flexion instead, to make up the difference
  5. E. Skip the warm-up; mobility has no effect on the deadlift
Show answer

Answer: B — Because the hamstrings cross both hip and knee, knee position changes their length and therefore available hip flexion: ~90° with the knee extended vs. ~120–135° with the knee flexed (apply anatomy/biomechanics, task 4.2.6). B uses that relationship correctly. A maximizes the limiting tension; C denies the two-joint principle; D substitutes risky lumbar flexion under load; E dismisses mobility's role in positioning.

Scenario 7. A member who recently started CrossFit reports a deep, localized ache in the hip that worsens with running and box jumps. There was no acute trauma. What is the correct action within your scope as a trainer?

  1. A. Diagnose a hip-flexor strain and prescribe a stretching routine
  2. B. Refer for medical evaluation to rule out a femoral-neck stress fracture, scale or remove high-impact work in the meantime, and document the concern
  3. C. Have them push through the pain to build durability
  4. D. Foam-roll the area aggressively and continue jumping
  5. E. Tell them it's just normal new-athlete soreness and ignore it
Show answer

Answer: B — The article specifically warns that the femoral neck is the femur's weakest link and that new athletes with hip pain, especially on high-impact activity, should be evaluated to rule out a stress fracture — a medical determination outside CCFT scope (task 1.1.2). The trainer refers, scales away from impact, and documents. A diagnoses (out of scope); C and D risk worsening a possible fracture; E dismisses a red-flag pain pattern.

Scenario 8. An athlete asks why CrossFit puts so much emphasis on 'driving the hips' in the deadlift, kettlebell swing, clean, and jump. Using this article, what is the most accurate teaching point?

  1. A. The hips are emphasized mainly because they look athletic, not for any mechanical reason
  2. B. The hip is the body's power-generation and transfer station, and the gluteus maximus and hamstrings produce the violent hip extension required in nearly every explosive athletic movement — so opening the hip forcefully is where the power comes from
  3. C. Power actually comes from the arms; the hips just stabilize
  4. D. The hips matter only in slow lifts, not explosive ones
  5. E. Hip extension is irrelevant once an athlete is advanced
Show answer

Answer: B — The article frames the hip as the power-generation/transfer station that initiates and directs nearly all complex movement, and names the glute max + hamstrings as producing the 'violent opening of the hip' required in nearly every explosive movement — the biomechanical basis for teaching hip-driven, powerful functional movements (tasks 3.1.1, 3.1.6, 3.1.10). A, C, D, and E all contradict the article's central thesis about the hip's role in generating power.

Why this is on the reading list

This article is on the CCFT reading list because the handstand is a foundational CrossFit gymnastics skill and the piece is a teaching manual: it shows how to progress an athlete from zero to a freestanding inverted hold using layered instruction, prerequisite strength screening, scaling, and fear management. It backs Domain 3 (Educating) most directly — teaching execution, layering, using progressions, spotting, and the technique-before-intensity relationship — while also supporting evaluating/correcting movement (D4) and risk management (D5/D7). The exam will not ask you to recite the strength checklist; it will ask you to make coaching decisions about how to teach, scale, and keep a novice safe going upside down.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 3.1.1 Teach proper execution of movements
  • 3.1.2 Layer instruction to meet athlete capability
  • 3.1.3 Use progressions to teach complex moves
  • 3.1.4 Teach and use correct spotting techniques
  • 3.1.6 Teach descriptive/defining characteristics of functional movements
  • 3.1.7 Teach importance of movements that produce little/no power (e.g., L-sit, back lever)
  • 3.1.10 Teach the relationship between technique and intensity (threshold training)
  • 3.1.12 Teach the principles of scaling
  • 3.2.1 Demonstrate proper movements
  • 3.2.2 Demonstrate movement faults
  • 3.2.3 Demonstrate movement progressions
  • 1.1.1 Screen athlete for medical issues / readiness (strength, mobility, fear assessment before inverting)
  • 1.2.1 Assess capacity/capability to perform functional movements
  • 4.1.1 Identify points of performance
  • 4.1.3 Identify faults in movement
  • 4.1.6 Identify root cause of faults
  • 4.2.1 Communicate cues to correct unsound mechanics
  • 4.2.6 Apply basic principles of anatomy and biomechanics
  • 5.2.2 Apply scaling to meet current physical and psychological needs of each athlete
  • 5.2.3 Manage risk for the athlete
  • 5.2.7 Arrange equipment, athletes, instructors to maximize safety
  • 5.2.6 Recognize warning signs for possible injury or overexertion

What to focus on while reading

  • The contrast between the 'old-school' handstand (large back arch, closed/not-fully-open shoulder girdle, toes over or beyond the head) and the 'modern' inverted lockout — highlight every cue that defines the correct vertical line.
  • The plumb-line standard: when viewing the body profile from the side, toes and ankles should be over and in line with the knees, hips, shoulders and hands (a stacked vertical line). This is the points-of-performance picture you must be able to recognize and demonstrate.
  • The definition and purpose of the 'hollow' / hollow-body brace: stabilization of the mid-spine, NOT done with enormous energy, a simple core contraction bringing the rib cage toward the hip. Note it produces the flattened lower back via anterior pelvic tilt.
  • The chin-tailbone relationship cue: raising the chin without engaging the core arches the body and makes the handstand less efficient. Note the sequencing fix — look with the EYES toward the ground first, before ever moving the chin.
  • Head/gaze progression: start with NEUTRAL head position until the athlete controls the core brace, THEN allow them to look toward hands/floor for a better focal point. This is layered instruction (3.1.2) in action.
  • The prerequisite-strength gate before inverting: the article says ASCERTAIN numbers for strict press, kettlebell swing, dead-hang pull-ups, bench press, etc. — i.e., screen upper-body strength before putting someone upside down.
  • The three risk factors named explicitly as a 'recipe for injury': strength, mobility, and FEAR. You must be able to identify which one is limiting a given athlete and respond to it.
  • The beginner dosing rule: limit beginners to five-second static holds with rest until basic strength is achieved — or scale accordingly. Note this number; it is the conservative starting prescription.
  • The full prerequisite/strength-development list for inversion (active hollow hold 20s, hollow-to-superman, burpees, scaled inversion holds, push-ups with active tension and externally cued hands, frog stand, overhead squats, thrusters/push presses with controlled negatives) — understand these as a PROGRESSION/scaling toolkit, not a list to memorize verbatim.
  • The claim that the handstand 'rivals the overhead squat in exposing an athlete's inflexibility and weakness,' most apparent at the SHOULDER GIRDLE and the HIP — note where to look for root-cause limitations.
  • The progression sequence for getting inverted: active lunge position → kick up while pressing the open shoulder up → press shoulders, hips and feet toward the sky. Note 'box, then against the wall, in various forms' as the staged path.
  • Spotting and EXIT-STRATEGY instructions: spot beginners until competency/safety is met; teach an exit — reverse-lunge back down from the kick-up if using the wall, or cartwheel out by quickly turning the hips. 'The way back down is the way they came up.'
  • The fear-management ramp: ramp up slowly with scales, partially inverted loads on tires/boxes, then kick up to a wall for five-second holds with perfect form.
  • The detailed points of performance for a balanced freestanding handstand (hands shoulder/'cubit' width, fingers spread wide and slightly gripping the floor, open/extended shoulders, neutral head with gaze slightly toward hands, tight trunk, rib cage shortened, lower back flattened via anterior pelvic tilt, glutes squeezed, hip open and neutral, quads squeezing legs straight, toes pointed up).
  • The conceptual framing that the handstand is a 'resting position' and a BALANCE move — once strength prerequisites are met, balance becomes the primary focus and strength becomes secondary. Note where balance is controlled: from the hands (wrist crease toward the fingers/phalanges, palms working up/down).
  • The methodology framing: the handstand is 'the foundational block' of gymnastics (as the squat is to weightlifting) and applies 'pure CrossFit methodology' — tie this to teaching the defining characteristics of functional movements and the role of low-/no-power skills.
  • The 'cubit' term = shoulder-width hand distance established from a sound push-up and hollow hold — note this connects the push-up base to the handstand.
  • Breathing note: the athlete must learn to breathe while holding tension — a subtle coaching point that bracing should not mean breath-holding for the whole skill.

Concepts to understand

  • Technique before intensity (threshold/charted progression): a novice is gated to short, perfect five-second holds and prerequisite strength work before adding volume, range of motion, or walking — you build mechanics and consistency before intensity. Be able to apply this to deciding whether an athlete is ready to add load/volume to an inverted skill.
  • Layered instruction: introduce one controllable element at a time — establish the hollow brace with a neutral head first, then add the gaze/focal-point change only after the brace holds. Be able to choose the correct NEXT layer for an athlete based on what they currently control.
  • Progression design for a complex/scary movement: box → wall → freestanding, and lower-skill drills (frog stand, scaled inversion holds, hollow holds) before full inversion. Understand how to select the entry point that matches the athlete's current capability.
  • Pre-screening readiness for an advanced movement: before inverting, assess upper-body strength (press, pull, swing), mobility (shoulder girdle, hip), and psychological readiness (fear). Understand that missing any one is a contraindication to loading the skill and dictates the scale.
  • Root-cause diagnosis of the arched (old-school) handstand: an excessive back arch usually traces to a lost hollow brace and/or a raised chin (chin-tailbone link) or limited shoulder mobility — not just 'try harder.' Be able to name the cause behind the visible fault.
  • The hollow-body brace as the engine of the position: a modest rib-toward-hip contraction with anterior pelvic tilt that creates the straight vertical line; understand WHY it matters (efficiency, balance, midline stability) so you can cue its absence.
  • Spotting and risk management as a teaching responsibility: the coach actively spots novices, arranges a safe setup, and ALWAYS gives an exit strategy (reverse lunge or cartwheel out) before the athlete commits to inversion. Understand spotting as integral to teaching, not optional.
  • Scaling to physical AND psychological needs simultaneously: fear is treated as a legitimate scaling variable — partial inversions on boxes/tires, wall support, and short holds reduce fear while building competence. Be able to scale for the fearful-but-strong athlete differently than the weak-but-fearless one.
  • Points of performance / sound mechanics for the inverted lockout: the stacked vertical plumb line (hands-shoulders-hips-ankles-toes), open shoulders, spread/gripping fingers, neutral head, tight trunk, squeezed glutes, straight squeezed legs, pointed toes — understand these as the standard you teach toward and evaluate against.
  • Balance mechanics: micro-adjustments come from the hands (shifting pressure from wrist crease toward fingers) and later from shoulders/elbows; understand that the goal is to keep the vertical line rigid and adjust at the hands rather than bending the body ('any angles in the vertical line are a big no-no').
  • The handstand as a low-/no-power but high-value skill: it produces little external power yet develops balance, midline stability, spatial awareness, isometric strength, and confidence — understand why CrossFit programs such movements and how to articulate their functional value to athletes.
  • Functional-movement framing: the handstand teaches that 'all training has a functional use' and applies CrossFit methodology — be able to connect this single skill to the broader definition and defining characteristics of functional movement when educating athletes.
  • Conservative dosing and patience: 'great rewards will come' only after small static holds are dialed in — understand the coaching posture of building slowly with success-based progression rather than rushing an athlete to a full freestanding handstand.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenario questions where a novice is struggling with an inverted hold and you must pick the best teaching action: choosing the correct progression entry point (box/wall vs. freestanding) for a fearful or weak athlete (3.1.2, 3.1.3, 5.2.2), identifying the root cause of an arched handstand and cueing the fix (4.1.6, 4.2.1, the hollow brace / chin-tailbone cue), deciding when an athlete is ready to add the gaze change or more volume (3.1.10, technique-before-intensity), and setting up safe inversion with spotting and an exit strategy (3.1.4, 5.2.3, 5.2.7). You may also see readiness/screening items asking what to assess before putting someone upside down (1.1.1, 1.2.1) and items asking you to articulate why a low-power skill like the handstand belongs in functional programming (3.1.6, 3.1.7).

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Hollow (hollow-body brace)
A stabilization of the mid-spine created by a modest core contraction that draws the rib cage toward the hips, flattening the lower back via anterior pelvic tilt. It is the bracing that creates and holds the straight vertical handstand line; it is meant to be subtle, not a maximal effort.
Inverted lockout
The modern, correct handstand position: an isometric upside-down hold where, viewed from the side, toes/ankles, knees, hips, shoulders and hands stack in one vertical line with open, locked-out shoulders.
Old-school handstand
The outdated, faulted version characterized by a large back arch, a closed (not fully open) shoulder girdle, and toes positioned over or beyond the head — the fault picture a coach must recognize and correct.
Open shoulder / open shoulder girdle
Full overhead shoulder extension/elevation so the arms are stacked vertically under the body; 'pressing the shoulders up toward the sky.' A closed shoulder girdle is a primary cause of the arched, inefficient handstand.
Anterior pelvic tilt (in this context)
The deliberate pelvic action used to flatten the lower back and shorten the front of the trunk in the handstand, working with the glute squeeze and hollow brace to remove the back arch and keep the body long and straight.
Cubit
Shoulder-width hand spacing for the handstand, established from a sound push-up and hollow-body hold; the foundational hand-placement width for a stable platform.
Chin-tailbone connection (cue)
A teaching cue capturing that the chin and the pelvis move together: raising the chin without re-engaging the core tilts the body into an arch. The fix is to look with the eyes toward the floor first, before moving the chin.
Frog stand
A low, balanced tuck-on-the-hands hold used as a beginner progression and strength/balance drill toward inversion (referenced as a ~10-second hold) — a scaled step that builds hand-balance and confidence before a full handstand.
Active lunge position
The tensioned lunge (standing or hands-on-floor/compromised) from which the athlete kicks up to inversion; 'active' means muscles are engaged, not relaxed, providing control and a safe starting and exit point.
Exit strategy
The pre-planned, taught way to come safely out of an inversion before kicking up — e.g., reverse-lunge the lead leg back down off the wall, or cartwheel out by quickly turning the hips. 'The way back down is the way they came up.'
Static (isometric) hold
A position held without movement, requiring body-weight control; beginners are limited to about five-second holds with rest until baseline strength is achieved or the movement is scaled.
Handstand as a 'resting position'
The idea that a correctly stacked, balanced handstand requires far less strength than it appears — once mechanics and balance are dialed in, balance (not brute strength) becomes the primary focus.
Spotting
The coach physically guarding and assisting a novice through inversion until competency and safety requirements are met; an active, helpful teaching duty for beginners, not a passive presence.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • Do NOT invert an athlete who has not demonstrated baseline upper-body strength — the article explicitly says to ascertain strict press, kettlebell swing, dead-hang pull-up, and bench press numbers first; strength, mobility, or fear deficits are 'a recipe for injury.'
  • Fear is a safety variable, not just a confidence issue: a fearful athlete who freezes upside down can fall and get hurt. Scale with boxes/tires/wall and short holds rather than forcing a full inversion.
  • Always establish and teach an exit strategy (reverse lunge or cartwheel out) BEFORE the athlete kicks up, especially against a wall — athletes who don't know how to come down can crash.
  • Actively spot novices; do not let a first-timer attempt a freestanding or wall handstand unspotted until competency and safety requirements are met.
  • Cap beginner exposure (around five-second holds with rest) to avoid failure-while-inverted; do not chase long holds, walking, or added range of motion before basic strength and control exist.
  • Setup/space safety: arrange the area so a fall is safe (clear of equipment, appropriate wall/box) — risk management and equipment/athlete arrangement are part of teaching this skill (maps to 5.2.7).

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. A strong, experienced member can kick to the wall but holds the position with a big arch in the lower back, ribs flared, and toes drifting past her head. Her shoulders have good overhead mobility. What is the BEST first coaching action?

  1. A. Add more volume — longer holds will strengthen the position and the arch will resolve on its own.
  2. B. Cue a hollow-body brace: draw the ribs toward the hips, flatten the low back via posterior tilt of the pelvis, and squeeze the glutes to stack the body vertically.
  3. C. Send her back to box-supported inversions because she is not ready for the wall.
  4. D. Tell her to look straight up at the ceiling to find better balance.
  5. E. Stop training handstands until she improves her overhead squat.
Show answer

Answer: B — The fault is the classic old-school arch, and the article's root cause is a missing hollow brace (rib cage toward hip, flattened low back, glutes squeezed). B targets the actual cause with a short, specific cue. A ignores the fault and adds intensity before mechanics. C is over-scaling — a strong, mobile athlete on the wall doesn't need to regress to the box; she needs the brace cue. D is wrong and counterproductive: raising the gaze/chin (the chin-tailbone link) increases the arch. E is irrelevant to fixing this hold now.

Scenario 2. A new athlete is eager to try a freestanding handstand on day one. He has solid push-ups and hollow holds but has never been inverted and is visibly nervous. What is the most appropriate progression?

  1. A. Have him attempt a freestanding handstand in the center of the room so he learns balance immediately.
  2. B. Skip handstands entirely until he asks again, since fear means he's not ready.
  3. C. Start with partial/box-supported inversions and active-lunge kick-ups to the wall for short five-second holds, spotting him and teaching an exit strategy.
  4. D. Have him hold a maximal wall handstand for as long as possible to push through the fear.
  5. E. Load a barbell overhead instead and revisit handstands next month.
Show answer

Answer: C — The article prescribes ramping fear down with scales — partial inversions on boxes/tires, then kicking up to a wall for short, perfect five-second holds — with active spotting and a taught exit strategy. C matches this exactly and respects both his readiness (good push-ups/hollow) and his fear. A skips the progression and the safety net. B abandons the athlete; fear is something you coach through with scaling, not a reason to quit. D ('push through' a maximal hold) is the failure-while-inverted risk the article warns against. E avoids the skill instead of scaling it.

Scenario 3. You are teaching a beginner the wall handstand. She can establish a decent hollow line with a neutral head, but the instant you tell her to look at her hands she loses the brace and arches. What should you do?

  1. A. Keep her cueing the neutral head and hollow brace for now; add the gaze-to-hands change later, once the brace holds reliably.
  2. B. Insist she keep looking at her hands until she gets used to it — the brace will come back.
  3. C. Have her close her eyes to remove the visual distraction.
  4. D. Move her to a freestanding handstand so she has to balance.
  5. E. Tell her the focal point doesn't matter and to look wherever feels natural.
Show answer

Answer: A — This is layered instruction (3.1.2). The article says to begin with a neutral head until the athlete controls the core brace, then allow the gaze change for a better focal point — and warns that newbies tend to drop the hollow as they raise the chin/look toward the floor. A keeps the layer she can control and defers the next layer until she's ready. B and D add a layer she can't yet hold, reinforcing the arch. C is not the prescribed method. E contradicts the article, which treats the focal point as a deliberate, sequenced coaching variable.

Scenario 4. Before letting a member attempt their first wall handstand, which assessment is MOST consistent with the article's approach to managing risk?

  1. A. Check only whether they can touch their toes.
  2. B. Ascertain baseline upper-body strength (e.g., strict press, dead-hang pull-ups, kettlebell swing) and gauge shoulder/hip mobility and fear before inverting.
  3. C. Have them sign a waiver and proceed — the wall removes all risk.
  4. D. Time how long they can hold a freestanding handstand.
  5. E. Measure their one-rep-max back squat.
Show answer

Answer: B — The article explicitly says to ascertain numbers for the strict press, kettlebell swing, dead-hang pull-ups, bench press, etc., and to know whether strength, mobility, or fear is an issue before getting someone inverted. B captures all three risk factors. A and E assess unrelated or insufficient qualities. C is false — the wall reduces but does not remove risk, and a waiver is not a substitute for a readiness screen. D asks them to perform the very skill they aren't ready for, which is the risk you're trying to avoid.

Scenario 5. An athlete asks why CrossFit bothers programming handstands when they 'don't move any weight.' Which explanation BEST reflects the article's framing of low-power skills?

  1. A. They're mostly a party trick, but they look impressive in competition.
  2. B. They build balance, midline/core stability, spatial awareness, isometric strength, and confidence, and — like the overhead squat — expose weakness and inflexibility, making the athlete a more efficient, functional human.
  3. C. They're only useful for former gymnasts.
  4. D. They replace the need for pressing strength work.
  5. E. They are programmed mainly to fill time in a warm-up.
Show answer

Answer: B — The article frames the handstand as a foundational block that develops balance, core control, spatial awareness, and isometric strength, and that 'rivals the overhead squat in exposing inflexibility and weakness' while building 'more efficient human beings.' B captures this and supports teaching the value of low-/no-power movements (3.1.7) and functional-movement characteristics (3.1.6). A trivializes it. C is false — the article says it should be a staple for the whole community, young and old. D is wrong; the handstand requires and complements pressing strength, it doesn't replace it. E understates its programmed purpose.

Scenario 6. While spotting a first-timer kicking up to the wall, what should you have ensured the athlete knows BEFORE they kick up?

  1. A. How to walk on their hands.
  2. B. Their max hold time so they can try to beat it.
  3. C. A clear exit strategy — how to reverse-lunge the lead leg back down or cartwheel out by turning the hips.
  4. D. How to press to a straddle handstand.
  5. E. Nothing — figuring out how to get down builds resilience.
Show answer

Answer: C — The article stresses having an exit strategy for beginners — reverse-lunge from the kick-up if using the wall, or cartwheel out by quickly turning the hips ('the way back down is the way they came up') — and active spotting until competency. C is the safety prerequisite. A and D are advanced skills not relevant to a first kick-up. B invites failure while inverted. E is exactly the unsafe approach the article warns against.

Scenario 7. A member can hold a wall handstand with a solid hollow line and now wants to progress toward a freestanding hold. According to the article, where does balance control primarily come from, and what must be preserved?

  1. A. From bending at the hips to shift the center of mass, keeping the legs relaxed.
  2. B. From small pressure adjustments in the hands (wrist crease toward the fingers), while keeping the rigid vertical line and hollow brace — no angles in the body.
  3. C. From kipping the legs back and forth to stay up.
  4. D. From widening the hands well beyond shoulder width for a bigger base.
  5. E. From looking around the room to spot a fixed point.
Show answer

Answer: B — The conclusion section says balance is found by adjusting on the hands alone — shifting pressure from the wrist crease toward the fingers — while keeping the integrity of the extended vertical body and hollow brace, because 'any angles in the vertical line are a big no-no.' B is correct. A and C introduce the body angles/movement the article forbids. D contradicts the cubit (shoulder-width) standard. E is not the described balance mechanism; the gaze stays slightly toward the hands.
