CFJ_Kilgore_Leverage.pdf

Open the PDF on Google Drive →

Why this is on the reading list

This article gives the coach the working biomechanics vocabulary the CCFT exam assumes when it asks you to identify the ROOT CAUSE of a fault and apply principles of anatomy and biomechanics (Domain 4) and to teach functional-movement characteristics and the technique-intensity relationship (Domain 3). Kilgore reframes every exercise as a system of levers, balance, and center of gravity, so a 'fault' becomes an inefficiency you can name (an extraneous lever arm) rather than something you only vaguely 'see.' Because the exam tests applied judgment, the payoff is that you can explain WHY keeping the load over mid-foot is efficient and HOW a small bar-position or balance change cascades into different forces, adaptation, and risk.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 4.2.6 Apply basic principles of anatomy and biomechanics
  • 4.1.6 Identify root cause of faults
  • 4.1.3 Identify faults in movement
  • 4.1.2 Identify sound mechanics
  • 4.1.4 Identify refinements of sound mechanics to optimize performance
  • 4.1.1 Identify points of performance
  • 3.1.6 Teach descriptive/defining characteristics of functional movements
  • 3.1.10 Teach the relationship between technique and intensity (threshold training)
  • 3.1.1 Teach proper execution of movements
  • 4.2.5 Refine sound mechanics to optimize performance
  • 1.2.1 Assess capacity/capability to perform functional movements

What to focus on while reading

  • The three entities that define any lever and their abbreviations: point of Force application (F = muscle attachment/action), point of Resistance application (R = the load), and the Axis/fulcrum (A = the joint). Be able to locate all three on a real lift.
  • The two arms: resistance arm (R to A) and force arm (F to A). Notice which arm is longer in each lever class, because that ratio is the mechanical advantage.
  • The defining order of each lever class, which is the only reliable way to classify one: first-class = F-A-R (axis in the middle, teeter-totter), second-class = F-R-A (resistance in the middle, wheelbarrow), third-class = R-F-A (force in the middle, biceps/elbow).
  • The body example given for each class: first-class = skull tilting on the atlas/cervical vertebrae; second-class = the push-up (whole body rotating over the ball of the foot); third-class = the biceps curl / elbow (and the baseball bat).
  • The four functions a first-class lever can perform: (1) balance forces, (2) change direction of force, (3) modify/amplify force, (4) modify speed or range of motion. Note that lever geometry decides which you get.
  • The trade-off baked into each class: second-class favors FORCE production (force arm longer); third-class favors RANGE OF MOTION and VELOCITY (resistance arm longer). This is why most human levers (third-class) trade strength for speed and reach.
  • Why bar position matters: placing the bar high on the traps versus low across the scapular spines alters moment arms and joint angles, which changes the forces the body generates and experiences, and therefore the adaptation, for good or bad.
  • The thesis sentence to highlight: inappropriate lever configurations or inadvertently created EXTRA lever arms produce poor technique, poor force transference, and poor fitness results.
  • The caveat that single-joint lever classification rarely holds: real CrossFit movements are COMPOUND, so multiple joints, muscles, and lever systems act at once. Use the squat as the worked example.
  • The squat correction to the 'quads only' myth: the squat is not a quadriceps-only/knee-only movement; the hip joint contributes greatly, and hamstrings and glutes are heavily involved. This is a root-cause lens, not trivia.
  • Definition and behavior of CENTER OF BALANCE: the ground-contact point above which body mass is balanced; it is 'plastic' (constantly shifting via unconscious muscle effort); on two feet it sits on the soles between the calcaneus (heel) and the metatarsals (ball of foot).
  • Definition and behavior of CENTER OF GRAVITY (center of mass): the point with equal mass above/below/front/back (intersection of the cardinal planes); in normal stance it sits about an inch above and a couple inches behind the navel; it MOVES when body conformation changes (e.g., raising a leg shifts it forward).
  • How external load moves the center of gravity: overhead load raises it, low-held load lowers it, and the bigger the load the bigger the deviation from the unloaded location. Connect this to overhead vs. ground-based lifts.
  • The balance rule for standing exercise: keep the center of mass within the boundaries of support (the footprints); if COG passes behind the heels you fall backward, if it passes beyond the toes you fall forward.
  • The corrective-reflex chain for a backward lean (knee back over ankle, hip over knee, shoulders over hips; arms/head may swing forward for big corrections) and the matching muscles in Figure 5 (COG too far back -> anterior chain: tibialis anterior, rectus abdominis, iliopsoas; COG too far forward -> posterior chain: gastrocnemius, gluteals, erector spinae).
  • The efficiency standard for stationary standing exercise: most efficient technique keeps the center of gravity directly over MID-FOOT, and moving the load in as straight a line as possible (close to the line between center of balance and point of load application) avoids inducing extraneous lever arms / extra work.
  • The definition of an 'extraneous lever arm': any lean or off-line load path that creates a moment you must produce extra force to counter, i.e., work that does not contribute directly to completing the movement.
  • The dynamic-movement example: walking as a 'controlled loss of balance forward' (COG is propelled past the trailing foot's support, the lead heel catches the load, COG and center of balance migrate heel-to-toe, repeat). Note how this differs from the stationary 'keep COG over mid-foot' rule.
  • The coaching mandate at the end: anatomy is fixed (you cannot retrain where muscles attach to change mechanical advantage), but you CAN teach efficient technique by routinely observing trainees, spotting erroneously introduced lever arms, and coaching them out. The two payoffs: faster fitness gains and safer sessions.
  • The role of the tendon: muscle force reaches bone via the tendon, which is why tendons are 'crucial to human movement.' A small but testable anatomy point.
  • The practical reason to know muscle attachment sites at BOTH ends: it lets you reason out, physically, how a muscle acts on its lever (which informs cueing and fault diagnosis).

Concepts to understand

  • The body is a collection of simple machines (levers): bones are the rigid frame that transfers force, joints are the axes of rotation, muscles generate the force, and tendons transmit that force to bone. Coaching movement is, mechanically, managing these levers.
  • A lever is fully described by F (force application), R (resistance application), and A (axis), plus the two arms (force arm F-to-A, resistance arm R-to-A). You classify a lever by which entity sits in the middle, NOT by what it looks like.
  • Lever class determines the mechanical trade-off, and you should be able to predict it: first-class (F-A-R) can do all four machine jobs depending on geometry; second-class (F-R-A) has the longer force arm and favors force; third-class (R-F-A, the most common in the body) has the longer resistance arm and favors range of motion and speed at the cost of force.
  • Mechanical advantage is geometric: moment = force x distance from the axis. The longer arm wins. This is why moving the fulcrum, or moving the load farther from the joint, changes how hard the system has to work, and it is the quantitative core of 'why technique matters.'
  • Small set-up changes are not cosmetic. Bar height on the back, foot position, or where a load is held shifts moment arms, joint angles, and the center of gravity, which changes the forces experienced and the adaptation produced, and can tip a movement from efficient/safe to inefficient/risky.
  • Real movements are compound: a single 'simple' lift like the squat is several lever systems, muscles, and joints acting together. Analyzing a fault means considering ALL contributing joints (e.g., hip AND knee in the squat), not just the obvious one, which is exactly how you find a root cause.
  • Center of balance vs. center of gravity are distinct and both move: center of balance is the ground-contact support point (plastic, on the soles between heel and ball of foot); center of gravity is the internal mass-balance point (shifts with limb position and with any external load). Stability requires the COG to stay over the base of support.
  • External load relocates the system's center of gravity (up for overhead, down for low loads, proportional to load size), which is why overhead and heavily loaded movements demand more precise balance management and tighter midline control.
  • An 'extraneous lever arm' is the operational definition of inefficient technique: any lean or off-line load path creates a moment the athlete must fight with extra muscular work that does not advance the rep. Eliminating these arms is the mechanical meaning of 'clean up the movement.'
  • Balance is maintained automatically by graded reflexive corrections; small, few corrections = efficient, large corrections (arm swing, a step, head roll) = the athlete was near or past their base-of-support limit. The size and number of corrections you observe is a readable signal of how off-line the movement is.
  • The efficiency standard for standing strength work is a straight, mid-foot-balanced load path: keep COG over mid-foot and move the load as close to a straight vertical line over the base of support as possible. Deviations from this line are the lever arms you coach out.
  • Dynamic locomotion intentionally violates the static rule: walking is controlled forward loss of balance. So 'keep COG over mid-foot' is context-dependent (stationary lifting) and not a universal command, which matters when you coach gait-like or traveling movements.
  • Anatomy is the fixed constraint; technique is the trainable variable. You cannot change a lever's geometry by training, so the coach's leverage is observation plus technique correction, and the two returns on it are performance (faster fitness gains via better force transfer) and safety.
  • This article supplies the 'why' behind CrossFit's mechanics-first ordering: mechanics (sound levers and balance) must precede intensity, because adding load or speed to an inefficient lever configuration amplifies bad force transference and injury risk rather than fitness.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenarios that hand you an athlete's movement and ask for the root cause or the best biomechanical explanation rather than a definition (4.1.6, 4.2.6): e.g., why a load drifting away from mid-foot or in front of the bar makes a lift harder and less safe, or why an overhead-loaded position is less forgiving of a backward lean. Items may give you a fault and several plausible cues and ask which addresses the actual lever/balance problem versus a symptom (4.1.3, 4.2.5). Teaching-flavored questions can ask you to explain, in athlete-friendly terms, why bar position or a straight bar path matters, or to justify mechanics-before-intensity (3.1.1, 3.1.10). You will not be asked to recite Archimedes or memorize figure captions; you will be asked to reason like a coach who understands levers, center of gravity, and the base of support.

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Lever
A simple machine made of a rigid bar that rotates around a fixed point; in the body, a bone rotating around a joint, driven by muscle force, used to move a load.
Point of force application (F)
Where the muscle attaches and applies its pulling force to the lever (the bone).
Point of resistance application (R)
Where the load to be moved acts on the lever (e.g., the weight in the hand, body weight, or an external implement).
Axis / fulcrum (A)
The fixed pivot the lever rotates around; in the body this is the joint being flexed or extended.
Resistance arm
The distance from the point of resistance (R) to the axis (A). A longer resistance arm makes the load harder to move but increases range of motion and speed.
Force arm
The distance from the point of force application (F) to the axis (A). A longer force arm increases the force the lever can produce against a load.
First-class lever (F-A-R)
Axis sits between force and resistance, like a teeter-totter (skull on the atlas). Can balance force, reverse force direction, amplify force, or change speed/ROM depending on arm lengths.
Second-class lever (F-R-A)
Resistance sits between axis and force, like a wheelbarrow (whole-body push-up over the ball of the foot). Force arm is longer, so it favors force production.
Third-class lever (R-F-A)
Force sits between resistance and axis, like the biceps/elbow or a baseball bat. The most common lever in the body; resistance arm is longer, so it favors range of motion and velocity at the cost of force.
Mechanical advantage
How much a lever multiplies or assists force, set by the geometry of the arms; quantified as moment = force x distance from the axis. The longer arm has the advantage.
Moment (moment arm)
The turning effect around the axis, equal to the applied force times its perpendicular distance from the axis. A load farther from the joint creates a larger moment the athlete must overcome.
Moment arm / lever arm
The perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of force. Coaching efficiency means minimizing unnecessary moment arms created by leaning or off-line loads.
Extraneous (unnecessary) lever arm
An off-line load path or lean that creates a moment the athlete must fight with extra muscular work that does not contribute to completing the rep, i.e., the mechanical signature of bad technique.
Center of balance
The ground-contact support point above which the body's mass is balanced; constantly shifting (plastic). On two feet it lies on the soles between the heel (calcaneus) and the ball of the foot (metatarsals).
Center of gravity (center of mass)
The internal point with equal mass above, below, in front, and behind it (intersection of the cardinal planes); normally about an inch above and a couple inches behind the navel. It moves when limb position or external load changes.
Base of support
The area bounded by the points of ground contact (the footprints). Balance is maintained only while the center of gravity stays within this area; passing the heels causes a backward fall, passing the toes a forward fall.
Compound movement
A movement in which multiple joints and muscles act simultaneously (e.g., the squat involves knees and hips, quads, hamstrings, and glutes), so it is composed of several lever systems at once.
Tendon
The connective tissue that transmits muscle force to bone; because muscle force reaches the lever only through the tendon, it is essential to producing movement.
Controlled loss of balance (walking)
Kilgore's description of gait: the center of gravity is deliberately propelled past the trailing foot's support, the lead heel catches the load, and balance migrates forward, repeating; an intentional, useful violation of the static mid-foot rule.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. An intermediate athlete's back squat keeps grinding and stalling out of the bottom, and the bar visibly drifts forward of mid-foot as she descends. Using a levers/center-of-gravity lens, what is the BEST coaching explanation and first correction?

  1. A. Her quads are simply too weak; program more leg extensions and retest in a month.
  2. B. The forward bar drift moves her center of gravity ahead of mid-foot, creating an extraneous lever arm (a larger moment about the hips/knees) she must fight; cue her to keep the bar over mid-foot and balanced through the heel/mid-foot so the load path stays vertical.
  3. C. She needs more intensity; add load so her body is forced to adapt to the position.
  4. D. The squat is a knee-dominant movement, so the issue is entirely at the knee; cue knees forward to use the quads more.
  5. E. Switch her to the leg press to remove the balance demand permanently.
Show answer

Answer: B — The forward drift is an off-line load path that shifts the center of gravity away from mid-foot, inducing an extraneous lever arm and a larger moment to overcome, exactly the inefficiency Kilgore describes. Restoring a vertical, mid-foot-balanced bar path is the root-cause fix. A and D misattribute a balance/lever problem to isolated muscle weakness and the article explicitly corrects the 'squat is just quads/knee' myth (the hip contributes greatly). C adds intensity to a faulty lever configuration, amplifying bad force transference and risk. E avoids teaching the skill rather than coaching it.

Scenario 2. You are explaining to a new member why you keep stressing where she places the barbell on her back. Which explanation is biomechanically correct per the article?

  1. A. Bar position is just a comfort preference and has no real effect on the lift.
  2. B. A higher versus lower bar position changes moment arms and joint angles, which alters the forces the body generates and experiences and therefore the adaptation, for better or worse, so position is a real mechanical variable, not cosmetics.
  3. C. A lower bar always makes the squat easier because it shortens every muscle.
  4. D. Bar position only matters for tall athletes; short athletes can place it anywhere.
  5. E. Where you place the bar changes which lever CLASS the squat is, turning it from third-class to first-class.
Show answer

Answer: B — Kilgore states that placing the bar high on the traps versus low across the scapular spines alters moment arms and joint angles, changing the forces generated/experienced and thus the adaptation, for good or bad. A and D dismiss a real mechanical effect. C overgeneralizes ('always easier') and ignores that the change can be good or bad depending on the athlete and goal. E misuses 'lever class' which is defined by which entity sits in the middle, not by bar height.

Scenario 3. During a heavy overhead-hold drill, an athlete repeatedly leans back, then makes large arm-swing and stepping corrections to stay upright; the same athlete is rock-steady with the load held at the hip. What is the BEST biomechanical read?

  1. A. The overhead position is inherently dangerous and should never be coached.
  2. B. The athlete is just not trying hard enough to stand still.
  3. C. Holding the load overhead raises the system's center of gravity, so the same backward lean pushes the center of gravity toward and past the base of support faster, demanding larger balance corrections; cue a tighter midline and keep the load stacked over mid-foot.
  4. D. The arm swing proves a shoulder mobility problem; stop the drill and stretch the shoulders only.
  5. E. The low hold is harder than the overhead hold, so you should load the overhead position more to make it feel easy.
Show answer

Answer: C — Per the article, a load supported overhead moves the center of gravity upward and the larger the deviation the more balance is challenged; large corrections (arm swing, a step) signal the COG is reaching the edge of the base of support. Cueing midline control and stacking the load over mid-foot addresses the actual balance/lever cause. A overreacts and abandons coaching. B ignores the involuntary reflexive nature of the corrections. D fixates on a symptom without evidence of a mobility cause. E inverts the difficulty and the mechanics.

Scenario 4. A coach claims, 'The squat is a quadriceps exercise, so to fix a weak squat I only need to watch the knee.' How should you respond, using the article's reasoning?

  1. A. Agree; the knee is the only joint that matters in the squat.
  2. B. The squat is a compound movement of multiple lever systems: the hip contributes greatly and the hamstrings and glutes are heavily involved, so analyzing a fault means considering the hip AND knee together, not the knee alone.
  3. C. Disagree, but only because the ankle is actually the single most important joint.
  4. D. Agree, because single-joint lever classification always holds for full lifts.
  5. E. It does not matter which joints you watch as long as the athlete moves more weight.
Show answer

Answer: B — Kilgore directly corrects the 'squat is just quads/knee' view, noting the hip contributes greatly and the hamstrings and glutes are heavily involved, so the squat is several lever systems at once. Root-cause analysis (task 4.1.6) requires looking across contributing joints. A and D ignore the compound nature the article emphasizes. C just swaps one single-joint tunnel vision for another. E abandons mechanics-first coaching in favor of load chasing.

Scenario 5. You want to teach an athlete the most efficient path for a heavy stationary deadlift-style pull. Based on the article's efficiency standard, which instruction is best?

  1. A. Move the bar in whatever arc feels natural; the path does not affect efficiency.
  2. B. Keep the load moving in as close to a straight vertical line as possible, staying near the line between your center of balance and the load, with your center of gravity over mid-foot, so you do not create extra lever arms and extra work.
  3. C. Let the bar swing away from the body at the top to build momentum.
  4. D. Lean back hard the whole way up to use your bodyweight as a counterweight.
  5. E. Keep the center of gravity behind your heels throughout to stay 'grounded.'
Show answer

Answer: B — The article's efficiency standard for stationary standing exercise is a mid-foot-balanced, straight-line load path close to the line between the center of balance and the point of load application, which avoids inducing extraneous lever arms. A and C invite off-line paths that create moments and extra work. D and E push the center of gravity outside or toward the edge of the base of support (a backward lean / COG behind the heels), which the article says forces large corrective work and risks a backward fall.

Scenario 6. While coaching a traveling lunge, a newer trainer insists the athletes must keep their center of gravity perfectly over mid-foot at every instant, 'just like in a squat.' What is the most accurate correction?

  1. A. The trainer is right; center of gravity must stay over mid-foot in every movement without exception.
  2. B. The 'keep COG over mid-foot' rule is the standard for STATIONARY standing exercise; locomotion is different. Walking and gait-like movement are a controlled forward loss of balance, where the COG is intentionally driven past the support foot and the lead foot catches it, so demanding a static mid-foot COG throughout is wrong for traveling movement.
  3. C. Center of gravity is a fixed point in the body and cannot move, so the cue is meaningless.
  4. D. Balance only matters with an external load, so unloaded lunges need no attention to the center of gravity.
  5. E. The athletes should keep the center of gravity behind the heels while traveling to stay safe.
Show answer

Answer: B — Kilgore frames walking as a 'controlled loss of balance forward,' where the COG is deliberately propelled past the trailing foot's support and the lead heel catches the load, an intentional, useful violation of the static mid-foot rule. So the static standard is context-specific. A over-applies a stationary rule to locomotion. C is false; the article stresses the COG moves with limb position and load. D is false; balance and the COG matter even unloaded (the COG shifts when you raise a leg). E would drive the COG outside the forward-moving base of support and cause a fall.

Scenario 7. An athlete asks why, if good leverage is so important, you do not just 'train her levers' to get longer force arms and lift more. What is the correct coaching answer from this article?

  1. A. You can train muscle attachment sites to migrate over months, lengthening force arms; just keep lifting heavy.
  2. B. Lever geometry is anatomically fixed: you cannot train to change where muscles attach to bones to improve mechanical advantage. What you CAN change is technique, by routinely observing movement, spotting erroneously introduced lever arms, and coaching them out, which yields faster fitness gains and safer sessions.
  3. C. Mechanical advantage is irrelevant to performance, so there is nothing to do either way.
  4. D. Only stretching changes leverage; add a long static-stretch block and her force arms will lengthen.
  5. E. Buy longer-limbed genetics; coaching cannot affect performance at all.
Show answer

Answer: B — The article's closing point: anatomy deals us a fairly static hand (we cannot train to change attachment sites and thus mechanical advantage), but we CAN teach efficient technique by observing trainees, identifying erroneously introduced lever arms, and coaching them out, with two payoffs, better performance/faster fitness gains and safer sessions. A and D claim attachment geometry is trainable, which the article denies. C dismisses leverage that the whole article argues matters. E is fatalistic and ignores the trainable variable (technique).

Scenario 8. Two athletes lose balance backward at the top of a heavy clean catch. Which muscle group is the body recruiting to pull them forward into balance, and what does the size of the correction tell you as a coach?

  1. A. Posterior muscles (gastrocnemius, gluteals, erector spinae) fire to pull them forward; small corrections mean a big problem.
  2. B. Anterior muscles (tibialis anterior, rectus abdominis, iliopsoas) fire to pull the body and center of gravity forward; smaller, fewer corrections mean a more efficient, in-balance athlete, while large corrections (a step, arm swing) signal the COG reached the edge of the base of support.
  3. C. No muscles are involved; balance is purely passive skeletal alignment.
  4. D. Anterior muscles fire, and the bigger the correction the better, because big corrections build more strength.
  5. E. Posterior muscles fire, and correction size tells you nothing about efficiency.
Show answer

Answer: B — Figure 5 states that when the center of gravity moves backward, anterior muscles, tibialis anterior, rectus abdominis, and iliopsoas, contract to pull the body and COG forward into balance (posterior muscles handle a forward COG). The article also notes that the fewer and smaller the corrections, the more efficient the athlete, so large corrections are a readable warning that the COG neared or passed the base-of-support limit. A names the wrong (posterior) muscles for a backward loss. C ignores the active reflexive corrections described. D wrongly treats big corrective work as a goal.

D3 · Educating 19% of exam Confidence tier: ___

Virtuosity.pdf

Open the PDF on Google Drive →

Why this is on the reading list

This is Greg Glassman's foundational 2005 open letter defining 'virtuosity' as 'performing the common uncommonly well' and naming the 'novice's curse' — the rush past fundamentals toward fancy, risky, original movements. It is the philosophical backbone of how a CrossFit trainer teaches: master the basics first, insist on sound mechanics, and earn the right to add complexity. It directly backs Domain 3 (Educating) tasks on teaching the definition of CrossFit, the technique-intensity relationship, progressions, and layering instruction, and it informs the mechanics-consistency-intensity sequencing that runs through Domains 4 and 5.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 3.1.3 Use progressions to teach complex moves
  • 3.1.2 Layer instruction to meet athlete capability
  • 3.1.10 Teach the relationship between technique and intensity (threshold training)
  • 3.1.1 Teach proper execution of movements
  • 3.1.5 Teach the definition of CrossFit
  • 3.1.9 Teach the goals of CrossFit programming and how goals are met (programming with variance)
  • 3.1.12 Teach the principles of scaling
  • 5.2.1 Apply mechanics-consistency-intensity to programming for safety and performance
  • 5.2.4 Plan lessons for a class period (warm-up, skill development, workout, cool-down)
  • 5.1.4 Lead by example
  • 7.1.1 Self-assess sessions according to the foundations of effective training
  • 2.1.1 Design single workouts using the CrossFit methodology

What to focus on while reading

  • The gymnastics scoring frame: a flawless routine scores only 9.7; the last 0.3 requires 'risk, originality, and virtuosity' — note that virtuosity is the rarest and most valuable of the three.
  • The precise definition of virtuosity: 'performing the common uncommonly well' — memorize the phrasing and, more importantly, understand it means excellence in the basics, not in the exotic.
  • Definitions of risk ('executing a movement likely to be missed or botched') and originality ('a movement or combination unique to the athlete') — and why novices gravitate to both.
  • Why audiences, coaches, AND athletes all readily recognize virtuosity, but audiences often miss risk and originality — virtuosity is the universal mark of mastery, genius, and beauty.
  • The 'novice's curse': rushing past fundamentals toward elaborate/sophisticated skills, producing 'excessive adornment, silly creativity, weak fundamentals,' lack of virtuosity, and DELAYED mastery.
  • The key insight that the curse 'afflicts learner and teacher alike' — coaches are tempted to teach fancy moves to entertain and impress, and that this is 'a sucker's move.'
  • The specific progression violation Glassman names: 'Teaching a snatch where there is not yet an overhead squat, teaching an overhead squat where there is not yet an air squat, is a colossal mistake.'
  • The four concrete harms of rushing advancement: increases chance of injury, delays advancement/progress, blunts rate of return on effort, and 'retards fitness.'
  • What insisting on basics produces: clients recognize you as a master trainer, they are 'awed not bored,' they advance faster in every measurable way, and you garner more respect.
  • Glassman's two named programming symptoms of lost fundamentals: rarely seeing 'short, intense couplets or triplets,' and rarely seeing trainers 'really nitpick the mechanics of fundamental movements.'
  • The structure of a sound hour-long session he lays out: warm up, practice a basic movement/skill or pursue a PR/max lift, discuss and critique efforts, then a tight couplet or triplet, or play.
  • The 'seasoning vs. main course' metaphor: tire flipping, basketball, relay races, tag, Hooverball are essential but are 'seasoning — like salt, pepper, and oregano,' not the main course.
  • The closing thesis: 'good enough never is' — CrossFit trainers have the tools to be the best on earth and should pursue the full 10.0, i.e., virtuosity.

Concepts to understand

  • Virtuosity as a coaching standard: excellence is demonstrated by doing ordinary, fundamental movements uncommonly well — a trainer pursues flawless air squats, push-ups, and deadlifts before chasing complex skills.
  • The novice's curse as a diagnostic lens: recognize it in BOTH athletes (who want to skip ahead) and trainers (who want to teach impressive moves) and understand it as the primary cause of weak fundamentals, injury, and delayed progress.
  • Mechanics before intensity: sound technique on fundamental movements must precede load, speed, and complexity — this is the conceptual seed of the mechanics → consistency → intensity hierarchy used to scale and program safely.
  • Progressions as non-negotiable prerequisites: a movement may only be taught once its foundational movement is owned (air squat → overhead squat → snatch); skipping a layer is a fault in coaching, not just in the athlete.
  • The trainer's job is to make the basics compelling, not to entertain — insisting on basics earns respect and produces faster, measurable gains; using flash to impress is a 'sucker's move' that sacrifices the client's results.
  • Fundamentals drive measurable fitness outcomes — recommitting to basics improves training, accelerates client advancement, and increases the coach's perceived professionalism and authority.
  • CrossFit programming epitomized by short, intense couplets and triplets executed with nitpicked mechanics — the simple, hard, well-executed workout is the main course; novelty and games are seasoning.
  • Session architecture that honors fundamentals: a complete hour includes warm-up, skill/strength practice, coaching/critique, and a tight metcon (or play) — structure that keeps the basics central while leaving room for variance.
  • Play as legitimate but secondary programming: relay races, sports, and games belong in good programming as 'seasoning,' but cannot replace the fundamental movements and conditioning that drive adaptation.
  • Leading by example through commitment to fundamentals: the coach's own discipline about basics models the standard and signals mastery to athletes more than displaying advanced skills would.
  • 'Good enough never is' as a professional ethic: continuous pursuit of refinement — chasing the last tenth of a point — is the standard a CCFT holds for their own coaching and their athletes' execution.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenarios that hand you a trainer or athlete eager to skip ahead — teaching a snatch to someone who can't overhead squat, programming complex gymnastics before bodyweight basics, or filling class with games instead of mechanics work — and ask for the best coaching response (tasks 3.1.3, 3.1.2, 5.2.1). Other items will test whether you can identify the technique-before-intensity principle, recognize the 'novice's curse' in a class description, or choose a class plan that keeps fundamentals central (tasks 3.1.10, 5.2.4, 2.1.1). Because the exam tests applied judgment, the right answer is almost always the one that reinforces sound fundamentals and earns the right to add complexity, rather than the one that entertains or impresses.

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Virtuosity
Performing the common uncommonly well — excellence demonstrated through mastery of fundamental movements rather than through difficult or novel ones. The mark of true mastery, genius, and beauty.
Risk (gymnastics sense)
Executing a movement that is likely to be missed or botched. Dramatic and appealing to novices, but worth little without sound execution.
Originality
A movement or combination of movements unique to the athlete — something not seen before. Like risk, it attracts novices but is not the mark of mastery.
Novice's curse
The compulsion to rush past fundamentals toward elaborate, sophisticated movements, resulting in excessive adornment, weak fundamentals, a lack of virtuosity, increased injury risk, and delayed mastery. It afflicts learners and teachers alike.
Fundamentals
The basic, foundational movements and skills (e.g., air squat) on which all advanced movements are built. Commitment to them is what drives real fitness gains and signals a master trainer.
Couplet / Triplet
A workout combining two (couplet) or three (triplet) movements, typically short and intense — the kind of programming Glassman says epitomizes CrossFit.
Threshold training / technique-intensity relationship
The principle that intensity should be added only after technique is sound; mechanics on fundamental movements come before load, speed, and complexity (Content Outline task 3.1.10).
Seasoning vs. main course
Glassman's metaphor: play (tire flips, sports, relays, Hooverball) is essential 'seasoning' in good programming but must not replace the 'main course' of fundamental movements and intense conditioning.
Master trainer
A coach whose instruction is recognizably simple, fundamental, and basic; one who insists on the basics and thereby awes rather than bores clients and advances them faster.
'Good enough never is'
Glassman's closing standard — the refusal to settle for a flawless-but-unremarkable performance; the relentless pursuit of the last tenth of a point, i.e., virtuosity.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • Rushing an athlete to advanced or loaded movements before fundamentals are sound directly increases injury risk — the article explicitly names this as a 'colossal mistake' that 'increases the chance of injury.' Honor mechanics-before-intensity as a safety practice (links to risk management, task 5.2.3).
  • A trainer programming complexity or novelty to entertain/impress rather than to drive adaptation is a coaching fault to correct, not a style choice — it blunts client results and is a self-assessment trigger (task 7.1.1).

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. A new member can perform a solid air squat but cannot yet hold a stable overhead position with an empty barbell. Eager to keep him engaged, he asks you to teach him the snatch today. What is the best coaching response?

  1. A. Teach the snatch now to keep him motivated and engaged while interest is high.
  2. B. Teach the overhead squat and other overhead-position progressions first, explaining that the snatch is built on positions he doesn't yet own.
  3. C. Skip both and put him straight into a heavy clean so he still gets a barbell lift.
  4. D. Tell him the snatch is too dangerous for members and he should never attempt it.
  5. E. Load a moderate barbell and let him attempt full snatches so he can feel the movement.
Show answer

Answer: B — Glassman names exactly this sequence — air squat → overhead squat → snatch — and calls skipping a layer 'a colossal mistake' that increases injury risk and delays progress. B respects the progression and layers instruction (tasks 3.1.3, 3.1.2). A and E rush advancement and raise injury risk; C substitutes an unrelated skill and still skips prerequisites; D is needlessly absolute and abandons coaching.

Scenario 2. Reviewing a colleague's class plan, you see it is built almost entirely around novel, complex gymnastics skills and games like Hooverball and relay races, with almost no fundamental movement practice or short intense couplets/triplets. Per Glassman's 'Virtuosity,' what is the most accurate critique?

  1. A. The plan is excellent because variety and novelty keep athletes entertained.
  2. B. The plan shows the 'novice's curse' — it elevates seasoning (play/novelty) over the main course (fundamentals and intensity) and will dilute the coach's efficacy.
  3. C. The plan is fine as long as the games are physically demanding.
  4. D. The only problem is that it lacks a cool-down.
  5. E. The plan is too conservative and should add even more advanced skills.
Show answer

Answer: B — Glassman explicitly warns that play is 'seasoning — like salt, pepper, and oregano,' not the main course, and that lost fundamentals show up as rarely-programmed couplets/triplets and un-nitpicked mechanics. B correctly identifies the novice's curse and the seasoning/main-course inversion. A, C, and E embrace the very error the article warns against; D names a real but trivial gap and misses the central problem.

Scenario 3. An experienced-looking coach tells you he avoids drilling basic movements because clients find them boring, so he keeps sessions full of flashy, advanced variations to impress them. According to the letter, how should you frame the impact of this approach?

  1. A. He's right; entertaining clients with advanced moves is the fastest way to build loyalty and results.
  2. B. It's a harmless personal coaching style with no effect on athlete outcomes.
  3. C. It's a 'sucker's move' — insisting on basics would actually awe clients, build respect, and advance them faster in every measurable way.
  4. D. It's acceptable as long as he occasionally reviews fundamentals once a month.
  5. E. The only fix is to stop coaching advanced athletes altogether.
Show answer

Answer: C — Glassman calls the urge to teach fancy movements to impress clients 'a sucker's move' and promises that really insisting on basics makes clients recognize a master trainer, leaves them 'awed not bored,' and advances them faster in every measurable way. C captures both the diagnosis and the payoff. A and B contradict the text; D treats fundamentals as occasional garnish; E is an unrelated overcorrection.

Scenario 4. You are planning a one-hour class and want it to reflect Glassman's commitment to fundamentals while still leaving room for variance. Which structure best fits the article's guidance?

  1. A. Spend the full hour learning one brand-new, complex skill the class has never seen.
  2. B. Warm up, practice a basic movement/skill or pursue a PR or max lift, discuss and critique efforts, then run a tight couplet or triplet (or play).
  3. C. Run back-to-back competitive games for the entire hour to maximize fun.
  4. D. Do only a long, single-modality endurance piece with no skill work or coaching.
  5. E. Have athletes free-style whatever movements they feel like for the hour.
Show answer

Answer: B — Glassman lays out almost this exact session: 'warm up, practice a basic movement or skill or pursue a new PR or max lift, discuss and critique the athletes' efforts, and then pound out a tight little couplet or triplet ... or just play.' B keeps fundamentals and coaching central while allowing intensity and play (tasks 5.2.4, 2.1.1). A over-indexes on novelty (novice's curse); C makes seasoning the main course; D omits skill and coaching; E abandons structure and mechanics.

Scenario 5. An athlete with sloppy mechanics on the overhead squat insists on adding heavy load because he wants to 'go hard' every day and feels light technique work is a waste. Using the technique-intensity principle implied by 'Virtuosity,' what is the best response?

  1. A. Add the heavy load as requested — intensity is what produces results, so mechanics can be cleaned up later.
  2. B. Reinforce that sound mechanics come before intensity; refine his positions at lighter load and add intensity as technique stabilizes.
  3. C. Tell him overhead squats aren't important and remove them from his training.
  4. D. Let him load heavy but only once per week so the risk is limited.
  5. E. Match his load to the strongest athlete in class so he stays motivated.
Show answer

Answer: B — The letter's core message — virtuosity through fundamentals, and the warning that rushing advancement increases injury risk and blunts return on effort — underlies the mechanics-before-intensity hierarchy (tasks 3.1.10, 5.2.1). B sequences technique before load and refines toward intensity. A and E load an unsound movement and invite injury; C abandons a foundational movement; D still adds load to broken mechanics, just less often, and ignores the root fault.

Scenario 6. A trainer asks you to define 'virtuosity' for a new staff member and explain why it matters for how they coach. Which explanation is most consistent with Glassman's letter?

  1. A. Virtuosity means performing rare, high-risk, original movements that wow the crowd.
  2. B. Virtuosity means 'performing the common uncommonly well' — so we coach toward flawless fundamentals, because that is the true mark of mastery.
  3. C. Virtuosity is just another word for working out at maximum intensity every session.
  4. D. Virtuosity is about programming as much variety and novelty as possible.
  5. E. Virtuosity means letting advanced athletes do whatever advanced movements they choose.
Show answer

Answer: B — Glassman defines virtuosity precisely as 'performing the common uncommonly well' and calls it the mark of true mastery, genius, and beauty — distinct from risk and originality, which attract novices. B states the definition and its coaching implication (teach toward excellent basics). A conflates virtuosity with risk/originality (the novice's curse); C, D, and E substitute intensity, novelty, or athlete free-rein for the actual definition.

D4 · Training 24% of exam Confidence tier: ___

60_07_Where_Barbells.pdf

Open the PDF on Google Drive →

Why this is on the reading list

This article makes the trainer a knowledgeable judge of the single most-used piece of equipment in a CrossFit gym: the barbell. It is assigned to D4 (Training) because evaluating and facilitating sound movement depends on equipment that behaves predictably — a bar that spins, doesn't bend, and won't fail under load. But its strongest, most testable hooks are actually in equipment maintenance and risk management (7.2.3) and arranging/maintaining safe equipment (5.2.7, 5.2.3): the piece explicitly warns that a cheap bolt-retained sleeve can slide off during a heavy squat with 'spectacular and very dangerous' consequences to lifter and spotters. Read it for applied judgment about bar selection, inspection, and maintenance — not to memorize manufacturers or psi numbers.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 7.2.3 Maintain/inspect equipment; keep facility clean and safe
  • 5.2.7 Arrange equipment, athletes, instructors to maximize safety
  • 5.2.3 Manage risk for the athlete
  • 4.2.6 Apply basic principles of anatomy and biomechanics
  • 2.2.3 Scale for athletes with sport-specific goals
  • 7.2.5 Assess insurance policy and other legal needs (equipment as a liability/risk factor)
  • 5.2.10 Manage logistics (ratio, equipment demands, duration, space)
  • 1.2.6 Quantify and track performance (equipment that reliably loads/spins enables valid measurement)

What to focus on while reading

  • The central claim up front: a good bar is the most important piece of equipment in a strength program — anchor every other detail to WHY this matters for a coach (safe, reliable, measurable training).
  • The two failure modes a coach must prevent: a bar that won't spin dependably (can't clean/snatch real weight) and a bar that bends or fails under load — note these are training-quality AND safety issues.
  • Olympic (weightlifting) vs powerlifting bar differences: WL bars are springy/'whippy' and thinner; PL bars are stiffer/'deader' and thicker. Tie each property to the lift it serves (whip helps the catch in clean/snatch; oscillation hurts stability in heavy squat/bench).
  • Why diameter matters: smaller diameter (28mm men / 25mm women WL; ~28-29mm+ for power bars) = faster rotation (higher angular velocity), easier hook grip, more whip — but needs higher-grade steel.
  • Men's vs women's WL bar specs: 20kg/28mm men, 15kg/25mm women; lighter 10kg and 5kg training bars exist for novices and children — directly relevant to scaling load for size, age, and skill.
  • Tensile strength vs yield strength — the two most important steel properties. Pin down the plain-English distinction: tensile = resistance to BREAKING; yield = resistance to BENDING (permanent set).
  • Elastic vs plastic deformation: elastic = bends and returns to straight; plastic = permanent bend/bow. A high yield strength keeps deformation elastic under normal loads.
  • The worked example: 195,000 psi tensile / 120,000 psi yield bar won't break but WILL eventually take a permanent bow; 195,000 / 175,000 stays straight. Lesson: the closer tensile and yield are (and the higher both), the better — and yield info is harder to get, so a smart buyer asks for BOTH.
  • Pound-test ratings (1500/1200/1000 etc.) are a STATIC test (forklift holds a loaded bar, no bounce/drop). Note the caveat: static ratings don't predict behavior under DYNAMIC (dropped, bounced) loading — exactly how CrossFit uses bars.
  • Sleeve retention systems and their failure risk: snap rings (preferred, can't fail, not exposed), roller pins (work but can shear if dropped hard on the end), and bolts ('the mark of a cheap, inferior product' that loosen over time) — this is the article's clearest safety hook.
  • The closing safety scenario: a loaded sleeve sliding off during a heavy attempt endangers both lifter and spotters — connect to equipment arrangement and risk management.
  • Sleeve rotation hardware: bushings (cheaper, wear faster without occasional lube, but well-maintained ones spin as well as bearings) vs needle bearings (faster, but soft ones can flatten if dropped wrong and stop spinning) vs sealed/maintenance-free assemblies for busy gyms.
  • Maintenance cues you can act on: oil bushings (e.g., a drop of 3-in-1 oil) periodically; recognize that dropping a bar wrong can flatten bearings; sealed bars reduce maintenance burden in a high-traffic facility.
  • Knurl characteristics: depth (shallow/medium/deep), coarseness (pattern size), presence/absence of a center knurl, and whether points are rolled (smoother) or left sharp (more friction) — note how knurl 'feel' affects grip security and which athletes/lifts benefit.
  • Finishes and their practical trade-offs: chrome/zinc (bright, club-preferred, chrome holds chalk poorly but cleans/de-bloods easily), black oxide (tacky grip favored by powerlifters), stainless (rust-free, best but 2-4x cost), bare steel.
  • Manufacturing/quality checks named: turning to size, checking straightness to tolerance, inspecting for cracks/pits/corrosion, X-ray for internal defects — these are the quality signals behind a 'good bar' and what wear/inspection looks for over time.
  • 'Four good bars vs one great bar' for general-purpose/institutional buyers — the budget-vs-quality trade a gym owner actually faces.

Concepts to understand

  • Equipment as a safety and performance variable: a coach is responsible for the gear athletes load and lift. Understand that bar quality is not a vanity purchase — a failing or non-spinning bar creates injury risk and degrades training quality.
  • Matching the bar to the goal/sport: understand that weightlifting bars (whippy, thinner, fast-spinning) suit cleans/jerks/snatches, while powerlifting bars (stiff, thicker, 'dead') suit heavy squat/bench/deadlift — so equipment selection is part of scaling for sport-specific goals.
  • Why bar diameter and whip matter biomechanically: smaller diameter spins faster and grips easier (hook grip) and flexes more to help the pull/catch; a stiffer thicker bar improves stability under very heavy static loads where oscillation would interfere.
  • Tensile vs yield strength as a usable buying/judgment heuristic: high tensile means it won't break; high yield means it won't take a permanent bend. The best bars have both high AND close together. A coach/owner who only checks tensile can still end up with a bent bar.
  • Elastic vs plastic deformation applied to inspection: a bar that bows under load and springs back is fine (elastic); a bar that stays bent is damaged (plastic deformation) and should be pulled or retired — this is a concrete inspection judgment.
  • Static vs dynamic load ratings: understand that a 'pound-test' number is measured statically and does NOT guarantee performance when bars are dropped or bounced (standard in CrossFit). Don't over-trust a static rating for a high-rep, drop-heavy environment.
  • Sleeve retention as the highest-consequence failure point: bolts loosen and can let a loaded sleeve slide off (catastrophic); snap rings and roller pins are far safer. Understand WHY this is the inspection item that most directly protects athletes and spotters.
  • Spin hardware and maintenance: bushings need occasional oil and well-maintained bushings rival bearings; needle bearings spin faster but can be ruined by bad drops; sealed assemblies trade maintenance for cost — a coach should know how the bars in their gym are built and maintained.
  • Knurl 'feel' and grip security: knurl depth/coarseness and center-knurl presence affect how the bar marries to the hands; understand that grip-related faults or slips can stem from worn, too-smooth, or inappropriate knurling, not just athlete technique.
  • Finish trade-offs for a gym context: chrome/zinc for appearance and easy cleaning (including blood after a pull), black oxide for tacky grip, stainless for longevity at a premium — practical for owner decisions and for understanding why a bar feels the way it does.
  • Quality and inspection signals: straightness tolerance, absence of cracks/pits/corrosion, and overall machining quality are what 'good' means; the same checks (plus monitoring for permanent bend and sleeve play) define ongoing equipment inspection.
  • Budget vs quality as a real coaching/ownership decision: 'four good bars vs one great bar' frames the trade institutions make; understand the safety floor (no failing or bolt-retained junk bars) that should never be crossed for budget reasons.

How the exam applies this

Expect equipment to surface as risk-management and facility-safety scenarios rather than trivia. A question may describe a bar with a loosening bolt-retained sleeve, a bar that no longer spins, or a bar with a visible permanent bend, and ask for the safest coaching action — pull it from service and inspect/maintain (7.2.3, 5.2.3, 5.2.7). Sport-specific scaling items may ask which bar suits a weightlifting vs powerlifting goal (2.2.3), and biomechanics items may probe why a whippy bar helps the catch or why a stiff bar improves heavy-squat stability (4.2.6). The exam will not ask you to recall manufacturers, prices, or exact psi figures — it tests the judgment those facts support.

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Barbell (bar) shaft
The central rod the lifter grips; its steel quality, diameter, and straightness determine how the bar performs and whether it survives heavy/dynamic loading.
Sleeve
The rotating end section where plates load; made from Drawn Over Mandrel (DOM) tubing, it lets plates spin independently of the shaft and is stopped by an inner flange.
Whip / 'whippy'
The springy flex of a bar. Desirable in the clean, jerk, and snatch because the rebound helps the catch; undesirable in heavy squat/bench where it causes destabilizing oscillation.
Weightlifting (Olympic) bar
A thinner (28mm men / 25mm women), springier, faster-spinning bar built to IWF specs for the dynamic Olympic lifts; men 20kg, women 15kg, with 10kg/5kg training versions.
Powerlifting (power) bar
A stiffer, thicker, 'deader' bar built so it won't oscillate under very heavy squat, bench, and deadlift loads; specialty squat and deadlift bars also exist.
Tensile strength
The stress (in psi) a material can take before BREAKING — i.e., resistance to snapping. High tensile means the bar is nearly impossible to break.
Yield strength
The stress (in psi) a material can take without PERMANENT deformation — i.e., resistance to bending. High yield (and close to tensile) keeps a bar from taking a lasting bow.
Elastic deformation
Temporary bend: the bar flexes under load and returns to straight when unloaded. Normal and acceptable.
Plastic deformation
Permanent bend or bow that remains after unloading. A sign the bar exceeded its yield strength and is damaged — a candidate for retirement.
Pound-test rating
A static strength rating (e.g., 1500-lb test): a loaded bar is held statically and passes if it shows no permanent bend. Higher is better, but it does NOT predict behavior under dropped/dynamic loads.
Knurl
The rough, checkered pressed pattern that grips the hands/shoulders/back. Varies by depth, coarseness, center-knurl presence, and whether points are rolled smooth or left sharp — all affecting grip 'feel' and security.
Center knurl
Knurling in the middle of the bar (present or absent depending on bar type) that aids grip for back-rack/squat positions; its presence/absence and width is a defining bar feature.
Finish (chrome / zinc / black oxide / stainless / bare)
The bar's coating. Affects appearance, corrosion resistance, and grip: black oxide is tacky (powerlifters), chrome/zinc are bright and clean easily but hold chalk less, stainless is rust-free but costly.
Bushing
A bronze/steel sleeve-bearing surface that lets the sleeve spin; cheaper than needle bearings, needs occasional oiling, and when well-maintained spins comparably well.
Needle bearing
Precision bearings that give a fast, free spin (good for cleans/snatches); faster than bushings but soft ones can flatten if the bar is dropped wrong, stopping the spin.
Sleeve retainer (snap ring / roller pin / bolt)
The hardware holding the sleeve on the shaft. Snap rings (preferred, can't fail), roller pins (work but can shear on hard end-drops), and bolts (cheap, loosen over time and can let a loaded sleeve slide off).
DOM tubing (Drawn Over Mandrel)
Straight, strong machine tubing pulled through a die under pressure; the standard material for bar sleeves because of its straightness and internal integrity.
Sealed (maintenance-free) sleeve assembly
A bar whose spin hardware is enclosed, reducing the maintenance burden — practical for busy/institutional gyms where regular oiling is unlikely.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • Bolt-retained sleeves are 'the mark of a cheap, inferior product': bolts loosen over time and from dropping, and a loaded sleeve sliding off during a heavy attempt is a serious injury hazard to the lifter and spotters — inspect for and retire these.
  • A bar with a visible PERMANENT bend/bow (plastic deformation) has been overloaded beyond its yield strength; it compromises safe loading and valid lifting and should be pulled from service.
  • A bar that no longer spins dependably (flattened needle bearings from a bad drop, or dry/worn bushings) makes Olympic lifts unsafe and degrades training — service or remove it before athletes load it heavy.
  • Trusting only a static pound-test rating for a drop-heavy CrossFit setting can mislead: static ratings don't guarantee performance under dynamic/dropped loads.
  • Routine inspection items the article implies: straightness, cracks/pits/corrosion, sleeve play, and retainer integrity — failing any of these is a safety stop, not a cosmetic issue.
  • Equipment selection is within scope, but bar materials engineering and competition certification are not coaching judgments to overstate — defer to manufacturer specs and qualified maintenance for anything beyond inspection and basic upkeep.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. During warm-up, you notice the loadable sleeve on one barbell wobbles and the end bolt that retains it has backed out slightly. An athlete is about to use it for a heavy back squat. What is the best action?

  1. A. Let the athlete proceed but tell them to re-rack carefully
  2. B. Tighten the bolt by hand and continue using the bar for the session
  3. C. Pull the bar from service immediately, move the athlete to a different bar, and tag the bar for inspection/repair
  4. D. Reduce the athlete's load by half and allow the lift on that bar
  5. E. Have a spotter stand at the loose end during the lift
Show answer

Answer: C — A loosening bolt-retained sleeve can let a loaded sleeve slide off mid-lift — described as spectacular and very dangerous to lifter and spotters. The only safe move is to remove the bar from use and inspect/repair it (7.2.3, 5.2.3, 5.2.7). Tightening by hand (B) or reducing load (D) still trusts a known-failing retainer; A and E do nothing about the failure point and put people in harm's way.

Scenario 2. A member training for a weightlifting meet complains that the gym's bars feel 'stiff and dead' and don't help in the snatch and clean. Which equipment explanation best fits, and what would you recommend?

  1. A. The bars are too whippy; switch to a power bar for the Olympic lifts
  2. B. The bars are stiff power-style bars; provide a weightlifting bar, which is thinner, springier (whippy), and spins faster to suit the dynamic lifts
  3. C. The bars need a center knurl removed to fix the snatch
  4. D. The issue is the finish (chrome); switch to black oxide to add whip
  5. E. Reduce the weight so the bar whips more
Show answer

Answer: B — Weightlifting bars are intentionally thinner, springier ('whippy'), and faster-spinning to serve the dynamic clean, jerk, and snatch, while power bars are stiffer and 'deader.' Matching the bar to the sport-specific goal is the fix (2.2.3, 4.2.6). Finish (D) and load (E) don't create whip; A reverses the relationship; center knurl (C) is unrelated to whip/spin.

Scenario 3. Two training bars carry the same tensile strength rating (195,000 psi). Bar 1 has a yield strength of 120,000 psi; Bar 2 has 175,000 psi. For a CrossFit gym doing heavy squats, deadlifts, and shrugs, which is the better choice and why?

  1. A. Bar 1, because lower yield strength makes it more forgiving
  2. B. Either — identical tensile strength means identical performance
  3. C. Bar 2, because its higher yield strength resists permanent bending; Bar 1 will likely develop a permanent bow over time
  4. D. Bar 1, because tensile strength is the only number that matters
  5. E. Bar 2, but only for Olympic lifting, not for squats and deadlifts
Show answer

Answer: C — Tensile strength resists breaking; yield strength resists permanent bending. With equal tensile but much higher yield, Bar 2 stays straight under heavy loads, while Bar 1 (low yield) will eventually take a permanent bow even though it won't break. The best bars have high AND close tensile/yield values — and a smart buyer asks for both, since yield info is often omitted.

Scenario 4. A vendor sells you a bar advertised as '1500-pound test' and you plan to use it for high-rep deadlifts and dropped cleans. What is the most accurate way to interpret that rating?

  1. A. It guarantees the bar will never bend under any condition
  2. B. It is a static rating (a loaded bar held without bounce or drop); it does not predict behavior under the dynamic, dropped loads typical of CrossFit, so ask for tensile and yield strength too
  3. C. It means the bar weighs 1500 pounds
  4. D. Pound-test ratings are more informative than tensile/yield strength
  5. E. It certifies the bar for international weightlifting competition
Show answer

Answer: B — Pound-test ratings are established statically (e.g., a forklift holding a loaded bar with no bounce/drop). They don't capture dynamic loading, which is exactly how CrossFit uses bars, so the article advises asking for tensile and yield strength for a fuller picture. A overstates it, C and E are wrong meanings, and D inverts the article's point that tensile/yield is the more informative index.

Scenario 5. An Olympic-style bar that used to spin freely now barely rotates after an athlete dropped it awkwardly from overhead. What is the most likely cause and the appropriate response?

  1. A. The knurl wore down; re-knurl the bar before next use
  2. B. The finish oxidized; refinish the bar
  3. C. A needle bearing likely flattened from the bad drop; remove the bar from heavy Olympic-lift use and have the spin hardware serviced or replaced
  4. D. The bar bent elastically; it will fix itself with more lifting
  5. E. Nothing is wrong; bar spin is not important for cleans and snatches
Show answer

Answer: C — Soft needle bearings can flatten when a bar is dropped wrong, which stops the bar from spinning. Free rotation is essential for safe, effective cleans and snatches, so the bar should be pulled from heavy Olympic use and serviced (7.2.3, 5.2.3). Knurl (A) and finish (B) don't affect spin; D misuses 'elastic'; E contradicts why fast spin matters for the dynamic lifts.

Scenario 6. You are outfitting a busy group-class gym on a limited budget. Which equipment decision best balances safety, durability, and cost based on this article's guidance?

  1. A. Buy the cheapest bolt-retained bars so you can afford more of them
  2. B. Buy several good-quality, snap-ring-retained, durable bars rather than one premium bar, and favor sealed/maintenance-free or easily-maintained spin assemblies for a high-traffic setting
  3. C. Buy only premium competition bars with exposed bolt retainers
  4. D. Prioritize bar finish color over retention and steel quality
  5. E. Skip inspection since new bars don't need maintenance
Show answer

Answer: B — For general-purpose/institutional use, several good bars can beat one great bar, and snap rings are the preferred (can't-fail) retainer; sealed or easily-maintained spin hardware suits a busy facility. The safety floor — no bolt-retained junk bars — must not be crossed for budget (A, C). Finish is largely aesthetic (D), and all equipment needs ongoing inspection/maintenance (E) per 7.2.3.

CFJ_Bench_Starr.pdf

Open the PDF on Google Drive →

Why this is on the reading list

Bill Starr's article is on the CCFT reading list because it is a deep, single-movement case study in the relationship between technique and safe loading — the core of Domain 4 (Training). It gives you a concrete vocabulary of bench-press points of performance, the specific faults coaches see (bridging, bouncing, false grip, cocked wrists, wandering feet), and the root causes behind them, which is exactly what a CCFT must identify and correct on the floor. It also backs Domain 3 (teaching execution and progressions), Domain 5 (spotting, equipment arrangement, risk management), and Domain 1/7 (injury risk and warning signs) because Starr frames the bench as 'the most dangerous exercise in all of strength training' and prescribes the spotting and bail-out protocols a trainer is responsible for.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 4.1.1 Identify points of performance
  • 4.1.2 Identify sound mechanics
  • 4.1.3 Identify faults in movement
  • 4.1.4 Identify refinements of sound mechanics to optimize performance
  • 4.1.5 Identify common themes in athletes' movements
  • 4.1.6 Identify root cause of faults
  • 4.2.1 Communicate cues to correct unsound mechanics
  • 4.2.2 Use multiple cueing strategies (visual, tactile, verbal)
  • 4.2.3 Utilize effective cues (short, specific, actionable)
  • 4.2.4 Reinforce sound mechanics
  • 4.2.5 Refine sound mechanics to optimize performance
  • 4.2.6 Apply basic principles of anatomy and biomechanics
  • 4.2.7 Address the most egregious fault first (triage)
  • 3.1.1 Teach proper execution of movements
  • 3.1.3 Use progressions to teach complex moves
  • 3.1.4 Teach and use correct spotting techniques
  • 3.1.10 Teach the relationship between technique and intensity (threshold training)
  • 3.2.2 Demonstrate movement faults
  • 5.2.1 Apply mechanics-consistency-intensity to programming for safety and performance
  • 5.2.3 Manage risk for the athlete
  • 5.2.6 Recognize warning signs for possible injury or overexertion
  • 5.2.7 Arrange equipment, athletes, instructors to maximize safety
  • 5.2.8 Educate athletes on personal responsibility in a workout setting
  • 1.1.2 Recognize conditions/injuries outside CCFT Scope of Practice that require referral
  • 2.2.3 Scale for athletes with sport-specific goals
  • 7.3.1 Create and follow an Emergency Action Plan (EAP)

What to focus on while reading

  • The grip standard: thumbs WRAPPED around the bar (never a false/thumbless grip), and the width that puts wrists directly above elbows so forearms stay vertical — highlight WHY (vertical pressing path = power; lateral pressing = wasted power and higher risk).
  • The specific cue for finding grip width: extend thumbs until they barely touch the smooth knurling center of the Olympic bar, then adjust so forearms are vertical.
  • Wrists must stay absolutely straight, not cocked or twisted — note both reasons given (twisting bleeds off power from chest/shoulders/arms, and small wrist joints injure easily and heal slowly).
  • The taping remedy for wandering/cocked wrists (a tactile correction tool), and the boundary: tight enough to hold, not so tight it cuts circulation.
  • Feet as the foundation: feet planted flat and squeezed to the floor; 'benching starts with the feet.' Highlight that loss of the foot base is what drives squirming and bridging.
  • The full-body tightness setup: squirm down into the bench, lock shoulder blades and glutes into the fabric, plant the feet — and hold that position the entire set.
  • The two banned faults named in a section header: bridging (lifting the butt/hips off the bench) and bouncing/rebounding the bar off the chest. Hunt for every place Starr explains the harm.
  • Bar path and bottom position: lower under control to a point at the END of the breastbone (low chest/sternum), pause 1 second, then the bar travels up in a slight backward arc to finish over the chin/neck — not further back.
  • The tempo prescription: lower slowly and controlled (more slow than fast), pause 1 second on the chest, then drive up forcefully like a 'boxing jab,' blending the start into the middle with no hesitation.
  • The breathing/bracing instruction: take a breath and hold it through the rep (Valsalva), exhale only at lockout — note the stated mechanism: positive intrathoracic pressure keeps the diaphragm locked and the rib cage rigid for a solid foundation.
  • Spotter responsibilities (3 of them): help lift the bar off the uprights, help rack it safely at the end, and rescue if stuck — and the explicit boundary that the spotter does NOT help move the bar through the sticking point.
  • The 'All-You Syndrome' and Starr's rule: if the spotter touches the bar before lockout, the rep does not count ('Strength training is not a team sport').
  • The prearranged liftoff signal ('Give me the weight on three…') and keeping pressure on the bar until you see it placed in the uprights — communication and handoff safety.
  • The solo bail-out protocol (no spotter): do NOT hesitate; tip one side so the plates slide off, which flips the bar and unloads the other end. Note this is a deliberately taught skill, not improvisation.
  • Why the bench is called 'the most dangerous exercise in all of strength training' — the bar is suspended directly over the face and chest, so a slipped grip or a stuck rep can be catastrophic.
  • The historical mechanism for rotator-cuff injuries: heavy OVERHEAD pressing strengthens the rotator cuff; the shift to bench-as-king in the '70s correlated with the rise of rotator-cuff injuries. Highlight the implication for balancing pressing patterns.
  • Starr's core thesis line to underline: the bench is 'not the true villain' — done with precise technique and not overworked it is excellent; sloppy form plus excessive volume/load is what traumatizes wrists, elbows, shoulders, rotator cuffs, and pecs.
  • The 'learn it right from the get-go' principle: bad habits, once grooved over time, almost never change — argues for coaching mechanics before load on novices.
  • Sport-specific programming examples (football: bench twice/week, heavy Monday wave + back-off sets of 10, lighter Friday volume) versus Olympic lifters (keep reps low — singles/doubles to build strength without pec hypertrophy or losing shoulder flexibility; stretch shoulders after every set and after the session).
  • The transfer claim: bench trains deltoids and triceps (used in pressing/jerking and 'every sport'), while pecs contribute to few athletic actions — Starr prefers a closer grip to bias delts/triceps over outer pecs.
  • The risk-vs-reward note on wide grip: a wide grip can yield a higher bench number but carries a higher injury risk (his only 11-year injury at Hopkins was a wide-gripper who tore his pecs twice).

Concepts to understand

  • Technique governs safe intensity: the bench is only safe and productive when mechanics are sound; load and volume amplify whatever technique exists — this is the mechanics→consistency→intensity logic applied to a single lift (3.1.10, 5.2.1).
  • Points of performance for the bench you can coach to: secure full grip, vertical forearms / wrists over elbows, straight wrists, planted/squeezed feet, locked shoulder blades and glutes (tight torso), controlled descent to the low sternum, 1-second pause, forceful straight-line drive arcing slightly back to over the chin, breath held to lockout (4.1.1, 4.1.2).
  • Fault recognition: bridging (hips off bench), bouncing/rebounding off the chest, false/thumbless grip, cocked or twisting wrists, feet dangling or moving/leaving the floor, grip too wide or too narrow, exhaling mid-rep — and the ability to spot each on the floor (4.1.3, 3.2.2).
  • Root-cause reasoning: squirming and bridging are usually SYMPTOMS of a lost foundation (feet not set / torso not tight), not standalone faults — fix the base and the compensations disappear (4.1.6).
  • Common themes across athletes: novices treat the bench as 'easy' and self-coach, grooving bad habits because coaches spend teaching time on the clean and squat — so the trainer must proactively teach the bench rather than assume it's intuitive (4.1.5, 3.1.1).
  • Refinement vs. correction: once mechanics are sound, optimizations (closer grip for vertical pressing, blending the start into the middle of the press, perfect bar groove, consistent bottom position) raise both performance and the loads that can be handled safely (4.1.4, 4.2.5).
  • Cueing toolkit: verbal ('thumbs around the bar,' 'wrists over elbows,' 'drive like a jab'), visual (demonstrating the false grip vs. wrapped grip, the bridge vs. flat butt), and tactile (taping the wrists to stop cocking) — choosing the strategy that fixes the specific fault (4.2.1, 4.2.2, 4.2.3).
  • Fault triage: with a brand-new lifter showing several faults at once, address the most dangerous one first — a false grip or bar-over-face-without-a-plan is a higher-order safety risk than a slightly wide grip (4.2.7).
  • Anatomy/biomechanics applied: vertical bar path lets the deltoids and triceps work efficiently; a wide grip shifts load to outer pecs and increases shoulder/pec injury risk; heavy overhead pressing strengthens the rotator cuff, so an all-bench upper-body diet leaves those stabilizers underdeveloped (4.2.6).
  • Spotting as a coachable, defined skill: the spotter exists for liftoff, re-rack, and rescue — not to assist the rep; understand the 'All-You Syndrome' as both a coaching-integrity issue and a data-integrity issue (the lift is no longer the athlete's true capacity) (3.1.4, 5.2.7).
  • Risk management and EAP thinking: because the loaded bar sits over the face/chest, the trainer must arrange spotting, teach the solo bail-out (dump the plates), and treat a stuck-with-no-spotter scenario as an emergency to be prevented and planned for (5.2.3, 5.2.6, 5.2.7, 7.3.1).
  • Warning signs and scope: persistent wrist/elbow/shoulder/pec pain from grinding ugly reps is a referral-worthy injury signal; a torn pec or serious elbow injury ends benching (and sometimes all strength training) — the trainer recognizes the warning signs and refers out, staying within scope (1.1.2, 5.2.6).
  • Personal responsibility and culture: 'anything goes' bench culture (bridging, bouncing, ego numbers for recruiters) is a coaching/culture failure; the trainer educates athletes that form is non-negotiable and that the number means nothing if the rep is illegitimate (5.2.8).
  • Sport-specific scaling and programming: bench frequency, rep schemes, and even whether to emphasize the lift depend on the athlete's sport and goal (football/throwers/wrestlers value it; Olympic lifters keep reps low and protect shoulder flexibility) — programming serves the goal, not tradition (2.2.3, 5.2.1).
  • Breathing and bracing as a performance and safety mechanism: holding the breath (Valsalva) creates intrathoracic pressure that stabilizes the trunk; exhaling early collapses the foundation and makes the rep harder — understand when this brace is appropriate and that it is a deliberate technique (4.2.6).
  • The 'learn it right first' principle: motor patterns grooved over time are extremely resistant to change, so investing coaching time in correct novice execution prevents years of fault and injury risk (3.1.1, 3.1.3).

How the exam applies this

Expect scenario items that drop you onto the floor with an athlete benching and ask for the best coaching action: spotting a fault and naming the root cause (4.1.3/4.1.6), choosing the most egregious fault to fix first (4.2.7), or selecting the right cue type — verbal, visual, or tactile, e.g., taping wrists (4.2.1/4.2.2/4.2.3). Other items test safety judgment: what a spotter should and should not do, how to handle a 'no spotter available' situation, and when persistent pain crosses into referral (3.1.4, 5.2.3, 5.2.6, 5.2.7, 1.1.2). You may also see programming/scaling questions that ask how bench prescription changes for a powerlifter or football player versus an Olympic lifter (2.2.3, 5.2.1), and conceptual items on the technique–intensity relationship and personal responsibility for sound mechanics (3.1.10, 5.2.8). The answer the exam wants is the experienced coach's call, not a memorized line from Starr.

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

False grip (thumbless grip)
Gripping the bar with thumbs on the same side as the fingers rather than wrapped around it. Starr bans it on the bench: it lets the bar slip and roll onto the lifter, and it puts the wrists in a poor position. Every bar-slip injury he saw came from a false grip.
Secure (full) grip
Thumbs wrapped completely around the bar so it cannot slip. The required, safe grip for benching; it also lets the lifter steer the bar back into the correct groove better than a false grip.
Vertical forearms / wrists-over-elbows
The grip-width standard: hands set so the wrists are stacked directly above the elbows, keeping the forearms vertical. This drives the bar straight up (efficient power) instead of pressing it laterally (wasted power, higher risk).
Cocked wrist
Bending or twisting the wrist back/around under the bar instead of keeping it straight and stacked. It bleeds power out of the press and exposes the small, slow-healing wrist joints to injury; taping is the fix.
Bridging
Lifting the hips/buttocks off the bench to arch excessively and shorten the press. A banned major form break — it is illegal in competition and a sign the lifter has lost a stable foundation. Cue: keep the butt locked to the bench.
Bouncing / rebounding
Crashing the bar onto the chest and using the rebound to jump-start the press. Banned: it robs the rep of legitimacy and traumatizes the pecs, elbows, and shoulders over time. Replaced by a controlled descent and a 1-second pause.
Sticking point
The hardest part of the press range where the bar tends to stall. A solid foundation (planted feet, tight torso) lets the lifter drive power up through the base to get past it — without resorting to squirming or bridging.
The pause (1-second)
A deliberate ~1-second hold with the bar motionless on the low chest before pressing. Builds control, eliminates bouncing, and prepares the athlete for heavy loads and competition standards.
Bottom position
Where the bar touches the body: at the end of the breastbone (low sternum). Establishing the same touch point every rep improves consistency and bar path.
Bar path / groove
The line the bar travels: straight up off the low chest, then arcing slightly backward to finish over the chin/neck — and no further back than that. Staying 'in the groove' is the efficient, repeatable line.
Foundation (the feet)
The base of the lift: feet planted flat and squeezed to the floor, shoulder blades and glutes locked into the bench. 'Benching starts with the feet'; losing the base is what triggers squirming and bridging.
Boxing-jab drive
Starr's cue for the press: after the pause, punch the bar up forcefully and continuously, blending the start of the drive directly into the mid-range so it climbs to lockout without hesitation.
Intrathoracic pressure (breath hold / Valsalva)
Pressure created in the chest cavity by holding a deep breath through the rep. It locks the diaphragm and stiffens the rib cage, giving a rigid trunk to press from. Exhale only at lockout; exhaling early collapses the foundation.
Spotter
