A training partner whose job is to help lift the bar off the uprights, help re-rack it safely, and rescue the lifter if stuck — but NOT to help move the bar through the sticking point.
All-You Syndrome
Starr's term for the common scene where a spotter is actually helping move the bar while yelling 'It's all you!' His rule: if the spotter touches the bar before lockout, the rep doesn't count — the lift is no longer the athlete's true effort.
Solo bail-out (dumping the bar)
The taught emergency procedure when stuck with no spotter: don't hesitate — tip one side so the plates slide off, which flips and unloads the other end. Ugly and noisy, but far safer than being pinned.
Rotator cuff
The group of small shoulder-stabilizing muscles. Starr notes these injuries became common only after the bench replaced overhead pressing as the upper-body lift of choice — heavy overhead work strengthens them, an all-bench diet does not.
Prearranged liftoff signal
An agreed verbal count for the handoff (e.g., 'Give me the weight on three. One, two, three.') so the lifter and spotter move the bar off the uprights together cleanly and safely.
Back-off set
A lighter, higher-rep set performed after heavier work (e.g., a set of 10 after fives) to add training volume/workload without the load of the top sets.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • The bench is the most dangerous lift in strength training because the loaded bar sits directly over the face and chest — a slipped grip or a stuck rep can be catastrophic. A CCFT must arrange spotting and never let a novice grind heavy benches unsupervised.
  • False/thumbless grip is a hard NO on the bench — it is the direct cause of bars slipping onto the lifter. Correct it immediately; this is a triage-first safety fault.
  • No spotter available is a managed-risk situation, not a 'go ahead anyway' — the athlete must know the bail-out (dump the plates), loads should be conservative, and the EAP applies if someone gets pinned (7.3.1).
  • Persistent wrist, elbow, shoulder, rotator-cuff, or pec pain from repeated bad-form reps is a warning sign of impending or actual injury; a torn pec or serious elbow injury is outside coaching scope and requires referral to a medical professional (1.1.2, 5.2.6).
  • An all-bench upper-body program with no overhead pressing under-trains the rotator cuff and shoulder stabilizers — a programming/risk concern the trainer should balance.
  • 'Ego number' bench culture (bridging, bouncing, wide-grip max-outs for recruiting numbers) raises injury risk and produces illegitimate lifts; the trainer is responsible for enforcing sound mechanics and educating athletes on personal responsibility (5.2.8).
  • Wide grip can add to the bench number but carries higher pec/shoulder injury risk — weigh reward against risk for the individual athlete and their goal.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. A new member is about to bench. As he unracks, you notice his thumbs are on the same side of the bar as his fingers (thumbless), his grip is slightly wider than his shoulders, and his feet are tucked back near the bench legs. He has no spotter. What is your best FIRST action?

  1. A. Let him complete the set and then cue all three issues at once afterward so you don't interrupt his rhythm
  2. B. Re-rack the bar, fix the thumbless grip to a wrapped secure grip, and get a spotter or set up the bail-out before he presses again
  3. C. Narrow his grip first so his forearms are vertical, then let him press
  4. D. Cue him to plant his feet flat and squeeze the floor, then let him press
  5. E. Add a back-off set of 10 to build his foundation before correcting anything
Show answer

Answer: B — Triage the most egregious, highest-risk fault first (4.2.7). A false/thumbless grip on a bar suspended over the face is the catastrophic-risk item — every bar-slip injury Starr cites came from it — and the lack of a spotter compounds it. Fix the grip and secure spotting/bail-out before any pressing. C and D address real but lower-order faults (width, feet) and ignore the dump-risk grip. A lets him press unsafely. E is a programming move irrelevant to an active safety hazard.

Scenario 2. An athlete's bench reps look fine until the weight gets heavy, then his hips lift off the bench (bridging) and he squirms to grind the bar past the sticking point. What is the root cause you should coach to?

  1. A. His triceps are weak, so program more triceps accessory work
  2. B. He is exhaling too early, so cue him to breathe out at the bottom
  3. C. He has lost his foundation — feet/torso aren't set and tight — so re-establish planted feet, squeezed glutes, and locked shoulder blades
  4. D. His grip is too narrow, so widen it to recruit the outer pecs
  5. E. The load is appropriate; bridging is a normal way to move heavy weight
Show answer

Answer: C — Starr is explicit that squirming and bridging are symptoms of a lost base: 'without a strong foundation, no source of additional power is available,' so the lifter bridges to set the bar back in motion. The root-cause fix (4.1.6) is to rebuild the foundation — feet planted and squeezed, glutes and shoulder blades locked into the bench. A and D treat unrelated guesses; B contradicts the breath-hold guidance; E endorses a banned, competition-illegal fault and a safety/integrity problem.

Scenario 3. Mid-set, a lifter starts to stall at the sticking point and his training partner grabs the bar and helps it to lockout while shouting 'It's all you!' How should you, the coach, handle this?

  1. A. Count the rep — the spotter barely touched it and the athlete did most of the work
  2. B. Do not count the rep, and re-teach that the spotter's job is liftoff, re-rack, and rescue only — not moving the bar through the sticking point
  3. C. Tell the spotter to push harder next time so the athlete can complete more reps
  4. D. Add weight next set since he clearly had more in the tank
  5. E. Stop the workout and refer the athlete to a physical therapist
Show answer

Answer: B — This is the 'All-You Syndrome.' Starr's rule: if the spotter touches the bar before lockout, the rep doesn't count, and a spotter's role is strictly liftoff, safe re-rack, and rescue — not assisting the rep (3.1.4, 5.2.7). Counting it (A) corrupts the athlete's true-capacity data and reinforces bad habits; C makes it worse; D bases a load increase on a fake rep; E is unwarranted — there's no injury signal here.

Scenario 4. A masters athlete who competes in Olympic weightlifting asks whether the bench press will hurt his snatch and clean & jerk by tightening his shoulders. Based on Starr's reasoning, what is the best coaching guidance?

  1. A. Avoid the bench entirely; it has no value for an Olympic lifter
  2. B. Bench heavy for high reps to maximize pec size and pressing strength
  3. C. Keep the reps low (singles and doubles) to build pressing strength without adding pec size, and stretch the shoulders after every set and after the session
  4. D. Replace all his overhead pressing with bench press to save the shoulders
  5. E. Use the widest possible grip to protect the shoulders
Show answer

Answer: C — Starr recommends Olympic lifters keep bench reps low (singles/doubles) to strengthen the deltoids and triceps — which transfer to pressing and jerking — without hypertrophying the pecs or compromising shoulder flexibility, and to stretch the shoulders after every set and the session (2.2.3, 5.2.1). He even reports the bench helping lifters set overhead world records. A overstates the case; B causes the exact pec/flexibility problem the athlete fears; D removes the overhead work that strengthens the rotator cuff; E raises injury risk.

Scenario 5. You're teaching bench technique to a beginner. Which sequence best reflects the correct setup and execution Starr describes?

  1. A. Wide grip with cocked wrists, feet up on the bench, bounce the bar off the chest, exhale on the way down
  2. B. Secure grip with vertical forearms and straight wrists, lock shoulder blades/glutes and plant the feet, take and hold a breath, lower under control to the low sternum, pause 1 second, then drive up forcefully and exhale at lockout
  3. C. Let the feet dangle for comfort, lower fast, no pause, press with a thumbless grip for extra thrust
  4. D. Take a breath and exhale immediately as you unrack, then press as fast as possible with a relaxed torso
  5. E. Bridge the hips to shorten the range, lower to the throat, and grind through the sticking point
Show answer

Answer: B — B is Starr's full sequence: secure wrapped grip, wrists over elbows / vertical forearms, locked shoulder blades and glutes with feet planted and squeezed, deep breath held (intrathoracic pressure) through the rep, controlled descent to the end of the breastbone, a 1-second pause, then a forceful straight-line drive arcing slightly back to over the chin, exhaling at lockout (3.1.1, 4.1.1, 4.1.2). Every other option strings together the exact faults Starr bans — false grip, cocked wrists, dangling feet, bouncing, bridging, early exhale, lowering to the throat.

Scenario 6. A lifter keeps cocking his wrists backward under the bar despite repeated verbal reminders to keep them straight. What is the most effective next coaching strategy?

  1. A. Tell him again, louder, to keep his wrists straight
  2. B. Switch to a tactile correction: tape the wrists firmly (not so tight it cuts circulation) to hold them straight and protect the joints
  3. C. Have him widen his grip so the wrists naturally straighten
  4. D. Add wrist-curl accessory work and revisit the bench next month
  5. E. Tell him to use a false grip so the wrists feel more natural
Show answer

Answer: B — When a verbal cue isn't landing, change the cueing modality (4.2.1, 4.2.2). Starr's specific tactile fix for cocking/wandering wrists is taping — tight enough to hold the wrists firmly but not so tight it cuts off circulation — which both stops the fault and protects the small joints. A just repeats a failed cue; C and D don't address the wrist position; E introduces the banned, dangerous false grip.

Scenario 7. During open gym, a member tells you he benches alone at home and asks what to do if he ever gets stuck with no spotter. What should you teach him?

  1. A. Hold the bar on his chest and wait for the energy to come back before trying again
  2. B. Roll the loaded bar down over his abs and stomach to the floor
  3. C. Don't hesitate — immediately tip one side of the bar so the plates slide off, which flips the bar and unloads the other end
  4. D. Yell for help and keep pressing until someone arrives
  5. E. Set up clips/collars extra tight so the plates can never come off
Show answer

Answer: C — Starr teaches the deliberate solo bail-out: don't hesitate, tip one end so the plates fall off, which flips the bar and unloads the other side (5.2.3, 5.2.6, 7.3.1). Waiting (A) only depletes energy while pinned. Rolling the loaded bar down the torso (B) is what Starr did before he knew better — it left his chest and abs black and blue and is the lesson he warns against. D risks getting fully pinned; E (tight collars) removes the very escape the bail-out depends on, making it more dangerous.

Scenario 8. A high-school athlete benches with heavy weight, bouncing the bar off his chest and bridging hard to hit a number for a recruiter, and over weeks he develops nagging shoulder and elbow pain that isn't going away. What is the most appropriate coaching response?

  1. A. Encourage the bridging and bounce since the recruiting number is what matters
  2. B. Diagnose the likely rotator-cuff tear and prescribe rehab exercises yourself
  3. C. Stop reinforcing the ego number, re-teach controlled reps without bounce/bridge, and refer the persistent joint pain to a medical professional
  4. D. Tape the shoulder and have him keep maxing twice a week
  5. E. Tell him the pain is normal for benching and to push through it
Show answer

Answer: C — Two CCFT duties combine here. First, enforce sound mechanics and educate on personal responsibility — the 'anything goes' recruiting culture (bounce, bridge, ego number) is exactly what Starr says traumatizes joints (5.2.8, 3.1.10). Second, persistent shoulder/elbow pain is a warning sign that is outside coaching scope: recognize it and refer out (1.1.2, 5.2.6). B oversteps scope by diagnosing/prescribing rehab; A, D, and E all push the athlete deeper into injury.

D4 · Training 24% of exam Confidence tier: ___

CFJ_CBT_Hermiz.pdf

Open the PDF on Google Drive →

Why this is on the reading list

This article ('Building Mental Toughness' by John Hermiz) explains the psychological mechanism behind CrossFit's 'never-quit' ethos: high-intensity work pushes athletes past the lactate threshold, producing genuine negative thoughts and emotions, and the coach's job is to train athletes to keep moving according to plan despite those feelings. For Domain 4 (Training), it gives the coach a framework for reading the difference between a fault driven by physical breakdown versus an athlete who is mentally negotiating with discomfort, and for cueing the athlete to push through safely. It also directly supports assessing psychological tolerance for training (1.1.4), balancing relentlessness with acknowledgement (4.2.8), and the technique-versus-intensity relationship (3.1.10), because intensity is exactly where mental toughness and movement quality collide.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 4.2.8 Balance relentlessness with acknowledgement of improvement
  • 4.2.4 Reinforce sound mechanics
  • 4.2.1 Communicate cues to correct unsound mechanics
  • 4.2.3 Utilize effective cues (short, specific, actionable)
  • 4.2.7 Address the most egregious fault first (triage)
  • 4.1.6 Identify root cause of faults (mental negotiation vs. physical breakdown)
  • 4.1.5 Identify common themes in athletes' movements (under fatigue)
  • 3.1.10 Teach the relationship between technique and intensity (threshold training)
  • 3.1.11 Teach relative intensity
  • 1.1.4 Assess psychological tolerance for training
  • 1.1.3 Assess for rhabdomyolysis risk
  • 2.2.5 Scale by skill level
  • 3.1.12 Teach the principles of scaling
  • 5.1.1 Provide athletes with goal setting
  • 5.1.3 Establish rapport and adapt approach based on athlete response
  • 5.2.3 Manage risk for the athlete
  • 5.2.6 Recognize warning signs for possible injury or overexertion
  • 1.2.4 Monitor athlete for signs of over- or under-training

What to focus on while reading

  • Hermiz's working definition of mental toughness: 'the ability to continue according to plan in a way that is in line with your values even though negative thoughts and emotions are pulling you in another direction' — and the layman's version: 'get present and move forward in a stressful situation.' Highlight both; the exam tests the applied concept, not the wording.
  • The 'medical model' of problem-solving (find it, remove it) and why it works in the OUTER world (small apartment, bad job) but BACKFIRES in the INNER world of thoughts and feelings.
  • The paradox stated explicitly: 'if you're not willing to have it, you've got it!' — unwillingness to feel a feeling increases its frequency and drives avoidance behavior.
  • Traditional cognitive therapy = identify maladaptive thoughts and REPLACE them. Third-wave CBT / ACT = do NOT remove the thoughts; instead INCREASE tolerance for them. Note this contrast — it is the spine of the article.
  • Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) named as the most renowned third-wave CBT form (reference 1: Hayes, Strosahl, Wilson).
  • 'Cognitive defusion': separating yourself from your thoughts/feelings — HAVING them rather than BEING them — which creates flexibility to choose behavior under stress.
  • 'Committed action': when you least feel like training, that is precisely the moment to act on your value and train anyway.
  • 'Acting from outside and in': feelings often change AFTER you start the behavior, not before — debunking the misconception that you must 'feel like it' first. Activity as a treatment for depression is the supporting example.
  • The physiology link: as exertion rises and the ANAEROBIC system supplies most of the energy, affective responses become more negative (reference 2: Lind, Welch, Ekkekakis).
  • Pain is triggered when work surpasses the LACTIC-ACID (lactate) threshold; byproducts (lactic acid, CO2) fire pain receptors → discomfort → negative affect → thoughts of quitting or self-scaling mid-workout (reference 3: Vecchiet et al.).
  • The predictable mid-workout negotiation: thoughts of 'lowering reps, sets, load' appear — the coach must learn to recognize these as normal threshold artifacts, not signals to stop.
  • 'Cognitive restructuring' from getting through hard workouts: a rule forms — 'A situation might seem hopeless and overwhelming, but if I keep going, I'll get through it' — which builds confidence that transfers OUTSIDE the gym.
  • The four practical rules at the end: (1) Start at the right level — beginners need success, use proper scaling, no one improves by constantly failing or getting injured; (2) Push the limit with realistic challenges; (3) Commit to the workout — quitting is not an option UNLESS there's a risk of injury; (4) Train yourself at observing thoughts/feelings — recognize the negotiating thoughts but don't buy into them.
  • The critical SAFETY caveat embedded in Rule 3: 'Quitting is not an option UNLESS there's a risk of injury.' Highlight this — it is the line between toughness coaching and reckless coaching.
  • Rule 1's injury warning: pushing through without preparation (the marathon analogy) carries 'a real risk of injury' — toughness is never an excuse to skip scaling or progression.
  • The author's credentials frame the authority: Level 1 trainer + psychologist specializing in behavior change — so the article is reconciling sports psychology with coaching practice.

Concepts to understand

  • Mental toughness is behavioral, not emotional: it is the capacity to keep executing the plan despite negative thoughts/feelings — a coach builds it by structuring repeated, survivable exposure to discomfort, not by eliminating the discomfort.
  • Negative thoughts and emotions during hard training are NORMAL and expected physiological byproducts of crossing the lactate threshold — the coach should treat them as predictable, not as a problem to fix or a reason to stop.
  • The inner/outer world distinction: trying to 'remove' an uncomfortable feeling (the medical model) is the wrong tool for the inner world and increases avoidance; tolerance, not removal, is the goal.
  • Cognitive defusion applied to coaching: cue the athlete to OBSERVE the thought ('I want to quit') as just a thought rather than a command, creating room to choose to keep moving.
  • Acting 'from outside and in': behavior change precedes mood change — getting an athlete to start (or restart) the work is more effective than waiting for them to feel ready; useful for the athlete who 'doesn't feel like it' today.
  • The technique-intensity relationship (threshold training): intensity is where mental toughness matters AND where mechanics break down — a coach must distinguish an athlete mentally negotiating from an athlete physically failing, because the correct response differs (push through vs. correct/scale/stop).
  • Triage of root cause (4.1.6): when an athlete slows or 'wants to drop the load,' ask whether the limiter is mental (capacity remains, mechanics sound) or physical/mechanical (form is degrading, fatigue is genuine) — only the former calls for toughness cueing.
  • Balancing relentlessness with acknowledgement (4.2.8): the never-quit spirit must be paired with recognizing real improvement and respecting genuine limits — relentlessness without acknowledgement burns athletes out; acknowledgement without relentlessness never builds toughness.
  • Scaling is the foundation of toughness, not its opposite: beginners must experience success, so proper scaling (2.2.5, 3.1.12) sets up the survivable challenge that builds confidence — failure and injury destroy it.
  • The safety boundary on 'never quit': pushing through is the default ONLY when there is no risk of injury; recognizing warning signs (5.2.6) and managing risk (5.2.3) override the toughness mandate every time.
  • Confidence is transferable and earned through completion: getting through hard workouts installs a generalizable rule ('if I keep going, I'll get through it') that the coach can name and reinforce to motivate athletes.
  • Assessing psychological tolerance (1.1.4): the coach reads each athlete's threshold for discomfort and tailors the challenge — realistic enough to succeed (Rule 1), hard enough to grow (Rule 2).
  • Distinguishing mental discomfort from medical danger: 'I feel like throwing up / I want to quit' can be normal threshold affect, OR it can co-occur with red-flag symptoms (disproportionate pain, dizziness beyond exertion) — the coach must not normalize away a genuine emergency or a rhabdo risk.
  • Cueing under fatigue should be short, specific, and present-focused ('get present, move forward') consistent with effective-cue principles (4.2.3) — long explanations fail when an athlete is past threshold.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenarios where an athlete mid-workout starts negotiating ('can I drop the weight?', 'I think I'm going to be sick') and you must choose the best coaching response — the key discrimination is whether the limiter is mental (sound mechanics, capacity remains → encourage and keep moving, task 4.2.8/4.2.4) versus physical/mechanical or medical (degrading form, warning signs → correct, scale, or stop, tasks 4.1.6/5.2.3/5.2.6/1.1.3). Other items test the principle that toughness is built through survivable, properly scaled challenge (2.2.5, 3.1.12) and that intensity is where technique and mental load intersect (3.1.10, 3.1.11). The article's safety caveat — push through UNLESS there's risk of injury — is the trap-avoider: any option that has the coach normalizing a genuine emergency to 'build toughness' is wrong.

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Mental toughness
The ability to keep executing your plan, consistent with your values, even while negative thoughts and emotions push you to stop or change course; in plain terms, getting present and moving forward under stress.
Medical model of problem-solving
Find the problem and remove it. Effective for outer-world problems (change a bad job, find a bigger apartment) but counterproductive when applied to inner-world thoughts and feelings.
Third-wave cognitive behavioral therapy (third-wave CBT)
A modern CBT approach whose goal is not to eliminate disturbing thoughts/emotions but to increase tolerance for them; the most renowned form is ACT.
Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT)
The leading third-wave CBT method (Hayes, Strosahl, Wilson). Treats negative thoughts and emotions as a normal part of life and works to raise tolerance for them rather than remove them.
Cognitive defusion
Separating yourself from your thoughts and feelings so you observe them from a distance — 'having' a thought rather than 'being' it — which frees you to choose your behavior under stress.
Committed action
Acting in line with your values precisely when you least feel like it; e.g., training on a day you're tired because health is your value.
Acting from outside and in
Start the behavior first; the feeling often follows. Counters the misconception that you must 'feel like it' before you can act. Underlies activity-based treatment of depression.
Cognitive restructuring
The shift that occurs after getting through tough situations, installing a usable rule: 'It may seem hopeless, but if I keep going, I'll get through it.'
Lactic-acid (lactate) threshold
The exertion point past which anaerobic byproducts (lactic acid, CO2) accumulate and fire pain receptors, producing discomfort and a more negative emotional response — where mental toughness is tested.
Anaerobic energy system
The energy pathway dominant at high intensity; as it supplies most of the energy, affective (emotional) responses tend to become more negative.
Affective response
The emotional reaction (positive or negative) to exertion; tends toward negative as intensity rises above threshold.
Avoidance behavior
Backing out of situations that trigger uncomfortable feelings; unwillingness to feel a feeling tends to increase that feeling and shrink the athlete's life — the cycle toughness training breaks.
Proper scaling (for confidence)
Setting the challenge at a level where the athlete can succeed; beginners need success, not failure or injury, because confidence — and toughness — is built on completion.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • Rule 3 boundary: 'Quitting is not an option UNLESS there's a risk of injury.' The never-quit ethos NEVER overrides athlete safety — a coach must stop or scale an athlete the moment injury risk appears, regardless of toughness goals.
  • Do not normalize genuine emergency symptoms as 'just mental toughness.' Nausea and the urge to vomit can be normal threshold affect, but disproportionate or persisting symptoms (severe localized pain, dark urine, confusion, dizziness beyond exertion) can signal rhabdomyolysis (1.1.3) or overexertion (5.2.6) requiring you to stop the athlete and refer — outside CCFT scope.
  • Pushing an underprepared or beginner athlete through (the marathon-without-preparation analogy) carries 'a real risk of injury' — toughness is not a substitute for progression and scaling.
  • Mental toughness coaching is not psychotherapy. ACT, cognitive defusion, and treating depression are clinical interventions; a CCFT coach borrows the behavioral principle (act according to plan) but must not diagnose or treat psychological conditions — refer athletes with mental-health needs to qualified professionals (scope-of-practice limitation).

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. Mid-WOD, an experienced athlete with sound, unchanging mechanics on thrusters slows down and says, 'I want to drop to a lighter bar — I feel like I'm going to throw up.' You see no form breakdown, no signs of a medical emergency, and the load is within their proven capacity. What is the BEST coaching response?

  1. A. Immediately reduce the load to the lighter bar so the athlete feels supported
  2. B. Acknowledge the feeling is normal at this intensity, give a short present-focused cue, and encourage them to stay with the plan
  3. C. Stop the athlete and end their workout to avoid any risk
  4. D. Tell them to ignore how they feel because feelings don't matter
  5. E. Explain in detail the physiology of the lactate threshold so they understand why they feel sick
Show answer

Answer: B — Mechanics are sound, capacity remains, and there are no emergency signs — so the limiter is mental negotiation at the lactate threshold, which is normal (article's core point). The coach reinforces sound mechanics and keeps the athlete moving (4.2.4, 4.2.8) with a short, present-focused cue (4.2.3). A drops the challenge prematurely and undercuts toughness-building; C is over-cautious with no warning signs; D is dismissive and damages rapport (5.1.3) — the article says acknowledge the feeling, not deny it; E is a long explanation an athlete past threshold can't absorb.

Scenario 2. During a heavy, high-rep workout, an athlete's deadlift form is visibly breaking down — rounding lumbar spine, hips shooting up early — and they're grinding each rep. They haven't complained. Applying the article's logic on toughness versus safety, what should you do FIRST?

  1. A. Praise their never-quit spirit and let them finish the prescribed reps
  2. B. Address the most egregious fault: stop or reduce the load to restore sound mechanics before continuing
  3. C. Say nothing, because interrupting would weaken their mental toughness
  4. D. Tell them to speed up to get through the set faster
  5. E. Add weight to challenge them since they aren't complaining
Show answer

Answer: B — This is physical/mechanical breakdown, not mental negotiation — the root cause is fatigue degrading technique (4.1.6), and the toughness mandate explicitly does NOT apply when there is risk of injury (Rule 3). The coach triages the most egregious fault first (4.2.7) and protects the athlete (5.2.3, 5.2.6) by correcting or scaling. A, C, and E let a dangerous fault continue under a misread 'toughness' rationale; D worsens it.

Scenario 3. A nervous beginner is intimidated by a benchmark workout and says, 'I don't think I can do this.' Based on Hermiz's rules for building toughness and confidence, the BEST approach is to:

  1. A. Have them attempt the workout exactly as Rx'd so they learn they can survive hard things
  2. B. Scale the workout so the challenge is hard but achievable, setting them up to experience success
  3. C. Excuse them from the workout entirely until they feel more confident
  4. D. Tell them their thoughts are just thoughts and to do the full version anyway
  5. E. Compare them to a fitter member to motivate them through competition
Show answer

Answer: B — Rule 1 — start at the right level: beginners need success, not failure or injury, and proper scaling is the tool (2.2.5, 3.1.12). Confidence and toughness are built on completion, so the coach calibrates a survivable challenge. A risks failure/injury that destroys confidence; C avoids the challenge entirely and builds nothing; D misapplies cognitive defusion while skipping the scaling the article requires; E damages rapport and ignores the individual's readiness (5.1.3, 1.1.4).

Scenario 4. An athlete tells you, 'I always plan to do the full workout, but once it gets hard my brain starts bargaining — three rounds is probably enough today.' Which coaching action best reflects the article's 'observe your thoughts' rule?

  1. A. Tell them to suppress and replace those thoughts with positive affirmations
  2. B. Help them learn to recognize that negotiating self-talk as normal and predictable, and not act on it, while keeping mechanics sound
  3. C. Advise them to lower their planned volume so the thoughts never appear
  4. D. Tell them the thoughts mean they're overtrained and should rest
  5. E. Ignore it, since self-talk has no effect on performance
Show answer

Answer: B — Rule 4 and cognitive defusion: train the athlete to recognize the bargaining thoughts as normal ('thoughts are just thoughts') and choose committed action rather than buy in. A is the old replace-the-thought (traditional CBT) model the article moves past; C removes the challenge that builds toughness; D misreads normal threshold self-talk as overtraining without evidence (1.2.4); E denies the phenomenon the whole article is built on.

Scenario 5. Two weeks into training, an athlete pushes hard through an unfamiliar high-volume workout despite your suggestion to scale. The next day they report severe, persistent soreness in one muscle group, swelling, and unusually dark urine. The article praises pushing through discomfort — how should you interpret and act on this?

  1. A. Celebrate it as a sign of mental toughness and program a similar workout to reinforce it
  2. B. Treat it as possible rhabdomyolysis, advise them to seek medical evaluation immediately, and do not train them through it
  3. C. Tell them it's normal lactic-acid discomfort and to train again today to flush it out
  4. D. Tell them to push through because quitting is never an option
  5. E. Give them nutrition advice to reduce the soreness
Show answer

Answer: B — These are classic rhabdomyolysis warning signs (severe localized pain, swelling, dark urine), which fall outside CCFT scope and require referral (1.1.3, 5.2.6, 5.2.3). The article's 'push through' principle explicitly stops at risk of injury — it never licenses normalizing a medical emergency. A, C, and D dangerously misapply toughness language to a red-flag situation; E delays urgent medical care and is outside scope.

Scenario 6. An athlete says they keep skipping their planned training days because by the time work ends they 'never feel like it.' Drawing on the article's 'acting from outside and in,' what guidance best helps?

  1. A. Tell them to wait until they genuinely feel motivated, then train
  2. B. Coach them to start the session regardless of how they feel, since the motivation often follows once the behavior begins
  3. C. Recommend they cut their training to only days they feel energetic
  4. D. Tell them feelings are irrelevant and willpower is all that matters
  5. E. Suggest they switch to a completely different sport
Show answer

Answer: B — 'Acting from outside and in' — behavior precedes mood; feelings often change after you start. Committed action means training even when you don't feel like it (supports goal adherence, 5.1.1, and reading psychological tolerance, 1.1.4). A reinforces the misconception the article debunks; C lets avoidance win; D is harsh and ignores the article's nuance (acknowledge feelings, then act); E abandons the goal instead of building the habit.

D4 · Training 24% of exam Confidence tier: ___

CFJ_Excellence_Bergeron_FINAL2.pdf

Open the PDF on Google Drive →

Why this is on the reading list

Ben Bergeron's 'The Pursuit of Excellence' is a philosophy-of-priorities piece: using Covey's golf-balls/pebbles/sand jar parable, it argues that an affiliate's success comes from pouring limited time and energy into what truly matters (members, relationships, and the coaching craft) rather than the 'sand' of marketing, pricing, and competition. For a D4 (Training) reader this article is largely tangential — it is fundamentally a Leadership/Management (D5) and Professional-Development (D7) article, not a movement-evaluation or cueing article. Its one genuine D4 anchor is that Bergeron explicitly names 'your ability (and the ability of your staff) to see and correct movement' and 'running fun and effective classes' as core 'pebbles' — i.e., the coaching skills D4 tests are, in his framework, non-negotiable priorities a trainer must protect time to develop. Read it to understand WHY the trainer's eye and continuing education are priorities, then expect the exam to test the actual seeing/correcting in other articles.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 4.2.8 Balance relentlessness with acknowledgement of improvement
  • 4.2.7 Address the most egregious fault first (triage) — as an instance of the article's prioritize-what-matters-most principle
  • 7.1.1 Self-assess sessions according to the foundations of effective training
  • 7.1.2 Pursue continuing education
  • 5.1.2 Create a culture/community of excellence and camaraderie
  • 5.1.3 Establish rapport and adapt approach based on athlete response
  • 5.1.4 Lead by example
  • 5.1.1 Provide athletes with goal setting (member improvement and results as the goal)

What to focus on while reading

  • Find the central thesis stated outright: 'the pursuit of excellence is the pursuit of improving the lives of your members.' This is the lens the whole article asks you to coach through.
  • Highlight the golf-balls/pebbles/sand/beers jar parable and what each tier maps to — you must be able to classify any given task into the right tier.
  • Golf balls = community, relationships with members and coaches, the health/happiness/results delivered daily, and the owner's integrity. Mark these as the irreducible priorities.
  • Pebbles = programming, continued education of coaching staff, the ability (yours and your staff's) to SEE AND CORRECT MOVEMENT, running fun and effective classes, and clean bathrooms. This is the article's only direct line into D4 — flag it.
  • Sand = marketing, worrying about new affiliates opening up, complex pricing, non-compete contracts, membership software, break-even analyses, cash-flow projections. Mark as 'noise/distraction,' important but never first.
  • Note the ordering principle: if you pour the sand in first, there is no room for the pebbles or golf balls. The SEQUENCE of attention is the lesson, not just the categories.
  • Highlight 'simple — not easy.' Bergeron warns that the hard interpersonal/coaching work (dealing with a coach or member not meeting expectations, fixing the rep-cutting member) is what people avoid by hiding in 'complex' busywork.
  • Flag the concrete relationship behaviors: spend time before/after class, talk about non-fitness topics, use names, look members in the eye, send flowers for an ill family member, take coaches to dinner — these are 'lead by example' and rapport (5.1.3/5.1.4) in action.
  • Mark the daily mantra 'Them not me' and the question 'What can I do today to improve my members' experience and their lives overall?' — a self-assessment heuristic (7.1.1).
  • Note the explicit example of addressing 'that problem member who seems to always be cutting reps or making other members uncomfortable' — a class-management and standards-enforcement obligation, not something to defer.
  • Highlight the closing principle: 'If you focus on delivering your very best to your clients, you can expect to have a great many clients.' Results-first, growth-follows — the inverse of chasing new members.
  • Note the author credentials (Level 1 Seminar Staff, 2011 Games-winning affiliate team, B.O.X. Seminar creator) — context for why CrossFit puts this on the reading list, but NOT exam-testable content.

Concepts to understand

  • Excellence is operationally defined here as improving members' lives — happiness, confidence, community belonging, health, wellness, fitness, and results. Understand it so you can recognize, in a scenario, which coaching choice actually serves the member versus serves the owner or the business optics.
  • The golf-balls/pebbles/sand hierarchy as a prioritization model: when time and energy are finite, fund the highest-impact-on-members items first. Apply this to triage of a coach's own attention during a class, not just business strategy.
  • Programming, staff continuing education, and the ability to see and correct movement are 'pebbles' — essential and high-value, but they only get oxygen if the relational 'golf balls' are protected first. Understand that the coaching craft D4 tests sits in this tier and must be deliberately invested in.
  • Sequence matters: low-value 'sand' (admin, marketing, competitor-watching) expands to fill all available time if you let it, crowding out what matters. Apply this as a guard against letting logistics or paperwork displace member coaching.
  • 'Simple, not easy' — the right priorities are conceptually obvious but emotionally hard; people avoid hard interpersonal/coaching confrontations by busying themselves with complex but low-stakes work. Recognize avoidance behavior in a coaching scenario.
  • Member-first, growth-second: delivering excellence to current members is the engine of retention and organic growth; chasing new members directly is the wrong primary focus. Understand the causal direction.
  • Relationship and rapport as deliberate practice: names, eye contact, genuine listening, time before/after class, and small gestures are the daily mechanics of building a culture of excellence and camaraderie (5.1.2/5.1.3) — not optional extras.
  • Investing in coaches as much as in yourself — developing staff is part of delivering member excellence, and it ties directly to 'continued education of your coaching staff' (a pebble) and to leadership (5.1.4).
  • Standards enforcement is a member-experience obligation: the rep-cutting / disruptive member must be addressed because tolerating it degrades the experience and culture for everyone — connect to managing the group (5.2) and balancing attention (5.2.9).
  • Self-assessment as a daily discipline: the 'Them not me / what can I do today to improve their experience' question is a repeatable self-check that maps onto self-assessing sessions against the foundations of effective training (7.1.1).
  • Balancing relentlessness with care: although this article does not use the seeing-and-correcting language directly, its 'deliver your very best to your members' ethos is the same disposition behind 4.2.8 — be relentless about improvement while keeping the member's experience and dignity central.

How the exam applies this

Expect this material to surface as judgment/prioritization scenarios rather than technical movement questions. A stem may describe an owner-coach torn between a marketing or admin task and a member/coaching need, and ask which to prioritize — the keyed answer favors the 'golf balls/pebbles' (member relationships, coaching craft, standards) over the 'sand,' linking to 5.1.2 and 7.1.2. Other items may test recognizing that growth follows from serving current members (not from chasing new ones), or that a disruptive/rep-cutting member must be addressed for the group's sake (5.2.9). On the D4 side specifically, the article reinforces only that the trainer's ability to see and correct movement and to keep developing it is a top-tier priority (7.1.1/7.1.2/4.2.8); the actual mechanics of identifying faults and cueing are tested from other readings.

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Pursuit of excellence
Bergeron's organizing principle (from Glassman's 'blind and relentless pursuit of excellence') — operationally, relentlessly working to improve the lives of your current members rather than chasing peripheral business metrics.
Golf balls
The irreducible priorities of the affiliate: community, relationships with members and coaches, the health/happiness/results delivered daily, and the owner's integrity. If only these survived, the business would still succeed.
Pebbles
The other things that genuinely matter: programming, continued education of coaching staff, the ability to see and correct movement, running fun and effective classes, and a clean facility. High-value but second in priority to the golf balls.
Sand
Everything else — marketing, competitor-watching, complex pricing, non-competes, membership software, break-even and cash-flow analyses. Important to a degree but 'noise' that must never be funded before the golf balls and pebbles.
The jar parable (Covey, First Things First)
If you fill the jar with sand first, there's no room for golf balls or pebbles; load the big rocks first and the small stuff still fits. A model for sequencing priorities under finite time and energy.
Beers
The parable's coda — no matter how full the jar (your life and business), there's always room for time with friends. A reminder that balance/relationships still fit.
Simple, not easy
The principle that the right priorities are easy to identify but emotionally hard to execute, so people retreat into complex busywork to avoid the hard relational/coaching work.
'Them not me'
Bergeron's daily mantra — orienting every decision around what will improve members' experience and lives rather than around the owner's convenience or income.
Affiliate / box
A licensed CrossFit gym; Bergeron writes as an affiliate owner-operator (CrossFit New England) coaching owners on running a 'world-class' affiliate.
Business of Excellence (B.O.X.) Seminar
Bergeron's seminar that teaches affiliate owners to turn their gyms into world-class affiliates — author context, not exam content.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • Do NOT treat this article as a source for movement-evaluation, fault-identification, cueing, anatomy, or biomechanics specifics — it contains none. Pulling 'D4 technical' answers from it would be a misread; its D4 relevance is limited to prioritizing the coaching craft and continuing education.
  • Member-experience obligation (not a clinical/safety scope issue): the 'problem member' who cuts reps or makes others uncomfortable must be addressed — this is standards and group-management, and the article frames ignoring it as a failure of excellence.
  • Author bio and credentials (Level 1 Seminar Staff, 2011 Games team, B.O.X. Seminar) are background only and are not testable content.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. A new affiliate owner-coach has two free hours this afternoon. Option A: build a six-month advertising campaign to attract new members. Option B: meet with a struggling coach to improve their ability to see and correct movement, then talk with a member who has been cutting reps. Using Bergeron's framework, which is the better use of the time, and why?

  1. A — new-member acquisition is the fastest path to revenue, so marketing should always come first.
  2. B — the coach's development and the member/standards issues are 'golf balls and pebbles' (people, coaching craft, integrity of the experience); marketing is 'sand' that should never be funded first.
  3. A — the advertising campaign is more concrete and measurable, which Bergeron says should be prioritized.
  4. B — but only because advertising is unethical for a CrossFit affiliate.
  5. Either is equally valid; Bergeron says all business tasks carry the same weight.
Show answer

Answer: B — B reflects the core thesis: pour finite time into what most improves current members — relationships, the coaching craft (seeing/correcting movement), and protecting the experience (the rep-cutting member). A is 'sand'; Bergeron warns that loading sand first leaves no room for what matters. The article never calls advertising unethical (so D is wrong), never says concrete/measurable tasks win (C), and explicitly rejects equal weighting (E).

Scenario 2. An owner is anxious because a new CrossFit gym opened a mile away and is undercutting on price. They want to spend the next month overhauling pricing tiers and writing non-compete contracts. What does Bergeron's 'pursuit of excellence' most directly recommend?

  1. Match the competitor's price immediately to avoid losing members.
  2. Redirect that energy toward delivering excellence to current members — relationships, coaching, results — because growth and retention follow from serving members, not from competitor-driven 'sand.'
  3. Launch an aggressive ad campaign to out-market the new gym.
  4. Draft the non-compete contracts first, since protecting the business legally is a 'golf ball.'
  5. Close early each day to scout the competitor's classes.
Show answer

Answer: B — Pricing tiers, non-competes, and competitor-watching are explicitly listed as 'sand.' Bergeron's prescription is member-first: 'If you focus on delivering your very best to your clients, you can expect to have a great many clients.' A, C, and E chase the competitor (sand). D miscategorizes legal/contract work as a golf ball — the article puts non-competes in the sand tier.

Scenario 3. Bergeron writes that pursuing excellence is 'simple — not easy.' In a coaching context, what behavior is he warning against?

  1. Spending too little time on programming design.
  2. Avoiding hard interpersonal or coaching work (e.g., confronting an underperforming coach or a disruptive member) by burying yourself in complex but low-stakes busywork.
  3. Failing to memorize the CrossFit definition of fitness.
  4. Over-scaling workouts for beginners.
  5. Neglecting to track benchmark times.
Show answer

Answer: B — Bergeron states it's 'easier to get distracted by the complexities of your business—like implementing a six-month advertising campaign—than it is to deal with a coach or member who isn't meeting expectations.' The warning is about using complexity as avoidance of the hard, high-value relational/coaching work. The other options aren't what 'simple, not easy' addresses.

Scenario 4. Classify each item correctly using Bergeron's jar: (1) the trainer's ability to see and correct movement, (2) cash-flow projections, (3) the owner's integrity and the relationships with members. Which mapping is correct?

  1. 1 = golf ball, 2 = pebble, 3 = sand.
  2. 1 = pebble, 2 = sand, 3 = golf ball.
  3. 1 = sand, 2 = golf ball, 3 = pebble.
  4. 1 = pebble, 2 = golf ball, 3 = sand.
  5. All three are golf balls.
Show answer

Answer: B — The article explicitly lists 'your ability (and the ability of your staff) to see and correct movement' among the pebbles, 'cash-flow projections' among the sand, and 'the relationships you have with your members and coaches' plus 'your integrity as an owner, boss, and coach' among the golf balls. Only B matches the text.

Scenario 5. A head coach has 20 minutes before class and notices: (a) the gym's social media is overdue for a post, (b) a long-time member's father just went into the hospital, and (c) a new athlete keeps no-repping themselves out of frustration. Consistent with Bergeron's priorities, what should the coach do first?

  1. Write and schedule the social media post so the gym stays visible.
  2. Acknowledge the member whose father is ill (a genuine human gesture) and plan to support the frustrated new athlete in class — people and their experience come before promotion.
  3. Ignore all three and start setting up equipment to save time.
  4. Tell the front desk to handle the member and the athlete so the coach can focus on marketing.
  5. Post on social media about the hospitalized member's situation to show the gym cares.
Show answer

Answer: B — Bergeron's golf balls are people and relationships ('if they have an ill family member, send flowers'; 'use their names and look them in the eye'), and the new athlete's struggle is a member-experience/coaching priority. Social media is sand (A). Delegating people away to chase marketing (D) inverts the priorities; E exploits a private situation for promotion, the opposite of integrity; C neglects the people entirely.

Scenario 6. How should a D4-focused (Training) candidate use this specific article when preparing for the seeing-and-correcting portions of the exam?

  1. Memorize its lists of faults and cueing strategies for movement correction.
  2. Treat it as a priorities/leadership piece: it justifies WHY developing the trainer's eye and pursuing continuing education are top priorities, but get the actual mechanics of fault identification and cueing from other readings.
  3. Skip it entirely — it has zero relevance to the CCFT exam.
  4. Use it as the primary source for anatomy and biomechanics principles (4.2.6).
  5. Use it to learn correct spotting techniques.
Show answer

Answer: B — The article contains no fault lists, cues, anatomy, or spotting content (so A, D, and E are misreads). It is not irrelevant either (C) — it explicitly elevates 'the ability to see and correct movement,' staff continuing education, and running effective classes as priorities, supporting 7.1.1/7.1.2 and the disposition behind 4.2.8. The honest use is as a leadership/priorities lens, with technical D4 skills sourced elsewhere.

D4 · Training 24% of exam Confidence tier: ___

CFJ_Kilgore_Movement101.pdf

Open the PDF on Google Drive →

Why this is on the reading list

This article gives the trainer the shared anatomical vocabulary used to describe where body parts are and how they move (anatomical position, directional pairs, the three cardinal planes and their axes, and the core movement terms flexion/extension, abduction/adduction, rotation, circumduction). On the CCFT exam, Domain 4 (Training, 24%) requires you to apply basic anatomy and biomechanics (4.2.6), identify sound mechanics and faults (4.1.x), and translate that understanding into cues (4.2.x). Kilgore's central thesis is the exam's core competency in miniature: a good coach must both understand the anatomical nature of a movement AND convert that knowledge into plain-language cues an athlete can act on. The piece also explicitly models cueing ("push your knees out" instead of "abduct your femurs"), which is exactly the applied-judgment the exam tests.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 4.2.6 Apply basic principles of anatomy and biomechanics
  • 4.1.1 Identify points of performance
  • 4.1.2 Identify sound mechanics
  • 4.1.3 Identify faults in movement
  • 4.1.4 Identify refinements of sound mechanics to optimize performance
  • 4.1.6 Identify root cause of faults
  • 4.2.1 Communicate cues to correct unsound mechanics
  • 4.2.2 Use multiple cueing strategies (visual, tactile, verbal)
  • 4.2.3 Utilize effective cues (short, specific, actionable)
  • 3.1.1 Teach proper execution of movements
  • 3.1.6 Teach descriptive/defining characteristics of functional movements
  • 3.2.2 Demonstrate movement faults
  • 1.2.1 Assess capacity/capability to perform functional movements

What to focus on while reading

  • The two coaching tasks Kilgore names at the end (Section: 'two tasks to be accomplished'): (1) understand the anatomical nature of the movement to DETECT segmental deviations from the reference standard of good technique, and (2) convey that feedback in vocabulary the athlete understands. Highlight this — it is the spine of the whole article and of Domain 4.
  • Anatomical position defined: flat on back, palms facing up. Note that it is an artificial reference construct, NOT how the body stands relaxed (relaxed standing = palms facing the hips/slightly rearward).
  • Why a single reference position matters — the 'magnetic north' / compass analogy. One agreed-upon reference lets any coach describe any location or movement unambiguously.
  • The four directional pairs and a worked example of each: Anterior/Posterior (toes anterior to heels; erector spinae posterior to abdominal cavity), Proximal/Distal (knee proximal to foot; hand distal to elbow), Superior/Inferior (head superior to pelvis; chin inferior to nose), Medial/Lateral (sternum medial to shoulders; shoulders lateral to sternum).
  • That these directional terms are RELATIVE — a structure is anterior/proximal/superior/medial only in relation to another named structure, and orientation can flip during exercise (the article's example: pelvis can be superior to the skull in an inverted position).
  • The three cardinal planes and exactly what each divides: Sagittal = right/left halves (passes front-to-back), Frontal = front/back halves (passes side-to-side, shoulder-to-shoulder), Transverse = top/bottom halves (passes at the waist, perpendicular to the long axis).
  • All three planes intersect at the body's center of gravity / center of mass — connect this to balance and bar-path concepts you will see elsewhere in the curriculum.
  • Axes of movement: every plane has an axis (the imaginary line a segment rotates around). Note the paper-folding mental model and the names — transverse axis, frontal axis, sagittal axis.
  • Kilgore's honest caveat that planes and axes are good anatomy knowledge but NOT practical cueing language ('when have you or any coach ... used these terms?'). Highlight this — the exam favors applied cueing over reciting plane/axis jargon.
  • The core movement descriptors with their plane and joint-angle behavior: Flexion = sagittal plane, joint angle DECREASES ('closing,' like closing a book, 180° to 0°); Extension = sagittal plane, joint angle INCREASES ('opening,' 0° to 180°).
  • The critical correction Kilgore stresses: it is the JOINT that flexes/extends, not the muscle. Muscles CONTRACT to flex or extend a joint. (He proves it with the photo showing flexion without muscular involvement.)
  • Abduction = frontal plane, segment moves AWAY from midline ('to abduct is to take away' / kidnapper mnemonic). Adduction = frontal plane, segment moves TOWARD midline.
  • Rotation = pivoting around the long axis of the body or a segment. Circumduction = distal segment traces a circle around the joint; it is a combination of flexion, abduction, extension, adduction in sequence, and can ONLY happen at joints that move in two or more planes (ball-and-socket).
  • The 'hyper-' prefix meaning: hyperextension, hyperabduction, hyperflexion, etc. specifically mean movement BEYOND the joint's normal range of motion — and Kilgore flags that 'hyper-anything is potentially injurious.' Mark this; it is the safety hook on the exam.
  • The two worked cueing translations Kilgore gives: 'abduct your femurs' -> 'push your knees out' (squat); 'internally rotate the humerus' -> 'point your elbows out' (clean set-up, which engages the lats for force application). These are model answers for cue-selection questions.
  • Table 1 (the term glossary) — scan it for the segment-specific terms you may not know: pronation/supination (hand to palms-down / palms-up), dorsiflexion/plantarflexion (ankle: toes up / toes down), inversion/eversion (sole toward midline / sole out), elevation/depression (up / down), protraction/retraction (shoulders forward / backward), internal/external rotation (rotate part anteriorly / posteriorly).
  • Note the article's framing that point 1 (the anatomy) is 'science applied to exercise' and point 2 (the athlete-friendly vocabulary) is 'the art of coaching' — and that failing at EITHER makes a less successful coach.

Concepts to understand

  • The dual mandate of coaching: you must (a) read the body anatomically to spot deviations from the standard of good technique, and (b) communicate the fix in language the athlete can immediately act on. Both are required; mastery of one without the other is insufficient. This is the lens for nearly every Domain 4 scenario.
  • Why a common reference standard exists: anatomical terms only work because everyone agrees on one neutral starting position. Understand that you describe positions and movements RELATIVE to a fixed reference, the way navigation depends on magnetic north.
  • Directional terms are relational and context-dependent: 'distal,' 'proximal,' 'superior,' etc. only have meaning between two structures, and the relationship can invert when the athlete changes orientation (e.g., inverted/handstand). Apply this rather than memorizing fixed labels.
  • Planes describe location/section of the body; movements happen 'in' or 'along' planes — but for COACHING you rarely cue in plane language. Understand planes well enough to analyze a movement, then translate, not recite.
  • Flexion vs. extension is fundamentally about whether a joint angle is closing (decreasing) or opening (increasing), and it occurs in the sagittal plane. Be able to read any joint in a CrossFit movement and say which is happening (e.g., hip opening at the top of a deadlift = extension).
  • Muscles contract; joints flex and extend. Understand this distinction so you cue and explain accurately and don't reinforce the common misconception that 'muscles flex.'
  • Abduction/adduction (away from / toward midline, frontal plane) and rotation (around the long axis) describe the other primary ways segments move; circumduction is the compound, multi-plane motion available only at ball-and-socket joints.
  • The 'hyper-' concept as a safety boundary: any movement taken beyond a joint's available range of motion is, by definition, hyper- and is potentially injurious. Recognize when a cue, load, or position is pushing an athlete past safe ROM.
  • Cue translation is a skill, not a nicety: the same anatomical fault can be fixed with everyday language. Understand WHY the plain cue works mechanically (e.g., 'point your elbows out' produces internal rotation of the humerus and lat engagement) so you pick cues that actually change the mechanics.
  • The science/art split: anatomical analysis is the science; athlete-appropriate vocabulary is the art. Effective coaching requires fluency in both registers and the ability to switch between them depending on the athlete in front of you.
  • Anatomical literacy supports root-cause analysis: knowing the joints, segments, and movement types lets you trace a visible fault (e.g., knees caving) back to what is actually happening anatomically (insufficient femoral abduction/external rotation) rather than chasing symptoms.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenario questions that hand you a described fault and ask for the BEST cue — the right answer is almost always the short, plain-language, athlete-actionable cue ('push your knees out'), not the technically-correct anatomical instruction ('abduct your femurs'), even though both describe the same correction (4.2.1, 4.2.3, 4.2.6). Other items will test whether you can correctly classify a movement (which joint is flexing vs. extending, abduction vs. adduction, what plane a motion occurs in) as part of evaluating mechanics (4.1.2, 4.1.3) and identifying root cause (4.1.6). Safety-flavored items may probe the 'hyper-' concept — recognizing when a position exceeds safe range of motion (4.2.6, and risk-management tasks elsewhere). The article's two-tasks framework is the rubric the exam uses to judge a coach: see the anatomy, then translate it.

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Anatomical position
The standard reference posture for describing the body: lying flat on the back with palms facing up. It is an artificial construct (not how the body stands relaxed) used so everyone describes locations and movements from the same starting point.
Anterior
In front of another structure. Example: the toes are anterior to the heels.
Posterior
Behind another structure. Example: the erector spinae (the long muscle group up the back) is posterior to the abdominal cavity.
Proximal
Closer to the center of the body or to the beginning of a limb than another structure. Example: the knee is proximal to the foot.
Distal
Farther from the center of the body or from the beginning of a limb than another structure. Example: the hand is distal to the elbow.
Superior
Higher than another structure in the standard orientation. Example: the head is superior to the pelvis.
Inferior
Lower than another structure. Example: the chin is inferior to the nose. Orientation can flip during exercise (e.g., when inverted).
Medial
Closer to the body's midline (the cardinal sagittal plane) than another structure. Example: the sternum is medial to both shoulders.
Lateral
Farther from the midline than another structure. Example: the shoulders are lateral to the sternum.
Sagittal plane
The plane that divides the body into right and left halves, passing from front (toe side) to back (heel side). Flexion and extension occur in this plane.
Frontal plane
The plane that divides the body into front and back halves, passing side-to-side (shoulder to shoulder). Abduction and adduction occur in this plane. Also called the coronal plane.
Transverse plane
The plane that divides the body into top and bottom halves (at the waist), perpendicular to the long axis of the body.
Cardinal planes
The three primary anatomical planes (sagittal, frontal, transverse). They intersect at the body's center of gravity / center of mass.
Center of gravity / center of mass
The body's theoretical balance point, where the three cardinal planes intersect. Relevant to balance and stability in loaded movements.
Axis of movement
The imaginary line around which a segment rotates within a given plane. Every plane has an axis (transverse, frontal, sagittal). Useful for analysis, but not typically used as a coaching cue.
Flexion
A movement in the sagittal plane in which the joint angle DECREASES (the joint 'closes,' like closing a book from 180° to 0°). Note: it is the joint that flexes, not the muscle.
Extension
A movement in the sagittal plane in which the joint angle INCREASES (the joint 'opens,' like opening a book from 0° to 180°). Example: the hip angle opens as you rise from sitting to standing.
Abduction
A frontal-plane movement that takes a body part AWAY from the midline. Memory aid: to abduct is to 'take away.'
Adduction
A frontal-plane movement that brings a body part TOWARD the midline (the opposite of abduction).
Rotation
A pivoting motion around the long axis of the body or of a body segment.
Internal (medial) rotation
Rotation of a part anteriorly (toward the front). Example cue context: 'point your elbows out' in a clean set-up internally rotates the humerus and engages the lats.
External (lateral) rotation
Rotation of a part posteriorly (toward the back).
Circumduction
A compound, circular movement where the distal segment traces a circle around the joint. It combines flexion, abduction, extension, and adduction in sequence and can occur only at joints that move in two or more planes (ball-and-socket, e.g., shoulder).
Pronation
Rotation of the hand to a palms-down orientation (at the elbow/wrist).
Supination
Rotation of the hand to a palms-up orientation (at the elbow/wrist).
Dorsiflexion
At the ankle, lifting the toes and ball of the foot up toward the shin.
Plantarflexion
At the ankle, pushing the toes and ball of the foot down (pointing the foot).
Inversion
Rolling the ankle so the sole of the foot faces the midline.
Eversion
Rolling the ankle so the sole of the foot faces outward.
Elevation / Depression
Movement of a segment upward (elevation) or downward (depression); commonly applied to the shoulders/scapulae.
Protraction / Retraction
Movement of the shoulders forward (protraction, a form of abduction) or backward (retraction, a form of adduction).
Hyper- (prefix)
Indicates movement BEYOND a joint's normal range-of-motion capacity (e.g., hyperextension, hyperabduction). Kilgore warns that 'hyper-anything is potentially injurious.'

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • 'Hyper-' movements exceed a joint's available range of motion and are potentially injurious — recognize hyperextension/hyperflexion/hyperabduction/hyperadduction in an athlete's positions and intervene before loading or speeding up the movement.
  • Do not cue an athlete into a range they don't have. Pushing for an extreme position (the article notes its extreme abduction/adduction photos are not achievable by most trainees and required years of ballet) without the requisite mobility risks injury.
  • Anatomy education here is for movement analysis and cueing only — it is NOT clinical diagnosis. Pain, suspected injury, or abnormal joint mechanics fall outside CCFT scope and warrant referral to a qualified medical professional.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. During a back squat, an athlete's knees collapse inward at the bottom. You understand this anatomically as insufficient abduction/external rotation of the femurs. What is the BEST coaching cue to fix it in the moment?

  1. A. 'Abduct and externally rotate your femurs.'
  2. B. 'Push your knees out.'
  3. C. 'Your femurs are adducting in the frontal plane — correct that.'
  4. D. 'Engage your hip external rotators around the sagittal axis.'
  5. E. 'Fix your knees.'
Show answer

Answer: B — Kilgore's whole point is that the coach must translate the correct anatomy into plain, actionable language. 'Push your knees out' is short, specific, and immediately actionable — it produces the femoral abduction/external rotation you want. A, C, and D are anatomically correct but useless as in-the-moment cues; most athletes can't act on jargon. E ('fix your knees') is plain but not specific — it doesn't tell the athlete WHAT to do.

Scenario 2. A new trainer claims 'the biceps flexes during a curl.' Based on Kilgore's article, which statement is the most accurate correction to teach?

  1. A. Correct as stated — muscles flex and extend.
  2. B. The biceps doesn't move the elbow; the brachialis does.
  3. C. The joint flexes; the muscle contracts to produce that flexion.
  4. D. Flexion only happens in the frontal plane, so a curl is actually adduction.
  5. E. Curls are extension, not flexion, because the weight goes up.
Show answer

Answer: C — Kilgore explicitly stresses that it is the JOINT that flexes or extends, while muscles CONTRACT to produce that movement. C captures this precisely. A repeats the common error. B is irrelevant to the point and inaccurate as a blanket claim. D is wrong — flexion occurs in the sagittal plane, and a curl is elbow flexion. E confuses the joint-angle definition: during the lifting phase of a curl the elbow angle decreases, which is flexion.

Scenario 3. At the top of a deadlift, an athlete stands fully upright and the hip angle has opened from a closed position to roughly straight. How should you correctly describe what happened at the hip, and in which plane?

  1. A. Hip flexion in the sagittal plane.
  2. B. Hip extension in the sagittal plane.
  3. C. Hip abduction in the frontal plane.
  4. D. Hip adduction in the frontal plane.
  5. E. Hip circumduction around the long axis.
Show answer

Answer: B — Opening a joint angle (it gets larger) is extension, and flexion/extension occur in the sagittal plane — Kilgore uses 'the hip angle opens as you rise from sitting to standing' as his example. So standing up at the top of a deadlift is hip extension in the sagittal plane. A is the opposite (closing). C and D are frontal-plane away/toward-midline movements, not what the hip is doing here. E is a compound multi-plane motion of ball-and-socket joints, not a simple stand-up.

Scenario 4. You're explaining the set-up for a clean and want the athlete to internally rotate the humerus so the lats engage for proper force application. Per Kilgore, what is the most effective way to communicate this to a typical trainee?

  1. A. 'Internally rotate your humerus.'
  2. B. 'Point your elbows out.'
  3. C. 'Rotate your arms anteriorly around the long axis.'
  4. D. 'Pronate your shoulders.'
  5. E. 'Abduct your scapulae toward neutral.'
Show answer

Answer: B — This is the exact translation Kilgore provides: say 'point your elbows out' rather than 'internally rotate the humerus,' and the athlete will engage the lats correctly. B is the plain, actionable cue. A and C are technically accurate but not athlete-friendly. D misuses 'pronate' (a forearm/hand term, not a shoulder action). E introduces scapular jargon that is both off-target and not actionable.

Scenario 5. An athlete with limited shoulder mobility is straining to force a deep overhead position, and you notice the joint being driven past its available range. Applying Kilgore's terminology and his safety note, how should you interpret and respond?

  1. A. This is normal extension; add load to build strength through the range.
  2. B. This is hyper-movement beyond the joint's ROM and is potentially injurious; scale the position rather than force it.
  3. C. This is circumduction, which is always safe at the shoulder.
  4. D. This is adduction; cue the athlete to pull the arms toward midline harder.
  5. E. This is anatomical position; no concern.
Show answer

Answer: B — Kilgore defines the 'hyper-' prefix as movement beyond the joint's normal range-of-motion capacity and warns that 'hyper-anything is potentially injurious.' Forcing a joint past its available range is exactly this, so the coaching response is to scale/modify, not to load or push harder. A and D would drive the athlete further into an unsafe position. C is false — circumduction is a movement type, not a guarantee of safety. E is simply incorrect terminology.

Scenario 6. Kilgore says effective coaching requires two tasks. Which option best states them and why both matter for the CCFT exam's Domain 4?

  1. A. Memorize all anatomical terms, then quiz athletes on them.
  2. B. Understand the anatomy of a movement to detect deviations from good technique, AND convey the correction in vocabulary the athlete understands.
  3. C. Always cue in plane-and-axis language so instructions are precise.
  4. D. Demonstrate every movement perfectly and never speak.
  5. E. Diagnose the athlete's joint pathology and prescribe corrective exercise.
Show answer

Answer: B — Kilgore names exactly these two tasks: (1) understand the anatomical nature of the movement to detect segmental deviations from the standard of good technique (the science), and (2) convey feedback in language the trainee understands (the art) — and failing at either makes a less successful coach. This is the spine of Domain 4 (apply anatomy/biomechanics, identify faults, cue effectively). A is rote memorization, which the exam explicitly does not reward. C contradicts the article — plane/axis terms are poor cues. D ignores half the mandate (communication). E is outside CCFT scope of practice (diagnosis/treatment).
