  • Coaching the diseased/terminal client (Michael): function and quality of life over performance, medical-team-set physiological limits (e.g., SpO2 above 90), drastically modified work-to-rest, mostly strength/isometric work, and the principle of continuing training no matter what — all within scope and under medical guidance.
  • CrossFit's model of aging: health = work capacity across broad time and modal domains throughout life; the more capacity built early and the more continuity of training across the lifespan, the larger the hedge against age-related loss ('use it or lose it'); training attenuates the negative effects of sedentary aging ('fountain-of-youth' effect).

How the exam applies this

Scenario items will describe a specific masters athlete (e.g., a 58-year-old returning after a break, a 44-year-old ex-athlete overreaching, a post-menopausal member avoiding double-unders, a diseased client) and ask what the experienced coach should DO. Expect the Masters Quadrant logic to drive 'how would you classify / what's the priority' questions (5.1.3, 2.2.1-2.2.5), referral/scope questions about cardiac symptoms, pelvic-floor signs, and medication (1.1.2, 6.2.4, 7.4.1), and risk-management questions about overuse, rep budgets, gradual load introduction, and the low-to-high-risk environment (5.2.3, 5.2.6). Mindset, goal-setting, motivation, setback-handling, and 'don't make masters feel abnormal' will surface as leadership items (5.1.1-5.1.4, 5.2.9). Programming/scaling items will test that wellness gets broad GPP while performance gets a narrower stimulus, that late masters run ~70-80% Rx'd with an extra rest day, and that complexity is scaled but never removed (2.1.2, 2.2.x, 3.1.10-3.1.12). The strongest distractors will be the four debunked myths stated as if true.

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Aging / masters athlete
In this guide, anyone 40 years and older (used interchangeably with 'aging athlete'); NOT the competition definition of 35+, and not necessarily a competitor. Athletes under 40 are called younger adults.
Masters Quadrant
A coaching classification framework built from four interacting variables (goals, age, fitness level, injury state) that yields 16 archetypes, each with distinct coaching priorities, risks, and scaling needs.
Archetype
A specific combination of the four quadrant variables (e.g., 'late deconditioned wellness uninjured') that tells the trainer how to adapt coaching style and programming for that athlete.
Goal orientation
Whether the athlete trains primarily for performance (competition, results, a specific event) or wellness (health, quality of life, real-world capability, social interaction). Determined by asking 'What is your reason for training?'
Early masters
A masters athlete aged 40-54; tends to still have active work/family demands, may deny aging, and is prone to overreaching/overestimating ability (false-positive belief).
Late masters
A masters athlete aged 55+; aging effects are more noticeable, neurological skills take longer to learn, strength is harder to build and lost faster with breaks, and they tend to under-reach (false-negative belief). Typically scaled to ~70-80% of Rx'd with an extra rest day.
Fit vs deconditioned
A judgment of current conditioning used to estimate how much the program must be scaled and graduated. Deconditioning has an amplified effect with age — more scaling, slower start, higher injury and dropout risk.
Injury state (uninjured / injured / diseased)
Whether the athlete has a limitation requiring modification. Uninjured athletes get the full program; injured/diseased athletes need modification, carry higher risk, and resolving the injury (or maximizing function) becomes the top priority. It's the limitation, not the diagnosis, that matters.
Relative intensity
Working to the boundary of an individual's current physical AND psychological tolerance, and not beyond. The mechanism that makes the same program universally scalable and high intensity safe for an older athlete.
Mechanics-consistency-intensity (the charter)
Teach correct mechanics first, achieve consistency second, then apply relative intensity — applied more conservatively and with more gradual intensity for masters; the primary risk-management and confidence-building tool.
Universal scalability
The principle that the CrossFit program does not need to change for any population; it only needs appropriate scaling — 'anyone can do it, and everyone should.'
Contraindication
Something that makes an activity or treatment inadvisable. Identifying contraindications for a diseased/medicated client requires guidance from the medical team and is outside the trainer's scope to determine independently.
Secondary overuse injury
An injury to uninjured body parts caused by over-programming the movements an injured athlete CAN still do, raising rep counts and stressing healthy tissue. A specific risk for injured masters.
Rep budget
A weekly cap on total repetitions of a high-risk movement (e.g., 150-200 pull-ups/week) summed across all WODs, warm-ups, and practice, used to prevent overuse injury. Being far under budget is also undesirable.
Poor recovery feedback loop
The self-reinforcing cycle in which believing age inhibits recovery leads to neglecting recovery strategies, which then produces actual poor recovery — to be broken by addressing lifestyle and mindset before blaming age.
Negative self-talk
An athlete's internal dialogue that hinders rather than helps progress (e.g., 'this is too heavy, I always miss'); the trainer must detect it and teach a better mental script.
Thought stopping
A mindset technique: the athlete recognizes negative self-talk, uses a mental or physical cue (e.g., stamping feet) as a trigger, and replaces it with a pre-practiced positive thought.
False-positive / false-negative belief
Inaccurate self-assessments of capacity. False-positive (think they're better than they are) leads to reckless overreaching and injury; false-negative (think they're worse than they are) leads to over-scaling and under-reaching. The coach's job is to build TRUE beliefs.
Rigid thinking
Masters athletes being set in their ways and unwilling to try new things, often anchored to strong opinions from prior experience; the trainer counters it with new positive experiences and similarly-aged high-capacity role models.
Successful / active aging
A late-life process characterized by high physical, psychological, cognitive, and social functioning; contrasted with sedentary aging, which produces functional decline and disease driven by inactivity rather than age.
Survival advantage / hedge against decline
The idea that becoming and remaining an athlete extends life and preserves function; the more work capacity built earlier in life and the more continuity of training, the larger the buffer against age-related loss.
On-ramp program (masters)
A graduated introduction (e.g., the 12-week, 3-day example) preparing a deconditioned late masters athlete for group classes — slower than a younger client's, with strength every session, extensive skill practice, and embedded teaching points before graduating to standard programming.
Movement substitution
Replacing a movement that must be excluded entirely (due to unresolvable pathology) with another that preserves the intended stimulus (e.g., snatch to split snatch, box jump to step-up, barbell deadlift to suitcase deadlift off blocks).
Masters progression
A skill-teaching progression with more steps and finer increments than a standard one, which may reduce the THINKING component, isolate the neurological pattern, and fix underlying strength/mobility first; box-jump progressions can need 15+ steps over months, pull-ups 2-3 years.
Scaling / substitution table
A personalized 'cheat sheet' (e.g., the Joe Smith example) listing each movement's Rx, max reps, weekly budget, scaling, and substitutions so the athlete can self-manage daily modifications without feeling a burden; the trainer reviews and updates it periodically.
SpO2 (blood oxygen saturation)
A monitored vital used with Michael's degenerative lung disease; the medical team set the limit (stay above 90, return to 95 before continuing). The trainer manages training within medically set physiological limits.
Work-to-rest ratio
The ratio of working time to rest; with Michael it was capped at no higher than 1:5 to keep SpO2 above 90, illustrating how a diseased client's program is reshaped around physiological limits.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • Cardiac referral triggers — any athlete (especially 55+ and/or deconditioned) with suspected coronary artery disease, chest pain, unexplained shortness of breath, dizziness, or who is on heart medication must be referred to a qualified medical practitioner before/for training; warning signs must never be ignored.
  • Medication side effects — older clients are more likely medicated; BP meds + cholesterol meds + exertion can cause muscle pain, dizziness, and confusion. Determining contraindications is outside the trainer's scope; get guidance from the medical team.
  • Pelvic floor / exertional urinary incontinence (leaking with jumping), and risk of pelvic organ prolapse with load-bearing — common in older women (and possible in older men); avoidance of jumping/running may be the signal. Do NOT normalize it; educate and refer to a qualified practitioner.
  • Post-menopausal reduced bone density and stress-fracture risk — be conservative with loads and volume and ensure the client has appropriate medical care.
  • Chronic injury or disease state — refer to a medical professional; never make the condition worse or inhibit recovery; resolve/manage as the highest priority before performance.
  • Diseased/terminal client — intensity may need to be reduced or removed; never advise on disease treatment or drug therapy; seek direct guidance from the medical team and stay within physiological limits they set (e.g., SpO2 above 90).
  • Poor mobility as a warning sign — decreased mobility raises risk in movements like the snatch; reduced range of motion can make specific patterns unsafe.
  • Deconditioned late masters require closer monitoring (affecting client-to-trainer ratio) because underlying medical conditions may be undetected — the trainer cannot know if there is hidden pathology, so use graduated introduction and relative intensity.
  • Hidden injuries from anxiety — an older athlete worried about being a burden may not disclose an injury; the coach must watch for non-disclosure and avoidance behaviors.
  • Irregular strenuous training raises cardiac risk — reduce intensity until a regular training pattern is re-established; older athletes should not train through pain, tightness, or fatigue the way a younger athlete might.
  • Common older-athlete injuries that resist healing — rotator cuff tears (often idiopathic, rarely heal in older athletes; err on less overhead volume) and Achilles/foot injuries; avoid contraindicated movements and manage overuse.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. A 59-year-old new member returns to exercise after 15 years sedentary. She ran competitively in her 30s and keeps insisting she should be doing workouts 'as Rx'd like I used to.' She has no diagnosed injuries. How should the experienced coach proceed?

  1. A. Let her go Rx'd to build confidence, since she has prior athletic experience
  2. B. Classify her as late / deconditioned / wellness / uninjured, scale conservatively with a graduated introduction, and use mindset coaching to build a true belief about her current capacity
  3. C. Tell her that at her age she should only walk and do light machines
  4. D. Put her straight into the competitive masters squad to channel her drive
  5. E. Avoid all complex gymnastics and weightlifting because she is 55+
Show answer

Answer: B — She is a late masters athlete who is currently deconditioned despite a prior athletic history, which is exactly the profile most likely to overreach and then quit from frustration. The quadrant calls for conservative, graduated scaling and active mindset work to replace her false-positive belief with a true one. A risks injury (deconditioning is amplified with age). C is the debunked 'just walk' myth. D ignores her wellness reality and deconditioning. E is the debunked 'simplify the program' myth — complexity is scaled, not removed.

Scenario 2. Mid-workout, a 61-year-old deconditioned member reports chest tightness and unexplained shortness of breath that does not ease with rest. He mentions he takes blood-pressure medication. What is the most appropriate action?

  1. A. Lower the intensity, give him extra rest, and let him finish the WOD scaled
  2. B. Tell him it's normal to be winded at his age and encourage him to push through
  3. C. Stop him, treat it as a medical red flag, and refer him to a qualified medical practitioner; do not let him continue until cleared
  4. D. Recommend he stop the blood-pressure medication before training next time
  5. E. Substitute the movements for lower-skill versions and continue
Show answer

Answer: C — Chest pain/tightness, unexplained shortness of breath, dizziness, and being on heart medication are explicit referral triggers — sudden cardiac death risk is elevated in older, deconditioned, non-habitual exercisers. The coach stops the session and refers. A, B, and E continue training through a cardiac warning sign. D is squarely outside scope of practice — never advise on medication.

Scenario 3. You program a masters wellness class. To prevent overuse injuries from pulling movements, what is the best application of the rep budget?

  1. A. Cap pull-up reps within each single workout but ignore warm-ups and skill practice
  2. B. Set a weekly pull-up rep cap (e.g., 150-200) and write the week's WODs, warm-ups, and practice so the total never exceeds it
  3. C. Eliminate pull-ups from masters programming entirely
  4. D. Let athletes do as many pull-ups as they want as long as form looks good
  5. E. Only count Rx'd pull-ups toward the budget, not scaled versions
Show answer

Answer: B — The rep budget is a weekly cap on a high-risk movement summed across ALL programming (WODs + warm-ups + extra practice), e.g., Fran 45 + Angie 100 + 30 in a warm-up = 175, in the safe zone. A and E undercount the true weekly volume. C needlessly removes a valuable movement (complexity is scaled, not removed). D ignores cumulative overuse risk, which is independent of single-set form.

Scenario 4. A 47-year-old early masters athlete, a former college athlete, consistently loads heavier than prescribed, cherry-picks workouts that favor his strengths, and resists rest days. What does the Masters Quadrant suggest about him and how to coach him?

  1. A. He has a false-negative belief and needs encouragement to attempt more
  2. B. He is under-reaching and should be pushed to go Rx'd on everything immediately
  3. C. He likely has a false-positive belief / tendency to overreach; rein in volume and load, address cherry-picking, and coach a true belief to reduce injury risk
  4. D. His behavior is ideal for a masters athlete and should be left alone
  5. E. He should be moved to a wellness track and discouraged from intensity
Show answer

Answer: C — Early masters typically overreach and hold false-positive beliefs (perceiving themselves as un-aged), and cherry-picking plus resisting rest days are classic tells. The coach moderates load/volume, confronts the cherry-picking (variance matters), and builds a true belief to prevent overreaching injuries. A and B describe the opposite (under-reaching) error. D ignores real injury risk. E misreads his goal orientation and wrongly strips intensity.

Scenario 5. An injured late masters athlete has a chronic shoulder issue that limits overhead pressing and pull-ups. You modify the program around the shoulder. Weeks later he develops elbow tendinopathy. What most likely happened and how should you adjust?

  1. A. He simply got unlucky; keep the program the same
  2. B. By repeatedly programming the lower-body and pulling movements he CAN do, volume on healthy areas climbed and caused a secondary overuse injury — reduce volume on the overused pattern and broaden the stimulus with substitutions
  3. C. The original shoulder injury spread to the elbow; refer him out of CrossFit permanently
  4. D. He needs more intensity to toughen the connective tissue
  5. E. Switch him to performance programming to distract him
Show answer

Answer: B — Injured masters are prone to secondary overuse injuries precisely because limiting one area concentrates volume on the movements that remain available, overstressing previously healthy tissue. The fix is to manage that volume (rep budget), vary the stimulus, and substitute to preserve training effect. A ignores the mechanism. C and D are wrong and unsafe. E does not address the volume problem.

Scenario 6. Your affiliate is new to coaching masters athletes and has only a handful of older members; your trainers are not yet confident scaling for them. What implementation does the guide recommend?

  1. A. Immediately build a fully integrated model so masters always train in general classes
  2. B. Refuse masters members until trainers are more experienced
  3. C. Start with separate masters classes/programming where trainer and client confidence is low, then migrate toward an integrated model as skill, confidence, and numbers grow
  4. D. Program every class to masters Rx'd so no one stands out
  5. E. Keep masters permanently separated regardless of how the gym develops
Show answer

Answer: C — The guide recommends a fully separated model where trainer/client confidence is lowest and a fully integrated model where it is highest, migrating over time as experience and the number of masters grow. A jumps to integration before the trainers can scale ad hoc. B and E are absolutes the guide rejects (it values autonomy and progression). D lowers the standard for everyone and can become a limiter.

Scenario 7. You are rewriting the hero WOD 'Barraza' (18-min AMRAP: 200-m run, 9 deadlifts at 275 lb, 6 burpee bar muscle-ups) as a 55+ Rx'd version. Besides reducing the deadlift load to about 80%, why also cut the time cap from 18 to 14 minutes?

  1. A. To make the workout easier and shorter for older athletes
  2. B. Because masters can't sustain 18 minutes of work
  3. C. To preserve the intended volume — lighter load lets athletes complete more rounds, so trimming the time keeps total volume near the original target of ~5-7 rounds
  4. D. Time caps are always shorter for any masters workout regardless of the stimulus
  5. E. To leave more time for the cool-down
Show answer

Answer: C — Reducing load without adjusting the clock would inflate rounds (and total volume), changing the stimulus and adding overuse risk. Cutting the cap to 14 minutes holds volume near the original 5-7 rounds, preserving the intended stimulus. A misstates the goal (scaling makes a workout accessible, not easy). B and D are overgeneralizations. E is not the programming rationale.

Scenario 8. A late masters athlete keeps freezing when attempting a box jump even onto a 10-lb plate, despite many sessions on a standard step-up to small-box to higher-box progression. What is the best coaching response?

  1. A. Tell her box jumps aren't for older athletes and drop them permanently
  2. B. Recognize that masters progressions may need to reduce the thinking component and address underlying strength/mobility first — restart with basic jumping/landing drills and calf-raise strength, building a 15-step progression as needed
  3. C. Add load to force her body to adapt faster
  4. D. Have her keep attempting the box jump every day until fear subsides
  5. E. Increase the box height to give her a clearer target
Show answer

Answer: B — Standard progressions reduce the effort component, but late masters often need the thinking/neurological component isolated and any underlying strength or mobility limitation fixed first (e.g., calf-raise strength before jumping). The guide's box-jump progression can require 15+ steps over months. A removes a valuable skill unnecessarily. C and E increase risk and demand. D ignores the missing strength/neurological foundation and can entrench fear.

Scenario 9. A terminally ill 70-year-old with a degenerative lung disease wants to keep training. His medical team says SpO2 must stay above 90 and return to 95 before he continues. How should the coach run his sessions?

  1. A. Program normal high-intensity metcons since intensity is always the priority
  2. B. Refuse to train him because disease is outside the trainer's scope
  3. C. Prioritize function and quality of life within the medically set limits — monitor SpO2, use long rest (e.g., up to a 1:5 work-to-rest ratio), avoid combined movements, and bias toward strength/isometric work
  4. D. Tell him to stop his oxygen therapy so it doesn't interfere with conditioning
  5. E. Push him to chase benchmark PRs to keep him motivated
Show answer

Answer: C — For a diseased/terminal client, intensity may be reduced or removed; the coach maximizes function and quality of life while staying within physiological limits set by the medical team (SpO2 above 90), using extended rest, avoiding movement combinations, and favoring strength/isometric work — exactly Michael's case. A ignores the disease and the oxygen limit. B abandons a client who can train safely under medical guidance. D is dangerous and outside scope. E disregards the physiological constraints.

Scenario 10. A 56-year-old member who recently had a wrist injury returns to training and seems withdrawn and hesitant, training alone off to the side. What is the most important leadership priority during this setback window?

  1. A. Give her space and let her come back on her own timeline
  2. B. Deliver a clear recovery/training plan quickly and keep her connected to the group (e.g., do her rehab within class), keeping routine as normal as possible to prevent self-deselection
  3. C. Tell her injuries are just part of aging and she should expect more of them
  4. D. Have her sit out entirely until she feels 100% confident again
  5. E. Push her back to full Rx'd to prove the injury didn't set her back
Show answer

Answer: B — Setbacks hit masters harder and there is a critical window in which delivering an effective plan and maintaining group connection preserves motivation; isolation leads to giving up (self-deselection). Doing rehab in class and keeping routine normal are explicitly recommended. A and D increase isolation. C is demotivating and reinforces self-limiting beliefs. E ignores the injury and risk.

Scenario 11. Two masters athletes ask why they should bother with intensity 'at their age.' Which response best reflects the guide's position on relative intensity and safety?

  1. A. They're right — older athletes should avoid intensity and train in moderation
  2. B. Intensity is the pathway to results at any age; applied RELATIVE to each individual's physical and psychological tolerance and governed by mechanics-consistency-intensity, it is appropriate and safe — risk comes from the condition, not the age
  3. C. They should max out every session to prove age is irrelevant
  4. D. Intensity should be replaced with long, slow endurance work for masters
  5. E. Only performance masters need intensity; wellness masters do not
Show answer

Answer: B — Intensity is the variable most associated with favorable adaptation, and it is made safe for older athletes by applying it relatively (to the boundary of current physical and psychological tolerance) under the mechanics-consistency-intensity charter; increased risk comes from health conditions, not age itself. A and D are the debunked 'avoid intensity' / 'just do endurance' myths. C ignores relative intensity and is reckless. E is false — barring specific health issues, all masters need relative intensity.

Why this is on the reading list

This article is on the CCFT reading list because it equips the trainer to do exactly what Domain 6 demands: give evidence-based nutrition and lifestyle guidance, correct a common athlete misconception (that sports drinks are 'necessary athletic fuel'), and steer clients toward whole-food sources of sugar and plain water. It directly backs the nutrition-guidance, dietary-strategy, food-label, health-marker, and lifestyle-guidance tasks under 6.1 and 6.2, while also reinforcing the scope-of-practice limits that separate a CrossFit trainer's hydration/added-sugar coaching from the medical management of a disease like diabetes. The Marinoff case (undiagnosed Type 1 diabetes presenting as thirst, polyuria, weakness, and weight loss) is a vivid prompt for recognizing when symptoms exceed scope and require referral.

  • 6.1.2 Assess athlete's nutrition
  • 6.1.3 Provide nutrition guidance

What to focus on while reading

  • The specific sugar loads cited so you can put real numbers behind a coaching conversation: 20 oz Gatorade G-Series = 34 g sugar / 136 cal; 24 oz Ion4 Powerade = 40 g sugar / 154 cal (high-fructose corn syrup), roughly 10 tsp of sugar; G2 = 12 g sugar in 20 oz but adds the artificial sweetener sucralose; 20 oz Coca-Cola = 64 g; Mountain Dew = 77 g.
  • The American Heart Association added-sugar ceilings: no more than ~100 cal (26 g)/day for women and ~150 cal (38 g)/day for men — and note that ONE 20-oz Gatorade can exceed a full day's allotment.
  • The dietitian's bottom line — refined sugar 'needs to be minimized for optimal health,' and with added sugar 'the lower, the better' — as the simple, defensible message a trainer can repeat.
  • The 'electrolyte myth': most athletes do NOT need to replace carbohydrates or electrolytes during typical training, and are usually better off with plain water; Gatorade also causes an insulin spike.
  • The practical threshold Vannata gives clients: electrolyte replacement is mostly a concern only when exercising continuously for MORE than two hours — a clean rule of thumb for everyday class members.
  • The alternative Vannata offers when a client is genuinely worried about electrolytes: coconut water instead of a sugary sports drink.
  • How a coach actually handles the conversation: Vannata leads with the sugar content, uses himself as a living example (water-only, no issues for years), and frames it as a cost/benefit trade-off that 'just isn't worth it' — i.e., persuasion over preaching.
  • Marketing literacy: ads pair high-profile athletes (e.g., Usain Bolt) with the product 'whether or not they actually use it,' and much marketing is aimed at children who see sports drinks as 'cool.'
  • Funding bias / 'science-washing': the Gatorade Sport Science Institute (GSSI) funds research and partners with credible bodies like the American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM), and Zinn's caution that you 'cannot trust research funded by the very company who wants to make money by selling their product.'
  • The whole-food framing of sugar from 'The Toxic Truth About Sugar' (Nature, 2012): evolutionarily, sugar was available only seasonally as fruit or guarded as honey — 'Nature made sugar hard to get; man made it easy'; global sugar consumption has tripled in 50 years.
  • The American Academy of Pediatrics warning that frequent/excessive caloric sports drinks substantially raise overweight/obesity risk in children and adolescents.
  • The diabetes red-flag cluster in Marinoff's story you must be able to recognize: frequent thirst, constant urination, muscle weakness, and unexplained weight loss — ignored for a month before diagnosis.
  • The blood-glucose numbers used for context: normal ~80–120 mg/dL; Marinoff measured 900 mg/dL at diagnosis; a diabetic coma is possible around 600 mg/dL — useful for appreciating how serious untreated high blood sugar is, NOT for the trainer to diagnose.
  • The end-state lifestyle picture: working with a nutritionist and endocrinologist, focusing on clean eating, getting the small remaining sugar in the diet from fruits and vegetables, and reporting steady all-day energy versus the prior 'up and down' from constant soda.
  • The policy/education angle: San Francisco warning labels on sugary-beverage ads ('contributes to obesity, diabetes and tooth decay') as an example of environmental nudges that support athlete education.

Concepts to understand

  • Sports drinks are a hidden, often unnecessary source of refined/added sugar — the trainer's job is to make the invisible sugar visible and reframe 'athletic fuel' marketing as a health-and-performance question, not an automatic necessity.
  • Added sugar should be minimized; practical targets (AHA: ~26 g/day women, ~38 g/day men) let a coach quantify how a single sports drink can blow past a daily budget, supporting concrete dietary-strategy guidance (food types AND amounts).
  • For the typical CrossFit class member, water is the default hydration choice; carbohydrate/electrolyte replacement is generally needed only for prolonged continuous effort (>~2 hours), so everyday WODs do not justify a sugary sports drink.
  • Reading the label is a teachable, repeatable skill: scan grams of sugar per serving, watch the serving-size vs. container-size trick (a 20-oz bottle is often more than one serving), and recognize that 'diet'/low-cal versions trade sugar for artificial sweeteners like sucralose.
  • Critical consumption of nutrition claims: industry-funded 'sport science' (e.g., GSSI) and athlete endorsements can manufacture credibility; a trainer should weigh conflicts of interest and prefer independent evidence and simple, robust principles.
  • Whole-food sourcing of carbohydrate/sugar (fruits, vegetables) is preferable to refined added sugar — consistent with CrossFit's broader 'eat meat and vegetables, nuts and seeds, some fruit, little starch and no sugar' stance and the 'Nature made it hard, man made it easy' logic.
  • Coaching technique for behavior change: lead with facts the client can verify, model the behavior yourself, and frame choices as a cost/benefit trade-off rather than moralizing — meet the athlete where they are and let them own the decision.
  • Recognizing medical red flags that exceed scope: a symptom cluster like excessive thirst, frequent urination, weakness, and unexplained weight loss is a refer-to-physician situation, not a nutrition-coaching situation — the trainer screens and refers, the physician/endocrinologist diagnoses and manages.
  • Scope-of-practice discipline: a CrossFit trainer can educate on added sugar, hydration, and general nutrition and review basic health markers conceptually, but must NOT diagnose disease, prescribe insulin/medication, or manage a diabetic's blood sugar — that is the lane of dietitians, nutritionists, and physicians.
  • Lifestyle and energy connection: stabilizing sugar intake can smooth out the 'energy up-and-down' of a high-sugar diet, tying nutrition guidance to the recovery/energy/performance outcomes athletes actually care about.
  • Environmental and marketing influences (advertising aimed at kids, warning-label policy) shape athlete beliefs; effective lifestyle education includes inoculating clients against misleading messaging, not just handing them facts.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenario questions where an athlete defends drinking Gatorade 'because it's a sports drink / for electrolytes' and you must choose the best coaching response — typically educate on added sugar and recommend water (6.1.3, 6.1.6, 6.2.3), not endorse or shame. Label-reading and meal-planning items (6.1.7, 6.1.8) may give you a nutrition fact panel and ask what to flag (grams of added sugar, serving-size deception, artificial sweeteners). Scope-and-referral items (1.1.2, 6.1.5, 6.2.4, 7.4.1) will present a client with thirst/polyuria/weight-loss or a request to manage their diabetes/medication, and the correct answer is to refer to a physician or registered dietitian rather than diagnose, prescribe, or manage it yourself. Marketing/evidence items may test whether you recognize industry-funded research and celebrity endorsement as reasons for skepticism, not proof of benefit.

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Added sugar (refined sugar)
Sugar put into a food or drink during processing (e.g., high-fructose corn syrup in sports drinks), as opposed to sugar that occurs naturally in whole fruit or vegetables; the type athletes should minimize.
High-fructose corn syrup (HFCS)
A common refined sweetener used in sodas and many sports drinks; the form of added sugar in Powerade cited in the article.
Sucralose
A no-calorie artificial sweetener used in lower-sugar products like G2 Gatorade; a reminder that 'less sugar' often means 'artificial sweetener added,' not 'healthier by default.'
Electrolytes
Minerals (sodium, potassium, etc.) lost in sweat; sports-drink marketing claims you must replace them, but for most athletes this is only a real concern during continuous exercise beyond about two hours.
Insulin spike
A rapid rise in the hormone insulin after consuming fast-absorbing sugar; cited as a reason plain water is usually a better intra-workout choice than a sugary drink.
Type 1 diabetes
An autoimmune disease in which the body produces little or no insulin and cannot regulate blood sugar; in this article it presents in a young adult and requires medical (endocrinologist) management — outside a trainer's scope.
Blood-sugar level (mg/dL)
Concentration of glucose in the blood; the article cites a normal range of roughly 80–120 mg/dL, ~600 mg/dL as a coma risk, and Marinoff's 900 mg/dL at diagnosis — context for severity, not a number a trainer measures or treats.
AHA added-sugar limits
American Heart Association guidance to cap added sugar at ~100 cal (26 g)/day for women and ~150 cal (38 g)/day for men — a benchmark for quantifying dietary strategy.
Gatorade Sport Science Institute (GSSI)
Gatorade's research arm that publishes studies and partners with bodies like the ACSM; used in the article to illustrate industry-funded 'science' and conflict of interest.
Conflict of interest / funding bias
When research is paid for by a company that profits from a favorable result, undermining its trustworthiness; the reason to favor independent evidence and simple robust principles.
Coconut water
A natural beverage suggested as a lower-sugar alternative for the rare client who genuinely needs electrolyte replacement.
Scope of practice
The boundary of what a CrossFit trainer is qualified and permitted to do — general nutrition and lifestyle education yes; diagnosing disease, prescribing medication, or managing a medical condition no (refer out).
Serving size vs. container size
A label-literacy trap: nutrition facts are per serving, but a single bottle (e.g., 20 oz) may contain more than one serving, multiplying the actual sugar consumed.
Sugar epidemic
The article's framing (echoing Nature's 'The Toxic Truth About Sugar') that tripled global sugar consumption over 50 years is driving widespread health harm — context for why minimizing added sugar matters.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • Symptom cluster of frequent thirst, constant urination, muscle weakness, and unexplained weight loss = possible undiagnosed diabetes; the trainer must recommend the athlete see a physician promptly, not coach through it (1.1.2, 6.2.4).
  • A client asking the trainer to manage their diabetes, set insulin doses, or 'fix' their blood sugar is outside scope — refer to a physician/endocrinologist and registered dietitian (6.1.5, 7.4.1).
  • Do not diagnose any medical condition or interpret lab/blood-glucose values as a diagnosis; basic health markers can be discussed generally but diagnosis and treatment belong to medical professionals (6.1.4, 7.4.1).
  • Artificial-sweetener products (e.g., sucralose in G2) are not automatically a 'healthy' swap; avoid implying they are problem-free.
  • Avoid blanket prescriptive nutrition mandates; provide education and options and respect that detailed individualized diet prescription for a diseased client is a dietitian's role.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. A 19-year-old member tells you he chugs a 20-oz Gatorade during every WOD because 'athletes need it for electrolytes and performance.' He does typical 12–20 minute metcons. What is the best coaching response?

  1. A. Agree — sports drinks are formulated for athletes, so it's a smart choice during training.
  2. B. Tell him sports drinks are poison and he should be ashamed of drinking them.
  3. C. Educate him that one 20-oz bottle has ~34 g of added sugar (often more than a day's recommended limit), that for short workouts water is the better default, and that electrolyte replacement mainly matters past ~2 hours of continuous effort.
  4. D. Refer him to a physician because consuming Gatorade is a medical issue.
  5. E. Tell him to switch to Mountain Dew since it tastes similar.
Show answer

Answer: C — C matches the article: make the hidden sugar visible, default to water for typical training, and reserve electrolyte concern for prolonged (>~2 hr) exercise. A endorses the marketing myth the article debunks. B is shaming, not coaching — effective change comes from facts and modeling, not moralizing. D misuses referral; drinking Gatorade is a nutrition-education matter, not a medical emergency. E increases added sugar (Mountain Dew = 77 g).

Scenario 2. During an intake conversation, a new athlete mentions she's been unusually thirsty for weeks, is urinating frequently, feels weak, and has lost weight without trying. What should you do?

  1. A. Build her a low-sugar meal plan and tell her the symptoms will resolve with clean eating.
  2. B. Reassure her it's just dehydration from training and recommend a sports drink.
  3. C. Recommend she see a physician promptly, because these symptoms can signal a medical condition outside your scope, and document the conversation.
  4. D. Tell her to test her own blood sugar and start avoiding all carbs until it normalizes.
  5. E. Ignore it — intake is about goals, not health history.
Show answer

Answer: C — C is correct: thirst, polyuria, weakness, and unexplained weight loss are the exact cluster that preceded Marinoff's Type 1 diabetes diagnosis. Recognizing and referring is within scope (1.1.1, 1.1.2, 6.2.4); diagnosing or managing it is not. A and D overstep scope by treating a likely medical condition with nutrition/coaching. B is both wrong and risky. E ignores a screening responsibility.

Scenario 3. A member shows you the label on a 20-oz lower-calorie sports drink and asks if it's a 'healthy' choice because it has only 12 g of sugar. What is the best label-literacy coaching point?

  1. A. Yes — under 15 g of sugar means it's healthy, drink as much as you want.
  2. B. Note that the lower sugar is achieved with an artificial sweetener (sucralose), check the serving size against the bottle size, and remind her that less added sugar is good but the drink still isn't a needed 'fuel' for normal training.
  3. C. Tell her the label is irrelevant because all sports drinks are identical.
  4. D. Tell her to drink the full-sugar version instead for better performance.
  5. E. Recommend she stop reading labels and just trust the brand.
Show answer

Answer: B — B teaches real label skills from the article: 'diet' versions swap sugar for sweeteners like sucralose, servings can be smaller than the container, and the broader point is that the drink isn't a necessity. A oversimplifies and ignores the sweetener and quantity. C and E discourage the exact label literacy task (6.1.7). D pushes more added sugar.

Scenario 4. An athlete says he trusts Gatorade because the Gatorade Sport Science Institute publishes research and partners with the American College of Sports Medicine. How should you frame the evidence question?

  1. A. That partnership proves Gatorade is scientifically necessary — accept the claim.
  2. B. Explain that research funded by the company selling the product carries a conflict of interest, so it should be weighed skeptically and checked against independent evidence and simple principles like minimizing added sugar.
  3. C. Tell him all sports science is fake and he should ignore science entirely.
  4. D. Tell him to drink it because Usain Bolt is in the commercials.
  5. E. Refuse to discuss it because evidence evaluation is outside a trainer's scope.
Show answer

Answer: B — B reflects Zinn's caution in the article: you can't fully trust research funded by the company that profits from the result; favor independent evidence and robust principles. A accepts manufactured credibility. C overcorrects into anti-science. D is the celebrity-endorsement fallacy the article warns about. E is wrong — helping athletes critically evaluate nutrition claims is squarely within lifestyle education (6.2.3).

Scenario 5. A client with diagnosed Type 1 diabetes asks you to set his insulin dosing and design a diet to manage his blood sugar around training. What is the appropriate action?

  1. A. Calculate his insulin doses and prescribe a precise carb plan yourself.
  2. B. Decline the medical management, refer him to his physician/endocrinologist and a registered dietitian, and stay in your lane by offering general nutrition education and supporting his clean-eating goals.
  3. C. Tell him diabetes can be reversed by CrossFit so he can stop his insulin.
  4. D. Avoid the topic entirely and refuse to coach him.
  5. E. Recommend he replace insulin with coconut water.
Show answer

Answer: B — B is correct: insulin dosing and disease-specific diet management belong to physicians and registered dietitians, not trainers (6.1.5, 6.2.4, 7.4.1); the trainer still coaches training and offers general nutrition education. A and C are dangerous scope violations (C could be fatal). D abandons the client unnecessarily — you can train him within scope. E is unsafe nonsense.

Scenario 6. You're helping a member outline a simple dietary strategy to cut added sugar. She wants the small amount of sugar she does eat to come from better sources. What guidance best fits CrossFit nutrition principles and this article?

  1. A. Replace meals with diet soda since it has no sugar.
  2. B. Get her remaining sugar from whole fruits and vegetables, default to water for hydration, and keep added sugar well under daily limits (~26 g women / ~38 g men).
  3. C. Tell her sugar amount doesn't matter as long as it's 'natural.'
  4. D. Have her load sports drinks before every class for energy.
  5. E. Tell her to eliminate all carbohydrates including vegetables.
Show answer

Answer: B — B aligns with the article and CrossFit's nutrition stance: minimize added sugar, source sugar from whole fruits/vegetables, hydrate with water, and quantify limits (6.1.6, 6.1.3). A relies on artificial sweeteners and skips real food. C ignores that amount still matters. D reintroduces the added-sugar problem. E is extreme and removes nutrient-dense vegetables the framework explicitly encourages.

CFJ_2016_06_Cancer-Saline4.pdf

Open the PDF on Google Drive →

Why this is on the reading list

This CrossFit Journal article presents the metabolic theory of cancer and the ketogenic diet as a potential adjuvant therapy, framing sugar, chronic carbohydrate intake, insulin, and systemic inflammation as drivers of disease. It is on the CCFT reading list to support Domain 6 Lifestyle Education: it gives a coach the scientific rationale behind why CrossFit emphasizes controlling sugar and refined carbohydrate intake, and it is a sharp illustration of where nutrition guidance ends and scope-of-practice limitations begin. The exam will not ask a coach to memorize survival percentages or study designs; it tests whether a coach can distinguish general dietary education from medical treatment and refer appropriately.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 6.1.3 Provide nutrition guidance
  • 6.1.5 Recognize nutrition scope-of-practice limitations
  • 6.1.6 Outline dietary strategies (food types and amounts)
  • 6.1.4 Review basic health markers (HDL, triglycerides, A1C, body fat %, lean mass, BP, bone density)
  • 6.1.1 Identify nutrition goals
  • 6.2.3 Provide additional lifestyle guidance
  • 6.2.4 Recognize scope-of-practice limitations
  • 1.1.2 Recognize conditions/injuries outside CCFT Scope of Practice that require referral
  • 7.4.1 Work within CCFT Scope of Practice

What to focus on while reading

  • The central claim: the article argues cancer may be primarily a mitochondrial METABOLIC disease, not (only) a genetic one — note that this is a contested scientific hypothesis presented by its proponents, not settled consensus or CrossFit doctrine.
  • The proposed causal chain: excess sugar/carbohydrate -> repeated blood-sugar spikes -> imbalanced metabolic hormones (especially insulin) -> systemic/chronic inflammation -> mitochondrial damage -> reactive oxygen species (ROS) -> DNA/protein/lipid damage and mutations -> carcinogenesis. Trace each link.
  • The Warburg Effect: damaged cells revert to aerobic glycolysis (oxygen-free fermentation), consuming large amounts of glucose for unbridled growth. Understand this as the 'sugar-feeds-tumors' mechanism in the article.
  • Seyfried's framing that all tumors 'are fermenting' and share the same metabolic malady — needing glucose and glutamine to survive — versus the 'thousand diseases' gene theory.
  • The ketogenic diet definition given in-text: a low-carbohydrate, high-fat diet that raises ketone bodies in the blood; note the ~50 g carbohydrate/day threshold for entering ketosis (varies with activity).
  • Why ketones are proposed to help: healthy cells (and neurons) can use ketones for fuel and ketones may act as neuroprotectors and anti-inflammatories, while most tumor cells reportedly cannot use ketone bodies.
  • Fine's distinct emphasis: it may be more about lowering INSULIN signaling than lowering blood glucose per se — cancers are described as dependent on insulin signaling; restricting carbohydrate reduces insulin (carbohydrate is the principal secretagogue for insulin release).
  • D'Agostino's 'garden' analogy: glucose = fertilizer, pre-cancer cells = seeds, ketogenic diet = removing the nutrients/'herbicide' so cancer can't take root. A coachable mental model for why sugar control matters generally.
  • The repeated, explicit framing that diet is proposed as an ADJUVANT (complement) to standard care (surgery, radiation, chemo), NOT a standalone cure — Fine: 'I doubt we can fight cancer with our forks alone.'
  • The animal/mouse studies and small human trials are illustrative of an emerging research area — capture that they are preliminary and that large-scale clinical trials are still lacking, not proof a coach can act on.
  • The prevention hook (Fine): if dietary habits changed in general, the same effects 'could be preventing cancers to begin with' — this is the legitimate lifestyle-education takeaway for a healthy gym population.
  • The 'Church of Gene Theory' section: institutional inertia and funding incentives. Useful context, but irrelevant to coaching scope — do not let it pull you into making medical claims.
  • Every place where a coach would have to STOP: any mention of treating, curing, or managing diagnosed cancer is medical territory outside CCFT scope.

Concepts to understand

  • Sugar/refined-carbohydrate excess as an inflammation driver: a coach should be able to explain in plain language WHY CrossFit nutrition guidance pushes to limit sugar and refined carbs — chronic blood-sugar spikes drive hormonal imbalance and systemic inflammation — without diagnosing or claiming disease causation for any individual.
  • Insulin as a hormonal lever: understand that carbohydrate intake is the primary driver of insulin secretion, and that chronically elevated insulin is associated with growth-promoting and pro-inflammatory effects. Apply this to general goal-setting (e.g., body composition, metabolic health) — not to treating illness.
  • The ketogenic diet as a dietary strategy (food types and amounts): low-carb, high-fat, roughly under ~50 g carbohydrate/day to reach ketosis. A coach can OUTLINE what this strategy is and how it generally works (6.1.6) and discuss it as one option among many for a healthy athlete's goals.
  • Therapeutic vs. general use: the article uses keto as a proposed cancer adjuvant therapy. A CCFT coach operates only in the general-wellness lane — outlining dietary strategies and goals for healthy athletes — and must never position any diet as a treatment, cure, or management plan for a diagnosed disease.
  • Adjuvant, not alternative: the strongest application concept is that even the researchers frame keto as a COMPLEMENT to medical care under physician supervision. By extension, a coach's role around any athlete with a medical condition is to support, defer to, and coordinate with medical providers — never to replace them.
  • Health markers as the coach's legitimate data: the article's themes (insulin, blood glucose, inflammation, body composition) map to the basic health markers a coach may review and track — A1C, triglycerides, HDL, body fat %, lean mass, blood pressure (6.1.4) — to set goals and monitor progress, while abnormal values trigger referral.
  • Hypothesis vs. consensus: understand that this is one camp's contested model. Apply intellectual honesty — a coach educates from established, defensible general nutrition principles and flags speculative claims as such rather than presenting them as proven.
  • Prevention framing for a healthy population: the defensible, in-scope message is that broadly improving diet (less sugar, controlled carbohydrate, better metabolic health) supports long-term health — general lifestyle education, not a medical promise.
  • Recognizing the referral line: any athlete who has, suspects, or asks about cancer (or any diagnosed medical condition) is outside CCFT scope — the coach refers to and defers to qualified medical and nutrition professionals (registered dietitian/physician).

How the exam applies this

Expect scenario items where an athlete with (or asking about) a serious diagnosis seeks dietary 'treatment' advice, or where a coach is tempted to make a medical claim from this article — the best answer almost always keeps the coach in the general-education lane and refers to a physician or registered dietitian (6.1.5, 6.2.4, 1.1.2, 7.4.1). Other items test whether a coach can correctly OUTLINE a dietary strategy like keto for a healthy athlete's stated goal and explain the sugar/insulin/inflammation rationale in plain terms (6.1.3, 6.1.6, 6.1.1). Some questions surface as health-marker interpretation — knowing which markers a coach may review and when an abnormal result warrants referral (6.1.4).

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Metabolic theory of cancer
The contested hypothesis (Seyfried) that cancer is fundamentally a disease of damaged mitochondria/cellular respiration, with most genetic mutations being a downstream effect rather than the root cause.
Mitochondria
The cell's 'powerhouse' organelles that convert nutrients into ATP (energy) via cellular respiration; the article frames their damage as the proposed origin of cancer.
Reactive oxygen species (ROS)
Cytotoxic byproducts of damaged mitochondria (described as 'chemical bombs inside cells') that damage proteins, lipids, and DNA, causing mutations.
Warburg Effect
The observation that cancer cells favor aerobic glycolysis — fermenting large amounts of glucose for energy even when oxygen is available — named for biochemist Otto Warburg.
Aerobic glycolysis (fermentation)
An oxygen-free energy pathway that consumes large amounts of glucose; in the article, the metabolism damaged cells revert to for rapid growth.
Ketogenic diet
A low-carbohydrate, high-fat diet that shifts metabolism to produce ketone bodies; the human body typically enters ketosis around 50 g carbohydrate/day (varies with activity).
Ketone bodies
An alternative fuel the liver makes from fat when insulin is low; usable by healthy cells (and neurons) but, per the article, not by most tumor cells; may act as anti-inflammatories and neuroprotectors.
Ketosis
The metabolic state in which the body is running substantially on ketones rather than glucose, induced by carbohydrate restriction.
Insulin
A hormone released mainly in response to carbohydrate intake; in the article, chronically high insulin is described as binding cancer-cell receptors and locking them into a 'permanent growth mode.'
Insulin signaling
The downstream growth-stimulating cascade triggered when insulin binds its receptor; Fine argues lowering it (via carb restriction) may slow cancer growth.
Secretagogue
A substance that triggers secretion; the article calls glucose (from carbohydrate) the principal secretagogue for pancreatic insulin release.
Systemic / chronic inflammation
Persistent, body-wide inflammation; the article links it to repeated blood-sugar spikes and to higher cancer risk via mitochondrial damage.
Glutamine
An amino acid that, alongside glucose, the article says tumor cells need to survive; cutting both is the proposed metabolic strategy.
Adjuvant therapy
A treatment given in addition to the primary/standard treatment; the researchers position the ketogenic diet as an adjuvant to radiation and chemotherapy, not a replacement.
Carcinogenesis
The process by which normal cells become cancerous; the article traces it from mitochondrial damage through ROS, mutation, and oncogene activation.
Oncogene
A gene that, when activated, can transform a normal cell into a cancer cell; the article says mitochondrial damage can trigger this activation.
Neuroprotective
Protecting nerve/brain cells from damage; ketones and the ketogenic diet are described as potentially shielding healthy neurons (including from radiation).
Scope of practice
The boundary of what a CCFT trainer is qualified and permitted to do — general fitness and lifestyle education only; diagnosing, treating, or prescribing for disease is outside it and requires referral.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • Cancer and any diagnosed disease are medical conditions outside CCFT scope of practice (1.1.2, 7.4.1) — a coach must never diagnose, treat, 'manage,' or claim to cure them with diet or exercise.
  • Never tell an athlete a diet will treat, cure, shrink, or prevent their cancer (or any disease). The researchers themselves frame keto as an unproven adjuvant under medical supervision — a coach making such a claim is practicing medicine without a license and exposes the athlete and business to harm and liability.
  • Recognize nutrition scope limits (6.1.5, 6.2.4): for medical nutrition therapy or any disease-specific diet, refer to a registered dietitian and the athlete's physician; the coach stays in general healthy-eating education.
  • An athlete with cancer, on chemotherapy/radiation, or with significant comorbidities requires medical clearance and physician coordination before and during training — defer programming decisions to the medical team.
  • Abnormal health markers (e.g., very high A1C/triglycerides, signs of metabolic disease) that a coach reviews are a referral trigger to a physician, not a prompt for the coach to prescribe a therapeutic protocol.
  • Do not present a contested scientific hypothesis as established fact; over-claiming erodes trust and can steer a vulnerable athlete away from proven medical care.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. A long-time member tells you privately she was just diagnosed with breast cancer and, citing 'an article about sugar and cancer,' asks you to put her on a ketogenic diet to 'starve the tumor' instead of starting the chemo her oncologist recommended. What is the best response?

  1. A. Design a strict ketogenic meal plan for her, since the article shows tumors need glucose and keto can shrink them.
  2. B. Tell her keto can replace chemo for her cancer type because most tumor cells can't use ketones.
  3. C. Express support, make clear that treating cancer is outside your scope, and strongly encourage her to follow her oncologist's plan and discuss any dietary changes with her physician and a registered dietitian.
  4. D. Tell her diet has nothing to do with cancer and she should ignore the article entirely.
  5. E. Quietly lower the carbs in her programming-day nutrition tips so she gets the benefit without you having to discuss it.
Show answer

Answer: C — Cancer treatment is squarely outside CCFT scope (1.1.2, 7.4.1, 6.1.5). The coach's job is to be supportive while deferring to the medical team and a registered dietitian. A is prescribing a therapeutic diet for a disease; B makes a dangerous, false medical claim that could lead her to refuse proven care; D is inaccurate and dismissive; E is deceptive and still amounts to unsanctioned medical intervention.

Scenario 2. A healthy 35-year-old athlete with no medical conditions wants to lose body fat and asks what you think about a low-carb/keto approach he read about in the cancer article. He has no contraindications. What is the most appropriate coaching action?

  1. A. Refuse to discuss diet at all because nutrition is always outside a coach's scope.
  2. B. Outline what a ketogenic strategy is (low-carb, high-fat, roughly under ~50 g carbs/day to reach ketosis), explain it as one option for his body-composition goal, and note you can track progress with simple markers — keeping it general healthy-eating guidance.
  3. C. Tell him keto will prevent him from ever getting cancer, citing the article.
  4. D. Prescribe an exact gram-by-gram therapeutic keto protocol modeled on the cancer trials in the article.
  5. E. Tell him carbs are dangerous and he must eliminate all carbohydrates permanently.
Show answer

Answer: B — For a healthy athlete, outlining dietary strategies and food types/amounts is in-scope general nutrition education (6.1.3, 6.1.6, 6.1.1). A is wrong because coaches CAN provide general nutrition guidance. C makes an unsupported medical/prevention claim. D copies a disease-treatment protocol and overreaches. E misstates the article (carbs in excess are the concern) and gives extreme, unqualified advice.

Scenario 3. During a nutrition chat, a member asks you to explain WHY CrossFit keeps telling him to cut back on sugar and refined carbs. Drawing on this article, what is the best plain-language explanation that stays within your scope?

  1. A. 'Sugar directly gives you cancer, so you must never eat it.'
  2. B. 'Eating a lot of sugar and refined carbs repeatedly spikes blood sugar and insulin, which can drive chronic inflammation and poorer metabolic health over time — so controlling them supports your long-term health and your body-composition goals.'
  3. C. 'There's no real reason; it's just a CrossFit rule.'
  4. D. 'Carbs are a poison and any amount will damage your mitochondria.'
  5. E. 'Cutting sugar will cure any disease you might have.'
Show answer

Answer: B — B accurately reflects the article's general mechanism (sugar/carb excess -> insulin/blood-sugar spikes -> chronic inflammation -> worse metabolic health) and frames it as general lifestyle education tied to the athlete's goals. A and E make false medical/causation claims about an individual; C abandons the coach's educational role; D overstates the article (the issue is excess and chronicity, not any carbohydrate at all).

Scenario 4. An athlete shows you recent bloodwork with a notably elevated A1C and high triglycerides and asks what it means and what she should do. What is the best coaching response?

  1. A. Diagnose her with pre-diabetes and prescribe a therapeutic ketogenic diet to reverse it.
  2. B. Tell her the numbers are meaningless for a CrossFitter and to ignore them.
  3. C. Note that these are markers you can help her track toward goals, but that interpreting abnormal results and any diagnosis or treatment is for her physician — recommend she follow up medically while you support healthy general nutrition and training habits.
  4. D. Assure her that as long as she does CrossFit, the numbers will fix themselves and no doctor is needed.
  5. E. Tell her to stop all carbohydrates immediately to bring the numbers down before her next workout.
Show answer

Answer: C — Reviewing basic health markers is in-scope (6.1.4), but interpreting abnormal values and diagnosing/treating is not (6.1.5, 1.1.2). C tracks the markers, refers for medical interpretation, and keeps the coach in general-education territory. A diagnoses and prescribes therapeutically; B and D dismiss a legitimate referral signal; E gives extreme, unqualified dietary orders.

Scenario 5. A coach on your team wants to start telling members that 'cancer is really a metabolic disease, not genetic' and that 'keto starves tumors,' using this article as proof. How should you advise him?

  1. A. Endorse it — the article proves cancer is metabolic, so it's safe to teach members this as fact.
  2. B. Caution that this is a contested scientific hypothesis, not established consensus or coaching content, and that making disease claims to members is outside scope and risky — keep nutrition talk to general healthy-eating principles and refer medical questions to physicians.
  3. C. Tell him to go further and offer members keto 'cancer-prevention' coaching packages.
  4. D. Tell him the article is worthless and members should never hear about nutrition science.
  5. E. Have him diagnose members' cancer risk from their diet logs so they know who to put on keto.
Show answer

Answer: B — The article presents one camp's contested model, not settled science, and coaches must not make disease claims (intellectual honesty + scope, 6.1.5, 7.4.1). B keeps the team in the general-education lane and defers medical claims to physicians. A overstates the evidence; C and E cross into practicing medicine and selling medical promises; D wrongly bans all legitimate general nutrition education.

Scenario 6. The article repeatedly frames the ketogenic diet as an 'adjuvant' to standard cancer care. For a CCFT coach, what is the correct takeaway from that framing?

  1. A. The diet is a proven standalone cure, so coaches can recommend it instead of medical care.
  2. B. Even the researchers position diet as a COMPLEMENT to physician-led treatment — so a coach's role around any athlete with a medical condition is to support and defer to the medical team, never to replace it.
  3. C. Because it's only adjuvant, diet is irrelevant and coaches should never discuss nutrition.
  4. D. Coaches should run their own clinical trials to prove it works before referring out.
  5. E. Adjuvant means the coach is now part of the medical treatment team and can manage the protocol.
Show answer

Answer: B — 'Adjuvant' explicitly means in-addition-to, under medical supervision — Fine says he doubts diet alone is the answer. B captures the scope-appropriate lesson: support and defer to medical providers (1.1.2, 6.1.5, 7.4.1). A inverts the meaning; C overcorrects against legitimate general nutrition education; D and E place the coach inside medical treatment, far outside CCFT scope.

D6 · Lifestyle Education 11% of exam Confidence tier: ___

CFJ_2016_10_Nutrition2-Synkowski3.pdf

Open the PDF on Google Drive →

Why this is on the reading list

This nutrition brief is on the CCFT reading list because Domain 6 (Lifestyle Education, 11% of the exam) requires a coach to give practical, scope-appropriate nutrition guidance, and carbohydrate selection is one of the most common questions athletes ask. It backs the 6.1.x cluster directly: providing nutrition guidance, outlining dietary strategies (food types and amounts), and recognizing scope-of-practice limits. Its core teaching—that there is no blanket 'good carb' or 'bad carb,' only the right carb for a specific athlete's goal and context—is exactly the kind of applied judgment the exam tests. A coach must be able to match a carbohydrate choice to an athlete's body-composition, health, satiety, and recovery needs rather than reciting a memorized rule.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 6.1.1 Identify nutrition goals
  • 6.1.2 Assess athlete's nutrition
  • 6.1.3 Provide nutrition guidance
  • 6.1.5 Recognize nutrition scope-of-practice limitations
  • 6.1.6 Outline dietary strategies (food types and amounts)
  • 6.1.7 Teach athletes how to read food labels
  • 6.1.8 Teach athletes how to build sample meal plans
  • 6.2.3 Provide additional lifestyle guidance

What to focus on while reading

  • The four decision criteria the brief gives for selecting a carbohydrate: total carbohydrate (for body composition), non-caloric constituents/micronutrients (for health), fiber (for satiety), and glucose vs. fructose (for recovery). These four lenses are the spine of the whole article—know what each one is FOR.
  • Why 'total carbohydrate grams' is the first consideration: overeating carbs from ANY source—even 'healthy' ones—can stymie health and performance goals. The source does not exempt you from the total.
  • The self-coaching question the article hands you: 'Do I want this food to represent X percent of my carbohydrate allotment for the day?' Notice this is a tool you can give an athlete, not just a fact.
  • The energy-use hierarchy: the body preferentially uses carbohydrate and protein for energy, storing fat until carbs and protein are metabolized—so excess protein and fat also affect body composition, not just carbs.
  • What 'non-caloric constituents' means: micronutrients (13 vitamins, 14 minerals) and phytonutrients (e.g., resveratrol, curcumin) provide little/no calories but drive long-term health—the reason to choose nutrient-dense whole foods.
  • Bruce Ames' 'triage' theory: when a vitamin/mineral is in short supply, the body spends it on immediate survival needs at the expense of long-term health—the rationale for nutrient density EVEN when current health markers look fine.
  • The rule that 'the closer a food is to its natural form, the higher the concentration of micronutrients and phytonutrients,' and that processing strips nutrients, adds dyes/chemicals, and adds 'empty calories' (lost opportunity to maximize health).
  • How fiber works: non-digestible, sometimes subtracted from carb totals, but aids satiety by slowing digestion, blunting the insulin spike/crash, and being less carbohydrate-dense—so you can eat a larger VOLUME and feel fuller.
  • The concrete volume comparison: ~5 cups of broccoli ≈ 2 cups of halved strawberries ≈ ½ cup of rice in total carbohydrate grams. This is the kind of label/portion reasoning you'd teach an athlete.
  • The consistency rule on fiber: decide to EITHER always count fiber toward carb grams OR always leave it out—pick one and stay consistent.
  • Glucose vs. fructose metabolism: plant foods (veg, legumes, nuts, grains) are mostly glucose chains; fruit and added sugar are ~50% fructose / 50% glucose; dairy galactose converts to glucose; everything else is glucose.
  • Why fructose is the WRONG post-workout carb: it does NOT spike insulin and does NOT refill muscle glycogen—it goes to the liver to fill liver glycogen or be converted to fat. Glucose is the one that drives the insulin/anabolism and muscle-glycogen refill.
  • The critical context qualifier: post-workout nutrition is LOW priority for a recreational athlete training once a day—day-long nutrition and the workout itself matter more. Priority rises with training VOLUME (multiple sessions/day) because of reduced refuel time.
  • Why fiber AND fructose should both be AVOIDED when fast-absorbing carbs are the goal (both slow or misdirect absorption).
  • The five 'choosing the most optimal' modifiers that override 'always eat greens': Variation (rotate sources for nutrient coverage), Realistic (you can't physically eat enough greens past ~100 g carb/day), Mass gain / compressed feeding window (target carb-dense, low-fiber foods to hit targets), Performance (lower-quality fast carbs near workouts for multi-session/endurance athletes who already have basics dialed in), and Enjoyment (treats aid adherence and social life—'and that's OK').
  • The donut-vs-orange and honey-vs-table-sugar examples—same carb grams, different non-caloric value—as the article's proof that macro counting alone hides health information.
  • The closing thesis to internalize: select the MAJORITY of carbs from a wide variety of whole, unprocessed foods, but the 'right tool for the right job' can be chosen without labeling any carb 'good' or 'bad.'
  • Author credibility/scope: E.C. Synkowski is CrossFit Seminar Staff Flowmaster and Training Dept. Program Manager pursuing a master's in human nutrition—note this is general nutrition education, NOT a prescription.

Concepts to understand

  • Carbohydrate quality is contextual, not absolute: the same food can be 'optimal' or 'suboptimal' depending on the athlete's goal (body composition, health, satiety, or recovery). A coach matches the carb to the job rather than declaring foods good or bad.
  • Total intake governs body composition first: no matter how nutrient-dense the source, consistently overeating carbohydrate grams undermines body-composition and performance goals—the athlete must know how a portion fits their daily allotment.
  • Non-caloric constituents (micronutrients + phytonutrients) are the health argument for whole foods: they add negligible calories but yield long-term health benefits, which is why a coach steers athletes toward nutrient-dense, minimally processed foods.
  • Triage theory explains WHY nutrient density matters even when an athlete 'feels fine': scarce vitamins/minerals get rationed to immediate needs, quietly mortgaging long-term health—so favorable current markers are not a reason to ignore food quality.
  • Fiber is a satiety and blood-sugar tool: it slows digestion, blunts the insulin spike/crash, and lowers carb density so the athlete eats more volume and feels fuller—useful for fat loss/appetite control, counterproductive when fast carbs are wanted.
  • Glucose vs. fructose is a recovery-timing concept: glucose drives the insulin response and refills MUSCLE glycogen (what high-intensity work needs); fructose does neither and is routed to the liver—so it's the wrong choice in the post-workout window.
  • Post-workout nutrition priority scales with training volume: trivial for the once-a-day recreational athlete (out-prioritized by overall daily nutrition and the workout itself), important for multi-session/endurance athletes with little refuel time.
  • Whole-food carbs deliver value that macro counting misses: matching carb grams (donut vs. orange, table sugar vs. honey) ignores micronutrients, phytonutrients, and fiber—so a coach teaches athletes to look past the gram count.
  • The 'optimal' choice is modulated by real life: variation, what's physically realistic, mass-gain or compressed-feeding goals, performance timing, and enjoyment/adherence all legitimately justify choosing a less 'nutrient-dense' carb at times.
  • Dietary indiscretions can be strategically useful: planned treats support long-term adherence and social enjoyment—an all-or-nothing 'perfect food only' stance often backfires.
  • Consistency in measurement beats perfection: deciding once whether to count or exclude fiber (and applying it consistently) is what makes carb tracking usable for an athlete.
  • Scope of practice frames all of this: a coach provides general carbohydrate education and strategy, not individualized medical-nutrition prescriptions or treatment of disease—referral to an RD/physician is required when needs exceed general guidance.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenario questions where an athlete states a specific goal (lose body fat, gain mass, recover between two-a-days, control hunger, improve health markers) and you must pick the best carbohydrate guidance—this is 6.1.3 and 6.1.6 in action. Items may give two foods with identical carb grams (orange vs. donut, honey vs. sugar) and ask what additional factors a coach should raise (6.1.2, 6.1.7), or present a post-workout fueling choice testing whether you know glucose—not fructose—refills muscle glycogen. Other items will probe judgment on when post-workout timing actually matters (once-a-day vs. multi-session athlete) and when a coach should stop educating and refer out (6.1.5). The right answer is almost always the context-dependent, scope-appropriate one—never a blanket 'this carb is bad.'

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Micronutrients
The 13 vitamins and 14 minerals the body needs in small amounts (e.g., magnesium for ATP production, iron for oxygen delivery, vitamin E as an antioxidant). They supply little/no calories but are essential to long-term health.
Phytonutrients (phytochemicals)
Plant-based compounds believed to promote health, such as resveratrol (wine) and curcumin (turmeric), linked to antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects. Thousands exist; many effects are still unknown.
Non-caloric constituents
Components of food (micronutrients and phytonutrients) that contribute essentially no calories but have long-term beneficial effects on health and performance—the 'health' reason to choose whole foods.
Empty calories
Calories—typically added sugar—that provide energy without micronutrients or phytonutrients. They represent a lost opportunity to maximize health.
Triage theory (Bruce Ames)
The idea that when a vitamin or mineral is in short supply, the body preferentially uses it for immediate survival needs at the expense of long-term health—the rationale for eating nutrient-dense foods even when current health markers look good.
Glucose
The carbohydrate the body uses for an insulin spike and to refill MUSCLE glycogen (needed for high-intensity effort). Plant foods—vegetables, legumes, nuts, grains—are primarily chains of glucose (cellulose, starch); dairy galactose converts to glucose.
Fructose
A sugar found in fruit and added sugar (fruit and table sugar are each ~50% fructose / 50% glucose). It does NOT spike insulin or refill muscle glycogen; it is sent to the liver to fill liver glycogen or be converted to fat—so it's a poor post-workout carb.
Muscle glycogen
Stored carbohydrate in muscle that fuels high-intensity efforts. Refilled by glucose (not fructose); the target of post-workout carbohydrate intake when recovery between sessions matters.
Liver glycogen
Stored carbohydrate in the liver. Fructose is routed here; once full, fructose is converted to fat. Liver glycogen does not directly fuel high-intensity muscular work the way muscle glycogen does.
Fiber
Non-digestible carbohydrate (sometimes subtracted from carb totals) that aids satiety by slowing digestion, blunting the insulin spike/crash, and lowering carb density—so you eat more volume and feel fuller. Should be avoided when fast-absorbing carbs are the goal.
Satiety
The feeling of fullness. High-fiber, low-carbohydrate-density foods increase satiety, helping with appetite control and fat-loss goals.
Carbohydrate density
How many carb grams are packed into a given food volume. Low-density (high-fiber) foods let you eat more and feel full; high-density foods help hit carb targets in a small volume (useful for mass gain or compressed feeding).
Carbohydrate allotment
An athlete's planned daily carbohydrate grams. The practical selection question is whether a given food is worth the percentage of that daily allotment it consumes.
Compressed feeding window
Eating all daily intake within a shorter time period (e.g., intermittent fasting). May justify choosing carb-dense, low-fiber foods to reach daily targets within the available time.
Post-workout window
The period after training when quickly absorbed carbohydrate can drive insulin/anabolism and muscle-glycogen refill. Low priority for once-a-day recreational athletes; increasingly important as training volume rises.
Dietary indiscretion
A treat or off-plan food not justified by its nutrient content. Used strategically, it can boost long-term adherence and support social enjoyment—so it is not automatically 'bad.'
Nutrient density
The amount of beneficial micronutrients and phytonutrients per calorie. Whole, unprocessed foods are the most nutrient-dense and, by promoting fullness, often reduce total caloric intake.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • Scope of practice: a coach provides general carbohydrate EDUCATION and strategy, not individualized medical-nutrition therapy, disease treatment, or diagnosis. When an athlete has a medical condition (diabetes, kidney/liver disease, eating disorder, GI disorder) or needs a clinical-grade plan, refer to a registered dietitian or physician (6.1.5).
  • Do not interpret or 'treat' an athlete's blood markers (A1C, lipids, etc.) as a clinician would—reviewing basic markers for education is in scope (6.1.4), but diagnosing or prescribing based on them is not.
  • Watch for disordered-eating signals around carb avoidance, fasting/compressed windows, or rigid 'good/bad' food beliefs; the article's anti-restriction, enjoyment-includes-treats stance is healthier, and clinical concerns warrant referral.
  • Aggressive carb manipulation around very high training volume should account for fueling adequacy; under-fueling a high-volume athlete is a performance and health risk, not just a programming detail.

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. An athlete just finished a single high-intensity metcon and is about to start a second hard session in 90 minutes. He asks what to eat right now to recover fastest. Which guidance best fits the article's reasoning?

  1. A. A piece of fruit, because fruit sugar refills muscle glycogen quickly
  2. B. A primarily glucose-based, low-fiber carbohydrate, because glucose drives the insulin response and refills muscle glycogen
  3. C. A high-fiber vegetable like broccoli, because fiber speeds absorption
  4. D. Skip carbs entirely; post-workout nutrition never matters
  5. E. A fructose source such as honey water, because the liver fuels high-intensity work
Show answer

Answer: B — With two hard sessions close together, fast muscle-glycogen refill matters, and that requires glucose with minimal fiber (fiber slows absorption). A and E are wrong because fructose goes to the liver and does NOT refill muscle glycogen or spike insulin. C is wrong because fiber slows absorption. D is wrong because post-workout timing DOES matter as training volume/density rises—the qualifier is that it's low priority only for the once-a-day recreational athlete.

Scenario 2. A general-fitness member training once a day asks where she should put her energy to improve results. She has heard she needs a special post-workout shake. What is the best coaching response per this brief?

  1. A. Yes, the post-workout shake is the single most important meal—prioritize it above all else
  2. B. For a once-a-day athlete, overall daily nutrition and the workout itself matter more than post-workout timing; dial those in first
  3. C. She should add fructose immediately after training to refill muscle glycogen
  4. D. Post-workout nutrition is equally critical for everyone regardless of training volume
  5. E. She should stop eating carbohydrates to improve body composition
Show answer

Answer: B — The article states post-workout nutrition is low priority for a recreational athlete working out once a day and is easily surpassed by attention to the workout and day-long nutrition. A and D overstate post-workout timing. C is wrong (fructose doesn't refill muscle glycogen). E is an extreme, non-individualized prescription the article rejects.
