Open the PDF on Google Drive →

Why this is on the reading list

This primer is the CCFT reading list's single deepest source for Domain 7 (Professional Responsibilities), which tests the trainer's duty to manage risk for the business, facility, and people in it. It directly backs the tasks on inspecting/maintaining equipment and keeping the facility safe (7.2.3), responding to extreme environmental conditions (7.2.4), assessing insurance and legal needs (7.2.5), building and following an Emergency Action Plan (7.3.1), and running an ethical practice within scope (7.4). It also reinforces obtaining informed consent and waivers (7.2.1) and ties into managing risk and arranging equipment/space for safety in Domain 5. The exam will not ask you to recite OSHA form numbers; it will hand you a gym scenario (a worn climbing rope, a client who vomits, a chemical spill, a treadmill malfunction, a power outage) and ask what a competent, responsible trainer does first.

Content Outline tasks this supports

  • 7.2.3 Maintain/inspect equipment; keep facility clean and safe
  • 7.2.4 Recognize and respond to extreme environmental conditions
  • 7.2.5 Assess insurance policy and other legal needs
  • 7.2.1 Obtain informed consent and waiver of liability from every athlete
  • 7.2.2 Obtain written, signed medical release when required
  • 7.3.1 Create and follow an Emergency Action Plan (EAP)
  • 7.4.1 Work within CCFT Scope of Practice
  • 7.4.2 Adhere to CrossFit Standards of Professional Practice and related legal agreements
  • 5.2.3 Manage risk for the athlete
  • 5.2.6 Recognize warning signs for possible injury or overexertion
  • 5.2.7 Arrange equipment, athletes, instructors to maximize safety
  • 5.2.8 Educate athletes on personal responsibility in a workout setting
  • 5.2.10 Manage logistics (ratio, equipment demands, duration, space)
  • 1.1.1 Screen athlete for medical issues (e.g., health questionnaire)

What to focus on while reading

  • The four OSHA elements of any health-and-safety program (management sets/supports policy with employee involvement; a responsible party does ongoing worksite hazard analysis; hazard prevention/control methods are implemented; supervisors and employees are trained) — these are the skeleton of 'manage risk for the business entity.'
  • The principle that authority can be delegated but responsibility cannot — the owner/manager remains responsible even when a task is assigned to an employee or independent-contractor trainer.
  • That trainers are often independent contractors and are bound by the SAME health-and-safety guidelines as owners and managers — you cannot disclaim responsibility by saying 'I'm just a contractor.'
  • The five-step risk-assessment process: Identify -> Analyze -> Solve -> Implement -> Evaluate. Know what each step accomplishes, not just the names.
  • Hazard identification is the most important step — if a hazard is not identified, its risk cannot be reduced or eliminated.
  • The risk-control hierarchy: eliminating risk is best; minimizing risk to the lowest practicable level is next best; for non-modifiable hazards, training and signage are acceptable remediation.
  • The legal standard 'so far as is reasonably practicable' — all risk cannot be eliminated, but the employer must make the workplace as safe as reasonably possible. The word 'practicable' is doing real work.
  • The 97% vs 3% statistic: only ~3% of worksite accidents stem from materials/equipment/environment; ~97% involve human factors. This reframes safety as a behavior/supervision problem, not just an equipment problem.
  • The categories of non-human hazards an assessor looks for in a gym: chemical, electrical, mechanical (crush/laceration/amputation from moving parts, plus ropes/rings/racks failing), ergonomic (trip/slip from cords and unstacked plates), radiation (tanning beds), and environment (sauna/outdoor heat or cold).
  • Treadmills are repeatedly called the single most dangerous / highest-injury piece of equipment in the gym (~24,400 injuries in 2014, ~39% of gym injuries, ~3 deaths/year) — counterintuitive but exam-relevant.
  • Bench press accounts for ~10 deaths/year (mostly in homes) — relevant to spotting and 'bail-out' judgment.
  • The seven required elements of an Emergency Action Plan (reporting procedures; evacuation procedures and exit routes; procedures for anyone who stays to run critical operations; method to account for everyone after evacuation; rescue/first-aid procedures; the person(s) to contact about the plan; the alert method).
  • When a WRITTEN plan is required vs. when verbal is allowed: in the U.S., a written health-and-safety policy and written fire/emergency plan are required at 10+ employees; the U.K. threshold is 5+. Below that, plans may be communicated verbally but writing is still recommended.
  • The three parts of an exit route: exit access (path leading to the exit door), exit (the protected portion between workspace and exit door), and exit discharge (where the exit leads directly outside).
  • Exit-route rules a trainer can violate by accident: routes must be permanent and unobstructed; doors must stay unlocked from the inside; at least two exit routes are common code; exit routes must be kept clear of equipment, stored plates, locked doors, and dead ends; routes must be lit and marked.
  • The U.K. minimum-exit guideline by capacity (<=60 -> 1 exit; 61-600 -> 2; >600 -> 3) and the principle that exit planning is governed by maximum building capacity, not the actual number present.
  • Fire-extinguisher operation acronym PASS: Pull the pin, Aim low at the base of the fire, Squeeze the lever, Sweep side to side; plus the practical rules — only fight a fire if you have an unobstructed escape route, stay 6-8 ft from the leading edge, and evacuation is the primary response.
  • Fire-extinguisher placement/maintenance: travel distance to any extinguisher <=75 ft for Class A fires, one on every floor and adjacent to stairways, monthly visual inspection, annual maintenance check.
  • Smoke-alarm basics: at least one per floor (including basement), mounted high/on ceiling, away from windows/ducts/doors and >=10 ft from cooking appliances; ionization responds faster to flaming fires, photoelectric to smoldering fires, dual-sensor gives best coverage; test monthly, replace batteries when chirping, replace alarms every ~10 years.
  • How a sprinkler differs from an extinguisher: heads open individually when heat melts a fusible link; the system works independently and lets all occupants evacuate (it is not an all-or-nothing dump).
  • The three chemical routes of entry: inhalation (fastest, most common, straight to bloodstream via lungs), absorption (skin/eyes, second most common; open cuts increase entry), ingestion (slowest/least effective, often via contaminated hands/food).
  • The five chemical health-hazard categories and what each does: toxic (dose-dependent organ/system damage, often delayed and away from entry point), corrosive (immediate tissue damage via oxidation; acids/bases), carcinogenic (DNA/metabolic damage, insidious/delayed, usually a critical dose), reproductive (infertility, miscarriage, birth defects; worst in first trimester), sensitizers (no first-exposure effect, allergic hypersensitivity after repeated exposure; e.g., latex, formaldehyde).
  • The danger of mixing common cleaners — bleach + ammonia produces toxic chloramine gas that can rapidly cause unconsciousness; in a closed container the evolving gas can explode it. This is a classic 'what's wrong with this picture' scenario.
  • What a Safety Data Sheet (SDS, formerly MSDS) is, that one must be kept for EVERY chemical used regardless of how rarely, and that it must be accessible to workers; know that an SDS has 16 standardized sections and that Section 4 covers first aid.
  • Chemical storage rules: store off the floor, no higher than eye level, heavier/larger containers on lower shelves, containers tightly closed and undamaged, labels legible; incompatible chemicals stored apart.
  • Secondary-container labeling — when you decant bleach into a spray bottle, that secondary container must be labeled with contents and hazard; the bottle of bleach must be distinguishable from the bottle of plant-misting water. Minimum U.S. label: product name, hazard category, other hazard statements, supplier name, supplier contact.
  • Universal precautions for biological fluids: treat ALL body fluids/materials as if infectious; the core elements are hand washing, barriers (gloves, masks, eye protection, gowns, CPR dam), and sanitation/decontamination of equipment before reuse.
  • Blood is the primary concern (hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV). Sweat, tears, urine, vomit, etc. are generally low-risk for HIV/hepatitis UNLESS visibly bloody, but can still carry other pathogens — notably MRSA spread skin-to-surface-to-skin via sweat.
  • The specific clean-up sequence for vomit/blood: keep everyone but the cleaner away -> don PPE (gloves, mask, eyewear, clothing) -> use absorbent disposable materials -> disinfect/sanitize -> bag, seal, and dispose of all materials.
  • The scope nuance: blood-borne-pathogen regulation (CFR 1910.1030) primarily targets occupations with anticipated exposure; ordinary gym first aid is a 'Good Samaritan' act, not occupational exposure — so a typical gym is NOT legally bound UNLESS it runs combat sports (boxing/wrestling/MMA) where bleeding is expected. But adopting the precautions anyway is recommended.
  • MRSA control via clothing as a barrier and regular surface cleaning — a programming/coaching lever you can pull (recommend clients wear clothing that blocks skin-to-surface contact).
  • The legal-safety triad for the business: screen customers before participation, obtain informed-consent AND waiver-of-liability forms from every customer, and carry liability insurance — plus keep complete, accurate records/forms per client.
  • The supervision statistic: ~80% of reviewed court cases cited lack or inadequacy of supervision as a contributing factor to injury. An unattended exercise floor is a liability.
  • The spotting reframe: 'no spotter, don't lift' is largely FALSE; untrained spotters are themselves a hazard; teaching trainees to safely dump/miss/bail out (as USA Weightlifting teaches) is often safer than mandating spotters.
  • Equipment-spacing guidance: design to disability-access (ADA / DDA) standards; ~36-48 inch walkways between free-weight/platform areas and ~24-36 inch walkways between machines; keep foot traffic clear of moving barbells, dumbbells, and machine parts.
  • The daily/weekly/monthly equipment-maintenance checklist specifics — DAILY: clean shared-contact surfaces (pull-up bars, barbell/dumbbell/kettlebell grips, med balls, jump-rope handles, rower handles, ab mats, box grips), check floors for slip/trip hazards, scan for items stored too close to workout space and for exposed sharp edges; WEEKLY: check daily-use gear for dangerous wear (jump ropes with exposed wire, pads under pull-up bars/rings/ropes, lifting-mat edges); MONTHLY: check stretch bands for joint separation, climbing ropes (especially at attachment points), pull-up-bar connections, rack anchoring to floor/wall/ceiling, and under floor mats/platforms where weights are dropped.
  • The warning against DIY/home-made equipment: do not use stretch bands made from inner tubes, storage shelves anchored only to drywall without studs, or DIY pull-up bars — increased failure risk.
  • Crash pads / matting requirements: pads under climbing ropes; concrete must NOT be exposed under pull-up bars or rings.
  • Record-keeping obligations relevant to risk: training records, equipment-inspection dates, chemical inventory + SDS file, and injury/illness records — and that the fitness industry (NAICS 713940) is NOT exempt from injury/illness recordkeeping. Serious incidents (fatality, hospitalization, amputation, loss of eye) must be reported regardless of size.
  • The 'novices are at highest risk' principle — new employees/trainers and new equipment/tasks carry the highest risk and require training BEFORE assuming duties.

Concepts to understand

  • Risk management as a continuous, proactive cycle, not a one-time document: Identify -> Analyze -> Solve -> Implement -> Evaluate, reviewed at least annually. Be able to place a given gym situation at the correct step and choose the next action.
  • The legal duty of care: owners/managers owe a safe workplace to employees AND a safe environment to customers, 'so far as is reasonably practicable.' Understand that 'practicable' means reasonable, achievable mitigation — not perfection — so the right answer is usually the proportionate, reasonable control, not an extreme one.
  • Delegation vs. responsibility: you can hand off the task but not the accountability. If an assigned employee fails to complete a safety task, it falls back on the owner/manager. Apply this when a scenario tries to let a manager off the hook.
  • Independent-contractor trainers are still fully bound by the gym's safety procedures and by general OSH/HSW law — 'contractor status' is not a safety or liability shield.
  • Hazard identification is the linchpin: unidentified hazards cannot be controlled, so the highest-leverage safety act is systematic, recurring inspection and observation (walk-throughs, step-by-step equipment review).
  • The control hierarchy: eliminate > minimize to lowest practicable level > administrative controls (training, rules, signage) for hazards that cannot be engineered out (e.g., a non-modifiable machine pulley). Choose the highest feasible control for the scenario.
  • Human factors dominate safety: since ~97% of incidents involve human behavior, supervision, instruction, enforcement of rules, and athlete education on personal responsibility are the most powerful risk controls a trainer has — more than equipment alone.
  • The Emergency Action Plan as an executable system: it is not enough to have a plan; it must be written (at scale), disseminated via training, name responsible people, be practiced with drills, and include accounting for all people after evacuation. Understand 'create AND follow.'
  • Egress integrity: an exit route only works if it is permanent, unobstructed, unlocked from inside, lit, marked, and free of stored equipment/plates — so day-to-day housekeeping IS emergency preparedness. Recognize when normal gym clutter has compromised egress.
  • Fire response priorities: evacuation first; an extinguisher is for small/containable fires only when you have a clear escape; PASS technique; know placement/inspection cadence well enough to spot a deficiency in a scenario.
  • Chemical safety reasoning by route of entry and hazard category: match the exposure scenario (vapor, splash, skin contact, swallowed) to the right protective action and the right hazard class, and recognize that effects can be immediate (corrosive) or delayed/insidious (toxic, carcinogen, sensitizer).
  • Chemical incompatibility and labeling discipline: never assume two cleaners can be combined; the bleach+ammonia -> chloramine example generalizes to 'mixing or mislabeling cleaning chemicals is a real injury vector.' Secondary containers must always be labeled.
  • SDS as the authoritative reference: when a chemical question arises (first aid, spill clean-up, storage, incompatibility), the correct professional move is to consult that chemical's SDS — and SDS files must exist for every chemical and be accessible.
  • Universal precautions and the 'treat everything as infectious' default: understand WHY (you cannot see pathogens) and the standard sequence of barrier -> contain -> disinfect -> dispose, plus that blood is the highest risk and bloody fluids escalate other fluids to blood-level caution.
  • Scope-of-practice nuance for blood-borne pathogens: recognize that a standard CrossFit gym is generally outside the strict regulation (Good Samaritan first aid) while a combat-sports gym is inside it — and that adopting the precautions voluntarily is still the responsible standard.
  • MRSA and surface hygiene as a coaching responsibility: cleaning shared-contact equipment and recommending barrier clothing are concrete, exam-relevant controls a trainer applies daily.
  • Legal safety as part of professional responsibility: informed consent + waiver of liability from every athlete, pre-participation screening, medical release when indicated, and liability insurance form the documentation/coverage backbone (7.2.1, 7.2.2, 7.2.5). Understand each is per-athlete and must be complete and accurate.
  • Supervision as the dominant liability factor: because ~80% of reviewed injury cases involved inadequate supervision, an attended, actively surveyed floor is both a safety control and a legal defense — even in self-service/pay-for-access models.
  • Spotting judgment: a competent trainer weighs whether a spotter is trained and competent before requiring one, and often teaches safe bail-out technique instead — directly relevant to managing risk and spotting tasks.
  • Environmental-condition response (heat/cold): saunas, non-climate-controlled spaces, and outdoor training raise hyperthermia/hypothermia risk; the responsible trainer plans for and adjusts to extreme conditions (7.2.4).
  • Layout and spacing as engineered safety: spacing per ADA/DDA and recommended walkway widths prevent strikes, entanglement, and trip/slip — connecting facility design to arranging equipment/athletes for safety (5.2.7, 5.2.10).
  • Preventive maintenance on a fixed cadence (daily/weekly/monthly) with documentation is the operational expression of 'maintain/inspect equipment; keep facility clean and safe' (7.2.3) — and inspecting load-bearing/overhead gear (ropes, pull-up bars, racks, rings, pads) is highest priority because failure there is catastrophic.
  • DIY-equipment risk: recognizing and removing home-made gear (inner-tube bands, drywall-anchored shelves, DIY pull-up bars) is a defensible risk-management decision a responsible trainer makes.

How the exam applies this

Expect scenario items that drop you into a live gym problem and ask for the single best next action of a responsible trainer. A frayed climbing rope at its attachment point, an unanchored rack, exposed concrete under a pull-up bar, or stretch bands made from inner tubes test equipment inspection and removal (7.2.3) plus risk management (5.2.3). A client vomiting mid-WOD, a bloody shin scrape on a bar, or a bleach-and-ammonia mixing mistake test biological-fluid precautions, chemical-route reasoning, and SDS use (7.2.3, 7.4.1). A power outage, fire, or evacuation tests whether you create and FOLLOW an EAP — reporting, evacuating by a clear route, and accounting for everyone (7.3.1). A new member at signup, a self-service floor with no coach watching, or a question about who carries liability tests informed consent, waivers, medical release, insurance, and the supervision-as-liability principle (7.2.1, 7.2.2, 7.2.5). A sauna day, a brutally hot outdoor session, or a question about who is responsible when a delegated safety task was skipped tests environmental response (7.2.4) and the 'authority delegates, responsibility doesn't' rule. The wrong answers will usually be the disproportionate action, the scope violation, the 'it's the contractor's problem' deflection, or the choice that ignores the highest-leverage control (supervision, inspection, or consulting the SDS).

Key terms (understand, don't memorize)

Health and safety (broad sense)
All relevant governmental and organizational regulations and procedures intended to prevent accident or injury in a workplace or public environment — a gym is both, so trainers and owners must apply these standards.
So far as is reasonably practicable
The legal standard (from the U.K. Health & Safety at Work Act and mirrored elsewhere) that an employer must make the workplace as safe as is reasonably achievable; it accepts that not all risk can be eliminated, so controls must be proportionate and reasonable.
Authority vs. responsibility
Authority to perform a safety task can be delegated to an employee, but ultimate responsibility cannot — if the task isn't done, accountability falls back on the owner or manager.
Worksite (hazard) analysis
An ongoing examination of premises, equipment, methods, and tasks to identify all existing and potential hazards so they can be eliminated or reduced to acceptable levels; one of OSHA's four program elements.
Risk-assessment process (Identify, Analyze, Solve, Implement, Evaluate)
The five-step cycle for managing hazards: find hazards, judge whether each risk is inherent or removable, decide a control, put it into action with assigned responsibility and dates, then review and update (at least annually).
Hazard vs. risk
A hazard is a thing/condition/process/person with the potential to cause harm; risk is the likelihood and magnitude of that harm occurring. The two words are often used interchangeably but are distinct.
Voluntary vs. involuntary risk
Voluntary risks are entered knowingly (e.g., choosing to run on a treadmill); involuntary risks occur without prior knowledge or consent (e.g., lightning, flood, an unexpected chemical exposure).
Control hierarchy (eliminate > minimize > administrative)
Best to eliminate a hazard; next best to minimize it to the lowest practicable level; for hazards that can't be engineered out, use administrative controls like training and signage.
Human factor (97%)
Only ~3% of worksite accidents stem from materials/equipment/environment; ~97% involve human behavior — making supervision, instruction, and athlete education the most powerful risk controls.
Emergency Action Plan (EAP)
A written-to-standard document covering how emergencies are reported, evacuation procedures and exit routes, accounting for everyone afterward, rescue/first aid, who to contact about the plan, and the alert method; it must be disseminated, practiced, and followed.
Exit route (means of egress)
A continuous, unobstructed path of travel to an exit; it has three parts — exit access (path to the exit door), exit (protected portion between workspace and door), and exit discharge (where it leads directly outside).
PASS
Fire-extinguisher operating sequence: Pull the pin, Aim low at the base of the fire, Squeeze the lever, Sweep side to side until the fire is out or the extinguisher is empty — used only with a clear escape route, staying 6-8 ft from the fire.
Class A fire / 75-foot rule
Ordinary combustible (paper, wood, cloth) fire; OSHA requires extinguishers placed so travel distance to one is 75 ft or less, with one on every floor and adjacent to stairways.
Ionization vs. photoelectric smoke alarm
Ionization alarms respond faster to flaming fires; photoelectric alarms respond faster to smoldering/smoking fires; dual-sensor units combine both for best coverage.
Sprinkler fusible link
A heat-sensitive element in each sprinkler head that melts at a set temperature to release water; heads activate individually (one near a small fire, many near a large one), letting occupants evacuate while the fire is contained.
Routes of entry (inhalation, absorption, ingestion)
The three ways a chemical enters the body: inhalation (fastest/most common, straight into the bloodstream via the lungs), absorption (skin/eyes; open cuts increase entry), and ingestion (slowest/least effective, often via contaminated hands or food).
Dose-dependent (toxic effect)
An effect whose severity or number of symptoms increases directly with the amount/duration of exposure — central to how toxic chemicals harm the body.
Corrosive chemical
A highly reactive chemical (acid or base) that causes immediate tissue damage on contact via oxidation; serious, immediate risk to skin, eyes, and tissues.
Carcinogen
A substance shown to cause cancer by damaging DNA or disrupting cellular metabolism; effects are insidious/delayed, usually with a critical dose above which risk becomes significant (e.g., asbestos, radon, tobacco smoke).
Reproductive hazard
An agent that harms reproductive health/function — infertility, miscarriage, birth defects — with effects most profound in the first trimester (e.g., lead, certain insecticides, diesel exhaust).
Sensitizer
A chemical that causes no effect on first exposure but provokes an immune-mediated allergic reaction (e.g., hives, eczema, asthma) after repeated exposures; latex and formaldehyde are common examples.
Globally Harmonized System (GHS)
An international standard that unifies chemical hazard classification, labeling, pictograms, and Safety Data Sheet format across countries; uses nine hazard pictograms.
Safety Data Sheet (SDS, formerly MSDS)
A 16-section manufacturer document describing a chemical's hazards and safe-use precautions; one must be kept and made accessible for every chemical in the gym (Section 4 covers first aid).
Primary vs. secondary container
A primary container is the manufacturer's original; a secondary container is one you fill on-site (e.g., a spray bottle) — both must be clearly labeled with contents and hazards so chemicals aren't mistaken for one another.
Chemical incompatibility (chloramine example)
Some chemicals react dangerously when combined; mixing bleach and ammonia evolves toxic chloramine gas that can rapidly cause unconsciousness and, in a closed container, an explosion — so incompatible chemicals must be stored and used apart.
Universal precautions
The practice of treating all blood and body fluids as if infectious; core elements are hand washing, barriers (gloves, masks, eye protection, gowns, CPR dam), and sanitation/decontamination of equipment before reuse.
Blood-borne pathogens
Disease agents carried in blood — chiefly hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV — that drive the biological-fluid precautions; blood poses the greatest transmission risk.
MRSA
Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, a skin bacterium that can spread person-to-surface-to-person via sweat; controlled by regular surface cleaning and recommending barrier clothing between skin and shared surfaces.
Good Samaritan act vs. occupational exposure
Rendering simple first aid for an unexpected gym injury is a Good Samaritan act, not occupational exposure, so a typical gym is outside the strict blood-borne-pathogen regulation — unless it runs combat sports where bleeding is expected.
Exposure-control plan
A written plan identifying tasks where exposure to blood/body fluids may occur, the schedule and procedures for universal precautions, PPE provision, cleaning/disposal, and training; required where the regulation applies and reviewed at least annually.
Informed consent and waiver of liability
Documents obtained from every customer acknowledging the risks of exercise and releasing the business from certain liability; part of the legal-safety backbone alongside screening and insurance.
Medical release
A written, signed clearance from a medical professional required when screening flags a condition, supporting safe participation and protecting the business.
Liability insurance
Coverage the gym must carry as part of managing legal risk, complementing screening, consent/waiver forms, and accurate per-client records.
Spotting vs. bail-out
Spotting assists a lifter under load but is dangerous if the spotter is untrained; teaching trainees to safely dump/miss/bail out of a failed rep (per USA Weightlifting) is often the safer risk control than mandating spotters.
Preventive maintenance checklist (daily/weekly/monthly)
A documented inspection cadence — daily cleaning of shared-contact surfaces and floor/hazard scans; weekly wear checks of high-use gear; monthly checks of bands, climbing ropes, pull-up bars, rack anchoring, and under mats/platforms.

Red flags & scope-of-practice

  • Equipment failure points: frayed climbing ropes (especially at attachment points), worn pull-up-bar/rack connections, ring tethers, jump ropes with exposed wire, and stretch bands separating at the joint — load-bearing/overhead failures are catastrophic and demand immediate removal from service.
  • Exposed concrete under pull-up bars, rings, or climbing ropes, and missing crash pads — a fall onto bare concrete is a serious injury risk that proper matting prevents.
  • DIY/home-made equipment: inner-tube stretch bands, DIY pull-up bars, and shelves anchored only to drywall (no studs) — increased failure risk; remove from use.
  • Chemical mixing hazard: combining bleach and ammonia (or other incompatible cleaners) produces toxic chloramine gas that can rapidly cause unconsciousness — never mix, never assume compatibility, consult the SDS.
  • Missing or inaccessible SDS for any chemical, or unlabeled secondary containers (e.g., an unmarked spray bottle that could be bleach or water) — both are scope/compliance failures and injury vectors.
  • Blocked, locked-from-inside, obstructed, unlit, or unmarked exit routes — stored plates, equipment, or clutter in egress paths is an emergency-preparedness failure even on an ordinary day.
  • No Emergency Action Plan, an unpracticed plan, or no method to account for all people after evacuation — 'having a plan' without dissemination, drills, and follow-through fails 7.3.1.
  • Blood on equipment or a client bleeding (shin scrape, torn callus): apply universal precautions — keep others away, glove up, contain, disinfect, bag and dispose; treat as infectious.
  • Vomit during/after high-intensity work: treat as potentially hazardous, restrict contact to the designated cleaner with PPE, then absorb, disinfect, and dispose.
  • Unsupervised exercise floor: ~80% of reviewed injury court cases cited inadequate supervision — an unattended floor is both a safety and a liability red flag, even in pay-for-access models.
  • Untrained spotters: mandating spotting without trained, competent spotters can endanger both lifter and spotter; consider teaching safe bail-out instead.
  • Environmental extremes: saunas, non-climate-controlled or outdoor sessions raise hyperthermia/hypothermia risk and must be planned for and adjusted (7.2.4); this is also where rhabdomyolysis and heat illness vigilance overlaps with screening.
  • Assigning a trainer to tasks they are not trained/authorized for (e.g., a yoga instructor running a strongman session) — never assign or undertake work that cannot be done safely; novices and new tasks carry the highest risk.
  • Treating 'I'm an independent contractor' as a liability shield — contractors are bound by the same safety guidelines and law as owners/managers.
  • Missing legal-safety documentation: no pre-participation screening, no informed-consent/waiver on file, no medical release when indicated, or no liability insurance — incomplete or inaccurate per-client records are a professional-responsibility failure.
  • Anything beyond CCFT scope (diagnosing a medical condition, providing medical treatment beyond basic first aid, prescribing): refer to the appropriate professional and stay within scope (7.4.1).

Self-test — application scenarios

Scenario 1. During warm-up you notice the gym's main climbing rope is visibly fraying right where it attaches to the ceiling anchor. Class starts in two minutes and the workout includes rope climbs. What is the best action?

  1. A. Run the class as written but tell athletes to climb gently and avoid the frayed section
  2. B. Take the rope out of service immediately, scale the rope-climb element for everyone, and report the damage for repair/inspection
  3. C. Let only the lighter, more experienced athletes use the rope since they stress it less
  4. D. Cut off the frayed section yourself and re-tie the rope so the workout can proceed
  5. E. Proceed and add a crash pad under the rope so a fall is cushioned
Show answer

Answer: B — A load-bearing/overhead failure is catastrophic, so the rope must be removed from service immediately and the element scaled while it's reported for repair/inspection (7.2.3, 5.2.3). A and C still expose athletes to a potential failure; D is unauthorized field modification that can increase failure risk; E (a pad) reduces fall consequences but does nothing about an in-use rope failure that could drop a climber from height.

Scenario 2. A new member finishes a hard interval workout, then vomits near the rowers. Several athletes are nearby finishing their rounds. What should you do first?

  1. A. Quickly mop it up with a towel before anyone notices and keep class moving
  2. B. Ask the member who vomited to clean it up since it's theirs
  3. C. Keep everyone except the designated cleaner away from it, then have that person don PPE (gloves, mask, eyewear) and follow absorb-disinfect-bag-dispose
  4. D. Spray disinfectant on it from a distance and continue the workout, cleaning after class
  5. E. Evacuate the gym and call for professional hazmat cleanup
Show answer

Answer: C — Treat all body fluids as potentially infectious: first prevent unintended contact by keeping everyone but the cleaner away, then the cleaner uses PPE and follows the contain/absorb -> disinfect -> bag and dispose sequence (7.2.3, universal precautions). A skips PPE and risks exposure; B is inappropriate (the sick member shouldn't be tasked, and contact must be limited to the trained cleaner); D leaves a hazard in a trafficked area and skips containment; E is a disproportionate overreaction for routine gym vomit.

Scenario 3. A coach is restocking cleaning supplies and, to save bottles, plans to combine a half-bottle of bleach cleaner with a half-bottle of an ammonia-based glass cleaner into one spray bottle. What should happen?

  1. A. Allow it, but label the new bottle clearly so no one confuses it
  2. B. Allow it only if the bottle is left open so fumes can escape
  3. C. Stop it — bleach and ammonia react to form toxic chloramine gas; never mix them, keep them in separate labeled containers, and consult the SDS
  4. D. Allow it as long as the coach wears gloves while mixing
  5. E. Allow it but store the mixed bottle outside in case it reacts
Show answer

Answer: C — Bleach + ammonia produces toxic chloramine gas that can rapidly cause unconsciousness, and a closed container can become a pressure/explosion hazard (chemical safety). The correct move is to never mix them, keep separate clearly labeled containers, and consult each chemical's SDS. Labeling (A), leaving it open (B), gloves (D), or outdoor storage (E) do nothing about the toxic reaction itself and still endanger people.

Scenario 4. A power outage knocks out lights and the front roll-up door's opener mid-class with about 25 athletes present. What is the most important immediate priority under your responsibilities?

  1. A. Wait by the breaker panel to restore power before doing anything else
  2. B. Execute the Emergency Action Plan: calmly direct athletes along a known clear exit route to the exit discharge and account for everyone outside
  3. C. Keep the class going by phone flashlight until power returns
  4. D. Tell athletes to find their own way out however they can
  5. E. Lock the doors so no one wanders into hazards in the dark
Show answer

Answer: B — This is exactly what an EAP exists for: report/respond, evacuate via a permanent, unobstructed, known route to the exit discharge, and account for all people afterward (7.3.1). A and C keep people in a darkened hazard; D abandons the accounting/direction duty and invites injury; E violates the rule that exit routes must remain unlocked from the inside and is dangerous during an evacuation.

Scenario 5. Your gym uses a pay-for-access model: members train on their own and a coach is 'on call' in the office. A member is loading a barbell with poor setup near a walkway. Considering liability and supervision, what is the best practice?

  1. A. Stay in the office — self-service members assume their own risk via the waiver
  2. B. Actively survey the floor, intervene to correct the unsafe setup and spacing, and ensure members were given use instruction/signage at signup
  3. C. Do nothing unless the member specifically asks for help
  4. D. Post a sign about safe lifting and consider the duty satisfied
  5. E. Cancel the pay-for-access model because it can't be made safe
Show answer

Answer: B — About 80% of reviewed injury court cases cited inadequate supervision, and an unattended floor is a liability even in self-service models; the trainer should actively survey, intervene, and ensure members received instruction/signage (5.2.7, 5.2.8, 7.2.5). A misreads the waiver — a signed waiver does not erase the duty to supervise; C and D are passive and leave a live hazard; E is an unnecessary overreaction since the model can be operated safely with supervision.

Scenario 6. A gym owner delegates the monthly equipment-inspection task to a part-time coach. One month the coach forgets, and a poorly anchored rack later tips during use. Who bears responsibility, and what's the lesson?

  1. A. Only the coach, because the task was assigned to them
  2. B. Only the equipment manufacturer, because the rack tipped
  3. C. The owner/manager retains responsibility — authority can be delegated but responsibility cannot — so the system must ensure the inspection actually gets done
  4. D. No one, because rack tip-overs are unforeseeable acts of nature
  5. E. The injured member, because they signed a waiver
Show answer

Answer: C — Authority to perform a safety task can be delegated, but ultimate responsibility cannot — if an assigned task isn't completed, accountability falls back on the owner/manager, who must ensure compliance happens (7.2.3, professional responsibility). A wrongly offloads all accountability to the contractor; B ignores that rack anchoring is a monthly inspection item; D is false (a tipping rack is a foreseeable, preventable hazard); E misuses the waiver, which does not excuse a known maintenance failure.

Scenario 7. Which scenario actually triggers the strict blood-borne-pathogen regulation (versus being handled as ordinary 'Good Samaritan' first aid)?

  1. A. A coach bandages a member's torn hand callus after a pull-up set
  2. B. The gym adds regular boxing and MMA sparring classes where bleeding is reasonably expected as a matter of course
  3. C. A member gets a minor shin scrape on a box jump
  4. D. A coach helps wipe up a member's bloody nose after an accidental bump
  5. E. A member sweats heavily onto a shared rower
Show answer

Answer: B — The regulation targets work where exposure to blood is reasonably anticipated as part of the job; a standard gym's incidental first aid is a Good Samaritan act, but offering combat sports where bleeding is expected as a matter of course brings the gym within the regulation (scope nuance, 7.4.1). A, C, and D are incidental/Good-Samaritan situations; E involves sweat, which is low-risk for HIV/hepatitis (though MRSA surface hygiene still applies) and is not the trigger.

Scenario 8. You're programming a sauna-and-conditioning session on a record-hot summer day, with part of the workout outdoors on the turf. What best reflects your professional responsibility for environmental conditions?

  1. A. Run it as planned; clients chose to come in, so heat is their responsibility
  2. B. Recognize the hyperthermia risk, adjust the session (shorten outdoor work, add hydration/cooling, watch for heat-illness signs), and scale or move work indoors as needed
  3. C. Cancel all training any time it's hot outside
  4. D. Skip warning clients so they don't get discouraged from training hard
  5. E. Push intensity harder to acclimate everyone to the heat quickly
Show answer

Answer: B — Recognizing and responding to extreme environmental conditions is a defined responsibility: a sauna plus a hot outdoor session raises hyperthermia risk, so the competent trainer adjusts the plan, hydrates/cools, monitors for heat-illness warning signs, and scales (7.2.4, 5.2.6, 5.2.3). A abdicates the duty of care; C is a disproportionate blanket cancellation; D withholds safety information; E recklessly increases the very risk you should be mitigating.

Scenario 9. A small grease fire flares up in the gym's break-room kitchenette. You've been trained on the extinguisher. What is the correct approach?

  1. A. Immediately stand right next to the fire and empty the extinguisher straight down onto the flames
  2. B. Only attempt it if you have a clear, unobstructed escape route; stay 6-8 ft back and use PASS — Pull, Aim at the base, Squeeze, Sweep — while evacuation remains the primary plan
  3. C. Throw water on it since water puts out fires
  4. D. Aim the extinguisher at the top of the flames and hold it steady
  5. E. Ignore the extinguisher entirely and just wait for the fire department
Show answer

Answer: B — Evacuation is the primary response; an extinguisher is for small/containable fires only when you have a clear escape, standing 6-8 ft from the leading edge and using PASS (aim low at the base) (fire safety). A removes your escape margin and stands too close; C (water on a grease fire) can spread it and is wrong; D aims too high — you must hit the base/fuel; E needlessly forgoes a trained, available control on a small fire when escape is assured.

Scenario 10. While organizing the cleaning closet, you find a spray bottle of clear liquid with no label sitting next to the plant-misting water. A new coach asks which is the bleach solution. What's the right professional response?

  1. A. Sniff each bottle to tell them apart
  2. B. Guess based on which shelf they're usually on
  3. C. Treat the unlabeled bottle as a hazard: do not use it until contents are confirmed and it's properly labeled, and require all secondary containers to carry contents and hazard info going forward
  4. D. Pour both out and refill from scratch without labeling, to save time
  5. E. Assume it's water since bleach is usually stored elsewhere
Show answer

Answer: C — Secondary containers must be labeled with contents and hazards precisely so bleach can't be confused with water; an unlabeled bottle is a hazard that shouldn't be used until identified and labeled (chemical safety/labeling). A (sniffing) risks inhalation exposure; B and E are unsafe guesses; D recreates the same unlabeled-container problem you're supposed to fix.
